"Lord of Secrets!
If one does not contemplate my own intrinsic nature, then 'I' and 'mine' arise"—the following explains the meaning of the continuity of mind.
In order to clarify the causes for the initial arising of the pure mind, [the text] first describes the irrational minds of ignorant, ordinary worldlings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*).
Regarding "beginningless birth and death," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Whether it be sentient beings or phenomena, the world has no beginning."
In a sutra, the Buddha said:
"Enveloped by ignorance and bound by craving, one wanders through birth and death, such that its beginning cannot be found.
Even when a bodhisattva contemplates this beginninglessness as empty, they do not fall into the view of having a beginning."
The meaning of "foolish child" is as previously explained.

As for the term "ordinary person" (*pṛthagjana*), the correct translation should be "distinctly born" (*visadṛśa-janman*). This means that due to ignorance, one follows karma to receive retribution without autonomy, falling into various realms of existence; because the categories of form and mind differ from one another, they are called "distinctly born."
That which they conceive as a self exists merely as a verbal designation and lacks any substantial reality; therefore, it is said that they are "clinging to the name of self.
To say "I have" is precisely what constitutes "that which belongs to the self" (ātmīya).

In this way, the grasping at "I" and "mine," such as the sixteen types of false views and so forth, varies infinitely according to the distinctions among phenomena; therefore, they are called "divisions.
Next, to explain the cause of false conceptualization, it says: "O Lord of Mysteries!"
If one does not contemplate the self-nature of that [self], then the notions of "I" and "mine" arise.
If one contemplates that all aggregates (skandhas) arise entirely from a multitude of conditions, then what therein could be the self?
"In what do I abide?
Do I exist as identical to the aggregates, or distinct from the aggregates?
If one can investigate in this manner with earnest scrutiny, one shall attain the right eye of wisdom.

However, they do not examine this for themselves; rather, they merely transmit it from one to another, having practiced this view as a tradition since time immemorial, asserting: "I am within the body, capable of performing actions and of nourishing and perfecting the sense faculties."
Only this is the ultimate path; all else is false speech.
For this reason, they are called "foolish children.
When the Sūtra says, "Furthermore, they calculate that there is time," it means they reckon that all things in heaven and earth, whether good or bad, have time as their cause.
As that verse says: "When the time comes, sentient beings ripen; when the time arrives, they are summoned and seized.
Time can awaken people; therefore, time is the cause."
Furthermore, others say:

Although all persons and things are not produced by time, time is nonetheless an unchanging cause and a substantially existent phenomenon (*dravyasat*). Because it is subtle, it cannot be perceived; however, its existence can be known through effects such as flowers and fruits.
Why is this? Because one knows that there is a cause by seeing the fruit.
At this time, because the dharma is indestructible, it is permanent.
Furthermore, it is because they do not contemplate the self-nature of time that such false conceptualizations arise.
When the Sūtra speaks of "the transformations of earth and so forth," it refers to those who each cling to earth, water, fire, wind, and space as being real.
Some say that earth is the cause of all things, because all sentient beings and all phenomena arise in dependence upon the earth.

Failing to contemplate the intrinsic nature of the earth and recognizing instead that it exists merely through the combination of various conditions, they give rise to this view, believing that by making offerings to the earth, one shall attain liberation.
Next, there are those who reckon that water can produce all things, and that fire and wind do likewise.
Or they reckon that all things arise from space, asserting that space is the cause of true liberation and should therefore be worshipped and served.
All of these should be explained in detail.

As the Sūtra says regarding the "Yogic Self": this refers to practitioners of meditative concentration who reckon the principle of the internal mind’s correspondence as the true self; they hold that it is eternally abiding and immovable, its true nature serene and still, and that this alone is the ultimate path, transcending cause and effect.
Because they do not contemplate the self-nature of the mind, they give rise to such views as taking this to be a true self; yet, merely abiding in this principle is called liberation.
As the Sūtra says: "Establishing purity, not establishing non-purity. Within this, there are two kinds of conceptualizations:
the former phrase refers to those who establish all dharmas, and practicing based on this is what they call "purity."

The next phrase means that this establishment is not the ultimate dharma; if there were no such establishment, that which is called the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) would be termed the true self (*ātman*). Furthermore, it is free from the purity cultivated in the preceding phrase, and is therefore said to be "without purity."
Because one does not contemplate the self-nature of the "self," such views arise, as explained in detail above.

As the Sūtra says: "Whether it be Īśvara, or emanation, or time," this refers to a class of non-Buddhists who reckon that Īśvara is eternal and that this sovereign being is capable of producing all things.

As it is argued in the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*: "If sentient beings were the sons of Īśvara, he should provide them only with pleasure and shield them from suffering, rather than inflicting suffering upon them; furthermore, they should attain the cessation of suffering and the acquisition of pleasure simply by making offerings to Īśvara."
In reality, it is not so; rather, one experiences the retribution for the causes and conditions of suffering and pleasure created by oneself, and it is not wrought by Īśvara.
Furthermore, if Īśvara were the creator of sentient beings, who then created this Īśvara?
"If [the Lord] were to create himself, that would not be so, for as with any object, it does not create itself.
If there were another creator, then he could not be called 'sovereign' (īśvara).
This is explained at length in that treatise.
Regarding the reckoning of "outflow," it is largely the same as "establishment.
In "establishment," all phenomena emerge from the mind;
here, in "outflow," all phenomena emerge from manual labor.
For example, it is like a potter who, through continuous molding and shaping, produces various distinct forms and appearances.

Next, regarding the term "time" (*kāla*): this differs slightly from the sectarian tenets of the aforementioned non-Buddhist schools, as they all belong to the category of those who posit Īśvara as the cause.
Commentary on the Mahāvairocana-abhisambodhi Sūtra, Scroll One Commentary on the Mahāvairocana-abhisambodhi Sūtra,
Scroll Two Recorded by the Śramaṇa Aśāri Yixing (Yī-háng) The Mahāvairocana-abhisambodhi Sūtra Commentary, Scroll One The Mahāvairocana-abhisambodhi Sūtra Commentary,
Scroll Two Recorded by the Śramaṇa Aśāri Yixing (Yī-háng)
The remainder of the first chapter, "Entering the Mantra Gate and Abiding in the Mind," states:
Regarding the term "Venerable and Noble One" (*bhadanta*), this refers to the deity Nārāyaṇa.
Non-Buddhists reckon that this deity is serene, eternally abiding, and immovable, yet possesses the ministers who create and fashion all things.
It is like a sovereign who governs through non-action, while his officials receive his mandates and carry them out.
Because the sovereign who is able to create has no one more noble or honorable than himself, he is called "noble and honorable."
Furthermore, according to the tenets of this school, those who are venerable and noble pervade all realms of earth, water, fire, wind, and space.
In the past, there was a master of treatises who, wishing to refute their tenets, went to a celestial shrine and sat upon the body of a divine image there to eat and drink.
The Westerners regard the remnants of food and drink as the ultimate impurity and are all collectively incensed.
The Master of Treatises said:
"According to your own tenets, is it not the case that the characteristics of earth, water, fire, wind, and space pervade all places?"
He replied, “It is so. The Master said:
"He is composed of earth, water, fire, and wind; I am likewise so.
Since we interpenetrate one another in this way, what is there that is not possible? Why then do you harbor such anger?
The assembly remained silent, unable to offer a rebuttal.
This false conceptualization also arises because one does not contemplate the self-nature of the "self.
As the Sūtra says regarding "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*): a certain class of non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) conceptualizes that all phenomena exist spontaneously, without any agent of creation.
Just as a lotus flower is born with a fresh and pure color—by whom was it dyed?
And by whom were the sharp points of thorns carved?
Therefore, one knows that all phenomena are inherently such of themselves.
A teacher raised this objection:

"Now we see with our own eyes that things such as boats, ships, houses, and dwellings constructed by people all arise from a multitude of conditions and do not form spontaneously; how then can you say they exist 'of themselves'?"
If it is argued that although [the nature] exists, it is not yet manifest, and therefore requires human effort to bring it forth, this is also incorrect.
Since it must be brought forth by human effort, it is something arising from conditions; it does not exist spontaneously.

The Sūtra states that "the internal self" refers to those who reckon that apart from the mind within the body, there exists a distinct nature of self capable of moving this body and performing various activities.
The opponent says: "If it were so, then I would be impermanent. Why is this?"
"If any phenomenon is a cause or arises from a cause, it is all impermanent.
If the self were impermanent, then the retribution for sins and merits would be entirely annihilated.
Such various arguments and principles are explained in detail within the section on comparative analysis.

The Sūtra states that "the measure of the person" (*pudgala-pramāṇa*) refers to calculating the size of the *ātman* as being equal to the human body; if the body is small, the *ātman* is small, and if the body is large, the *ātman* is large.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
"Some calculate that the size of the *ātman* follows that of the human body, and at the time of death and dissolution, the *ātman* likewise emerges first."
It is exactly the same as this.
However, that school regards the self (*ātman*) as an eternal and sovereign phenomenon;
since it now appears to vary according to the size of the body, it is clearly impermanent, and thus we know their position is incorrect.
Regarding the term "universal adornment" (*paryanta-śobha*) mentioned in the Sūtra, it refers to the calculation that this self (*ātman*) is capable of creating all phenomena.
However, the notion that such superior and universal adornments of the world are my own work differs slightly from the calculation of the Lord (*īśvara*).
As it says in the treatise, refuting Īśvara: "For what reason does Īśvara not make all people happy and all people miserable?
Since there are those who suffer and those who are happy, one should know that [suffering and happiness] arise from attachment and aversion; therefore, he is not sovereign."

Now, if the so-called "Omnipresent Adornment" (Vibhūṣaṇa) can indeed create various merits and pleasures, yet cannot use such pleasure to ward off suffering, how can it be called omnipresent, eternal, and sovereign?

As for the scripture’s statement, “If there were a life-span,” this refers to certain non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) who calculate that all phenomena—even the four great elements, grasses, trees, and so forth—possess a life-span.
Just as grass and trees continue to grow even after being cut down, one should know that they possess life.
Furthermore, since they close up at night, one should know that they also possess consciousness, for this is due to their sleeping.
An objector says:
"If one sees that when *liǎn* grass is cut it grows back again, one takes this as evidence that it possesses life;
yet when a person has a limb severed, it does not grow back—how can it be that they lack life?"
Just as the *hehun* tree has its sleep while the flow of water continues day and night without ceasing—how could this be considered constant wakefulness?
All such states arise because one does not contemplate the self-nature of the Self, and thus various deluded views are produced.

The Sūtra speaks of "pudgala," which refers to those schools who assert that there exists a "grasper of aggregates" (saṃskāra-grāhaka), all of whom maintain it is a single self (*ātman*) that merely receives different names according to its various functions.
If there were something that proceeds from this world to a future world, then the *vijñāna*-soul would be eternal.
If the *vijñāna*-soul were eternal, how could there be death and birth?
Death is defined as ceasing at this place, and birth is defined as emerging at that place; therefore, one cannot say that the soul is eternal.
If there were impermanence, then there would be no self.
For instance, within the Buddha-dharma, there are the Vātsīputrīyas and the Sarvāstivādins; these two schools maintain that dharmas exist throughout the three periods of time.

If the past, future, and present were definitively existent, then it would be identical to the existence of a *pudgala* (a self or person); this would result in the loss of the three seals of the Dharma taught by the Buddha. Thus, the various Bodhisattvas of the West employ diverse forms of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to refute those sectarian tenets.

The Sūtra states, "If it is consciousness," meaning that there is a class of people who cling to this consciousness as being omnipresent, asserting that it pervades everything down to earth, water, fire, wind, and the realm of space, such that consciousness completely fills them all.
This is also not the case.
If the consciousness-spirit were all-pervading and eternal, it should be able to see, hear, perceive, and know by itself.
Yet, in reality, consciousness arises only through the conjunction of the sense organs and their objects; thus, your consciousness-spirit would be rendered useless.
Furthermore, if the consciousness-spirit were omnipresent throughout the five destinies, how could there be further death and birth?
Thus, we know it is not so.
The sūtra states that "ālaya" carries the meaning of grasping and storing, and it also carries the meaning of a "dwelling."

This school maintains that there exists the ālayavijñāna, which is able to sustain this body; it performs all actions and contains within it the myriad phenomena—when gathered together, they are non-existent, yet when unfolded, they fill the world.
This is not the same as the meaning of the eighth consciousness (*aṣṭamavijñāna*) within the Buddha-dharma.

However, when the World-Honored One spoke with intentional ambiguity (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*) of the *tathāgatagarbha* as the *ālayavijñāna*, if those within the Buddha-dharma do not contemplate the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of their own minds but instead engage in conceptual discrimination and attachment, they likewise possess the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*).

The Sūtra says, "the knower and the seer," meaning that there are non-Buddhists who reckon that within the body there exists a knower and a seer capable of cognizing matters such as suffering and pleasure.
Furthermore, there are those who reckon that the one capable of seeing is the true self.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The eye beholding form is called the seer; the five consciousnesses cognizing objects are called the knower."
"All these are my own conceptualizations; they are different names for the same reality according to their respective functions.
The objector says: "If you claim that 'that which can see' is the self, then is it not the case that 'that which can hear, touch, and cognize' is also the self?"
If all [the six faculties] were identical, then the objects of the six faculties would not know one another; one could not become six, nor could six become one.
If there were something that was not the self, this too would be subject to the same doubt.
Therefore, we know that it is only through the conjunction of the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) that there is cognition and perception; there is no separate self (*ātman*).
A sūtra speaks of "the grasper and the grasped," referring to those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who claim:

"Apart from consciousness within the body, there exists a separate grasper which is the true self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*); this is able to move the body, speech, and mind to perform all various activities."
Some may say: "The grasper is merely consciousness, while that which is grasped as its object is called the 'True Self'; this self pervades all places."
However, the nature of the internal and external aggregates—body, sensation, mind, and phenomena—all arises from conditions and lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Within this, even the grasped object and the grasping subject cannot be found; how much less so, then, can there be a "self"?
This statement is also made because one does not contemplate the self-nature of the self.
When the Sūtra speaks of "internal knowledge" and "external knowledge," these are also alternative names for the knower.
This is divided into two views:
some reckon that internal cognition is the self, asserting that there is a distinct internal cognizer within the body who is the true self;
others reckon that external cognition is the self, asserting that the one capable of cognizing external objects and realms is the true self.

The scripture states that "Śānta-brahman" refers to a doctrine largely identical to the sectarian tenets of the knowers (Vedantins), differing only in its specific school; thus, it is singled out here.

As for the scriptural passage "If *manuṣya*," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* translates it as "human being" (*ren*), which refers to the grasping at a person (*pudgala-grāha*); in its full translation, it should be called "human birth" (*rensheng*).
This belongs to the class of non-Buddhist schools that worship Īśvara; they maintain that humans are born from Īśvara himself, and thus it is named accordingly.
The Tripitaka Master of the Tang dynasty translated this as "Mind-born" (Yìshēng), which is incorrect.
"Manas" refers to the mind; the current term "manu" is a phonetic shift with a different meaning, and is thus an error.

When the Sūtra says "māṇava," this refers to a class of non-Buddhist followers of Viṣṇu; it should correctly be translated as "Superior Self" (Śreṣṭhātman), signifying that the self is the most excellent and sublime within the body and mind.
"He constantly observes within his heart that there is a 'self' about one inch in size.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* also states: "There are those who reckon that the spirit (ātman) resides within the heart, as subtle as a mustard seed."
Purity is called "pure matter" (*rūpa*); it may be like a bean or a grain of wheat, even as small as one inch.
At the moment of first receiving a body, it is received first of all, resembling the skeletal frame of a statue.
"When his body is fully formed, it is like a statue already adorned.
The Tripitaka Master of the Tang dynasty translated this as "Māṇava" (儒童), which is incorrect.
"Māṇava" in Sanskrit is translated here as "Nà" (納); the meanings are distinct, so [the former] is an error. These two names are the interpretation of Ācārya Bodhi.

Regarding the scriptural passage "Constantly Born in Samādhi": those non-Buddhists reckon that the self is eternally abiding and indestructible, naturally and constantly born without further rebirth; it is for this reason that it is so named.
The Sūtra states, "Sound is not sound. This refers to the Śabdika-tīrthikas (the non-Buddhist proponents of sound).
If sound were manifest, they would calculate that the essence of sound exists inherently and is merely manifested in dependence upon conditions, its essential nature being eternally abiding.
If sound were produced, one would calculate that sound is produced from its own primary cause, yet arises dependently upon conditions; once produced, it would abide eternally.
Within this, there is further internal differentiation in their calculations, as explained extensively elsewhere.

Regarding "non-sound," this differs from the previous position; for while that [position] maintains that sound is pervasive and eternal, this school entirely negates it as non-existent, falling into the view that there are no dharmas of good or evil, nor even any locus for sounds or syllables, taking this very [absence] to be reality.
The Sūtra says: "O Lord of Mysteries!
In this way, my own portion has, from time immemorial, been associated with conceptual differentiation; there are those who seek liberation through accordance with the correct principle."
In the sutras, thirty matters are briefly presented; however, if categorized according to their specific distinctions, they are immeasurable and boundless.
For example, when a person attains the four dhyānas while seated, they immediately reckon this dharma to be the true and eternal principle.
Or one might give rise to this thought:
"I am an attainer of dhyāna.
All such instances are associated with the category of the self; other cases may be understood by analogy.

This is all because they do not contemplate the true reality of the self; rather, from time immemorial, they have inherited and practiced this view, each claiming for themselves that there is a Great Master, a Bhagavān, who possesses all-knowing vision and, through the excellent cultivation of yoga, has realized this Dharma and teaches it to the world.
This alone is the ultimate path; there is no other path.
It is like when, at the beginning of the eon, a single deity was first born in the Brahma realm and had this thought:
"If only there were other sentient beings who might come to dwell together with me."
"How excellent! At that time, there was one whose life had ended in a higher realm and who had come to be born among them; the one born first spoke to him, saying:
"It is by the power of my mindfulness that you have been able to be born here."
"You are indeed born from me.
Yet they also thought: "This Honored One is able to give birth to us."
They then followed one another’s lead, reckoning themselves to be the first possessors of a self.
From that time onward, they claimed that this Brahmā Deva was the creator of the world.
In this manner, various divergent views arose in succession, beyond all calculation.

Those who seek liberation through conformity to principle—“conformity to principle” being the Sanskrit term *yogin*, referring to practitioners of yoga from antiquity—are so called because they have attained true liberation, which is the source of all things, and now conform to that practice in their quest for liberation. Thus, it is said.
All that above constitutes minds that destroy internal and external causes and effects and contradict principle.
Next, the initial mind that accords with principle is explained; "accordance with the wholesome" refers precisely to the eight worldly minds.
The Sūtra says: "Lord of Mysteries!
Foolish, ordinary worldlings are like rams; at times, a single notion of a dharma arises in them, namely, the observance of the fast."
He contemplates this small portion, gives rise to joy, and practices it repeatedly.
"O Lord of Secrets!

This is the initial seed from which wholesome karma arises": the ram is among animals the most inferior in nature; it thinks only of water, grass, and sexual desire, knowing nothing else. Therefore, following the linguistic conventions of the West, it serves as a metaphor for the ignorant, ordinary person who does not understand the causes and effects of good and evil.

Since time immemorial, there has been a succession of transmission in the world regarding the name of "wholesome dharmas"; yet, though one seeks them in various ways with a mind that contradicts reason, they cannot be found.
Later, a thought suddenly arose within him:
"I shall now practice moderation in eating and observe the fast.
This was indeed a wholesome dharma, yet it was still not the Eightfold Precepts (aṣṭāṅga-śīla) within the Buddha-dharma.

Because he restrains himself by means of moderation in eating, he perceives that his worldly affairs have diminished, making it easy for him to obtain food and drink without the toil of seeking them out; at that time, a mind of slight non-attachment arises, and his heart becomes joyful and finds peace.

Because one perceives these benefits, one practices them repeatedly; this is precisely the initial subtle consciousness that discerns the causes and effects of good and evil, and is therefore called the "seed-consciousness."
The Sūtra states: "Taking this as a cause, on the six days of fasting (ṣaḍ-upoṣadha), one gives to parents, sons, daughters, and relatives.

This is the second 'tooth-seed'. Regarding these six days of fasting, they are the same as those mentioned in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* where it is said that "ancient seers possessing the five supernatural powers (pañcābhijñā) exhorted people to abstain from food on these days."
"Having thus conformed to wholesome dharmas, one also avoids the calamities and misfortunes of ghosts and spirits," as it is explained at length therein.

Because one sees that by ceasing covetous seeking, one gains benefit and happiness within, and because one desires to cultivate this dharma so that it may increase, on the day of observing the fast, one gives away one's own wealth and property to one's six kin, thinking to oneself:
"I am free from the anxiety of needing protection, yet I cause others to love and respect me, and I obtain the reputation for filial piety and righteousness.
Seeing this cause and effect, he gives rise to joy.
Because of this joy, the wholesome mind gradually increases, just as a sprout grows from a seed.

The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, to bestow this gift upon those who are not one's relatives or acquaintances constitutes the third 'bud-seed'"; this refers to the desire to perfect these wholesome dharmas of observing the fast, cultivating a mind of non-attachment, wisdom, and relinquishment.

Through repeated practice, the virtuous mind gradually increases; one is then further able to give to those who are neither kin nor acquaintances, because one perceives the merit, benefit, and excellence of this impartial mind of giving.

At that time, the "good sprout" (śubhāṅkura) increases and expands even further; it is like a stem flourishing before the actual production of the karma, and is therefore called the "bud stage" (arbuda-bīja).

The Sūtra states: "Furthermore, giving this to one of great capacity and high virtue is the fourth 'leaf stage' (patra-bīja). This means that one has already been able to practice wisdom and renunciation, and taking this as a cause, one gradually becomes capable of discerning the objects to which one gives.
Such a person’s virtuous conduct is lofty and supreme; I should now draw near to them and make offerings.
This is precisely how the nature of wisdom gradually unfolds, serving as the gradual means of encountering a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).

The Sūtra states: "Furthermore, with this gift, one joyfully bestows it upon performers of music and the like, as well as offering it to venerable elders. This means that as the nature of wisdom gradually unfolds, one further discriminates the objects of giving; seeing the benefit of altruism therein, one rewards the merit of performers of music because they are able to transform the great assembly and cause them to rejoice.
There are many such instances as these, which is why it is said that they are "equal.

Venerable elders and seniors who have seen and heard much, as well as those of noble learning and conduct who serve as models for the world, give with sincere joy because their giving brings benefit to many; likewise, because my own mind is doubly joyful at the time of giving, this is precisely the "seed of flowers."

As for the sutra’s statement, “Furthermore, by means of this giving, one gives rise to a heart of affection and makes offerings; this is the sixth fruit of accomplishment,” it means that when one’s practice has reached full maturity, it is not merely a matter of joy alone; rather, one is further able to bestow gifts with a heart of affection upon those who possess noble conduct.

Furthermore, by virtue of the causes and conditions of previous giving, one gains the benefit of hearing the Dharma; knowing that the person inwardly harbors superior virtues—namely, the capacity for renunciation of desire and so forth—one associates with, draws close to, and makes offerings to them.
Looking toward the initial seed, it is precisely the mind that realizes the fruit.
"Furthermore, O Lord of Mysteries!

That 'guarding the precepts leads to birth in heaven' is the seventh seed of enjoyment" means that having already been able to perform the rites of fasting and giving, one perceives their benefits and thus understands that the unwholesome actions of the three karmas are all causes and conditions for decline and affliction; thinking, "I shall abandon them and abide in the guarding of the precepts," [one acts accordingly].

By virtue of guarding the precepts, one obtains various beneficial rewards in the present life: great renown, peace and happiness of body and mind, a further increase in virtuous qualities, and upon the end of life, rebirth in the heavens.
For example, it is like planting a fruit; once it has matured, one enjoys its actual fruit, and thus it is called the "seed of enjoyment.

Furthermore, it is said that from a single seed, hundreds or thousands of fruits are produced; each of these fruits, in turn, gives rise to many more, proliferating and nourishing one another beyond measure.
Now, this mind that experiences the fruit likewise becomes the seed for the subsequent mind; it is just like this, and is therefore called the "seed of experience.
As the Sūtra says: "O Lord of Mysteries!"
While transmigrating through the cycle of birth and death with this mind, he hears these words from a virtuous friend:

"This is Mahādeva, the god who bestows all happiness; if one makes offerings to him with sincere devotion, all one's wishes will be fulfilled—namely, Maheśvara and the others. Upon hearing this, his heart is filled with joy, and he practices accordingly with earnest respect and reverence.
"Lord of Secrets!
This is called the eighth stage of the infant-like mind, which is the fearless reliance for the cycle of birth and death of foolish, ordinary beings.

Having known those who practice the noble path, one should approach and make offerings to them; furthermore, seeing that upholding the precepts can give rise to wholesome benefits, one gradually comes to recognize cause and effect."

Now, having further heard the words of the spiritual friend that this Great Deva can bestow all happiness, and that if one reverently recognizes and makes offerings to him, all aspirations will be fulfilled, one is then able to give rise to a mind of refuge.
Although they have not yet heard the Buddha-dharma, they know that these devas have attained this wholesome retribution by practicing virtuous deeds.

Furthermore, they gradually develop faith and understanding, distinguishing the superior field of merit; upon hearing the extraordinary excellence of the Buddha-dharma, they will surely be able to take refuge and accept it with conviction. Thus, this is the highest state of mind in the world.

Question: Previously it was stated that [theories concerning] Īśvara and others are all false conceptions; now, however, you say that taking refuge in these is a superior worldly mind. How does this differ from what was said before?
The answer is:
Previously, this was a mind that did not recognize cause and effect, merely calculating that all phenomena were created by Īśvara and other such deities.

Now, because his roots of goodness have matured, he seeks a refuge from fear within the cycle of birth and death; desiring to emulate those [noble ones] in practicing causes with the hope of accomplishing superior fruits, he is therefore not the same as his previous calculation.
"Śaṅkara" is an alternative name for Maheśvara.
"Kṛṣṇa"—the Sanskrit term being Rudra—is a member of the retinue of Īśvara.
“Nāgarāja” refers to the great nāgas.
“Kuvera” and others are all the Great Devas venerated by the world.
“Brahmāṇī” is the honored deity worshipped by the world.
However, within the Buddha-dharma, the Brahma King has transcended desire and possesses no consorts or queens.

From "Padma" (Pāṭhuma) downward—namely the Takṣaka Dragon, the Vāsuki Dragon, the Śaṅkha Dragon, the Karkoṭaka Dragon, the Mahāpadma Dragon, the Kulika Dragon, the Mahāpanini Dragon, the Āditya Dragon, the Sāta Dragon, and the Nanda Dragon—all such dragons are honored deities venerated by the world.
"Divine Transcendents" (ṛṣi) refers to the various seers possessing the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*); as their number is immeasurable, their names are not listed here.
The *Veda* consists of the four types of illuminating treatises (*vidyā*) expounded by Brahmā.
The "Great Veda Master" is one who upholds that scripture and is capable of instructing others; because he can reveal the practice for transcending desire, he should be taken as a refuge.

Within that class of beings, the Brahma King is like the Buddha; the four Vedas are like the twelve divisions of the scriptures; and those who transmit this Dharma are like the harmonious Saṃgha. At that time, hearing of such worldly Triple Gems, they joyfully take refuge and practice in accordance with them; this is the eighth basis of fearlessness for ordinary worldlings within the cycle of birth and death.
As for the passage in the Sūtra which states, “O Lord of Secrets!

Furthermore, regarding the supreme practice, by abiding in the supremacy within what has been taught therein, the wisdom that seeks liberation arises,” this means that within this very eighth basis of fearlessness, there is further a supreme mind.
Having heard what was said above regarding how one should offer worship and take refuge in all the Bhagavāns of the world, he subsequently gave rise to this thought:
"Among these Three Jewels, which is the most excellent?"
"I shall select those that are wholesome and practice them accordingly.
By the power of his previous roots of goodness, he attained a distinguished state within the teachings spoken by him, and the wisdom seeking liberation arose.

However, because they do not yet understand the principle of dependent origination, their wisdom that contemplates emptiness does not transcend the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism; thus it is said that "the permanent and the impermanent are empty. They merely follow such teachings as these and diligently practice and study them.
Within this, there are further two types:
the arising of the wisdom that seeks liberation is called the "excellent mind," and having realized the dharma of emptiness is called the "resolute mind.
If these are explained separately from the preceding [categories], there are ten minds in total.
The World-Honored One, wishing to contrast this with the supramundane wisdom that contemplates emptiness, next says:
"Lord of Mysteries!

It is not that those who understand the meaning of emptiness and non-emptiness, who comprehend the cessation of permanence and annihilation, and who—though performing the contemplation of equality as neither existent nor non-existent—have severed all conceptual proliferation, yet are still unable to simultaneously abandon these views, because they have not understood the principle of true causes and conditions."

However, within the Buddha-dharma, because one knows that things exist through causes and conditions, one is free from the view of non-existence; because one contemplates that their intrinsic nature is empty, the view of existence does not arise.
If one is free from the views of existence and non-existence, one does not fall into the extremes of nihilism or eternalism.

If one does not penetrate this meaning of emptiness, then even if one does not cling to existence or non-existence and remains beyond words and free from marks, one ultimately uses a conceptualizing mind to construct this so-called "non-conceptual" mind.
It is like the Brahmacārin Dīrghanakha, who contemplated the true mark of all dharmas and, while not accepting any dharma, accepted this very view.
Now, true emptiness is free from conceptual discrimination; how could one discriminate emptiness?
If one does not understand the meaning of emptiness, then even if they single-mindedly apply themselves with diligence to seek liberation, they will not be able to know nirvana.
Therefore, the Buddha said:
"If you wish to seek nirvana, you should thoroughly understand the emptiness of dependent origination, which is free from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism."

Because that initial seed-mind diminishes a portion of the defilement of greed, it accords with a small degree of pure mind; from this point onward, fasting and giving gradually increase, which is precisely the power of the pure mind beginning to sprout.
Through this habitual perfuming, one is able to discern the proper objects of refuge, and the wisdom seeking liberation arises.
If, however, one does not encounter favorable conditions, one will again fall back into the views of nihilism, eternalism, or emptiness, and thus enter into false views.

Nevertheless, the seeds of these eight consciousnesses never perish; if one hears the Buddha-dharma, one merely [realizes] that [the self] is empty of both annihilation and permanence, and by contemplating the emptiness of dependent origination, one immediately enters the right path.

If there are those who are like unconditioned seeds—people in whom [the potential] has not yet arisen—then even if one explains it to them in various ways, they will ultimately be unable to believe or understand it.

Furthermore, when a practitioner, at the eighth moment of mind, seeks birth and death and relies upon fearlessness, if they encounter a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) who explains for them the true refuge in the Triple Gem, they will be able to believe and accept it because they gradually come to recognize the causes and effects of the present life.
Setting this matter aside for a moment:
suppose, while that person is practicing the fast, they encounter a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) who says to them,
"For what benefit do you observe this fast and give these offerings?"

He replied: "I observe that the causes and conditions for seeking protection involve various forms of sorrow and suffering; whereas by practicing few desires and giving, one attains joyful and peaceful dwelling."
Then the spiritual friend said:
"Excellent, son of good family!

As the Buddha has taught, because sentient beings are driven by stinginess and greed, they experience various forms of sorrow and suffering in the present life; at the end of their lives, due to these causes and conditions, they fall into the evil realms."

Because the mind is free from the defilement of stinginess and greed, one will enjoy peace and happiness in the present life and attain great renown; at the end of life, one will be reborn in heaven, and subsequently attain nirvana.
Therefore, you should now once again receive the eightfold precepts with a most excellent mind.
Having heard this, they immediately accepted it in faith and practiced according to the instructions.

However, for those who lack the spiritual capacity (*gotra*), one speaks only of how worldly suffering and pleasure are all created by Īśvara, or are transformations of the earth and other elements, or have time as their cause; such people cannot even believe in this small portion of the eightfold fast (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*) which is peaceful and pure, let alone in other profound matters.
Question: What serves as the cause for these eight minds, which are the original seeds? Answer:
Since time immemorial in the world, there have been the names "good" and "evil," and from this, seeds [of such concepts] have arisen.

For example, at the beginning of the kalpa, when sentient beings were greedy for the "earth-fat" (*pṛthivī-parpaṭaka*), those who ate much were then considered "unwholesome" and those who ate little were considered "wholesome."
Some, seeing that the causes and conditions of eating much give rise to various faults and afflictions, think to themselves:
"It would not be well for me to eat little of this flavor now,
constantly admonishing myself with moderation."

However, these sentient beings do not yet recognize the retribution of cause and effect in future lives; they merely transmit from one to another, regarding benevolence, righteousness, shame, and remorse as wholesome dharmas. Those who are able to practice in this manner are collectively praised by the world.

Furthermore, it is like when a minor kalpa is coming to an end, sentient beings suddenly give rise to the resolve for awakening; they recognize the faults and afflictions of worldly unwholesome dharmas and exhort one another to collectively practice virtuous deeds.

At that time, there is likewise no spiritual friend who exhorts and guides one toward this; you should know that it is entirely due to the power of the causes and conditions of the permeation of the true mark of one's own mind.
Just as with the original seed, when even a speck of dust’s worth of mental defilement is removed, the power of the pure mind is revealed accordingly, even down to the measure of that speck of dust.

Although it is said that they arise from the seeds of goodness, in reality, this is precisely "non-arising arising. Because of this nature of firmness, they never perish within the consciousness-mind of sentient beings; until one reaches the Great Vajra Wheel of the actual limit of one's own mind, there is no other place for them to abide.

The fruit of separation again becomes a seed, which grows and increases through successive stages; yet it does not transcend the gateway of the letter A. Therefore, it is said: "The supreme Mahāyāna phrase is the characteristic of the continuous arising of the mind."
"The great secrets of all Buddhas cannot be known by those of external paths.
The *Parable of the Herbs* chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra* also intends this very point.

Furthermore, when a practitioner takes refuge in the Triple Gem and accords with the Tathāgata’s discipline, receiving the eightfold precepts for a single day, they attain tranquility and bliss because they are protected by the noble precepts.
Because of this peace and happiness, one places faith in the conduct of the noble ones and practices it repeatedly; this is called the "initial seed.

To cause these virtues to increase, one cultivates various wholesome deeds, up to the point where, through the purity and certainty of ethical discipline (*śīla*), one is reborn in heaven and subsequently attains *nirvāṇa*; this is called the "seed of enjoyment."

Furthermore, by virtue of associating with spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), one hears the benefits of the True Dharma and does not give rise to a mind of seeking refuge elsewhere; this is the eighth true ground for fearlessness for ordinary beings wandering in the flow of saṃsāra.

Furthermore, within this superior dwelling, there arises the wisdom seeking liberation; through contemplation and investigation, a definitive conception is produced, from which the initial seed-mind of the śrāvaka-bodhi is immediately generated.
All of these should be explained in detail by following the preceding text.

Thus, from the first stage up through each of the stages of the Three Vehicles, all possess the ten mental states; even in the tenth stage, they possess the seeds, sprouts, buds, leaves, flowers, and fruits, until the wisdom seeking the Buddha-ground arises, whereby one contemplates ultimate emptiness and reaches the Diamond Limit (*vajra-koṭi*).
At that time, Vajrapāṇi again requested the Buddha, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One would explain that mind.
Having spoken thus, [the Buddha replied:]
The Buddha addressed the Lord of Secrets, Vajrapāṇi, saying: “Lord of Secrets, listen attentively! As for the characteristics of the mind, they are:
a mind of desire and a mind without desire; a mind of hatred and a mind of loving-kindness; a mind of delusion and a mind of wisdom; and so on, up to: what is the mind that undergoes rebirth?”
"This means that when various beings cultivate karmic actions and are born, their minds possess such a common nature.
This answers the phrase concerning the characteristics of the various minds within the preceding question.
First, the names of the sixty types of mind are listed; next, their characteristics are explained.
"Lord of Secrets! What is a covetous mind?
It is that which accords with defiled phenomena. This means being attached to preceding objects, which is precisely the defilement of the pure mind.
If one practices in accordance with this dharma, it is called a mind possessed of craving.
Because mental phenomena are subtle and difficult to discern, one should simply observe the activities they perform; there will inevitably be signs manifested externally.
For example, by observing the appearance of smoke, the nature of fire can be known through inference.
Therefore, most of these phrases clarify the meaning by following the principles of cultivation, as they may be understood through such analogies.

All of these are states of mind that arise in various combinations with wholesome factors prior to the emergence of the supramundane mind. If the practitioner skillfully discerns the true from the false—just as a farmer diligently weeds out the noxious grasses to protect the noble seedlings—the power of the pure mind will gradually increase.
Do not assume that these are merely matters of causal phenomena and thus treat these ultimate words with negligence, allowing the mind to sink into them without self-awareness.
Second: "What is a mind free from greed?"

"Conforming to undefiled phenomena" means that it is contrary to the preceding mind, such that one does not even give rise to aspiration or delight toward the wholesome states that ought to be pursued.

Therefore, while non-attachment and wholesome dharmas both obstruct the arising of goodness, they differ in that the latter is associated with a mind free from defilement; this must be most carefully examined.

Consequently, a practitioner should simply contemplate the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the greedy mind, whereby the mind naturally becomes untainted by greed; one should not give rise to such unwise practice of non-greed.
Regarding the third [point], "What is the mind of anger?

It refers to that which accords with the phenomena of wrath": "wrath" refers to the arousal of the mind of anger manifesting outwardly; because mental phenomena are difficult to discern, it is explained by way of its conformity to the practice of the phenomena of wrath.
If such signs of non-quiescence repeatedly arise, one should know that these are the signs of a mind of anger.
However, if one observes within these various conditions that the mind of anger itself has no place of abiding, then this hindrance will not arise.
Regarding the fourth [point], "What is a mind of loving-kindness?
It refers to practicing in accordance with the dharma of loving-kindness": this loving-kindness is likewise the opposite of hatred.
Loving-kindness that is a mental defilement arising from attachment and views is not produced from wholesome seeds.
The upper character "compassion" (ci) refers to the internal mind; the lower character "compassion" refers to the activities performed through external manifestations.
Once this has been realized, one simply remedies those failings that obstruct the Path and progressively cultivates the immeasurable mind of compassion; this is the specific antidote.
The fifth [question]: "What is a deluded mind?

It refers to practicing in accordance with non-contemplation of dharmas. This means not contemplating the preceding words regarding good and evil, right and wrong, but instead accepting them immediately upon encountering them.

In all undertakings one performs, if one cannot first use the mind of wisdom to discern and deliberate upon right and wrong, such numerous errors and failures as these are all characteristics of the deluded mind.
Regarding the sixth point, "What is the mind of wisdom?

It refers to practicing in accordance with the sublime and superior dharmas": this means that among the various teachings spoken, such a person uses wisdom to discern what is superior and what is inferior, what should be accepted and what should not be accepted; they take up the superior elements and practice them, which is precisely the characteristic of non-delusion.
However, the methods for transcending humanity cannot be fathomed by the calculations of intellectual power; only those with faith can enter them.
Therefore, observing that worldly wisdom, eloquence, and cleverness are difficult [to overcome], this serves as their antidote.
Seventh, what is the resolute mind?
It refers to following instructions and practicing them exactly as taught.
Eighth, what is the doubting mind?

Regarding the phrase "constantly collecting and maintaining uncertain matters" and so forth: first, one now discriminates the doubting mind so that the characteristics of the decisive mind may be easily understood and clearly realized.
This means that whenever such a person hears anything, they immediately give rise to an indecisive mind.
For example, at the time of receiving the precepts, one may spontaneously give rise to doubt, thinking:
"Have I now certainly obtained the precepts, or have I not obtained them?
Or one may doubt the teacher or the Dharma; all such cases are like this.
It is like a person traveling on a road who, because of doubt, is unable to move forward.
As a verse in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "Even as when observing a forked path, one who seeks benefit should follow [the right way]."
This is their antidote.

Furthermore, "resolute mind" means that upon hearing the Dharma teachings and instructions from virtuous friends and others, one does not give rise to doubt or hesitation, but instead practices them with a sincere heart.
Nevertheless, one should also observe with wisdom and give rise to a mind of right certainty.
Regarding the ninth [point], "What is a darkened mind?

It refers to giving rise to a state of doubt regarding things that are free from doubt": this means that regarding such matters as the Four Truths, impurity, impermanence, and so forth, which a wise person of the world should not doubt, those who hear of them harbor hesitation, like seeing a stump at night and giving rise to various kinds of speculative thoughts.
If one perceives such signs, one should know that they are caused by a darkened mind.
Regarding the tenth [point], "What is the luminous mind?

It refers to practicing without doubt or hesitation regarding the Dharma that is free from doubt": this means that regarding the definitive Dharma-seal, which is not a dharma subject to suspicion, one is able to have immediate faith upon hearing it; one should know that this is the luminous mind.
However, within this context, both excess and deficiency constitute minds that obstruct the Path; rather, wisdom that abides in the middle is their antidote.
The eleventh [question]: "What is the mind of accumulation?"

Regarding the phrase "taking the immeasurable as the nature of the one," it means that once this person has given rise to faith and understanding regarding a single matter, they further hear various distinct teachings and integrate them all together into one.

It is like a person who, having mastered one samādhi, sees the various superior matters of the countless dharma-gates in other sūtras and teachings, yet claims that all of them describe this very state of concentrated mind and that there is no other dharma apart from it; therefore, it is called the "accumulated mind."
Regarding the twelfth [point], "What is a contentious mind?

It is characterized by mutual assertion and refutation": this means that upon hearing the teachings spoken by others, one constantly delights in debating right and wrong, asserting that "this principle ought to be so" or "that matter is not thus."
Even if what is said is reasonable, they will employ various skillful means to seek out its flaws and faults, desiring to cause it to fall into error.
Should another come to question them, they likewise seek out his shortcomings, saying:
"This question is perverse; I should not answer it."
When such signs appear, one should know that this is the mind of contention.
Thirteenth: "What is the mind of strife?

It refers to giving rise to notions of right and wrong regarding oneself. This means harboring a mind of right and wrong within; for instance, having finished contemplating a single point, one immediately posits alternative views to seek out its faults.

Although one may receive instruction from others with a virtuous mind, once it has been received, one still examines for oneself what is gained and lost, thinking, "This matter is appropriate," or "This is not appropriate."
When many such signs appear, one should know that this is a contentious mind.
Regarding the fourteenth [point], "What is a non-contentious mind?

It is the relinquishing of both 'is' and 'is not,'" according to the Sanskrit original, the word for "conditioned nature" (*saṃskṛtatva*) should be appended to all instances following the sixty minds; this can be understood by analogy.

This means that his mind harbors no partiality; although he previously held such views based on his own long-standing study and practice, upon hearing a different teaching that accords with reason, he immediately accepts and practices it.
Or, having previously considered something to be right, upon hearing that others consider it unwholesome, one is immediately able to reform it.
With no attachments in the mind, both right and wrong are relinquished.
If such characteristics are present, one should know this is the mind free from contention.
To be aware of a mind that is indeterminate and free from contention, and to cultivate the mind of non-contention regarding the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena—this is their antidote.
Fifteenth: "What is the celestial mind?"

Regarding the phrase "accomplishment through mental reflection and mindfulness": it is like how the various devas, by virtue of the karmic fruition of their previous lives, have whatever they require arise according to their minds without the application of effort.
One should know that such frequent arising of aspirations and desires is the mind of a deva;
it is also due to having previously been born in the higher realms that such habits persist.
Just as with practitioners of mantra who, without aspiring for far-reaching and great fruits, are merely led by their own minds, they are able to obstruct the pure bodhicitta.
One should know for oneself and not covet worldly *siddhi*; this is its antidote.
Regarding the sixteenth [point], "What is the mind of an asura?

It is that which delights in dwelling within birth and death": *Asura* is composed of *a*, meaning "not," and *sura*, meaning "deva. Because their karmic retribution resembles that of the devas, yet their conduct, actions, and abodes differ, they are given this name.
Although such a person knows there is the benefit of liberation, they take deep delight in the pleasures of the retributive fruits of birth and death and are unable to advance toward it.
If a practitioner possesses these characteristics, one should know that this is the mind of an asura.
It is also because they were previously born in this realm in past lives that they possess these habits.
Contemplating impermanence, suffering, and so forth, serves as their antidote.
Seventeenth: "What is the mind of a nāga?"
"Regarding 'contemplating vast wealth,' this means frequently forming this thought:
'By what skillful means shall I obtain such vast wealth and exquisite, precious jewels?'"
To possess such thoughts of excessive greed and insatiability is the very mind of the dragon realm.
Furthermore, because they have originally come from within the dragon realm, they give rise to this habituation.
Excessive joy causes practitioners to seek worldly *siddhis*, which obstructs the supramundane pure mind.
Contemplating few desires, contentment, impermanence, and so forth, serves as the antidote to that.
Regarding the eighteenth [point], "What is the human mind?
It is the contemplation of benefiting others," this means one takes pleasure in pursuing the thought:
"Such-and-such a person has been kind to me; I shall employ such-and-such skillful means to bring them great benefit."
"Such-and-such a person once did me harm; I shall now repay them.
Such various schemes for managing people and benefiting oneself are all merely matters of the human mind.

One should mindfully observe one's own mental activities and seek the benefits of the Dharma early; one should not engage in distracted deliberations regarding external conditions, for this is their antidote.
Nineteenth: "What is the female mind?"
Regarding the phrase "conforming to the nature of desire," this too is the mind of the human realm, differing only in that it is characterized by excessive desire.
As the Sūtra says: "Women have a hundred times more desire than men; they constantly dwell upon the pleasures they have experienced, or imagine the countenances, complexions, and postures of others."
This can cause the practitioner to obscure their pure mind;
it is also because they have frequently been born as women in past lives and still possess those habitual tendencies.
Within this context, contemplating the true nature of the body through the applications of mindfulness on impurity (*aśubha-smṛtyupasthāna*) and other methods serves as the antidote to that.
Twenty: "What is the mind of *īśvara*? It refers to the thought:

'May I have everything according to my wish. Here, *īśvara* refers to the celestial deity worshipped by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). According to their school, they maintain that the god *Īśvara* can, by mere thought, create all sentient beings as well as phenomena such as suffering and pleasure.
Those who practice this dharma should also constantly maintain mindfulness, vowing to become like their chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā).
If a practitioner of mantras frequently contemplates such siddhi, I shall grant accomplishment in accordance with that contemplation.
One should know that this mind of self-mastery is likewise made so by prior habituation.
One should observe that all phenomena belong entirely to a multitude of causes and conditions and possess no self-mastery; this is that which is to be counteracted.
Twenty-first: "What is the 'merchant's mind'?

It refers to practicing in accordance with the method of first gathering and subsequently dividing. This means that just as a worldly merchant first prioritizes the accumulation of goods, and only thereafter contemplates their analysis, thinking:
"This item should be used in such-and-such a place, and that item should be used in another place; thus, great profit may be obtained."
If a practitioner first attends to internal and external studies until they are fully mastered, they may then deliberate:
"This is a worldly scripture; it should be applied in such a manner."
"This application of the Dharma of the two vehicles should be used to receive such-and-such a person;
these provisions of the Mahāyāna are what is required for such-and-such conditions.
This is called the "merchant's mind."
This is also due to the influence of past habituation.
Cultivating swift wisdom is the remedy for this.

That is to say, as soon as one hears any teaching, one should immediately contemplate its causes, conditions, and functional applications; why wait until one has accumulated extensive learning before seeking its practical application?
Twenty-second: "What is the mind of a farmer?
It refers to following extensive initial learning and subsequently seeking the Dharma. This is like a student of agriculture who asks an experienced farmer:
"How does one know that the soil is fertile and excellent?"
What is meant by plowing, sowing, weeding, and hoeing?
What is meant by observing the seasons?
And what is meant by harvesting and storing?
Having thus understood each of these points, one then applies effort.
This mind is likewise: first, one must consult the wise and extensively hear the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa), and only thereafter practice them.
All of this is brought about by the force of past habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
That which is to be counteracted is the faculty of sharp intelligence.

For example, upon hearing that the aggregates (*skandha*) are impermanent, one immediately understands that the same applies to the elements (*dhātu*), the sense bases (*āyatana*), and dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); all such cases are like this.
Furthermore, if a poisoned arrow has entered the body, how could one wait for the three months of the farming season to conduct extensive inquiries before extracting it?
Twenty-third: "What is meant by 'the heart of the river'?"

Regarding the phrase "practicing in accordance with the two extremes based on causes": this nature of mind relies simultaneously upon both extremes; at times it practices permanence, and at times it practices annihilation, or it may concurrently believe in both the heterodox and the orthodox. This is like a river that relies upon both its banks; the objects drifting within it are likewise not fixed to either side.
Regarding the remedy herein: it means that if a practitioner concentrates their mind on a single object, they will be able to reach their goal.
If the mind is not fixedly maintained, there is no principle by which one could accomplish all tasks simultaneously.
Twenty-fourth: "What is the 'pond-like mind'?
It refers to the dharma of following after craving without satiety. This is like a pond: even if various waters flow into it, it is never satisfied.
This mind is likewise: if fame, wealth, kinsmen, and other such matters gather around it, it is never satisfied; this is even so regarding the teachings one has studied.
Just as one who has already obtained milk-rice does not strive to eat it hastily, nor further craves other flavors;
therein, having few desires and knowing contentment serves as the antidote.
Twenty-fifth: "What is the 'well-mind'? "
Regarding the phrase "to contemplate in this way, profoundly and even more profoundly": it is like looking down into a well; its depth is difficult to ascertain. This nature of mind is likewise:

whatever one contemplates or values is profound and far-reaching, such that all matters, whether wholesome or unwholesome, are intended to be immeasurable by others. Even those who walk, stay, or work together with one do not recognize the movements of their mind; know that this is the "well-like mind."
The Dharma-door of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and the characteristics of virtuous persons are both clearly manifest and easy to understand; these serve as their antidotes.
Regarding the twenty-sixth [point], "How does one guard the mind?

It means that this mind alone is real, while other minds are unreal": it is like when worldly people, for the sake of protecting their own bodies, wealth, and possessions, employ various defenses such as surrounding walls and multi-storied towers to prevent them from being harmed by others.
This mind is likewise; it constantly guards the body and mind, even as a tortoise withdraws its six limbs, so that they are not harmed by external objects.
That is to say, this practice alone is the treasure, while all other conditioned activities are unreal.
Those who study as śrāvakas often give rise to this mind.
It is countered by the practice of protecting others as well.

Furthermore, there are those who seek to preserve their own understanding and do not wish for it to be harmed by various dissenting arguments from others, asserting that all other views are entirely unreal; this too is such a case.
Twenty-seventh: "What is a stingy mind?

It refers to acting in accordance with the principle of seeking for oneself while also giving to others. This means that whatever this person does is entirely for their own sake; therefore, they are fond of keeping secret and begrudging their wealth, skills, and even wholesome dharmas, rather than bestowing them upon others.
One who possesses these signs knows this to be a mind of stinginess.
To counteract it, one should cultivate mindfulness of giving and impermanence.
One should reflect: "Wealth, possessions, and skills—when the time of impermanence arrives, none of these will follow me."
However, this present body cannot be preserved for even a single moment; why then should one begrudge it?
Regarding the twenty-eighth [question], "What is the mind of a wildcat?

It refers to practicing the method of gradual progress": this is like a cat or wildcat stalking and catching birds; it remains still with its breath held, not striving for haste, but waiting until the bird is within reach before seizing it.

This person is likewise: having encountered and heard various essential teachings, they merely take them to heart, receive them, and retain them, yet do not put them into practice, hoping instead that when favorable conditions converge, they will then courageously and vigorously apply themselves.
Furthermore, it is like a cat or a wildcat that, despite receiving various forms of compassionate care and upbringing, fails to recognize its debt of gratitude.
If a person merely accepts another's kindness and benevolent words yet does not bear them in mind to repay them, such a person possesses the heart of a wildcat.
To act immediately upon hearing the teaching without waiting for the proper time or place, and to constantly keep in mind [the teacher's] kindness and virtue, serves as the antidote.
Twenty-ninth: "What is the dog-like mind?

It refers to being satisfied with having obtained only a small portion. This means that because dogs possess the causes and conditions of meager merit, their aspirations are base and inferior; thus, upon encountering even a small amount of coarse and lowly food, they immediately give rise to satisfaction.
If one were to exceed this slightly, it would not be what was originally intended.
This mind is likewise: having heard but a small portion of the wholesome Dharma, one considers practice to be inexhaustible and no longer seeks further superior matters.
This arises from the habitual tendencies of the śrāvaka lineage.
It is countered by the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*).
Furthermore, the mind is like the great ocean: it neither rejects the small nor overflows with the much.
The thirtieth: "What is the mind of a garuḍa?

It is said to be the dharma of following and relying upon its own faction as wings. This bird constantly relies upon its two wings to support its body; wherever it goes, it acts according to its will and achieves great power, yet if even a single feather were missing, it would be incapable of anything.
This mind is likewise; it constantly longs for many companions and supporters with whom to cooperate in order to accomplish its tasks.
Furthermore, it gives rise to its resolve only because of the actions of others and cannot advance on its own.
Just as when seeing someone practicing virtue, one should think: "If they can do it, why should I not?
One should thus conceive the courageous and heroic bodhicitta, like a lion king who does not rely on companions, as an antidote to its opposing factors.
Regarding the thirty-first [point], "What is the rat-like mind?

It refers to contemplating the severing of all fetters": Just as a rat, upon seeing another's chest or basket tied with ropes and the like, will immediately and unreasonably damage them, yet does not form the thought:
"By severing these, I shall obtain such benefit."
"Yet one does not act for it with any purpose.
This mind is likewise: whatever attachments or accomplishments it possesses, it seeks out opportunities to create gaps and ruins them."
Chapter Thirty-two, "The Mind of Chanting": This section is missing from the Sanskrit manuscript and is not explained.
The Ācārya said: "This is a metaphor for the transmission of the sound of the Dharma."

It is like a person of this world who, having mastered the melodies from others and attained skillfulness, then performs them for others, producing all manner of exquisite and beautiful sounds that bring joy to those who hear them.

This mind desires to hear the sublime Dharma from others; I shall, for the sake of sentient beings, explain it through various phrases and expressions, adorning and analyzing it, so that this wondrous sound may be heard and known everywhere.
"Most of these are the residual habits of the śrāvakas, which can also obstruct the pure mind.
One should reflect: 'I shall attain the wisdom of self-realization within, and thereafter manifest in various physical forms to expound it'—this is the remedy for them."
Thirty-third: "What is the dancing mind?

It refers to practicing such dharmas with the thought, 'I shall ascend through various supernatural transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*). Just as people in the world speak of 'dancing' when their limbs are dispersed and moved, so too are these supernatural transformations; they manifest various unprecedented events to cause the minds of those before them to become pure and their eyes to rejoice."
Most of these are the residual habits of those who possessed the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
If one is biased toward such methods for attaining *siddhi* and pursues them with longing, this likewise obstructs the pure mind.

One should instead contemplate the Samādhi of Removing Obstructions (*Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin*), maintaining a mind free from distraction and movement; manifesting supernatural transformations through empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) without arising from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). One must not crave minor worldly signs of efficacy, for this is what is to be remedied.
Thirty-fourth: "What is the mind that beats the drum?
It refers to cultivating this Dharma with the thought, 'I shall beat the Dharma-drum. The drum can serve as a warning to sentient beings, causing them to attain awakening."
If a practitioner forms this thought:
"Sentient beings have been in a state of long-term slumber; I shall cultivate various kinds of unimpeded eloquence and beat the great Dharma drum to awaken them."
It can also obstruct the pure mind.

One should contemplate attaining the *dhāraṇī* of immeasurable speech at an early date, so as to universally proclaim to all beings with the wondrous sound of a celestial drum; one must not allow minor worldly gains to hinder the causes and conditions of the Great Matter—this is the remedy for that.
Thirty-fifth: "What is the 'dwelling-mind'?

It refers to practicing in accordance with the methods for protecting one's own body. This means that just as a person constructs a house to shelter and defend their body, thereby escaping various harmful conditions such as cold, heat, wind, rain, thieves, and malicious insects.

This mind is also like that: "I shall maintain the precepts and cultivate goodness to protect myself, so that in this life and future lives I may remain far removed from the manifold sufferings of the evil realms.
This is mostly the practice of the śrāvakas.
One should contemplate rescuing and protecting all sentient beings rather than oneself alone; this is what is to be remedied.
Regarding the thirty-sixth [point], "What is the lion-like mind?
It refers to practicing all dharmas without any timidity": just as a lion among all beasts is victorious wherever it goes and possesses no timidity whatsoever.
This mind is likewise: in all matters, it desires to excel all others and its heart is not timid.
It thinks to itself, "There is no difficult task; none can contend with me to determine our relative superiority."

Once one has awakened to this knowledge oneself, one should give rise to the mind of the Lion of the Śākyas, so that all sentient beings may be universally supreme, without any distinction of superior or inferior; this is what is to be remedied.
Regarding the thirty-seventh [point], "What is the owl-like mind?
It refers to constantly contemplating in the dark night": this bird is incapable of anything during the great light of day, yet its six faculties are sharp and keen at night.

If a practitioner, although having heard something during the day, recites and studies it with a clouded mind and fails to attain skillfulness therein, yet upon reaching the dark night, they reflect upon what was done and deliberate upon it again, they will then attain clarity.
Even when practicing meditative contemplation and so forth, a dark place is superior.

Once one has become aware of this, one should maintain an equanimity toward light and darkness, ensuring that the mental application is free from the distinction between day and night; this is the remedy for what is to be countered.
Thirty-eighth: "What is the 'crow-mind'?

It refers to the state of being constantly apprehensive and fearful in all circumstances. This means that just as a crow, even when approached and nurtured by a person with a benevolent heart, may at times watch for an opportunity to strike and harbor a sense of suspicion and dread; such is its nature at all times.
This mind is likewise; even when a virtuous friend seeks to benefit them, or when someone attempts to lead them astray, it reacts with uniform suspicion and obstruction, harboring doubt and fear.
Even when observing the precepts and cultivating goodness, it maintains a heart of alarm and dread toward birth and death.
If one has become aware [of this], one should cultivate a mind of stability and fearlessness;
this is its antidote. (39) "What is the rākṣasa-mind?
It refers to initiating what is unwholesome amidst the wholesome. This means that when a person perceives something as a wholesome deed, they instead form an unwholesome interpretation of it.
The Buddha taught that constructing various stūpas and temples yields immeasurable merit; yet they, on the contrary, say:
"Because of this, countless small insects are needlessly harmed and the donors are troubled; what benefit will there be from this?"
"One shall experience the retribution of suffering.
"Initiation" refers to the arising of such unwholesome states of mind.
In this context, one should simply contemplate the virtues and benefits [of the remedy], not dwelling upon those [unwholesome states] which are to be counteracted.
Fortieth: "What is 'thorn-like in mind'?

It refers to having a nature of committing evil in all circumstances. This is like a thicket of thorns; in every place it causes much harm and obstruction, leaving those who approach it in a state of unease.
This mind is likewise: if one performs virtuous deeds such as great acts of giving, once they have been completed, one immediately gives rise to a sense of regret;
if one has committed an evil deed, one further reflects upon it and harbors shame and fear.
Therefore, one will constantly harbor regret and experience mental agitation and restlessness.
As for the remedial method herein: if one has committed an offense, one must swiftly strive to confess and eliminate it; do not give rise to agitation or remorse.
Regarding the good deeds one performs, one should reflect upon them personally and give rise to a mind of joy.
Forty-first: "What is the cave-like mind?

It refers to practicing in accordance with the methods for entering a cave. This means that various nāgas, asuras, and others all reside within deep caves beneath the earth or at the bottom of the ocean.
There are many divine elixirs there that can grant longevity and mastery.

The practitioner may think that within those realms there are many beautiful women, as upright and handsome as the gods, so that one need have no fear of premature death and may indulge freely in the five desires.
Or one might think of remaining there, where one could live for the duration of a kalpa and behold the Buddhas of the future;
these are all the mind of a cave-dweller.

One should instead contemplate practicing according to the Dharma, so that in this very life one may see the path of the light of the Dharma and even attain Buddhahood. One should not linger on the road, harboring thoughts of the methods of the world’s immortals; this is the remedy for those [attachments].
Forty-second: "What is the wind-mind?
It is characterized by the nature of arising everywhere. This is because the nature of wind is dispersal, due to its lack of stability.

The mind of this person is likewise; it universally plants roots of goodness in all places—meaning it ensures a share [of merit] within the worldly heterodox paths, among various celestial deities, and within the practices of the Three Vehicles—and forms this thought:
"Just as when many seeds are sown everywhere, there will inevitably be those that sprout."
"One should have a mind like this wind.

One should reflect that a stony field is barren and wastes the seeds sown; one should seek instead a fertile field of merit that is rich and lush. By cultivating with single-minded intent, the harvest will surely be great—this is the remedy for that."
Forty-third: "What is the water-like mind?

It refers to practicing in accordance with the washing away of all unwholesome dharmas. This means that just as the nature of water is pure and clean, even if it is temporarily defiled by various impurities, it becomes clear when settled and is further able to wash away those stains and filth.
The mind of this person is also like this: it constantly desires to reveal its defilements and evils, and to repent and wash away the manifold transgressions of the three karmas.
Because one perceives these defilements and this purity, [one realizes that] "if I act in such a way, it will obstruct the pure mind."

One should simply contemplate the true mark of the mind and realize that, from the very beginning, defiled phenomena have never arisen; by doing so, one can naturally eliminate all hindrances, which constitutes the practice of their remedy.
Forty-fourth: "What is the fire-like mind?
It is characterized by being blazing and intensely hot. Just as the nature of fire is brilliant and swift, so too is this person's mind:
when performing wholesome deeds, they can accomplish immeasurable merit in a mere instant; yet when committing evil, they likewise accomplish extremely grave karma in a short time.
