Regarding the practice of remediation herein, one should reflect that a fierce and violent mind causes much ruin and injury; therefore, by means of the water of gentle kindness and compassion, one should skillfully extinguish it, while ensuring that the blazing activities of virtue remain constant—this is its antidote.
The forty-fifth, "Mud-like Mind," is missing from the Sanskrit manuscript and is not explained.
The Ācārya said: "This is a mind that is exclusively characterized by ignorance."
One cannot even distinguish or remember matters close at hand before one's eyes; therefore, the Vinaya says it is "like a lump of clay.
Furthermore, it is like a muddy quagmire: because it is soft and yielding, it is difficult to cross over.
It is necessary to have something to rely upon; that is to say, one must depend on such things as bridges and planks to be able to cross over.

If one realizes that such expedients exist, one must necessarily rely upon virtuous friends to bring these expedients to fruition; only then can ignorance be gradually dispelled and the nature of wisdom be restored.
Regarding the forty-sixth [section], "What is the mind of manifest color?
It means that its nature is to resemble them": for example, just as with dyes such as blue, yellow, red, or white, if a plain silk thread is immersed in them, it immediately becomes the same color.

The mind of this person is also like this: when seeing or hearing wholesome dharmas, it follows and practices them; when seeing or hearing unwholesome matters, it likewise conforms to and trains in them; even with regard to neutral matters, it is the same, shifting according to the circumstances as it encounters various objects.

Once the practitioner has become self-aware, they should mindfully and single-mindedly seek the Dharma of personal realization; not awakening through another, nor being turned by external conditions—this is the remedy for that.
Forty-seventh: "What is the 'board-like mind'?

It refers to practicing the Dharma according to one's capacity and abandoning other virtues. This means that just as a wooden board floating in water can carry various objects only up to its own limit, and once that limit is exceeded it can no longer support them and will eventually tip over and cast them away; so too is this mind.
The mind of this person is also like this: having discerned the karma of wholesome dharmas and performed a single task according to his own capacity, he then says:
"I have followed my predecessors and practiced only this dharma; I know nothing else."
"Furthermore, practicing the eight precepts of the fast without ever relinquishing them, and not aspiring to practice any other virtues;
because one has generated the vast mind and trains in the conduct of bodhi—this is what is to be countered."
Regarding the forty-eighth [point], "What is a deluded mind?
It means that what is grasped is different from what is intended": it is like a person who, due to being confused, intends to go east but instead goes west.

The mind of this person is likewise: though he intends to practice the contemplation of impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*), he instead grasps at signs of purity and yet claims, "I am now practicing the contemplation of impurity.
When practicing impermanence and non-self (*anitya-anātman*), he instead acts within the inversion of permanence and self, yet claims, "I am now practicing impermanence and non-self."
This is caused by the distraction of the mind.
One should therefore bring the mind to single-minded concentration and observe with careful discernment, tranquility, and non-erroneous insight; this is the remedy for that [distraction].
Forty-ninth: "What is the mind of poison?
It refers to practicing in accordance with the dharmas that lead to non-arising. Here, "poison" refers to the various evil poisons of dragons, snakes, medicinal herbs, and so forth.
It is like a person who, having been poisoned and fallen into a swoon, is turning toward the realm of death with no further prospect of life.

This person’s mind is likewise: neither wholesome nor unwholesome thoughts arise, and ultimately not even any thought whatsoever can be produced; it merely proceeds spontaneously, gradually entering into a state where there is neither cause nor effect. Therefore, it is called the "dharma of the state of non-arising."
Once the practitioner has awakened to this realization themselves, they should give rise to great compassion and manifold virtues, remaining free from the emptiness of nihilism;
this is what is called the "wondrous medicine of ambrosia. (50) What is the "noose-heart"?

Regarding the statement, "Its nature consists in dwelling everywhere in the bondage of the self," it is like a person bound by a snare, such that even their hands, feet, limbs, and joints cannot move.
This mind, being thus, falls into the bondage of the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
This view can bind the practitioner’s mind; even in all circumstances, it remains constantly constrained and unable to emerge on its own, constituting the most grievous obstacle.
Having thus become aware, one should swiftly use the sword of right wisdom regarding dependent origination to cut away the hindrances and coverings that are to be counteracted.
Fifty-first: "What is the shackled mind?"

Regarding the phrase "having the nature of causing the two feet to remain stationary": that which is applied to the hands is called *nigaḍa* (handcuffs), and that which is applied to the feet is called *śṛṅkhalā* (fetters).
Just as when a person is held by fetters, their two feet come to rest and they are unable to move forward.

This mind is likewise; it constantly delights in sitting upright and remaining in silent stillness to cultivate a concentrated mind and investigate the meaning of the Dharma. Because it is constrained by these [practices], it is called the "shackled mind."
Regarding the practice of remediation herein, one should at all times and in all places contemplate and cultivate it so that stillness and agitation are uninterrupted;
this is what is to be countered. Fifty-second: "What is the cloud-like mind?"

Regarding the phrase "constantly forming the thought of bringing down rain": for example, during the three months of summer in the Western regions, torrential rains are particularly severe; because they persistently drench and obscure the crops, the minds of the common people are filled with anxiety, joy, and worry, becoming densely clouded and increasingly abundant. Therefore, it is said that one forms the thought of bringing down rain at such a time.

Having become aware of this, one should practice the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*), remaining free from worldly sorrow and joy and conforming to the joy of the Dharma; these are the factors to be counteracted.
Fifty-third: "What is the field-mind (*kṣetra-citta*)?"

Regarding the phrase "constantly practicing in this way with one's own body": it is like a person who possesses fertile and excellent fields, who constantly cultivates, plows, and weeds them, employing various skillful means to ensure they become pure.
This person is likewise; they constantly delight in tending to their body, bathing and anointing it with incense, flowers, and delicacies, striving to keep it radiant, pure, and well-adorned.

Having become aware of this, one should constantly reflect on redirecting this power to cultivate the mind; by planting these various offerings as seeds in the field of merit, one brings about the attainment of supreme fruits—this is the remedy for that [obstacle].
Fifty-fourth: "What is the salt-like mind?
It refers to when one's thoughts are further increased by subsequent thoughts. This is like the nature of salt, which is salty; wherever it enters, it increases the salty flavor.

The mind of this person is also like this: regarding the object of thought, he further applies repeated reflection; just as when recollecting the desire-realm form, this thought arises, he then further investigates within himself:
"From whom does this mind arise?"
"What kind of appearance does it have?
If one observes this mind and remains undecided, one further reflects: "What causes and conditions give rise to this anxiety of seeking?
If one proceeds in this manner, there will be no end to it.
Once you have attained this awakening, you should single-mindedly settle the mind upon the principle of reality, striving to penetrate it thoroughly.

Furthermore, the nature of the mind is free from discursive thought and cannot be known through conceptualization; do not further increase the mental factors (*caitta*) upon the basis of discrimination.
Fifty-fifth: "What is the razor-like mind?
It refers to relying solely upon the method of shaving. This means that the removal of hair and beard is the mark of one who has left the secular world to become a renunciant.
It means that this person thinks only thus:
"I have already eliminated worldly appearances so that unwholesome dharmas cannot proliferate again; what more is there to seek?"
"You should know that this mind is most evil; because it establishes its own limits, it can shave away all roots of goodness so that they may not grow.

You should keep in mind that which all worthies and sages must sever—namely, the root of the three poisons dwelling in the ground of ignorance (avidyā-vāsabhūmi). If one can shave this away so that deluded thoughts do not arise, only then is one called a true renunciant."
Fifty-sixth: "What is the mind equal to Mount Meru?
It is that which has the nature of constant reflection and mental exaltation. This means that just as Mount Sumeru rises far above all other peaks such that none can surpass it, so too is this mind.

The mind of this person is likewise; it is constantly characterized by arrogance, such that even toward those who should be respected—such as teachers, monks, and parents—they are unable to humble their minds, remaining like a tall banner that cannot be bent or lowered.
If one attempts to disturb him, he must inevitably remain unyielding, never altering his constant conduct.
Through patience and humility, he regards all sentient beings as his great teachers; this serves as the remedy for that which is to be countered.
Fifty-seventh: "What is the mind equal to the ocean?
It refers to dwelling while constantly experiencing one's own body in this manner. This is like the great ocean, into which the hundred rivers flow; it swallows and contains them without limit.

This mind is likewise; regarding all superior qualities, it attributes them solely to itself, thinking that others have no such counterparts. It constantly maintains these many virtues of its own and dwells enjoying them for its private use.
The former mind strives for height, while this mind strives for breadth; therefore, it is said to be equal to the ocean.

Once the practitioner has attained such awareness, they should reflect that the immeasurable ocean of great merit of the Three Worthies and Ten Sages is successively deep and vast, whereas their own mental cultivation has never yet attained even a speck or a drop of it; thus, they should not give rise to a mind of great arrogance.
Fifty-eighth: "What is the mind that is like a perforated vessel?

It refers to that which was previously determined [to be stable], but later undergoes transformation and becomes unstable by nature. For example, it is like a vessel that is solid and strong, yet later encounters conditions that cause it to develop holes, rendering it incapable of holding anything.
This mind is also like this: at first it retains much that is upheld, but later it gradually becomes permeated by leaks.

Or, when one first resolves upon the mind and receives the precepts, they are complete and without deficiency; yet before long, the phenomena of leakage gradually arise, just as water cannot remain in a vessel that has already been broken.
All such instances as these are termed "piercing the heart.
Therefore, a practitioner should always ensure that whatever they undertake has both a beginning and an end.
Furthermore, knowing that one's nature is prone to frequent change and alteration—which most effectively obstructs the firm resolve for bodhicitta—one should apply the appropriate antidotes thereto.
Fifty-ninth: "What is the mind that takes birth?

It refers to the minds of those who have cultivated various karmic actions, which are of a similar nature [to those actions]. This means that just as a person receives good or evil retribution due to white or black karma, because of the various mixtures of their deeds, they receive various immeasurable and distinct bodies.
This mind is likewise; since all the practices one cultivates are intended for rebirth, one should know that the resulting fruits will also encompass both good and evil.
Therefore, the practitioner should mindfully discern between good and evil, eliminate what is unwholesome, and purely cultivate wholesome dharmas (*śukla-dharma*).

Within this goodness, one further uses wisdom to remove coarse impurities; proceeding through such stages in succession, until one attains the singular, pure, and sublime fruit of clarified butter (*sarpis*), which is that which is to be remedied.
The sixtieth mind is missing from the Sanskrit manuscript. The Ācārya said:
"One 'monkey-mind' is lacking."
The nature of a monkey is that its body and mind are distracted and never rest for even a moment.
It is the same with the practitioner: their nature is restless and unstable, so they grasp at many objects of perception, just as a monkey releases one thing only to seize another.
To speak roughly, all sentient beings are thus; however, this is stated here with reference to those in whom [certain afflictions] predominate.
Within this context, that which is to be counteracted is the failure to follow [the mind] and instead allowing thoughts to scatter, thereby binding the object of focus to a single point.
It is just as when a monkey is tied to a pillar; it can no longer indulge its impulses by leaping and bounding about. This is what is to be disciplined.

Now, regarding these sixty mental states, they may at times arise because the practitioner’s innate nature is biased toward them, or because the mind is activated by past habits during the practice of the Way. They may arise simultaneously or sequentially; one must remain attentive and maintain awareness at all times, so that one naturally accords with the pure bodhicitta.
When an ācārya levels and cultivates the mind-ground for a disciple, he should likewise eliminate each [state of mind] one by one.
As the Sūtra says: "O Lord of Secrets!

Counting one, two, three, four, and five, there are a total of one hundred and sixty states of mind. Transcending the three worldly false attachments, the supramundane mind arises, and so on, until one-fourth has passed into the stage of faith and understanding. This, too, is an answer concerning the various mental conceptions and the distinctions among states of mind.
Due to the existence of ignorance (*avidyā*), five fundamental afflictions arise within the mind, namely: greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt.
The reason why the five views (*dṛṣṭi*) are not mentioned here is that they belong to the category of afflictions associated with views, which are mostly included among the sixty mental states.

These five root afflictions are counted twice for the first, making ten; twice for the second, making twenty; twice for the third, making forty; twice for the fourth, making eighty; and twice for the fifth, making one hundred and sixty mental states. Thus it is said: "Counting one, two, three, four, and five twice results in one hundred and sixty mental states."
Because the afflicted minds of sentient beings constantly rely on two dharmas and fail to attain the Middle Way, they follow the diversity of phenomena and immediately divide them into two.
Within these two, they are further subdivided through successive stages; their names and characteristics are fully explained as set forth in the *Śatasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
If one further classifies them according to the nine grades—superior, middling, and inferior—and so forth, they even amount to eighty thousand afflictions; if expanded, they are immeasurable.

It is like a single seed producing five primary roots, and each of those primary roots being split into two branches; by the time one reaches the fifth splitting, there are one hundred and sixty minor branches.
From this, as they further divided and separated, the branches and leaves became beyond counting.

Furthermore, it was like at the beginning of the kalpa, when all humans were born by transformation, took thought as their food, and possessed natural bodily radiance, living in peace, happiness, and without obstruction.

However, because they did not know the true nature of the mind, they gradually became attached to the essence of the earth; due to the varying amounts of the flavor they consumed, their physical appearances changed accordingly, and from this, the mind of competition—of right and wrong, victory and defeat—arose.
Because of their prideful minds, their merit and benefits declined, and the fertility of the earth vanished; even the surface of the earth, its forests, and its vines disappeared.

Next, they ate naturally growing non-glutinous rice, and for the first time there appeared the categories of male and female; subsequently, various unrighteous acts such as lust, theft, killing, and lying arose in succession.
These matters are explained in detail within the *Āgamas*.

From that time onward, there have been various lineages and diverse local customs; various karmas, afflictions, and fetters have arisen; various destinies of sentient beings have been formed; and various bodies composed of the five aggregates have been constructed. Unless one is an omniscient person (*sarvajña*), one cannot exhaustively investigate their myriad details.

The reason the various ācāryas employ this analogy is that they wish to demonstrate how a single mind of ignorance, according to its objects, differentiates and disperses, thereby forming incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) false attachments.

Regarding "transcending the three worldly false attachments and giving rise to a supramundane mind": if one takes the pure bodhicitta as the supramundane mind, this constitutes the practice of a *yogin* that transcends three eons.
The Sanskrit term *kalpa* has two meanings:
first, a period of time; second, deluded attachment.
According to the standard interpretation, one attains perfect enlightenment after passing through three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

According to the esoteric interpretation, transcending one kalpa through the practice of a yogin means that one passes beyond the one hundred and sixty mental states and other such layers of coarse, deluded attachment; this is termed one asaṃkhyeya-kalpa.

Having transcended two kalpas of yogic practice and further crossed over one set of one hundred and sixty mental states—the first layer of subtle deluded attachments—it is called the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa.

For a practitioner of the Mantra Gate, this further exceeds one kalpa; by crossing over another set of one hundred and sixty mental states—the layer of extremely subtle deluded attachments—they attain the initial mind of the Buddha’s wisdom. Thus, it is said that Buddhahood is attained through three asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
If one transcends these three types of false attachments within a single lifetime, then one attains Buddhahood in that very life; what need is there to discuss the duration of time?
However, regarding the first stage, at the very moment one first realizes that there is only the aggregates and no self, this is termed the arising of a supramundane mind.
To transcend the sixty mental states of the world and depart from the three poisons—the root of which arises from the inversion of self—is called "transcending the three false attachments.

Furthermore, there are three false attachments, namely: attachment to the faculties (*indriya*), attachment to objects (*viṣaya*), and attachment to the realms (*dhātu*) that detain one during spiritual practice.

The "faculties" (indriya) refer to the six faculties; the "objects" (viṣaya) refer to the six sense-fields; and the "elements" (dhātu) refer to the six consciousness-elements. Since the twelve internal and external elements consist precisely of these faculties and objects, they are mentioned together.
These are the three fruits where those in training (śaikṣa) linger; therefore, it is said that they "remain and dwell" while practicing.

Furthermore, there are three types of false attachments—namely, the stumps of karma and afflictions, as well as the seeds of ignorance—which are the three most difficult points to sever for noble ones who are beyond training (aśaikṣa). Thus, there are three sets of three such false attachments.

When a practitioner of the Mahāyāna first attains the supramundane initial resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda*), they are exactly equal to those who have attained the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) of the Hīnayāna; yet, they do not fall into the fixed state (*niyāma*) of the Śrāvaka.

This is because, from the very moment they first generate the resolve, they understand that the nature of the mind is merely obscured by the inversion of self (*ātma-viparyāsa*), though it has not yet been manifested before them.

At that time, he observes with precision that the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) all arise from conditions and are impermanent and subject to change; within these, what is the self (*ātman*)?

By investigating in this manner, he realizes that the self is fundamentally unarisen, crosses over the net of immeasurable views, and the purity of the bodhicitta increases slightly in its brilliance.
It is by the power of having attained the bodhicitta that one does not fall into the stages of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

Nevertheless, such a practitioner may still harbor attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) within the mind; thus, when practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), or the various perfections (*pāramitā*), although they do not give rise to the inversion of self (*ātman-viparyāsa*) therein, their minds remain fixed upon and linger in such dharmas as dhyāna and wisdom, unable to swiftly reach bodhi.
Because they lack skillful means for crossing over according to reality, this is called "prolonged dwelling in cultivation.
Nevertheless, they are somewhat detached from the three attachments of the lower stages and are able to uproot the seeds of fundamental ignorance—the root of karma and afflictions.
One gives rise to knowledge of the twelve links of dependent origination; such a profoundly deep dharma has its nature and characteristics eternally as they are, whether a Buddha appears or not.

As previously stated, various doctrinal tenets—such as establishing purity, not establishing it, or neither purity nor impurity—are all inconsistent with reality. Even great masters of treatises such as Dīrghanakha and Sñātika, who used the sharp faculties of their own wisdom to investigate the true mark of all dharmas, were likewise unable to fathom or measure it.
The meaning of these twelve links of dependent origination is explained in detail in such sūtras as the *Śālistamba-sūtra*.

As for the term "tranquil stillness" (*zhanji*), "stillness" (*ji*) has the meaning of non-arising; that is to say, because the five root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) and the one hundred and sixty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are all ultimately non-arising, it is called "stillness."

"Profound" (*zhan*) signifies the meaning of extreme depth. It is like a clear pool ten thousand fathoms deep, tranquil and as transparent as a mirror; one who gazes upon it cannot fathom its depth. Thus it is said that when three animals cross a river, each reaches only as far as their respective tracks allow; only the Great Fragrant Elephant King is able to gradually enter deeper until he reaches the very source and bottom.

In this regard, those of the three vehicles alike attain the true reality of all phenomena through the path of wordlessness; however, because the śrāvaka enters the nature of phenomena most superficially, they feel aversion and fear toward birth and death, claiming for themselves that they have already attained nirvāṇa and conceiving the notion of having reached liberation.

The entry of the pratyekabuddha is somewhat deeper; therefore, he is not particularly anxious regarding birth and death, yet he is unable to give rise to great compassion through the power of skillful means.

When a bodhisattva awakens to such dharmas, they immediately know that the defilements of this mind are gradually being removed, whereby the pure mind gradually manifests. At that time, one attains the power of the bodhicitta’s diligent application and is able, by means of the path of non-abiding, to train in the various gateways of liberation.
Therefore, although they share the same single dharma as before, there are differences in their ascent and descent.
As the Sūtra says, "That which cannot be known by any non-Buddhists," this school explains that there are two kinds of non-Buddhists:
the external non-Buddhists, who are like those who see a clear pool and, conversely, give rise to fear, not daring to approach it; and [the internal non-Buddhists].

Although those of both internal and external paths can swim within it, finding relief from heat, removing defilements, and attaining the joy of coolness, they do not realize that within this there are immeasurable jewel-kings.
"First, they do not enter and thus do not recognize it; second, they enter but do not recognize it; therefore, it is said that no heterodox practitioners can know it.

Regarding the phrase "the former Buddhas proclaimed that which is free from all faults," this means that throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, all Buddhas possess only this single gate to entice and lead the deluded masses out of the burning house.

In this state, there is no further obstruction and conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) does not arise; thus, among all teachers who employ various logical measures (*hetu-pramāṇa*), none are able to find fault with it.

Nevertheless, because one has not yet transcended the obstacles to the Dharma, it is not yet called the truly pure *bodhicitta*. It is like a lotus that has already left the turbid mud but has not yet emerged from the water; hence the Sūtra says, "The supramundane mind dwells within the aggregates."

For although the practitioner’s mind of profound stillness has become manifest within yoga, when engaging with phenomena, the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses still require mental attention; because of their weariness with and fear of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), they remain attached to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*). Nevertheless, by the power of the bodhicitta, this occurs spontaneously without depending on external instruction.

When such wisdom arises accordingly, one is able to direct the mind toward the aggregates and so forth, cultivating the skillful means of detachment and observing the emptiness of intrinsic nature through five types of analogies.

Regarding the first phrase, "observing the mass of foam": it is like bubbles floating on water; although they can be seen with the eyes in various forms, when their essential nature is sought, it is utterly unfindable.

The aggregate of form is likewise: whether coarse or subtle, there is nothing that does not arise from a multitude of conditions. That which arises from conditions has no inherent nature; this is precisely the fundamental non-arising of form.
Regarding the next phrase, "floating bubbles": they are like the bubbles on the surface of water during a summer downpour, which likewise depend solely upon a multitude of conditions.
When observed through the fourfold analysis, they are entirely devoid of arising or ceasing.

The aggregate of sensation is likewise: all feelings of suffering, pleasure, and so forth arise from the conjunction of the faculties and their objects; since they lack intrinsic nature by virtue of their dependence on conditions, this is precisely the original non-arising of sensation.

Regarding the term "mirage" in the subsequent phrase: it is like the vapors rising from the earth in the spring months, which appear as water when viewed under the sunlight; those deluded by thirst give rise to a longing mind and rush toward it in vain effort, only to find themselves moving further and further away from it.

Sentient beings are likewise; not knowing that the nature of dependent origination is empty, they give rise to the notion of a self-existent dharma. If one awakens to the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), then this very notion is fundamentally non-arising.

Next, regarding "the plantain tree": it is like a person seeking the solid core within a plantain tree; even if one strips it away piece by piece until reaching the subtlest particle (*paramāṇu*), nothing can be found.
The aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) is likewise: when even a single atom enters the realm of motion, there is nothing that does not arise from a multitude of conditions.
Since that which arises from conditions lacks intrinsic nature, this is precisely the fundamental non-arising of formations.

Next, regarding "illusory phenomena": just as in the world, the power of spells and medicines can delude the human mind and manifest all kinds of unprecedented events, so too is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

From the initial emergence of the illusory mind of a single moment of ignorance (*avidyā*) into the triple world, if one investigates its ultimate source, it is entirely devoid of arising or ceasing, coming or going.
One should know that because things arising from various conditions lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they are likewise fundamentally unarisen.
Although these five similes are taught in the *Śrāvaka* sūtras, their underlying intent clarifies the absence of self (*anātman*).
The five similes presented here are intended to clarify that the nature of the aggregates (*skandha*) is empty.

Just as one contemplates the five aggregates, it should be understood that the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the six sense-faculties, the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and so forth, should all be explained in detail through extensive analysis, as taught in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

When the practitioner observes in this manner, they penetrate the emptiness of all phenomena through the gateway of non-substantiality, thereby attaining liberation from one layer of inversion regarding phenomena and comprehending the nature of the mind.
Thus, one is not shaken by the grasper or the grasped within the aggregates, elements, and sense bases; therefore, this is called "realizing the realm of tranquility.

When realizing this realm of tranquility, one gradually transcends the spheres of the two vehicles, like a lotus flower that, though not yet in full bloom, already slightly emerges above the clear stream.
The practitioner is likewise; because the mind no longer sinks into the aggregates (skandhas), it is called "transmundane mind" (*lokottara-citta*).
According to a correct translation, it should be termed "mind that has transcended the world."
"O Lord of Secrets!

'That which is free from the net of karmic afflictions consisting of the continuity of the eight minds of opposition and compliance' refers to what was previously described as the seeds, roots, sprouts, and so forth, as well as taking refuge in the Three Jewels and practicing the wholesome dharmas of fasting and giving for the sake of the vehicles of humans and devas—all these are called the eight minds of worldly compliance."

If those of the three vehicles first give rise to the aspiration for the Way, up until the point where they uproot the seeds of ignorance—the fundamental source of karma and afflictions—that give rise to the twelve links of dependent origination, this is called the "eight minds that oppose the world."
Alternatively, these may be divided according to the various stages such as the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), each having its own eight mental states.

Because Mahayana practitioners realize that the nature of all aggregates (*skandha*) is empty, they neither grasp at nor reject any phenomena within all dharmas. By simultaneously abandoning the eight mental states of opposition and compliance, as well as the two inversions regarding the self and the aggregates, and the two types of nets of karma and afflictions (*kleśa*), this is called the "yogic practice that transcends one eon."
Yoga is translated as "correspondence" (xiāngyìng); if addressed with a feminine suffix, it is called *yoginī*.
What is meant by "correspondence" refers to a person whose contemplative practice accords with principle.

According to the conventional explanation, this Bodhisattva has, from the moment of first generating the resolve for enlightenment, passed through one great asaṃkhyeya kalpa before finally realizing such a realm of tranquility.
In the Secret Mantra Vehicle now, merely crossing over this single layer of deluded attachment is equivalent to transcending one asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
When the practitioner has not yet passed beyond this kalpa, yet their stage is equal to that of a pratyekabuddha, it is called the "Ultimate Place Beyond Words."

At that time, the mind becomes stagnant within the signs of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). If one loses the skillful means (*upāya*), one will mostly fall into the stages of the two vehicles and realize the limited nirvāṇa.
However, through the power of the bodhicitta, one is able to once again give rise to compassionate vows; from this point onward, the paths of the three vehicles begin to diverge.

However, since the person and phenomena observed are both empty, this does not differ significantly from the various schools such as the *Tattvasiddhi*; it merely constitutes this contemplation of equality based on the principle of partial truth (*ekadeśa-satya*). Therefore, when the supramundane minds of the three vehicles—superior, middling, and inferior—are discussed collectively, they span one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, and it is only upon reaching the second *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* that they diverge from the two vehicles.
The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, Guhyakādhipati!
The practice of the Mahāyāna gives rise to the mind of the vehicle of non-conditioning and the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya). Why is this?"

"That those who practiced in such a manner in the past observed the aggregates and the ālayavijñāna, knowing their intrinsic nature to be like an illusion, a mirage, a shadow, an echo, a whirling firebrand, and a city of Gandharvas," refers precisely to clarifying the second stage of contemplation: the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
The Brahma-sound *maṃpala* signifies both "meaningless" and "the meaning of others.

What is called the vehicle of other-conditions refers to the making of the great vow of equality: to practice the bodhisattva path for the sake of all sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm; and even for those icchantikas and followers of the two vehicles who have not yet entered the stage of certainty, one should use various skillful means to subdue and gather them in, so that all may universally enter this vehicle together.
Based on this objectless great compassion (*anālambana-mahākaruṇā*), it is called the Vehicle of Other-Conditioning (*parapratyaya-yāna*).

Furthermore, as for the Objectless Vehicle (*anālambana-yāna*), upon reaching this *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, one is finally able to observe the profound and subtle *ādāna-vijñāna* and realize that the three realms are mind-only (*cittamātra*), such that not a single dharma can be found apart from the mind.
Because one proceeds upon the path to great enlightenment by means of this mind of non-conditionality, it is called the Vehicle of Non-conditionality (*anālambana-yāna*).
This mind of the Vehicle of Non-conditionality is itself the nature of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).

Because when a practitioner first cultivates contemplative practice during the initial eon, the mind sinks into the aggregates (skandhas), they therefore contemplate the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya) through the five gates of emptiness regarding the absence of intrinsic nature.

However, in relation to the Middle Way of dependent origination, this still belongs to the *pratipakṣasiddhānta* (the standpoint of therapeutic remedies). If one loses the skillful means (*upāya*) of Prajñā, one falls into nihilism; such a person is called one who "misappropriates emptiness" (*durgṛhītaśūnyatā*) and is confused with those who follow the Vaipulya path.

Now, in the Mahāyāna, the characteristic of emptiness is unattainable, and even that characteristic of emptiness is unattainable. Although one contemplates all phenomena as being non-existent, yet there is nothing among all phenomena that is made empty; therefore, one must depart from both existence and non-existence to contemplate the nature of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).

In order to purify and eliminate the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), one should follow the ancient Bodhisattvas in training in the contemplation of the aggregates (*skandha*) and the ālayavijñāna; this is precisely the intended meaning of the eight consciousnesses, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), and the three absences of nature (*triniḥsvabhāvatā*) found in such sutras as the *Laṅkāvatāra* and the *Saṃdhinirmocana*.
The sūtra’s statement that “one knows self-nature” means precisely knowing that the three realms are mind-only.

The six metaphors—the illusion, the mirage, the shadow, the echo, the whirling firebrand, and the city of the gandharvas—all dualistically distinguish between existence and non-existence to clarify the meaning of the dependent origination of the aggregates and the ālayavijñāna; this differs further from the previous five metaphors regarding the observation of the emptiness of intrinsic nature during the kalpas.
*Ālaya* means "containing" or "storing" in its semantic sense; it is correctly translated as "abode.
This refers to the fact that the various aggregates (*skandhas*) arise within it and cease within it; it is thus the nesting place or lair of the aggregates, and is named accordingly.
However, the ālayavijñāna has three meanings:
first, the meaning of differentiation; second, the meaning of causal condition; and third, the meaning of ultimate reality (*tattva*).

As stated in the verse seeking ultimate reality in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, because it is "free from duality and the basis of delusion, beyond description and conceptual proliferation," one should know that all three natures (*trisvabhāva*) are equally ultimate reality.
That which is called "separation from duality" refers to the reality of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), because both subject and object are ultimately non-existent.
"The basis of delusion" refers to the reality of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), because it gives rise to all conceptual constructions.
"Without speech and without conceptual proliferation" refers to the reality of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), because it is by its very nature free from conceptual proliferation.

Next, the verse providing an analogy for seeking that reality states: "Just as there is a magician, so is false discrimination explained; just as there are those magical illusions, so are the two kinds of delusion explained."
The commentary states:

Just as a magician, relying on the power of incantations, transforms wood, stone, and so forth into causes for delusion, so too is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) of false conceptualization; it gives rise to various forms of discrimination that serve as the cause for inversion.
Furthermore, just as various appearances such as illusions, gold, and so forth manifest, so too does the nature of conceptual construction (parikalpita-svabhāva) that arises;
because of the grasper and the grasped, the two delusions manifest at all times.
The following verse states: "Because it lacks intrinsic nature like that, one enters the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);
because it can be apprehended like that, one penetrates the reality of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The intended meaning here is as follows:

Just as those illusory phenomena lack any substantial reality, this analogy shows that the two natures—the dependent and the imagined—likewise lack substantial reality; through this principle, one attains penetration into the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).

Furthermore, just as the substance of a magical illusion can be perceived by a magician, so too is it with false discrimination; through this principle, one attains penetration into the reality of conventional truth.
Furthermore, a verse states: "Because those phenomena lack intrinsic nature, one attains the true object.
Through such a transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti), one attains the true meaning.
The commentary explains:
If a person realizes that those illusory phenomena lack intrinsic substance, they immediately attain the actual reality of the wood and so forth.

When Bodhisattvas realize that both types of delusion lack intrinsic substance and attain the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), they immediately attain the meaning of true nature (*tathatā*).
Furthermore, a verse states: "This thing exists there, yet that which has its own essence does not exist there.
Because that which has an essence is non-existent, it is therefore said to be an illusion.
This verse clarifies that illusory phenomena exist and yet do not exist.
Why is this? That which exists refers to the phenomena of illusory images, because they appear therein.
That which does not exist refers to their substantial reality, because it cannot be apprehended.
Thus, existence and non-existence are non-dual; for this reason, it is said that they are an illusion.

Furthermore, a verse states: "Non-existence is not non-existence, and that which is not non-existence is existence. Since non-existence and existence are non-dual, it is therefore called an illusion."
This verse clarifies that illusory phenomena are non-existent yet existent.
Why is this? They are non-existent because those illusory phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), owing to the absence of any substantial reality.
Yet it exists; that is to say, illusory phenomena are not without substance, because they manifest as images.
Thus, non-substantiality and substantiality are non-dual; for this reason, they are said to be illusions.
This illusion is a metaphor for the aggregates; therefore, one should know that false discrimination exists yet is non-existent. Why is this?
Because although those two images appear, their substantial reality cannot be apprehended; thus, it is said that the substance of form and so forth is itself without substance.
Furthermore, false discrimination exists though it does not exist.

Why is this? Because those two are entirely devoid of substantial reality, yet there is the manifestation of their reflections; therefore, it is said that form and the like are non-dual in being both without substance and with substance.
Because existence and non-existence are non-dual, one is able to refute both reification and denial, as well as the inclination toward the quiescence of the Hīnayāna.
Why is this so? Because there is no intrinsic nature, and since one knows there is no intrinsic nature, one should not establish any [ontological] position.
Because there is substantiality and because one knows the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one should not engage in disparagement.
Furthermore, since those two are non-different, one should not become weary of substantiality and enter the lesser nirvāṇa.
That verse further states: "The illusory image and the grasping of the illusion are said to be two due to delusion;
likewise, although those two do not exist, the two are perceived.
The skeletal image and the grasping of the skeleton are also said to be two through contemplation."
"Though non-dual, it is spoken of as dual; that which is apprehended is likewise so.
The meaning of the preceding verse is this:
deluded persons, regarding both the illusory image and the grasping of the illusion, speak of the existence of two things—the grasper and the grasped—due to their delusion.
Although those two do not exist, they are perceived because they appear through delusion.
The meaning of the subsequent verse is as follows:

it is the same for the practitioner; regarding the skeletal image and the grasping of the skeleton, it is said that there are the two things—the subject that observes and the object observed—by virtue of contemplation.
Although those two do not exist, the two can still be apprehended because they appear through observation.
Question: Having observed in this manner, what phenomenon serves as the object to be remedied?

Therefore, he further spoke two verses, saying: "One should know the nature of that which is to be remedied; namely, the delusive characteristics of those phenomena. Such a nature, whether existent or non-existent, is neither real nor unreal, like a magical illusion."

"One should know that the entities which serve as the remedies—such as the applications of mindfulness and other dharmas—are likewise without intrinsic characteristics; they are like illusions, and so too is this [reality].
The meaning of the preceding verse is:
"What is the entity that is to be remedied?"
This is precisely delusion regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Delusion regarding the characteristics of phenomena means that [one perceives] such-and-such an essence.
However, such an essence can be said to exist by virtue of false conceptualization (*abhūtaparikalpa*).
It is also said that they do not exist, because the two entities of grasper and grasped are no different from non-existence.
Thus, existence is like an illusion and non-existence is also like an illusion; therefore, this characteristic is said to be like an illusion.
The meaning of the subsequent verse is as follows:

The essence of that which is capable of counteracting [afflictions] is precisely all phenomena—namely, the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth taught by the Buddha—because they possess such and such an essence.
That essence, too, is entirely like an illusion.
Why is this? Because it exists as such and has such an essence as it is grasped by ordinary worldlings;
yet, as the Buddhas have taught, it lacks such an essence as it is thus and thus, and thus its essence is without marks.

Furthermore, although the Buddha, the World-Honored One, manifests entering the womb, being born, leaving the city, renouncing the world, and attaining equal and perfect enlightenment, these appear as reflections despite being devoid of marks; therefore, he is like an illusion.
Question: If all phenomena are equally like illusions, for what reason is one [phenomenon] the antidote and another the object to be remedied?
The verse answers: "Just as a powerful illusory master causes other illusory kings to retreat."
"By means of such pure dharmas, one is able to bring the defiled dharmas to an end. For this reason,
although a Bodhisattva cultivates all manner of practices...
Yet there is nothing to be attained.

That treatise clarifies the observation of the aggregates and the ālayavijñāna, understanding their intrinsic nature to be like an illusion; this most closely accords with the present sutra, and therefore it is set forth in full.
One should know that mirages, shadows, echoes, fire-wheels, and the city of the Gandharvas should also be explained extensively in this same manner.

Although the five metaphors of the preceding section included foam, bubbles, and plantain trees, they are not discussed here because these three things still involve the analysis of constituent parts (*dharmapravicaya*) to clarify the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

However, the intended meaning of the metaphors of illusions, mirages, and so forth herein is to clarify the emptiness of the reality of consciousness-only, which is difficult to comprehend; since this refers to the transformation and dissolution of coarse characteristics, it is not discussed here.
The practitioner understands that all aggregates are mind-only; this is precisely knowing the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena.
When one has not yet realized such an intrinsic nature, because of the fear of falling into the attainment of something existent, one cannot contemplate existence according to the ultimate principle;
and because of the fear of falling into nihilistic annihilation, one cannot contemplate emptiness according to the ultimate principle.
It is not merely that one has failed to see existence clearly, nor is it that one’s vision of emptiness remains incomplete.

Now, by means of gates such as "illusion-like," one illuminates the non-duality of existence and emptiness; yet even the marks of the two kinds of emptiness—of persons and phenomena—are no longer to be grasped by the mind. This is called truly entering the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), for one thereby awakens to the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*).
The Sūtra says: "O Lord of Mysteries!
Thus abandoning selflessness, the sovereign of the mind attains mastery and realizes that one's own mind is fundamentally unarisen.
The "sovereign of the mind" is the *cittarāja* (mind-king).

Because one does not stagnate in existence or non-existence, the mind is free from obstruction; thus, the wondrous activities one undertakes can be accomplished according to one's will, and for this reason it is said that the "Mind-King is Sovereign.
That the Mind-King is sovereign clarifies that this is precisely the pure *bodhicitta*.
Furthermore, there is another turning that clarifies and illuminates even more excellently than the previous kalpa.
The mind-king is like the water in a pond, pure by nature from the beginning.
The purification of mental factors is like the clearing away of adventitious dust.
Therefore, when one realizes this nature of purity, one is immediately able to self-awaken to the fact that the mind is fundamentally unborn. Why is this?
Because the mind cannot be apprehended at either its prior or subsequent limits.
For example, the waves of the great ocean arise from conditions; therefore, they are not non-existent before and non-existent after.
Yet the nature of water is not like this: when waves arise from conditions, the nature of water is not non-existent beforehand;
when the causes and conditions for the waves cease, the nature of water is not non-existent afterward.
The mind-king is also like this: it has no prior or posterior limits, because those limits have been severed.
Although it encounters the winds of objects and arises or ceases according to conditions, the nature of the mind is eternally without arising or ceasing.
To realize that this mind is fundamentally unarisen is to gradually enter the gateway of the letter A.
At that time, one further abandons the subtle, false attachments—one layer of dust-like afflictions numbering one hundred and sixty minds and so forth—known as the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
Therefore, a sutra states: "To know the nature of one's own mind is the practice of a *yogin* that transcends two kalpas.

Regarding the meanings herein—such as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the causes and conditions of birth and death, and the arising of aspiration—these are explained in detail in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, and the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*.
For now, I shall clarify the essential tenets and therefore do not explain them in detail.

Nevertheless, having traced the origin and examined the conclusion above, from the initial arousal of even a hair’s breadth of goodness up to the transcendence of the two obstacles of persons and dharmas—whether existent or non-existent—though the ultimate principle has been brilliantly manifest, becoming increasingly subtle and profound, it remains merely a remedy for the defilements external to the mind; it has yet to reveal the various inconceivable secrets within this very mind, which will only be explained from here on.
If one does not provide such a clarification, then ordinary people will each cling to their prior habits and will be unable to perceive its subtlety.
As the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, Guhyakādhipati!"

The statement, "The Bodhisattvas who practice the Bodhisattva path through the gateway of mantras have accumulated immeasurable merit and wisdom over countless, innumerable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas; having fully cultivated all practices with immeasurable wisdom and skillful means, they have achieved complete perfection," is intended to clarify the mind that transcends the third kalpa.
It should be understood that this is merely a preliminary praise of his merits so that those who see or hear of him may have faith, joy, and respect.

It is like other teachings concerning bodhisattvas who practice the path of skillful means as an antidote, gradually removing the defilements of the mind over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, some of whom attain enlightenment while others do not.
Now, this teaching for bodhisattvas is not like that; they take the mantra itself as their vehicle and directly enter the gate of the pure bodhicitta.
When one perceives this path of the heart-mantra (cittavidyā), the merit and wisdom cultivated by bodhisattvas over countless eons are spontaneously perfected.
For example, suppose there is a person who travels by boat or carriage across difficult and perilous paths for five hundred yojanas to reach their destination.

Then there is another person who flies directly through the air by means of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). Although the route traversed and the place reached are no different, the vehicles used are distinct.

Furthermore, the reason the World-Honored One previously explained the various characteristics of the mind in detail as above was to instruct practitioners of the Mantra-gate: when they reach such a state, they must clearly recognize it; they must not claim to have reached it before they have, thereby lingering midway.
Furthermore, just as when the crown prince of a wheel-turning monarch is first born, he is endowed with all the marks in their entirety without any deficiency;
although he is not yet able to master all the arts or govern the four continents, he is already capable of upholding the seven treasures and accomplishing the noble householder’s lineage.
Why is this? Because he is the very embodiment of the Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin).

It is likewise for the practitioner of mantra when first entering the pure bodhicitta: although they have not yet fulfilled the myriad practices of Samantabhadra or perfected the skillful means of great compassion over countless asaṃkhyeya kalpas, all such Tathāgata qualities are already accomplished within them.
Why is this? It is because he is the very embodiment of the Dharmakāya of Vairocana.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas, [he] has fully accomplished all wisdom and skillful means."
Furthermore, just as a prince at birth is already venerated and sought after by dragons, spirits, and the common people, so too is it with the initial arousal of the pure bodhicitta;
it serves as a great refuge for those in the world of devas and humans who have lost their way on the right path.
According to what is elucidated in the various conventional treatises, when this mind is realized, one is immediately named a Buddha.
Therefore, Śāriputra and all other śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, even by exhausting the power of their intellectual faculties, are unable to fathom it.
The Sūtra states: "That which is called transcending all stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

This is because when the practitioner attains this mind, they immediately know that the pure land of Śākyamuni is not destroyed, they perceive the Buddha’s lifespan as vast and long, and they see their own original bodies together with the Bodhisattvas such as Viśiṣṭacāritra and others who have leaped forth from the earth, all assembled in one place.

Although those who cultivate the path of antidotes may stand in proximity to the stage of the successor to the Buddha, they do not recognize even a single person; therefore, this matter is called "secret.

Furthermore, while within a mind of ultimate purity, these Bodhisattvas can universally assemble all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-realm in the ten directions, and they themselves can personally travel everywhere throughout the ten directions to make offerings to spiritual friends and inquire after the True Dharma; yet, they alone understand this clearly, while gods and humans alike are unable to know it.
For this reason, it is further called "esoteric.

Although during the first two kalpas it was said that they had transcended the stages of the Two Vehicles, and although Subhūti and others were able, through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, to expound extensively upon the emptiness of both persons and phenomena, they nevertheless felt shock and doubt regarding this esoteric One Vehicle, not knowing where it was headed. This is precisely what is meant by "directly passing beyond the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas."

At that time, the gods of great majesty and virtue, unable to perceive the locus upon which the Bodhisattva’s mind relied, all gave rise to reverent faith; thus Śakra Devānām Indra made this vow, saying:
"This Superior Person shall before long attain Buddhahood."
"If he attains Buddhahood, I shall offer auspicious grass.
The Four Heavenly Kings also gave rise to this thought, saying:
"When this Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, we shall present him with an alms bowl."
The Brahma King also gave rise to this thought:
"When this Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, I shall request him to turn the wheel of Dharma.
Therefore, it is said that he approaches and pays homage.
Having concluded the praise of the merits of entering the gateway of mantras, one might ask:
by what further method does the practitioner enter this gateway?
Therefore, the sutra continues: "That is to say, emptiness."
Emptiness is the very nature of one's own mind, which is equal to space.
The aforementioned passage from "immeasurable like space" up to "the manifestation of perfect enlightenment" is a metaphor for this mind.

In previous kalpas, I realized that all phenomena are mind-only and that there are no phenomena external to the mind; now, I observe that this very mind is the Tathāgata’s spontaneous wisdom, and it is also the Vairocana-body pervading all things.
Because the mind is thus, all phenomena are also thus.
Since both the sense faculties and their objects enter the gateway of the letter A, it is said that they are "detached from faculties and objects.
Because reflected images do not emerge from the light of eternal quiescence, they are said to be "without marks" (animitta).

By means of the wisdom that realizes the true mark of the mind, one awakens to the true mark of the mind; since both object and wisdom are *prajñāpāramitā*, it is said that there is "no objective realm.

When these ten metaphors within this context are compared to the preceding ten metaphors, they further constitute conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); therefore, it is said that one "transcends all conceptual proliferations."

In the third stage, the one hundred and sixty subtle mental states are eliminated, along with the seeds of afflictions, karma, and lifespan; thereupon, the sprouts of the Buddha-tree arise. Therefore, it is said: "All Buddha-dharmas are equal to space and boundless."

Arising in dependence upon this continuity, one enters the *dharmadhātu* without destroying causes and conditions; likewise, not moving from the *dharmadhātu* is itself dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

One should know that the arising and ceasing of causes and conditions is the arising and ceasing of the *dharmadhātu*, and the non-arising and non-ceasing of the *dharmadhātu* is the non-arising and non-ceasing of causes and conditions. Therefore, it is said: "Transcending the realms of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)."
Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, all phenomena abide as such by their very nature; therefore, it is said that they are "free from all conditioned activity.
As stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā*: "All phenomena tend toward the eye; they do not transcend this tendency."
It is just as the hundred rivers flow toward the sea and have nowhere else to go.
Therefore, you should know that the eye is itself the primary limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Within this primary limit of reality, even the eye cannot be apprehended; how much less, then, can there be going or not-going?
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; therefore, it is said: "one is detached from the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

When a practitioner attains such subtle wisdom, they observe that all defiled and pure phenomena, down to even the smallest fraction, are like atoms (*paramāṇu*), none of which do not arise from conditions.

If that which arises from conditions lacks intrinsic nature, then that which lacks intrinsic nature is fundamentally unarisen; that which is fundamentally unarisen is the limit of reality of the mind (*cittasya bhūtakoṭi*), and even this limit of reality of the mind cannot be apprehended. Therefore, it is said: "The mind arises as the ultimate absence of intrinsic nature."
Viewed in relation to the preceding two stages, this mind is like a lotus in full bloom;

viewed in relation to the subsequent two states of mind, it is as if the fruit has returned to become a seed. Therefore, it is said: "Such an initial mind is taught by the Buddha to be the cause for attaining Buddhahood; thus, while it is liberated from karma and afflictions, it nonetheless fully relies upon karma and afflictions."
Regarding the phrase "spoken by the Buddha" herein, the World-Honored One takes the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time as witnesses.
He states that through this one causal condition, he opens up pure knowledge and vision for sentient beings; thus, his Way is mysteriously identical [to theirs].

When the practitioner is liberated from all karma and afflictions, they immediately realize that there is no karma or affliction that is not the Buddha’s work; since these were originally non-existent as bonds, whom could one possibly liberate?

Just as a skilled physician transforms poison into medicine to eliminate all ailments, and just as space transcends all characteristics yet serves as the basis for all phenomena, when one dwells in this inconceivable liberation, one is a true Arhat;
unattached to the conditioned or the unconditioned, such a person deserves vast offerings from all the world.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The world honors and reveres him; one should always make offerings to him.

Furthermore, because the Ācārya wishes to clarify that he should be so honored, he provides a comprehensive discourse on the beginning and end of the three kalpas, employing the analogy of a precious jewel.
It is like a wish-fulfilling jewel that lies within a stone ore; because worldly people do not recognize it, they discard it upon the road, no different from common rubble.
However, one who discerns precious gems perceives even a subtle sign; as soon as a mere reflection appears externally, they recognize it. First, they use sharp iron to grind away the dull stone.

Once they are near the king of jewels, the stone gradually softens; they then consume it with various medicinal herbs so that the impurities of the ore are digested, yet without damaging its essential substance.

At that time, although the coarse impurities have been removed, there still remain subtle impurities; having already washed it with alkaline water and polished it with clean cloth, one brings it to brilliance through various skillful means.
Once it has been brought forth and displayed, it is placed upon a high banner; it can universally rain down all manner of objects according to every request.

At that time, the people of the world conceive a sense of wonder and marvel, honoring this treasure as they would the Great Deity (Mahādeva), because it is able to fulfill all their hopes and aspirations.
Yet this jewel, at a single moment, universally accords with the minds of the multitude; according to what each obtains, there are various differences.
Now, were these various objects already present within the jewel beforehand?
Did they not exist previously?
If they existed previously, how could this small pearl suddenly contain so many objects?
If they did not exist previously, how could it suddenly rain down so many objects?
If even the nature of jewels in this world is already inconceivable, how much more so the jewel of the bodhicitta of sentient beings?

Therefore, as soon as spiritual friends perceive the eight worldly concerns beginning to stir within sentient beings, they immediately recognize them as true jewels, knowing that there is the principle of being able to excavate them.
Just as one who has frequently perceived a particular mark recognizes it as a treasure upon encountering it, so too it is with the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
having long since realized and known that they have personally attained the path of Great Enlightenment through even a single hair’s breadth of goodness.

Therefore, perceiving their mental dispositions, he rejoices greatly and employs skillful means to guide them forward so that they may receive the Three Refuges, as has already been explained in detail.

It is like taking a piece of stubborn stone home and, next, using three kinds of "three-minds" to uproot the roots of karma and afflictions—the seeds of ignorance—just as one uses sharp iron to excavate and remove the coarse ore.
Next, one contemplates the selflessness of phenomena within the vehicle of non-referentiality, like gradually reaching a soft spot to digest it with medicinal substances without causing injury.
Next, one gives rise to the mind of ultimate lack of intrinsic nature, like polishing it with ash and water until it is extremely radiant and pure.
At that time, being born into the family of the Buddha is called "placing [the child] upon a high banner and raining down various jewels.
For this reason, one is worthy of receiving the vast offerings renowned throughout the world.
If a practitioner directly perceives the jewel of the mind through the gateway of mantras— just as a seer skilled in incantations uses supernatural power to retrieve it—
then although there may be differences in skill versus clumsiness or ease versus difficulty, there is ultimately no different path for obtaining the jewel.

Therefore, this sutra extensively elucidates the characteristics of the mind from the shallow to the profound, all for the purpose of revealing the fundamental and derivative causes and conditions of bodhicitta.
If one were to rely merely on the conventional *dharmalakṣaṇa* (characteristics of phenomena), one could not say: "I now fully reveal and expand upon the great secrets of all Buddhas."
The scripture states: "O Lord of Mysteries!

On the stages of faith, understanding, and practice, one contemplates the three minds; through the wisdom of the immeasurable pāramitās, one contemplates the four means of integration (saṃgrahavastu). On the stage of faith and understanding, there is the immeasurable and inconceivable state beyond opposition; therein, the ten minds are established and boundless wisdom arises. This is the core tenet of this sutra.

From the pure bodhicitta upward through the ten stages (bhūmi), all are practices within the sphere of faith and understanding; only the Tathāgata is named the ultimate stage of omniscience (sarvajñatā-bhūmi).

As stated in the *Avataṃsaka*, a Bodhisattva of the first stage is able to believe in the entry into the original practices of the Tathāgata; believe in the accomplishment of the various pāramitās; believe in the entry into the various supreme stages; believe in the accomplishment of the powers; believe in the fulfillment of the fearlessnesses; believe in the growth of the indestructible, unshared Buddha-dharmas; believe in the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas; believe in the emergence of the Buddha-realm without center or periphery; believe in the successive entry into the immeasurable realms of the Tathāgata; and believe in the accomplishment of the fruit. Regarding such matters, their mind is ultimately indestructible and no longer turns according to other conditions; therefore, it is called the Stage of Practice through Resolute Belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), and is also called the Stage of Reaching Cultivation.
To observe the three minds is precisely the causal root of the ultimate mind.

If discussed in general terms regarding the stage of faith and understanding (*śraddhābhūmi*), it refers to when a Bodhisattva of the first stage attains this space-like, stainless bodhicitta; at that time, they spontaneously give rise to ten great vows within the ten inexhaustible realms, eventually fulfilling millions of *asaṃkhyeya* great vows. Thus, this bodhicitta serves as the cause.

From the second stage onward, the further cultivation of the ten thousand practices of great compassion constitutes inexhaustible great vows; these take root within the ten dharma realms and gradually increase until they reach full maturity.
From the eighth stage onward, all are termed the Stage of Expedient Means (*upāya-bhūmi*).
The *Buddha-nature Treatise* (*Foxing lun*) states: "The realms from the eighth stage upward are identical; it is merely that they are designated as descending stages based on expedient means."
If one contemplates each individual stage (*bhūmi*), there are likewise three minds within it.
For example, when one enters the first stage by means of many sets of ten causal conditions, these are termed "causal conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Once firmly established, one purifies this stage through various practices of the ten thousand deeds of great compassion; this is called the "Root.
To explain the characteristics of the fruit of purifying the stage and its skillful means is called the "Ultimate."
All other matters should be understood accordingly.
In this sutra, the immeasurable *pāramitās* and the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) constitute the stage of "purifying the ground" (*bhūmi-śodhana*).

From this point onward, the practitioner is free from all relative opposition and transcends the stage of the inconceivable mental measure (*cittamātra*). Therein, ten minds and boundless wisdom arise; this is the fruit-phase of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).

The *Avataṃsaka* states: "Having made the ten great vows, one then attains a beneficial mind, a supple mind, a compliant mind, a tranquil mind, a disciplined mind, a mind of cessation, a humble mind, a moistening mind, an immovable mind, and an unclouded mind."

Next, one further accomplishes ten kinds of dharmas that purify the stages (*bhūmi*), namely: faith, loving-kindness, compassion, equanimity, and tirelessness; knowledge of the various sūtras and śāstras; skillful understanding of worldly dharmas; a sense of shame and dread of blame; firm causal power; making offerings to all Buddhas; and practicing in accordance with the teachings.

Furthermore, having dwelled in this stage, one thoroughly understands the obstacles of the various stages; thoroughly understands the formation and destruction of the stages; thoroughly understands the characteristics and fruits of the stages; thoroughly understands the attainment and cultivation of the stages; thoroughly understands the purification of the dharmas of the stages; thoroughly understands the transition and progression through the stages; thoroughly understands what is possible and impossible regarding each stage; thoroughly understands the superior wisdom of each stage; thoroughly understands the non-retrogression of each stage; and thoroughly understands the purification of all bodhisattva stages, up to and including the entry into the stage of a Tathāgata.

There are many such sets of ten mental states; if they were to be analyzed in detail, there would be millions of asaṃkhyeya gateways of liberation. Therefore, it is said that "boundless wisdom arises."
Furthermore, based on the preceding three minds, they are explained as ten minds.
If discussed generally regarding the stage of faith and understanding (*śraddhā-vimukti-bhūmi*), then the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) serves as the seed;
the second stage serves as the sprout.
The third stage is the bud;
the fourth stage is the leaf;
the fifth stage is the flower.
The sixth stage is the fruit;
the seventh stage is the seed for enjoyment;
and the eighth stage is the basis of fearlessness, which is the fruit among fruits.
In the ninth stage (*bhūmi*), there arises the wisdom that seeks advancement toward the Buddha-stage; this is the most excellent mind.
In the tenth stage, this mind becomes definitive.
These two minds have no distinct objective sphere; they are merely differentiated from the eighth mind through the transformation of skillful means.
If within each and every stage (*bhūmi*), one likewise possesses these ten mental states in their entirety—

for instance, when abiding in the first stage, accomplishing the purification of the dharmas of all stages and knowing the characteristics of all stages— this constitutes having first completed the understanding of one stage.
Taking this as the cause, wisdom increases and one further understands the second stage (*dvitīyā bhūmiḥ*).
This can be known by inferring through the categories of the ten mental states.
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* contains numerous sets of ten dharma-gates; these should likewise be extensively analyzed and explained according to this sequence.
However, the central tenet of this scripture is that one enters the adamantine treasure-store from the very first stage (*bhūmi*).
According to the oral transmission of the Ācārya, every single term in the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* must be interpreted in two ways:
first, the shallow and exoteric interpretation; second, the profound and esoteric interpretation.

If one does not penetrate such secret designations and merely explains them according to the literal text, then the causal phenomena will pertain to the "Chapter on the Ten Abodes" (*Daśabhūmika*). However,
if one understands the generation of the sixteen great bodhisattvas of the *Vajraśekhara*,
one shall naturally realize and know it for oneself.

As for the statement in the sutra, "All that I have spoken is obtained by relying upon this," it refers to the aforementioned realm of the inexhaustible adornments of the stage of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*), as well as other immeasurable sūtras; there is no fruit of all practices praised by the Buddha that is not obtained through this. Therefore, other sūtras extensively praise the trunk, leaves, flowers, and fruits of the king of śāla trees in this manner.

In this sutra, only the seeds of this king of trees and the causes and conditions for their growth and birth are clarified; it is impossible that such a fruit could be produced apart from these causes and conditions.
Is it not for this reason that the *Mahāvairocana Sūtra* is called the King of Sūtras?

Furthermore, the sūtra raises further benefits to encourage practice, saying: "Therefore, the wise should contemplate this stage of faith and understanding of omniscience, and further transcend all others to ascend and abide in this stage."

This is precisely the initial entry into this stage of the Ground of Resolute Belief (*adhimukti-bhūmi*); furthermore, by transcending one layer of subtle afflictions consisting of one hundred and sixty mental states, it is called "crossing over the three great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*."

When the practitioner first contemplates emptiness, they realize that all phenomena enter the ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi) of the mind; looking downward, they see no sentient beings to be delivered, and looking upward, they see no Buddhas to be sought. At that time, the myriad practices come to rest, which is termed the ultimate.

If one abides in this state, one neither regresses to fall into the stages of the two vehicles nor advances to attain the stages of the higher Bodhisattvas; this is called the arising of attachment to dharmas, and it is also termed an indeterminate mind.

Nevertheless, through the power of the bodhicitta and the sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgatas, one is further able to give rise to compassionate vows; at that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions simultaneously appear before one and exhort them.
Because of receiving the Buddha’s instruction, one gives rise to a mind of ultimate selflessness, such that even the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the mind cannot be apprehended.
Although one is liberated from all karma and afflictions (*kleśa*), karma and afflictions nevertheless remain fully present.
Upon reaching this inconceivable stage, it is called the true stage of being detached from the two vehicles.
Within the meaning of the preceding three phrases, the Buddha-stage is further opened as the supreme expedient mind.
Upon reaching this fourth mental state, it is called the ultimate stage of all-knowledge; therefore, it is said that "this one-quarter transcends the stage of faith and understanding."
Commentary on the Mahāvairocana Sūtra, Scroll Two;
Commentary on the Mahāvairocana Sūtra, Scroll Three;
Recorded by the Śramaṇa Aśāri Yixing.
The remainder of the "Chapter on Abiding in the Mind upon Entering the Mantra Gate" states:
At that time, Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"May the Savior of the World expound the characteristics of the mind.

How many kinds of grounds for fearlessness do Bodhisattvas attain, up to the attainment of fearlessness regarding the equality of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena?"—this is likewise an answer to the preceding statement concerning the characteristics of the mind.

Since Vajrapāṇi had heard this teaching that bodhisattvas directly ascend to the bodhisattva stages via the gateway of mantras, he asked the Bhagavān: "When these bodhisattvas practice this path, how many kinds of grounds for fearlessness are there?"
The Buddha again refers back to the three preceding kalpas to provide a comparative explanation.
The Sanskrit term *aśvāsa* should be correctly translated as "revival" (*suxi*).

It is like a person who, when seized by a powerful assailant, has his throat constricted and his breath cut off until he is on the verge of fainting, yet suddenly receives release and returns to life.
