As for the statement in the Sūtra, "First, one should prostrate to all Tathāgatas and awaken the Earth Deity with these verses," it means that when the Ācārya is about to awaken the Earth Deity, he first directs his mind to contemplate the body of Vairocana, which is adorned with inexhaustible ornaments and pervades the entire Dharma-realm; all Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the three periods of time are likewise so, each possessing an inexhaustibly adorned body that pervades the Dharma-realm.

From the ten stages of abiding up to the first stage, the Bodhisattvas possess partially realized bodies of adornment that are immeasurable and boundless, filling the Dharma-realm without any gaps, like oil within sesame seeds.
One should contemplate this body as reaching before all the holy ones and perform prostrations with utmost sincerity through the three purified karmas.

By virtue of these causes and conditions, one shall obtain immeasurable merit; one should then, with an unerring mind, bestow it upon those disciples, making the vow that they may quickly achieve unsurpassed bodhi without hindrance or difficulty. Next, one should recite a verse to awaken the earth deities.
For example, when Śākyamuni Buddha first sat at the site of enlightenment, he said to Māra:
"Because you practiced the gift of inexhaustibility in a previous life, you have now attained this body as the Lord of the Devas."

"However, since immeasurable kalpas past, I have practiced such great acts of giving in incalculable numbers; even my own flesh, hands, and feet I have not begrudged. How can you compare me with him and determine our relative superiority?"
The Māra said:
"As for the merit I have performed, you have already served as its witness.
But who shall bear witness to your own meritorious deeds?"
"If there were no witness, you would fall into defeat.
At that time, the Bodhisattva extended his right hand and pointed toward the earth, speaking these words of truth:
"In the past, I practiced the path of the Bodhisattva upon this very ground, performing various difficult and ascetic practices; the Earth Deity bears witness to this."
"You should know that this finger is itself the Body Secret Seal (*kāyaguhyamudrā*).
At that time, immeasurable earth deities emerged from the ground, manifesting their upper bodies to bear witness; consequently, the hosts of Māra’s army retreated and dispersed."

Now, because the Ācārya wishes to cause his disciple to succeed to the rank of the Tathāgata before long, he likewise uses this seal to awaken the Earth Goddess. At that time, the Earth Goddess gives rise to great joy and reflects:
"This Son of the Buddha is now able to establish the causal conditions for a great undertaking; it is to protect us and ensure we suffer no harm or affliction that he has awakened us."
"I shall employ skillful means to protect it and cause it to be free from all demonic activities.
By the power of these various conditions, he immediately caused this earth to become identical to vajra.
The Āryā verses that have been explained are known as spontaneously accomplished mantras (*svayambhū-siddha-mantra*).
When performing ritual acts, one should recite them in their original Sanskrit; they are now recorded here in full.
Recite this seven times, pressing the five fingers of the right hand against the ground:

*Tadyathā | Oṃ gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā*. Translation: "O you who are the protector of the celestial kin (*devatā-jñāti-rakṣaka*)," with the word *at* (the syllable *a*) entering into the following phrase.
“Samantabuddhānām” means “of all Buddhas”; “śāstṝṇām” means “of the Teachers,” which carries the sense of being a guide. Translated, it reads:
“Of all the Buddhas, the Teachers.”
"Jalaye caryāye viśeṣeṇa" is translated as: "The excellence of practice."
"Bhūmi" means "pure ground," "pāramitā" means "reaching the other shore," and "sūtra" means "equality. The translation states:
the meaning of "pure ground" (bhūmi) and "perfection" (pāramitā) is combined with the word "equality" (sūtra).
“Māra-tama-ya-se-niun-yung-ya-tha-zhu-ya-hao-ke-nan-po. Translated as:
“Like destroying the host of Māra’s armies.”
*Śākyasiṃha-jagat-trātā*. Translation: "The Lion of the Śākyas, Savior of the World."
*Tathāgato ’ham māraṃ mārayāmi* (or *māraye*). Translation:
"I, too, shall subdue Māra."
「Maṇḍalale maṇḍala-ālikhya moheṃ yam |」 Translated: "I draw the maṇḍala."
The meaning of the verse is that he first addresses the Earth Goddess, saying:

"O celestial maiden who personally guards this great earth, you have already made offerings to and drawn near all the Buddhas, the Teachers; you have cultivated sublime practices to purify the stages (*bhūmi*), and have fully perfected the perfections (*pāramitā*) and various other virtues."
As extensively clarified through the examination of dharmas in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, it is for this reason that [the text] says "and so forth.

In the present translation, five characters are made into a single verse-line, which cannot preserve [the original] in its entirety; nevertheless, these manifold virtues are already contained within the *bhūmi-pāramitā*.

The following verse expresses the intent of this exhortation: I speak these words of truth. Just as when the World-Honored One was in the Bodhi-maṇḍala and subdued the hosts of Māra, you appeared within that great assembly to act as a witness; for this reason, the World-Honored One is titled the Lion of the Śākyas, who can stride alone without fear to rescue and protect the world.
I now likewise wish to follow the path traversed by the Buddha and succeed to the work of the Tathāgata; for this reason, I have painted this maṇḍala.

Although I have not yet attained everything that is identical to the Tathāgata, by virtue of being empowered by the three secrets of Vairocana, I am also able to manifest the body of a Buddha and universally assemble the great assembly of all maṇḍalas.
Therefore, you should now likewise manifest as a witness, so that the hosts of Māra cannot destroy or corrupt [this rite].

Furthermore, the Earth Goddess is a female deity; "female" (nārī) signifies *samādhi*, which is precisely the *samādhi* of the World-Honored One Vairocana for protecting and sustaining the mind-ground of all sentient beings.

World-Honored One of Suchness, in the past, when you were at the Bodhi-maṇḍala subduing the Māra King of the Dwelling Place of Ignorance and his sands-of-Ganges-like host, you repeatedly extended the five powers with the hand of Prajñāpāramitā to press upon the mental ground of all sentient beings; at that time, your samādhi manifested to act as a witness. Consequently, the four kinds of māra-armies of the immeasurable sentient beings who were to be saved were thereby dispersed and scattered. For this reason, you are named Śāntakarmasiṃha, the one capable of saving the world through sovereign supernormal powers.

I now likewise desire to level and cultivate the minds of my disciples and paint the Great Compassion Maṇḍala; you, too, should act as a witness to this, so that the hosts of the four Māra armies may be subdued.

Furthermore, to explain this by means of the gateway of syllables (*akṣaramukha*): this *ariṣa* possesses immeasurable meanings; yet, if one seeks its ultimate essence, it resides precisely within the other syllable.

In the Sanskrit sound, *tathā* signifies "suchness" (*tathatā*); within the long-drawn-out vowel *ā* of the word *tathā*, the sound *a* is inherently contained, because all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen.
Just as there is neither increase nor decrease regarding the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), one should likewise awaken all the Earth Goddesses through this very principle.

When reciting the verse, one should kneel with both knees touching the ground, extend the five fingers of the wisdom hand with the palms flat against the earth, and only then recite this *āryā* verse.
Seal it once and seven times, and empower it sevenfold; this is what is called the "correspondence of mantra and mudrā. The Ācārya said:

"When one wishes to perform this rite, first empower one's own body with the self-nature of the Samaya-Dharmadhātu-Vajra, as described in the ritual for making offerings. Having purified the ground of the mind and this site of practice by means of the letter-gateway *ra*, within the yoga, first generate a wind-wheel in the shape of a half-moon empowered by the syllable *ha*; next, generate a water-wheel empowered by the syllable *ba*; and next, generate a vajra-ground-wheel empowered by the syllable *a*."

First, one should clearly contemplate with focused attention on the Truths, skillfully regulating the mind and the breath. Recite the gateway of the letter *A* continuously and without interruption for the duration of a single breath; when strength is exhausted and the breath returns, recite it again—whether for one breath or three breaths—until a sensation of awakening or contact is felt.

By means of such skillful methods of single-pointed concentration, one immediately enters samādhi and beholds the great assembly of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas adorned with secrets; alternatively, one may personally perceive the various faults within and without the earth.

Regarding the statement in the Sūtra, "One should make offerings with scented unguents, flowers, and so forth," this is not merely for the purpose of awakening [the deity]; one should also make offerings of various incenses, flowers, lamps, and lights to the Buddhas of the ten directions as well as to the Earth Goddess.

However, within this context, there are three kinds of grounds: namely, purifying one’s own mental ground, the disciple’s mental ground, and the ground of the path through the syllable-gateway *ra*; all of these are sustained by the syllable-gateway *a* to be rendered adamantine (*vajra*).
If one explains the meaning of offering according to the secret interpretation, it is likewise so.

If the ācārya dedicates the various merits of the pure bodhicitta to the seal of the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñājñāna*), this is itself an offering to all Buddhas and the holders of the ground within his own dharmadhātu.

Dedicate these merits to the disciple to assist in the causes and conditions for attaining Buddhahood; this is equivalent to making offerings to all Buddhas and the Earth-Holders within the mind-dharmadhātu of the disciple.
If one uses these to adorn this vajra-maṇḍala, it is equivalent to making a Dharma-offering to all Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Having made the offering, one should further take refuge in all Tathāgatas.
This can be understood through the illustrative explanation.
As the Sūtra says: "Thereafter, one prepares the ground;

according to the proper sequence, one shall be endowed with all virtues. This means that whenever one wishes to construct a maṇḍala, one must first perform such rites before proceeding to excavate and select the site for treatment.

It also encompasses the threefold meaning of the stages (*bhūmi*) through both exoteric and esoteric interpretations; furthermore, as it is taught in the sūtras, it possesses all constituent parts in their proper sequence, and is therefore said to "be endowed with all virtues."

At that time, Vajrapāṇi, desiring to elucidate the profound and secret intent of the Tathāgata and to sever the doubts of future disciples, prostrated his head at the feet of the World-Honored One and spoke in verse:

"The Buddha-dharma is free from all marks, even not conforming to the path of suchness (*dharmatā*). This means that I have personally heard from the Buddha that the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena is far removed from all marks; it is the abode of the Dharma-Buddha, dwelling in the station of the Dharma.

Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, it is eternally quiescent and inconceivable; it is beyond the reach of thought or discrimination, and cannot be expressed through inference, measurement, or analogy.
If the characteristics of phenomena were eternally thus, they could not be produced by any Buddha, much less could the various characteristics of conditioned things be accumulated.

For what reason, then, does the Greatly Valiant One, the God among Gods, now teach these conditioned matters such as selecting the site and constructing the mandala, as well as the sequential practices of mantras, so that practitioners may prepare various incenses, flowers, and offerings; engage in verbal discourse according to their mental observation and reflection; train in physical mudrās and dignified deportment; and direct the mind toward the color, appearance, form, and position of the *iṣṭadevatā*?
Since these are conditioned and possess characteristics, how can they truly accord with the unconditioned and signless path that is the very nature of reality?
We only pray that the World-Honored One will reveal the profound meaning herein, so as to eliminate the world’s deluded attachments to words and sentiments of doubt and slander.
From "At that time, the Bhagavat" onwards, the World-Honored One answers in verse.

Regarding the initial statement, "Listen well to the characteristics of dharmas," it is because the meaning of the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is extremely profound and difficult to perceive; therefore, he exhorts them to listen attentively.

Now, the Dharma is eternally without intrinsic nature; arising from a multitude of conditions, it is precisely the characteristic of the eight consciousnesses, transcending all conceptual proliferation.
Where else would you seek the signless and unconditioned Dharma?
Therefore, the subsequent verse states: “The Dharma is free from discrimination and all conceptual constructions,” and so forth.

If one realizes that all phenomena are fundamentally without marks in this way, then one perceives the true nature of the mind, which has been eternally unborn from the very beginning. At that time, all actions of body, speech, and mind are like space and are inexhaustible; hence it is said: “I have attained supreme perfect enlightenment, ultimately like space.”

However, because all ignorant, childish, and ordinary worldlings do not know things as they truly are, they falsely and erroneously cling to various objects, namely "time," "direction," "various characteristics," and so forth.
"Enveloped by the ignorance of craving": they are constantly moistened by the waters of craving and shrouded by ignorance.
If I were to abandon skillful means and directly preach such a Dharma of self-realization to sentient beings, how could they possibly understand it or proceed toward liberation?

Therefore, the following verse clarifies the intention behind establishing the teaching, stating: "It is for the sake of delivering those beings that it is taught in accordance with skillful means (*upāya*).
The Buddha’s intent was this:

since the characteristics of the Dharma (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are so profound that they cannot be directly proclaimed, I have relied upon the power of skillful means to entrust them to the constituent parts and requisites of this maṇḍala, so that beginners may find a ground upon which to fix their minds and ensure that their practice is not in vain.

Because he has received the Buddha’s empowerment and has further attained the observation of the ten phrases of dependent origination, he is able to sport with supernatural powers within the unmoving true reality (*dharmatā*). He universally observes all spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and adorns all Buddha-lands. He does not wish to cause practitioners to abandon all practices and dwell in signlessness (*animitta*), nor does he wish to cause them to cling to practices and dwell in the realm of signs (*sanimitta*). Therefore, it is said: "Although one speaks of time, place, and the actions performed, in reality there is no time, no place, no action, and no agent; all those dharmas abide solely in the true reality."
If all conditioned phenomena abide entirely within the true nature of reality (dharmatā), how could one act like that deluded person who either wishes to flee from space or desires to cling to space?
Furthermore, within this context, the Ācārya explains at length the parable of the three vehicles from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Just as that elder’s sons were young and ignorant, and although he exhorted them with various kind words in an attempt to lead them out of the fire, he was ultimately unable to do so.
At that time, the elder observed that the boy’s deep inclination was fixed solely upon play; he then employed a skillful means and said to him:
"Outside this gate, there are three kinds of exquisite chariots."
"You all should go and take them; you may enjoy yourselves as you please.

At that time, because those sons heard the name of "play" and it suited their wishes, their hearts were filled with vigor and they rushed out in competition. Yet, when they obtained the jewel-adorned vehicles, the most magnificent of all, it was not what their original intentions had envisioned.

This maṇḍala dharma-gate is likewise so: the Tathāgata employs the causal conditions, phenomena, and characteristics of the world as models and metaphors to illustrate the inconceivable dharma-realm, thereby reaching down to accommodate the various capacities of sentient beings.
If one can take up this practice, one will be able to cultivate with courageous progress through universal gateways of faith and understanding.

Furthermore, when one receives the empowerment of the Three Mysteries and personally perceives the path of the luminous mind, one will realize that all various names and phrases are the secret names of the Tathāgata; this is not something that can be conceived by ordinary sentiments.

To say that "reciting for three months" refers merely to a ninety-day period is a misunderstanding; it actually represents the threefold expedient means within the inherently pure and perfectly luminous state.

How could it be interpreted as nothing more than a span of ninety days? Furthermore, the Buddha Ratnaketu of the East signifies the initial arousal of the pure bodhicitta; how could he be understood as merely representing one of the four directions?

By analogy with this, all other dharma-gates may be understood through the mind; therefore it is said: "In reality there is no time or direction, and so forth, until 'dwelling solely in the true mark'."

Furthermore, the World-Honored One’s great compassion is limitless; out of pity for those sentient beings of future ages who possess heavy obstructions and dull faculties and are unable to enter the Dharma-realm instantaneously, he has established within this profound and secret treasury the *parivarta-dhāraṇī* (the revolving dhāraṇī) along with provisional expedients of a shallow and concise nature. By contemplating and practicing within the sphere of phenomenal forms, even the accomplishment of worldly *siddhi* will not be in vain; through the secret support of the three mysteries, one shall ultimately attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
Therefore, the following verse says: "Furthermore, Lord of Mysteries!

In the future age, sentient beings of inferior intelligence, shrouded by delusion and craving, will rely solely upon signs; they will constantly delight in the views of annihilationism and eternalism, and in the signs of good and evil regarding time, place, and actions. Blind and ignorant, they will seek after fruits, not knowing how to understand this path."
"It is for the sake of delivering them that I speak according to skillful means.

Therefore, those who transmit the Dharma should skillfully discern the faculties and conditions of others, as well as understand the specific proportions of the various Dharma gates; they should administer medicine according to the illness, ensuring that the teaching does not miss the capacity of the recipient.
If one were to suddenly explain the profound meaning of emptiness to those who are attached to signs, it would cause them fear and doubt, thereby increasing their lack of faith.

If one were to suddenly bestow shallow and abbreviated teachings upon those of sharp faculties and deep wisdom, they would consider it inconsistent with the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) true path and thus give rise to contempt.

Since it would be of no benefit to others and would further violate one's own samaya, one should first abide in yoga and contemplate the fundamental and derivative causes and conditions of that [question].

Having understood this thoroughly, one should contemplate the intent within these questions and answers to employ skillful means (*upāya*) to reveal the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*). By integrating this into all gates of expedient means (*upāyamukha*) to provide instruction, one will be able to bring great benefit to many; thus, obstacles and difficulties will not arise.
The Sūtra states: "O Lord of Mysteries!

Among the locations thus described, whichever site is selected must be made firm through consecration; one should take *gomaya* and *gomutra* from an unbaked earthen vessel, mix them together, and smear [the ground] with them. Next, purify it by sprinkling with scented water while reciting mantras. As taught therein, whenever a maṇḍala is constructed, it must be completed within seven days.

On the first day, the ācārya should abide in the essential nature of the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana; thereafter, the rites for summoning the Earth Goddess (Pṛthivīdevī) and the expedient means for adorning the body are all as explained in the sequence of the offerings.
Having issued the warning, one should immediately empower the site with the mantra of Acala, and then dig the earth, selecting and preparing it according to the ritual rules.

One should first dig a pit at the center measuring one cubit; once the selection is complete, fill it back in again. If the soil exceeds the original level, it is considered superior ground; if it remains as it was, it is middling; and if it does not reach the original level, it is inferior.

Having thus successively eliminated all defects, he finely refined the excavated earth and filled it back in little by little; moistening it with cow's urine, he tamped it until it was firm and level, as smooth as the palm of a hand.
Next, one should apply a mixture of *gomaya* (cow dung) and *gomutra* (cow urine).
To explain this briefly: these are cow dung and its liquid, used for the sake of purification according to the local customs of that region.
Explaining it according to the secret interpretation: *Gau* has the meaning of "action" (*caryā*); because one enters the gate of the letter *A*, all phenomena are thus without action.
*Ma* has the meaning of "self" (*ātman*), and *I* has the meaning of "vehicle" (*yāna*).
Why are all phenomena without activity?
Because in all phenomena, a self cannot be found.
If there is no self, then there is neither that which is mounted nor a mounter; this is what is called the Mahāyāna.
*Gumuo* (瞿摸) has the same meaning as explained previously.
*Tala* (怛囉) signifies "suchness" (*tathatā*) free from dust and defilement; it is the true mark (*dharmatā*) of the mind.
If a practitioner can thus purify the ground of the mind, they will be ultimately pure and free from all obstacles.

Once the site has been selected and leveled, and its dimensions determined, one should dig a pit at the center of the maṇḍala approximately one cubit deep, using the mantra for accomplishing all tasks.

Consecrate the five jewels, the five grains, and the five medicines and place them therein; the methods for removing impurities and performing exorcisms are all as explained in the *Pūjā-vidhi* (Ritual of Offerings).

If one provides a profound and esoteric interpretation, these are the five jewels of the five wisdoms established within the *bodhicitta*. Because they can give rise to the five kinds of wholesome sprouts and eliminate the five kinds of faults and afflictions, they are called the "five grains" and "five medicines."

Having thus completed the arrangement, one should further smear it with clean plaster to make it perfectly level and even. One should take the consecration vases and fill them with pure water, ensuring they are not overfilled; having inserted various flowers and fruits and placed within them the five jewels, grains, and medicinal herbs, one should set them at the locations where the treasures were buried.

From the third day after the flask has been set out, one should daily recite the Vidyārāja-mantra one hundred and eight times during the three periods of the day to consecrate this flask; thereafter, one may perform other activities.

On the evening of the fourth day, next use the incense-water mantra to consecrate the incense water, either one hundred and eight times or up to one thousand times, and then sprinkle it for purification.
The mantra is as follows:
"Namaḥ samantabuddhānām apratihata-same gagaṇa-same samantānugate prākṛti-viśodhani dharmadhātu-viśodhani svāhā. The first phrase is the universal homage to all Buddhas.

Just as the three bodies of Vairocana pervade all places, so too do all Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the three periods of time; having now universally taken refuge in them all with a universal mind, one then recites this mantra, desiring that these World-Honored Ones not transgress their original vows, and thus collectively empower it to serve as a witness.
The same applies to all subsequent mantras, so they will not be explained in detail here.

Regarding the second phrase, the initial letter *A* serves as the essence of the mantra, which is to say, it is the seed-syllable (*bīja*). All other letter-gates serve merely to adorn this syllable, for this letter-gate is the very source of the bodhicitta.

Now, regarding this Maṇḍala King Born from the Treasury of Great Compassion that is being constructed: first, one must sprinkle it with scented water for purification; this is done entirely to treat such a ground of the mind so that it may be freed from all defilements and impurities.
If one discusses external objects, they too are the supported Vajra Ground of Mind; therefore, all other syllables serve to establish this gateway of letters.
The syllable *A* signifies the meaning that all phenomena are fundamentally unborn (*anutpāda*).
Next, regarding the syllable *pala*: *pa* is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and *la* is named "dust" (*rajas*).

Because all syllables enter the gateway of the syllable *a*, they are inherently unborn as dust and defilement; that dust and defilement are inherently unborn is the ultimate truth, and the ultimate truth is what is called the pure bodhicitta.
Next is the syllable *ti*. Its primary form is the gateway of the syllable *ta*; because it carries the sound of *samādhi*, it is transformed into *ti*.
*Ti* has the meaning of "mind" (*citta*) and also the meaning of "suchness" (*tathatā*).
The suchness of the true nature of one’s own mind is precisely the pure bodhicitta.
This pure bodhicitta, which is entirely free from attachment to all phenomena, is called the Lotus Samādhi.
One who dwells in this samādhi finds that even the two—the dharmas and their mark of emptiness—are both unobtainable; this is because it is the "Great Emptiness" (mahāśūnyatā) of all Buddhas.
Next, the gate of the syllables *sa* and *ma* is explained: because it possesses the sound of samādhi through the equalization of concentration and wisdom, it is called *samaya*.
In this context, the explanation is provided solely by way of the letter-gate (akṣaramukha).

As in various Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras, which extensively expound the letter-gate "A" through various causes, conditions, and parables—such as the four *siddhāntas* and the four types of non-arising—it possesses immeasurable phrases and meanings.
Furthermore, because the sound "A" is present within all speech, every single letter-gateway (akṣaramukha) contains all letter-gateways.
If one attains this meaning, one should be able to expound them with sovereign mastery and fluidity; it is impossible to discuss them exhaustively here.
Furthermore, within mantras there are both the meaning of individual syllables (*akṣarārtha*) and the meaning of phrases (*padārtha*).
The meaning of the syllables has already been explained as before.

As for the meaning of the phrase, this *apratisama* signifies "unequaled" and "without counterpart. This means that this King of Maṇḍalas of the Mind-Ground transcends all speech and metaphors; since there is not even a single dharma that can serve as its equal, it is called "unequaled."
Why is this so? Because it fully contains the meanings explained by the aforementioned gates of syllables (*akṣaramukha*).

The meaning of the third phrase—“space and so forth”—states that this ground of mind (*cittabhūmi*) is ultimately pure, without conceptual differentiation (*avikalpa*), and without limits, being identical to space.
Furthermore, the gateway of the letter *ga* signifies "action" (*gati*).
That is the Great Emptiness, in the sense of mastery over all phenomena.

Because one enters the gateway of the letter *a* by means of the letter *ga*, all phenomena have from the very beginning been entirely without action; it is within these phenomena that the Tathāgata has reached the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Furthermore, there is nothing further to be practiced; because there is no practice, one abides in the great emptiness and attains mastery over all phenomena, for my mind-ground is ultimately equal to this great emptiness.
One should know that the mental ground of the disciple and the site of the path are likewise so; therefore, it is said they are "equal to space.

Regarding the meaning of the fourth phrase, "equal and conforming": because the vajra-ground is equal to space, it is able to pervade the realms of all sentient beings equally, universally manifesting bodies that accord with their various types; thus, it is fit to be depicted as a maṇḍala.
Furthermore, "sa" has the meaning of outflows (*āsrava*), while "ma" has the meaning of self (*ātman*) and the meaning of significance.
Since these realms of sentient beings are fundamentally unarisen, they are all suchness (*tathatā*); therefore, the dharma-realm and the realm of sentient beings are ultimately equal.

"Effort" refers to the Great Emptiness Samādhi. When the Tathāgata dwells in this Great Emptiness Samādhi, there is no practice, no arrival, and no coming or going; yet he is able to manifest in response to conditions according to the measure of his own mind. Therefore, it is said that he "responds equally."
The meaning of the fifth phrase, "inherently pure," further explains the gate of the letter A—the pure bodhicitta—and the significance of the fragrant water.

The Tathāgata, by means of the fragrance of the dharma-realm attained through meditative equipoise, blends it with the water of great compassion and samādhi; this enables him to universally sprinkle the mental ground of all sentient beings, thereby removing their defilements.
Why is this so? Because its intrinsic nature is pure.
Just as the nature of water is fundamentally pure, it is therefore able to cleanse all defilements.
The Tathāgata’s fragrant water is likewise; because it is fundamentally pure, it is able to purify the minds of all sentient beings.
Next, the meaning of the sixth phrase is clarified: it refers to the purification of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Just as scented water is sprinkled upon the ground to remove impurities, so too is the Tathāgata;

with the fragrance of naturally pure precepts blended with the water of naturally pure compassion, he sprinkles it everywhere upon the naturally pure mental ground of sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm, in order to completely purify all conceptual proliferation.
Furthermore, one should expand upon this by means of the various syllable-gates (akṣaramukha); because all Tathāgatas have spoken such a great vow in common, it is called a mantra.

Furthermore, the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*); the realm of sentient beings is the realm of mind (*cittadhātu*); the realm of mind is intrinsically pure (*prakṛtiviśuddha*); that which is intrinsically pure is that which pervades all things equally like space; and that which is equal to space is the gate of the letter A, which is the peerless among the peerless.
Just as space is boundless, one should know that the gateway of the letter A is also boundless.
Just as space is unstained, unchanging, and immovable, one should know that the gateway of the letter A is also unstained, unchanging, and immovable.

Just as space is free from all marks yet contains all phenomena, and is free from all activity yet enables the worldly affairs of the world to be accomplished, so too is the gateway of the letter A: it is without mark and without activity, yet is fully endowed with inexhaustible adornments and accomplishes the inconceivable karma of the universal gate.
In this manner, one should explain it with mastery through various gateways.

Furthermore, there are immeasurable and boundless unprecedented dharmas that cannot be illustrated by the analogy of space; therefore, the letter A-gate is the seed-syllable of mantra, transcending all analogies.
The final phrase is "Svāhā," which carries the meaning of awakening.
Because all Tathāgatas, when originally practicing the bodhisattva path, together perceived this same principle, they resolutely uttered the lion’s roar with words of truth:
"I shall, by means of this gateway of the letter A, universally purify the inexhaustible realm of sentient beings."
If this vow of mine is not false, then for all sentient beings who recite these words of my sincerity without violating the Dharma rules, I shall fulfill all their wishes exactly as they are made.

"I now proclaim this mantra in accordance with the Tathāgata’s samaya-teaching; may it not contradict his original vow, so that my place of practice (maṇḍala) may be fully adorned and purified—thus I say 'svāhā'."
Regarding the fact that the various mantras below conclude with "svāhā," their meaning is largely the same.
Whenever one brings forth the five inner treasures, one should immediately pay homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions as previously described and address them, saying:
"Tomorrow I shall perform the invitation ceremony for the Dharma."
From this third day onward, one should gradually determine the dimensions and orientation of the maṇḍala, whether it be four cubits or twelve cubits, and so forth.
Up to the abodes of the various noble deities, one should mark them all with white sandalwood paste.
If the ācārya is unable to record and maintain [the details] in full, he should instead depict their forms or write down their names to ensure that each is clearly distinguished.
Once the purification by sprinkling scented water is completed, one should use white sandalwood to smear and construct a circular maṇḍala measuring twelve finger-widths in diameter.

First, place the position of the World-Honored One Vairocana in the central matrix (garbha). Next, in the eastern direction, at the site of Mahāvīra, place the positions of all the Tathāgatas. In the southeastern quadrant, at the site of Cintāmaṇi, place the positions of all the Bodhisattvas. Next, in the northeastern quadrant, at the site of Gagananetra, place the position of the Buddha-Mother.

Next, place the position of Padmapāṇi to the right of Vairocana; next, place the position of Vajrapāṇi to the left of Vairocana; next, place the position of the noble Acala in the southwest corner; and place the position of Trailokyavijaya in the northwest direction.
Directly to the west is the location of the main entrance, which is where the ācārya resides and where the yoga of making offerings is practiced.
As the Sūtra states, "First, my own body," this refers to the position of Vairocana; thus, the five Buddhas should all be installed together upon a single altar.
"The second, 'the various saviors,' refers to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, who are also divided into two categories.
The third, 'those equal thereto,' refers to the Mother of the Buddhas."
The Tathāgata is named "Unequaled" (asama), yet the Prajñāpāramitā is "equal to the unequaled" (asamasama); therefore, it is said that they are equal.
The fourth is Padmapāṇi; the fifth is the Lord of the Vajra Family; and the sixth is called Acala, by which Trailokyavijaya may be understood.
These are all the Vidyādharas who accomplish all activities; one should know that by citing these six stages, all the deities are encompassed.
Having performed this in such a manner, one should arrange incense, flowers, and articles of offering according to the ritual procedures for the sequence of worship.

Thereafter, one visualizes the creation of a precious lotus-flower pedestal and a palace of jewel-kings, within which a seat is spread. Upon the seat is placed a white lotus-flower pedestal, upon which the letter-gateway *A* is transformed into the body of the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana. He is the color of Jāmbūnada and purple-polished gold; like a bodhisattva image, his head bears a topknot of hair shaped like a crown. His entire body radiates light of various colors, and he wears a garment of fine silk (*śāṭaka*). This is the insignia of the attainment of Perfect Enlightenment by the deity of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven.

The noble celestial hosts of that realm possess robes so light and exquisite that they weigh nothing even in the slightest measure; their essential nature is pure and majestic, requiring no external adornments. Therefore, the World-Honored One condescended to manifest an appearance identical to theirs.

If one provides a profound and esoteric interpretation: the Tathāgata’s marks of sublime adornment are naturally and inherently complete without diminution; they are not produced through artificial effort, and therefore he does not use external jewels as ornaments.

Even Bodhisattvas up to the tenth stage can only perceive the body sustained by empowerment by virtue of receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power; because that eternally quiescent essence is as subtle as a hair in a sieve, this analogy is employed.
Jambūnada gold is also naturally pure in its nature, and its color is the deepest; this illustrates that the essence of the Buddha’s vajra-wisdom is most profound and subtle.
That his entire body emits various kinds of light signifies the universal gateway that reveals great wisdom and illumination.

Next, upon the eight petals in the four directions, one should visualize the Buddhas of the four directions: in the east, visualize the Tathāgata Ratnaketu, possessing a color like the rising sun, with red and white hues radiating together.
The "jewel banner" (ratnadhvaja) signifies the arousal of the bodhicitta.

It is like a military general who leads a great host; he must first obtain the banner and standard before his divisions can be unified, whereby he is able to defeat enemy nations and achieve great renown and merit.

The myriad practices of the Tathāgata are likewise thus: taking the vow for omniscience as his banner and standard, he subdues the hosts of the four māras beneath the Bodhi tree; it is for this reason that he is so named.
The color is like the morning sun; this is also the meaning of its corresponding significance.

To the south is the Buddha Contemplating the King of Śāla Trees in Full Bloom, whose physical form is golden and universally radiates light, serving as the sign of his abiding in the Samādhi of Freedom from Defilement.

Beginning from the seed of the bodhicitta, one nurtures the myriad practices of great compassion; now, having attained universal enlightenment, the myriad virtues have blossomed, and thus this name was given.
"Free from defilement" (vimala) is the meaning of the Great Emptiness (mahā-śūnyatā).
When this Great Emptiness is realized, it is like pure gold that has been refined a hundred times so that all impurities have vanished; the marks and signs of the Buddha’s body are likewise.

This is the most exquisite gold in the world; compared to the gold of Jambudvīpa, its color is paler and somewhat turbid, unable to match the natural, mirror-like clarity and purity of the former. Because the Buddha appearing upon flowers and leaves arises from the conditions of mental construction (*citta-mātra*), there is a distinction between them.
Next, one contemplates Akṣobhya Buddha in the north, appearing in the aspect of dwelling in tranquil meditative absorption, free from heat and cool.
This is the Tathāgata’s wisdom of nirvāṇa; therefore, it is called "Immovable" (Akṣobhya) in meaning, but this is not his original name.

His original name should be called Tathāgata Drum-Sound; like a celestial drum, he has no form or appearance and no dwelling place, yet he is able to manifest the sound of the Dharma to awaken sentient beings.
The Great Parinirvāṇa is likewise; it is not like that of the two vehicles, which is eternally quiescent and utterly devoid of sublime function, and thus it is used as a metaphor.

Next, one contemplates Amitāyus Buddha in the western quarter. This is the expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata; because the realm of sentient beings is inexhaustible, the great compassion and expedient means of all Buddhas are likewise without end, and for this reason he is named Amitāyus.
His Brahma-voice is such that he is called the Benevolent One (*muni*).
Furthermore, because he has conquered the four Māras, he is called the Victorious One (*jina*).
Thus, the verse fully translates these meanings, referring to him as the Benevolent Victor (*munijina*).
These two Buddhas are also of a true golden color; with their eyes slightly closed and looking downward, they assume the form of the Samādhi of Quiescence. All Buddhas are exemplified in this manner.
At the four corners of the flower pedestal are four bodhisattvas, as described in the subsequent text.
Regarding the position of all Tathāgatas, one need only visualize a single Buddha within the golden altar; this is identical to the bodies of all Buddhas.
The others should each follow the positions of the deities within their respective sūtras, transforming the syllables into the bodies [of the deities] so that each one is clearly understood.

Regarding the method of transforming syllables in a maṇḍala, every deity employs its own fundamental seed-syllable (*bīja*), or else uses a general seed-syllable common to various families, such as *a*, *svā*, and so forth for the three families.

If one fears that a practitioner of shallow capacity cannot perform such rapid rotation, they should simply contemplate the letter-gateway A (A-kāra) as producing immeasurable light; wherever that light reaches, the body of that honored one will immediately appear.
On the night of the ritual service, one should likewise release them all.

Whenever practicing meditative cultivation, one should first stabilize the body with the five-syllable mantra as described in the *Pūjāvidhi*; then, one should visualize one’s own mind as an eight-petaled lotus flower.
The Ācārya said:

"The ordinary person’s *vilīḍha*-heart is shaped like a lotus bud that has not yet opened; it is bound by sinews and veins to form eight divisions—the male [heart] pointing upward and the female [heart] pointing downward."
First, visualize this lotus so that it fully blossoms, serving as an eight-petaled white lotus seat.

Upon this pedestal, one should visualize the syllable *A*, the color of a vajra; within its head, place the King of Pervasive Radiance of a Hundred Lights (*Śataraśmiparipūrṇaprabharāja*), and gaze upon him with stainless eyes.
By means of this self-consecration, one immediately becomes the body of Vairocana.
Through this expedient, one contemplates the body of Vairocana so that it is non-dual and indistinguishable from one's own body.
Furthermore, the space between the two vidyārājas is called the "Buddha-chamber.

When the drawing of the maṇḍala is completed, the ācārya shall move his seat and exit through the eastern gate; at this location of the Buddha-chamber, he should place the deity of his choice or the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, contained within a precious golden vessel, and offer it with solemn adornment.
Alternatively, one may place the rosary held in hand, or the vajra, the vajra-bell, and so forth.

Furthermore, whenever one intends to select and prepare a site, one should personally contemplate a wish-fulfilling jewel upon a lotus in one’s heart, transparent both inside and out. When observing it with focused attention, all signs of good and evil will appear within it.
The ācārya should then employ wisdom and skillful means to select and refine it, ensuring it becomes firm, stable, and upright; he should observe the disciple’s mind in this same manner.
The profound and secret significance herein can be grasped through the power of intention alone.

The practitioner dwells in the Buddha-chamber; as described above, having completed the visualization of the Noble Lord, one should transform the syllable *ā* into *vaṃ*, empower oneself as Vajrasattva, and present offerings such as perfumed water and flowers according to the ritual, all as extensively explained in the sequential procedures.
Thereupon, one should arouse the mind of great compassion with utmost sincerity and earnestness, reciting the *Āryā* verses of invitation as they appear in the sūtra.
The Sanskrit text is preserved here as follows:

*samantāvalokite mame sarvair nārhaṃ kārūṇikatama bhūmi-pāla kuru suputre śvasane jñāti-bandhave* The meaning of this verse is as follows: "O you who look upon all beings, for my sake, O Worthy One, most compassionate one, protect the earth and act [for its benefit], together with your sons, O Wind, relative and kinsman!"
O Buddhas, you who possess great compassion, we pray only that you hold us in your mindful regard.
We now make this request: together with the sons of the Buddhas, please descend tomorrow to act as witnesses for the ritual of receiving and upholding the ground.
Within the Brahma-sound of mindful recollection, there is already the intention of inviting [the deities] to attend.

○ Three: All Bodhisattvas; ○ Five: Vajrapāṇi of Fire; ○ Seven: The Holy Acala; ○ Two: The Position of All Buddhas of the Eastern Wood; ○ One: The Position of the Five Tathāgatas; ○ Nine: The Position of the Western Golden Ācārya.
This is the position for the White Sandalwood Maṇḍala.
[The deities are: 4. Māmakī, Ākāśanetrī; 6. Vajrapāṇi, Padmapāṇi; 8. Trailokyavijaya.

On the evening of the fifth day, one should again prepare all the ritual procedures in their proper order, adorn oneself well, and visualize entering the positions of the maṇḍala. Having completed each stage—including the invitation and the sealing protection—one should recite the mantra of Acala or Trailokyavijaya in conjunction with its corresponding mudrā exactly one hundred and eight times to consecrate this site.
The Ācārya said:
"From the third day onward, during the three sessions of recitation each day, one should recite the Acala mantra one hundred and eight times to consecrate the ground."
This applies not only here, but should be employed in all instances.
Furthermore, from the first day until the third day, if any obstacles or difficulties arise, one should immediately withdraw and cease the practice.

If the application of white sandalwood paste has already been completed, even if various demonic obstacles arise such that the two [substances] do not harmonize, one must diligently apply skillful means to ensure that it is successfully accomplished.
"The remainder is as explained in the *Guhya* [Tantra].
On the fifth night, having finished reciting the *Acala* mantra, one should next employ the body of Mahāvairocana Tathāgata;

that is, one should recite and maintain the *Dharaṇīdhara* mantra and perform the *Samaya-mudrā*. The mantra is spoken as follows: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ sarvatathāgatādhiṣṭhitādhiṣṭhite ajarivimale samarasapralambhe svāhā.* The first phrase is the homage to all Buddhas.
The meaning of the second and third phrases is that it is empowered by the empowerment of all Tathāgatas. This signifies:
just as that Vajra-maṇḍala was empowered by the combined spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of all Tathāgatas, so now shall this ground likewise be.
Furthermore, I have already leveled and purified the ground of the disciples' pure mind; this is the site for the mandala of the Great Compassion Treasury of the Tathāgata Cittarāja.
I now utter words of truth, which are empowered by the spiritual power of all Tathāgatas, so that it may become firm and immovable.
The fourth phrase says *ajāre*, which means "immovable.
The fifth phrase says *vimale*, which means "stainless.
The meaning of this is as follows:
By means of the true empowerment of the spiritual powers of all Tathāgatas, it is made firm and immovable.
Not only is it rendered immovable, but it is also caused to be free from all defilements.
Precisely because the first syllable *A* of the fourth line constitutes the essence of the mantra,
by what dharma does the Tathāgata empower it so that it remains ultimately unshakable?
This means that by means of this very *akṣara*-gate, such power and function exist.
The sixth phrase has the meaning of mindfulness and upholding (*dhāraṇa*).
It is like a bhikṣu performing the *karmavācanā* ritual, causing the community of monks to be single-minded and harmonious as they collectively receive and uphold it.
This mantra is likewise: having completed the empowerment with the syllable A, one requests all Tathāgatas to remember their original vows, whereby they collectively uphold it.
The seventh phrase has the meaning of "purity by nature" (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*); this serves as a further explanation of the preceding phrase.
Why do all Buddhas maintain their mental focus through empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*)?
It is because of purity by nature.
If all phenomena enter the gateway of the letter A, they are from the very beginning unmoving and stainless.

For this reason, the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time are all identical in their precepts and identical in their views; it is for this reason that they collectively provide empowerment and support.
Regarding the final phrase "svāhā": it is like adding a seal of approval at the conclusion of a *saṃgha-karman* (formal ecclesiastical act). It means:
"If the truthful words I have uttered are certainly without error, may all Buddhas, not transgressing their *samaya*, cause what has been performed to be perfected."
All the meanings of the words herein shall also be explained in detail.
At that time, the ācārya should go outside the maṇḍala of all Tathāgatas in the east and, facing east, recite and maintain the mantra three or seven times; this will be of great benefit and virtue.
Next, he should go to the south, then to the west, and then to the north, in each case reciting and maintaining it while turning his back toward the white sandalwood seat.
Having completed one circuit in this manner, proceed next to the position of Ākāśanetra; there, face the northeast with your back to the altar and recite it.
Next go to the southeast, then to the southwest, and then to the northwest.

Furthermore, when one cycle is completed, one should again perform prostrations with utmost sincerity and offer various kinds of offerings; then, taking the seat of the ācārya and sitting facing east, one should recite the mantra as originally received and maintained, abiding in the samādhi of the tutelary deity, all according to what is explained in the sequence of the offerings.
Furthermore, recite the mantras of the deities in the positions of white sandalwood in sequence, while binding their respective mudrās. The Ācārya says:
"First, recite the mantra of the Lord of the Family, Vairocana, one hundred and eight times; for the remaining eight positions, recite their mantras according to their length."

If one is further able to recite, it is also permissible to maintain the four bodhisattvas of the second court, the principal deities such as Śākyamuni of the third court, and even to recite all the positions in their entirety.

Regarding the white sandalwood seat, once it has been smeared with mud and dried, and the fragrant water has been sprinkled, one may proceed to construct it; it need not necessarily wait for the fourth day.
After it has been set up, one must always perform the recitation in accordance with this.
The same may be understood to apply to the night of the Dharma-rite.

As for the night of receiving and maintaining [the precepts], once the Ācārya has completed the ritual recitation according to the Dharma, he shall extol all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas with the *vajra-gāthā*.

When one is utterly exhausted from sitting in meditation, one should perform the ritual protection of the body according to the rules at this very site where the altar is placed, and then lie down facing east.

One should generate a heart of supreme great compassion and pity for the disciples to be initiated. Furthermore, once the *Guhya-tantra* has been received and maintained upon the ground, there is also the method for binding the *sūtra* and receiving the names of the disciples.

When he sleeps peacefully, he should contemplate that within the heart-lotus pedestal, the syllable *ma* represents the gate of all dharmas being ungraspable as a self; this is precisely the unobstructed bodhicitta.
It is also like a wish-fulfilling jewel.
Furthermore, it is said:
"This wish-fulfilling jewel is nothing other than the gateway of the letter A."

That ācārya shall, within a dream, either see immeasurable Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of great renown manifesting various activities—namely, guiding and transforming sentient beings according to their diverse capacities through the three wheels—or personally arrange and establish the Karuṇāsambhava Maṇḍala; or else, with subtle and wondrous voices, they shall comfort and exhort him, saying:
"Out of compassion for sentient beings, you have now constructed this maṇḍala."
"Excellent, Mahāsattva!
What you have painted is most subtle and exquisite.
Regarding such various realms as these, the ācārya should skillfully discern them with a mind of wisdom.
One should know that the noble ones have already consecrated this ground; thus, one may perform rites according to one's will.
If there are obstacles, one should employ the appropriate methods of *homā* (fire ritual) to purify them, and with great diligence and courage, one must ensure that the rite is accomplished.

Furthermore, if one encounters a preceptor who has realized the Truths, then within the wish-fulfilling jewel of the pure bodhicitta of the Lotus Samādhi, one will naturally and clearly perceive, without obstruction, the causes and conditions of both hindrances and their absence; the Buddha will manifest before one’s mind to entrust the teachings and resolve all doubts.

If one perceives the activities of Māra as they arise, one should employ great wisdom and great skillful means to perform the rite of homa in a transformative manner; one must ensure that the mind held remains unshakable and non-regressive, capable of establishing the maṇḍala of the dharmadhātu, and only then may one rest.

Furthermore, from the initial moment the Ācārya has awakened the Earth Goddess, he must not abandon this site of the maṇḍala; he should constantly perform empowerment and recitation therein while observing it with careful scrutiny, immediately repairing any part that is uneven or incorrect.

Furthermore, one should contemplate that all requisite conditions and components must be fully prepared in advance, so as not to encounter deficiencies at the time of the ritual and thereby give rise to doubt.

From the moment one has completed the personal observance of the site (*bhūmiparigraha*), one should immediately delineate the boundaries and fix the orientations; it is only on the night of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) that one should fashion the various deities.
If one is unable to achieve success quickly, there is no fault in practicing gradually from the stage of Holding the Ground (Dharaṇī) onwards.

As the Sūtra states: "Furthermore, on another day, beginning with the reception of those to be converted and ending with the bestowing of scented water so that their minds may be purified," this clarifies the branches of receiving, establishing, and protecting disciples.
Having completed the reception and upholding of the stages, the following clarifies the ritual for the disciple to be performed at night; thus it says, "on another day.
Consequently, this provides a detailed analysis of the characteristics of the disciples who are fit to be delivered.

Regarding the verse, "If the disciple has faith," this means that the ācārya, having observed the disciple's present faculties or their causes and conditions from long ago, finds that they can directly believe without doubt and without any fear amidst these three kinds of secret skillful means within inconceivable dependent origination; such a person is then fit to be accepted.
The remainder is as explained in the section on the teacher’s qualities.
As for the verse stating, “born into a pure lineage,” this refers to being born into one of the four great lineages, such as the Brahmins and so forth.
If they are outcasts (caṇḍāla) and so forth, because they have inherited and practiced impure matters according to their family traditions, their lineage is generally corrupt and evil.

If one were to confer upon them the empowerment for transmitting the Dharma to cause the Great Dharma to circulate, it would give rise to the contempt of others or become a cause and condition for the depletion of the Dharma.
Just as when a bhikṣu receives full ordination, those who have brought disgrace upon the Saṃgha or belong to an extremely low caste are excluded;
if one merely establishes a karmic connection to receive the Dharma, such cases are not under discussion here.
Furthermore, if since long ago there has ever been the causal condition for generating the bodhicitta, one is born into the lineage of the Tathāgata; this is the most preeminent clan.

Regarding the verse that says, "Reverencing the Triple Gem," this means to give rise to a heart of profound sincerity and humble submission toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and to always delight in drawing near to them, making offerings, honoring, and praising them.

You should know that this person possesses the causal conditions for practicing the Way from previous lives; even as the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging did, they are said to deeply respect all sentient beings and to have faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha Treasures.

Regarding the phrase "adorned with profound wisdom": such boundless dharmas of the Buddha, which are like space, cannot be borne by the mental vessels of those with inferior wisdom; therefore, it is for those who adorn themselves with the nature of wisdom that is deep and sharp that these teachings are expounded.
"Enduring without weariness" means possessing capability and being free from retreat or discouragement. This term in the Sanskrit original is distinct from *kṣānti* (patience);

it refers to the ability to undertake all manner of difficult and arduous tasks for the sake of seeking the Dharma. Even if one fails once, one resumes the practice with renewed resolve, continuing until the vow is fulfilled—just as one would empty the great ocean by drawing out its waters drop by drop.
If a person’s disposition is such as this, they may transmit the Dharma.
Regarding "pure śīla without defect":

this refers to the lay and monastic vows, even down to the various prohibitions naturally undertaken; according to what one upholds, one protects them with a profound mind so that there is no violation or deficiency.

If one possesses such a nature, even when entering the samaya—the equality of the great vow—one should remain respectful and compliant without contravening it; therefore, such a person is fit to receive the transmission of the Dharma.
Regarding "patience without parsimony," this is divided here into two phrases.

"Patience" means that amidst the eight great winds of internal and external favorable and adverse conditions, the mind remains calmly enduring and unshakable, as explained in detail in the *Prajñāpāramitā* (Jìdù) within the section on the *Śīlapāramitā*.

It should be known that such a person will certainly not violate the grave prohibitions of a Vidyādhara, nor will they engage in conduct that is detrimental to sentient beings; therefore, they are fit to transmit the Dharma.

Regarding non-avarice: this means that one should always keep in mind the giving away of all wealth and the Dharma to others; even when seekers come, one’s heart is free from contempt or stinginess, as is explained in detail in the *Prajñāpāramitā* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra) concerning the dāna-pāramitā.
It should be known that such a person will certainly not violate the grave prohibitions of the Vidyādhara nor be stingy with the True Dharma;
therefore, they are fit to receive the transmission. "Valiant and firm in conduct and vows" is also divided into two phrases.
"Courageous and robust" refers to the courageous seed-nature of the bodhicitta within the virtues of an ācārya.

When practicing the path, even when encountering various terrifying forms and sounds, their mind does not become timid or weak; they remain free from thoughts of fear even when facing birth and death. Because they correctly follow the conduct of great beings, the Bodhisattvas, they should be granted the transmission.
Regarding "firmly practicing the vows," this refers to the essential core of one's aspiration; the Sanskrit term differs in meaning from a mere general prayer.
If one establishes a personal resolve to recite it three times each day, then it shall be maintained until the end of one's life.

Although he encountered various and diverse circumstances, his practice was never interrupted from beginning to end; since such a matter possesses both a commencement and a conclusion, and because he did not fail in his original vow while practicing the bodhisattva path, he is thus capable of transmitting the Dharma.

Regarding these ten virtues of a disciple thus described, one should know that it is extremely rare to find someone who possesses them all together; however, if a person has even a partial excellence sufficient for a single master to bring them to completion, they should indeed be accepted.

Furthermore, when a śrāvaka receives full ordination, one examines various impediments and obstacles—namely, being too young or too old, physical defects, various illnesses, and so forth—and immediately excludes them for fear of causing resentment or reproach among the white-robed laity.
Now, this Mahāyāna is not like that; it merely requires that those with the potential for the Way be saved, so that even if there are various other faults, none of them are taken into account.

Regarding the statement in the verse, "Either ten, eight, or seven; or five, two, one, or four," this refers to the limited number of disciples for whom an ācārya may perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) within a single session of the maṇḍala.

In this context, they are counted by skipping numbers: that is, from one to two, from two skipping to four, from four to five, from five skipping to seven, from seven to eight, and from eight skipping to ten people.
Therefore, within a single maṇḍala, one may not simultaneously bestow initiation upon three, six, or nine persons.
This is the secret intention of the Tathāgata, which the ācārya does not explain.
Furthermore, as in the *Mahāvaipulya-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one must not exceed ten persons.

Beyond this number, I fear that the Ācārya’s mental capacity may not be sufficient to encompass them all; therefore, one should wait for future circumstances to perform the ritual separately for those others.

Furthermore, regarding those with fewer than ten people, this refers to cases where they simultaneously resolve their minds, each relinquishing all internal and external possessions to make offerings to the Three Jewels and collectively accomplish the maṇḍala; therefore, they may perform the ritual procedures at the same time.

If a person merely encounters a site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and claims that such karmic conditions for the Dharma are difficult to encounter, requesting initiation for the sake of universal salvation, it is not appropriate to confer upon them the empowerment of an ācārya.

If, however, one exceeds this number, or seeks merely to establish a karmic connection by receiving mantras and mudrās within the dharma of a single-gate principal deity, then one does not rely upon such numerical limits.

The ācārya should likewise arouse great compassion; for anyone capable of generating even a slight degree of wholesome mind, he shall cause them to produce and establish the seed of bodhicitta. Therefore, it is said that "or perhaps even more than this."
The Sūtra states: "At that time, Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
'World-Honored One!
What should this maṇḍala be named?'"
"What is the meaning of 'maṇḍala'?
This question arises because the Tathāgata has restricted the assembly by selecting specific individuals, leading those who have not yet attained realization to give rise to further doubts.

Vajrapāṇi himself requested the World-Honored One to proclaim this realm of empowerment, expounding the Great Maṇḍala King Born from the Matrix of Great Compassion; this is the equality of great compassion, which is beyond all measure.

Now, regarding what the World-Honored One has taught, although there are those who may transmit his virtues, they do not exceed ten people; it appears that these are merely those who follow and turn [the wheel], and are not the specific embodiments themselves. Therefore, he asks: "What should this maṇḍala be named?"

Furthermore, "maṇḍala" carries the meaning of being circular and complete; since the present enumeration is limited and restrictive, it appears that the principle is not yet fully realized. Therefore, he asks again: what is the meaning of "maṇḍala" in this context?
There are two questions in total.
Within the World-Honored One’s response, he first answers regarding the name and subsequently answers regarding the meaning.
Within the answer concerning the name, he further clarifies the original intent.
Now, "maṇḍala" carries the meaning of "generation. It is here named the maṇḍala that generates all Buddhas. One plants the seeds of the bodhicitta within the ground of the mind of omniscience;

it is moistened by the water of great compassion, illuminated by the sun of great wisdom, fanned by the wind of great skillful means, and rendered unimpeded by the emptiness of great emptiness. This enables the sprouts of the inconceivable nature of phenomena (dharmatā) to grow stage by stage, until they fully pervade the dharma-realm as the king of trees—the Buddha. Therefore, it is designated by the term "generation."

Now, when thunder and rain arise to bring about release, those whose husks have already cracked sprout first; it cannot be because the nature and allotment of plants and trees differ in their capacity for flourishing that the impartial bestowal of the rain is thereby rendered limited.
Next, regarding the explanation of the meaning: the Sanskrit term *maṇḍala* carries the sense of churning curdled milk to produce clarified butter (*sarpis*).

*Maṇḍala* signifies the most refined and pure essence of that butter which gathers and floats upon the surface; because this refined essence does not undergo further transformation, it is further termed "solid" (*khara*).
The pure and wondrous flavors are in perfect harmony with one another, unmixed by any other substances; thus, they possess the sense of being a "congregation" (*maṇḍala*).
Therefore, the Buddha said:
"It is a flavor of ultimate incomparability and a flavor unsurpassed; for this reason, it is called a *maṇḍala*."

By means of the three kinds of secret skillful means, one churns the milk of the Buddha-nature within sentient beings, passing through the five flavors until the sublime nectar of wondrous enlightenment (amṛta) is achieved.

Pure, refined, and subtly harmonious, it cannot be further increased; it is the supreme among all vajra wisdom seals gathered together, the foremost within the flavor of the true, eternal, and unchanging nectar. This is the meaning of the maṇḍala.
The scripture states, "Furthermore, O Lord of Mysteries," and so forth, extensively expounding the meaning of the maṇḍala to resolve doubts and remove obstacles.
This section is further divided into three parts:

first, it clarifies that the perfect altar of the dharma-realm is universally accessible and limitless; second, it clarifies the reasons for restricting access and distinguishing among sentient beings; and finally, the concluding sentence exhorts the ācārya to give rise to impartial compassionate vows.

Regarding the first passage, the phrase "Compassion for the boundless realm of sentient beings is the broad meaning of the Maṇḍala born from the Matrix of Great Compassion" means that when a practitioner perceives the central matrix for themselves, they immediately know that all sentient beings possess the causal conditions for attaining Buddhahood; therefore, the Maṇḍala of Great Compassion that arises therein also pervades the entire Dharma-realm.

Furthermore, for example, if a multitude of Vajradhara Bodhisattvas, numbering as many as the atoms in ten worlds, each take one gate as the presiding lord of the maṇḍala while the others serve as their retinue, then a single type of maṇḍala is thus formed.
Thus they revolve without end, beyond the reach of calculation or analogy.
How much more so, then, can one enumerate the various infinite gateways by which each is adorned, and the diverse skillful means used to attract and guide sentient beings?

If a practitioner, within this single-syllable dharma-gate, condenses the extensive into the concise and expands the concise into the extensive, giving rise to the wealth of the Dharma to bestow universally upon all without ever ceasing or exhausting it, they are then said to be well-versed in the broad meaning of the maṇḍala.
Next it says: "Lord of Mysteries!
The Tathāgata has been empowered by the accumulation of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* over immeasurable kalpas; therefore, he possesses immeasurable virtues."
"One should know it thus" explains the origin of this broad meaning.

For example, regarding the various spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) who enter the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, each has attained a profound and boundless mastery of the Dharma within their own particular gate; yet, they do not know one another's [realizations].

When the Tathāgata formerly practiced the bodhisattva path, he universally approached as many spiritual friends as there are atoms in such Buddha-fields; regarding each and every treasury of their merits, he attained the ultimate, peerless, and unsurpassed flavor.

Because such internally realized virtues are immeasurable and boundless, the manifestations of the dharma-gates and their retinues sustained by his empowerment are likewise immeasurable and boundless.
That practitioner of the mantra-gate should broaden and clarify their mind, forming this understanding:
having already known that internal virtues are limitless, one next clarifies how the mandala of the original ground delivers limitless beings.
Why is this? Because it accords with the vow of great compassion.
Therefore, the sutra text continues: "O Lord of Secrets!"
It is not for the sake of a single sentient being that the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment;
nor for two, nor for many. It is out of compassion for all sentient beings—both those with remainder and those without remainder—that the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment.
"By the power of the vow of great compassion, one expounds the Dharma within the realm of immeasurable sentient beings according to their inherent nature.
Regarding the meaning of generating the bodhicitta herein, it is explained in detail in the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter (*Gandavyūha-sūtra*) and in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Regarding those for whom there is no further explanation:

it is as when the Buddha bestows a prediction of enlightenment in his very presence, saying, "A certain sentient being shall become a Buddha in a certain eon, with the name of such-and-such a Tathāgata, and possess such-and-such a land, retinue, and lineage."
Because it is recorded with complete clarity, it is called "unremainderd prediction" (anupadhiśeṣa-vyākaraṇa).
As for "with remainder prediction" (sopadhiśeṣa-vyākaraṇa), it is as when one tells sentient beings:
"In the future, at the time of a certain Buddha, you shall exhaust these karmic offenses; such-and-such a Tathāgata will grant you a prediction [of enlightenment]."
This is of that nature.
Furthermore, as the World-Honored One has said:

"Whether I am in the world or have entered parinirvāṇa, all those who hear even a single line or a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, I shall bestow upon them the prediction of unsurpassed bodhi."
This is called an answer without remainder.

If one says that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, that their production of roots of goodness continues in succession without interruption, and that they shall eventually attain unsurpassed bodhi.
This is called an answer with remainder.

I originally came to attain equal and perfect enlightenment for the sake of these sentient beings; how much more so now that my vow has been fulfilled? I shall open the treasure within the minds of sentient beings and bestow it upon them according to their own nature—how could there be any limit to this?

Furthermore, based on a single instance of one who propagates the sutras in this degenerate age with shallow practice, it is said that the ritual proceedings for a single period are limited to ten people at most.
From here on, the second sentence explains the reason for this restriction on the number of participants and the exclusion of the multitude.
The Sūtra states: "O Lord of Mysteries!

Those who lack the latencies of past practice in the Mahāyāna and have never contemplated the conduct of the Mantra Vehicle cannot, even in the slightest degree, see, hear, rejoice in, or accept it with faith."
Furthermore, O Vajrasattva!

As for the statement, "If those sentient beings have previously advanced through the immeasurable gateways of the path of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mahāyāna and have practiced therein, it is for their sake that these names and numbers are established," this means:

if sentient beings have not long planted roots of virtue in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas in the past, and have never cultivated this Secret Vehicle, they will be unable to believe or accept it upon hearing it in haste.

If a transmitter of the Dharma merely preaches according to their own wholesome intentions or by guessing at the capacities of others, it may instead increase the listener's slander and sever their roots of goodness.
Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "Those who lack wisdom and harbor doubt or regret shall suffer eternal loss."

Among all sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions, those who aspire to become śrāvakas are few; those who seek to become pratyekabuddhas are even fewer still; and those who seek the Mahāyāna are extremely rare. While seeking the Mahāyāna is still considered easy, it is most difficult to have faith in this Dharma.
Therefore, when viewed with the universal eye, those capable of receiving this Dharma are as few as the grains of dust or drops of water in Mount Sumeru or the great ocean.
Since one must protect their minds, it was only at the appropriate time that I spoke of it; how could I have failed to provide a concise summary by establishing these names and categories?
What is called "advancing through immeasurable gates" simultaneously explains the meaning of the term *maṇḍala*. Now, *maṇḍala* means "gathering.

Here, the true merits of the Tathāgata are gathered in one place; even the wheels of the various wisdom-seals (*jñāna-mudrā*), as numerous as the atoms in ten worlds, converge like spokes toward the hub to assist the Great Sun, the Sovereign Mind-King, so that all sentient beings may advance through the universal gate. For this reason, it is called a *maṇḍala*.

Regarding what is called "abbreviating this by establishing names and numbers": for instance, using the fivefold transformation of the letter *A* to encompass the Tathāgata’s boundless internal virtues, and using the hundred luminosities of the wheel of syllables (*akṣaracakra*) to subsume the Tathāgata’s universal eye dharma-gates—this is what is meant by "abbreviation of names."

Using skillful means as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field, he opened an eight-petaled mandala; using infinite great compassion, he established a limit of ten persons—this is but a brief enumeration of the numbers.
Nevertheless, those who study it may attain awakening and entry by clarifying the Way through any single dharma; this is precisely to universally enter all gates of dhāraṇī.
Just as seeing the king through a single gate is equivalent to entering all his thousands of gates and myriad doors,
if one cannot act according to what has been taught, then even though one may provide extensive explanations using various literary expressions, it will be of no benefit.
Therefore, in the third section, the limited number of names is explained next; this does not obstruct the extensive treatment that follows.

Thus, the Sūtra says: "That ācārya should also, with a mind of great compassion, establish such a vow: for the sake of liberating the entire realm of sentient beings without exception, he should embrace immeasurable sentient beings, acting as the causal condition for the seed of bodhi."

It means that by constructing this maṇḍala, whoever sees, hears, touches, or knows it—even down to those who merely raise a hand, bow their head, or rejoice for a single thought-moment—will all certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Therefore, although an ācārya may not be permitted to err by bestowing the full-branch initiation (sakalāṅga-abhiṣeka) upon one for whom the karmic capacity is lacking, how could the conditions of the "tied-bead" or the "poisonous drum" ever be averted?
Therefore, one should exercise the mind of great compassion, striving to ensure that it is widely and thoroughly pervaded.
Furthermore, it is like a person who possesses a secret treasure; fearing that it might be observed by thieves, they conceal it with a covering garment.
This maṇḍala dharma-gate is likewise: because the secret treasury cannot be directly proclaimed, the esoteric intent is turned and concealed by means of expedient signs.
The present statement that the limit is ten persons refers merely to the maṇḍala of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).

However, the ācārya himself should cultivate and level the ground of his own mind and paint the Maṇḍala of Great Compassion; he should universally deliver sentient beings, for the more there are, the better. One must not interpret this according to the literal words alone.
Commentary on the Mahāvairocana Sūtra, Scroll Four.
Commentary on the Mahāvairocana Sūtra, Scroll Five.
