Recorded by the Śramaṇa Acharya Yi-hang.
The remainder of the verses from the "Chapter on the Requisites for Entering the Maṇḍala" states:
"The practitioner who upholds the mantra-words," which clarifies the skillful means for protecting and establishing the constituent parts of the disciple.

Upon reaching the sixth night, the master and his disciples shall all bathe for purification, don fresh and clean garments, and carry the ritual offerings. They should proceed to the site where the white sandalwood maṇḍala was previously constructed and, according to the rite, perform the consecration (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of themselves, the practice site, and all the disciples.
The expedient means for protecting the disciples are as explained below in the section on entering the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).

At that time, the *ācārya*, according to the sequential ritual rules, performs the offerings in full; he visualizes the deities at the stations of white sandalwood as being in union with their respective secret mudrās, and recites their mantras.

Guhya said: "Place the hands upon the *maṇḍala* of the central womb and recite the mantra once; in this manner, recite it once for each station up to seven times, and the same applies to the remaining positions."
Next, one should preach the Dharma to the disciples in accordance with their capacities to guide their minds, instructing them in the three refuges and the repentance of prior transgressions.
Once they have repented, their bodies and minds will be as pure as bright pearls, enabling them to truly give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.
Therefore, next, cause them to generate the mind of *kṛti* (compassionate resolve), all according to what is explained in the ritual for making offerings.

Next, one should present them with scented ointments, flowers, and so forth, instructing them to direct their minds toward making offerings to the various deities; thereafter, one shall confer upon them the precepts of unobstructed wisdom of the three periods of time.
This method for receiving the Bodhisattva precepts has its own distinct code of conduct.

The reason a bodhisattva resolves to undertake the training in skillful means is solely to accomplish the pure wisdom of the Tathāgata, so as to realize and penetrate all phenomena of the three periods of time without obstruction in a single thought-moment.

For those who abide in this precept, from the very moment they first perceive the clarity of the Path, there arises such inconceivable power; because this precept is intimately capable of generating the Buddha-wisdom, and because the disciplinary codes of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) are limited, it is therefore named the "Unobstructed Wisdom of the Three Times."

Next, one should provide a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) and have the disciples chew it; by means of this, one should immediately observe whether those individuals possess the signs of being fit vessels (*bhājana*) or unfit vessels.

The reason for performing this rite is that it accords with the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) of that region, and it is performed through the application of secret skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) as an empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

Whenever the people of India invite monks for a meal, or even when they invite one another as laypeople, they first send a tooth-stick, adorned with various kinds of incense and flowers, and present it to them; one should know that this signifies an invitation for a meal on the following day.

The reason for acting in this way is to manifest a heart of love and respect; fearing that he might have pre-existing conditions such as phlegm or undigested food which, upon receiving my offerings, might be provoked and cause him distress, I first protect and alert him with a benevolent mind. This causes him to first purify his physical vessel, perhaps by consuming *harītakī* and other remedies, so that on the following day he may eat and drink at his pleasure without any violation or affliction, remaining peaceful and happy in body and mind.
Now the Ācārya is likewise: when bestowing the *yank-chi* (tooth-stick) upon the disciple, he should immediately employ this expedient means to explain the profound Dharma, saying:

"I am now about to bestow upon you the Buddha-nature, the *amṛta* (clarified butter), the flavor that rescues from all faults. Having already instructed you to resolve upon Bodhicitta to purify and eliminate the karmic obstacles of the three activities (*trikarma*), and having used the tusks of subduing through the unimpeded wisdom of the three periods of time to devour all afflictions, I now wish to further utilize this secret empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) to wash away the defects and maladies of body and mind."
"You must also purify your verbal transgressions; wherever you travel, do not propagate [these teachings] recklessly.
Tomorrow, I shall bestow upon you the nectar of immortality so that all may be fully satisfied."
He should take a piece of Udumbara or Aśvattha wood that is straight and well-proportioned, neither too coarse nor too fine, measuring twelve finger-widths (dvādaśa-aṅgula).
Regarding all methods of measurement, one should use the side of the upper phalanx of the thumb and pinch it against [the other fingers]; this is the correct measure.
These two pieces of wood are the Bodhi trees of past Buddhas; if such are unavailable, one should seek wood that contains sap, such as the mulberry or the *śyāmāka* tree.

One should mark the distinction between the upper and lower parts, taking the tips of the branches as the upper and the roots as the lower. These should be washed with scented water, then smeared [with fragrant paste] and incensed.
At the lower end, wrap white thread around the flower to serve as an ornament and also as a marker, so that the upper and lower ends may be easily distinguished.
One should press it with the hand while reciting the *Acala-mantra* one hundred or one thousand times; these preparations should be strictly completed in advance.

Once the precepts have been received, the master shall take one tooth-stick and offer it to the various Honored Ones; the remainder shall be distributed to the disciples, who are to exit the altar, face either east or north, and chew them while squatting in accordance with the ritual rules.
Having chewed it, one should cast it straight toward the direction one is facing to examine its signs.

If the end of the chewed portion points outward, this person’s *siddhi* will not be accomplished; if it points toward the body, *siddhi* will be accomplished. If, after being thrown far away, it returns near the body, this is a sign that accomplishment will occur before long. If the head stands upright pointing upward, accomplishment will be even swifter; if the head points downward, this person shall enter the palace of the asuras or nāgas. If it remains suspended in the air, one should know that this person has already achieved accomplishment.
Furthermore, facing north is the highest accomplishment, facing west is middling accomplishment, and facing south is the lowest accomplishment.

Nevertheless, if a person first casts [the seed] toward the east, yet the place where they chew faces east, this constitutes turning one's back on the body, and accomplishment will not be attained; other cases should be understood by analogy according to these directions.
The remainder is as explained in the *Guhya* [Tantra].
Next, one should perform the rite of the vajra-thread (*vajrasūtra*).
In making the thread, one should select fine, high-quality fibers, wash them with scented water until they are perfectly pure, and have a clean maiden join them together with her right hand.
Combine threads of five colors; one should hold each color while reciting the mantra of one of the five Tathāgatas, and then empower them all collectively with the mantra for accomplishing all tasks.
The same applies to the threads for constructing the maṇḍala.
Regarding the colors of the five Tathāgatas: Vairocana Buddha is sustained by the color white; Ratnasaṃbhava by red; Padmaprabha by yellow; Amitāyus by blue; and Dundubhisvara by black.

The ācārya first takes three strands of thread himself, forms them into a vajra-knot, and ties it upon his left arm to protect himself; he then proceeds to tie one upon the arm of each disciple in turn.
When one thus receives a disciple, entering the maṇḍala constitutes the removal of all obstacles and difficulties.
As for the method of the vajra-binding, it cannot be explained in detail; it must be received directly from the face of the ācārya.
Furthermore, the five-colored threads represent the five wisdoms of the Tathāgata, as well as the five dharmas of faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
Because these five dharmas thread together and encompass all gates of teaching, they are called *sūtra*; in ancient translations, this was termed the "Thread Sūtra" (*xián jīng*).

If the Vidyācārya who has realized the Truth can, through the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s five wisdoms, take the five kinds of roots of goodness within the disciple’s bodhicitta and thread them with all practices, binding and upholding them upon the arm of yoga, so that they shall pass through birth and death without ever being lost or damaged.
If one can thus receive disciples, it is called "skillfully performing the vajra-binding. The Ācārya said:
"When performing the ritual for disciples on this night, the offerings should be reduced by half compared to those of the seventh night."

Furthermore, one should observe their dispositions and capacities, extol the Secret Teaching (Guhyamantra), inspire in them a longing for it, and strengthen their resolve, while also explaining the ten types of skillful means and precepts.
"However, regarding this unimpeded wisdom-vow of the three times, all those who have formed a karmic connection with it shall be permitted to hear it.
As for the four root [vows] and the samaya, these should be whispered into the ear in a single verse; only those who have received the complete-branch initiation (kalaśābhiṣeka) should hear them."
The two verses of instruction he taught are also *āryā* stanzas; it would be even better if one could recite the Sanskrit original in its entirety.
They are listed below: *Anityaṃ* (from now on), *yauṣmākaṃ*, *tvaṃ*, *nirātma-dṛṣṭi-rahitam-anupama-rūpaṃ*, *jīvaloka-mahā-tārakam*.
*Ma-bhi-da-ya-ye-nā sarva-jñena buddha-yānena saṃpūrṇaṃ ca bodhisattva-rakṣā śāsanīya-sarvabhadra-ari* [The Blessed One said:
"O Great Compassionate One, by means of the omniscient Buddha-vehicle, may there be fulfillment and protection for the Bodhisattvas;
may this be taught as the auspiciousness of all noble ones."
Dvayaṃ kṣetraṃ saṃgraha-jayamāna-janma-mahodaya-nayena, arthaviniścaye tannayena mahāyāne śrāvaka-hīnam-udbhava-pañcāśat.
The meaning of the verse "Dvayaṃ pratītya" is as follows:
From this day forward, you have already attained incomparable benefit, and your status is equal to that of the Great Self (Mahātman).
The "Great Self" refers to all Tathāgatas who have attained the eightfold mastery over themselves and possess sovereignty over all phenomena, as well as the Mahāsattvas.
It further states: "All Tathāgatas, together with the assembly of Mahāsattvas within this teaching, have all already taken you under their protection."
"This teaching" refers to the ten Buddha-fields, Vajra Bodhisattvas, and others within this secret Mahāyāna teaching.
Next, the phrase "accomplishing the great task" means that which is capable of accomplishing the great task.

It is capable of accomplishing the causal conditions for the Great Matter, namely, the revealing, showing, awakening to, and entering into the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision; therefore, the meaning is expressed through the assembly in the Sūtra.

It further states: "On the morrow, you shall give birth to the Mahāyāna," which means that having entered the Maṇḍala of Great Compassion and received empowerment, you shall be born into the lineage of all Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, by departing from birth through conditions and karma, one attains the birth of Great Emptiness; therefore, it is called "birth in the Mahāyāna.
When the Ācārya has thus finished instructing and sealing [the disciple], he then directs him to sit in order outside the maṇḍala, facing east.
The ācārya shall further perform offerings, and with a heart of utmost sincerity, invite the various honored ones, saying:
"On the morrow, out of compassion for my disciple, I shall establish the Mahākaruṇā-garbha-maṇḍala to make offerings to the various holy honored ones, providing sustenance according to my ability."
"I only pray that you will look upon me with compassion and mindfulness, and tomorrow, assemble in full within the maṇḍala to bestow your empowerment.
The general meaning is as such; the remaining details are as explained in the *Guhya* [Tantra].
After he has made his three earnest requests, he shall proclaim verses of the vajra-words to praise the various deities, and then perform the ritual dismissal according to the Dharma.

He shall further expound the essential points of the teaching extensively for the disciple, instructing him to maintain mindfulness and contemplation, and to lie down upon auspicious grass (śarī-grass) facing west.

If, within his dreams, he encounters various objects or experiences, he should report them all to his teacher upon waking; thus, the signs indicating whether or not the practitioner’s *siddhi* will be accomplished may be known.
If the ācārya who has realized the truths abides in profound yoga himself, he will clearly perceive the disciple’s fundamental and derivative conditions and roots without error;
even if he does not perform such formal rituals or follows the practices of conventional truth, there is no fault whatsoever.
If one has not yet seen a teacher who has realized the Truths, one should instead carefully rely upon the rules of the Dharma so as not to let them fall into decline or loss.

As for what the Sūtra says regarding "seeing the dwelling place of the Saṃgha in a dream," it refers to seeing a pure, subtle, and exquisitely adorned site; entering therein, prostrating, kneeling, and circumambulating, and encountering various auspicious and virtuous events.

Regarding "gardens and groves," this refers to seeing exceptionally flourishing landscapes with an abundance of flowers and fruits; or personally gathering them, or ascending trees to pluck them, or walking through the air.

"Halls and chambers" refers to various flowered rooms and ornate windows, exquisitely and uniquely adorned, wherein one dwells in sovereign enjoyment with body and mind in a state of blissful contentment.

"Towers and pavilions" refers to multi-storied terraces, open and spacious, from which one gazes afar across the four quarters, beholding various sublime landscapes so that the spirit and mood become joyful and expansive.
All such instances as these are auspicious.
The significance of these dharma-gates is also as explained in the section on selecting a site for a monastery.
If they are contrary to this—such as seeing stūpas or monasteries that are burning, collapsing, or overgrown with filth—then these are not auspicious dreams.

The banner (*dhvaja*) refers to a precious standard, lofty and magnificent, appearing before one; or it is used to direct the multitude so that none fail to obey its command. It is an image representing the establishment of the great bodhicitta and the fulfillment of the myriad practices.

The canopy refers to the five-colored, variegated plumage of the peacock's tail and the like; whether suspended in the air to provide shade above, or bestowed by a person and held while traveling, it is an image symbolizing the universal covering of compassionate vows.

The maṇi jewel is also said to be perfectly luminous and penetrating; alternatively, it can produce various objects to bestow upon all people. This is the image of the pure mind, the treasure of awakening, and the four means of attraction (saṃgrahavastu) for benefiting others.

The sword refers to one that is polished, reflective, and transparent, as well as refined, firm, and sharp; whether bestowed by another or grasped by oneself, it is the image of the accomplishment of the nature of wisdom.

Pleasant flowers refer to various kinds of flowers growing in water or on land; according to their respective natures and categories, they are classified as superior, middling, or inferior—just as, for example, white is considered superior in color and sweet and rich flavor is considered superior in taste. These are all signs of the auspicious unfolding of wholesome sprouts, which one should discern with the mind.
A woman is the image of samādhi, and a man is the image of wisdom; one should also take as objects those who are upright, majestic, virtuous, and beloved by others.
"Intimate relatives" refers to parents and the like.
"Virtuous friends" refers to those who transmit the Dharma, such as superiors and spiritual mentors (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Whether one sees a herd of cows grazing with abundant milk, or whether people are milking them or drinking from them themselves, these are all images of the supreme flavor of the *mahāmaitrī* maṇḍala, like the finest essence of clarified butter (*sarpis*).

If one sees that the sutra scrolls are pure white and stainless, neatly arranged and beautifully adorned, with the color of the characters distinct and clear, recording various kinds of sublime matters, this is an auspicious sign;
if the volumes are soiled and damaged, or the characters and meanings are incomplete and deficient, one should know it to be inauspicious.

Or one may see various Buddhas personally stroking their heads and bestowing face-to-face prophecies, consoling and encouraging them with subtle and wondrous voices; or one may see śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others, even up to those dwelling in mid-air, manifesting immeasurable supernatural transformations—all of these should be carefully discerned according to the specific circumstances to recognize the causes and conditions for such manifestations.

Regarding "various fruits," this refers to rare, precious, and wonderful fruits seldom seen in the world, whether they are bestowed by someone or descend from the sky; these are all manifestations of the *siddhi*.
If one crosses rivers, ponds, or great oceans, or even dreams of drinking them all until they are exhausted in an instant, these are all auspicious signs;
however, if one is adrift, drowning, or among those for whom there is no rescue, one should know that this is inauspicious.

Or one may hear various pleasant sounds in the air, such as the chanting of Dharma-sounds and the performance of music, or the praise of the merits of the Triple Gem—all of which the mind delights to hear;

or it may say "Auspiciousness," or say "You shall receive the fruits you desire. Such instances are all auspicious dreams, which should be distinguished according to their superior, middling, or inferior categories.
Just as with temple buildings and the like, there is a distinction between those that rest upon the ground and those suspended in space;
likewise, among the people seen therein, there are differences such as male and female, or saint and ordinary person.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "One should examine and distinguish them with careful attention."

If these are contrary to the auspicious signs described previously—such as dreaming that one's body is being pursued by a mad elephant or other such creatures in a state of terror and peril; or riding upon a camel or a donkey; or seeing loathsome, wicked persons with tattered and ruined clothing; or seeing oneself lying face down in green mud and filth; or various impurities falling from the sky—all of these are contrary signs.
If the ācārya is one who practices the profound path, he shall naturally, within the context of yoga, fully know the matters of the disciple's dreams as well as the causes and conditions for them.
When the disciple rises at dawn and reports to the teacher, the teacher should, according to the circumstances, exhort and inspire him in order to sever the net of his doubts.

If one observes that a person lacks the capacity for accomplishment, then one should not bestow the Dharma upon them in its entirety; this is because one fears they will fail to produce results for a long time, or might give rise to doubt and slander.
Alternatively, as Guhya states, one should perform the homa for pacifying calamities; once all obstacles have been cleared away, one may then summon [the deity] to enter.
If various extraordinary visions appear, one should console and encourage them with Dharma words so that they attain joy.
That which is called "abiding well in the precepts" is, in Sanskrit, referred to as *suvrata*; this is an honorific title for a disciple, similar to such terms as "Son of the Buddha."
The verses spoken in the Sūtra are also Āryā; it is even better to recite them from the Sanskrit original, which is preserved here on the left:
*Iṣāgramalagavaraśrīde mahāyānam*. (Iṣā = this; agra = path; mala = wish; gava = excellent;
śrī = virtue; de = great; mahā = great; yāna = vehicle.)
HŪṂ. Protect the great, protect the mind, O Nārāyaṇa!

You who are firm, you who are the source of all emanations, you who are sought after, you who have accomplished the vast, you who are established in the state of others, the Tathāgata, the one possessing the *jñāna* of the *vajra*-family, the Great Nāga, the equal... Sa-ma.
*Lokeśvara*, who is like a stūpa; *asti*, there is;
*nāsti*, there is not; *vayaḥ*, youth; *kālāntara*, at another time; *ākāśa*, space; *miva*.
Ayathāyathā-lam-gu-ya-yan-bi-lan-shen-ao; sarva, all; dharma, phenomena;
apratigha-jñāna, that which even worldly wisdom cannot comprehend; amala-ālaya-sarva, the stainless storehouse of all.
*Prapañca-hetunā* means "by the cause of conceptual proliferation"; *prapañca* refers to conceptual proliferation, which is so called because it is devoid of reality;
*prapañcita* also refers to conceptual proliferation, stated here for emphasis;
*sarva* means "all"; *kṛtya* means "that which is to be done"; *rādu*.
Anupama-saṃdhā-nirvāṇa-samavasaraṇe 'nuttare dhyāna-mārga-vilāsini.
*Chikhan* (勅閑) means "extraordinary" (*viśiṣṭa*). *Rabise* (羅避設) means "attainment" (*prāpti*). *Tadane* (他捺曳) means "path" (*mārga*).
*Saddharmam* (薩𭍑哆) means "to abide. Generally, when the Sanskrit original concludes a verse, it adds a concluding particle pronounced as *iti*.
The first half-verse praises the path of the Secret Vehicle (*guhyayāna*).
The sublime vow refers to the vow for omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

If one enters this gate of pure bodhi, one then illuminates and perceives the path of clarity within the mental dharmas; that is to say, the Great Bodhi-path of the Buddhas of the past. Therefore, it is called this sublime path of vows.
The meaning of the "Great Mind" (*mahācitta*) is as previously explained in the section on the *mahāsattva*.

All great-minded beings of the past, future, and present who mount this precious vehicle proceed directly to the site of enlightenment; therefore, it is called the Great Vehicle of the Great Mind (*mahācitta-mahāyāna*).

The next verse praises the merit of the practitioner who has resolved upon bodhicitta; it bestows the prediction of great enlightenment by means of the "Dharma-seal of the certain attainment of all Tathāgatas. Thus it says: "Since you are now able to aspire with resolve, you shall achieve the Great Dragon of the Tathāgata’s spontaneous wisdom, whom the world honors like a stūpa."

"Self-existent wisdom" (svayambhū-jñāna) refers to the wisdom by which the Tathāgata has personally awakened to and realized for himself; it is the dharma never before heard or known, which manifests spontaneously and clearly before him without any obstruction, and thus receives this name.
Mahānāga is an epithet of the Tathāgata, used as a metaphor for his inconceivable and boundless great activity.

Caitya is translated as "Accumulation of Merit" (Puṇyaskandha), meaning that the entire mass of merits of all Buddhas is contained therein; therefore, worldly people all offer worship and pay homage to it in order to seek merit.
Now that you have resolved to attain bodhicitta, you are likewise able to encompass the boundless mass of merit of all Tathāgatas; therefore, the world should revere you as if you were a stūpa.
Next, there is one and a half verses that reveal the seal of the true aspect of the pure bodhicitta; this is precisely the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to make it pure.

"Transcending both existence and non-existence" refers to the inconceivable Middle Way arising from manifold conditions, which surpasses the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, and is neither existent nor non-existent. Because it is a realm where all mental measures (*cittamātra*) cannot operate, it is called the "Stainless Space Vajra Wisdom Seal."

That all dharmas are profoundly deep and mysterious is because the nature of the mind is profoundly deep; one should know that the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and so forth, up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), are likewise profoundly deep, for no dharma whatsoever transcends the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the mind.
Such a true reality can only be known by a Buddha and a Buddha; it is beyond the reach of conceptualization or discrimination, and is therefore called "profound and mysterious."

Regarding the phrase "that which worldly wisdom cannot comprehend": this nature of the mind cannot be conceived by any of those in the world who possess intelligence, keen faculties, or sharp wit. Even if great masters of treatises, such as the Brahmin Dīrghanakha, were to employ various causes, conditions, analogies, and metaphors to measure it through inference, it would ultimately remain beyond their domain. To contemplate it with arduous effort only serves to drive one to madness; it can be entered only by those whose power of faith is firm, relying upon these secret expedient means.

Regarding "that which has no storehouse" (*anālaya*), what is called "difficult to comprehend" refers precisely to this state of being without a storehouse. Because one knows the aggregates and the *ālayavijñāna* as they truly are—namely, that they are fundamentally unarisen—one has nothing to grasp and no storehouse. At that time, all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) of mind, mentation, and consciousness are entirely purified; the Dharma-realm shines forth perfectly like the autumn moon in the sky. Therefore, the next phrase says: "free from all conceptual proliferation."

The Sanskrit original states: "Free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and false imagination (*vikalpa*). Since the phrasing here is abbreviated within the verse yet the meaning remains unchanged, it is not preserved in full.

The subsequent phrase, "because conceptual proliferation is fundamentally non-existent," would, if the Sanskrit were preserved in its entirety, state: "because conceptual proliferation is without conceptual proliferation. This is because all conceptual proliferations arise from a multitude of conditions and possess no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because they lack intrinsic nature, they are primordially unarisen; thus, the preceding phrase is explained as "these very conceptual proliferations are themselves without proliferation.
Now, speaking in accordance with the intended meaning, it is said that they are "originally non-existent."
Next, there are two phrases that clarify the ultimate skillful means of this pure bodhicitta; by transcending all deluded karma, one is able to accomplish the wisdom-karma of the Tathāgata.
The universal gate of guidance and benefit is nothing other than a great causal condition; therefore, all that is performed is peerless, and thus it is said that "all karma is incomparable."
Next, the preceding phrase is further explained by providing a general overview of the grand framework of the provisional and the real; thus it says, "Always relying upon the two truths.
This is precisely what the treatise states: "The Buddhas, in preaching the Dharma, always rely upon the two truths."

However, the central tenet of this sutra is that the various skillful means involving constituent parts all conform to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); by virtue of these causes and conditions, attaining the seal of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna-mudrā*) is itself ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Therefore, conventional truth serves as the cause and ultimate truth as the fruit. The cause is like the four flavors, all of which are impermanent; the fruit is like *mākṣika* (clarified butter), which is eternal.

However, when viewed through the ten phrases of dependent origination, the true reality of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is itself the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); therefore, the provisional and the real are mutually identical, and both are inconceivable.

Although these two lines of text are concise, they enable the practitioner to have no further doubts regarding the skillful means (*upāya*) of all Tathāgatas; therefore, one should extend this principle by analogy so that the meaning of the text permeates the entire work.

Having briefly expounded the path to great enlightenment, he again provides a concluding exhortation for its upholding; thus it says, "This vehicle is supreme; may you abide in this path. This also serves to reiterate the meaning of the bestowal of the prophecy.
"At that time, Vajradhara Abiding in Non-conceptual Elaboration addressed the Buddha, saying:

'I pray that you will expound the precepts of unimpeded wisdom of the three times, so that no bodhisattva may dwell therein, and thereby cause all Buddhas and bodhisattvas to rejoice. This is because the preceding text had only spoken of receiving the unobstructed precepts of the three times without yet revealing their characteristics; therefore, Vajradhara Abiding in Non-elaboration (niṣprapañca) of the Vajrayāna posed this inquiry to bring forth [the teaching]."
Furthermore, the reason the World-Honored One speaks only in response to questions is also to clarify the entrustment of the Dharma-gate through mutual illumination.

This present pure precept takes as its essence the abiding in the Vajra-Wisdom Seal free from conceptual proliferation; therefore, he specifically addresses this Honored One, desiring that the correspondence between person and Dharma be transmitted with a designated locus for its preservation.
The Ācārya spoke again:

"These characteristics of the precepts are also mantras of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). When transmitting them, it is most excellent to first recite and uphold the Sanskrit original, and subsequently explain it through the vernacular language."
Now they are listed in full on the left:
Śrīṇu (listen well), kula-putra (son of noble family),
dānta-parākrama (if one who possesses self-restraint and valor).
Ayukula-puṭra, son of noble family; yakṣa-vajramāna, [the body, speech, and mind];
me-kaṭrāṇi-kṣapuna-raṃ (these are combined into one); akriśa, do not act; sarama.
Homage to the Dharma, the Peaceful One, all dharmas. What is the meaning of *yathā*?
It means "just as. *Tathāgata* means "thus come. *Pūjā* means "offering" to one's own body.
*Buddhabodhisattvavaiyāvṛtya* refers to service for the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. *Jñāna...* [the remainder of the text follows].
*Kaśmānti tu*, why is that? *Arye adya mama vaṃ*.
If one’s own self (*ātman*) is *pariṣad* (an assembly), or if it is *tyajati* (to abandon/give), then for those *tattvabodhatariyāṇām*.
*Āvaraṇa-kaṣāya-vāsanā-kleśa-mūrcchita-sattva-stūtra-yaṃ kathaṃ nāma svayaṃ-nuttara-jñāna-ātmaka-iti?
Deha iti ucyate.* [How is it that the body is called the self of unsurpassed primordial wisdom? It is called "body."
*Vākcittam* means body, speech, and mind; *tathāgata-kula* means "of the lineage of the Tathāgatas";

*kulaputra* means "son of good family"; *kṣānti-vīrya-dhyāna-samādhi-pratilabdha* means "one who has attained patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and samādhi"; *bodhisattva* means "an enlightened being."
Yebha vitta-vyam, one shall attain yatkasama-stu.
Why is this? Because of the *ārya-gaja-madana-saṃparitīrtha*.
One abandons that body, speech, and mind, as well as the *śikṣā-kṛt*.
Rahaśa, this is what should be studied. Gṛhṇa bodhisattva mahāsattva, O Bodhisattva Mahāsattva! Gṛhṇa, [take hold of] the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva!

Regarding the phrase "O Son of the Buddha, listen attentively," which serves as an introductory exhortation: *kula* in Sanskrit carries the meanings of "clan" or "section," while *putra* means "son. Thus, it signifies "Son of the Buddha."
If explained according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one born into any of the four castes is called a member of a great clan;

thus, they are termed "sons of noble family" (*kulaputra*). Now, having been born into the family of the Tathāgata, one is the most preeminent among all clans; therefore, one is termed a "son of noble family."
The Ācārya said: "One should understand the intent; to say 'son of the Buddha' implies attachment to the literal meaning.

As the Sūtra says: "If a son of noble family abides in these precepts, he should unify his body, speech, and mind into one. These precepts are called *śīla* in Sanskrit, which carries the sense of being co-arisen and co-accomplished through conditions. They are, in fact, the accumulation of wisdom, skillful means, and so forth.
If it is *śīla*, it carries the meaning of purity alone.

Furthermore, *trivara* has the meaning of equality. When the Buddha says that body, speech, and mind are unified as one, this refers to abiding in the Dharma-gate of the three equalities; therefore, it is named the "unobstructed precepts of the three periods of time."

Just as the Buddha briefly gave this instruction to the śrāvakas, saying, "These three paths of karmic action, when purified, constitute the path of the Great Sage," after twelve years he gradually expounded their meaning, establishing the various forms of discipline (vinaya).

Now, the meaning of the concise precepts for the Vidyādhara is likewise: if the practitioner’s three karmas and skillful means are entirely in accord with the state of the three equalities, one should know that they possess the ethical discipline (vinaya) of all Buddhas.

Furthermore, "tearing asunder the net of all conceptions" is the meaning of *tribhava*. This refers to the net of various views of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), which, with its warp and woof mutually supporting one another, is interwoven in layers; therefore, it is called a "net."

Now, when the practitioner contemplates that the karmas of body and speech have no separate substance of their own, and that by subsuming the derivative to the fundamental, they are but this single mind—wherein the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of this mind is eternally the equal *dharmadhātu*—then while abiding in this precept, all various karmas of body, speech, and mind are of one and the same mark. All nets of immeasurable views are entirely purified and removed; therefore, it is called "abiding in the Vajra Seal of Non-conceptual Elaboration."

The Sūtra states: "Not performing any dharmas" means that the various five aggregates depend upon afflictions, afflictions depend upon karma, and these various karmas all arise from body, speech, and mind.
Just as the ten paths of wholesome and unwholesome karma are categorized according to body, speech, and mind, when their ramifications are fully investigated, they are immeasurable and boundless.

Therefore, regarding the three types of action, whatever one practices constitutes a path of progress; to lose this progress is to fall into perverted conceptions. From these perverted conceptions, immeasurable mental images arise, and being obstructed by these various signs, one fails to attain the unimpeded wisdom of a Buddha.

Now, when a practitioner deeply contemplates the ten phrases of dependent origination and realizes that the three types of karma ultimately do not arise, and that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is inherently such that it is eternally without activity, this is called abiding in unconditioned precepts (*asaṃskṛta-śīla*).
If even such pure precepts are not made by the Tathāgata, how much less could one who abides in these precepts create any phenomena?
As the Sūtra says: "What is meant by 'precepts'?"
This refers to observing the relinquishing of one's own body and offering it to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Why is this?
Because if one relinquishes one's own body, one relinquishes those three things.
"What are the three?
They are body, speech, and mind. Next, this clarifies that by upholding the unconditioned precepts (*avijñapti-śīla*), one is endowed with wisdom and skillful means.
The practitioner contemplates that within the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the body, the body cannot be apprehended; this is precisely the liberation of the Tathāgata.

Therefore, one should completely relinquish this body to offer it to all Tathāgatas; from this point forward, whether moving or staying, acting or performing, whatever one does shall be for the sake of the liberation of the Tathāgatas, and not for one's own body.

Although one may zealously cultivate myriad practices to adorn buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is inherently so; it is not something produced through effort.
One who can practice and cultivate in this manner is said to possess an infinite mass of merit and an inexhaustible river of merit.

By casting even a single drop of the roots of goodness one has cultivated into the ocean of the Dharma-realm, one receives the ultimate salvation for the realm of sentient beings, which is likewise inexhaustible.

The Ācārya said: "In the recitation of the Sanskrit original, there is a verse that says: 'If there is one who is liberated and upholds this Dharma of liberation, and makes offerings to those who are liberated, this merit is the most supreme.'"

"If a practitioner of mantras does not understand such pure precepts, then even though they recite mantras with their mouth, maintain secret mudrās with their body, and abide in the samādhi of the deity with their mind, fully performing the successive rituals and making offerings to the various honored ones, they are still merely engaged in the fabrication of phenomena. As long as they have not escaped the net of self and person, how can they be called a Bodhisattva?"
Therefore, the Sūtra continues: "For this reason, son of good family, one is named a bodhisattva by virtue of receiving the precepts of body, speech, and mind.
Why is this? Because one is detached from that [defiled] body, speech, and mind."
"A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should train in this way.

Regarding what is to be trained in here, the old translation calls it *śikṣāpada* (or *śaikṣa-dharma*), which is like the fifth section of the *Prātimokṣa*, summarizing the rules of conduct and decorum found in the *Vinayavastu*.
It is the same for those who study the Mahāyāna: they should maintain these precepts as skillful means to universally enter into all mantra practices.
If one’s precepts are deficient and yet one can accomplish the bodhisattva conduct, such a thing is impossible.

The scripture states: "On the following day, having empowered oneself as Vajrasattva, one should prostrate to the World-Honored One Vairocana. This refers to the day after receiving the precepts, specifically the evening of the seventh day.

When performing various tasks such as constructing a maṇḍala, one should always empower oneself with Vajrasattva; that is to say, one should contemplate that one's own body is none other than Vajradhara.
The skillful means therein are as explained in the sūtra text of the lower volume and in the sequence of offerings.
If one encounters a Vidyācārya who has realized the Truths, he abides in the mind of Vajrasattva, which is the so-called "unequaled bodhicitta."
By virtue of this secret empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), there shall be nothing that can obstruct or destroy whatever is undertaken.

Next, one should direct the mind as before and pay homage to the Tathāgata Vairocana. Thereafter, one should empower the purification flask by reciting the Trailokyavijaya mantra; this is also the mantra for accomplishing all activities.

First, one should take a pure flask according to the Dharma and draw clean water, filtering it according to the ritual. Within it, place the five jewels and the five grains; furthermore, take various scented waters and various wonderful flowers and fruits, inserting their branches into the vessel. Adorn it in every way, and tie a fresh, clean cloth around its neck. All these should be performed according to the sequence of offerings, removing defilements and purifying with the *dharmadhātu* seed-syllable, and then performing the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
In general, there is no fixed limit for the number of recitations of mantras; they should be calculated by the number of syllables, as explained in the Susiddhi [Tantra].
Furthermore, therein, one should construct the maṇḍalas of the three families as appropriate and consecrate each with the heart-mantra or the mother-mantra of that respective family.

In this present sutra, the mantras for accomplishing all tasks are employed through empowerment; since these mantras include both extensive and concise versions, the specific number of recitations is not detailed here and should be determined according to one's own intention.
If the practitioner is of the highest capacity, they should recite it one hundred times; for those of intermediate capacity, five hundred times; and for those of lesser capacity, one thousand times.
Once the consecration is complete, the object should be placed outside the sandalwood gate previously delineated with white sandalwood paste.
Those who wish to enter the maṇḍala should first sprinkle [the water] upon them with this, so that their latent obstacles may be purified and they may then behold the maṇḍala.

Furthermore, one should prepare perfumed water in a separate vessel, blending various exquisite fragrances such as saffron, camphor, and sandalwood, and likewise empower it with mantras; this should then be given to them to drink in small amounts.

This is called the Vajra Water; through secret empowerment, even the heavy obstructions of the hells are entirely extinguished, so that one becomes pure both internally and externally, fit to be a vessel for the Dharma.
The Ācārya said: "This is called the water of oath;

it also accords with worldly convention, like the rite of a solemn pledge. It causes one to take this fragrant water before all the holy ones and make a self-vow of heart, ensuring that one shall never retreat from the vow for great bodhi."

Furthermore, by blending the fragrance of unimpeded ethical discipline with the water of the pure and white mind—the gateway of the syllable VAṂ—all who drink from or touch it will certainly attain unsurpassed bodhi.
When one has thus purified the mind, one is fit to enter the secret maṇḍala.
From the passage beginning "At that time, the Vajradhara Lord of Secrets questioned the Buddha in verse," the text clarifies the constituent parts for the construction of the maṇḍala.
In this verse, the Buddha is first praised:
"May the All-Knowing One, the foremost among all preachers of the Dharma, explain that period of time.
This period of time refers to the duration from the initial drawing of the maṇḍala until its completion.

Next, regarding the statement, "At what time will the great assembly gather universally, manifesting spiritual omens? this refers to the time when all the universal gate bodies corresponding to various types within the Great Compassion Womb Matrix (Mahākaruṇā-garbha) gather universally at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), manifest before one's eyes through the empowerment of supernatural power (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and display their majestic efficacy.

If a disciple’s faculties are pure and sharp, and their capacity for deliverance is profound, they may at this very moment personally behold the boundless assembly of sages; just as those seated at the assembly on Vulture Peak see them together, there is no difference in seeing the various Buddhas of the three transformations and their manifested bodies within the Pure Land.

It should be understood that at that time, it is precisely when the maṇḍala-ācārya transmits and upholds words of truth and performs the deeds of the Tathāgata; therefore, it is said that one should "earnestly maintain the mantra."
Having spoken this verse, at that time the World-Honored One addressed the Holder of Vajra-Wisdom, saying:
"One should always construct a maṇḍala during this night."
This refers to the completion of the Dharma-ritual during this seventh night.
Within this context, the period from after sunset until the appearance of the dawn light is collectively termed "night."

At the onset of the first watch of the night, one should immediately prepare the drawings for the various deities and arrange the ritual offerings; these must all be dispatched before the appearance of the dawn light.
If one violates this rule, obstacles will arise, and even the dwelling place where one resides will become inauspicious.

However, in the profound and secret exegesis, "time" refers precisely to the auspicious convergence of the conditions for the Way; or, through the skillful means of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), one may condense a hundred kalpas into a single night, or expand a single night into a hundred kalpas. Length and brevity depend upon conditions and have no fixed limit.

If the ācārya is one of limited practice, he must strictly adhere to the ritual rules: during the daytime, he should demarcate the boundaries and use white sandalwood powder and other materials to define the positions and divisions of the various deities.
When the day approaches its close, prepare incense, flowers, lamps, candles, and so forth; all should have been prepared in advance.

Guhyasamāja states: "In a certain location on the northern side of the maṇḍala, use white [powder] to draw the boundary and employ the mantra for accomplishing tasks to clear away all obstacles, and then arrange the various offerings."

The Ācārya said: "If you are unable to complete the painting of all the Venerable Ones within a single night, it is not contrary to principle to proceed gradually, beginning from the fifth day after the consecration of the site."
Furthermore, there are three other types of expedient means consisting of honored forms, seals (*mudrā*), and syllables (*akṣara*), as explained in the following text.
The Sūtra speaks of the "Dharma-transmitting Ācārya"; once the proper timing is known, one clearly understands the ritual procedures for their construction and establishment.

When the sun has set, the ācārya and his assistant disciples, having each bathed according to the dharma and donned fresh, clean robes, shall generate the mind of great compassion and, carrying the offerings, proceed to the site of the maṇḍala.
First, one should perform the empowerment according to the specific rites for each individual, as explained in the sequence of offerings.
Next, one should protect oneself in accordance with the Dharma.
Summon the disciples to be initiated; provide protection for them, sprinkle them with scented water, and have them all sit together in order.
Thereafter, the ācārya goes before the entrance of the maṇḍala, extends his mind universally, and prostrates with his head to all the Buddhas of the ten directions, as described above.
Thereafter, holding a five-colored thread, one stands facing the position of the maṇḍala and wears it upon the crown of the head.
Next, one visualizes oneself as Vairocana; this is what is meant in the Sūtra by the phrase, "One performs the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) upon oneself as Mahāvairocana."

Why is this so? Because Mahāvairocana Tathāgata is the ācārya of this Great Compassion Womb Matrix (Mahākaruṇā-garbha). Therefore, when a practitioner performs the duties of an ācārya, they should immediately regard themselves as Vairocana.
When performing various ritual activities within the maṇḍala of conditions, one should manifest oneself as Vajrasattva.
The method for this empowerment is as explained in the subsequent sections and in the *Pūjāvidhi*.
Furthermore, the practitioner should know that the eight directions are to be protected; all mandalas that are constructed revolve according to these.

Indra is in the east, and proceeding in order, one reaches Yama in the south, Varuṇa in the west, Vaiśravaṇa in the north, Īśānī in the northeast, Agni (Homa) in the southeast, Nairṛti in the southwest, and Vāyu in the northwest.

The deities in the upper section mostly rely on the right side of Śakra, while those in the lower section mostly rely on the right side of the Nāga Honored Ones; "upper" refers to those dwelling in the sky, and "lower" refers to those dwelling on the earth.

Furthermore, within the circular center, the threefold layers of the Womb Realm (garbhadhātu) and the city walls have all been pre-marked so that the cardinal directions and intermediate points are equal and the positions on the diagram are predetermined; it is essential that the position of Vairocana be situated at the heart of the fivefold heap of jewels.

When reaching this stage of delineating the various features, the ācārya first proceeds to the Indra direction (East) and performs the ritual prostrations according to the rules; next, he stands facing north in the Agni direction (Southeast), while his assistant disciple remains in the Īśāna direction (Northeast), holding the cord to establish the outer boundary accordingly.
The disciple then proceeds to circumambulate clockwise to the nairṛtya direction; the master likewise turns clockwise to face west and holds [the object] opposite him.
The ācārya then again circumambulates clockwise to the vāyu direction; the disciple likewise turns clockwise to face north and holds [the object] opposite him.
The disciple again circumambulates to the right until reaching Aiśānī, while the master likewise turns to the right, facing east, and holds [the cord] together with him.
When one complete circuit has been finished, he causes it to be aligned precisely in the space above, perfectly even and level.
Upon reaching the second circuit, one likewise turns to the right as before, marking the lines in succession to form the boundary paths.
Next, one determines the four intermediate directions accordingly.
The Ācārya should again circumambulate to the south-west (Nairṛti), while the disciple, previously stationed at the north-east (Īśāna), turns to the right to face him and hold [the cord].

The disciple then circumambulates clockwise again until reaching the Vāyu direction; the master immediately turns clockwise to the Homa direction, and the disciple likewise turns clockwise to face him as they hold [the object], ensuring it is level with the navel and fixed in its position within the air.
The disciple then circumambulates to the right again, reaching the nairṛti direction; the master then turns to the right and draws a line from the īśāna position directly opposite him.
The disciple then circumambulates to the right again, reaching the homa direction; the master then turns to the right and likewise draws a line from the vāyu direction directly opposite him.

The Ācārya said: "As for the four cardinal directions and the cross-shaped boundary lines, although they are not explicitly mentioned in the sūtras, they must necessarily exist in principle; furthermore, they must also be fixed by stretching the cords while circling to the right."

Having thus completed the determination of the external boundaries and the characteristics of the eight directions, one should next enter the interior; first, determine the external boundary of the central womb, likewise using the previously described method of rotating the cord to mark out the four square directions.
Once the characteristics of the eight directions have been fixed, they shall not be altered again.
Next, fix the outer boundary of the first layer, and then fix the outer boundary of the second layer; these follow the same procedure as the central matrix.
Regarding their dimensions of breadth and width, each successive layer should be reduced by half.

For example, if the central matrix (garbhadhātu) measures eight feet in length and breadth, the first layer should be four feet wide, the second layer two feet wide, and the third layer one foot wide.
The Ācārya said: "The fundamental method is thus.
If you fear that there may be a great disparity between large and small [quantities], you may slightly adjust them according to your own judgment; there is no loss in principle."
Having thus completed the division, each of these sections is further divided into three parts, one within another.
The innermost section is the circumambulatory path; therefore, it is called "the path traversed by the sons of the Buddha."

The next inner portion is the place for arranging the various offering articles, and the subsequent outer portion is the place for arranging the seats of the deities; therefore, these two portions both constitute the stations of the noble deities.

Next, beyond this, one should again establish a surrounding boundary; within this space, one should direct the mind to observe and universally invite and make offerings to all the deities corresponding to their respective positions and directions.

The reason for this is that if the ācārya should forget or err during the ritual proceedings, such as failing to properly arrange the various deities or omitting those who should be summoned but lack a designated position, one should direct the mind toward this [central area] to perform offerings for them all.
Regarding this division of the three stages of the site: first, within the inner portion of the first outer boundary, select a small area as the boundary for the enclosure.
As for its width and extent, one should determine it according to one's own judgment, ensuring that there is sufficient space for the seating arrangement.

Within this boundary for the objects of focus, divide it into three equal parts. First, one should determine the internal boundary for the seating of the deities; next, determine the intermediate boundary for the circumambulation and offerings. Thus concludes the first layer.
Next, in the second layer, one likewise divides it gradually from the outside toward the inside.
Next, one divides the third layer; as stated in the preceding text, the light emanating from below the navel of Mahāvairocana constitutes this third layer.
The light emitted from above the navel up to the throat constitutes the second stage;
the light from above the throat up to the crown of the head constitutes the first stage.
The womb within it is the eight-petaled lotus of Vairocana’s own mind.

As for the vajra-disciples who together establish the maṇḍala, they must thoroughly master the essential points of the mantra-dharma; by drawing near to the teacher, they will be able to assist one another without any omission.
If such a person cannot be found, one should instead take someone who has already received empowerment according to the Dharma and instruct them to perform the rite when the occasion arises.
Furthermore, if even such a person is unavailable, one should plant a ritual stake (kīla) to serve as a substitute.

First, drive a stake beneath the master’s position in the southeast (Agni) direction; next, place one in the northeast (Īśāna) direction and draw a line between them. The master first mentally notes that the stake in the southeast is his own position, and then draws the line from Īśāna to the northwest (Nairṛti). The rest should be understood by following this same procedure.
The Ācārya further said:

"If one wishes to draw the guiding line together, it is necessary to select those disciples who are to receive the empowerment; first, sprinkle them with consecrated perfumed water and perform the ritual together."
"The painted positions for the sandalwood [altar] and so forth should be covered with objects for the time being, so that they are not seen.

Regarding the four gates of the Vaipulya [mandala], this means that each successive courtyard is provided with four gates, arranged so that they are perfectly centered and equal; one gate is opened facing west to facilitate entry and exit, while the remaining gates are cross-segmented with lines.

Guhya said: "Whenever a direction opens a gate, one should divide that quarter into nine parts according to its breadth and width; taking one central part as the gate, the remaining eight parts are then divided such that four parts are obtained on each side of the gate."
"The gates through which one enters and exits should be made somewhat wide; all other gates should be closed by drawing them with white powder. The Ācārya said:
"Having completed the demarcation using the vajra-line to form a horizontal barrier, it shall be like a vajra that cannot be transgressed; whoever transgresses it violates the samaya."
"Furthermore, the main entrance of the hall faces west; if there is a specific cause or condition for opening it toward another direction, there is no fault in principle.
The rest is as explained in the text below.

Regarding the phrase, “With a sincere and profound mind, one manifests the assembly of all the Honored Ones,” this means that at the time of painting, one first abides in *yoga* and contemplates this great assembly of the maṇḍala. One must clearly and fully visualize each and every form, color, appearance, dignified demeanor, category, seat, and mudrā as being present before one. Thereafter, with a boundless and earnestly reverent mind, one paints it; even the proportions of large and small, or the density of spacing, must be made uniform and harmonious. Therefore, it is said: “Thus one creates the various forms, well-discriminated and perfectly balanced.”
"The wondrous white lotus within the heart" refers to the fundamental mind of sentient beings, the secret emblem of the exquisite *puṇḍarīka* flower of the sublime Dharma.
Its eight petals form a circular and perfectly symmetrical shape, like that of a flower in full bloom.
This lotus pedestal is the natural wisdom of the true mark (*dharmatā*), and the lotus petals are the skillful means of great compassion (*mahākaruṇopāya*).

It is precisely for this reason that this treasury is called the body of the Great Compassion Womb Maṇḍala; the remaining three layers flow forth from these self-realized merits and serve as the gateways to the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) for all spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

The four petals of the square [mandala] represent the four wisdoms of the Tathāgata, and the four petals at the corners represent the four practices of the Tathāgata; manifesting as these eight kinds of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), each holds the seal of adamantine wisdom (*vajraprajñāmudrā*), which is why it is said that they "emerge everywhere from between the petals."

These sixteen dharmas are each equal to the dharma-realm; there is not even the slightest degree of inequality among them, and thus their defining characteristics are in perfect accord with the profound mystery.

Briefly summarized, the ten thousand virtues of the Tathāgata are condensed into sixteen finger-widths; yet when extended, they are immeasurable and boundless. Therefore, this maṇḍala has a minimum measurement of sixteen finger-widths, while its maximum is limitless.

The "pollen of the temples" refers to all the gates of samādhi, the gates of dhāraṇī, the six perfections, the eighteen kinds of emptiness, and so forth, as described in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
From each and every filament of the ear-ornaments, by virtue of the power of empowerment, there manifest the various types of majestic retinues within the threefold maṇḍalas.
This is the secret transmission of the Tathāgata; it cannot be fully expressed through brush and ink, and thus it is entrusted to images to instruct practitioners.
Those who grasp its profound meaning will naturally comprehend it in silence.

From within this flower pedestal of the true nature (*dharmatā*), there is manifested the sign of the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana; its meaning has already been explained as previously stated.
As for the remaining eight secret mudrās, they will be described below in the text and illustrations.

Next, in the inner court of the eastern direction, above the Great Tathāgata Vairocana, one should paint the seal of Sarvajña (the All-Knowing One) in the shape of a triangle with its apex pointing downward, surrounded by pure white light-flames, resting upon a white lotus flower.
This is the Great Heroic Seal (*mahāvīra-mudrā*) of all Tathāgatas of the ten directions and three periods of time; it is also called the Heart Seal (*hṛdaya-mudrā*) of the Buddhas.

The triangle signifies the meaning of subduing and removing obstacles; that is to say, while seated beneath the Bodhi tree, the Buddha subdued the four Māras through his majestic and powerful might, thereby attaining Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

The brilliant white is the color of great compassion; it is for this very purpose that the Tathāgata, through the power of his lion-like, vigorous, and great diligence, emanates rays of great compassion that constantly pervade the entire Dharma-realm—hence it is said to be "universally pervasive."
Next, to the north of Mahāvīra, one reaches the northern quarter where Akāśanetra is placed; she is the Mother of Vairocana Buddha.
The iconography of the Mother of Buddhas is as extensively described in the "Chapter on the Mother of Buddhas" (*Buddhamātṛparivarta*) of the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Pure gold is the essence of the suchness of reality;
the phrase "ultimate purity" is its external ornamentation within the gates of teaching, which is why it is said, "using white silk as clothing."

When all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) ceases, the radiance of the sun of the mind shines upon everything without exception; hence it is said, "pervasive illumination like the light of the sun.
Only those who possess a tranquil and single-minded heart can perceive this, and thus its manifestation is like the image of a celestial maiden abiding in meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).
Next, to the south of Mahāvīra, reaching the southern quarter, one forms the Cintāmaṇi seal of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
This is the accumulation of the boundless practices and vows of the pure bodhicitta, which can constantly and universally rain down all mundane and supramundane wealth and treasures.
All the Saviors manifest such jewels from within the naturally pure lotus throne; therefore, it is said that they "dwell upon white lotuses. The Ācārya says:
"This is a seal that applies universally to all; it may also be placed in every direction."
"If the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not mention the specific mudrās to be held in their sūtras, one should likewise hold these; thus, all priceless jewels will be obtained.
Generally, this first layer consists of the Buddha’s body adorned with various virtues above, and the Buddha’s vidyādhara messengers below; both are termed the "Tathāgata Section."
The right side represents the Tathāgata’s samādhi of great compassion, which can nourish and flourish all manner of goodness; therefore, it is called the Lotus Family (Padmakula).
The left side represents the Tathāgata’s power and function of great wisdom, which can shatter and destroy the three obstructions; therefore, it is called the Vajra Family (Vajrakula).
Therefore, entering the gateway of the letter *A*, all dharmas are unborn; this is the meaning of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Entering the gateway of the letter *Sa*, all dharmas are free from defilement and attachment; this is the meaning of the lotus.
Entering the syllable-gateway *ja*, all phenomena are beyond verbal expression; this is the meaning of "vajra.
This is intended to mean that, as in the "Chapter on the Wheel of Syllables" (*Akṣaracakravatīparivarta*) below, these three syllables encompass the hundred luminosities (*vidyā*).
The Sūtra states: "To the right of Mahāvairocana, place Mahāvīra Avalokiteśvara. This is the lord of the Padma family.
It means that because the Tathāgata has ultimately contemplated the ten phrases of dependent origination and attained this universal-eye lotus, he is named Avalokiteśvara.
Because he practices the conduct of the Tathāgata, he is called a Bodhisattva.
"The Immeasurable Life appears at the crown" clarifies that the ultimate fruit of this practice is precisely the Tathāgata’s wisdom of universal gateways and skillful means.
This image and the body of the Bodhisattva both display an expression of joyful, smiling serenity, abiding in the bliss of the present dharma (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
The color of Avalokiteśvara’s body is like that of the pure moon or like a *śaṅkha*—that is, a most excellent conch shell.
Or it is like the *kumuda* flower; this flower originates in the West and is also exceedingly fresh and white.
One should take these three metaphors together to describe its light as fresh, lustrous, and penetrating—the very pinnacle of whiteness.
Next, to the right of Avalokiteśvara, one should paint the Bodhisattva Tārā.
All the holy beings face toward Mahāvairocana; thus, "to the right of Avalokiteśvara" means facing west from his seat, and this principle applies to all others as well.
This is the samādhi of Avalokiteśvara; therefore, she manifests in the form of a woman.

"Tārā" has the meaning of "eye," and the blue lotus has the meaning of "pure and stainless. Because she embraces all sentient beings with such universal eyes—neither before nor after [the present moment]—she appears as a middle-aged woman, her appearance being neither too old nor too young.

Blue is the color of subjugation, and white is the color of great compassion; their excellence lies in the integration of these two functions, which causes the two colors to harmonize. For this reason, it is neither blue nor white.
The image has its palms joined, holding this blue lotus within them; both hands and faces are turned toward Avalokiteśvara, appearing as if in a gentle smile.

Its entire body is encircled by a halo of pure golden color, and it wears white robes. On its head is a topknot fashioned in the style of a celestial tiara, which differs from the hair-crown of Mahāvairocana.

To the left of Avalokiteśvara is placed the noble Bhṛkuṭī; her body has four hands: the right hand holds a garland of various flowers, one hand performs the varada mudrā, the left hand holds a lotus flower, and one hand grasps a kamaṇḍalu.
His face has three eyes, resembling the image of Maheśvara.
On his head he wears a hair-crown, shaped like the topknot-crown of Vairocana.
As for what is called "holding," it is like saying that the earth holds all things; this carries the meaning of supporting and sustaining.

His body is pure white, encircled by a halo of light; within this light are present the three colors—yellow, red, and white—and because it is not purely white, purely red, or purely yellow, it is said to have "no single master."

Generally, yellow is the color of augmentation; white is the color for pacifying calamities; and red is the color for subjugation. Since these three powers are all contained within the light of this samādhi, they are therefore employed as its insignia.

Next, to the left of Mahāpratisarā, one should paint the Honored One Mahāsthāmaprāpta. He is called "Great Power" because his majesty and influence are sovereign, like those of a worldly king or a great minister.
This noble being is so named because he has attained such a state of mastery over great compassion.

The reason for holding the unfurled lotuses is that once the flower-pedestal of Vairocana’s ultimate wisdom has borne fruit, he again takes such seeds and scatters them universally into the waters of the minds of all sentient beings, causing further unfurled lotuses to arise.

The traces of this Honored One are identical to those of this place; he is also able to universally protect the latent sprouts of goodness in all sentient beings, ensuring they are not destroyed or injured, but rather increase with every thought-moment. He is precisely the Vidyārāja of the Lotus Family.
Next, to the left of the Vidyārāja, paint the Vidyārājñī Yaśodharā, translated as "She Who Holds Renown.
Her body is of true golden color, adorned with various necklaces and ornaments so that she is exceedingly beautiful, like the image of a goddess.
In his right hand he holds a branch of exquisite white flowers, with fruits and leaves interspersed, long-stemmed and luxuriantly beautiful.
Among the flowers, some are still buds, some are about to open, and some are in full bloom—whether five, ten, or even several dozen.
The left hand holds the *utpala* flower, which is likewise a supreme flower of the Western direction.

Because the Great Power Vidyārāja presides over the establishment of the seeds of bodhi for all sentient beings, while this consort presides over the containment and production of the various merits therein, her attire and insignia are all consistent with this meaning.
To the right of Tārā, place Paṇḍaravāsinī, translated as "White Abode," so named because this Honored One always dwells within a white lotus flower.
She also wears a crown of matted hair reaching toward the heavens and is clad in pure white garments; with her left hand, she holds a blossoming lotus flower.
From this most pure and white place, the Universal Eye (Samantacakṣus) is born; therefore, this samādhi is named the Mother of the Lotus Family.
Next, below Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, place Hayagrīva, translated as "Horse-Head.
His body is neither yellow nor red, having the color of the newly risen sun.
Adorned with white lotus flowers as necklaces and other ornaments, his body is majestic;

his radiant flames are fierce and brilliant like a garland, his fingernails are long and sharp, and two fangs protrude upward from his mouth. His hair on the head resembles the mane of a lion, and he assumes an expression of extreme roaring fury—this is the Wrathful Vidyārāja of the Lotus Family.
Just as the precious horse of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) traverses the four continents, its mind never ceasing to move at any time or in any place;
so too is the great power of the bodhisattvas' diligence.

The reason he attains such majestic and fierce power, undaunted by life or limb as he subdues many within the heavy obstacles of birth and death, is precisely because of his pure and great compassionate heart; therefore, he adorns his own body with a necklace of white lotuses.
Having thus completed the ritual establishment of the various retinues of Avalokiteśvara,
next, to the left of Mahāvairocana Tathāgata, one should install the Vidyārāja of the Vajra Family, namely Vajrapāṇi, who is capable of fulfilling all wishes.
Its color is like that of the *pāṭalī* flower, which is a pale yellow;
or it is like an emerald (*marakata*), which is a green *vajra*-gem, appearing like the manifest color of space.
Because the color of the pure dharma-realm is blended with adamantine wisdom, his body is yellowish-white.
This wisdom-body is like space, indestructible, and such that no one can subdue it; therefore, the manifest color of space is used as its emblem.
This means: if any phenomenon, even down to its smallest fraction such as an atom, were perceivable, it would be subject to impermanence and the transformations of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Therefore, the wisdom of ultimate emptiness is the foremost among all firm natures.
The secret mudrā it upholds is the five-pronged vajra.

The wisdoms of the five Tathāgatas all encompass both provisional and ultimate functions, yet they hold them within with the hand of adamantine wisdom; therefore, it is said that the left hand holds a *vajra*.
This mudrā should be universally encircled by a garland of light; hence it is said that "light-flames arise all around.

He wears a three-peaked jewel crown upon his head, its shape like the letter *śa*; between the peaks, they take the form of crescent moons, both upright and inverted. His body is adorned with various exquisite miscellaneous jewels and all manner of necklaces.

This means that when the *prajñāpāramitā* reaches the mind of the stage of fruition (*phalabhūmi*), it is renamed "all-aspect wisdom" (*sarvākārajñatā*); therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] "wears a crown of various jewels upon his head."

By means of this wondrous wisdom, one extensively traverses all phenomena, freely revolving them to give rise to the adornments of the infinite Dharma-realm; therefore, it is said that they are interspersed and mutually adorned.
"Vast and numerous" means their number is immeasurable.
Next, to the right of the Lord of the Vajra Family, one places Mañjuśrī (Maṅ-mang-ki), who is the Mother of the Vajra Family.
She also holds the vajra-wisdom scepter, and her body is adorned with various necklaces and ornaments.
This is the samādhi that gives birth to the vajra-intelligence power, namely the Vajra-samādhi.
Next, to the right of the Family Mother, place the Great Powerful Vajra-Needle; Suji translates this as "Vajra-needle," which holds a single-pronged *vajra* as its emblem.

This Vajra is the wisdom that is singular in its mark and singular in its object, firm and sharp; by means of it, one penetrates all phenomena without anything remaining unpenetrated, and for this reason it is called the "Vajra Needle."

Beneath them are two messengers, both in the form of women; they kneel on their right knees, smiling and gazing up at him with blinking eyes. Their appearance is humble yet full, and they are a pale yellow color; they take the vajra as their emblem. This is the samādhi that destroys heavy obscurations.
Next, to the left of Vajradhara, place Vajraśaṅkara, translated as "Vajra-Chain.

His mudrā consists of holding a linked chain, both ends of which are fashioned in the shape of a vajra; beneath the chain there are also two female messengers, no different from those of the Vajrasūcī messenger.
Because this seal of wisdom gathers and sustains all stubborn and difficult-to-transform sentient beings, causing them not to regress from unsurpassed bodhi, it is named accordingly.
Next, below Vajradhara, one should place the wrathful vidyādhara known as Candramaṇḍala, who subdues all great obstructors of the three times.

His face has three eyes and four fangs protrude; his complexion is like the color of clouds during the summer rains, he displays a form of great laughter, and he wears a necklace made of vajra-jewels.
This is the samādhi of the Vajradhara for protecting sentient beings through immeasurable gateways of great power and majesty;
he is surrounded by an immeasurable retinue.
They were all lowly yet full;
they assumed wrathful forms, even with a single body possessing hundreds of thousands of hands, brandishing various weapons that stood up in a terrifying array.
If it is impossible to depict them all, one should instead draw one or two messengers, or even five or six, all of whom should stand upon lotuses.

This is intended to clarify that within the heart of these lotuses, all the power of courageous and great diligence is spontaneously accomplished by the very nature of reality (*dharmatā*), and does not come from any other source.
Having completed the establishment of the retinue of Vajrasattva,
one next proceeds to the western direction to paint the Tathāgata-vidyādharas and the assembly of Vajradharas.
Various forms, colors, natures, and types of secret mudrās and insignia are all manifested within the diagrams.

Each and every honored one possesses the great wisdom-light that pervades the entire dharma-realm, and the secrets of their body, speech, and mind likewise pervade the dharma-realm; therefore, it is said: "Universally emitting perfect light for the sake of all sentient beings."
Below this, in the direction of Nairṛti, one should draw the Tathāgata messenger Acala, appearing in the form of a youth.

His right hand holds the seal of the Great Wisdom Sword (*mahāprajñā-khaḍga-mudrā*), and his left hand holds a noose (*pāśa*). He has a topknot (*uṣṇīṣa*) on his head, with his hair curled and hanging over his left shoulder. His left eye is slightly closed, and he bites his upper lip on the right side with his lower teeth; the lower lip on the left side is slightly turned outward. On his forehead is a mark (*tilaka*) resembling the ripples of water, and he sits upon a stone.
His body is lowly yet full and robust; he displays a posture of fierce wrath and an appearance of extreme indignation—this is the characteristic mark of his secret mudrā.

Although this Honored One attained Buddhahood long ago upon the flower pedestal of Vairocana, by virtue of his samaya and original vow, he manifests the form of one who has first resolved upon the Great Mind and whose physical marks are incomplete, serving as a servant and attendant to the Tathāgata and performing all manner of tasks.
The reason for holding a sharp blade and a lasso is to carry out the command of the Tathāgata’s wrathful activity, intending to slay all sentient beings.

The lasso is the skillful means of the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) within the bodhicitta; by binding with it those who have not been subdued, one cuts their endless life-force of karma with the sharp blade of wisdom, causing them to attain birth in the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*).
If the seeds of karma and lifespan are eliminated, then the winds of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) will also all subside; therefore, one should keep the mouth closed.

With the intention of looking with "one eye," it is made clear that the Tathāgata regards all sentient beings with an impartial gaze such that none may be excused; thus, whatever deeds this Honored One performs, they are solely for the sake of this single purpose.

It stabilizes the heavy obstructions and the underlying rock so that they no longer move, thereby forming the Wondrous High Mountain King of the pure bodhicitta; hence it is said, "dwelling securely upon the rock."

Furthermore, at the lower northwest corner, one should visualize the wrathful Vidyārāja Trailokyavijaya, wearing a jeweled crown and holding a five-pronged vajra seal; he gazes up at Vairocana in the manner of one awaiting instructions and commands.
Regarding the verse’s phrase “disregarding one's own body and life,” it means that one should assume an expression of ultimate wrath, showing no regard for one's life.

This refers to the desire to summon all sentient beings of the *dharmadhātu* so that they all submit to the majestic command of the Dharma King; this is also a mantra for accomplishing all activities (*sarvakarmasādhana*).

Those who are cleansed and destroyed by the great sovereign power of the wisdom of these five Tathāgatas all reach the adornment of the stage of fruition; it is not merely that they realize a partial emptiness free from all obstacles.
