Now, this sutra possesses the causes and conditions for the eight mental states—those that oppose the world and those that accord with the world—to continue and increase in succession; even unto the pure bodhicitta, which takes the five-syllable gateway as its condition to give rise to the root of great compassion, such that the Buddha’s śāla tree grows and spreads, filling the entire dharma realm.

However, because all phenomena, by means of these five letter-gates, are fundamentally unborn, beyond verbal expression, pure by nature, devoid of causes and conditions, and characterized like space, they cannot be nurtured or increased.

Furthermore, from the letter *A* onwards, they are explained through successive interpretation until one reaches the ultimate equality of all phenomena, wherein there is neither high nor low. Because there is no high or low, it should be known that there is likewise no increase.
Regarding the statement, “The letter-gateway *ṇa*: because enmity (*pratigha*) is unattainable in all phenomena,” the Sanskrit term is *ṇamara*, which carries the meaning of enmity.
Just as in the world, enemies retaliate against one another, it is therefore called "opposition" (*prati-gha*).
Furthermore, what was previously termed "waging war against an enemy" refers to mutual engagement between two parties;
whereas "hostile opposition" in this context carries the sense of avoiding an avenger. These Sanskrit terms are distinct from one another.
In the Vinaya, the Buddha taught that if one repays enmity with enmity, the enmity will never cease; only by being without enmity can enmity be extinguished.
He further stated that women are the enemies of those who practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
The *Anantārthasūtra* also states that the enemies of birth and death naturally disintegrate.

One realizes the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), which is half of the Buddha-land’s treasures; therefore, when a practitioner encounters the gateway of the letter *Na*, they know that all phenomena possess their opposites, which is termed "knowing the characteristics of letters."

Furthermore, because all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen and even their growth cannot be apprehended, one should know that adversaries likewise are fundamentally unarisen and possess no growth whatsoever.
Therefore, the Tathāgata ultimately has no adversary; this is the true meaning of the gateway of letters known as "Ṭa.

Regarding the gateway of the letter "Ṭa," it is because the grasping and maintaining of all dharmas cannot be apprehended. In the Sanskrit language, *ṭaṅka* carries the meaning of "grasping" or "maintaining."
By placing a bindu (dot) above the letter *ca*, it is transformed into the sound *ṅa*; thus, their essence is identical.
Furthermore, what is called *kṣara* is also another name for this.
The Sūtra states that he was possessed by a ghostly specter, or as it is also said, held by a non-human being.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that his possession was entirely the work of the *Bhūta* spirit named Kṣayamkara.
Because they are attached to one another and do not separate, it is given this name.
As for the sun, moon, and the five planets, because they also follow one another from beginning to end, the Sanskrit term is *graha*, which is translated as "the nine graspers" (*jiuzhi*).
The month when the [solar] signs truly meet at one point is called *ṛtu-prāpta* in the Indian calendar;
this carries the meaning of "being possessed," which is different from the sense of *dhāraṇī*.

Upon seeing this gateway of the letter *ṭa*, one immediately understands that all sentient beings, since beginningless time, have been possessed by the four Māras and are unable to abandon them—this is the characteristic of names.
Now, because one observes through various gateways such as the letter A that all phenomena are ultimately unattainable, one should know that all phenomena are without enmity or opposition.

Because enmity is fundamentally unarisen, one ultimately does not, by means of the equal dharma-realm, cling to the equal dharma-realm; therefore, it is said that the grasping and maintaining of all dharmas are unobtainable.
Regarding the phrase "The gateway of the letter *ta*: because the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena cannot be apprehended," the Sanskrit term *tathatā* means "suchness.
Within the phonetic flow of the word, there is also the sound of "attainment" (*lābha*); thus, the realization of suchness is precisely the meaning of liberation.

As for what is called the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena: when all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) arising from various unreal views are extinguished, it remains eternally as its original nature, indestructible.
If one perceives the gateway of the letter "Da" (the first syllable), one immediately knows that all phenomena are the mark of suchness (*tathatā*); this is called the "mark of the syllable."
However, there is a class of non-Buddhists who postulate a nature such as *tathatā* (suchness), claiming that if one knows and perceives this, it is called liberation.
Although they speak thus, they are merely applying a different name to the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
Nāgārjuna maintained that when the Śrāvaka sūtras speak of the "abiding of dharmas" (dharmasthiti), this also refers to the suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena.
Because their penetration was not yet profound, they gave rise to the notion of "extinction" (nirvāṇa), believing they had realized parinirvāṇa.

However, saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are mutually dependent phenomena. If one knows that saṃsāra has, from the very beginningless limit, always been of the same nature as nirvāṇa, then in relation to what would it be called "nirvāṇa"?
Therefore, all dharmas are ultimately neither real nor unreal, neither suchness nor different.
The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* also states: "The limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of nirvāṇa and the limit of the world (*lokānta*)—between these two limits, there is not even the slightest distinction."

Because there is no differentiation, all dharmas are without enmity; because there is no enmity, there is no grasping; and because there is no grasping, there is likewise neither suchness nor liberation.
Regarding the phrase "The letter-tha gate: because the locus of all dharmas cannot be apprehended," in the Sanskrit language *sthāna* has the meaning of "locus" as well as "abiding."
Just as when a person ascends from this dwelling place to another, the place upon which they rely is called a "dwelling," so too it is with the stages of the noble ones (*ārya*).
Because they serve as the basis and the place of rest for the mental traces of those practicing the path, they are designated by various names.

When one sees the character "tha," one immediately knows that all phenomena are without exception established in dependence upon conditions; thus, one should know that they all have a basis upon which they rely—this is the characteristic of the character.

However, since all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, and even suchness and liberation cannot be apprehended, there is neither going nor coming, neither proceeding nor abiding; within such a state of quiescent extinction, how could there be any sequence of stages?
Furthermore, when entering the gateway of the letter *ta*, because one realizes that all phenomena are empty, one does not abide within saṃsāra;
and because even this suchness (*tathatā*) is unattainable, one does not abide within nirvāṇa.

At that time, the spheres of activity are completely stilled and all stages are exhausted; being without dependence throughout all places, this is called abiding in the Great Abiding of the Tathāgata by means of the dharma of non-abiding.
Regarding the statement, “The gateway of the letter *na*: because giving (*dāna*) is unattainable in all phenomena,” the Sanskrit term *dāna* means the act of relinquishing or giving.
If one perceives the letter *na*, one immediately knows that all phenomena possess the characteristic of being relinquishable.
Why is this? Because all phenomena arise and dissolve in dependence upon conditions and possess no stable abiding.
If one becomes attached to them and gives rise to craving therein, one will inevitably be consumed by it.

Even for Bodhisattvas up to the tenth stage, because they have not yet reached the further shore of relinquishment regarding the pure and sublime merits produced within their own stages, they still possess inconceivable retrogression; therefore, this is not called the state of supreme peace and bliss.
Now, because one observes that all phenomena are unarisen, the giver, the recipient, and the gift are all fundamentally unarisen from the very beginning.

Even unto all phenomena, there is no place of abiding; because there is no place of abiding, these three things likewise have no place of abiding. Therefore, when the Buddha sat at the site of enlightenment, he neither attained anything nor relinquished anything. Within the treasury of empty space, there is nothing accumulated, yet it flows forth through universal gates to bestow gifts upon all living beings. This is called seeing the true mark of *dāna*, and it is also called being fully endowed with the *dānapāramitā*.
Furthermore, the secret treasury of the Tathāgata is entirely natural, meaning it cannot be transmitted to others.
When it is bestowed upon another, it is merely opened and revealed within the chamber of the sentient being's own mind.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The fact that all dharmas cannot be apprehended through giving is called the 'Gate of Letters' (akṣaramukha) in its true sense.

Regarding the phrase, "The gate of the letter *Dha*: because the *dharmadhātu* of all dharmas cannot be apprehended," the Sanskrit is *dharma-dhātu*, which is translated as "Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*). Here, "realm" (*dhātu*) carries the meaning of "essence" (*svabhāva*) and "division" (*vibhāga*).
The relics of the Buddha are also called the *tathāgatadhātu*, meaning they are the constituent parts of the Tathāgata.
If one perceives the gateway of the syllable *dhā*, one immediately knows that all phenomena possess a substance—that is, they take the *dharmadhātu* as their substance.
Why is this so? Because if one is separated from the true mark of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), the essential nature and meaning of all phenomena cannot be established.
Now, the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is precisely the mind-realm (*cittadhātu*); since the mind-realm is fundamentally unarisen, one should know that the Dharma-realm is also fundamentally unarisen.
Since even the mind-element is neither attained nor relinquished, one should know that the dharma-element is likewise neither attained nor relinquished.
If even relinquishment itself does not exist, there is no dharma to be relinquished; how much less could there be anything attained?
If the dharma-realm were a phenomenon that could be apprehended as a characteristic, it would be produced from a multitude of causes and conditions.
If it were produced from a multitude of causes and conditions, one should know that it lacks an intrinsic essence of its own; how much less could it serve as the essence of all phenomena?
Therefore, the dharma-realm is solely the self-realized eternal mind; there is no separate dharma.
Furthermore, the great giving of the Tathāgata is what is called the Great Compassion Maṇḍala.
The Dharma-realm is precisely the universal gate of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Such a true mark cannot be shown to others through the power of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*); therefore, no dharma can be apprehended.

Regarding the statement, "The gateway of the letter *pa* [is so called] because the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) of all phenomena cannot be apprehended": in Sanskrit this is *paramārtha*, which is translated as "ultimate truth" (*dìyī yì*) or "supreme truth" (*shèngyì*).
*Satya* is translated here as *di* (truth). The meaning of truth is explained through the gateway of the letter *sa*.
Now, this gateway of the letter *pa* precisely clarifies the characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Nāgārjuna said:
"The ultimate truth is called the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), for it is neither broken nor destroyed."
Furthermore, among all phenomena, the foremost is called *nirvāṇa*. As the *Abhidharma* states: "What is the unsurpassed phenomenon?
It is the cessation through wisdom (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)."
The exhaustion of conditions through wisdom is itself nirvāṇa.

If one sees the letter *pa*, one knows that all phenomena do not depart from the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), and that the ultimate truth does not depart from the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; this is the characteristic of the letter.
If the true meaning of the letter-gate is such, then even the ultimate truth (paramārtha) cannot be apprehended. Why is this?
Because there is neither craving nor attachment.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* further states: "Because sentient beings are attached to the sound of 'nirvāṇa,' they engage in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) regarding its existence or non-existence.
To destroy this attachment, it is taught that nirvāṇa is empty; this is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*)."
"It is not that which is attained within the minds of the sages, because the sages do not grasp at signs (*nimitta*) among all phenomena.

Furthermore, since all phenomena enter the equal Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), there is neither high nor low; how could one wish to establish distinctions of superiority or inferiority within the dharma of non-arising (*anutpāda*)?
Therefore, the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is unattainable.
Regarding the phrase "the gateway of the letter Pha: all dharmas are not solid, like a mass of foam," the Sanskrit term is *phenapinda*, which is translated as "mass of foam."

It is like waves surging and colliding in a great body of water, forming a mass of foam; various characteristics arise therein, and through their coalescence and mutual support, they eventually attain a state of solidity.

However, when one observes each stage from the coarse to the subtle, it is merely a condition arising from further conditions; it cannot be grasped or touched, and possesses no substantial nature at all.
Upon reaching its fundamental limit, the entire substance is water, and there is nothing that has been produced.
The various five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) in this world are likewise thus.

Now, if one observes by subsuming the branches back to the root and reducing the large to the small—down to the point of a single fine filament or a hair-tip—even these slight, individual movements are all successively produced through conditions. If they arise from a multitude of conditions, they possess no self-nature (*svabhāva*). If they lack self-nature, one should know that such arising is non-arising; reaching the ultimate limit of primordial non-arising, it is nothing other than the ocean of the mind-essence.
Yet, following the deluded sentiments of the six realms of existence, there subsequently arises the designation of "worlds.
Now, the ocean of the mind-nature is precisely the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), and the dharma-realm is precisely the ultimate nirvana.
If one can see in this way, then even though great waves surge and toss about, manifesting various universal form-bodies, they do not destroy the nature of clarity and stillness.
Regarding the phrase "The letter-mā gate: because bondage is unobtainable in all dharmas," the Sanskrit term is *bandha*, which is translated here as "bondage.
For example, when a person is constrained by shackles, they cannot move or turn; this is the meaning of bondage.
If one unties these knots through skillful means, it is called liberation.
Apart from the cord binding the body, there is no separate dharma of bondage or liberation.
It is like Śakra, Lord of the Devas, who bound the Asura King with a subtle fetter and placed him atop the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
When the thought arises to return, the five fetters are already upon one's body; yet when one ceases that thought, the fetters naturally dissolve.
If even the snares of Pāpīyān exceed this by hundreds of thousands of times, how much more so the fetters of karma, afflictions, and the unconditioned?

To state it briefly: that which is apart from all causes and conditions and does not fall within the category of any phenomena is called "unbound"; this is the meaning of the term. The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:

"If there were a sentient being existing separately from the five aggregates, then the aggregates would bind that sentient being; however, in reality, there is no sentient being apart from the five aggregates."
If afflictions existed separately from the five aggregates, they should separately bind the five aggregates; however, in reality, there are no separate afflictions apart from the five aggregates.
Through such various causes and conditions, one should know that there is no binding; where there is no binding, there is no liberation.
Because there is neither bondage nor liberation, nirvāṇa is itself saṃsāra, and saṃsāra is itself nirvāṇa.
This is explained in detail in the "Chapter on Contemplating Bondage and Liberation.
Furthermore, if all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen and are like a mass of foam, who therein could be the one who liberates?
Who is it that is bound? Therefore, all bonds are unapprehendable. Regarding the statement, "The gateway of the letter *ba*:

because all phenomena and all existences (*bhava*) are unapprehendable," in Sanskrit this is *bhava*, which is translated here as "existence. Existence refers to the three realms of existence, up to and including the twenty-five states of existence.

If one sees the letter BA, one immediately knows that all dharmas possess causes and conditions; because they arise from the conjunction of various conditions, they are said to "exist," yet they lack any fixed nature.
Why is this so? If a dharma were fixedly possessed of the characteristic of existence, then it would ultimately never possess the characteristic of non-existence; this would constitute permanence.

For example, regarding what is said of the three periods of time: if there were the characteristic of a dharma within the future, and that dharma, upon arriving in the present and transitioning into the past, did not abandon its original characteristic, then one would fall into the view of eternalism.
If one asserts that existence and non-existence are fixed, then this non-existence must have previously existed and now no longer does; this constitutes the view of annihilationism.
Because of these two views, one distances oneself from the Buddha-dharma.
As explained at length in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* in the chapter refuting existence and non-existence, we now observe that all phenomena arise from conditions;

this is precisely the meaning of their primordial non-arising (*anutpāda*). Because they are primordially unarisen, there is no action and no activity, and so forth, up to neither bondage nor liberation.
Therefore, because the gateway of the letter *ba* arises from conditions, it fully possesses all gateways of letters.
If one possesses all gateways of letters, this is the King of Samādhis Samādhi, which is able to shatter the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*).
For this reason, Śākyamuni is called the Dharma King who shatters existence (*bhava*).

Regarding the phrase "The gateway of the letter Ya: because all dharmas and all vehicles (*yāna*) are unattainable," the Sanskrit term is *yāna*, which is translated here as "vehicle" (*chéng*) and is also termed the "path" (*mārga*).
Just as when a person rides in a boat or a carriage, they are able to carry heavy loads and travel great distances to reach their destination;

so too, upon seeing the "wild" (野) letter-gateway, one knows that all sentient beings, through various causes and conditions, have each a vehicle by which they proceed toward the retributions of birth and death or toward nirvana. One also knows that these immeasurable vehicles are all in fact the Buddha-vehicle; this is called the characteristic of the letter.
Now, observing that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, they are thus without activity and without abiding, neither moving nor retreating;
herein, who is there to be a rider, and what dharma should one ride?

Furthermore, this vehicle emerges from the three realms of existence and proceeds to *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) over five hundred *yojanas*. Since there is not a single point among these that is not a real location, by which path does it wish to travel, and to what destination does it intend to go?
Therefore, because all vehicles are unattainable, it is called the Mahāyāna path.

Regarding the statement, "The letter-gateway *ra* [indicates that] all dharmas are free from all dust and defilement (*rajas*)," in Sanskrit, *rajas* (raśi) carries the meaning of dust and defilement.
"Dust" (*rajas*) is the sphere of activity for deluded perceptions; thus, it is said that the six faculties, such as the eye, engage with the six objects, such as form.

If one perceives the letter-gateway *ra*, one knows that all phenomena which are seen, heard, touched, or cognized are merely the characteristics of dust. This is like a clean garment stained by dust and grime, or like drifting motes of dust agitating the great void so that the sun and moon lose their clarity—this is the characteristic of the letter.
The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* seeks to see phenomena through various approaches, yet no seer is found.
If there is no seer, who could employ the act of seeing to distinguish external forms—that which sees and that which is seen?
Because one sees that phenomena are non-existent, the four factors of consciousness, contact, sensation, and craving are all absent.
Because craving is absent, the twelve links of dependent origination are likewise absent.
Therefore, when the eye perceives form, this is itself the mark of nirvāṇa; the same applies by analogy to the other sense objects.

Furthermore, by means of the gateway of the letter A, one should successively observe all sensory objects; because they are fundamentally unarisen and devoid of fabrication, and even because there is neither a vehicle to be mounted nor a rider, one should know that all phenomena which are seen, heard, touched, or known are entirely the pure Dharma-realm. How could the pure Dharma-realm ever defile the six sense faculties of the Tathāgata?

In the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra*, it is stated that because the Buddha’s eye of permanence is complete and undiminished, he clearly perceives permanent form; this applies likewise to the mind and mental objects (*dharmas*). This is the true meaning of the syllable-gateway *ra*.

Regarding the statement, "The letter-gateway *la*: because all phenomena (*dharma*) and all characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are unattainable," the Sanskrit term is *lakṣa*, which is translated here as "characteristic" (*xiāng*).
Some say: "There is no distinction between nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); it is as when one says that the nature of fire is precisely its characteristic of heat. Others say:
There is a slight distinction: "nature" (svabhāva) refers to its essence, while "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) refers to what can be recognized.
For example, for a son of the Śākya, the observance of the prohibitive precepts is his nature, whereas shaving the head, wearing the cut and dyed robes, and so forth, are his characteristics.
If one sees the letter-gateway *la*, one knows that all phenomena (*dharma*) possess characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
These characteristics are further of two kinds:
first, the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), which refers to the characteristics of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; [the second is the specific characteristic].

"Distinction" refers to the fact that although all phenomena are impermanent and without self, they each possess their own specific characteristics. For example: earth has the characteristic of solidity, water of moisture, fire of heat, and wind of motion; renunciation has the characteristic of giving, non-regret and non-affliction have the characteristic of ethical discipline, the mind’s lack of fluctuation has the characteristic of patience, the arousal of effort has the characteristic of diligence, the gathering of the mind has the characteristic of meditative concentration, non-attachment has the characteristic of wisdom, the ability to accomplish tasks has the characteristic of skillful means, the weaving of birth and death has the characteristic of the mundane world, and the absence of such weaving has the characteristic of nirvana, and so forth.
Now, observing that the essential nature of both conditioned and unconditioned phenomena is empty, with whom would these characteristics be characteristics?
This is explained in detail in the "Chapter on the Three Characteristics" of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* and in the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*.

Furthermore, within the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the various characteristics such as the one hundred and sixty types of mind are fundamentally unarisen and thus devoid of volitional construction (*abhisamskāra*). Because there is no volitional construction, there is ultimately no objective dust (*rajas*); because there is no objective dust, it is free from all marks (*nimitta*).
Because it is free from all signs, it is called the self-realized *sambodhi* of all Buddhas.
Regarding the statement, "The gateway of the syllable *va*: because the path of speech regarding all phenomena is severed," in the Sanskrit language *va* corresponds to *vāk*, which means speech.

When one sees the syllable VA, one immediately knows that all phenomena do not depart from the ground of language, because there is no phenomenon among them that does not possess causes and conditions.
If a dharma is originally unarisen, it is free from all causes and conditions; therefore, the path of language is cut off.
Furthermore, if a dharma possesses the characteristic of being produced, it can be proclaimed; if it is unproduced, the path of language is cut off.

If the characteristic of space were itself a characteristic, it could be described; however, since the characteristics of all phenomena are like the characteristic of space and are likewise without characteristics, the path of language is cut off.
If a phenomenon possesses activity, transformation, and appearance, it can be explained; if it lacks activity, lacks transformation, and lacks appearance, the path of language is cut off.

As long as phenomena possess characteristics, they can be proclaimed; however, since all phenomena are now devoid of all characteristics, they cannot be indicated nor transmitted to others. Therefore, the path of language is severed.

Furthermore, the signless is also without fixed characteristics; one should know that all dharmas are both characterized and signless, and neither characterized nor signless. Just as those three eyes are inconceivable, the path of language is thus cut off.
Other dharma-gates may be understood by analogy with this.
Regarding the "gate of the letter Śa," it is because the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is quiescent (*śānti*). In Sanskrit, this is called *śānti*, which is translated here as "quiescence" (*ji*).
Just as worldly ordinary people, who attain a slight degree of tranquility and still the clamor of their movements, are also said to have attained "quiescence";
and even those of the two vehicles, who eternally sever the cycle of all conditioned activities and realize nirvana, are also said to have attained "quiescence."
Yet it is not that their fundamental nature is eternally quiescent. Why is this so?
Because all dharmas, from the very beginning, have always been characterized by inherent extinction; within the three realms and six paths, what is not nirvana?
When untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) arises, how does it differ from that of an ordinary person?
Yet, you alone conceive of nirvāṇa within this state; is this not a perversion?
Furthermore, if all dharmas are by nature quiescent, then among the forty-two stages, which one is not the stage of the Tathāgata?
Which one is not the stage of an ordinary person?
If Maitreya Bodhisattva has attained the prediction of birth in his final life because his fundamental nature is quiescent, then all sentient beings should likewise attain such a prediction.

If all sentient beings can practice ordinary worldly affairs without hindering their state within the quiescence of the fundamental nature, then Maitreya Bodhisattva should also practice ordinary worldly affairs.
Now, to form such discriminative conceptions—is this not idle proliferation (*prapañca*)?

When one enters the gateway of the letter *Śa*, one knows that all phenomena are equal and without high or low; they are eternally unmoving yet accomplish all things. Therefore, it is said that within liberation there is vast capacity for reception, and that Great Parinirvāṇa can establish great meaning—all of which is due to this.

Regarding the phrase, “The gateway of the letter *sa* [is that] all dharmas are dull by nature,” if the Sanskrit original were preserved in its literal form, it would state that their nature is identical to that of the insentient.
"Insentient" (*wán*) means, for example, like wood or stone, having no capacity for cognition or for the sensation of touch.
What is called "sameness" (sāmya) is a statement made for the purpose of providing an analogy; it does not mean that [the subject] is unilaterally identical to that [object].
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states, "Prajñā is without cognition, because its intrinsic nature is dull," which accords with the meaning of this "gate of letters" (akṣara-mukha).
Therefore, those who adorn their writings merely preserve the terminology of ancient translations.

Now, that which is by nature dull is precisely the ultimate non-conceptual mind; it is neither ignorant nor wise, neither clever nor foolish; it has no consciousness, no intellect, no delusion, and no awakening. It cannot be moved by any phenomena whatsoever, being nothing other than the single, pure, and solid ground of vajra.

Why is this so? It is because people in the world do not err in their taking and rejecting; thus, they prize wisdom and discard folly, honoring *nirvāṇa* while disparaging birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
Now, since all things are fundamentally unborn and, ultimately, all things are fundamentally quiescent by nature, who is sharp and who is dull?
It is like that diamond blade: because it encounters non-solid objects and because it is used predominantly on one side, it is called "sharp."

If every direction one turns toward were entirely composed of vajra, and if the entire body were perfectly spherical such that it could not be used for specific purposes, then the characteristic of sharpness would likewise revert to dullness.
Regarding the phrase "The gateway of the letter *sa*: because all phenomena and all truths (*satya*) are unattainable," the Sanskrit term is *sattya*, which is translated here as "truth" (*di*).
Truth (*satya*) means knowing the true nature of all phenomena as it is, without inversion or error. As it is said: "The sun might be made cold, and the moon might be made hot;
but what the Buddha has taught regarding the Truth of Suffering cannot be made otherwise."
“Accumulation is the true cause; there is no other cause.
When the cause ceases, the fruit ceases. The path that extinguishes suffering is the true path; there is no other path.”
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "To understand suffering as being without suffering, there is therefore no suffering, but rather the True Truth (*satyadharma*).
The same applies to the other three truths.
This extends even to the analysis of the four truths having immeasurable aspects and the single ultimate truth (*ekasatyadharma*), as explained in the "Chapter on Noble Conduct" (*Āryacaryā-varga*).
This is the characteristic of the gateway of syllables.

However, because all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, ultimately signless, cut off from language, quiescent by nature, and inert by their own essence, one should know that there is neither seeing nor abandoning, neither realization nor cultivation.

Thus, seeing, severing, realizing, and cultivating are all the inconceivable Dharma-realm; they are simultaneously emptiness, the provisional, and the Middle Way. Being neither real nor false, they possess no fixed characteristics that can be demonstrated; therefore, it is said that the truths are unattainable.
The meaning of this is also extensively explained in the "Chapter on the Four Truths" of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*.
Regarding the statement, "The gateway of the syllable *ha*, because the cause of all phenomena cannot be apprehended," the Sanskrit term is *hetu*, which carries the meaning of "cause."
There are six kinds of causes, as well as five kinds of causes within the meaning of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), as explained in detail in the *Abhidharma*.
If one sees the gateway of the letter *ha*, one immediately knows that there are no phenomena whatsoever that do not arise from causes and conditions; this is the characteristic of the syllable.

Since all phenomena are established through mutual dependence on causes, one should know that the final [phenomenon] has no basis; therefore, it is said that non-abiding is the root of all phenomena. Why is this so?

As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* observes through various gateways that the causes and conditions of all phenomena are entirely non-arising, one should know that the myriad dharmas are mind-only. The true nature of the mind is itself the omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), which is the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) of all Buddhas. This dharma-realm is the very essence of all phenomena; it cannot function as a cause.
Speaking from this perspective, the cause is also the dharma-realm, the conditions are also the dharma-realm, and the phenomena produced by causes and conditions are also the dharma-realm.
The previously mentioned "gate of the letter A" proceeds from the fundamental to the derivative, ultimately arriving at such a state.
Now, the gateway of the letter *ha* likewise returns from the derivative to the fundamental, ultimately arriving at such a state.

The letter *a*, being unborn from the beginning, gives rise to all dharmas; now, by taking the absence of causal dependence as the cause of all dharmas, the beginning and end converge. Thus, the underlying purport of the intermediate stages can all be understood.

Furthermore, regarding the characteristics of the wheel of syllables (*akṣara-cakra*) within this *Pratyāhāra-dhāraṇī*: it means explaining the meaning of all syllables by means of a single syllable, and explaining the meaning of a single syllable by means of all syllables; establishing the meaning of all syllables through the meaning of a single syllable, and establishing the meaning of a single syllable through the meaning of all syllables; and subverting the meaning of all syllables through the meaning of a single syllable, and subverting the meaning of a single syllable through the meaning of all syllables.
Regarding the principle that "one syllable is all syllables," the examples of rotating in reverse or forward order can be understood by analogy.
How does one explain all syllables through a single syllable?
For instance, when explaining the syllable *Śākya*, by observing its fundamental non-arising through various causes and conditions, one immediately perceives the meaning of "that which is uncreated."
Even when explaining the syllable *ha*, one contemplates primordial non-arising through various causes and conditions, thereby perceiving the meaning of causelessness.
How, then, does one explain a single syllable by means of all syllables?

As when explaining the gateway of the letter *a*, by contemplating through various causes and conditions that there is no conditioned activity (*anabhisaṃskāra*), one immediately perceives the meaning of primordial non-arising (*mūlājāti*).
Likewise, by contemplating through various causes and conditions that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are without cause, one immediately perceives the meaning of primordial non-arising.
The same applies to all other characters, which shall be explained in detail.
How is it that all characters establish a single character?
It means that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, because they are without activity, like space in being signless, without formation, without conjunction, and even without cause.
How does one syllable become all syllables?
It is because all phenomena are without activity, for they are originally unarisen; and so on, up to all phenomena being without cause, for they are originally unarisen.
How does one refute the "single character" by means of all characters?
For example, if someone maintains that all phenomena have an origin and a birth, one should refute their statement as follows:
"If all phenomena are devoid of volitional construction (saṃskāra) and yet you say they have birth, this meaning is not tenable."
Furthermore, if one claims that phenomena arise despite their causes being unapprehendable, this meaning is untenable.
How does a single word refute all words?
For example, if someone clings to the existence of a creator, one should refute their statement as follows:
If the principle that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen has already been established, yet one claims they have an agent, this is not tenable.
Furthermore, regarding those who cling to the existence of causes, he likewise refutes their statement:
"If the principle that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen has already been established, yet one claims they have a cause, this is not tenable."

What is meant by "reversing and following the rotation"? It is as follows: if a phenomenon is fundamentally unarisen, then there is no volitional construction; if there is no volitional construction, then it is like space, being without marks; if it is like space and without marks, then there is no activity; if there is no activity, then there is no conjunction; if there is no conjunction, then there is no transition or change. Furthermore, if there is no cause, one should know that phenomena are fundamentally unarisen—this is called "following."

If dharmas have no cause, then the truths cannot be apprehended; if the truths cannot be apprehended, then their intrinsic nature is dull; if their intrinsic nature is dull, one should know that their fundamental nature is quiescent; if they are fundamentally quiescent, one should know they are signless; and so on, until: if they are fundamentally unarisen, one should know they are causeless.
Thus, these eight categories of meaning are explained through their free and revolving exposition.
Furthermore, what is now called "all phenomena" (sarvadharma) is merely a general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
If one follows the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, each phenomenon from form (*rūpa*) up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) is explained individually and distinctly; thus, the meanings are immeasurable.

Furthermore, each individual gate should be distinguished according to the sequence of its shallow and deep aspects as presented in the "Chapter on Abiding in the Mind through Mantras," for since the gates are transformed by means of syllables, their meanings also differ.
For this reason, one is able to give birth to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *dhāraṇīs* of revolving.
Furthermore, because all the Tathāgata’s speech is nothing other than mantra, one should universally enter into all *sūtras* by means of the meaning of these syllables.

Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If a bodhisattva hears the syllable 'A' within any discourse, they immediately understand its meaning: that all dharmas are, from the very beginning, characterized by non-arising (*anutpāda-lakṣaṇa*). 'A-ti'—in the language of Qin, this means 'the beginning.'"
Anūpāda means "non-arising" in the language of Qin.

If one hears the syllable *ra*, one should understand its meaning accordingly: all phenomena are devoid of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). The syllable *ra* means "defilement" (*rajas*) in the language of Qin.
If one hears the syllable *pa*, one immediately knows that all phenomena enter into *paramārtha-pāramitā*—*paramārtha* being the Qin (Chinese) term for "ultimate truth.
If one hears the syllable *cha*, one immediately knows that all conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*) are non-activities, *cārikā*—*cārikā* being the Qin term for "activity."
If one hears the syllable *na*, one immediately knows that all dharmas are neither gained nor lost, neither coming nor going—*na* being the Qin (Chinese) word for "not.
This is explained in detail in the "Chapter on the Four Foundations of Mindfulness" (*Catur-smṛtyupasthāna-varga*) of that treatise.

Furthermore, among all names and expressions, those containing the sound "a" entirely enter the gateway of the letter A; those containing the sound "ka" entirely enter the gateway of the letter Ka; and so on, up to those containing the sound "ha," which entirely enter the gateway of the letter Ha.
Therefore, within this single gateway of the letter *ha*, there are infinite meanings; it is not that the gateway of the letter *ha* contains only the meaning of "no cause.
One should know that the same principle applies to all other gateways of letters.
Furthermore, for example, *sata* has the meaning of "truth" (*satya*). Therefore, a sutra says: "The gateway of the letter *sa*:

the truth of all phenomena is unattainable. Moreover, *sata* has the meaning of "attachment. Therefore, in the *Dharmapūjā-sūtra*, it says: "The gateway of the letter *sa*: all phenomena are free from defiled attachment."
Furthermore, *bha-va* has the meaning of "existence"; therefore, a sutra states: "The syllable-gateway *bha*: in all dharmas, existence is unobtainable.
Moreover, *bhāvanā* has the meaning of "contemplation"; therefore, in the *Pūjāvidhi*, it says: "The syllable-gateway *bha*: all dharmas are free from all contemplations."
The rest are all omitted here.
Therefore, both the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter (*Lokadhātu-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* both explain the forty-two letter-gates.

The "Chapter on Letters" in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, and the "Chapter on the Sovereign King of Dhāraṇīs" in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* each provide explanations of the Siddham letters; their meanings are either identical to or consistent with those taught in this sūtra.
If one grasps this meaning, then all the sutras will be clearly and coherently integrated, without any contradiction or obstruction.
Furthermore, the fact that each and every "gate of letters" (akṣaramukha) states that [the object] is unobtainable is for the purpose of clarifying the meaning of the Middle Way.
For now, let us explain this by means of the gateway of the letter *ca*.

It is like observing the reflection of a face in a mirror: with the original object as the cause and the clean mirror as the condition, a reflected image appears once more; this is what is meant by "the dharma that is produced" being seen.

Because the appearance of beauty and ugliness manifests before one without error, it is called "existence"; because when sought through various skillful means, they are entirely unobtainable, it is called "emptiness. This existence and this emptiness both do not transcend the substance of the mirror; they are one within a single name.
The three characteristics are neither identical nor different, yet they are both identical and different; therefore, worldly scholars cannot conceive of them. Now, the gateway of Mantra is likewise:

with the contemplation of the mind as the cause and the three secrets as the conditions, the oceanic assembly of the universal gate manifests before one without error, and is thus called "existence. Yet, when sought through various means, it is utterly unobtainable, and is thus called "emptiness. Since both this existence and this emptiness do not transcend the Dharma-realm, they are called the "Middle."
The three truths are different yet identical, and non-different yet distinct; this cannot be conceived by those who follow any of the provisional vehicles.
Other dharma-gates are all like this, and it is impossible to cite them all exhaustively.
The Sūtra states: "O Lord of Secrets!

*Aṅgāṅga-maṅga* possesses mastery over all samādhis; it can swiftly accomplish all tasks, and whatever aims and benefits are pursued will all be fulfilled. Within the five classes of sounds—ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa—there are likewise five syllables each. Of these, the first through the fourth syllables are all gateways to wisdom, as has already been explained above.
The fifth group of characters are all gates of realization, which shall now be explained together.

In Sanskrit script, these five characters are all marked with a circular dot (*bindu*); for instance, as in the four characters *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, and *gha*, when extended to the eleventh vowel sound, a dot is placed above the initial letter.
If one wishes to eliminate this dot, yet adds characters such as the "upward-facing" (仰) character upon the subsequent syllables, those characters become no different from having a dot.

Furthermore, among the twelve phonemes of the Sanskrit script, the first is the essence (*dharmakāya*); the second is practice (*saṃbhogakāya*); from the third onwards, those increased by various strokes are called samādhi; the eleventh, with a dot placed above it, is realization (*nirmāṇakāya*); and the twelfth, with two dots placed beside it, is parinirvāṇa.

If this syllable *yaṅ* can pervade the sound of the samādhi of wisdom, one should know that it signifies the meaning of "Great Emptiness" (*mahāśūnyatā*); therefore, it is explained separately and is not discussed in conjunction with the preceding syllables.
These five characters from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* also fully clarify the meaning of the word "letter.
Now, the Vairocana school employs these five characters to elucidate the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*).
The Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*) is the locus of realization; as there is no dharma that can be expressed, it is represented solely by a circular dot (*bindu*).
Furthermore, although this circular dot has no gateways within its own essence, it pervades all dharmic gateways, just as space is free from all characteristics yet contains all manifestations.
Therefore, if any letter-gate is provided with the bindu (the dot of emptiness), it possesses the function of mastery and is fully capable of accomplishing all matters.

For instance, the letter-gate A represents the wondrous wisdom of non-arising, which all sentient beings equally possess; yet, because they do not personally realize and know it themselves, they are like a poor woman who cannot access the power of a treasure store buried beneath her home.

When it is brought forth through skillful means, it is like opening a treasury; when one enters into realization, it is as if a jewel mine has appeared before one. At that time, one may enjoy its benefits at will, and whatever is sought will certainly be obtained. Therefore, it is said that by adding this *bindu* (the dot), all meaningful purposes are accomplished.

Next, regarding the verse spoken by the World-Honored One, "The gate of mantra-samādhi fulfills all vows," the complete Sanskrit original should include the word *mārga* (path) following the word *mantra*. When the practitioner focuses single-mindedly on the letter *A*, it is called the *A*-letter samādhi.
This *a*-syllable samādhi is precisely the gate to the path of the heart-vidyā; all other syllables are likewise so.
Regarding "all vows," the Sanskrit term is *sarvaśa*; these are the vows prayed for by the mind.
It means that for all sentient beings who cultivate this gate of samādhi, every aspiration and pursuit shall be brought to fulfillment.
When these vows are fulfilled, that is precisely the inconceivable fruit of all Tathāgatas.
If even the eternally abiding fruit and the teacherless wisdom can be bestowed upon sentient beings, how much more so the aspirations for worldly *siddhi*?
Furthermore, whether a Buddha exists or not, the dharmatā of the sounds, syllables, and true reality (*dharmatā*) of each of the Tathāgata’s samādhi-gates remains thus.
This is precisely why it does not flow; this is the Tathāgata’s original ground, the *dharmakāya*.

Because he wishes to universally bestow this *dharmakāya* upon all sentient beings, he employs his sovereign spiritual power (*ṛddhibala*) to empower these naturally occurring sounds and syllables. Therefore, these sounds and syllables are the bodies empowered by all Buddhas.

This body sustained by empowerment can universally manifest bodies that accord with all types of beings, being present everywhere; one should know that the empowerment of sounds and syllables is likewise so.
Therefore, if the practitioner single-mindedly and attentively contemplates these sounds and characters, they will naturally behold the Buddha’s body of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna-kāya*).

If one beholds the body of empowerment, one beholds the Dharma-body of the original ground (*mūla-dharmakāya*); and when the Dharma-body of the original ground is beheld, that is precisely the practitioner’s own self. Thus, each and every gateway is the inconceivable fruit of the Tathāgata, which does not come from any other place.

Regarding the phrase "Endowed with all supreme vows, the definitive meaning of mantras," the Sanskrit original exists in its entirety and should read: "Endowed with all existing supreme vows, the definitive true meaning of mantras."

Regarding "supreme vow" (*vara*) herein, the Sanskrit term is *vara*, which signifies being endowed with various merits—namely, samādhi, dhāraṇī, powers, fearlessnesses, and so forth—and carries the meaning of having fulfilled all aspirations and being fully equipped with all that is sought; its Sanskrit phonetic form differs from that of the previous word for "vow" (*praṇidhāna*).

Regarding what is called "certainty": take, for example, the gateway of the letter A; whether it be the sound or the character, its entire substance is non-arising, and thus the meaning of that sound and character is entirely non-arising in its very substance.
When one realizes it, one realizes only this non-arising; in the interim, there is no further intermingling nor any alternative path.

When one perceives this true meaning, even if the Buddhas of the ten directions were to appear simultaneously and speak various similar *pāramitās* in an attempt to alter one's mind, one would not give rise to doubt or confusion; therefore, it is called "decisive."

Furthermore, those who are fully endowed with the multitude of supreme vows possess the Tathāgata’s internally realized merits, numbering as many as the atoms within ten world-systems; because these are definitive, each one becomes a vajra-seal.
From this body of self-realization, there further arises a body of empowerment; therefore, it is said to "transcend the three periods of time.

Regarding "stainless and equal to space," this refers to the inconceivable ground of mind that is pure and stainless; by means of great skillful means, one draws the Universal Gate Maṇḍala upon this ground.

Therefore, the sutra continues by saying, "Abiding in the inconceivable mind, one undertakes all activities. In the Sanskrit original, this is fully expressed as "the ground of the mind" (*cittabhūmi*); however, because five characters constitute a single verse-line, it could not be written out in full here.
However, since the ground (*bhūmi*) is itself the essence of the mind, it is simply said that one "abides in the inconceivable mind.

Within the gateway of mantra-samādhi, although there exists such inconceivable fruit-virtue as to be capable of providing for an entire nation and bestowing gifts upon all sentient beings, [it is still called the ground].

If sentient beings are unable to conceive the thought that [the Buddhas] are difficult to encounter, and thus fail to make offerings and practice, it would be like a king’s sumptuous meal laid out before him, yet he has no intention to eat or drink; how then could the Buddhas be of any help?

Therefore, the Sūtra continues: "If one reaches the stage of cultivation, one is granted the inconceivable fruit. This stage of cultivation is precisely the first Dharma-gate of the Radiance of Enlightenment within the pure bodhicitta.
For example, after a śrāvaka has realized the truths (satyadarśana), they further enter the stage of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).

In this same way, within each of the hundred syllables of the gate of illumination, this bodhisattva perceives a world-ocean of lotus-womb maṇḍalas, the characteristics of whose adornments are all entirely distinct.

First, from the gateway of the syllable *kha*, within the great wheel of space (*mahā-ākāśa-cakra*), one generates the great wind-wheel (*mahā-vāyu-cakra*) by means of the gateway of the syllable *ha*. Next, upon that, one generates the ocean of fragrant water (*gandhodaka-samudra*) by means of the gateway of the syllable *va*. Then, upon that, one generates the vajra-ground and the mountain of the vajra-wheel (*vajracakraparvata*) by means of the gateway of the syllable *a*. The remainder is as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Within each of these world-systems of the Bodhi-maṇḍala in the hundred Lotus-treasury worlds, there are ten world-systems of bodhisattvas, vajradharas, and others who serve as their retinues.

This practitioner of yoga, without rising from his seat, is able to reach all such assemblies of Buddhas and can also successively seek out various spiritual friends; therefore, it is said that a Bodhisattva of the first stage transforms a hundred Buddha-lands, which is more than merely a matter of visual perception.
Furthermore, one is able to transform these hundred lotus-treasures into one's own body.

Upon reaching the fulfillment of the ten stages of mind—beginning with the sprout, stem, and flower-pod of the first bhūmi—one opens up ten gates of liberation from within a single gate of illumination, thereby manifesting a thousand worlds; all of these are inconceivable fruits bestowed according to one's respective capacity.

Upon reaching the boundary of the eleventh stage, within the gate of the luminous cloud-ocean of space, one perceives within each and every instance the various characteristics, forms, and types of the Lotus Treasury Adorned World-Sphere, all distinct from one another; by taking these as one's own body with sovereign mastery and unimpededness, this is called the fulfillment of the inconceivable fruit.
Next follow two verses that exhort faith and provide a seal of confirmation; thus it says, "This is the foremost reality, revealed by all Buddhas.
Herein, "revealed" refers to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, which is identical in meaning to the *Lotus Sūtra*.
The subsequent half-verse states: "If one knows this teaching of the Dharma, one shall attain all *siddhis*.
This cites the common path of all Buddhas to exhort faith in conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

If a practitioner of mantra clearly understands the sequential methods within these dharma teachings and practices according to the instructions with resolute faith, they shall attain the accomplishment of all siddhis.

If this explanation were not accepted, it would mean that the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time have committed the sin of violating their original vows and deceiving sentient beings.
The following verse exhorts one to abide in the ultimate truth.
Furthermore, these Siddhaṃ letters are recited and maintained even by young children; as for practices such as *homa* and offerings, even the Vedic seers (*ṛṣi*) all perform them together.
Now, the reason why this Mantra Vehicle alone is established as secret is that it is empowered by the true meaning.
If one merely recites mantras orally without contemplating their meaning, one may only achieve mundane benefits; how could one possibly realize the vajra-nature?

Therefore, the verse says: "The most supreme and true sound, the mantra and the characteristics of the mantra—when the practitioner contemplates these with discernment, they attain the indestructible word.

This sound is the very essence of the speech-secret (vāgguhya) within the Mantra-gate; it is like the foremost meaning of reality within the syllable *A*, namely, primordial non-arising (*ādi-anutpanna*).

The initial mention of "mantra" refers to it as it is called with the plural voice in the Sanskrit original; this is a general indication of the characteristics of the hundred-syllable gate (śatākṣara-mukha) and the wheel of conventional syllables (saṃvṛti-akṣara-cakra).
The subsequent mention of the "characteristics of the mantra" refers to the true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) of this mantra.
This very reality of the mantra, through the power of contemplative reflection, enters each and every lotus pedestal.
A "phrase" (*pada*) is the place where the traces of thought come to rest.
As the Sūtra says: "At that time, Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets, addressed the Buddha, saying:"
"How rare it is, World-Honored One!
Regarding the 'Dharma of the Path of the Inconceivable Mantra-Marks' spoken by the Buddha: just as in the Śrāvaka Dharma, there are no written characters within liberation."
Vimalakīrti does not depart from words and letters when he explains the characteristics of liberation; therefore, it is called "inconceivable liberation.

Now, this wheel of syllables is likewise: the signless Dharmakāya produces various sounds and syllables, and various sounds and syllables constitute the signless Dharmakāya. Therefore, it is called the "inconceivable characteristic of mantra."

"Neither shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor intended for all sentient beings universally"—this sutra is the secret treasure of the Dharma King; it is not shown falsely to those who are base and lowly.

Just as when Śākyamuni appeared in the world for over forty years, it was only after Śāriputra and others had made earnest requests three times that he finally briefly expounded the meaning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

This present body of the fundamental stage is, moreover, the profound and secret locus of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; thus, the "Life Span" chapter states: "I am always on Vulture Peak and in other dwelling places," up to: "My pure land is not destroyed, yet the multitudes see it consumed by fire. This is precisely the meaning of the Yoga of this school.
Furthermore, it was only after the Bodhisattva of the Stage of Rebirth (Upapatti-bhūmi) had earnestly requested it three times that [the Buddha] finally spoke of it.
If one lacks the capacity for sudden enlightenment, the teaching will not enter their hands; therefore, it is not universally bestowed upon all sentient beings.

This also summarizes the preceding verse regarding reaching the stage of practice and receiving the inconceivable fruit; it is followed by two verses on receiving the explanation and exhorting faith to seal the teaching. Therefore, it says: "If one has faith in this True Word (Mantra) path, all dharmas of merit shall be fulfilled."
"When these are fulfilled, they constitute the complete possession of all supreme vows.
Thus concludes the extensive explanation of the branches of the mantra.
Vajradhara, following upon the preceding text, requested the Buddha to next explain the sequence required for entering the maṇḍala.

In the verses spoken by the World-Honored One, the initial response to the two lines concerning the offering of incense, flowers, and so forth, along with various precious vases, is collectively termed the "limbs of worship.
Among these various articles of offering, the presentation of flowers is explained first.

In all offerings presented, one should carefully distinguish each according to the nature and category of the respective deities and their positions within the maṇḍala, ensuring that their color, fragrance, flavor, and texture are pleasing to the human mind.
As for those inauspicious flowers found on land or in water, they may only be used for the purpose of subjugation (*dharṣaṇa*).
Among the three colors—white, yellow, and red—the white color should be used for the Tathāgata family, the yellow for the Lotus family, and the red for the Vajra family.
Furthermore, one should follow the orientations of the maṇḍala: for a circular altar, use white; for a square altar, use yellow; for a triangular altar, use red.
Furthermore, the Buddhas use white, the Bodhisattvas use yellow, and the worldly deities use red.

As for the other incenses and so forth, one should likewise apply this same principle, incorporating relevant passages from the Susiddhi, Guhyasamāja, and other texts as appropriate; it is not necessary to record them all here in full.
*Padma* refers to the red lotus.
Generally, all water-born flowers, such as blue, red, and white lotuses, may be offered to the various deities.
Regarding "the *bunāga* flower of the nāgas," this *bunāga* is the *nāgapuṣpa* (dragon-tree) flower.
The World-Honored One Maitreya shall attain Buddhahood beneath this tree.
As for its name, "Dragon Flower" (Nāgapuṣpa), it is a flower held in high esteem among dragons; its species is quite common in the Western Regions.

As for the *kimsuka* flower, the *mallika* flower, the *tagara* flower, the *campaka* flower, the *aśoka* flower, the *tilaka* flower, the *pāṭala* flower, and the *sāla* tree flower—all these belong to India and cannot be fully identified here in this land.
Regarding the scriptural passage, "These various rare and exquisite flowers," the Sanskrit original includes the particle *vā* (or).
This indicates that these various flowers may all be used interchangeably; therefore, they are cited here as representative examples.

However, whether they originate in other regions or not, provided they are pleasing to the human mind and regarded by the world as auspicious, all such things may be offered; one should attend to each of them with care and distinguish them well.

Regarding the phrase "gathering [flowers] to make garlands," this refers to adorning [the deity] with a variegated arrangement, whether by stringing or binding them together. Because the practitioner’s mind is earnest, pure, and profound, it causes all the Honored Ones to rejoice and provide protective mindfulness.
Next, the fragrant unguents are explained.
As for sandalwood, *śrīkhaṇḍa*, saffron, and *dūrvā* grass—these are the *moxu* (sweet clover) incense of the Western Regions; they differ slightly from the *moxu* incense found here [in China].
"And other excellent unguents" refers to such as agallochum, spikenard, clove, cinnamon bark, western nutmeg (*kakkola*), and vetiver, as described in the Susiddhi and Guhya-samāja tantras.

Furthermore, it is said that among the fragrant ointments (*vilepana*), one must not use parts of sentient beings, lac (*manjiṣṭhā*), or those consumed by insects; rather, one should take pure and excellent substances and grind them with water.
If making an offering to the Buddha, one should use fresh and high-quality saffron or black agarwood, blended with camphor.

For the Lotus Family, one should use white sandalwood; for the Vajra Family, one should likewise use white sandalwood. For all other deities, one may blend them as desired, provided that camphor is added to whichever incense is combined.

Next, the method for burning incense is explained: one should use aloeswood (*agaru*), pine resin, *vālana* incense, camphor, and white sandalwood. In the West, white sandalwood is called *mālayu*; this is the name of a mountain, referring to what is stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "Aside from Mount Mālaya, there is no other place where sandalwood grows."
White resin (śrīkhaṇḍa) is the sap of the sāla tree.
As for the incense śrīvāseka, it resembles the *xūnlù* (frankincense) of this region.
"Śrī" carries the meaning of "possessing virtue and auspiciousness"; because it is said that even the celestial deities all delight in this incense, it is named accordingly.
Regarding the phrase, "And other types of incense, whose fragrance is praised as beautiful by the world," it is also as explained above.
Guhyi says: "For the category of offerings to the Buddha, one should burn incense made by blending white sandalwood and aloeswood."
"The resin of that tree is fragrant; it is for making offerings to the Lotus family.
Black aloeswood and guggulu are for making offerings to the Vajra family.
Alternatively, one may prepare incense according to those specific rites, blending all ingredients together to present as an offering to the various deities.

Regarding the phrase "one should follow the instructions of the Dharma," this refers to the purification through mantras, mudrās, and consecrations (*adhiṣṭhāna*), as explained in the sequence of offerings.
Other items, such as unguents and flowers, should be understood by analogy with these.

Next, regarding the statement "offering various foods according to the teachings," as found in the extensive versions of the sutras, each type of food offering has its own specific method of preparation.
As for their profound and secret significance, each one corresponds precisely to a particular dharma-gate.

Since these specific methods are not present here, one simply performs the construction, protection, and empowerment according to the ritual procedures of the Susiddhi and other texts; this is what is meant by "following the instructions.

Regarding milk-rice (*kṣīrayaṣṭi*), there are many varieties of gruel in the West, prepared either with sesame oil or with various beans and medicinal flavors, as explained extensively in such texts as the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Bhaiṣajyavastu*.
However, milk-rice is considered the most excellent.
When making food offerings, one should further add ghee, sugar, and so forth to ensure that both color and flavor are complete, and then present it first.
Furthermore, there are many varieties of rice in the western regions, and milk-rice (pāyasa) is considered the most excellent.

When offering this food, it should be accompanied by various flavors such as granulated sugar, salt, and ginger; one should also present soup, prepared according to the culinary methods of that region or following local customs.

As for *modaka*, one should boil various cakes in clarified butter (*sarpis*), blending them with various flavors and the three kinds of pungent medicines (*kaṭuka*), and thus making them manifoldly adorned.
As for *maṇḍaka*, these are thin cakes of this region.

The *patra-piṇḍaka* (leaf-cake) follows the baking method of India: flour is mixed with sugar, honey, and various flavors, then boiled in clarified butter and oil until it becomes exceedingly sweet and delicious.

As for the *śarkarā-piṇḍaka* (sugar-cake), this sugar is called *khaṇḍa*; its appearance is like that of the sugar produced in Yizhou (Yunnan), being extremely bright white and crumbling upon touch; this is used to mix with water.
First, one makes cakes from flour and soaks them repeatedly within it; only then does one eat them.
"Pure and exquisite" means making diligent efforts to ensure they are refined and clean, so that both color and fragrance are fully present.
Pūlaka, translated as "stuffed cake," is prepared by blending various superior flavors for the sake of those with discerning tastes.

There are two types of *antarāsa* cakes: some have holes pierced into them, while others are shaped like layers of tangled thread with numerous intervening cavities, further enriched with a variety of flavors.
The *matsyaśiras* cake is also coated with *kṛsara*, and further smeared with sugar and honey.
The *purnaka* cake is made from leavened dough and placed in a mold; it is cooked in ghee and oil, appearing like bubbles floating upon water, and is exceedingly lovely.
“Free from sorrow” refers to rolls made with sugar and flour.
“Pātra-food” refers to steamed dumplings made from flour that do not rise.
As for the phrase “such various delicacies,” it means that one should offer, according to one’s inclination, whatever superior flavors and exquisite fruits exist in various regions and countries.
The white sugar, rock honey, granulated sugar, and ghee-honey should each be placed separately.

Regarding "various kinds of syrups and drinks," the methods for preparing syrups in the Western Regions are numerous; they are all blended with fragrant medicinal herbs, making them delicious and effective for curing illnesses.
As for grape juice and other such non-seasonal drinks, they are as described in the *Vinaya*.
Regarding the consumption of milk and curd, one should likewise use pippali or kakkola, following the dietary methods prescribed by medical science.

Generally speaking, the Westerners' methods for preparing food and the sequence of their eating and drinking largely rely on medical arts; these possess the merit of nourishing one's nature and protecting the body, which is why they mostly live out their natural lifespans and rarely suffer the calamity of premature death.

Whenever food is placed, one should smear it all over with fragrant ointments; within the food hall, lotus leaves, lily leaves, or plantain leaves, and so forth, should be spread everywhere until they completely cover the area.
Regarding the absence [of a cloth], one should use a new, clean white cotton cloth or a clean piece of fabric, wash it thoroughly with pure water, and smear it everywhere with incense.

When arranging the food, one should add offerings for the principal deities: namely, Vairocana of the Central Womb Realm; in the second enclosure, Avalokiteśvara and Vajrapāṇi; in the next enclosure, the four bodhisattvas beginning with Mañjuśrī; and in the outer enclosure, Śākyamuni and one's own chosen tutelary deity (iṣṭadevatā).
If one part is assigned to the other positions, the principal deities should receive two parts.
Alternatively, if two parts are assigned to the others, Gohi states: "The lord of the maṇḍala should be increased by a multiple of that number."

Although there are such differences in rank and status, one should nevertheless offer worship with an impartial mind to all beings, from the Buddhas above down to the worldly ghosts and spirits below, ensuring that the offerings are both abundant and equal for all.
As for those who are unable to prepare [the offerings], they should simply make offerings to the Lord of the Family.
Alternatively, they may place the food within the inner courtyard and mentally offer it to all the deities.
The same principle applies to the incense, flowers, and other items presented.
Next, regarding the offering of lamps: there are many varieties of fragrant oils, such as *campaka* oil, *sumana* flower-scented oil, and so forth. As for the method of preparing these oils:

one should take fresh flowers, string them according to the method used for making garlands, and suspend them in the sun while supporting them with an oil vessel. Using an implement, one should collect the oil from the flowers and pour it back onto them; once it has fallen back into the vessel, one collects it again and pours it over the flowers once more.
In this manner, they proceeded in a continuous cycle from sunrise until sunset, at which point they ceased.
On the following day, they again took fresh flowers and prepared them as before, continuing until the fragrance of the oil was equal to the fragrance of the flowers, after which they stopped.
Regarding the vessels for the food offerings, the lamps, and so forth, those made of various precious gems are supreme.
If one cannot provide these, silver, copper, and the like may be used; even new and clean earthenware vessels will suffice for the purpose.

Regarding "silk banners and canopies on all four sides": if one possesses the means and resources, one should place them individually before each honored image, and it is best to use various precious gems as well.
If one cannot afford to provide colored powders or even paintings, when painting, one must use pure materials and must not use glue or similar substances.
If one cannot create them extensively, at the very least, one should place a canopy in each of the four directions.

The gate insignia, bells, and so forth, should all be fashioned with various adornments according to one's capacity, while also conforming to the characteristics shown in the "Chapter on Entering the Secret Maṇḍala."
Commentary on the Mahāvairocana Sūtra on the Attainment of Buddhahood,
Scroll Seven Commentary on the Mahāvairocana Sūtra on the Attainment of Buddhahood,
Scroll Eight Recorded by the Śramaṇa Acharya Yi-hsing (Ichigyō)
The remainder of the second chapter, "The Chapter on the Requisites for Entering the Maṇḍala," states in the Sūtra:

"Or one may make offerings with the mind; all [offerings] are performed in this way. As the World-Honored One has taught, among all offerings, the mind is supreme. Just as with each of the aforementioned individual offering substances, one should direct the mind so that it pervades the entire Dharmadhātu, sustaining them with mantras and secret mudrās, as explained in detail within the sequence of offerings.

Alternatively, one may contemplate the Great Jewel Tree King pervading all worlds, fully adorned with the characteristics of the Bodhi Tree King as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. From within it, every requisite for enjoyment emerges in inexhaustible abundance; reaching before all worthies and sages, it provides vast offerings and universally delivers all sentient beings.

Having thus directed the mind, one should employ the empowerment of the Vajra-Queen of the Space-Treasury (Gaganagañja-vajrārāṇī), and accomplishment will naturally be achieved according to one's wishes.
Next, the method for the auspicious vase (kalaśa) is explained; it should be made of precious materials such as gold or silver.
As for the vessel up to the point where there is nothing [else], it should be made of porcelain or clean earthenware; it must be perfectly round and well-formed, and moreover, it must not leak.
As described in the *Vinaya*, one should use a strainer as a skillful means to observe that the water is pure, and then fill the vessel with it to the brim.
The five treasures, the five grains, and the five medicines are explained in the *Guhya-samāja*.
However, as for these five medicines, they all originate from the Five Indic Regions; they cannot be found everywhere in this land.
Take the various powdered fragrant ointments as previously described and mix them with water, adding camphor and bezoar.

At the mouth of the flask, insert a precious flower—or whatever famous flowers are available in the local region—using those that are excellent, complete, and well-formed; arrange these flowers, fruits, branches, and leaves in an alternating pattern so that they hang down in a most magnificent display.
Wrap the neck with colored silk, tie a flower garland, and anoint it with various fragrances.
Perform the rites of protection and purification according to the procedures explained in the section on the sequence of offerings.
Within the central *garbhadhātu*, five vases should be placed; the central vase for Mahāvairocana is placed upon the flower pedestal, while the others are set within the outer petals.
Whenever food offerings are presented to the central *garbhadhātu*, the four Buddhas and four Bodhisattvas each occupy their respective seats within the flower pedestal.
Those who pay homage to Vairocana should place [the vases] before the flower altar.
If one has the capacity, one should place a vase before each and every deity.
If this is not possible, one should place them before the principal deities according to the internal and external directions.
Place one vase at each of the four gates and one vase at each of the four corners; outside the gates, there is another vase, which is consecrated with the mantra and mudrā of Trailokyavijaya.
When intending to enter or exit, one should sprinkle water upon oneself for protection; likewise, when summoning disciples to enter, one should also use it to sprinkle them.
Furthermore, a separate flask should be placed at the site of the *homa* ritual, with approximately one hundred or so flasks in total.
The Sūtra states that "six vases" is the minimum requirement.
One should place one vase at each of the four sides of the central womb; furthermore, the single vase outside the gate must certainly not be omitted.

If eighteen vases are used, place one vase in the central womb; in the second enclosure, place four vases for Mahāvīra, Padma, Vajrapāṇi, and the gatekeepers; and in the second enclosure, place one vase each for the four great bodhisattvas, namely Mañjuśrī and the others.
For the four gates and four corners of the outer enclosure of the flask, as well as outside the gates, these [flasks] are sufficient for their respective purposes.
If there are many who wish to receive initiation, one flask must be prepared for each person; none may be lacking.

As with the incense bottle, so it is with all the *argha* vessels; they should be made of gold, silver, white crystal, and so forth, or even of conch shell, wrought copper, stone, wood, or tree leaves and new earthenware. Filled with various perfumed waters and containing famous flowers, each should be placed individually in the same locations where the previous bottles were set.

Furthermore, one should offer pure robes to each of the honored ones; as previously stated, for the principal deities, one should also double the amount according to the method for offering food, which is why it says "each offers [robes] along with garments."
If one is unable to provide these, one should simply place them before the principal deities.
Alternatively, using a chest or casket according to what one possesses, one should place it within the Garbhadhātu Maṇḍala and offer it mentally to all the deities.
In general, when offering womb-mandala implements, they should be placed within one layer of empty space outside the womb.
If offering to nameless deities, they should be placed within the inner perimeter of the three-layered boundary.

Furthermore, when making offerings, one should first present *argha* water, next offer unguents, then flowers, incense, and food and drink, and finally offer lamps; the sequence in the scriptural text is not fixed.
Furthermore, regarding the profound and esoteric interpretation: "unguent" (*vilepana*) signifies purity.

Just as worldly unguents can cleanse filth and eliminate feverish affliction, so too does the practitioner now wash away the stains of the one hundred and sixty kinds of conceptual proliferation within the *bodhicitta* by means of the space-like *argha* offering. By applying the unguent of the unconditioned precepts (*asaṃskṛta-śīla*), the feverish afflictions of birth and death are extinguished, and the nature of coolness is attained; therefore, it is called "unguent."
That which is called "flower" signifies arising from compassion (*karuṇā*).
