It refers to these seeds of the pure mind blooming as the myriad practices within the Womb of Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā-garbha*), thereby adorning the Bodhi-tree of the Buddha; therefore, they are called flowers.
Incense represents the meaning of pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
Just as when the celestial king of trees (kalpavṛkṣa) is in full bloom, its fragrance naturally spreads both against and with the wind, so too is the fragrance of Bodhi:

according to each individual merit, it is incinerated by the fire of wisdom and fanned by the wind of liberation; through the sovereign power of compassionate vows, it turns everywhere to universally perfume all things. Therefore, it is called "burning incense."

Food and drink are the unsurpassed nectar, the flavor of neither birth nor death. If one partakes of this fruit and its merit matures, there will be no flavor superior to it; at that time, it is called "entering realization," and for this reason it is termed "food."

What is called a "lamp" signifies the Tathāgata’s radiance that destroys darkness; it means that when one reaches the stage of fruition, the obscurations of the mind are entirely exhausted, and the inexhaustible wisdom is transformed to shine universally upon all sentient beings—therefore, it is called a lamp. To explain this in a vertical sense, each and every stage (bhūmi) possesses these five meanings;
to explain it in a horizontal sense, each and every gate (dvāra) likewise possesses these five meanings.

For example, although the various foods explained above are identical in their suitability to the palate, they possess diverse flavors according to the skillful handling of the person preparing the meal.
One should know that other incenses, flowers, and so forth follow this same principle.

If a practitioner is skillfully able to perform the Vajra dance through the five-syllable gate (*pañcākṣaramukha*) to universally respond to sentient beings—just as one blends the five flavors, arranges the five colors, harmonizes the five tones, or compounds the five medicines—then although their fundamental natures do not exceed these five types, they undergo a thousand transformations and ten thousand shifts with inexhaustible ingenuity.

It should be known that such a person understands the meaning of the *samādhi* of ointment-incense, as well as the meanings of the *samādhis* of flowers, burning incense, food and drink, and lamps; they also understand the meaning of these five kinds of *dhāraṇīs*.
By making offerings with such various Dharma-gates and ritual implements to the Mind-King Tathāgata, one can cause all the Honored Ones to rejoice, and whatever is sought will surely be obtained.

If one uses the underlying intent herein to reflect back upon conventional worldly incense, flowers, and the like, one will naturally come to know the nature and scope of their application; thus, through immeasurable skillful means, they give rise [to benefit] upon contacting any object.

The Sūtra states: "Having performed the offerings in this manner, one next leads those who are to be converted. The following clarifies the branches of empowerment and instruction, as well as the branch of homa, at the time of performing the actual ritual procedure.
Within the context of the instructions on empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), there are the answers to the three questions posed by Vajrapāṇi: namely, how should one lead the disciple?
How should one confer the initiation (*abhiṣeka*)?
And how should one make offerings to the master?
Having finished asking these three questions, one then asks about the site for the homa.
In this present response, after first explaining the initiation of the disciple, the homa is clarified; only then are the remaining two questions answered.
However, since *homa* applies to all ritual procedures and not merely to the empowerment of disciples, it is appropriate to treat it as a distinct subsidiary component.

In the preceding fascicle, the layout of the maṇḍala was already explained for the time of the actual performance on the seventh night; here, the specific components required are separately clarified, which is why the textual flow is interrupted.
Now, following the preceding text, I shall explain this in sequential order.

Once the ācārya has finished drawing the maṇḍala and has thoroughly inspected it to ensure it is complete and perfect, he should then go outside and perform the ritual purification according to the dharma.

As previously described, direct your mind to universally prostrate to all Tathāgatas; repent of and take refuge in them to purify your own three karmas. Thereafter, according to the ritual of offering, bind the samaya-mantras and so forth to protect your body.

All the various articles for offering should likewise be purified by removing impurities and dispelling obstacles through the Amoghapāśa-mantra; they must be fully prepared in advance according to the ritual rules.
Furthermore, one should don the Vajra-armour and other accoutrements, ensuring each is applied exactly according to the ritual rules.
The Ācārya said:
"When forming the body of the Tathāgata, one uses the Tathāgata armor; when forming the Vajra body, one uses the Vajra armor; they should be employed by switching between them accordingly."

Furthermore, according to the Susiddhi and other tantras, it is especially excellent to adorn one’s own body with the various marks such as the *uṣṇīṣa* (crown protuberance) and the circular halo (*prabhāmaṇḍala*) of the Tathāgata; alternatively, one may use them universally, or perform them using the *sarvakarmika-mantra* (mantra for accomplishing all matters).

Having performed this, one then proceeds to the position within the maṇḍala and sits according to what is appropriate, abiding in yoga. First, one purifies the mind everywhere by means of the syllable-gateway *ra*;

next, one purifies the site of the practice, eliminating all afflictions so that it becomes identical to empty space. Thereafter, by means of the syllable *ha*, one generates a great wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*); upon the wind-circle, by means of the syllable *va*, one generates an ocean of fragrant water; and then, by means of the syllable-gateway *a*, one generates the vajra-ground and Sumeru, the King of Mountains.
One should know that this maṇḍala is situated upon it; as in the sequence of offerings, one should skillfully visualize it with various adornments, sustained by the Ākāśagarbha.
Next, at each of the positions of the deities within every maṇḍala, one should visualize their respective seed-syllables; from these syllables, all transform into the bodies of the deities.

If that ācārya perceives that the realization of the Path has not yet been integrated and fears that it may prolong the ritual period, he should simply contemplate the letter *A* upon the lotus pedestal within the central womb; from this gateway of letters (*akṣaramukha*), immeasurable light radiates forth, universally illuminating the seats of all the deities, whereupon the deities immediately manifest.
At that time, through skillful means, one contemplates that these deities are non-dual and indistinguishable from one's own body; thus, the deities are present within the body itself.
The Ācārya says: "If a practitioner has not yet established themselves in yoga, how could they be able to construct such a mandala ritual?"
Even at the very moment of its initial establishment, one has already contemplated it within one's own body before drawing it.

If one is a master of profound practice, then one is always accompanied by such a sacred assembly from the *Mahākaruṇā-garbha*, and realizes that this is none other than one’s own mind; thus, like those ten phrases on dependent origination, it is ultimately ungraspable.

Having thus visualized the Principal Deity, one next directs the mind to create various jeweled vehicles, consecrating them with the mantra and mudrā of Acala; with these, one welcomes the assembly of sages and purifies the path.
Next, perform the invocation: Guhyapati says, "One should invite each deity with their respective root mantra, or one may invite all the deities collectively using the mantra of the Maṇḍala Lord."
Alternatively, one may rely on what is taught in the fundamental scriptures and employ the mantras and mudrās for invocation according to one’s preference, whether in expanded or abbreviated form.

Furthermore, according to the tenet of this sūtra, the invited deities receive the invitation while remaining in their original seats; they arrive at this maṇḍala through the appearance of non-coming, which differs from the coarse expedient means that involve the conceptual distinction between "this" and "that."
Once the great assembly has gathered, one should employ the Immovable Vidyā to dispel obstructors, then reveal the three types of samaya and perform the empowerment.
Next, one should offer argha water and provide seats, speaking these words:
"Welcome, World-Honored One!"
Welcome, World-Honored One!
You have come down here by the power of your original vows.
We pray that you will grant your empowerment, accept this invitation, and partake of these humble offerings.
"Out of great compassion, please graciously accept [this].

At that time, because the Ācārya wishes to perform the Vajra-activity, he further uses the Immovable Wisdom-Sword to eliminate his own bodily obstructions, transforming himself into Vajrasattva to subdue the activities of Māra.

One should again bind the boundaries of all directions with the sword of wisdom; furthermore, one should once more bind the perimeter using the mantra and mudrā of the Tathāgata’s Great Boundary. One should protect each direction with the four great guardians, and then universally protect them all by maintaining the Great Guardian of Intolerance.
The Ācārya said:
"In constructing a maṇḍala, from the very beginning one should employ Acala, or else use Trailokyavijaya to protect and maintain this site."
During each session of recitation in the interim, one should perform the ritual boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*) according to the rules, and upon completion, release it.
When reaching the night of the ritual performance, one should further prepare the vajra-thread and fully establish the boundary within it.

Regarding the location of the consecration homa altar, one should further demarcate a perimeter with thread outside the maṇḍala so that it connects with the inner boundary, and therein establish the gates for entry and exit.

Regarding the statement that the outer boundary of the maṇḍala is universally enclosed by cutting with the vajra-line: at the time of performing the homa offering, one should likewise apply this visualization.
At the gateway, the raised vajra-line should be made to allow for the coming and going of all the deities.
Furthermore, when performing the boundary-binding (*sīmā-bandha*), one should simply carry out the ritual procedures as usual at one's original seat.
If one wishes to perform a circumambulation once to bind the perimeter, this too will be fully accomplished.

If, once the boundary has been established, it is suddenly broken due to deluded thoughts, or if various demonic activities arise, one should immediately recite and maintain the Great Protection of Akṣobhya.

If one wishes to remain unobstructed at all times, one should first employ the Great Protection (mahārakṣā) for the perimeter and the ritual offerings; should obstructions arise later, one must employ it once again.

Next, one should perform prostrations and offer *argha* water; using the Great Wisdom Knife, one should sprinkle it over all the ritual implements, purifying them with the inconceivable mind of the *dharmadhātu*.
When offering scented unguents, one should remain focused on the *unguents-mantra* while holding them.
When making offerings in succession, one should further apply the specific mantra of each respective deity—whether collectively or individually, or using the mantra one personally maintains.
The remaining offerings should be treated in the same manner.
Furthermore, one should perform the mental offering ritual, reciting the Gaganagañja-dhāraṇī and praising with the Vajrāriṣa chant.
Next, one goes outside again to offer food to the spirits of the wilderness.
According to the diagram, one offers to the Vināyakas outside the eastern gate and to the Gṛhakṣatas outside the southern gate.
As for those possessed by *māra* spirits, offer *śigru* outside the western gate.
As for those who spread pestilence, offer *śatapuṣpī* outside the northern gate.
Place four positions on each side of every gate.
However, Ghoṣaka says: "These are all rākṣasas, piśācas, bhūtas, and various classes of non-human beings who consume flesh and blood; some dwell upon the ground, while others dwell in forests."
Furthermore, whatever the mind conceives of or clings to, each shall be summoned from its respective direction and offered universally.

All food intended as offerings for the maṇḍala should be taken and combined into one place; likewise, all incense, flowers, and so forth should also be set aside individually and placed together in one spot.

The ācārya should give rise to a mind of infinite great compassion and the gift of Dharma; within the yoga, he should visualize various articles for enjoyment and distribute them by consecrating them with the *ākāśagarbha-vajra-jñāna-mantra*.
When these spirits and deities receive their offerings, they do not create obstacles for the maṇḍala.
One should begin from the east as the primary direction, then proceed to the south, west, and north.
Having thus completed one circuit, he again offered food in the northeast; next, he proceeded to the southeast, the southwest, and the northwest.

Having completed another circuit, he returned to the east of the altar to offer food to the spirits of the upper regions, and next proceeded to the west of the altar to offer food to the spirits of the lower regions.
In general, the food is offered three times.

Among all ritual matters, this rite is particularly difficult; at such a time, various extremely terrifying forms may appear before one’s eyes, or great sounds such as the roar of thunder or the howling of jackals may be heard—encountering such various extraordinary signs, the ācārya must maintain a firm and composed mind.
Furthermore, when wishing to give, one should first further protect one's body so that every action conforms to the Dharma.
If the food is exhausted and the recipient asks for more, one should give it again, ensuring it is abundant and generous so as to bring them joy.
If the materials are few, one should simply offer whatever is available.
Generally, regarding the offerings within the altar, one should maintain a mind of equanimity and must not allow for any deficiency or omission.
Ghoṣila said: "If, while serving food, there is an error or a deficiency, one should immediately make up for it and still request that [the recipient] accept it with joy.
If the types of food served are not complete, one should use other items to fulfill the required number."
When the distribution of food to all directions was complete, he washed his hands and sprinkled water for purification, then burned incense as an offering before the gate.
Next, he entered within to present *argha* and burn incense, and with a focused mind, he offered garments as a supplementary gift.

Thereafter, one should sit upon the yoga-seat and sustain the body with the five wheel-syllables; placing the King of Pervasive Radiance of a Hundred Lights at the head, one should gaze with stainless eyes at the syllable "Na" (the letterless) at the heart-lotus pedestal, and only then perform the universal gate recitation.
First, the mantra manifests vividly within the moon-disc of Vairocana’s heart; thereafter, one recites it while displaying the secret mudrā.
Having completed the circuit of the central Garbhadhātu, one proceeds next to the deities of the second enclosure, continuing until the very end.

One may perform the recitation while visualizing each [deity] appearing before one; or, identifying oneself as that deity, visualize the syllables of the mantra upon the moon at its heart and perform the recitation; or even instantaneously manifesting the body of the maṇḍala and performing the recitation—this depends on the power of the practitioner’s mental visualization.

If one is unable to do so, one should recite the mantra of the Lord of the Family one hundred times with a single-minded focus, and recite seven times each for the remaining principal deities, while forming their respective mudrās, as described in detail in the sequence of offerings.

Once the Ācārya has completed these ritual procedures, he should again prostrate with a sincere heart to all the Honored Ones. Thereafter, he shall summon each of the disciples one by one to enter, purifying them by sprinkling the aforementioned scented water. He shall then give them unguent to apply to their hands and next provide pure flowers. He should briefly proclaim the true meaning of bodhicitta from the "Chapter on Abiding in the Mind" (*Cittotpāda-paṭala*), causing them to recognize their own refuge, generate the authentic resolve for awakening (*samyak-cittotpāda*), and mindfully recollect all Buddhas with utmost sincerity and reverence.

Why is this so? Because a practitioner who is able to give rise to the Buddha-mind is a child of the Buddha; they shall receive the position of consecration as a Dharma Prince and be born into the lineage of the Tathāgata. Therefore, in all their movements and actions, they must never forget the Buddhas.
In this sutra, whenever it is about to expound any mantra, it invariably states, "I universally take refuge in all Buddhas"; this is precisely that meaning.

Regarding the term "Pure Buddhas" (viśuddha-buddha): in the Śrāvaka teachings, even Arhats are called "Buddhas," and other Mahāyāna sūtras of provisional meaning also contain the sense of attaining Buddhahood; however, they cannot be designated as "Pure."
Now, to clarify that the fundamental mind is the eternal Buddha, it is distinguished by the character "Pure" (Jing).
In a literal translation from the Sanskrit original, this would be called the "Buddha Family" (Fubu) in the Buddhist tradition; this carries the meaning of a lineage, clan, or category.

At that time, the ācārya contemplates the disciple’s body as the five wheels (*pañcacakra*) and sustains it with the five syllables; furthermore, by placing the syllable *A* and the others within the lotus-heart (*hṛdayapuṣkara*), he causes it to become identical with the essence of Mahāvairocana.

Seal the crown of the head with the Buddha-samaya-mudrā; next, seal the heart with the Dharmadhātu-janma-mudrā; and again, form the Dharma-cakra-pravartana-mudrā and seal the navel, reciting the respective mantras three times for each.
Next, one transforms the syllable *A* within that mind into the syllable *Va*, binds the Vajrasattva mudrā upon all the limbs—namely, the five locations—and seals them.
The reason for doing so is that one desires to accomplish those vajra activities.
At that time, the ācārya should also further protect and sustain himself by means of the samaya and other [practices].

Next, take a new, clean white cotton cloth or another kind of silk fabric; first, purify it according to the ritual using the Acala mantra, and then apply it three times with the King of Mantras of the respective family.
When constructing the Maṇḍala of Mahāvairocana, one should employ the mantra of Vairocana; the same applies to Padmapāṇi and Vajrapāṇi.

Cover the disciple’s face completely with this pure, dyed silk, and while generating a profound mind of compassion and protective mindfulness, whisper the samaya precepts into their ear, ensuring that no others who have not yet entered the maṇḍala hear the sound.
This verse shall be explained in the chapter on the practice of the *Cakravarti-maṇḍala*.

Furthermore, one should visualize that upon his crown there is the syllable *ra*, with a bindu placed above it; thus it is said, "adorned with the great empty dot (*mahābindu*)," which refers to the syllable *raṃ*.
The four sides of these syllables are entirely surrounded by blazing flames, like a continuous garland of flowers.
From within the syllables, bright white light flows forth everywhere, like the radiance of the pure, full moon.
By means of the empowerment of this mind of the pure *dharmadhātu*, one is able to eliminate all internal and external obstacles.
Next, they are led to the first gate, where the two nāga kings Sunanda and Upasunanda guard it, causing them to stand precisely at the gateway so that they neither advance nor retreat.

The master shall form the samaya-mudrā for the disciple, recite that mantra three times, and place a flower upon the mudrā; he shall then cause the disciple, with a mind of utmost sincerity, to scatter it toward the maṇḍala.

Wherever the flower arrives, one should know that this is precisely the Dharma-gate of the practitioner’s past causes and conditions and their spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra); one should then proceed with practice by relying upon this very gate of skillful means.
Guhya said: "When about to enter the maṇḍala, the ācārya should speak these words:

'I, [Name], having constructed this maṇḍala according to the Dharma, shall lead the disciple in; according to their merit, spiritual lineage, and capacity as a vessel for accomplishment, I pray that you will manifest your signs within this maṇḍala.'"
Once the flowers have been scattered, one should next uncover the face so that they may behold the maṇḍala, and with a heart of joy, address them, saying:
"Now, observe this wondrous maṇḍala and give rise to profound reverence and faith."

You have now been born into the family of all Buddhas; all the Vidyārājas and Honored Ones together bestow their protective empowerment upon you, and all auspiciousness and siddhis shall manifest before you.
Therefore, firmly maintain the samaya precepts and diligently practice the teachings of the mantra dharma.

Next, he instructs the disciple to universally make offerings of incense, flowers, and so forth to the holy assembly of the maṇḍala. He then bestows the fundamental mantra and mudrā upon him within the ritual site (maṇḍala), instructing him to sit in one place and recite them; subsequently, he leads the remaining persons inside.

In all cases, the ācārya should observe where the flower falls to discern its nature and category; if it falls upon the head of the Buddha, one will achieve the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa and the hair-curl marks (ūrṇā-kośa).
If it falls upon the face, one should achieve the Buddha-eye.
Regarding the divisions within the body, one should know that the various minds are accomplished.
If it falls upon the lower parts, the various messengers and so forth are accomplished.

Furthermore, according to the upper, middle, and lower parts of the Buddha’s body, one knows the accomplishment of the upper, middle, and lower [levels]; this is likewise true for the lotus and the vajra.
As for the other deities, one need only know their upper, middle, and lower characteristics.
If the flower falls far from that honored one, it will only be accomplished after a long time.
If it falls within the hall of offerings, bestow the mantra of whichever honored one it belongs to.
If [the seed-syllable] falls between two deities, one should observe its distance from them.

If it first falls within the inner court and is then moved to the outer court, that person lacks sufficient faith; yet if they persist in recitation with effort, they may attain the lower level of accomplishment.
Those who fall into the various realms, paths, or courtyards of practice lack a resolute mind and shall not attain accomplishment.
If they wish to cast [the ritual object] again, they should perform a homa and only then cast it.
The remainder is as explained there.
Next, one should perform the *śāntika* homa for the disciples; this is the *śāntika* rite, which may also be translated as "pacification."
Next, this constitutes one branch.

Now, in the Tathāgata’s response, because he follows the sequence of ritual practice, his explanation of the branch of empowerment and instruction is not yet complete; it is precisely at this juncture that he teaches *homā* (fire sacrifice), or perhaps it may be considered as forming a single branch together with the methods of consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and so forth.
As for the scripture stating, "Perform the silent homa; the homa abides according to the ritual," the aforementioned term "homa" refers to the performance of this specific homa rite.
Next, regarding the term *homa*, this is an instruction for the practitioner.
When performing *homa*, one must abide according to the ritual rules; therefore, it is stated emphatically.

Within this context, from the empowerment of oneself through the yoga method up to the invitation and the boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*), all are based on the skillful means of recitation; thus, it says "one should abide according to the ritual rules."

Regarding the phrase, "From the initial central matrix (garbhadhātu) to the second outer [court], one should maintain a mind free of doubt within the maṇḍala": the preceding secret terminology designates the court of Śākyamuni’s retinue as the second; thus, it is intended that what lies outside the great maṇḍala corresponds to the central matrix.
Furthermore, the ācārya stands outside, facing the maṇḍala; within these two positions, he establishes the fire altar (homa-sthaṇḍila).
Because it is a secret terminology in the Sanskrit original, it says: "The ācārya constructs the homa altar within the maṇḍala."
If one does not receive [this teaching] from a master, one will frequently lose its essential meaning; furthermore, it might be constructed within the maṇḍala court itself.
Now, as for the consecration altar (abhiṣeka-maṇḍala), it must be positioned directly facing the central womb (garbha); therefore, this altar may be moved slightly toward the south.
Up to and including the southwest corner, all [positions] are to be viewed as three groups in relation to one another; there is no error in principle.
A mind free from doubt and hesitation is precisely the intent of *śāntika* (pacification); one should perform it with single-minded focus and without distraction.

If a practitioner dwells in the gateway of the syllable *śa* and contemplates all phenomena as eternally quiescent, such that doubt and regret are exhausted and hindrances and obstructions are purified, this is precisely the fundamental intent of quiescent *homa*.

Regarding the method for constructing the maṇḍala: take one cubit as the length and width measured by one’s own forearm; its depth shall be half that. A border is to be placed all around, four finger-joints wide, and its height shall be the same.
In general, homa altars may be square, circular, or triangular, varying according to the ritual objective; however, for the rites performed herein, one should employ a square altar.
It should be smeared with *gomaya* and *gomutra*, and sprinkled with scented water.
Regarding the "inner-and-outer Vajra Seal," it means that one should draw a *vajra* within the hearth. Why is this so?
*Homa* is the fire of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, which can incinerate all calamities and misfortunes born of karmic causes and conditions, utterly purifying them until nothing remains.

The square altar is named Mahendra; it signifies the meaning of the King of Mind. It clarifies that the seal of this fire of wisdom exhausts the very source and bottom of reality. Arising from the nature of the vajra, it is therefore identical to the vajra and indestructible.
In the subsequent "Chapter on Mundane and Supramundane Homa," the World-Honored One himself will explain the causes and conditions in detail.
If a practitioner of mantra merely performs mundane homa without understanding the secret intent within this [teaching], would it not then be indistinguishable from the Vedic fire-sacrifices?
Therefore, the translator has combined the names of the various wisdoms, hoping that both the shallow and deep exegeses may be presented together for their respective utility.

As the Sūtra states: "To the right of the Master’s position, the implements for the homa are arranged. Suppose the gate of the Great Maṇḍala opens toward the west; the fire altar (homa-kunda) should then be situated to the west of the Great Altar, and the Ācārya, in turn, sits to the west of the fire altar, facing east.
The various implements and requisites for use in the homa ritual should be placed to the south of the master’s position.
The fuel for the homa should consist of milky wood, such as that of the *śāla* or *udumbara* trees.

Alternatively, one may cut a stalk of *Euryale ferox* (*niuxi*) to a length of twelve finger-widths; these must all be freshly harvested and moistened. Selecting those with straight, orderly nodes, one should observe their orientation and place them so that they point uniformly upward or downward, sprinkling them with scented water to purify them, ensuring the roots face toward oneself.
When you wish to ignite it, dip both ends into milk, curd, ghee, and honey, and cast them into the furnace.
Alternatively, it is especially effective to use agarwood sticks four finger-joints long and as thick as a thumb, which have been dipped in storax and used one hundred and eight times.

Regarding the various foods, incense, flowers, and other offerings to be presented within the maṇḍala, take each of them individually and, using the *karmavidhi-mantra*, purify them according to the ritual rules and place them to the right of the seat.
The argha vessel should be placed on the left side.
As for the various foods to be offered, they should be mixed with ghee, curd, and so forth, and placed together in a single vessel.
Furthermore, the five grains should also be moistened with ghee, oil, and the like, combined into one place, and set in a separate vessel; all should be prepared in advance.

If one provides a profound and esoteric interpretation, these components of the *homa* signify the meaning of manifold causes and conditions; it is through these causes and conditions that the calamities of the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*) are produced.
Now, by taking these very same elements as fuel for the fire of wisdom, one makes offerings to the Universal Gate Body (*samantamukha-kāya*), thereby augmenting its inconceivable power.
The Sūtra says: "Taking afflictions as firewood and wisdom as fire, by these causes and conditions, the meal of nirvāṇa is prepared, so that all disciples may enjoy it with delight."
This is the meaning. Furthermore, when performing the ritual for a disciple, one should have them sit in a squatting posture upon a mat of fresh *kuśa* grass to the north of the *ācārya*.
The ācārya should likewise sit upon a mat of *kuśa* grass; he must not use items such as couches or cushions.
There are briefly three reasons for using fresh *kuśa* grass:
first, its nature is pure and it provides a pleasant touch when removed from its source, which can eliminate the practitioner’s mind of dullness, lassitude, and arrogance.
Second, this is *kuśa* grass; the World-Honored One used it as a seat to realize *bodhi*, and for this reason, it can eliminate all obstacles.
Third, by means of this auspicious *kuśa* grass, the nature of wisdom is symbolized.

This grass has many sharp thorns on both sides; if one sits, lies down, or grasps it without skillful means, one will instead be injured by them, but if one handles it with care according to its direction, it cannot cause harm.

All dharmas are likewise: if one contemplates them in accordance with the principle of truth, all afflictions possess the function of inherent purity; yet if one loses the skillful means, they can destroy the body of wisdom. Therefore, this is used as a symbolic representation of the Dharma-gate.

If one constructs a maṇḍala upon a large rock or on an upper story of a multi-storied pavilion where it is impossible to dig a pit for a hearth, one should instead use colored powders to paint it, making it as distinct and magnificent as possible; this may then serve its purpose, and is called a "concise" method for preparing a site for homa.
If the maṇḍala constructed within the chamber is cramped, one should go outside and construct a hearth according to the ritual rules at a location from which the site of the maṇḍala is visible.

All four sides of the hearth should be encircled with fresh *kuśa* grass, arranged so that they turn to the right; they should be layered one over another in sequence, with their tips protruding. The remainder is as explained in the "Homa Chapter."

Furthermore, it should be surrounded on all sides and made broad and thick so as not to leave any exposed ground; one should sprinkle it everywhere with scented water, using the empowerment for accomplishing all matters—the *bhūmiparikarman-mantra* (ground-preparation mantra) explained in the preceding text.
Regarding the ritual procedure for homa within this context: once the ācārya has first completed the offerings and recitations within the maṇḍala, he should next go outside and perform the fire rite.

Facing east, seated upon an auspicious seat, first take firewood and dry fuel and place them in the hearth; sprinkle clarified butter (*ghṛta*) over them and ignite them. Then place wet fuel, and having performed the purification by sprinkling while reciting the *karmasādhana-mantra* to remove impurities and expel obstacles, one should abide in yoga. By means of the seed-syllable of the Fire God (*Agni*), transform it into the Lord of Fire within the triangular maṇḍala, selecting whichever of the twelve fire deities shown in the [lower] chapter corresponds to the specific ritual activity.

Once you have attained union, you should contemplate that the body of the Fire Lord and your own body are non-dual and indistinguishable; as it is with the Fire Lord, so too should you know the fire maṇḍala to be.
One should contemplate that these three locations are all of one and the same nature, and thereafter invoke the deity Agni with his mantra.
The Susiddhi states: "When wishing to perform the invocation, first speak these words:
'I now invoke the foremost of the fire-gods, the sage among deities, who is revered by those who practice the Brahma-conduct; I pray that you descend to this place to accept and receive the homa.'"
Next, the mantra of the Fire Deity (Agni) is spoken as follows:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām agnayai svāhā*. The first phrase, "Homage to all Buddhas," has a meaning as previously explained.
The second phrase is *Agnaye*, which means "fire.
In this context, the initial letter *A* serves as the seed-syllable; because all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, it is identical to the essence of vajra-wisdom.

This practice of righteousness is such that, because all dharmas are fundamentally unarisen, although one is fully endowed with the myriad practices, there is nothing to be practiced; therefore, it is called "self-awakening without a teacher."
If this is self-awakening without a teacher, it is identical to the Great Emptiness that pervades all places; therefore, it is of the same essence as the letter NA.
Because all phenomena are without teacher and without practice, they naturally pervade all places; thus, without moving from within the triple world, one arrives at *sarvajñā* (omniscience).
Therefore, when there is neither vehicle nor one who rides it, that is the Mahāyāna.
The reason for adding the term "samādhi" is to clarify that this vehicle maintains an equal balance between concentration and wisdom.

When all Buddhas practiced the bodhisattva path, they all used such fires of wisdom to incinerate all mental defilements and to blaze forth the light of the True Dharma; therefore, to speak of them according to reality is itself the realization of mantras.
When performing the invocation, one should add the words *īkṣe īkṣe*; when performing the dismissal, one adds the words *gaccha gaccha*.
The forms of the mudrās are as described in the subsequent chapter.

Having completed the invocation, first purify [the site] three times with *argha* perfumed water and offer three libations of water for rinsing the mouth. Then, taking various grains, clarified butter (*sarpis*), curd (*dadhi*), and other substances, perform the *homa* offering to the Fire Deity (*Agnideva*) by reciting the aforementioned mantra three times.

In all homa rites, one should first fill the large ladle with pure ghee and offer it into the fire; next, burn wood; then, the homa-rice; then, various grains or milk porridge; and finally, burn lotuses and other offerings as desired.
All that is offered during this interval should be done with a small ladle; thus the Sūtra says, "One should hold a vessel full and thereby make an offering.

Having made the offering, one should again sprinkle scented water and pour *argha* (water of respect), just as a person rinses their mouth with water after eating. Furthermore, one should offer incense, flowers, and so forth, and then direct the mind to escort the Fire God (*Agni*) back to his original seat.

Next, one should invoke the various deities. First, take a flower and purify it by reciting the *siddhi-mantra* to remove impurities; empower it with the *kula-adhipati-mantra*, hold it with both hands joined, and with mind and voice say:
"I pray that all the honored ones will empower this place and accept my humble offering."
One should then cast it from across the hearth toward the maṇḍala.

When about to cast it, according to its distance, one should first visualize this flower reaching all the seats of the deities, forming a corresponding seat for each according to their type. Furthermore, one should employ it to accomplish various tasks; having removed impurities and purified it within the hearth, one may then invite the deities.

One may invite each of those Honored Ones individually by means of their respective mantras, or invite them according to the retinue of a particular section, or even invite them all at once using the King of Mantras.

Furthermore, since this fire hearth is identical to the realm of fire, when inviting, one should simply visualize that the various Honored Ones descend from their original seats; when the ritual is completed, they likewise return to their original places without the appearance of departure.

For each homa performed for a single deity, one should sprinkle the hearth with scented water and provide water for rinsing the mouth; as the subsequent text states, one should offer these seven times while reciting the Śāntika-mantra.
When each of these has been completed, perform one hundred and eight more *homa* offerings, and once again offer clarified butter (*ghṛta*) from a full vessel for one round.
If one is unable to do even this, one should make offerings collectively one hundred and eight times, or one thousand and eighty times, while reciting:
"Whatever is here, may all the Honored Ones together accept this offering."
Next, one should go on almsround everywhere to inspire joy.
Having made offerings according to the Dharma, one should then perform repentance, dedicate the merit, and chant the Vajra verses, ensuring that the incense burning does not cease.

Furthermore, having offered arghya water and then prostrated to the deities, one summons the disciples. Following the ritual procedures such as scattering flowers as described above, and once the instructions have been fully delivered, one leads each disciple individually to the site of the homa. To the left of the ācārya, they remain crouching with a mind of reverence.

The Master grasps the right thumb of the disciple with his left hand and recites the *Śāntika* mantra; for each recitation, he offers a fire-oblation (*homa*). This is done twenty-one times, and the disciples perform it in the same manner.
Guhya says: "Furthermore, smear incense upon your hands, press them against the [disciple's] chest, and dispatch them by reciting the mantra as you wish.
Now, we shall explain this mantra for pacifying calamities.

*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām amoghaśāntika śāntikara-praśama-dharma-ujjvālāpavaya sarvabhāvadharmasamantaprabhā svāhā.* The essence of this mantra is the initial *ā* (long *ā*), which is pronounced with urgency. *Ā* signifies that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are fundamentally unarisen; it is the essence of the fire of Vajra-wisdom. When the bindu (*am*) is added, it becomes the fire of Vajra-wisdom in its fundamental mode of arising. The two dots beside the *samādhi* vowel (*m*) signify the meaning of *nirvāṇa*.

It is said that by entering this gateway of the syllable A, because one is fully endowed with the practice of wisdom, one is able to incinerate and eliminate all hindrances and obscurations, thereby attaining the great quiescence of *nirvāṇa*.
This is precisely the meaning underlying its designation as the "Mantra for Quelling Calamities."

Furthermore, when performing the ritual procedure, one should contemplate this syllable as being surrounded by a garland of light. Emerging from fire, it is endowed with three colors: its primary body is yellowish-white; its samādhi is painted red like Jambūnada gold; and the two side-dots are black like the fire at the end of an eon.

Because its intrinsic nature is pure white, it possesses the function of pacification; combined with yellow, it has the function of enrichment; red is for the functions of subjugation and incineration; and black is for the functions of crushing great obstacles and summoning.

Furthermore, this scriptural form is a gateway of skillful means; one should know that it is identical in nature to the color of great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*), yet possesses all manner of activities.

Moreover, among the twelve fires mentioned in the subsequent text: the wisdom-fire of the syllable *A*; the fire of the fulfillment of practice, which is the painting of samādhi; the wind-drying fire, which possesses the meaning of summoning; the *lohita* fire, which possesses the meaning of subjugation; the *mṛṣṭa* fire, which is the blending of yellow and red; the wrathful fire, which is a combination of red and black; and the *jaṭhara* fire, which is endowed with a multitude of colors.
To state it briefly, it fully possesses twelve kinds of functions, which shall be explained in detail below.
Each subsequent phrase serves to explain the preceding one.
The first phrase, *mahāśānti*, carries the meaning of "Great Quiescence."

*Bha* (蘗多) has the meaning of "gone" (*gata*). It signifies that by virtue of the meaning of this single syllable, the Tathāgata has gone to and arrived at the Great Nirvāṇa, which is the eternally quiescent fundamental nature.

The essence of the syllable *A* is fundamental quiescence; because it possesses the stroke of samādhi, it is the Sugata; because it possesses the dot of purification, it is Nirvāṇa. Being unmoving in this very place, one acts and arrives simultaneously; being identical to the great void and pervading all things without exception, it is called "Great Quiescence."

The next phrase is *saṃdhikāra*, which carries the meaning of "creating tranquility. This is because it is said that through the fulfillment of the skillful means (*upāya*) of this gateway of letters, one constantly and pervasively manifests throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time. By universally performing the activities of the Universal Gate (*samantamukha-karman*), one brings sentient beings to accomplishment and causes them all to depart toward the midst of Great Tranquility; therefore, it is called "creating tranquility."

Next, regarding the phrase *praśamadharmānirjāta*: *pra* means "supreme," and *śama* means "realizing this tranquility. This is a re-explanation of the preceding term; because it is made tranquil, it is the tranquility within tranquility.

Why is this so? Because quiescence is ultimately unattainable, one constantly acts; because acting is ultimately unattainable, one is constantly quiescent. Since this cannot be conceived by any in the world, it is called "supreme."
Dharma is the Dharma; "jue" (覺) means that which is manifold, which is birth.
From what does it arise?
It arises precisely from this inconceivable karma of quiescence.
Because movement and stillness are ultimately equal, from the phrase "originally unborn," the root, stem, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are fully produced, forming the King of Bodhi Trees.
Just as the element of fire can both burn and nourish, so too is the diamond-like fire of wisdom: it uses the *bindu* of purification to burn away defilements, and the *bindu* of samādhi to nourish.
Next, it says *abhāva sarvabhāva*, which further explains the preceding phrase; thus, it says they are "without intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*).
All intrinsic natures are quiescent by their very nature and arise from conditions; therefore, they lack intrinsic nature.
That which arises from conditions is inherently quiescent; therefore, it constitutes the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena.
By this principle, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) does not arise, and great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*) emerges.
Next, it says *dharmasamantaprabhāta*, which further explains the preceding phrase.
For this reason, the Tathāgata is equal toward all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), meaning that he has realized unsurpassed bodhi.

*Prāpti* (attainment) means the sense of "obtaining"; because there is nothing to be obtained, one attains this phrase of equality. The rest is as explained above. Whenever performing *homa*, various signs may appear:

sometimes the fire does not burn, or it burns and then quickly extinguishes, or it is not very intense; or smoke arises without flame, or the smoke is extremely turbid; or it produces sounds like those of donkeys and other such animals, which people find unpleasant to hear; or it says things such as "it will not be accomplished. One should know that these are signs of obstacles and failure.

If, amidst smoke and flames, various wondrous forms such as jeweled vases, jeweled nets, or lion-drawn chariots appear; or if sounds like those of bells, gongs, conchs, and other musical instruments resound; or if the voices of auspicious accomplishment emerge—know that these are the signs of unimpeded *siddhi*.

Furthermore, regarding those who skillfully perform *homā*, they shall receive direct oral instructions therein and come to clearly understand the signs of both success and failure (*saṃvarta-vivarta*).

In all *homā* rites, one should act according to the specific task at hand, employing either a mind of tranquility, joy, or ferocity. The garments worn should be white, yellow, or red, and one should sit facing north, east, or south, as appropriate.
These maṇḍalas also differ in being circular, square, or triangular, and their colors may likewise be known.
As for the firewood for the homa: for the rite of pacification (śāntika), use the uppermost branches of trees;
for the rite of increase (pauṣṭika), use the middle branches of trees.
For rites of subjugation, one should use tree roots.
For rites of pacification, one should use ghee, milk, barley, honey, and milk porridge, as well as tips of *kuśa* grass, *mujana* flowers, white sandalwood, and *aśoka* wood.
If one wishes to increase prosperity, one should employ milk porridge, curd-rice, honey, milk-curd porridge, sesame, *devadāru*, *tagara*, *śatāvarī*, *nāgapuṣpa*, various grains, and so forth.
If it is a matter of subduing, one should use red or white mustard seeds, mustard oil, poison, bones, hair, or various thorny wood such as thorns.
Although the sūtra does not provide a complete enumeration, one should infer it by analogy.
Furthermore, as with the number of *sū* seeds burned, the same applies to sesame seeds; for the others, the amount may be according to one's preference.
At both the beginning and the end, one should perform the *ghṛta-homa* (ghee-oblation); all other ritual procedures are likewise.
In every case of a *śānti-homa* (pacification rite), one must first perform the *abhicāra* (subjugation) method.
If the mantra being employed contains a subjugating meaning, one should recite it exactly according to its original form.
If it lacks such a meaning, one must augment it in accordance with the ritual rules.

Using mustard seeds and other substances appropriate for subjugation, perform homa seven times or twice seven times; next, visualize the phrases and meanings appropriate for enrichment along with their offerings and perform them likewise seven times or twice seven times, only then fully performing the rite for pacifying calamities.
When performing an *āpyāyana* (augmenting) homa, one must first perform the *abhicāra* (subjugating) rite; only then can the *āpyāyana* rite be fully accomplished.
As for the *abhicāra* homa, a single method suffices for its completion, and it does not require the preliminary preparations (*pūrvopāya*).
One should know that this maṇḍala possesses three types of ritual activities.
Guhyaka said: "After the consecration is completed, one must further perform the homa according to the dharma."

First, one should burn ghee one hundred times using the mantra of the Maṇḍala Lord; next, one should offer rice mixed with ghee, honey, and curd one hundred times using the mantra of Śānti; then, one should offer sesame seeds one hundred times; only after this should one extensively display the maṇḍala.

When the ritual is concluded and about to be dispersed, the preceptor should sprinkle himself with water and again offer *argha* (consecrated water), making offerings to each of the deities in succession.

Next, perform *homa* eight hundred times for the Lord of the Maṇḍala; then one hundred times with the *śāntika-mantra*; then twenty-one times with the Family Heart-mantra (*kula-hṛdaya*). Then, using the mantra of each individual deity, perform *homa* seven times each with cow’s ghee. Thereafter, perform *homa* at will with the root-holding mantra (*mūla-dhāraṇī*), and only then proceed with the rites of dissolving the boundary (*sīmā-bandha-vimocana*) and the dismissal (*visarjana*).
Alternatively, it is also permissible to rely on the previously mentioned general method.
In this present sūtra, the three syllables *a-sva-va* are, as explained in the "Chapter on the Wheel of Syllables" (*Akṣaracakravatīpatala*), the heart-mantras (*hṛdayamantra*) of the three families.
If it is on other occasions for the three types of ritual activities, once the recitation has been completed within the *tāna* [mandala], one should immediately exit and perform the *homa*.

Alternatively, if performing a *siddhi-homa*, the five locations must be aligned in a straight line: first, the principal deity; second, the fire pit; third, the object to be accomplished; fourth, the vessel for the clarified butter (*ghṛta*); and fifth, the seat of the *ācārya*.

Regarding the objects to be offered, first cover them with clean leaves; for each item such as clarified butter (*sarpis*) that is taken up, place a fuel-stick (*samidh*) upon the leaf before finally setting it on fire.
If one is to accomplish the benefit of sentient beings, one should draw their images at the place where the substances are kept; the rest is as explained above.
If performing homa for the sake of humans, one should recite each name individually before casting [the substances] into the fire.

If there is no maṇḍala and one performs only the homa rite, one should draw a single-layered maṇḍala around the hearth and arrange the seats for the various deities; whether one intends to invite the deities for offerings extensively or concisely is left to one's discretion.

The Susiddhi states: "Once the homa is completed, one should take pure water and empower it with the respective root mantra; then, circling the hand around the hearth, one should sprinkle the water three times."
One must again invite the Fire Deity (*Agnideva*) to receive the remaining offerings, and so forth, until one visualizes him returning to his original seat.

As for the remaining grains, clarified butter (*ghṛta*), honey (*madhu*), and curd (*dadhi*), combine them all in one place and perform *homā* by reciting the Fire Deity’s mantra three times over them. Once again perform the mudrās for protecting the body and the directions, and only after releasing the boundary (*sīmābandha*) may you dismiss the deities.

Guhya said: "On the sixth night, having completed the rite for becoming a disciple, one first performs the *vaśīkaraṇa-homa* (subjugation homa) in order to eliminate obstacles; next, one performs the homa with the *kulahṛdaya-mantra* (family-heart mantra) for the sake of self-increase; thereafter, one performs the *śānti-homa* (pacification homa) with the *śānti-mantra*."

When the time arrives to perform the ritual, if there are frequent signs of inauspiciousness, one should perform a pacifying homa using the *mātṛkā* mantra, burning ghee and fuel wood one hundred times each.
"On the day following the performance of the rite, in order to fulfill any deficiencies, one should further perform eight hundred *śānti-homa* offerings.

Now, this fire-rite is also a difficult matter among its constituent parts; because it serves to eliminate calamities and obstacles while augmenting the majestic power of the True Dharma, those who create difficulties all seek to find an opportunity within it. If one does not understand each detail clearly, one will surely bring harm upon oneself; therefore, one must not act recklessly or arbitrarily.

The Sūtra states: "When the practitioner has completed the homa, they should be instructed to offer a counter-offering. The following section, which answers the Lord of Secrets' question regarding how to make offerings to the master, still pertains to the branch of empowerment and instruction.

The reason I instruct my disciples to offer gifts is not out of greed for these objects or to seek them for myself; rather, it is so that they may give rise to roots of goodness and achieve the merit of empowerment.

If a disciple can, with all their various internal and external material resources, seek the causes and conditions for the Great Matter without any stinginess or regret, and with utmost sincerity and reverence offer these in gratitude to those who transmit the Dharma, they will be able to destroy immeasurable obstacles from past lives.
Furthermore, seeing for oneself the benefits of giving (*dāna*), one gives rise to a heart of profound joy and gratitude, thinking:

"I now relinquish this worldly wealth so cherished, which is shared by the five families and fraught with many afflictions, to purchase the unsurpassed treasure of the True Dharma; I shall bestow it universally upon all sentient beings, never exhausting it."

Having reflected thus, his mind becomes joyful; because of this joy, he is freed from doubt and regret; being free from doubt and regret, he attains and abides in inner tranquility and bliss; thereafter, by bathing him with the water of the Dharma, he is able to be forever cleansed of dust and defilement.

If one possesses nothing, one should even offer one's own body as an act of service to the teacher; that is, to serve and provide for the ācārya with this very body, never wearying of toil or suffering and never abandoning him, seeking the True Dharma even at the cost of one's life, for the sake of attaining the Way.

At that time, the Ācārya, moved by his earnest sincerity and giving rise to a heart of compassionate concern, instructed him in profound and secret skillful means; even the mantras and spiritual practices he himself had received and maintained, he bestowed upon him within the ritual enclosure, having performed the rites and dedicated them for his use.
One attains great accomplishment with little exertion of effort; this is the supreme among all forms of giving.
Guhyasamāja states: "The disciple should, at the site of the homa, prostrate with a sincere heart before the ācārya."
"First, one should offer garments cut into two circles, and only thereafter bestow other wealth.

Furthermore, that text states that once the consecration is completed and the characteristics of the maṇḍala have been extensively displayed, one should first instruct [the disciple] in the mantras and mudrās before making the offering.
This differs from other sūtras; one may employ it as appropriate.

When the sūtra states, "Having already bestowed empowerment, one should summon [the deity] and address them," this means that from the initial invocation and entry onward, all are skillful means of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Now, in order to inspire their minds, he further instructs them, saying:

"This supreme field of merit is that which all Buddhas have proclaimed, for the sake of extensively benefiting all sentient beings. This means that the World-Honored One perceives that sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been constantly destitute of internal and external resources; because they lack mastery over whatever they undertake, they fall into states of no leisure due to these causes and conditions, and are thus unable to swiftly attain unsurpassed bodhi.
Therefore, by means of the same power of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), this unsurpassed field of merit is proclaimed.
Within this treasury of great compassion, the vast ocean of all universal gateways (*sarvadvāra*) is entirely gathered therein.

Because one now extensively plants infinite roots of goodness within this state, from this life until the end of the future, one will constantly manifest as a wish-fulfilling jewel body and a space-treasury body, capable of fulfilling all the aspirations of oneself and others; therefore, it is said that one "extensively benefits all sentient beings."

Furthermore, having already completed offerings to the Sangha of the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-saṃgha*) and those who transmit the Dharma, one is further instructed to make offerings to the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) harmonious Sangha.

When making offerings to the harmonious Sangha, all members of the monastic community throughout the ten directions—both ordinary and noble—share in the merit; therefore, this merit is as inconceivable as the clouds and oceans of space.
"To obtain the great fruit" refers to ultimate benefit.

If one plants merit within this [teaching], it is like consuming a diamond; it will never be digested, but will persist until reaching the limit of the Diamond Ground (*vajrabhūmi*), only then coming to rest.
Therefore, Master Daosheng said:
"Even a single hair’s worth of goodness all tends toward the fruit of Buddhahood.
Next, to clarify the rare aspirations of the world, he further explains worldly benefits, namely: "Inexhaustible great wealth; the world says it follows one throughout successive births."
This is the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly consensus) of this world; therefore, it is called "worldly teaching.
For example, because Bakula offered a single *harītakī* fruit to the Saṃgha, for ninety-one kalpas he has remained free from illness and has never met an untimely death.
Because Aniruddha offered a single meal to a pratyekabuddha, he has also been born together with a treasure store throughout immeasurable kalpas.
As explained in detail in the *Jātaka-sūtra*, it is therefore said that he is "constantly born in their company."
Furthermore, it is stated in the Vinaya of the Sarvāstivāda school:

"The four great disciples—Mahākāśyapa, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and Subhūti—are like the 'Vessel of the Wise' (bhadraghaṭa). If a person makes offerings with a pure mind and seeks worldly rewards in this present life, there is nothing that will not be fulfilled according to their wishes."

How much more so for one who gives to the entire Saṃgha! One should know that all such virtuous persons throughout the worlds of the ten directions are included therein; even the noble ones who have attained no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) rely upon the power of the Saṃgha if they wish to prolong their lives and remain in the world.

Therefore, now that you desire to accomplish the fruit of siddhi, you must ensure that the practice of giving (dāna) you cultivate is complete and without deficiency; furthermore, you should, with a joyful mind, make offerings to the Saṃgha present in the world of conventional truth (saṃvṛti).

Because the Sangha of the ten directions cannot be assembled in its entirety, one gives simply to those who are present and gathered within the boundary; this is equivalent to giving to the entire Sangha.

The Sūtra states: "At that time, the World-Honored One Vairocana again addressed the Vajradhara Lord of Secrets. The following clarifies the method of empowerment (*abhiṣeka*), which also belongs to the section on the instructions for empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
However, this consecration (abhiṣeka) also applies to other ritual matters, or it may be considered a distinct subsidiary branch [of the rite].
The Ācārya constructs a second maṇḍala, which should face the central maṇḍala and be situated two cubits (hasta) away from the great maṇḍala.
The second is the meaning of "subsequent minor," which refers to speaking in terms of relative dependence.
Generally, the fire-hearth should be situated in the center; however, if the location is inconvenient, it may be gradually moved toward the south, even as far as facing the southwest corner.
This consecration mandala is situated to the north of the fire mandala; it should also be made equal on all four sides, with only a single gate, which opens toward the mandala.
On the four corners outside of this mandala, one should draw the four Vajradharas; in the fire direction—that is, the southeast—one places Avikalpapraveśa.
In the Nairṛti direction, place Gaganāmala; in the Vāyu direction, place Vimalanetra; and in the Īśāna direction, place Citravastradhara.
In the center of the maṇḍala, fashion a great eight-petaled lotus king, complete with filaments and stamens.

Upon four of its petals, place the four companion Bodhisattvas: on the Śakra side is Dhāraṇīśvara Bodhisattva; on the Yama side is Smṛtidhara Bodhisattva; on the Nāga side is Hitacitta Bodhisattva; and on the Yakṣa side is Kāruṇika Bodhisattva.

Upon the petals at the four corners are placed the four followers of the Teaching: in the southeast direction is the one named Citrāṃbara (Wearing Variegated Garments); in the southwest direction is the one named Pūrṇamanoratha (Fulfilling Wishes); in the northwest direction is the one named Asaṅga (Unobstructed); and in the northeast direction is the one named Vimukti (Liberation).

The Sūtra states: "In the center, one displays the Dharma-realm, the inconceivable color. This refers to this syllable *raṃ* being rendered in pure white; it is the emblem of the inconceivable Dharma-realm.

Furthermore, regarding the profound and esoteric interpretation: the square mandala is the Great Indra-hṛdaya-vajradhātu; abiding in non-conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) is the primordial, intrinsically pure wisdom of the three times that is free from obstruction. This is the precept.

By virtue of this precept, all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) are stilled; because conceptual proliferations are stilled, one attains untaught great wisdom (*mahāprajñā*). With all dust and obscurations utterly exhausted, it is like the pure void; therefore, it is named "Stainless Space" (*ākāśavimala*).
Just as when the sky is free from defilement and obstruction, one can see everything throughout the ten directions as far as the eye can reach, so it is with *prajñā*:
because it is free from all marks (*nimitta*), there is nothing of any kind that is not seen, heard, sensed, or known; therefore, it is called the "stainless eye."

Just as one with clear vision is able to perform all tasks with ease and mastery, so too, having now universally observed all faculties and conditions through unimpeded compassion, he shall manifest in various physical forms to guide and benefit them; therefore, he is said to wear robes of variegated colors.

If these four kinds of vajra-wisdom seals are fully present and without deficiency within a single mind, one is then able to stabilize this ground of the mind and is capable of sustaining the wisdom-body of empowerment. This is just as the area beneath the Bodhi tree, from the surface of the vajra-ground upward, is entirely firm and solid; therefore, when the Tathāgata attained enlightenment, he neither tilted nor sank.
The four companions refer to the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), which are the companions of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*).

It is said that when this pure dharma-realm mind-king accomplishes these four dharmas and is able to perform the four kinds of Tathāgata activities, it is then fit for consecration and the reception of the rank of Dharma King.
The initial statement, "The Sovereign King of Dhāraṇīs," refers precisely to the thorough penetration of the gateway of the letter A.
Upon seeing this King of Mantras, one immediately attains mastery over all gateways of dhāraṇī; therefore, it is so named.
Furthermore, by virtue of mastery over dhāraṇī, one accomplishes the Tathāgata’s念覺如意 (nianjue ruyi) Samādhirāja, which is able to sustain ten thousand Buddha-lands.

Just as the secret treasures within a dragon palace can sustain the great ocean so that it does not overflow, and can likewise sustain it so that it does not run dry, it is therefore called "mindfulness-sustenance" (念持).

Having already attained such a treasure of mindfulness, one then recollects the original vow to universally rain down the wealth of the Dharma, filling the entire Dharmadhātu and bestowing it upon all sentient beings; this is called the mind of benefit.
Having brought forth inexhaustible resources to perform boundless great acts of giving, yet inferior sentient beings have no intention to enjoy them and are unwilling to seek them.
For this reason, he gives rise to great compassion and employs various skillful means to discipline these impoverished sons; therefore it is said: "The compassionate ones are the Bodhisattvas."
To speak of "receiving the teaching" means that by means of these four gates, one performs the deeds of the Tathāgata through subduing and gathering [beings].
It should be known that wearing robes of variegated colors is the activity performed by the Sovereign King of Dhāraṇīs.
Fulfilling all wishes is the work performed by the King of Wish-fulfilling Jewels that one holds in mind.
Being free from all obstructions is the work performed by the Dharma-gift of great compassion.
Liberation is the activity performed through the skillful means of great compassion to uproot suffering sentient beings;
therefore, it is called the "four who uphold the teachings.
Furthermore, regarding the "vases composed of the four jewels," these are the jewels of the four virtues of Vairocana, placed at the four corners of the central womb as described above.

Having performed the empowerment through Acala Vidyārāja, furthermore, four Bodhisattvas each hold a flask: Samantabhadra is the treasure of inexhaustible vows and practices; Maitreya is the treasure of inexhaustible benefit for sentient beings; Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin is the treasure of inexhaustible pure knowledge and vision; and Sarvadurgatipariśodhana is the treasure of inexhaustible great compassion and skillful means.

Furthermore, Samantabhadra is the pure bodhicitta that pervades the entire dharma-realm; Maitreya is the emergence of the roots, sprouts, stems, and leaves of this pure mind within the womb-treasury; Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin is the manifestation and full blooming of the wondrous adornment of flowers and fruits upon this king of trees of pure awakening; and Sarvadurgatipariśodhana is the gathering of these fruits to be sown again in the fields of all sentient beings.

In this manner, they revolve and arise in mutual succession without end; therefore, using these four precious vases filled with various precious medicinal herbs and grains soaked in naturally pure perfumed water, one pours them over the inconceivable *dharmadhātu-citta* within the lotus pedestal. For this reason, it is named the "Son of the Dharma King."

It should be understood that one precious vase corresponds to the spiritual resonance of one bodhisattva, one vajra-holder, and one messenger; this may be known by correlating them with the dharma-gate of their respective directions.
Whenever one intends to perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), one should empower the seat and its furnishings with the *karmakara-mantra* and place them upon the lotus pedestal.

The *ācārya* shall again protect the disciple’s body according to the ritual; first, he shall employ Acala Vidyārāja to eliminate all obstacles, then employ the three types of *samaya* to empower the three places, and finally employ Vajrasattva to empower the limbs. Having done so, he shall cause the disciple to sit within it according to the auspicious seating posture (*śrī-āsana*).
All the unguents, flowers, lamps, *argha* water, and so forth, have already been consecrated according to the ritual;

this is exactly as in the procedure above. First, the *ācārya* should offer him scented water; next, he should use unguents to smear his entire body; then, he should adorn his body with flower garlands and crowns as necklaces; next, he should offer incense to fumigate him, arrange various lamps before him, and present various foods.
In total, these offering substances comprise thirteen seats, namely: the four Vajras, the four Bodhisattvas, the four Messengers, and the Disciples.
The offerings for the Disciples should be made most abundantly, as if making offerings to the Principal Deity itself.

Alternatively, one may arrange their positions within the great maṇḍala and make offerings; at the time of the empowerment, one should simply invoke them by reciting their names to bestow blessings upon the disciple.
As for those four bodhisattvas, they should each be placed in one of the directions within the first enclosure.
The messenger stands at the lower side of the gate, flanking it on either side.

Furthermore, prepare a new, clean white parasol; suspend flower garlands and white silk ribbons above it, and first employ the Acala mantra to remove impurities and eliminate obstacles, holding it with the mantra of Mahāvairocana Tathāgata.

The Ācārya himself holds [the vessel] to cover its top, while further commanding others to hold a pure yak-tail whisk, a fan, and an incense burner, all of which have been consecrated with the *viniścaya-mantra*.

Furthermore, place within a chest garments along with various auspicious objects—namely, golden *śrīvatsa* marks, bright mirrors, the wheel-treasure (*cakraratna*), conch shells, and the like—and offer them while holding a vase made of the four precious substances. Accompany this with the performance of music that captivates the mind; the details of this melody are fully contained within the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
When offering scented ointment, there is a specific song for the offering of scented ointment; the same applies to flowers, lamps, food, drink, and so forth.
Every chant is a mantra, and every dance is nothing other than a mudrā. Even if there is no one who understands them, the ācārya should perform them himself.
If one cannot do so, one cannot be said to have mastered a multitude of arts.

As for what is called "gathering the mind," it is like when people of the world see beautiful forms or sounds and their hearts become intoxicated by them; their emotions are focused upon that object and no longer attend to other conditions.

Now, this Vajra music is likewise able to move the hearts of people; it is just as when the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa himself performed the *Rāṣṭrapāla* melody, and upon hearing it, five hundred princes simultaneously left their homes to enter the Path—this is precisely its significance.
In the *Guhya*, it simply states: "If one attains proficiency, one should perform music.
As for the scriptural passage, "Auspicious verses (*gāthā*) and so forth, extensive and exquisite words," there are three types of such verses:
first, those called *maṅgala* (auspicious); second, those called *śrī* (glory/auspiciousness); and third, those called *atiśrī* (supreme auspiciousness). All of these are *āryā-gāthās*.
Using this to gladden and console the mind, it further serves the purpose of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), which the *ācārya* shall explain himself.
Next, regarding the section below, I have set forth one type of auspicious rite; what is employed here in this region is roughly complete.
While reciting these verses, one should personally hold a white fly-whisk and sweep over one’s own body.

When the recitation is complete, the ācārya shall again prostrate to all the deities of the maṇḍala and, for the sake of empowerment, address them with utmost sincerity. Then, holding the precious vase, he shall slowly circumambulate the maṇḍala three times and further perform the consecration according to the ritual rules.

Having gone to the disciple's location, he first uses the syllable RAṂ as fire to incinerate their body until it is entirely reduced to ashes; only then does he consecrate them in succession with the four vases.

Having performed the consecration, one visualizes the syllable VAM within this ash; it is pure white in color, and from it arise five syllables, namely A, VAṂ, RAṂ, HAṂ, and KHAṂ, which sustain the five wheels.
Next, it is taught that the syllable *Aṃ* is situated upon the crown of the head, transforming into the Central Womb (Garbhadhātu).

Furthermore, from this syllable, three layers of radiant flames arise; one layer encircles the area above the throat, and wherever it reaches, the various deities manifest accordingly, thereby forming the first court of the maṇḍala.
Next, a single layer of light encircles the heart; as the various deities manifest accordingly, they form the second tier of the maṇḍala.
Next, a single layer of light encircles the navel; as the various deities manifest accordingly, they form the third tier of the maṇḍala.
At that time, the disciples shall become the bodies of the maṇḍala; to explain this more deeply, they are the bodies of the universal dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Next, they should be led to a single location where the ācārya personally dresses them, crowns their heads with white silk, anoints their bodies with incense, and adorns them with flower garlands. They should be offered worship according to the ritual, including the burning of incense and lamps, as well as the binding of the *vajrasūtra* around their upper arms and the wearing of armlets and rings; the methods for these preparations are explained in the section on the *siddhi*-offering.

Furthermore, the ācārya first empowers the golden vessel with the syllable RAṂ; he empowers the bright mirror, the Dharma wheel, and the Dharma conch with the syllable MAṂ; and he empowers the wheel and the śaṅkha shell with the mantra.

Furthermore, before the disciple, one should polish their eyes with a golden mirror and recite this verse for them: "One should contemplate the letter-gateway *ra* to purify the defilements and obscurations within the eyes."

Next, he again manifests a clear mirror before him and speaks this verse for him: "One should contemplate the gateway of the syllable *maṃ* to purify the defilements and obstructions within one's mind.

Next, he places the Dharma-wheel between his two feet and hands a conch shell into his right hand, while speaking these verses for him; each [action] is performed while maintaining it with its respective mantra.

Why is this so? If that practitioner can, with the pure eye, directly observe the mirror of their own mind, they will thereby achieve great bodhi; having achieved great bodhi, they shall then turn the wheel of Dharma.

Turning the Wheel of Dharma is not for the purpose of setting limits upon a certain number of sentient beings; rather, it is intended to awaken all sentient beings, and for this reason, the great conch of the Dharma is blown.
In all the Secret Mantra teachings, the profound intent is explained through the phenomena of causes and conditions as metaphors; therefore, the transmission is conducted in this manner.

Next, the Ācārya shall hold an umbrella to cover [the disciple] from above and lead him to circumambulate the maṇḍala three times: first circling the first processional courtyard, then the second processional courtyard, and finally the third processional courtyard.
When proceeding in this manner, the ācārya should recite verses such as the *Maṅgala-gāthā* or the *Paramamaṅgala-gāthā*, or otherwise recite auspicious Sanskrit texts.

Once this is completed, they proceed to the western gate where two nāgas stand in attendance; there, he should cause [the disciple] to perform prostrations with great devotion, while holding the parasol over him, raising and lowering it as needed to provide shade.
One should then recite for them the Samaya verses, namely the four grave prohibitions within the Secret Treasury; these are all Āryā verses, which shall be explained below.
Guhya said: "After the disciple has arrived at the western gate and performed prostrations, the ācārya should address the honored ones, saying:
'I, [Name], have already completed the consecration for [Name]; I now entrust him to the honored ones to uphold the Vidyā-piṭaka.'"
Having spoken these words, one should have him set down his parasol and stand up, and before the maṇḍala, one should explain the samaya precepts to him:
"You have now completed the attainment of the maṇḍala vidyā-ācārya; all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, the lords of mantras, and all the celestial deities already know you."
"If one sees sentient beings who are capable of being vessels for the Dharma, out of compassion for them, one should establish a maṇḍala for them and provide instruction.
Furthermore, within this very sūtra, there are verses for the transmission of the dharma conch.

Just as when the people of the Western lands receive the *abhiṣeka* initiation, they take the waters of the four great oceans and all the rivers within their realm, together with precious medicines, grains, and so forth, and fashion a map of the territory; they then have this youth sit upon a lion throne adorned with various rare jewels, while his retinue, according to their respective ranks and sizes, attend upon him in order.

The Vedic Brahmin preceptor sat upon the elephant-treasure and followed behind him; holding this precious water, he poured it over the tips of the elephant’s tusks so that it fell upon the crown of the king’s head, and thereafter proclaimed a decree to inform the multitude, further extolling the methods by which ancient and former sage-kings governed their people and saved the age.
One who practices in accordance with this shall obtain a long life, with flourishing roots and branches, and succeed to the kingly lineage of a Wheel-Turning Monarch (Cakravartin).
If one does not perform such deeds, they shall naturally fall from their station, losing their life and leaving no heirs.
In this manner, each one is instructed individually.
However, the consecration of this Dharma Prince is not like that.

A great map of the Dharmadhātu of the Secret Adornment Buddha-land is displayed; he sits upon the lion-throne of sovereign spiritual powers of the Lotus of the Sublime Dharma, and his mind is consecrated with the water of innate purity, wisdom, and compassion, which contains all myriad virtues.
