At that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas, down to the eight classes of sentient beings, were all filled with joy, offering praise and generating deep reverence.
Then the ācārya instructed them using the bequeathed teachings of the Dharma King.
From this point forward, one shall be born into the family of the Tathāgata and will certainly succeed to the rank of a Buddha.
If one does not clearly understand in this manner, one will fail to recognize the dignity of the True Dharma.

this is his celebration; *hitakaraṃ* (beneficial), *prathamam* (the foremost),
*praśamanaṃ* (the pacifier) of all sentient beings.

The three verses: *tryakṣara* (three syllables), *maṅgala* (auspiciousness)—just as that celebration; *tuṣita* (Tuṣita), *nirvāṇa* (the Tuṣita heaven), *vimāna* (palace); *īśvara* (Lord), *anucara* (attendants)—likewise; *iha* (here), *vātala* (wind), *jagat* (sentient beings), *hita* (benefit); *seṇḍana* (with Indra), *surendra* (the Lord of Gods); *parivṛta* (surrounded), *tathāgata* (Tathāgata); *tamaṅgala* (that auspiciousness), *bhavatu* (may it be); *śāntika* (pacification), *kara* (making); *tava* (your), *adya* (today).

Catur-akṣara-praveśa-mong-bla-ra (The Four-Syllable Entrance into the Auspicious); tadyathā (it is as follows): Pu-ra (the city-palace); Va-jra (the Victorious One); Ka-pi-la (formerly called Kapilavastu); Ārya-nāma (the name of the Noble One); Deva-mahā-tama-videha-viśva-tāpasya vandye (O you who are to be venerated by the gods, the great, the darkness-dispelling, and the all-pervading ascetic); Acintya-dharma-tathāgata-tan-mong-bla-ra bhavatu śānti-karaṇa-tvayi (May the inconceivable Dharma of the Tathāgata bring about peace for you this very day).

The five verses: *Om* (entry), *Mong-bla-raṅ* (that celebration), *Ki-sa-la* (youthful branch), *Yu* (light), *Jva-la* (light), *Pu-śpa* (flower), *Ka-ti* (ornament), *Ra-me-ca* (delight), *Li-mi-ni* (name of a garden), *Va-niṅ* (garden), *Ma-hu* (immeasurable), *Ni-wa* (heaven), *Rus-kye* (dwelling place), *Na-tha-shya* (the Teacher), *Ran-ma-ni* (birth), *Wa-bu-wa* (time), *Ba-wa-da-ka-shya* (those who have reached the end), *Ta-mong-bla-raṅ* (that celebration), *Ba-wa-du-de* (attainment), *Shan-tsi-ka-raṅ* (peaceful), *Da-wa-ni* (you, today).
Ṣaḍgave, pramuñca! Vicitra, khaṇḍa, śāntaya, duḥśīya, tābūvanam, maṇijyotirātra, ardharātre, acirāt, devagaṇāḥ, parivṛtya māṃ namanti, kṛtyāḥ, ṭaṅkilaṃ, bhavantu, śāntikaṃ, tava adya.

The seven verses: *jaye jaye maṅgale* (Victory! Victory! Auspiciousness!), like that celebration; *bhogavati rājādhirāja* (O Sovereign Queen of Kings); *yanamaḥ kṛtas-tasmai nadyāḥ* (Homage to her who has been made by the river); *sattvārthapratimukta-parivāraḥ* (She whose retinue is released for the sake of sentient beings); *khecarapañjara* (The cage of sky-goers); *śaṅkhinī-tathā* (Like the conch-bearer); *maṅgaladāṃ dākinīm* (To the *dākinī* who bestows auspiciousness); *udbhava-svanāśam* (Arising and the destruction of one's own [delusion]); *tad maṅgalaṃ bhavatu* (May that be auspicious); *bhavatu śaṅkhakāram* (May it be like the sound of a conch); *tava nityam* (For you, eternally). Today.

*Oṃ aṣṭamahāmudrā-pratimandita-sarva-loka-viśeṣa-mahā-bala-vikurvaṇa-samanta-gata-sarva-deva-nāga-yakṣa-rākṣasa-gandharva-asura-garuḍa-kinnara-mahoraga-ādīn sarvān vaśīkuru svāhā.* Eight verses [are recited] to enter *maṅgala* (auspiciousness), just as that celebration [is performed]. *Bhagavat* is the World-Honored One (*bhagavān*). *Śrīmān* is the King (*rāja*). *Mūrdhni* is the crown of the head. *Maitrī* is a compassionate heart. *Mālinam* is power (*bala*). *Vijeti* means to subdue them. *Amogham* is immeasurable. *Maṅgalam* is auspiciousness. *Prakāram* refers to various kinds. *Sarvabhūtam* means all beings. *Nabho-viśvam* means throughout the human world. *Upary-upari mālinam* means reaching up to the heavens. *Tad maṅgalam* is that auspiciousness. *Bhavatu* means may it be attained. *Śāntika-lam* means peaceful action. *Tava idānīm* means "for you today."

Navāhe maṅgale tadvat prāvṛḍ-uttaravāre | Dharmacakre vārāṇasī-kauśāmbi-vastu-sugatasya śāstur adbhute bhūte vartamāne pravartite || Today, on this auspicious ninth day, like that very [occasion], during the excellent rainy season, at the Wheel of Dharma in Vārāṇasī, at Kauśāmbī, the abode of the Sugata, the Teacher, on this marvelous and wondrous event occurring in the world, at this present time, it has been set in motion.

*Daśagāthā-ṛṣi-praveśa-maṅgala*: Just as that [is] a celebration (*maṅgala*), *kṛta-maṅgala* means "to perform benefit. *Prathama* means "first. *Padavittaṃ* (three syllables) means "auspicious" (*śubha*), "essence" (*sāra*), and "merit" (*puṇya*). *Kīrti-karaṇa* means "benefiting. *Māriye* means "holy one" (*ārya*). *Jana* means "multitude. *Viniścitam* means "praising and extolling. *Kṛtsnānugata* means "pervasive. *Jagad-āha* means "he said to the world. *Bhagavan* means "World-Honored One" (*Bhagavat*). *Munīśvara* means "Lion of Sages. *Tat maṅgalam* means "that celebration. *Bhavatu* means "may it be. *Śāntikaraṇam* means "making peace. *Tavādya* means "for you today."
Bearing auspicious and manifold virtues, possessing the radiance of a golden mountain of marks,
the Teacher of the Three Times has extinguished the three defilements and opened the eye of perfect enlightenment, like the leaves of a water-born plant.
This is the primary auspicious blessing that benefits sentient beings.
(The preceding verse clarifies that all occurrences of good fortune arise solely because the Tathāgata has appeared in the world.)

Therefore, in Sanskrit it is called *lakṣmī* (pronounced with a triple *saṃdhi*), which is translated as "auspicious sign" (*jiāngxiángxiàng*), or "possessing signs" (*jùxiàng*). It also carries the meanings of excellence and celebration, auspiciousness, prosperity, consolation, majestic power, and excellent appearance.
One should know that this name encompasses all meritorious qualities; thus, it is spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).
The next phrase, "blossoming," also carries the sense of awakening.
"Water-born" is an alternative name for the lotus flower.

Because it possesses such meanings, the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world brings great benefit; thus, it is called "the foremost auspicious celebration," or "auspicious celebration" (*jìqìng*), or "excellent celebration" (*jiāqìng*), which are essentially the same in their general sense.
And that which he has proclaimed—the supreme, unshakable Dharma—has been revealed throughout the three realms; humans and devas should make offerings to it.
This sublime Dharma can bring about the eternal peace of all sentient beings.
This is the second auspicious joy in the world.
(Right) All that the World-Honored One has taught ultimately reaches the foremost limit of reality; therefore, it is called the "Unshakable Dharma."
In Sanskrit, *khyāta* (pronounced *khie chi ye fan duo*) means "to proclaim" and also "to reveal.

Here, the term "three realms" (*tridhātu*) is correctly rendered in the Sanskrit original as "three times" (*tryadhvan*), which intends to encompass the past, present, and future, as well as the three states of existence (*tribhava*).
Because it can universally demonstrate the foremost reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) in the world, all humans and devas should make offerings to this Dharma in order to repay its great kindness.
In the Sanskrit language it is called *śāntikara*; translated, it means "to bring about tranquility."
This "making" is the sense of being able to cause and being able to attain.

This Dharma can cause sentient beings to realize that the original nature of all phenomena is eternally quiescent, such that all internal and external obstacles ultimately do not arise; therefore, it is called "eternal quiescence."
The following is an example of this:
because it is through the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world that one is able to proclaim this Dharma, it is called the second excellence.
Being in accord with the sublime and wondrous Dharma, one obtains the blessing of extensive learning.
The Sangha of those worthy of offerings, a field of merit for humans, devas, and asuras—
rich in auspiciousness and shame, a community of preeminent virtue—
is the third source of blessing in the world.
The term on the right, *saddharma* in Sanskrit, is translated as "Right Dharma" or "Sublime Dharma"; it is retained here in its entirety for the sake of completing the phrase.

Within this context, the corresponding term is *yukti* in Sanskrit, which carries the meaning of "being appropriate" or "fitting," signifying a profound accord or correspondence; this differs slightly from the sense of *yoga*.

The next phrase refers to the "joy of much hearing" (*bahuśrutya-ānanda*); because practicing this Dharma in accordance with reason is a source of great celebration, it is called the "joy of much hearing.
According to a correct translation, it should be rendered as "abundance of hearing," but here I follow the traditional translation.

Furthermore, this "Arhat" (Arhant) differs from the Sanskrit term *Arhat*; here, "Arhat" carries the meaning that all devas, humans, and others ought to make offerings to him for the sake of seeking merit.

The first part of the second verse says "wealthy" (*bhoga*), which has the same meaning as the previous "wealthy in renown"; it also carries the sense of being fully endowed and free from lack—being wealthy in auspiciousness, wealthy in shame and dread of blame, and wealthy in merit.
The final phrase, "the assembly" (*zhòng*), is merely a designation for a multitude; its Sanskrit name differs from *saṃgha*, as *saṃgha* additionally carries the meaning of "harmony.
Because the treasury of the True Dharma has appeared in the world, there are those who practice and those who are directed toward the fruit; hence it is called the "third auspicious occasion."
Just as when he was in Tuṣita Heaven, the joy of being hidden in the celestial palace,
and his descent from heaven to benefit all living beings;
just as Śakra and the hosts of devas followed him like attendants when he departed.
"Now you have attained equality with them, / And experience the sublime joy of tranquility.

Regarding this term *garbha*, in the Sanskrit sound it is called *garbha* (or *gala-pa*). It signifies the "womb" (*garbha*) of the center, or the "womb" of the central matrix (*madhyama-garbha-tantra*); its meaning differs from that of *piṭaka* or *kośa*.

As it is extensively explained in such sutras as the *Avataṃsaka*, when a Bodhisattva dwells in a celestial palace or descends from the heavens, there arise immeasurable and boundless auspicious and celebratory events throughout all worlds.
The *Sūtra* states that they are indeed the host of devas; however, in order to distinguish them from [ordinary] devas, they are called asuras.
Treatises such as the *Lishi apitan lun* (Abhidharmakośa-śāstra) refer to them as "non-devas" (*asura*).

Furthermore, *Tathāgata* is translated as "Thus-Come" (*Rúlái*) or "Thus-Gone" (*Rùqù*). This means that one has gone from the path of suchness to enter into *nirvāṇa*, never to be born again; hence this name is given.
It is for the sake of explaining that it is more convenient in meaning to say [the Buddha] descended from heaven; thus, the phrasing is reciprocal.
If there were a Bodhisattva in the stage of "Successor" (Upapadya) in Tuṣita Heaven, then the seed of the Buddhas in the world would not be severed.

If a person receives the stage of empowerment within the Secret Treasury, they may even attain perfect enlightenment within a single lifetime; therefore, it is said that their celebration is equal to that [of the former].
Just as when the supreme palace city of Kapilavastu was filled with joy,
the gods of great majesty praised him and paid him homage;
so too is he inconceivable, the one who has come according to reality.
You have now attained equality with them, and experience the sublime joy of tranquility.
(In the Sanskrit original, the sense of "time" is contained within the word for "joy" [kṣaṇa]; the same applies to subsequent examples.)
This refers to the time when the Bodhisattva dwelt in the womb; at that time, there were immeasurable auspicious and celebratory events throughout all worlds.
This is also explained in detail in the "Entering the Dharma Realm" and "Leaving the World" chapters of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Furthermore, immeasurable multitudes of great bodhisattvas from the ten directions gather within his belly for the purpose of hearing the Dharma; therefore, this is inconceivable.

Following the previous verse’s treatment of the meaning of "going away" (*yāti*), it is now explained by means of "coming to attain perfect enlightenment," which is likewise more convenient for the flow of the argument.

Just as all the devas of great majesty and power offer praise and prostrations even while a Bodhisattva is still within the womb, so too do you now entrust your holy embryo within the Matrix of the Buddha-Mother Ākāśanetra;
for this reason, the eight classes of beings, including the nāgas and spirits, all revere you. Thus it is said that you share in their celebration.
As if in a garden of blossoms at a festival, where radiant flowers provide universal adornment,
so too is the grove of delight for the bhikṣuṇīs, where immeasurable hosts of devas dwell.
When the Teacher of the Path was first born, he possessed a final body that marks the end of all existence.
Now you have attained equality with them, achieving the sublime joy of tranquility.
In the Sanskrit language, this is called *kisa-layu*; it refers to a flower on a forest tree that is accompanied by both twigs and leaves.
Next, it says *puṣpa*, which refers directly to the substance of the flower.

Since names such as "flower garland" (*mālā*) and "scattered flowers" (*avakīrṇa-puṣpa*) all employ this term, the preceding line uses "flower garden" (*puṣpārāma*) to distinguish it [from other meanings].

When the Bodhisattva was first born, there were also immeasurable auspicious omens and celebrations throughout all worlds; even the countless hosts of devas gathered at the Lumbinī Grove for the purpose of making offerings.
Furthermore, there are immeasurable and inconceivable numbers of Bodhisattvas of liberation who, like dark clouds enveloping the moon, descend to birth simultaneously.

You now likewise take your initial birth within the Secret Treasury; all the gateways of the Dharma as your retinue have already begun to sprout. If you can courageously advance in practice, you will also possess the final body at the end of birth and death; therefore, it is said that you share in their celebration.
Just as there is joy when the various sufferings of household life are extinguished, so too,
with a heart full of gladness at midnight, he went to the place of ascetic practice.
He was like the hosts of devas who, paying homage, gathered around him.
Now you have attained equality with them, And experience the joy of tranquility.

This refers to when the Bodhisattva first left the household life; the term "extinction" (*nirodha*) used by Brahmā signifies the removal of various forms of suffering, which implicitly includes the meaning of leaving the household life—namely, abandoning the various sufferings of attachment and the bonds of affection associated with domestic life.
Regarding the "place of ascetic practice" (*duṣkaracaryā*), in Sanskrit it is correctly translated as the "place for cultivating the body.

For instance, when the Bodhisattva first set out from Uruvilvā to proceed toward this place for cultivating the body, there were immeasurable and boundless auspicious and celebratory events throughout the entire world, as described in detail in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and other texts.

At that time, the hosts of Śuddhāvāsa devas, down to the world-protectors (Lokapālas), were all greatly rejoiced; knowing that the Udumbara flower of the Perfectly Enlightened One would soon blossom, they all prostrated themselves, circumambulated him, or personally escorted him by attending upon his horse’s hooves.

Now you, too, within this Secret Treasury, have for the first time parted from the parents of ignorance and are proceeding toward the place where one cultivates the body at the Path of the Initial Illumination of Dharma.

You should know that the gods of the Pure Abodes and others likewise rejoice and pay homage, knowing that before long you will become equal to the World-Honored One; thus it is said that you obtain such celebration as they do.
Commentary on the Mahāvairocana Sūtra, Scroll Eight;
Commentary on the Mahāvairocana Sūtra, Scroll Nine;
Recorded by the Śramaṇa Aśāli Yixing.
The remainder of Chapter Two, "Entering the Maṇḍala with All Requisites":
Furthermore, like that Dragon King, when he was joyfully prostrated in reverence,
the multitude of birds on the riverbank circled him in a procession.
"Having attained the rare and profound meaning of tranquility, you who were about to destroy all states of existence, now share in that state and experience the sublime joy of peace.

At this time, the Bodhisattva had reached the very depths of asceticism and realized its lack of benefit; having accepted the milk-rice from the cowherd woman, he bathed in the river with his marks and signs of perfection fully manifest. At that moment, as he drew closer to the Way of the Buddha, there appeared the auspicious omen of countless blue jays, as described in detail in the *Mūlapravṛtti-sūtra* (The Sutra of Past Deeds).
This bird’s proper name is *saṃsā* (搡沙); it resembles a small blue magpie and is what is commonly called the "Immortal Bird" (*ṛṣi-pakṣin*) among the local people.

After the Bodhisattva had finished his ablutions, he contemplated the mind that is fundamentally quiescent in all phenomena; clearly beholding the path to Great Enlightenment, he gave rise to a sense of wonder and realized for himself that he would surely be able to destroy all states of existence through his great power. At that time, immeasurable and boundless auspicious events arose in the world.

Now you, too, within this Secret Treasury, have cast aside the various exhausting practices of body and spirit that yield no benefit among the ninety-five heterodox paths; you have consumed the single-flavored milk gruel of the letter *A*, thereby augmenting your eternal life, physical form, and strength; you have bathed your body with the pure water of the Dharma and clearly recognized the Great Way of the Mind-King. As you are about to proceed to the site where Vairocana sits upon the Bodhimanda, it is said that you shall share in that same celebration.
Just as when the Bhagavān sat beneath the King of Trees, he brought forth joy;
by the power of his mind of loving-kindness, he shattered the immeasurable armies of Māra.
Assuming various forms according to the needs of beings, he pervaded the worlds of devas and humans.
Now you have attained equality with them, achieving the sublime joy of tranquility.

When the World-Honored One sat at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, subduing the celestial Māras and attaining Perfect Awakening, all manner of mundane and supramundane auspicious celebrations occurred, like the celestial king of trees in full bloom during the month of spring.
Having already fulfilled all his aspirations while practicing the bodhisattva path, he immediately manifests his form-body everywhere throughout the worlds to enlighten and transform sentient beings.

Furthermore, regarding the term "army of Māra" (*mārasena*) mentioned herein: in its original Sanskrit pronunciation it is *pakṣa*, which carries the meaning of "wings," "partisans," or "allies. What is now rendered according to the ancient translation is merely an interpretation of the underlying sense.

Now that you have resolved to attain Bodhicitta, you should know that you have already sat securely at the foot of the king of trees, the Bodhi-śāla; through the Tathāgata’s power of empowerment, you have completely subdued the hosts of Māra.

If one remains firm and immovable from this state, and upon attaining the vision of the luminous path of the mind, one achieves perfect enlightenment at the very moment of first generating the bodhicitta; because one universally manifests the maṇḍala-body through the Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin-samādhi, it is said that one attains a celebration equal to theirs.
When the Sugata, the Guide, dwelt at Vārāṇasī and first turned the most unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma, that auspicious and joyous occasion was marvelous and unprecedented;
yet now, the time of the world has come to its end.
You have now attained equality with them, achieving the sublime joy of tranquility.
For ten reasons, the World-Honored One turned the wheel of the True Dharma, as explained at length in the *Avataṃsaka* and other scriptures.

In Sanskrit, it is called *pravarāvatāra*, which carries the meaning of "supremely excellent" or "extraordinary. This refers to that which is the foremost in the world and beyond which nothing superior exists; hence, it is called "the most unsurpassed."
Furthermore, World-Honored One, all that you have spoken is for the sake of a great cause and condition; therefore, it is called "most unsurpassed.
It has never been heard before in any world, nor can it be turned back by others; therefore, it is called "extraordinary."
This is unprecedented—though the Sanskrit original correctly calls it "marvelous" (*āścarya*), I have here translated it according to its meaning.

Having personally crossed over all realms of existence (*bhava*), they cause immeasurable sentient beings to abide in their final physical body (*antima-deha*), even causing the coarse burdens (*dauṣṭhulya*) of the mind-born existence to be forever exhausted.

You are now likewise so: if, in this very life, you attain the *samādhi* of the Removal of Obstacles (*apāvaraṇa*), the *dhāraṇī* of speech, and give rise to sovereign supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), you will also be able to turn the wheel of Dharma just as Vairocana does; therefore, it is said that you shall share in his rejoicing.
Just as for the sake of benefit, for the most auspicious and meaningful celebration,
and for the abundance of welfare and advantage, one praises the assembly of noble ones;
so too does one universally proclaim the virtues of the Honored One, the Sage, the Lion of the Śākyas.
Now you have attained equality with them, achieving the sublime joy of tranquility.
In the Sanskrit original it is *hita*, translated as "benefit.
Next is *kṣema*, which is translated as "well-being" (or "security").
*Kāraṇa* is translated as "beneficial.
Although their original names differ, those who transmit them have no means to distinguish between them.
It is like the terms *chūzāi*, *shǒujī*, *zhàozǔ*, and *yuántāi*; although they all ultimately refer to the beginning, there are nevertheless slight differences among them.
The first phrase signifies "benefit" and carries the sense of "causing benefit," thereby concluding the verse of praise for the Buddha.
The second phrase speaks of the "supreme auspiciousness," thereby concluding the verse of praise for the Dharma.
The next two lines clarify the supreme fruits accomplished through the practice of making offerings; they serve as a concluding eulogy for the *saṃgha*.
The subsequent two lines conclude the summary of the seven verses concerning the original practices of Śākyamuni. To state it briefly: all such merits as these, you have now fully attained.

The time when the World-Honored One entered parinirvāṇa was no different from the time he attained perfect enlightenment; however, according to conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), it is said that the merit of sentient beings in the three realms has been exhausted, and for this reason, he remained silent and did not speak.
However, the reconciliation herein of the Three Jewels and the original practices of the Tathāgata is precisely the meaning of the Great Nirvāṇa.
Within these eleven verses, there are immeasurable meanings, which shall be explained in detail through a comprehensive analysis according to the various sūtras.

Fearing that it might hinder the explanation of the meaning of the maṇḍala, I shall now briefly clarify only the glosses. The Verse of the Golden Staff: *Suvarṇadaṇḍa* (Sanskrit): *suvarṇa* means "gold"; *daṇḍa* means "staff. *Ajñāna* (Sanskrit): "Ignorance.

*Bhaṭṭāraka* (Sanskrit): "Lord" or "Venerable One. *Vajra-putra* (Sanskrit): "Son of the Vajra," i.e., a disciple of the Buddha. *Apanaya* (Sanskrit): "Remove" or "Eliminate. *Ārya* (Sanskrit): "Noble One. *Sādhu* (Sanskrit): "Excellent" or "Well done. *Śalākā-cāra* (Sanskrit): "One who skillfully employs the staff. *Maitreya* (Sanskrit): "Maitreya. *Rāja-jīvaka* (Sanskrit): "King Jīvaka," the physician-king. *Iha-loka-kṣema* (Sanskrit): "Peace in this world. *Maitreya* (Sanskrit): "Maitreya. *Purā* (Sanskrit): "As before" or "Just as. (Note: The phonetic transcriptions provided in the source text have been rendered here according to standard Sanskrit transliteration conventions.)
O Son of the Buddha!
The Buddha shall remove for you the film of ignorance, just as a master physician in the world skillfully employs a golden probe.

In the western method of treating the eyes, a golden instrument is used; it is rounded and smooth at both ends and slender in the middle, shaped like a pestle, approximately four or five inches in length. When in use, medicine is applied to both ends, and one end is inserted into each eye to apply the salve.
The "Golden Scalpel" in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is also of this kind.

All sentient beings inherently possess the Buddha-nature of knowledge and vision within their minds and eyes; however, because it is obscured by the cataracts of ignorance, the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena cannot manifest clearly before them.
If one were to let an unskilled physician attempt to save it, not only would it be ineffective, but it might even further increase the cataracts or damage the pupil.

The Tathāgata’s skillful means are fully perfected; he is like a master goldsmith who uses a golden probe: unlike the former case, he does not cause injury where injury must not be inflicted. He is like a master carpenter from Ying wielding his axe with all his strength to remove impurities, yet taking care never to harm the parts that must not be injured.

If there is a discrepancy of even a hair’s breadth in the expansion or contraction [of the visual faculty], it will be obscured by "severed emptiness" (*chōnkū*), and unimpeded knowledge and vision (*anāvaraṇa-jñāna-darśana*) will not be realized.

Furthermore, the nature of seeing forms within these diseased eyes is established by the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), whether a King of Physicians exists in the world or not; it merely becomes clear when meeting with a favorable opportunity for treatment, rather than being newly created through the efficacy of prescriptions and medicines.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* contains the parable of the blind man, which shall be explained in detail here.
As for the various and diverse skillful means (*upāya*) of all Buddhas, when their ultimate intent is examined, they all converge upon this very point.

The Verse on the Bright Mirror (*Pratibimba-gāthā*). In the Sanskrit original: *pratibimba* means "image"; *ākāra* means "form"; *dharma* means "phenomena" (*dharmas*); *accha* means "clear"; *śuddha* means "pure"; *anāvila* means "unclouded"; *anupalepa* means "unstained"; *vira-padya* means "beyond speech"; *hetu* means "cause"; *karma* means "action"; *samutpāda* means "arising."
All phenomena are formless, clear and pure, free from defilement;
they are without grasping and beyond verbal expression, arising solely from causes and karma.
Knowing these phenomena thus, one realizes that their intrinsic nature is undefiled.
You are peerless in the world; you have arisen from the Buddha-mind.

(In the Sanskrit original, the first phrase simply says "image" (*bimba*), yet as it connects with the textual flow of the "Dharma without marks" (*animitta-dharma*), the meaning clarifies that the Dharma is without form or image.)
The nature is fundamentally pure, like a bright mirror that is limpid and clear, free from defilement yet capable of universally manifesting all images.

One should know that these images do not arise from within the mirror, nor do they arise from external objects, nor do they arise from both together, nor do they exist without causes and conditions. All manner of conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) are inconsistent with this; furthermore, they cannot be grasped, for they belong solely to a multitude of causes and conditions.

When conditions conjoin, there is no arising; when conditions disperse, there is no ceasing. Thus, one speaks of impermanence without annihilation, and of neither going nor coming. One should know that the image is the mirror, and the mirror is the image.
When one can understand in this way, one immediately perceives the true mark of all phenomena (*dharmas*) and realizes that the intrinsic nature of the mind is fundamentally free from defilement.
Because the mind is like a mirror and the mirror reflects the mind, it is said that the mind sees itself and the mind knows itself; wisdom and the mirror are non-dual and indistinguishable.
The reason for decisively removing the film over the eyes is precisely to perceive this Dharma-realm; therefore, it is clarified by itself.

When one attains resonance with this, one immediately obtains the Samādhi of the Removal of Obscurations within the Universal Gate Maṇḍala, and is able to perform incomparable benefit for all sentient beings—whether termed "without opposition" or "without measure," meaning it cannot be quantified.
Because one is able to personally give birth to the Buddha-mind within oneself, one is called a child of the Buddha-mind.
Since one is born from the Buddha-mind, it is said: "You are born from the Buddha-mind. *Dharmacakra-dharmaśaṅkha-gāthā* (in Sanskrit:

*anadya adya prabṛtya parato lokasya cakram mārīca-tāraṇam abhyudgata-samantadharma-śaṅkham*). [The meaning is: The wheel of the Dharma, the conch of the Dharma; from this day forward, for the sake of the world, the wheel that rescues [beings] has arisen, pervading everywhere with the Dharma-conch. (Note: The provided Chinese text contains a transcription of the Sanskrit title *Dharmacakra-dharmaśaṅkha-gāthā* interspersed with its phonetic rendering and a brief explanation of its components.)

*Eka-gāthā-nāsti-tattva-dvaya-kṣepa-paryanta-vimala-vijñāna-śrī-saṃketa-niḥsaṃśaya-citta-prakāśa-svaloka-mantra-caryā-nayana-vijaya.* A single verse (*eka-gāthā*). There is no such thing (*nāsti*). The reality (*tattva*) of the two [extremes] (*dvaya*). Casting away (*kṣepa*) the limit (*paryanta*). Immaculate wisdom (*vimala-vijñāna*). The glorious convention (*śrī-saṃketa*). Without doubt (*niḥsaṃśaya*). The mind (*citta*). Revealed (*prakāśa*). One’s own world (*svaloka*). The mantra (*mantra*). Conduct (*caryā*). The method (*naya*). Victory (*vijaya*).

The two verses are as follows in the Sanskrit language: *kṛta-praṇidhāna-buddhānām upakāriṇe jaye ca kṣate ca vajradhare sarvāṇi rakṣa tvaṃ sarvadā śam*. [In Chinese: "Kṛta" means "made"; "praṇidhāna" means "vow"; "buddhānām" refers to "all Buddhas"; "upakāriṇe" means "to the benefactor"; "jaye" means "in victory"; "ca" means "and"; "kṣate" means "in defeat"; "vajradhare" refers to "Vajrapāṇi"; "sarvāṇi" means "all"; "rakṣa" means "protect"; "tvaṃ" means "you"; "sarvadā" means "always"; and "śam" means "peace."
From this very day, you shall turn the wheel that saves the world;
its sound shall pervade everywhere as you blow the unsurpassed Dharma conch.
Do not give rise to divergent wisdom, but with a mind free from doubt, [proceed].
Revealing to the world the mantra practices of the supreme path,
May you always make such aspirations and proclaim the Buddha’s virtues;
Then all Vajradharas shall protect and keep you in mind.
Just as the wheels of syllables revolve and form a single unity, so too it is with the wheels of seals and the body.
Therefore, when one understands the meaning of the Circular Mirror Maṇḍala, one simultaneously understands the meaning of turning the wheel of Dharma within the Secret Treasury.
When turning this wheel of Dharma, one uses a single voice to universally awaken sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions; therefore, it is called "blowing the great dharma conch.
Within the term *brahma-svara* (Brahma-voice), there is the sense of sound, the sense of blowing forth, and the sense of causing that sound to be heard everywhere.
Diverse wisdom is the wisdom of discriminative delusion.
A mind free from doubt is the state in which doubt and regret are forever exhausted, abiding in true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
Because one abides in true wisdom, one is able to definitively utter the lion’s roar, revealing to humans and devas the unsurpassed Dharma for practicing the path of mantra.

If you can make such a vow as this—to repay the great kindness of the True Dharma and proclaim the Buddha’s benevolent virtues at all places and at all times—then you shall be an envoy of the Tathāgata, performing the work of the Tathāgata; therefore, all Vajradharas shall protect and keep you in mind.

Furthermore, O King of Your Mind, when you first entered the Path of the Illumination of Dharma and attained Buddhahood by turning the Wheel of Dharma, there were already immeasurable and boundless Vajra-Wisdom Seals (Vajrajñānamudrā) that circled around you, assisted you, and protected you together; how much more so, then, is the majestic power possessed at the time of the ultimate attainment of Buddhahood by the King of Mind, Vairocana?
Therefore, for the sake of this Dharma, one should exert great diligence.

The Samaya-gāthā (Samaya-verse): *Samaya-samaya* (Sanskrit: *anīya-prabṛṃha*). From this day forward, you shall be a true son of the Buddha (*tathāgata-putra*). Do not spare your life (*abhīta-vikrama*). Never (*kālaṃ na*)—the final syllable is pronounced with a long sound—shall you abandon (*apara-tyaja*). The True Dharma (*saddharma*) and the Bodhicitta (*bodhicitta*) must never (*mātra-parityaja*) be forsaken.

One verse: *maṅku* (to be stingy), *sarvadharmeṣu* (in all phenomena), *sattvānām* (of all sentient beings), *na manye* (I do not think), *hitakriyāyai* (for the sake of performing benefit), *iti* (thus), *samayaḥ* (the commitment/samaya), *buddhaḥ* (the Buddha), *saṃketaḥ* (the convention), *deśitaḥ* (taught), *sattvasya* (of you, O being), *susthitasamaye* (well-established in the samaya).

The two verses: *yathā* (as), *svāhā* (self), *dvīṃ* (life-force), *rakṣa* (protect), *tathāgata* (also protect), *ime* (thus), *tvaṃ* (you), *pratinirvṛtti* (returning), *śuśrūṣe* (I shall serve), *gurūn* (the gurus), *śiṣyaḥ* (disciple), *tvam* (you), *śāstāraṃ* (the Teacher), *bhajiṣye* (I shall revere), *vatsala* (affectionate one).

The three verses: *āryāye* means "in accordance with the teaching"; *svāhā* means "all that exists"; *sarvamanas-kṛte* means "that which is made by the mind"; *naḥ* means "for us"; *tatra* means "regarding this doubt"; *tanmanasi* means "in the heart."
O Son of the Buddha, from this day forward, for the sake of not begrudging your own body or life,
you must not abandon the True Dharma, forsake the Bodhicitta,
be stingy with any teaching, or fail to act for the benefit of sentient beings.
The Buddha has taught the samaya: you who dwell well in the precepts should protect them just as you would your own life;
guard the precepts in this same way, with utmost sincerity and reverence, bowing your head at the feet of the Holy Honored One.
"Practice according to the instructions you have received; do not give rise to a mind of doubt.

As for what was previously mentioned regarding the single verse spoken in the "ear-whispered" transmission, it is like the *Mahāsāṃghika* school’s conferral of the six mindfulnesses (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) or the *Sarvāstivāda* school’s conferral of the five-period dharma; by this one may verify whether the full precepts (*upasampadā*) were previously received.

Now, regarding these four precepts, just as when the full ordination has been completed and their characteristics have been briefly shown, one should know that they are precisely the four *pārājika* offenses within the Secret Treasury.
Just as when a person’s head is severed for another, their life-force is no longer sustained, and thus all their limbs become incapable of function and will soon fall apart;
so too, these four fundamental precepts are the life-force of the Mantra Vehicle and the life-force of the True Dharma.
If one violates this, they are like a corpse within the Secret Treasury; even if they cultivate various meritorious practices, they will soon fall into ruin.

Regarding the first precept, which states that one should not abandon the True Dharma: one should embrace, practice, uphold, and recite all the authentic teachings of the Tathāgatas, with a mind like the great ocean that never tires of swallowing the hundred rivers.

If one develops a mind of rejection toward any dharma-gate, whether it be of definitive or provisional meaning among the various vehicles—for instance, if within the Śrāvaka vehicle one speaks with the mouth or conceives in the mind a thought of abandoning even a single dharma regarding a person capable of acting as a vessel—one also constitutes a breach of the precepts.
Although one who possesses the Vinaya does not fall from the ranks of the Saṃgha, this is not because it is not a transgression of the precepts;
however, since this secret Mahāyāna ultimately has no sense of relinquishment, it constitutes a grave offense.

Furthermore, all these Dharma-gates were accumulated by the World-Honored One of Great Compassion over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas; they have been expounded for the sake of universally benefiting all sentient beings through every door, just as one cannot discard a single character from a wheel of syllables.
If a follower of the Śrāvaka-yāna abandons even a single precept, their purpose is severed, their harmony is lost, and they forfeit their discipline;
how much more so for the Mahāyāna?

Regarding the second precept—that one must not abandon the bodhicitta—the bodhicitta is like the standard of a great general amidst the myriad practices of a Bodhisattva. If a great general loses his standard, it means the three armies have been defeated and have fallen into a state of defeat; therefore, this constitutes a pārājika offense.
There are those who, though they cherish and revere the Dharma-treasury of the Three Vehicles and do not abandon it in their hearts, nevertheless think:
"The various difficult practices and ascetic austerities of the unsurpassed Mahāyāna are not within my capacity."
"Furthermore, I shall attain parinirvāṇa within the Lesser Vehicle," some say; or they say,
"I shall extensively plant roots of goodness and make offerings to the Triple Gem, so as to long receive the blessings and rewards of humans and devas."
"Unsurpassed Bodhi is the sphere of practice for great beings such as Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī;
how could I possibly attain it now?
To thus withdraw from the vow for Bodhi through various causes and conditions such as these is equivalent to severing one's own life-root and constitutes the offense of a pārājika.

Furthermore, this bodhicitta ultimately possesses no possibility of retrogression; therefore, it is not like the śrāvaka teachings, wherein even one who has abandoned the three refuges and regressed to the status of a layperson or an outsider is still permitted by the Buddha out of his compassion and pity.

Regarding the third precept, "one should not be stingy with any of the dharmas": there may be someone who, though they do not abandon the true Dharma nor depart from the bodhicitta, is nevertheless stingy with the true Dharma and refuses to bestow it upon others according to their capacity; such a person also commits a pārājika offense.

Why is this so? It is because it is only through the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world that this True Dharma exists; even a single phrase or a single verse was not obtained without the World-Honored One relinquishing his body and life to serve as its servant.
This is the inherited wealth of all sentient beings, not intended for the sake of a single being alone.
Yet now, they have secretly claimed it as their own; therefore, within this Secret Treasury, this is equivalent to stealing the property of the Triple Gem.
Briefly stated, there are four kinds of teachings: namely, the three vehicles and the secret vehicle.
Although one should not be parsimonious, one must nevertheless observe sentient beings and assess their faculties before bestowing them.
If one recklessly speaks of profound and secret matters, causing others to give rise to doubt and sever their roots of goodness, then one commits a *pārājika* offense under the fourth precept.

As for those who are simply stingy with their wealth and refuse to practice giving, they commit an offense within the ten types of skillful precepts; this is described as an offense of the lower grade.
Regarding the fourth precept—“Do not act in ways that fail to benefit any sentient being”—this is a practice contrary to the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).

The four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) constitute the four reliances within the bodhisattva’s complete ethical discipline. At the time of first receiving the precepts, one must first explain these prohibitions and obstacles; only if the candidate can uphold them should they be received. If they cannot uphold them, they are not a *mahāsattva*, and the precepts must not be conferred upon them.

Why is this so? Because when a Bodhisattva gives rise to the mind of omniscience, it is fundamentally for the purpose of universally gathering all sentient beings and acting as the causal condition for them to enter the path through the three vehicles.
Now, on the contrary, you act in opposition to the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and give rise to causes and conditions that obstruct sentient beings from the Path.

Since all sentient beings share the same essence as the wheel of syllables (*akṣaracakra*) and cannot be separated from one another, to damage the roots of goodness of even a single sentient being, or to abandon the practice of benefiting them, constitutes an offense of defeat (*pārājika*).

For example, within the Śrāvaka Dharma, the abandonment of even one member of the seven assemblies constitutes the meaning of non-harmony and results in the severance and loss of the complete *vinaya* discipline.

However, when one commits acts such as sexual misconduct, theft, killing, or lying due to a mind afflicted by secondary defilements (*upakleśa*), yet does not damage the wholesome conditions for the Three Vehicles, this is like the *sthūlātyaya* offense in the Śrāvaka Dharma; it is subsumed under the training rules concerning preliminary preparations (*prayoga-śikṣāpada*).
The following is the instruction and admonition of the Ācārya.

Regarding the "Samaya" spoken of by the Buddha, this term is present in both the Sanskrit and Chinese versions of the text; it signifies that the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time have all together proclaimed this Samaya, practicing together the single path of true reality, with no other way.
Now, all those assembled within the maṇḍala manifest as witnesses.

In Sanskrit, this is called *sumudra*, which is translated as "one who abides well in the precepts" (*śīla-susthita*); because they abide well in the *samaya*, they are also called "one who abides well in the precepts. This is an alternative designation for the name of the Buddha's sons (*jinaputra*).
Just as you protect the life and body of your biological parents, so too should you now cherish this life of wisdom, the Dharma-body.
Now that you have completed receiving the full ordination, you should proceed to pay respectful homage with utmost sincerity to those venerable ones and then withdraw.
From this day forward, in all that you do, you must fully rely upon the teachings of the mantra-dharma and practice according to what is taught.

Like those who have newly received the precepts, you must first consult your teacher regarding all undertakings; do not act impulsively or exclusively out of your own judgment, lest it give rise to evil, heterodox views, doubt, or regret.

Furthermore, the Ācārya has taught that within the Vidyādharapiṭaka, the two sections of the Prātimokṣa-sūtras are each individual mantras capable of accomplishing all tasks, because the Tathāgata has empowered these for his disciples.
The verses herein are likewise; when performing the ritual, one should recite the Sanskrit original and provide an extensive explanation by means of the *mātṛkā* (gateways of letters).
"At that time, Vajrapāṇi addressed the Buddha, up until the point where they saw the World-Honored One together."
This is because once the full ordination has been completed, one attains the merit of non-action (*avijñapti*) within the gateway of mantras.

Just as in the Śrāvaka Dharma, when the full precepts have been received, for each individual training rule—such as those concerning sexual misconduct, theft, killing, or lying—one attains the merit of non-action regarding every single sentient being throughout the trichiliocosm; this river of merit flows continuously until the end of life.
Even regarding the precept against drinking alcohol, for every swallow by all sentient beings, there arises the merit of non-action (*avijñapti*).

Regarding the precepts against destroying life and digging the earth, for every single atom of grass and trees from the very limit of the diamond realm (*vajratala*) downward, there arises the merit of non-action.

For this reason, although they are ordinary persons possessing all the fetters and latent tendencies, they are included among the number of those worthy of offerings (arhats) and may participate together with the noble ones who have nothing further to learn (aśaikṣas) in the performance of sacred rites.

Now, within this Secret Treasury, by virtue of the first precept, one gives rise to the merit of non-action throughout all treasuries of the true Dharma in the ten directions and the three periods of time.
By virtue of the second precept, one gives rise to the dharma of unconditioned merit within all bodhisattva practices throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time.
By virtue of the third precept, one gives rise to unconditioned merit within all gateways for saving sentient beings throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time.

By virtue of the fourth precept, one generates the merit of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*) toward all sentient beings throughout the ten directions and three periods of time, as well as within the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).
It is not limited merely to a single lifetime, nor is its scope restricted to the three thousandfold world system.

Furthermore, all the disciplinary codes (*vinaya*) of the śrāvakas are produced through causes and conditions; they ultimately culminate in *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and return to the extinction of ashes.

Now, this bodhisattva discipline originates fundamentally from omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and ultimately flows toward the ocean of *sarvajña*; from its beginning to its end, it is ultimately equal in being like a vajra.

Furthermore, just as within the Śrāvaka-dharma there are various stages—such as those with full afflictions, those in training (śaikṣa), and those beyond training (aśaikṣa)—yet the unmanifest restraint (avijñapti-saṃvara) they generate does not differ in terms of superiority or inferiority.

Now, this bodhisattva discipline is likewise so: although there are different stages from the initial generation of the mind up to the forty-second ground, once one universally initiates non-conceptual roots of goodness throughout the entire dharma-realm at a single moment, there is no difference whatsoever between this and that of the Tathāgata in terms of increase or decrease.

Furthermore, at the moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, all merits are equal to those of the Tathāgata; from that point onward, throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, one constantly advances with ever-increasing distinction, becoming increasingly profound and vast in an inconceivable manner.
For this reason, it is called the merit of non-action within the Secret Treasury.
As the sutra says: "Vajrapāṇi asked:
'If these sons and daughters of good family enter this Great Compassion Treasury Maṇḍala, how much of an accumulation of merit do they obtain?'"
The Buddha said:

"From the first generation of the mind of awakening until the attainment of the state of a Tathāgata, the mass of merit possessed by that son or daughter of good family is equal to that mass of merit."
"This merit is beyond the reach of the conceptual deliberations of all sentient beings; only the Buddhas can truly know it.
Now, merely indicating the point of entry is intended to lead one to comprehend the perfect meaning; therefore, it is said: "One should understand this Dharma-gate in this way."

For example, when the crown prince of a wheel-turning monarch is still within the womb, he is already able to sustain the four continents so that their merit and virtue do not diminish, and the eight classes of spirits all revere him; how much more so is the benefit he brings about once he has ascended to the position of consecrated sovereignty?
Therefore, the Buddha said:

"Because their accumulation of merit is equal to that of the Tathāgata, you should know that they are children born from the mouth of the Buddha and from the heart of the Buddha; in whatever direction they reside, there the Buddha is present performing the work of a Buddha."
It is just as in the Śrāvaka sūtras, where the Buddha said: "I have no business in whatever region Śāriputra may travel;
for all sentient beings make offerings to and draw near to the Tathāgata because he is able to produce inexhaustible merit and wisdom."

Now, the mass of merit possessed by these sons and daughters of good family is equal to that of the Tathāgata. Therefore, out of great compassion, the World-Honored One entrusts all sentient beings with this: those who delight in making offerings to the Buddha should make offerings to these sons and daughters of good family;
and those who wish to see the Buddha should simply contemplate them.
The mass of merit acquired when first entering the worldly maṇḍala is equal to that of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, the mass of merit acquired when first entering the profound and secret yoga maṇḍala is likewise equal to that of the Tathāgata.

...and so on, as explained at length: whenever one enters the maṇḍala of each respective stage, the mass of merit generated is entirely equal to that of the Tathāgata; therein there is both distinction and non-distinction.
Because he perceives such a Vajradhātu, he is named Vajrapāṇi;
because he perceives such a Dharmadhātu, he is named Samantabhadra.
Therefore, this supreme upper-hand Honored One and the entire assembly of Vajra Bodhisattvas spoke with one voice, saying:
“From this day forward, we should respectfully honor and make offerings to these sons and daughters of good family. Why is this?
Because they see the same Buddha, the World-Honored One.”

It is just as when the ministers of a Wheel-Turning King, because they clearly recognize the king’s lineage, see that his appearance in the world brings great benefit and purpose; desiring that the seven treasures never vanish, they all pay sincere homage to the Prince within the womb and protect him, not with words of mere artifice.

Guhya said: "After the ācārya has performed the homa as previously described, he should sprinkle pure water upon the heads of the disciples, extensively show them the positions within the maṇḍala, and instruct them in the great mudrās and the mantras of the vidyārājas, commanding them to sit in one place and recite them."

Next, having instructed them to make offerings of incense and flowers to the principal deity and all other deities, they sit down in order; the master himself recites the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for them to hear.
Next, the samaya precepts shall be explained in their entirety:

"From this day forward, you must always revere and make offerings to the Triple Gem, to all bodhisattvas, and to all mantra-deities; you must constantly give rise to faith and understanding toward the Mahāyāna sūtras; and whenever you see anyone who has received the samaya, you should feel love and joy."
One should always maintain reverence toward the Venerable Ones; one should not harbor resentment toward them, nor should one place faith in or study the scriptures of non-Buddhist paths.

To all who come seeking, one should give according to one's ability; one should always arouse compassion for all sentient beings, diligently cultivate all meritorious qualities, and constantly delight in the Mahāyāna.
"One must not be negligent or abandon the practice of mantra; furthermore, these secret dharmas should not be explained to those who lack the samaya.
This is the general outline; the details are extensively clarified in the first chapter of the *Pūjāvidhi*.

Having thus given these instructions, he shall show each person the mantra and mudrā of their respective tutelary deity (iṣṭadevatā) along with the corresponding family (kula), and explain the primary maṇḍala; thereafter, he shall perform the final homa.
When the homa is completed, once again protect the body according to the ritual rules and offer food to the various directions.

Having finished the offerings, wash the hands and sprinkle water for purification; then, together with the disciples, present incense, flowers, and other offerings in succession to all the honored ones, prostrating with a sincere heart and requesting their joyful acceptance.

Furthermore, holding the argha water, each should dismiss [the deities] according to the ritual with their respective root mantras; alternatively, one may dismiss them all at once by relying on the original teaching or using the mantra of the maṇḍala’s presiding deity, following the same procedure as the method for invitation.
All food offerings should be given to the poor; they should not be given for dogs, crows, or the like to devour.
All wealth and property should be taken by the ācārya and used as he pleases; if he cannot use it, it should be offered to the Triple Gem.

One should offer parasols, fly-whisks, and the like to the Buddha; unguents, incense for burning, and so forth to the Dharma; and robes, vases, utensils, and the like to the Buddha and the Saṅgha of the four directions.
If there is no Saṅgha, they should be given to the seven classes of followers. The disciples [of the practitioner] may not use even a small portion of these; if they do, they violate their samaya.
This is as explained extensively therein.

"At that time, Vairocana again surveyed the entire assembly and addressed the Vajradhara Lord of Secrets and others," and so forth, clarifies the mantra components required for the ritual activities of the maṇḍala.
The Ācārya should understand this; therefore, it is explained next.
Because he is about to reveal the treasury of the Tathāgata’s secret speech, he again surveys the entire assembly and bestows empowerment upon them.

Just as when a Buddha in his physical body is about to utter words of truth, he may manifest the mark of the broad and long tongue, covering his entire face, and address those ready for deliverance, saying:
"Have you ever seen in the scriptures any person with such physical marks who has spoken false or deceptive words?"

If, within the Mahāyāna, there are instances where the mark of the tongue is shown to pervade the trichiliocosm, now, because the World-Honored One is about to preach the Tathāgata’s impartial speech, he clarifies that this wheel of speech—both horizontally and vertically—pervades the entire dharma-realm; therefore, it is called the mark of the broad and long wheel of speech.
Regarding this character "xiang" (相), in the Sanskrit original it is correctly called *maṇḍala*.

Previously, the *maṇḍala* of the body of the Universal Gate was revealed; now, the *maṇḍala* of the speech of the Universal Gate is further displayed. Like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*), which is tranquil and mindless and possesses no fixed form, yet can universally respond to all things so as to satisfy their hearts, it is therefore named the "Skillful-Colored Maṇi."

Furthermore, from the body of the skillful-colored mani-jewel, there issued forth the speech of the skillful-colored mani-jewel, and the mind of the skillful-colored mani-jewel was revealed; they universally rained down the wealth of the Dharma, fulfilling the various rare aspirations of sentient beings throughout the entire dharma-realm.

In this way, the traces that respond to sentient beings constantly pervade the ten directions and the three periods of time; through immeasurable gateways, they plant the roots of all virtues, dwelling at all times in indestructible conduct. This signifies that within all undertakings, nothing can obstruct or destroy them; therefore, it is called the "Mantra Phrase of the Peerless Power of the Three Periods."
This is a general explanation of the source from which all mantras arise.

As for the "great powers," "great protections," and so forth explained in the subsequent text, these are the functions manifested according to the capacities of beings, produced from the wish-fulfilling jewel wheel.

At that time, the entire great assembly, realizing that their mental vessels were pure and being sustained by the inconceivable empowerment of the Tathāgata, became capable of receiving the Great Dharma. Immediately, through immeasurable gateways, they all spoke with one voice, petitioning the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
Now is indeed the right time, Sugata!
Now is indeed the right time.
According to the Sanskrit original, the former period is called *kāla*, which refers to a long duration of time, such as a year divided into three parts and so forth.
The latter period is called *samaya*, which refers to a short duration within that time, such as the further sub-divisions within the six periods of a day and night, and so forth.
It is like someone saying:
"Now is precisely the time for spring cultivation; having encountered this abundant rain, you should hasten to sow the seeds and not let the opportunity pass."
Therefore, it is stated twice.

At that time, having accepted the invitation, the World-Honored One, intending to expound the Great Power and Great Protection Vidyārājñī, dwelt in the Samādhi of the High Peak of the Pure Dharma Banner that Fulfills All Wishes and Manifests the Broad and Long Tongue Mark to Pervasively Cover All Buddha-fields.

Regarding the term "emerging" (*niṣkrānta*) used here, the correct translation from the Sanskrit original should be "arising" (*utpāda*). The older translations may render it as "exertion" (*vikrīḍita*), which is a figurative expression based on the underlying meaning:
that the emergence of this mark of the broad and long tongue is precisely the Tathāgata’s manifestation of great supernormal power through exertion.

This samādhi is the foremost among the universal applications of the skillful-colored maṇi-gems that pervade all buddha-fields through the Tathāgata’s mark of the broad and long tongue; it is like the banner of a great general, and is therefore called the "Pure Dharma Banner."
In Sanskrit it is called *dhvaja*, which is translated here as "banner" (*chāng*).
In Sanskrit it is called *ketu*, which is translated here as "standard" (*qí*).

Their characteristics differ slightly: a banner is merely adorned with various multicolored streamers and insignia, while a standard is largely similar in form but further distinguished by the addition of flags and secret emblems—such as the various shapes of tortoises, dragons, birds, and beasts painted by military strategists—to serve as signals for the three armies.
In some places, it is also translated as "banner" (*dhvaja*); therefore, they are combined here.
If the Sanskrit original were preserved in full, it should be rendered as "the banner of the pure Dharma.

Just as a great general establishes a banner atop a high peak to clearly perceive the terrain’s advantages and disadvantages, the enemy’s disposition, and commands a host of a million men such that their every movement and speech follows his will—ensuring victory in battle and success in assault—so too is this [the banner of the Dharma].
If an unskilled general is ignorant of the situation and loses his banner and standard, then the men will each have different hearts and defeat will follow upon his heels.
It is the same with the pure bodhicitta as the banner and standard of the myriad practices.

Abiding firmly and immovably upon the mountain of the Middle Way, the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one universally contemplates the ten directions through the *gati-gāminī* samādhi. Thus, one clearly perceives the superior and inferior qualities of the materials for the immeasurable gates of liberation, as well as the appropriate applications for each, along with the causes and conditions of the open and obstructed paths across all stages (*bhūmi*). Consequently, one is able to sustain immeasurable merit and universally protect all sentient beings; whatever one undertakes cannot be hindered or destroyed.
At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought:

"Since first resolving my mind toward enlightenment, I have always used this courageous and steadfast bodhicitta to protect and uphold the True Dharma and all sentient beings. Amidst various difficult and painful practices, I have remained as unyielding as a diamond, never retreating, precisely for the sake of accomplishing such a samādhi and universally protecting all Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions."
"Now my aspirations are all fulfilled; the time has come for that which was to be done.
Thereupon, he uttered these vidyā-mantra verses, producing a voice that pervaded the entire dharma-realm of all Tathāgatas and took pity upon the realm of sentient beings without exception.

If what I have spoken is truthful and not false, then whoever recites, upholds, and practices it shall possess power no different from my own; therefore, it is called "Great Power" and "Great Protection."
The Ācārya said: " 'Ming' (明) has the meaning of the radiance of great wisdom (*mahāprajñā*).
As for 'Fei' (妃), in Sanskrit it is *rājñī*; this is the word *rāja* pronounced with a feminine suffix. Therefore, those who transmit the teachings explain its meaning as 'consort' (*fei*)."
The Consort is the meaning of samādhi, namely the Samādhi of the Matrix of Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā-garbha-samādhi*).
This samādhi is the mother of all Buddha-sons.
These Buddha-sons are none other than the bodhicitta, the pure banner of the Dharma.

Just as that embryo, from the very moment of the kalala stage, is contained and protected so as not to be harmed by various conditions, gradually growing until its birth; thereafter, one continues to guard it with diligent care and nourishes it with milk.
Therefore, it is said that a mother’s kindness is the deepest and her virtue is difficult to repay.

As for “arising from this samādhi,” the moments of entering, abiding in, and emerging from it are all the inconceivable dharma-realm; they are not like worldly meditative concentrations where movement and stillness obstruct one another, nor do they have moments of regression or interruption.

Namaḥ sarvatathāgatebhyaḥ | Sarvavidyādhipatibhyaḥ | Viśvamukhebhyaḥ | Svāhā | Khaṃ raṅkṣa mahāmāle | Sarvatathāgata-bhūrṇiye nirdhaṭe | Hūṃ hūṃ traṭ traṭ aparājite svāhā || The first phrase is the taking of refuge in all the Tathāgatas.
The next phrase, which states that it can remove all obstacles, fears, and the like, praises the Tathāgata’s virtue of possessing all great powers and great protection.
Furthermore, the subsequent phrase praises the immeasurable dharma-gates.

Viśva also carries the meaning of "skillful means" (upāya); that is to say, the immeasurable gateways of skillful means, which are the universal activities of the Samādhi of Contemplating the High Peak of the Dharma Banner.
Now, wishing to explain this vidyā-queen, he first pays homage to the merits of all Tathāgatas in this manner.
Next, he says "sarvatha," which is a general reference to the merits of all Buddhas, intended to cause them to enter together through the single-syllable gate.
Next, there are the two syllables *haṃ* and *khaṃ*, which constitute the very essence of the mantra and are also called its "seed" (*bīja*).
All subsequent phrases below serve as further explanations of these two gates.

The syllable *Ha* signifies the meaning of "cause. That which is called the Mahāyāna cause is precisely the bodhicitta; because all causes are fundamentally unarisen and even transcend causes and conditions, it is named the pure bodhicitta. This is the true cause for attaining Buddhahood and the seed of the banner of the True Dharma.
The dot above the letter *ka* signifies the meaning of entering into realization; therefore, the sound is shifted to become *haṃ*.

*Kha* is the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*); with the dot above it, the sound is shifted to become *khaṃ*, which is the realization of this Great Emptiness named Prajñāpāramitā, the Mother of Buddhas—this is precisely the meaning of the *vidyārājñī* (Wisdom Consort).
Within this *ākāśagarbha* (Space-Treasury), one nurtures the seeds of the true cause; this is the meaning of "Great Protection" (*mahārakṣā*).
Furthermore, the gateway of the syllable *kha* is like space, ultimately pure and devoid of all things; it is the realm of objects known through the contemplation of the high peak.

The syllable *ha* is the banner of enlightenment (*bodhidhvaja*) and also the power of mastery (*vaśitā*). Because these two syllables are in correspondence, it is like a great general who is able to defeat enemies.

Furthermore, the gateway of the syllable *ha* is the jewel of the bodhicitta; because it is in union with the gateway of the syllable *kha*, the treasury of space (*ākāśagarbha*), it becomes a mani-jewel of exquisite color, capable of fulfilling all hopes and aspirations.
In this present mantra, these missing characters are absent; they are fully contained in the subsequent passage.
The next phrase says *rakṣa*, which carries the meaning of "protection.

It is like a person who, when terrified by calamities or misfortunes, relies upon a powerful great man or gains the security of a high city and deep moat, thereby remaining at ease and free from anxiety.
Although those enemies may employ various expedients, they can do nothing against him.

It is the same for the practitioner: by relying on the King of Bodhicitta and taking the matrix of Prajñā as his citadel, he becomes indestructible like space; this is a further explanation of the previous meaning.
The next phrase is *mahā-māri*, translated as "Great Power" (*da-li*).

The syllable *ha* signifies that within the *bodhicitta* all the powers of the Tathāgatas are fully present; now, because it is joined with the syllable *kha*, it is freed from all bonds and no longer encounters any obstruction. Like the wind freely swirling in the midst of space, it is therefore called "Great Power."

Furthermore, because the syllable *ha* possesses sovereign power and is conjoined with the immeasurable gateways of skillful means of the syllable *kha*, it is like a strong man who is fully endowed with a thousand kinds of arts and abilities; thus, no one among the multitude can overcome him, and for this reason he is called "Great Power."
The seventh phrase explains the source of this great power; thus it says, "arising from the merits of all Tathāgatas.

This great, adamantine power originally arises from the vajra-lineage of the Buddhas. Furthermore, since immeasurable kalpas past, one has constantly cultivated the myriad virtues of the *dharmakṣara* (the letter-syllable) by means of this *hā*-syllable as the true cause, each and every one of them being indestructible like a vajra.

Now that all virtues are fulfilled and all powers are fully prepared, you shall further, by means of this Samādhi of the High Peak of the Dharma Banner, utterly crush the enemies of the Dharma-realm and universally protect all sentient beings.
Next, one utters words of truth, namely the syllable *hūṃ*.
*Hūṃ* is a sound that terrifies others; it is repeated because one instance destroys external obstacles and the other destroys internal obstacles.
Furthermore, the external refers to the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the internal refers to the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Regarding the interpretation of this gateway of the syllable, by what dharma does the Tathāgata terrify these hindrances?
It is precisely by means of this gateway of the syllable *ha*.

The drawing of the lower *samādhi* represents the complete cultivation of the ten thousand practices; the presence of the great *bindu* (dot) above signifies that the ten thousand virtues have already been perfected.
The syllable *HA* is the *samādhi* of the banner of the Dharma-pinnacle; because it is conjoined with the *bindu*, it is the *samādhi* of the High Peak Contemplation.

Regarding the statement that the syllable *HA* is the seed of all Tathāgatas: the upper dot (*bindu*) is the mother of the Vidyārājñī, and the lower stroke represents the daily increase of the fetal portion.
By virtue of this meaning, as soon as it utters its sound, the armies of Māra are shattered and destroyed.
Next, it says *taraṭa*, which carries the meaning of rebuking and subduing.
It is like when a lion roars in a fit of rage; there are no wild beasts that are not terrified and subdued.

Furthermore, the repetition of these words refers to the fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), as well as their antidotes, including all afflictions within the realm (*dhātu*) and those beyond the realm.
The final phrase says *apratihata*, which means "unimpeded and incomparable power," thereby concluding and upholding the preceding text.
For these reasons, she is called the Great Power, Great Protection Vidyārājñī.
*Svāhā* serves to awaken all Buddhas so that they may act as witnesses; it also carries the meaning of mindfulness and upholding, as has been explained previously.

As the Sūtra says: "At that time, when all Tathāgatas and the assembly of Buddha-sons had spoken this vidyā, immediately the entire buddha-field shook in six ways. This means that when Mahāvairocana Tathāgata uttered this sound that pervades the dharma-realm, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, by virtue of their non-dual state, spoke it together with one voice.

Now, this empowered phrase is fully endowed with majestic power; furthermore, by virtue of the Tathāgata’s words of truth, at that very moment the Buddha-fields of the ten directions shook in six ways, manifesting the reality and non-falsity of the Buddha’s great vow.
Regarding the meaning of the six kinds of earthquakes, their characteristics are fully explained in other sūtras.
Now, according to the secret interpretation of this school, the "six kinds" refer to the six root afflictions: greed, hatred, delusion, views, pride, and doubt.

The minds of all sentient beings have long been held fast by these heavy defilements and were unable to arise on their own; now, moved by the sincere resolve of the World-Honored One, they have all cracked open and spread apart, and the seeds of the Buddha-nature have sprouted—hence it is said that there are six kinds of earth tremors.

At that time, all the bodhisattvas, upon seeing these two kinds of causes and conditions for the earthquake—the superficial and the profound and secret—had their minds blossom of their own accord; attaining what they had never experienced before, they praised the World-Honored One Vairocana with subtle and wondrous verses.

As for the statement in the sutra, "in the presence of all Buddhas," it means that when the Buddha spoke this vidyā-mantra, the bodhisattvas and others of the worlds of the ten directions each saw it being spoken before their respective Buddhas; therefore, they all simultaneously understood it with a single voice.
This passage is sent to attest to the power of the Great Protection (*mahārakṣā*).
Regarding the verse, the phrase "the Buddhas are most extraordinary" should, according to the extant Sanskrit original, be rendered as "How marvelous! All Buddhas! (*āścaryam sarvabuddhānām*).
"To expound this mantra of great power" means that the bodhisattvas in each and every world simultaneously comprehend the mantras spoken by all the Buddhas of the ten directions.

Because it is protected and sustained by the Buddhas of the ten directions, it is like a vajra city—thick, solid, and so high that it cannot be ascended, and further encircled by a boiling moat so deep that it cannot be crossed; therefore, all those who create obstacles are unable to invade or oppress it.

Regarding the phrase "abiding by means of that protection of the mind," it means that practitioners are able to abide while protecting their body and mind through these mantras and secret mudrās; therefore, all obstructors, such as the Vināyakas and Rākṣasas of hideous form, naturally retreat and disperse.
Furthermore, regarding this syllable *vī*, if one follows the Sanskrit pronunciation, it also contains the sound *va*, which means "to dwell" or "to remain firmly within the heart.

To provide a profound interpretation: it is said that a person possessing this pure bodhicitta dwells with their mind protected by the true meaning of this consort (*vidyā-rājñī*). Therefore, the three types of heavy obstacles, the various evil rākṣasas, and so forth, all flee and disperse, unable to harm their roots of goodness.
Even down to the moment when one gives rise to the thought of recollection, there is likewise such power and efficacy; therefore, the final phrase further confirms this.
The Sūtra says: "The Bhagavat, through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the vast Dharma-realm, at that very moment dwelt in the *dharmadhātu-garbha-samādhi*."

Regarding the phrase "Emerging from this samādhi, he speaks of entering the Vidyādhara of the Buddha-samaya": the Sanskrit term *vipula* carries the meaning of "vast" or "extensive," signifying that which is profoundly and boundlessly expansive, beyond all measure.
The intrinsic nature of all such phenomena is called the Vimala Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

The true reality of all Buddhas, the true reality of mantras, and the true reality of sentient beings are all the Vimala Dharma-realm; because they mutually empower one another through this, it is called the empowerment of the Dharma-realm.

Furthermore, just as through the causal conditions of the union of a man and a woman, the seed is entrusted to the womb without being lost or destroyed—this is the meaning of mutual empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*)—so too, when the Buddhas, the kings, and the vidyārājñīs unite, they together produce the seed of Vimalaprabha, which is sustained by the Womb of Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā-garbha*) without being lost or destroyed; therefore, it is called the empowerment of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-adhiṣṭhāna*).

The World-Honored One universally empowered all sentient beings, completing the process of making them all equal seeds; immediately thereafter, he entered the Samādhi of the Womb-Treasury Pervading the Dharma-Dhātu. He observed that each and every seed was the inexhaustible adornment of the universal gate retinue of Vairocana upon a lotus pedestal, no different from the Great Compassion Maṇḍala.
Yet sentient beings are unable to realize this for themselves; therefore, they are said to dwell within the *garbha* (womb) of the Sage.
When they emerge from this treasury, it is the liberation of the Tathāgata.
Having thus observed in this manner, the Bhagavān immediately arose from samādhi and spoke the vidyādhara-samaya.
Samaya means equality, it means the original vow, it means the removal of obstacles, and it means awakening.

Regarding "equality," it means that when the Tathāgata directly realizes this samādhi, he perceives that the various bodies, speech, and minds of all sentient beings are entirely equal to those of the Tathāgata; their meditative concentration, wisdom, and the body of the true mark (dharmatākāya) are also ultimately equal.
Therefore, he utters words of truth to inform all sentient beings:

"If what I have said is certainly not false, then when all sentient beings utter these words of truth, may they likewise receive the empowerment of the three secrets, attaining inexhaustible adornments equal to those of the Tathāgata."
For this reason, it is able to perform the activity of the vajra; therefore, it is called *samaya*.
Regarding the "original vow": when the Tathāgata realized this *samaya*, he saw that all sentient beings possess the potential for Buddhahood, and immediately established this great vow:
"From now on, through the universal gate and by means of immeasurable expedient means, I shall cause all sentient beings to attain unsurpassed bodhi."
Until the realm of sentient beings is exhausted, my activities shall never cease.
If there are sentient beings who, following my original vow, utter these words of truth, I shall cause all their undertakings to become entirely of the nature of vajra.
Therefore, it is called *samaya*. Regarding the "removal of obstacles":

the Tathāgata perceives that all sentient beings possess the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata; yet, due solely to a single moment of ignorance (*avidyā*), they fail to realize it, even though it is ever present before their eyes.
Therefore, he utters these words of truth:
"I shall now employ various skillful means to universally dispel the cataracts from the eyes of all sentient beings.

If this vow of mine is destined to be fulfilled, then whenever sentient beings follow my skillful means and speak these words of truth, may they, throughout their entire lives, obtain the stainless eye with all obscurations completely exhausted."
Therefore, it is called *samaya*.

Regarding the meaning of "awakening": because all sentient beings are in the sleep of ignorance and thus do not themselves realize such merits, the Tathāgata moves them with truthful words to cause them to awaken.
This is also to alert all bodhisattvas and others, causing them to arise from the caves of profound meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and learn the lion’s stretch.

If there are practitioners of mantras who proclaim this samaya, we Buddhas shall likewise remember and uphold our original vows without transgression; it is just as when a king, having established his own laws, subsequently respects and complies with them himself. Therefore, it is called *samaya*.
The "Vidyādhara" (Holder of Wisdom) is called *dhāraṇī* in Sanskrit.

"Wisdom" (*vidyā*) refers to the total retention of all gateways of wisdom and enlightened conduct; because one does not allow even a single instance of these to be lost or leaked from the time this samaya vow was first undertaken until its conclusion, one is thus named an "Entrant into the Buddha’s Samaya Vidyādhara."
