*Namo samantabuddhānām asame trimaye samaye svāhā*. The first phrase, "I take refuge in all Buddhas," is explained as above.
The next phrase says "without equal," followed by "threefold equality"; taken together with the subsequent phrase, this refers to the *samaya* of the threefold equality that is without equal.
Furthermore, *a* signifies that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen; it is the very essence of the *dharmadhātu*.
*Sa* has the meaning of "truth.
*Mi* has the meaning of "samādhi.
*Ma* signifies "self-realized great emptiness" as well as "self."

When the World-Honored One realized this samādhi, he observed that the power of mind of each and every sentient being was a universal mandala equal to his own; therefore, there was nothing further to be compared or contrasted with, and thus it is called "unequaled."

The "threefold equality" refers to the equality of the three periods of time, the equality of the three causes, the equality of the three paths of action, and the equality of the three vehicles; this serves as a further explanation of the meaning of why there is no equal to the preceding phrase.
*Tāra* means that the mind is in accordance with its true nature (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*).

All defilements are fundamentally non-arising; the various skillful means of the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time are all for the sake of this one great causal event (*ekamahā-kārya-hetu-pratyaya*), which is precisely the meaning of removing obstacles.

The conclusion states: "Samaya" refers to the definitive lion’s roar that explains the meaning of the equality of all phenomena; it is the establishment of a great vow to cause all beings to become like oneself; it is the desire to universally open the pure knowledge and vision for all sentient beings; and it is used to awaken both sentient beings and all Buddhas. Therefore, this Samaya is called the Vajra Vow of Truth of All Tathāgatas.
If one does not first maintain this recollection, one shall not be permitted to perform any ritual activities of the mantras.

After the World-Honored One had proclaimed this samaya by means of the wheels of body, speech, and mind that pervade all buddha-fields, there was not a single member of the assembly of all the Buddha-sons who did not hear it.
Having heard this, one must not dare to transgress any of the dharmas of mantra. Why is this so?
If a bodhisattva forms various views of inequality regarding sentient beings and all phenomena, they then violate the samaya dharma.
If one forms various limited or discriminatory thoughts regarding this vow of equality, one also transgresses the samaya dharma.
If whatever one does conforms to worldly fame and profit rather than being for the sake of the great causal conditions, one also transgresses the samaya dharma.
If one is negligent and indolent, failing to awaken the mind, one also transgresses the samaya laws.
Because of such transgression of the samaya, various obstacles arise; thus, one harms oneself and others, resulting in no benefit or merit.
Therefore, all Bodhisattvas uphold this samaya as they would protect their own lives, not daring to transgress it.

As for the scripture stating, "At that time, the Bhagavat further spoke the Mantra of the Arising of the Dharmadhātu," it means that when the World-Honored One previously entered the *dharmadhātu-garbha-samādhi*, he saw that all sentient beings possess the seed of bodhi and are equal to all Buddhas; thus, he spoke the *vidyā* of entering the Buddha-samaya.
By means of this vidyā-dhara, one attains entry into the equality of the Buddha’s precepts; this is precisely the meaning of "entrusting the holy embryo.

At that time, the World-Honored One again observed all sentient beings with his universal eye, seeing that they were all fully endowed with the holy embryo and born into the family of the Buddha; at that time, Anantavyūha was likewise equal to the Tathāgata.
Having arisen from this samādhi, he immediately spoke the mantra for the arising of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Furthermore, observing with the universal eye (*samantacakṣus*), he saw that each and every sentient being was fully accomplished in vajra-activities; at that time, the inexhaustible adornments were likewise equal to those of the Tathāgata.
Having arisen from this samādhi, he then spoke the mantra of Vajrasattva;
therefore, these three are all termed *samaya*.
Furthermore, by virtue of entering the Buddha-samaya, one is not permitted to meet an untimely death within the *garbhadhātu*.
Because he is born from the *dharmadhātu*, at the moment of his first emergence from the womb, he is free from all obstructions.
Because he is Vajrasattva, he is able to manage household affairs and master all arts and crafts.

Furthermore, through the empowerment of the Secret Womb Matrix (*garbhadhātu*) of the Buddha’s Samaya, there is the empowerment of the two tiers of retinues consisting of the Bodhisattvas born from the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātujāta*) and the Vajrasattvas; and through the empowerment of Vajrasattva, various forms according to their respective types are manifested. Entering the Buddha’s Samaya is like a lotus treasury; being born from the Dharma-realm is like a blooming lotus; and Vajrasattva is like the accomplishment of a lotus that returns to its seed. Therefore, these three kinds are all termed "Samaya."
*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ dharmadhātu-svabhāvā-guhya dharmadhātu-svabhāvā.* This is the meaning of the *dharmadhātu*.
*Sarvabhāva* refers to self-nature (*svabhāva*), which is also called original nature (*prakṛti*).
The trace of the phrase is the meaning of "self.
Regarding the meaning of that phrase: "self" refers to the self-nature of the *dharmadhātu*.
Because it is the definitive lion's roar, it declares that both "self" and all sentient beings are the self-nature of the *dharmadhātu*; this is the meaning of equality.
"I shall employ various skillful means to cause all sentient beings to fully realize and know this; this is the meaning of my original vow.

Because they will know that I am the very nature of the *dharmadhātu*, they will be able to eliminate all conceptual discrimination and open up pure knowledge and vision; this is the meaning of removing obstructions."
I pray that all Buddhas will remember and uphold their original vows, so that this body of mine may become identical to the self-nature of Vairocana’s Dharma-realm; this is the meaning of awakening.
This shall now be explained extensively by means of the *akṣara-dvāra* (gateways of syllables).
*Namaḥ samantavajrāṇāṃ vajratama kuṭaṅga*. Since the first phrase is intended to proclaim the mantra of Vajrasattva, one takes refuge in all the vajras.
This means that those who uphold the Tathāgata’s vajra-wisdom through immeasurable gateways are all caused to remember, maintain, and protect it.
The next phrase, *vajratma-ko-hum*, means that one’s own body is identical to the vajra.
Vajra is the very nature of the dharmadhātu; because it accomplishes great, firm, and indestructible power, it is designated by an alternative term as "vajra.
The Tathāgata, with his universal eye, perceives that the essence of vajra-wisdom in all sentient beings is no different from his own; this is the meaning of equality.

Because sentient beings do not awaken to this themselves, one performs various vajra activities through immeasurable gateways of vajra wisdom; the essential purpose of this original vow is to destroy such great obstacles and lead them to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Thus, this ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi) is called the stainless eye and the vajra-eye; it carries the meaning of removing obstructions.
By means of this lion’s roar, it causes the Buddha-fields of the ten directions to tremble; it carries the meaning of awakening.
Therefore, it is called *samaya*.
Furthermore, by means of the first three *samayas*, the practitioner of mantra-ritual attains a body equal to the secret body, speech, and mind of the Tathāgata.
By means of the second samaya, one attains a body of sublime majesty, identical to the Tathāgata’s empowerment within the Palace of the Dharma-realm.
By means of the third samaya, this body and its environment are rendered entirely vajra-like, surrounded by an immeasurable assembly of Vajradharas.

The Buddha taught that the first samaya is for one's own enjoyment; the second samaya is for the sake of accomplishing the dharma-nature body for all bodhisattvas; and the third samaya is for the sake of subduing and gathering sentient beings according to their respective types.

The Buddha taught that the first samaya is for the purpose of establishing the Great Compassion Womb Maṇḍala; the second samaya is for performing the activities of the Vairocana Ācārya; and the third samaya is for performing the activities of the Vajradhara disciple.

The first samaya is for the purpose of empowering the retinue of the Tathāgatas; the second samaya is for the purpose of empowering the retinue of the Lotus Family; and the third samaya is for the purpose of empowering the retinue of the Vajra Family.
For this reason, the Buddha taught the three samayas.
Next, regarding the explanation of the Vajra Armor mantra: it is for the purpose of adorning the body of Vajrasattva.
Having already made the vajra vow, the practitioner, desiring to destroy all obstacles for the sake of all sentient beings, dons the armor of vajra with firm and powerful diligence.
Furthermore, for example, each of the six pāramitās is identical to the true mark (lakṣaṇa), all being like a vajra, indestructible.
Moreover, within each individual pāramitā, all five pāramitās are fully present; therefore, they are perfectly integrated and dense, without any gaps or fissures.

As with the six perfections, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the eighteen kinds of emptiness, the one hundred and eight samādhis, the five hundred dhāraṇīs, and so forth, all should be explained in detail.

Because they are clad in the Tathāgata’s adamantine armor (*vajra-kavaca*), though they revolve through the six realms of existence, passing from birth to death, they cannot be harmed by any afflictions, karma, or suffering.

To explain this in a more superficial and concise manner: because the practitioner empowers themselves with this mantra, all devas, nāgas, and other beings perceive them as identical to the body of Vajrasattva. Their entire bodies are covered in adamantine armor, which is dense and seamless, with light like a fierce flame; therefore, none of those who would create obstacles can cause them harm.
*Namaḥ samantavajrāṇāṃ vajrakavaca hūṃ*. Vajra is the diamond; *kavaca* means armor.
The Tathāgata, with his diamond eye, universally beholds all sentient beings, and there are none who are not protected by this diamond armor. Therefore, he proclaims it with words of truth.
The syllable *va* is taken as the essence of the mantra; *va* signifies that all phenomena are beyond verbal expression.

If something were within the sphere of conceptual proliferation and verbal expression, it would be entirely subject to refutation and transformation, lacking any solidity; therefore, the syllable *va* is taken as the essence.
The subsequent words all provide further explanations.
Why are all phenomena beyond verbal expression?
Because their arising cannot be apprehended.
Why is it that birth cannot be attained?
Because its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is pure.
This intrinsic purity is precisely the body of Vajrasattva.
Next, the meaning of "armor" (kavaca) is explained.

If a phenomenon is something produced through conditioning, one should know that it exists merely as a conventional designation, subject to transformation according to conditions; since it cannot even maintain its own nature, how could it possibly resist the sharp arrows of the six sense objects?

Now, observing that the adamantine essence is adorned with inexhaustibility and is entirely free from all conditioned activity, it is therefore firm and indestructible; since it cannot be affected by the hundred negations, it is called the "adamantine armor."
The final syllable *hūṃ* is the sound of fearlessness; it also signifies sovereign power and joy.

When one realizes this gateway of the letter *ha* through the perfection of meditative concentration and wisdom, one knows for oneself that one will certainly be able to destroy all obstacles and universally protect sentient beings; therefore, there is great joy.

Next, regarding the mantra of the Tathāgata’s eye: it is like the King of Golden-Winged Birds (Garuḍa), who is endowed with sovereign power and possesses complete and firm wings; furthermore, having attained eyes of extreme clarity and sharpness, he gazes down upon the great ocean from the midst of the void as if looking at a reflection in a mirror, and is thus able to seize various nāgas at will and with ease.

It should be known that the practitioner of mantras is likewise so: because they empower themselves with these Tathāgata-pure eyes, the ocean-like assembly of the maṇḍala shall appear before them; they will fully perceive all root conditions and obstructing dharmas, whereby all vajra activities will be accomplished according to their wishes. Therefore, this is explained next.
Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ tathāgatākṣivijayavairocana svāhā. Within the meaning of this phrase, *tathāgatākṣi* refers to the eye of the Tathāgata.
Next, it says *vairocana*, which has the meaning of "contemplation"; it means to contemplate with the eye of the Tathāgata.
It takes the initial syllable *ta* as its essence; *ta* signifies the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena. Because all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, even this suchness is unattainable.
Therefore, the Tathāgata contemplates all dharmas as ultimately neither identical nor different; though they cannot be seen, he perceives them clearly.
As it is with the Buddhas, so it is with the eyes of all sentient beings.
When a practitioner utters this word of truth, they receive the empowerment of the inconceivable Buddha-eye and gradually attain the purification of their vision.
Next are the six types of mantras for unguents and so forth; as these are all required when entering the maṇḍala to perform offerings, they are explained in this chapter.

The Mantra for Incense: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ viśuddha-gandhu-nirbhāva svāhā*. Regarding the meaning of these phrases: *viśuddha* means "pure," *gandhu* means "fragrance," and *nirbhāva* means "to produce"; thus, it signifies "the production of pure fragrance."
The essence of this consists of the initial subtle syllable *mi*; by adding the stroke of the letter *i* to the letter *va*, the sound is transformed into *mi*.
The letter *va* signifies "vajra" and the sense of being "beyond verbal expression."
Samādhi has the meaning of abiding.
Thus, when concentration and wisdom are in equilibrium, this is precisely abiding in the non-conceptual Vajra-holder’s precept of unobstructed knowledge throughout the three times.

Such is the fragrance of the precepts: its nature is fundamentally quiescent, neither coming nor going, yet it constantly pervades the entire Dharma-realm; therefore, it is called the "Pure Ointment Fragrance.
Although all sentient beings equally possess it, because they have not yet resolved their minds toward enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), this fragrance has not yet been manifested.
I have now thoroughly anointed my Dharma-body with this fragrance of precepts; therefore, I am able to universally diffuse this pure fragrance to all.
[The Flower Mantra, followed by the Flower Mantra.]

*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ mahāmaitryābhyudgate svāhā.* In the meaning of this phrase, *mahāmaitrī* means "great loving-kindness" (*maitrī*), and *abhyudgata* means "arising"; thus, it refers to the sense of the arising of great loving-kindness.
The syllable *ma* constitutes the essence of the mantra; it is the syllable *maṃ* with the addition of the *samādhi-stroke*, and for this reason it is pronounced with a shifted vowel tone.
*Maṃ* signifies "mind" (*citta*) and "self" (*ātman*), and is also called "Great Emptiness" (*mahāśūnyatā*).

It is said that this lotus of the mind was previously unable to grow because it was entangled by the false notion of "self. Now, because one has personally realized the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the mind, the eight petals, stamens, and filaments gradually unfold from within the treasury of compassion; therefore, it is said to be "born from great kindness."

Furthermore, the seeds of the sovereign tree-king of the pure bodhicitta grow and flourish from the ground of compassion, blossoming with the flowers of myriad virtues; through skillful means, they bear fruit. Therefore, it is said that they arise from great loving-kindness.
This shall now be explained extensively by means of the *akṣara-mukha* (gateways of syllables).
Regarding the incense mantra, following the incense mantra:

*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ dharmadhātvanugate svāhā*. In the meaning of this phrase, *dharmadhātu* signifies the "Dharma-realm"; *anugate* signifies "following after," as well as "pervading everywhere," "departing," or "advancing without ceasing. Translated, it means "pervading the Dharma-realm."
It takes the initial syllable of the phrase as its essence.

Because the realm of sentient beings is fundamentally unarisen, even the fixed characteristics of the dharma-realm cannot be apprehended; thus, this dharma-realm is profound and vast, boundless and immeasurable.
Because the practitioner of yoga constantly and preeminently advances without ceasing, their physical, verbal, and mental activities entirely pervade such a dharmadhātu.
Even when making an offering of a single flower to the Buddha, it likewise pervades such a dharmadhātu; this is precisely the meaning of "incense."
Next is the mantra for food and drink:

*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām, ararakaṣe kaṣemaline naminamaline mahāmale svāhā*. Regarding this, the initial *arara* signifies a sound that is unpleasant to hear; it carries the meaning of an unwholesome sound.
It is like a person shouting and clamoring loudly, causing the minds of those who hear it to lack tranquility.
Next, the word "karara" is used to stop that previous unwholesome loud noise; it carries the meaning of being serene, indifferent, and profoundly still.
In this context, the meaning is that the true sustenance consists of the joy of the Dharma and the delight of dhyāna; it is for this reason that the matter is addressed by means of this metaphor.

As for the characteristics of the syllable-wheel (*akṣara-cakra*), "A" signifies the primordial beginning (*ādyanutpanna*). Because this primordial beginning exists, there are two kinds of defilements: namely, the afflictions (*kleśa*) and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Because of these two kinds of defilements, there arises the clamor of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

Now, since all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, these two kinds of defilements are also fundamentally unarisen; this is precisely the opening of the gate of nectar and the preparation of the meal of *nirvāṇa*, and for this reason it is called "A-ra-ra."

Furthermore, if a person diligently cultivates the myriad practices in the hope of attaining such a flavor of the Dharma, because of their conditioned effort, the two obscurations will arise once more; this is not the true nectar-flavor of eternal life, physical vigor, and strength.

Now, because all phenomena are without fabrication, the flavor of internal realization is not obtained from another; it is like having eaten milk gruel and requiring nothing more. Therefore, it is said that one ceases the preceding unwholesome sounds.

Regarding *mālinda-nami*: generally, in the West, the food offered during sacrificial feasts—ranging from offerings made to the Buddhas above to those for spirits and ghosts below—is collectively termed *mālinda*.
The meaning of this phrase is: "I have already partaken of and presented this food."
Next, regarding the phrase *māmalaṃdana*, its meaning is this: having accepted the food offered by me, you shall in turn grant me sublime food.
It is like people in the world who offer sumptuous delicacies to a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) in order to ensure that they lack nothing for food and drink in both this life and future lives.

Therefore, I now empower this offering of worldly sustenance with the food of inexhaustible Dharma and present it to all the Honored Ones; may you in turn grant my aspirations, so that I may always be suffused with the flavor of neither birth nor death.
Next, regarding the term *mahāphalgu*, it means that among all foods, they are doubly vast, abundant, and exquisite.

By using this to analyze the preceding phrase, it means: "That which I now offer and that for which I pray are all of the most incomparable flavor and unsurpassed taste; I do not seek food of limited measure."
Next is the *Dīpa-pradīpa-mantra*:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ tathāgatārciḥ-spharaṇā-vyavasāna-gaganaudariye svāhā*. Regarding the meaning of these words: *tathāgata* refers to the Tathāgata; *arciḥ* refers to radiant light.
Next, it says: *saprāṇe* means "universal"; *avabhāsana* means "all darknesses"; and *gaganaudariya* means "limitless, equal to space."
The mental discourse [states] that the Tathāgata’s flame-light universally pervades all darkness, equal to space and without limit.

This mantra takes many syllables at the beginning of its phrases as its essence; like the true reality (*tattva*) of the mind, it is the great wisdom-light of Vairocana, which shines universally throughout the world, pervading everything without exception.

What is called "all darkness" is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*); because ignorance is fundamentally unarisen, its essence is itself illumination. Therefore, the Tathāgata’s radiance pervades all darkness.
Regarding the statement "equal to space," because ignorance is equal to space and immeasurable, the light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is likewise equal to space and immeasurable.
Up to and including old age and death, because they are like space and immeasurable, the light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is likewise like space and immeasurable.
As it is with the twelve links of dependent origination, so too are all phenomena explained.
Because its meaning is thus definitive, it is called the Lamp-Illuminating Mantra.
To offer this consecrated lamp-light to the Buddha is the foremost among all offerings.
Next is the *argha* mantra: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ gaganasamāsamasvāhā*.
Regarding the meaning of these words: *gagana* means "space"; *sama* means "equal"; and *asama* means "unequaled. This refers to being equal to space and yet without equal.
The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is equal to empty space because its fundamental nature is pure, because it is free from discrimination, and because it is without limit.
Nevertheless, it possesses immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable merits that cannot be illustrated by that empty space; therefore, it is said to be "without equal."
Furthermore, "asama" (a-sama) has the meaning of "unequal. Those who are unequal are the followers of the Two Vehicles.
Since [this state] is now equal to empty space and also equal to this very "inequality," it is said to be "equal to empty space and without equal."

Taking the initial syllable *ga* as the essence of the mantra, neither coming nor going within the realm of sentient beings can be apprehended, nor can the characteristic of coming and going within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) be apprehended; because the "thus-coming" and "thus-going" of the Tathāgata cannot be apprehended, it is called the "Great Emptiness."
By bathing the stainless body with this pure water of great emptiness, one realizes the true meaning of the *argha* offering.
Following this, there are four mantras which likewise represent the marks of adornment for the maṇḍala-ācārya; therefore, they are explained within this chapter.
The Tathāgata-Uṣṇīṣa Mantra: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ gaganānantaspharaṇaviśuddhadharmanirjāta svāhā*.

Regarding the meaning of these phrases: *gaganānantam* means the infinity of space; *spharaṇa* means pervasive; *viśuddha* means pure; and *dharmanirjāta* means born from the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
This statement regarding the Tathāgata’s uṣṇīṣa is like space: it transcends all measure and number, and is universally pure.
One should know that such a uṣṇīṣa is born from the matrix of the dharmadhātu, and is not born from the matrix of worldly parents.
This mantra also takes the syllable *ga* as its essence.

It refers to the mark of the Tathāgata’s topknot (*uṣṇīṣa*), which is devoid of the marks of coming and going and is identical to great emptiness; yet all sentient beings perceive it through the marks of coming and going. Therefore, although it pervades the ten directions, one cannot see its limits.
If a practitioner, with a mind of certain resolve, knows for themselves that their own cranial protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) is likewise so, this is called the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa mantra.
When the ācārya manifests himself as Vairocana, he loosens his topknot and then binds it once more.

If one is a renunciant, one should form a fist with the right hand and place it upon the crown of the head; then, by reciting this mantra to empower it, no devas or other celestial beings will be able to see the mark on the crown of one's head.
Next is the Tathāgata-kavaca-mantra:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ vajrajvālāviśara huṃ*. Regarding the meaning of these words: *vajrajvālā* means "diamond light," and *viśara* means "pervasive."

To say that this vajra-light of wisdom pervades all, is able to eliminate the obscurations of the darkness of birth and death, and is also able to outshine them, is the meaning of the Tathāgata’s armor.
This mantra takes the final syllable *hūṃ* as its essence and is fully endowed with the three gates of liberation.

Specifically, the syllable *na* above it, together with the nasal bindu (*anusvāra*), signifies "great emptiness" (*mahāśūnyatā*), which is the gate of liberation through emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*).
The essential nature is the syllable HA; because it is free from causes and conditions, it is the gate of liberation of signlessness (animitta-vimokṣamukha).
Below is the samādhi-line of the syllable U; because it is fundamentally unborn, it is the gate of liberation of wishlessness (apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha).
These three gates cannot be entered by any obstacles whatsoever.
Because this light of wisdom universally adorns the body, it is called the "armor of the Tathāgata."

Upon examining the secret mudrās, it appears that the Sanskrit manuscript is incomplete; I suspect this is the Vidyā-mantra of the Halo of Vajrasattva, and one should further seek out other Sanskrit manuscripts.
Following the Tathāgata’s Circular Halo Mantra:

*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ jvala-mālī-tathāgata-ṛddhi-svāhā*. In this mantra, *jvala* has the meaning of "flame-light," and *mālī* has the meaning of "garland. Because the garland of flames forms a continuous, unbroken circle, it is called the "Tathāgata’s Circular Halo."
The next phrase says *tathāgata-ṛji*, which carries the meaning of the Tathāgata’s radiance; this is the light of pure clarity.
Although its name differs from that of the *Jvālāmālā* (Flame Garland) light in the Sanskrit sound, it is precisely this word *ṛji* that constitutes the essence of the mantra.
The syllable *ra* above signifies the meaning of defilement (*rajas*), while the syllable *ca* as the lower body signifies the meaning of transformation.
Because it enters the gateway of the syllable *a*, it is inherently free from defilement and subject to no transformation; this is the light of the Tathāgata’s eternal quiescence.

Furthermore, it carries the resonance of the *ī* syllable samādhi, signifying that this light of eternal quiescence is fully endowed with both concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*); therefore, it is eternally illuminating while remaining quiescent, and eternally quiescent while remaining illuminating.

Because the ācārya has empowered his body in this way, all the devas and other celestial beings are completely enveloped by the Tathāgata’s flaming garland; he is fierce and difficult to behold, like the orb of the sun, and therefore no obstructors can find an opportunity against him.
The Mantra of the Tathāgata’s Tongue Appearance.

*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ mahāmahā tathāgatīrgha-satyadharma-pratiṣṭhitastava*. In this phrase, "mahāmahā" means "the Great, the Non-Great. "Tathāgatīrgha" means the tongue of the Tathāgata; because the appearance of this tongue is so broad and long that it completely covers all Buddha-fields, it is called "Great."

Because this "Great" (Mahā) has nothing superior to it, nothing with which it can be contrasted, and because even its characteristic marks (lakṣaṇa) cannot be apprehended, it is called "Non-Great" (Amahā).

"To be able to utter this teaching is for the great benefit of all sentient beings.
I shall now reveal it to you; I will answer everything according to your questions.
The Buddha said, "Obstacles arise from one's own mind, resulting from past compliance with stinginess."
Because those causes have been eliminated, this thought is the bodhicitta;

By recollecting the bodhicitta, one is able to eliminate the causes of all obstacles.

Within this, there is the character "you" (yu), which in the Sanskrit sound also carries the meaning of "arising.

Constantly contemplating the Great Being who is immovable, one can eliminate all that acts as an obstacle.
Regarding the one who shall bind this secret mudrā: this is none other than the previously mentioned Acala Vidyārāja.
By virtue of his great vows, the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata manifests this form within the signless state to protect all practitioners of the mantra path.

Lord of Mysteries, one should recite the letter-gateway *A* regarding the wind element; there is also a specific meaning here.

This continues the teachings of the former Buddhas: when constructing a maṇḍala, if a great wind arises as an obstacle because the rite is being performed in the open air, it must be restrained.

Regarding the method for obstructing water, one should contemplate the syllable *raṃ*, which manifests as a great red flame pervading the interior of the body; this garland of flames then issues forth from within the body and spreads over the exterior of the body like a wreath.

Alternatively, when all obstacles have subsided, one should again recite the mantra while abiding within the great, immovable, and powerful fundamental maṇḍala. Furthermore, another expedient means (upāya) is clarified: this expedient means removes all obstacles and is none other than the previously mentioned Acala Vidyārāja.

If they remain defiant and refuse to obey the instruction or depart, even to the point that their life-force must be severed, the practitioner of recitation should give rise to a mind of compassion and think: "May I not cause them to lose their lives."

However, the intended meaning here is that what constitutes an "obstruction" refers to dharmas such as stinginess and greed that arise from the mind, which are capable of creating all manner of obstacles for the practitioner.

This present Acala Vidyārāja is the Great Bodhicitta of the Knowledge of All-Knowledge; one should know that this mind is of great power and ferocity, capable of eternally destroying all faults associated with the eyes and other faculties, thereby causing them to be forever severed—this is the meaning of "death."
As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*:

All of these are esoteric expressions.

As for what is called "the end of life," it means that all mental phenomena are forever severed and one enters the nature of non-arising dharmas; thus, within this state, one receives the prediction of Buddhahood from all Buddhas—it is not killing.
At that time, the various devas, seeing that the Lord of the Trichiliocosm had taken his own life because he did not comply with the samayas, were filled with awe and said to one another:

They immediately went together to the place where the Buddha was, and within the great maṇḍala, they obtained the benefit of the Dharma.

"By the power of this Great King, I have now received the prediction of attaining Buddhahood; you should know that he is truly the most honored among all Buddhas. Why is this so?

Maheśvara, the lord of the three thousandfold world system, is none other than the self-mind of sentient beings—namely, the ground of beginningless ignorance—which attains sovereignty over all delusions; it can be subdued by nothing except the great bodhicitta.
Having severed their life-force, one realizes the realm of tranquility.
That which is called "birth" is precisely the arising of the gateway to the Buddha-wisdom.
Therefore, the practitioner of the mantra path should contemplate the secret words of all Buddhas one by one.

These bodhisattvas are all the virtues of Vairocana Tathāgata’s internal realization; in order to widely open these gates of knowledge and vision, each bodhisattva expounds a single gate.

At that time, the Buddha—through the empowerment of the intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*) of those Vajradharas and Bodhisattvas who are inexhaustible—addressed the sons of good family, speaking these mantra-words for the purification of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) as they have been realized. However, since this equal dharma-realm has neither movement nor arrival, how could there be coming and going?

Therefore, it is next described as "the great among the great," which refers to the realization of the Great Middle Way (madhyama-mahā) through equality and non-obstruction; this Great Emptiness (mahā-śūnyatā) is the realm of the Buddha.
Now, this mantra takes the syllable *ha* as its essence; *ha* signifies joy (*hṛṣṭi*), which is what is meant by the "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) practiced by Bodhisattvas.

If sentient beings uphold, recite, or contemplate this Dharma-gate, they will enter the gate of Samantabhadra and, before long, attain the power of mastery in the Samādhi of the Adornment of the Buddha-realm.

Giving rise to great compassion that accords with the *dharmadhātu* and being able to universally bestow the bliss of the true Dharma upon all sentient beings—this is the gateway through which he enters.
Just as he himself has attained realization, he enters into *samādhi* and utters the mantra; therefore, it is said that "his own mind speaks."
The explanation of the meaning is as above.
*Aśvajña* means "the unconquerable. *Jña* means "victory," and *a* means "none" (*asarvasattva*), referring to all sentient beings.

That which is "born" refers to the phenomena of birth, old age, sickness, and death—the process of all cyclic existence. Yet, in its very essence, it is eternally non-arising; this is the meaning of the syllable *A*.
Because one knows that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is non-arising, all sentient beings thereby become unsurpassed, supreme, and peerless.

Furthermore, because they know that the essence of all phenomena is unarisen, they penetrate and discern the mental natures of all sentient beings; there is nothing they do not clearly perceive through their manifest awakening, and they bring to fruition whatever each being is capable of attaining according to their needs.
This is the supreme among forms of loving-kindness, bestowed universally upon sentient beings without end.
Therefore, if there are sentient beings who can thoroughly penetrate, receive, uphold, recite, and practice this Dharma, they will before long become equal to the conduct of Maitreya.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha entered the Samādhi of the Pure Realm and spoke from his own mind as follows: "To abide in this samādhi means to be able to know that the fundamental nature of one's own mind is pure, and to thoroughly comprehend such a realm of the pure Dharma-realm; this is precisely the secret treasury of the Great Emptiness."
Furthermore, this Ākāśagarbha is the Great Compassion Womb (Mahākaruṇā-garbha), which is able to nurture and bring to fruition the bodhicitta.

*Ā* is the meaning of space (*ākāśa*); *samanta* and so forth mean that all phenomena are equal to space. *Nujjota* means "thoroughly knowing. *Vicitra-vastra* refers to variegated garments; it signifies various wonderful manifest colors. *Va* is garment; *ra* is holding; *dha* is wearing. Thus, this Guṇākara is one who wears various garments. This mantra takes the syllable *ā* as its essence. *Ā* is the essence of primordial non-arising (*anādikāla-anutpanna*); here, this *ā* is in the second tone, which signifies emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Because they are fundamentally unborn, they are identical to space; thus, all phenomena are equal to space, and one should personally realize this understanding.
The "variegated-colored robe" refers to the Dharma-gate of being adorned with myriad virtues.
If a person can realize this samādhi of emptiness, they will be able to adorn their body with myriad virtues, just as one clearly perceives manifest colors within a pure void.
The remainder is to be understood according to what was previously explained.
At that time, when the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin enters the mantra of the Samādhi of the Power of Compassion (*karuṇā-bala-samādhi*), it is precisely the compassion of the *dharmatā*.

By the power of mastery, one is able to eliminate all obscurations and hindrances of all sentient beings; having attained mastery over these very obstacles, one is able to abide within them while simultaneously removing them—this is the great compassion of the Tathāgata.
The meanings of *ā* are "subduing" (*avaśa*) and "gathering and subduing. This is the essence of the mantra. The letter *A* is primordial non-arising (*anādikāla-anutpanna*).

The long vowel is the second syllable, which is the Vajra-samādhi; furthermore, by adding the bindu (the dot), it signifies the meaning of "subduing. *Sattva* refers to the benefit of many sentient beings. *Prajvalita* means "arousing" or "causing to arise. *Tara-tara*—the *ta* is the sense of suchness (*tathatā*); *ra* contains the letter *la*, which signifies "stainless," and by adding a dot, it becomes the letter *ma*, which is the realization of Great Emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*). Within *tara-tara*, the letter *ra* signifies "dustless," and by adding a dot, it is the realization of Great Emptiness. The meaning of this mantra is as follows: [Note: The provided text appears to be a commentary on the *Hṛdaya-mantra* (Heart Sūtra) mantra, specifically analyzing its phonetic components and their symbolic significance.]
Abiding in suchness, one employs this power of mastery to eliminate all veils and obscurations of dust and defilement, thereby realizing emptiness.
The emptiness within emptiness is the meaning of "Great Emptiness" (mahāśūnyatā).

This characteristic is subtle and difficult to eliminate; therefore, it is taught everywhere that one must break through ignorance through samādhi to purify the delusive characteristics inherent in its own substance. For this reason, it is stated repeatedly, and the two characters *lánlán* are further emphasized.

Furthermore, regarding the explanation of the characteristics: because of abiding in the syllable *Ṣa*, one is able to bring great benefit to all sentient beings, giving rise to this nature and removing all defilements.
If there are sentient beings who enter this gateway of mantras, they will before long become equal in virtue to those bodhisattvas.
When performing contemplation, one takes only the single character of the fundamental essence as primary; when reciting, one employs the full verbal expression.
This is precisely the seed-syllable (*bīja-akṣara*).
Furthermore, regarding the sequential explanation of all syllables: for instance, if the syllable *ma* (惡) comes first, each subsequent syllable is used to explain it in turn.
According to the aforementioned "gate of letters," that which is not all-pervasive cannot be called "universal.
Because one observes sentient beings with this universal eye, one is named Avalokiteśvara (the One Who Observes with Sovereign Freedom).
Having entered this samādhi, various rays of light issue forth from his heart, and within these rays appear the mantras of this Dharma-gate.

*Sarvatathāgata* refers to all Tathāgatas, meaning the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time. It is called the "Contemplation of All Tathāgatas" because it is identical to that which those Buddhas contemplate; it is thus the Contemplation of Equality and the Contemplation of the Universal Eye (*samantacakṣus*). *Kāruṇīmaya* means "having great compassion as its essence. Just as a golden statue is called a "golden person" because its very substance is pure gold, so too is this Bodhisattva, whose essence is purely great compassion. *Rara rara* signifies "dust" (*rajas*); by entering the gate of the letter *A*, it becomes free from dust.

The reason for the three layers is that they signify the removal of the defilements and obstructions of ordinary beings. HŪṂ signifies the sense of "terror"; through the power of great, fierce, and sovereign majesty, it terrifies those three layers of defilement and obstruction, causing them to be purified so that one attains identity with the Buddha-eye.
Ja: this final syllable is the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
All the other syllables serve to explain the meaning of this syllable; that is, "arising and non-arising" is the meaning of the syllable *ja*.
Alternatively, one may take the initial syllable *sa* as the essence and employ it in the same manner; this has the meaning of "awakening.
Within the syllable *hūṃ*, there is the syllable *ha*, which signifies "joy"; above it is the great dot (*bindu*) of emptiness, which represents *samādhi*, and below it is the stroke of *samādhi*.
In this context, the "lower" and "drawn" characters also refer to samādhi; it is the practice within these two samādhis.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time are identical in this contemplation, and therefore it is called "equal contemplation."
Mahāsthāmaprāpta also enters this samādhi, just as Avalokiteśvara does, because he is his retinue. The character *rán* (髯) carries the meaning of "arising.

There are two instances of it because the first refers to the arising of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and the second refers to the arising of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Entering the gateway of the letter *A* means that these two types of arising are, in their entirety, non-arising.
The dot above signifies the meaning of Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*), which refers to the arising of Great Emptiness upon the removal of the two obscurations.
The syllable *sa* is the essence of the seed-mantra; *sa* carries the meaning of immovability (*akṣobhya*).
The phenomena of immobility and movement are characterized by arising and ceasing; whatever phenomena arise and cease possess the marks of stability and movement.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Both moving and non-moving phenomena are all marks of instability."
The addition of two dots to the side is identical to *nirvāṇa*, which signifies the meaning of firm abiding.

Having already abandoned the two obstacles and being identical to the great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*), one firmly abides in this state just as all Buddhas abide; this is the stage of Great Power (*mahāsthāna*).

For example, when a person in the world holds a high official position, possesses great wealth and power, and intimidates many people, they are called a person of influence; this influence is precisely their position.
To say that one transcends two births and is equal to the birth of a Buddha is precisely the stage of the Tathāgata.
Because one attains this great rank and great power, one is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta (He Who Has Attained Great Power).
Next, the Honored One Tārā is also a retinue of Avalokiteśvara; the samādhi she enters is also as previously described.
*Karuṇā* has the meaning of "compassion" (*karuṇā*). What is called compassion is *tāpapha-ja*, which means that it arises from one who possesses compassion.
The Compassionate One is Avalokiteśvara; this Bodhisattva was born from the eyes of that Honored One.

To perceive the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is called the Universal Eye (*samantacakṣus*), which means seeing the essence of suchness (*tathatā*). He was born from this eye-samādhi. *Tāre*, *tāre*, *nitāre*—these have the meaning of "deliverance."

However, this mantra takes the initial letter *ta* as its essence; within the two instances of *ta*, the first character *ta* signifies *tathatā* (suchness), while the dot (*bindu*) beside it is the letter *a*, which represents the practice of suchness.
The syllable *ra* represents the sense objects (*viṣaya*). These six sense objects are themselves the great ocean of birth and death.
By contemplating this nature of suchness (*tathatā*), all afflictions (*kleśa*) are identical to suchness and fundamentally unarisen; this is the meaning of crossing the great ocean.
To be able to cross this great ocean of birth and death is precisely to attain liberation regarding all phenomena.

The repetition of the term is explained as "ultimate crossing" (Sanskrit: *atyanta-tāraṇa*) by Śakra and Brahmā; having attained liberation oneself, one further universally delivers all sentient beings, which is called "ultimate crossing."
If a person has not yet attained liberation for themselves yet attempts to liberate others, this is improper.
If one has liberated oneself and is also able to liberate others, such a thing is possible.

Furthermore, the letter *ta* is the very essence of the Tathāgata; by contemplating suchness (*tathatā*), one crosses the great ocean of worldly afflictions and attains the self-body of the Tathāgata.
As in the *Mahāvaipulya* [Sūtra], there are five hundred Tārās who all arise from the eyes of Avalokiteśvara; they are all the samādhis of Amitābha’s sisters.
Next, Bhṛkuṭī enters samādhi as previously described.

*Sarva-pāyāḥ* means all terrors; *tārasaṃni* is also terror; *hūṃ hūṃ* also has the meaning of terror; *sphoṭaya* means to destroy or harm. Regarding the breaking of obstacles, *svāhā*. The reason for repeating "terror" is that the former refers to having fear, while the latter refers to being fearless.
All sentient beings possess fear because they have not yet attained the state of fearlessness.

Yet, within this context, they give rise to indolence and arrogance, clinging to the self and exalting themselves; therefore, [the Bodhisattva] causes them to fear him, so as to lead them away from having fear and enable them to attain fearlessness.
It is repeated because, by causing fear of that [obstacle], it brings about freedom from fear.
"Destruction" (saṃhāra) refers precisely to the shattering of all obstructions.
Furthermore, this mantra takes the syllable *tara* as its essence, and all the other syllables serve to explain it.
"Mostly" (duō) represents *tathatā* (suchness).
"Luo" (*luó*) represents the dust (*rajas*), and the single dot in the corner represents *a*; *a* signifies action (*karma*).

The essence of all afflictions (*kleśa*) is identical to suchness; by means of this practice of suchness, one is able to subdue and destroy the banners of all views of birth-and-death, pride, and self-clinging. This is the meaning of "great subjugation."
Within the great assembly of the Buddha, at that time, various Vajrapāṇis manifested forms of great terror and subjugation, appearing as if there were no one capable of subduing them.

Then, from within the furrow on Avalokiteśvara’s forehead, this Bodhisattva appeared; in the West, the wrinkles on the forehead are called *bhrūkuṭi*, just as people today have wrinkles on their foreheads when they are angry.
This Bodhisattva manifested himself in the form of a great wrathful deity; at that time, all the Vajras were struck with fear and entered into the body of Vajragarbha.
Then, that Bhīṣmāntaka approached the presence of Vajragarbha, who was likewise seized by great terror and entered beneath the seat of the Tathāgata, saying: "May the Buddha protect me!"
Then the Buddha said to that Vijayā: "Sister! Stay!"
Then Vajrapāṇi, having immediately come to a halt, addressed the Buddha:
"I shall carry out whatever the Buddha commands.
At that time, the fear of all the Vajradharas was also dispelled, and they all rejoiced greatly, saying these words:
"It is most rare that this Great Compassionate One can manifest such great power and majesty.
We should inquire regarding the secret intent herein.
Next, he addressed the Bodhisattva of the Abode, ensuring that the original Sanskrit sounds were preserved.
*Tathāgata* means "Thus-Come One. *Viśaya* means "realm.
The realm of the Tathāgata is that which arises from suchness (*tathatā*) and *sambhava*. *Padma* refers to the white lotus; because she wears a garland of *padma* flowers, she is named *Mārīcī*.
This is it. This *liṅ* has the meaning of "place" and the meaning of "abiding. Furthermore, this mantra takes the initial syllable *taḥ* as its essence; that is to say, it is *tathatā* (Suchness).
Suchness is the realm of all Buddhas, and it is from that that I am now born.
That which is white is the bodhicitta; to abide in this bodhicitta is to abide in one's own dwelling place.
This bodhicitta arises from the realm of the Buddhas; it abides eternally herein and is able to give birth to all Buddhas.
This is the Mother of Avalokiteśvara, who is the presiding deity of the Lotus Family.
Next is Hayagrīva Bodhisattva.
*Hūṃ* signifies "to terrify"; *khāda* means "to devour," referring to the devouring of all obstacles.
This mantra takes the syllable *kha* as its essence; the syllable *kha* is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and the dot in the corner is the practice (*caryā*).
"Dā" has the meaning of "bestowing. That which is called emptiness is precisely the true mark of all phenomena (*dharmatā*).
By practicing this very path, one attains the fruit of the true mark, and furthermore, one constantly bestows it upon others.
Now, as for the term "consuming" (*cham-shi*), it means that by means of this practice of emptiness, one consumes all dharmas that can obstruct bodhi.
*Pañca* and *paṭha* refer to the three realms of desire, form, and formlessness.
*Ja* means "to arise.
When these two characters are combined, they signify the meaning of "conforming to destruction" (*saṃvarta*). *Sa-pu-ṭa* means "completely shattering until nothing remains.

This refers to using this practice of emptiness to destroy all phenomena so that none remain, with the exception of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), for everything else is an obstacle to Bodhi.
Because he has completely devoured and destroyed all [obstacles] until they are exhausted, he attains fierce majesty and great power.
This Bodhisattva is the Vidyārāja of the Lotus Family.
Next is the mantra of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva.
At that time, this bodhisattva enters the samādhi of the indestructible vajra-practice.
"Vajra" is the bodhicitta; this bodhicitta is itself indestructible, and proceeding by means of it is "vajra-practice."
HA HA HA. The upper character *ha* is the essence of the mantra.
*Ha* signifies "action," as well as "laughter" and "joy. Entering the gateway of the letter *a* means to depart from joy;
since joy is a phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing, the fact that there are three [instances of *ha*] corresponds to the practices of the Three Vehicles.
This bodhisattva benefits sentient beings through various Dharma gates.

*Sutanu-sū* means "good" (*su*) and "son" (*tanu*); thus, it refers to a "good son. It also carries the meaning of "pliancy" (*praśrabdhi*). Because he is truly able to practice this conduct that benefits sentient beings, he is a true son of the Buddha; born from a virtuous nature, he is therefore called a "good son."
Because they are born from the Buddha, they are called "sons of the Buddha.
These bodhisattvas are able to expound various practice-gates of the three vehicles to benefit sentient beings, as explained in detail in the *Daśacakra Sūtra*.

Next, Mañjuśrī enters the samādhi of the Buddha’s empowerment and supernatural power (*adhiṣṭhāna-rddhi*). This empowerment samādhi is as described at the beginning of the aforementioned *Vairocana Sūtra*.
*Hī hī* has the meaning of summoning; *kumāra-kā* means "youth," which signifies summoning [him] to recall his original vow. Furthermore, *ku* has the meaning of "to destroy."
Māra refers to the retinue of Māra, namely the four Māras.
This mantra takes the syllable *ma* as its essence; it signifies Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*), and by realizing this Great Emptiness, one destroys all Māras.

"Vimuktipathasthita" means that this youth is said to abide in the path of liberation, which is the liberation of all Buddhas, namely Great Nirvāṇa. "Samara samara" means "remember, remember. "Pratijñām" refers to the vow previously established. The meaning of this mantra is:
"Hī hī, O youth who abides in the path of liberation, remember the vow you previously established!"
All Buddhas attain Buddhahood through the Dharma-body and enter the secret essence of body, speech, and mind; among all those with minds, none can equal them.
Nevertheless, because they remember their original vows, they employ the power of mastery to return to the realm of birth and death to rescue and deliver sentient beings.
The meaning of this mantra is likewise: this youth has long since attained Buddhahood in the Dharma-body; therefore, he is requested to deliver sentient beings by recollecting his original vows.

By virtue of the original vow of this Bodhisattva, all who see, hear, touch, know, or even merely remember me shall attain definitive certainty in the three vehicles, and ultimately fulfill all their aspirations.

This Bodhisattva has long since attained Buddhahood, being known as the Tathāgata Samantadarśin or, alternatively, the Tathāgata Samantamukha; through the power of his great compassion and empowerment, he manifests in the form of a youth.
Next is the Vajra Invincible Samādhi.
Because there is nothing equal to it, it is called "Invincible.
Since one realizes the vajra-body of all Buddhas through this and is able to uphold the wisdom of all Buddhas, it is called "Vajradhara" (Holder of the Vajra).
"I take refuge in all the Vajras" means that "Vajra" is the wisdom-seal (*jñāna-mudrā*) of all Buddhas, which is another name for the Buddhas themselves.
*Caṇḍa* means extremely fierce.

The ultimate among evils; it refers to one whose manifested form is so violent and malevolent that there is none surpassing it, even to the point of devouring all the world until nothing remains—the ultimate among evils. Mahāluṣaṇa: this is the Great Wrathful One.

Among the most evil, he is moreover exceedingly wrathful; this refers to the Buddha’s foremost majesty and ferocity, who destroys the world and its very nests, causing all to enter the Dharma-realm and return to the Vajra-realm. *HŪṂ*—this is the essence of the mantra, meaning "without fear."

The syllable HA represents this practice: the upper dot is the Great Emptiness (mahāśūnyatā), and the stroke below is meditative concentration (samādhi). This so-called "Samādhi of the Practice of Great Emptiness" is an alternative name for the Great Vajra Samādhi.
This is because she is able to subdue all others, and there is none superior to her.
Next is the Vajra Mother, known as Māmakī.
*Mā* signifies "mother," and *māmakī* also carries the sense of "many"; she is thus the mother of all vajras, from whom the wisdom of all vajras arises.
*Taraṭa Taraṭa*. Here, the syllable *ta-ra* constitutes the essence. For the most part, it signifies *tathatā* (suchness);
*ra* signifies being free from dust and defilement; and *i* signifies *samādhi*. Thus, it is the *samādhi* of stainless *tathatā*, from which the wisdom of all *vajras* arises.
The syllable *Ṭha* is incomplete; it is a half-body. That its body is destroyed and not formed signifies death.
By means of this samādhi, one kills those who dwell in the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*), because the dwelling in ignorance has already been killed.

If *tathatā* (the ultimate truth) also carries the sense of "arising," it is because by thoroughly realizing suchness (*tathatā*), defilements and obscurations are purified, and one attains a supreme arising; therefore, it is the mother of all.
That which is born from the Invincible is the birth of all Vajras.
The Vajra is the Invincible One, and it is also that which gives birth to all Invincible Persons.
This birth from the Invincible is also called the birth from Amṛta.
Next is the Vajraśṛṅkhalā mantra:

*panta panta ya*. Regarding this syllable *va*, it is because there is the syllable *na* beneath it; by adding this syllable *na* above the *va*, that *na* is precisely the bindu of great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*).
If there is a dot above the binding [syllable], it is immediately the syllable *ṭa*, and it is not necessary to add *na*.
In this context, the syllable *phaṃ* serves as the heart-syllable; it carries the meaning of "binding," which is the Vajra-binding.
*Panta* has the meaning of "universal protection"; it refers to binding that [object] everywhere.
To bind that [object] everywhere is precisely to bind the essence of that *dharmadhātu*.
The single point signifies the meaning of pervading all places.
Having fully realized the vajra-nature of the dharmadhātu, one binds it so that it cannot be destroyed; this is the meaning of binding and protection.
*Mudra mudra* means "firmness.
Having already performed the vajra-binding, one binds it further upon itself to make it firm; *vajrotpāda* means "the arising of the vajra."
It arises from the Vajradhātu; that is, it is born from the vajra-wisdom of all Buddhas. *Sarvatrāpratihatā*: this means "unassailable by anyone."

Just as the substance of a vajra jewel cannot be harmed by anything, so too, when consciousness realizes this vajra nature, it becomes as firm and dense as a vajra bond; therefore, nothing can harm it.
The vajra-bind is itself the gapless *tathatā*. Next is the mantra for the Wrathful Moon Pressing the Vajra:
*HṚĪḤ*, with the syllable *hṛ* as its heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*).
*Hṛ* has the meaning of "gathering" and also the meaning of "invoking.
The presence of the syllable *ha* signifies "action," while the presence of the syllable *ra* signifies "freedom from dust and defilement. Adding the stroke [on top] signifies "samādhi."
When these two points are adjacent, they are identical to nirvāṇa; this is the full possession of the merits of all Buddhas, and may I likewise be so.
Next, the syllable *HŪṂ* has the meaning of "to terrify."

To swiftly fulfill these merits of all Buddhas, one employs the practice of the stainless samādhi of firm and powerful progress, which is identical to the path of nirvāṇa, thereby causing all demons of great terror to retreat and disperse.
*Bhaṇṭa* has the meaning of "reproaching"; it refers to reproaching all demonic obstacles (*māra-vighna*) so that they are extinguished and vanish. Next is the Vajrasūcī-mantra:
*Sarvadharma*, which means "all phenomena."
The syllable *sa* above serves as the seed-syllable (*bīja*). *Niṣpeṣaṇī* means "piercing. *Vajrasūcī* is the "vajra-needle. *Varadā* means "bestowing excellent vows.
The intended meaning is that the needle signifies sharp wisdom.
Piercing through with this wisdom, as sharp as a vajra-iron drill, there is no dharma that it does not penetrate.
When wisdom reaches the intent of the dharma-nature, this is the meaning of the "vajra needle," which refers to piercing through ignorance to reach the limit of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*).
Next, regarding the mantra of Sarvadhara-vajrin:

at that time, as many vajras as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields entered the Vajra Invincible Samādhi; they became indistinguishable from Vajrapāṇi himself, and from their own hearts they emitted inconceivable light, within which this mantra appeared.
One should know that the remaining retinues exist accordingly. HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ.
Taking the first syllable as the essence, this is also the Great Emptiness-Practice Samādhi.
This samādhi is the practitioner of the Great Vajra, the Unconquerable.
Because one enters this samādhi, it is called "Great Emptiness" (Mahāśūnyatā), the practice of samādhi.
The three syllables signify the meaning of "multitude"; since all sentient beings are spoken of as being many vajras, the three syllables are combined.
*Bantha bantha bantha hā*: the meaning of "obstructing" is the same as above.
I [the author] say that the repetition refers to the scolding of the three obstructions. *Danda danda ja* means "arising"; the dot above is Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*).
Having already shattered all obstacles, one shall attain birth in the Great Emptiness, which is the birth of all Buddhas.
The birth of Vajra-wisdom is the birth of the Dharmakāya of all Buddhas.
This is precisely the meaning of the passage in the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* concerning the birth of this "unborn body.

Next, those who faithfully follow the instructions recite this mantra; this refers to those who remain constantly by the side of the tutelary deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), receiving commands to come and go as required for whatever task is to be performed.

Furthermore, as with the aforementioned Vajras, one enters the Great Vajra Invincible Samādhi and recites the mantra; this mantra is to be employed by all the families who follow the instructions in common.
The syllable *he* at the beginning is the seed-syllable; it also carries the meaning of summoning. This *ha* represents conduct and joy, while the *e* within it represents samādhi.
"One who values the Way" refers to practicing the ultimate practice and speaking with ultimate composure.
*Kañjiraye* means "why not enter the subtle quickly?
This is the meaning of an exhortation.

Just as when a person issues a command, why do you delay this task instead of performing it quickly? *Ari-hana ari-hana*. To "hold" means to maintain the previously explained samādhi of Vajra-conduct.

The second layer explains that these words have the meaning of "guarding. Having grasped and firmly held [the practice], one guards it so as not to let it be lost, ensuring it is not seized or taken away by various obstacles, thereby causing the samādhi of Vajra-conduct to be swiftly accomplished. *Khāda khāda* has the meaning of "devouring."
It is said "to eat" because one consumes and utterly devours all afflictions until they are exhausted; thus it is stated again.

In my view, this refers to eating the afflictions both within and without the realm (*dhātu*); therefore, *pāripūri* is mentioned again, meaning "complete fulfillment," signifying that one has eaten them to the point of total satisfaction.
This means to fulfill all the sublime vows of the practitioner and cause them to be satisfied.
The first vow is the Vajracaryā-samaya; *sarvākāraṃ svabhūtiṃ* (with the long vowel in *svabhūtiṃ*) refers to the original vow that was established.
One should fulfill them in accordance with the vows previously established by those [beings].

The preceding phrase speaks of "fulfillment," while this subsequent phrase speaks of "the vows originally established"; these are connected and are to be employed for the messengers of all three families.
Next, Śākyamuni Tathāgata entered the *ratnasthiti-samādhi*.
Jewels emerged from that state, hence it is named "Jewel-Abode" (*ratnasthiti*).
It is like the great ocean, which produces all kinds of jewels; once one reaches that island, whatever one requires according to one's wishes is there in no shortage.
After the Buddha had entered this samādhi, various kinds of light issued forth from his face; within these lights, this mantra appeared, pervading all buddha-fields.
One should know that all other mantras are explained in this same manner.

*Sarvakleśān* means "all afflictions"; *niḥsūdana* means "to subdue. Combined with the preceding phrase, it means "to subdue all afflictions. *Sarvadharmavaśitāprāpta* means "attained mastery over all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*). Combined with the preceding phrase, it means "having attained mastery within all phenomena," for by removing all obstacles, one attains mastery. *Gagana* means "space. Within *sama*, there is the sound *a*; *sama-sama* means "without equal," which is to say, "equal to space."
This practice is equal to emptiness, boundless, and pure; it is sovereign and unimpeded in all respects.
It is identical to names.
In the following phrase, its connection with the letter *a* signifies that it is without equal.

Those who are "unequal" are the followers of the Two Vehicles; they are called "unequal" because they possess deficiencies. This is the intent behind the employment of provisional means (*upāya*). Nevertheless, this mantra has the initial syllable *saṃ* as its essence.
The syllable *sa* signifies both "outflow" (*āsrava*) and "solidity. Entering the gateway of the letter *a*, there is neither outflow nor solidity.
If there were solidity, it would be a phenomenon subject to arising, ceasing, decay, and destruction.

If one causes it to be identical with the letter A, this solidity is primordially unarisen; thus, within all phenomena, one attains mastery equal to space and becomes able to serve as an island of jewels for all.

I maintain that Śākyamuni, by the power of his great compassion, enabled even those whose bodies were as dense and compact as vajra-candālī to shatter their views and enter the Buddha-dharma, bestowing upon them the vow for the Great Jewel.
Is it not that by attaining mastery over all phenomena, one is able to shatter all that is most solid?
Next is the Mantra of the Heroic Mark; this is the adornment accomplished through the immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata.
This is an accumulation of merit; therefore, she manifests in the form of a woman of Samādhi.
She is a member of Śākyamuni’s retinue, and having likewise entered the Jewel-Abode Samādhi, she has spoken this mantra.

Varadā means "granting wishes"; it is able to grant the wishes of all sentient beings. Varapradā means "obtaining wishes," which refers to the attainment of those wishes; it is like a person who possesses jewels and is thus able to give them to others.
"By my own accomplishment of this vow, I am able to bestow [blessings] upon others with mastery, causing them all to be fully satisfied, HŪṂ. This *citta* is the seed-syllable.

The syllable HA represents the practice identical to Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*). Below it is the syllable U, which is *samādhi*; the nasal dot (*bindu*) above is the *samādhi* of the practice of Great Emptiness.
Because one attains the place of the precious treasure by advancing through this practice, one is able to freely grant others the fulfillment of their wishes.

Next, regarding "the crown of all Buddhas": the crown of all Buddhas refers to the crowns of as many Buddhas as there are atoms in ten Buddha-fields. "Crown" carries the meaning of being supreme and preeminent; it is situated at the very top of the body.
This is an alternative name for the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*).

This form of the deity is identical to that of Śākyamuni, fully endowed with the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*), with the sole distinction being that the topknot within the crown is fashioned in the style of a Bodhisattva’s hair-knot.
Furthermore, abiding in the Jewel-Abode Samādhi, he spoke this mantra: *Vam*.

The first character, *Vam* (pronounced with a retroflex *ṇ*), serves as the seed syllable; it carries the meaning of "bondage. Entering the gateway of the letter *A* signifies the meaning of "freedom from bondage."
Furthermore, "bondage" (bandha) signifies the severance of the path of language; it is like the dot placed above a letter, which is identical to the great void (mahāśūnya).
Because [the practitioner] has already accomplished [this] and must cause it to be fully accomplished, it is stated three times.
"Hūṃ" signifies the meaning of terror; by means of its majestic and fierce power, it universally shatters all bonds, making them identical with the great void.
"Phaṭ" signifies the meaning of non-arising; because the body is destroyed so as not to allow for further arising, one must inevitably die.

This means that by shattering all phenomena so that nothing remains unpenetrated, one causes them all never to arise again; being identical to the great emptiness and the liberation of all Buddhas, one thereby enters the pinnacle of the Buddha’s unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
Next is the Mantra of Aparājita.
He is a member of Śākyamuni’s retinue and likewise entered the Jewel-Abode Samādhi, reciting the mantra as described above.

This is an emanation of Śākyamuni who, concealing his immeasurable and sovereign supernatural powers, manifests in the form of this wrathful Vidyārāja in order to subdue sentient beings and exhaust all obstacles.
*Ḍhī ḍhī*: take the first syllable as the body [of the mantra], and use the first syllable *ḍhī* as the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
*Da* signifies the meaning of the *dharmadhātu*.

*Ra* signifies the meaning of the various defilements that constitute dust-obstructions; if one enters the gateway of the syllable *a*, there are no dust-obstructions, which is precisely the *dharmadhātu*.
One should know that because it is identical to the *dharmadhātu*, where else could there be any dust?
This is the meaning of "Great Emptiness" (*mahāśūnyatā*).
If a person abides in this samādhi, then all veils and hindrances will be destroyed without exception.
To speak of it again is the meaning of utterly destroying the veil of dust.
Therefore, one speaks of the *arajasa-samādhi*, which is the so-called gateway of the syllable *laṃ*.
Next, one speaks of the syllable *ra-laṃ* (a conjunct) as being this samādhi; that is, the non-arising of all obstructions and the attainment of the arising of great emptiness.

These seed-syllables are adorned with various forms of concentration and wisdom; therefore, one can attain mastery within the cycle of birth and death and, sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, destroy the armies of the four māras.
"Invincible" (Ajita) means that there is nothing which cannot be destroyed.
Next is the consort Ajitā, who takes the form of a woman.
It is taught that by reciting this mantra, one enters samādhi, as previously described.

*Abhirati-śrī* means "invincible. *Jayantī* is another name for it, which carries the meaning of "victory in battle" and the sense of "being able to subjugate others. *Vaijayantī* signifies the completion of the act of crushing and subduing.
In this context, the syllable *ṭa* signifies "battle.

When the Buddha sat at the site of enlightenment, he engaged in battle with the four māras through the power of this samādhi and attained great might, such that none could cause him harm; this was due to the power of this samādhi.
The third syllable serves as the seed for the next, the mantra of the Earth Deity (Pṛthivī).
Since the earth can sustain all things, and all things depend upon it to grow and flourish, one should know that this is none other than the Buddha-mind.
Just as the Tathāgata’s mind can sustain all things, he entered deeply into the Samādhi of Sustaining the Root and spoke this mantra.
This, too, is merely a skillful means and an emanation-body of Śākyamuni.
*Pṛthivī* is the name of the Earth Goddess; one should employ that very name as a mantra.
If a person recites and practices it, they will before long also attain the mind-ground of the Tathāgata.
Taking the third syllable of the mantra as the seed-syllable signifies the meaning of being beyond verbal expression.
Within it lies the sound "I," which is samādhi; by entering this samādhi that transcends names and words, one realizes the ground of the mind.
This samādhi is named "Universal Support" (Pūrvacara), because as a samādhi it is identical to the great earth.
The final syllable *vye* has the meaning of "binding. *Jana* means "place."
The term "Ī" is a sound used to point to an object; it refers directly to the essence of that mantra.

Because of this samādhi of the mind-ground which transcends words, one proceeds upon the vehicle of liberation (vaimukhya-yāna). Next, Viṣṇu has many alternative names, which are specifically names for Nārāyaṇa.
This is an emanation of the Buddha; the samādhi is the same as before.
Viṣṇu-fei (毘瑟紐) is formed by taking his original name as the mantra, using the first syllable as the seed-syllable.
"Vi" has the meaning of "emptiness," and "śnu" has the meaning of "advancing" or "arising"; thus, one advances by means of emptiness.
This refers to how this deity rides upon a garuḍa bird and travels through the air.
I maintain that Śākyamuni, among the five classes of Buddhas, rides upon a *garuḍa*; this is precisely the meaning of "advancing through space.

Next is Rudra, who is also an emanation of a Buddha; he is an emanation of Maheśvara, also named Īśāna Rudra. His original name itself serves as the mantra, with the syllable *ru* as its heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*).
*Dhara* has the meaning of "bestowing" (*anupradāna*), as if one who already possesses much is able to bestow it upon others.
What is referred to as the various *yānas*; *yāna* is the meaning of the character *ji* (已).
Having personally realized such a precious vehicle, one is able to bestow it universally upon all sentient beings.
"Lu" refers to the samādhi free from dust and defilement; having attained this samādhi oneself, one further bestows it upon others.
Next is the mantra of the Wind Deity.
He is also an emanation of the Buddha; his samādhi is as described previously.
*Vāyo vāya*. This takes the deity's own name as the mantra, with the syllable *vā* as its essence.
*Vai* has the meaning of "bondage. Entering the gateway of the syllable *a* signifies the absence of bondage, which is liberation (*mokṣa*).
The dot (*bindu*) beside the syllable *a* signifies "conduct" (*caryā*).
The third syllable, *Vai*, signifies the meaning of ineffability; furthermore, adding the syllable *I* constitutes the *samaya*.
These various vehicles deliver all beings by means of the unimpeded vehicle.
Next is the Heaven of Beautiful Sound (Sudharmā).
These gods excel in chanting beautiful songs; they differ slightly from the gandharvas, who are musicians.
"Sarasvatī" is the name for Beautiful Sound. It takes the initial syllable *sa* as its essence, which carries the meaning of "firmness."

If there were anything that remained firm, it would possess the characteristics of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing; however, by entering the letter A, which is fundamentally without firmness, there is neither formation nor destruction.
All other letters serve to explain this point.

I say that by means of this wondrous voice one delights sentient beings; that one’s speech is gentle and pleasing, causing the hearts of the multitude to rejoice, means that one explains the lack of solidity so they may know impermanence, thereby verifying the attainment of the Tathāgata’s firm Dharma.
Next is Nīti, the lord of the rākṣasas, who is also an emanation of the Buddha.
*Rākṣasa* means "eater. *Sa* has the meaning of "firmness."
All [of these] have the sense of being able to devour; they constantly devour sentient beings.
The Tathāgata is likewise: he is able to consume all sentient beings who possess the obscurations of dust, never reaching satiety.
Regarding *dhipatiye*: the syllable *dhi* contains the sound *dhā*, which is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Adding *i* constitutes the samādhi, namely the "Dharma-realm Samādhi.
*Pati* means "to abide"; abiding in this Dharma-realm Samādhi is called "Sublime Abiding" (*supratiṣṭhita*).
To contemplate all defilements and obstructions as being the *dharmadhātu* is the meaning of entering the *dharmadhātu*, which is the sense of devouring and taking them into one's belly.
The final syllable *ye* represents the vehicle (*yāna*); this vehicle is unsurpassed in its swiftness.
The seed-syllable of the essence of the *dhātu*-gate.
Next is the mantra of King Yama;
this, too, is an emanation of the Buddha.
*Vibhatsava* (Vibhasvata) is also a mantra by its original name.

Taking the first syllable as its essence, it is further explained as the "Samādhi of Non-Bondage. *Vi-bha* signifies firm abiding, and it also means the removal of all bonds; that is to say, removing bonds through principle rather than through what is not the Dharma.
Within the syllable *ṭva* there are many sounds, which are suchness (*tathatā*); the syllable *sa* carries the meaning of firmness.
The syllable *ya* is the vehicle; by mounting this vehicle of suchness one advances toward practice. The dot of the syllable *a* situated to its side is practice itself.
To proceed while abiding in the suchness (*tathatā*) of the vehicle is itself the attainment of perfect enlightenment.
Next is the mantra of birth and death.
This is the Vidyārāja Yama; it is also recited according to one’s realization for the sake of accomplishing the Maṇḍala of the Arising of Great Compassion.
"Mr̥tyu" (pronounced with the *mr̥* and *tyu* combined) signifies death.
Death has the meaning of killing and severing; its fundamental nature is termed "killing. Based on the original intention:

"I shall sever the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) of all sentient beings"—wherein the life-faculty is precisely the beginningless ignorance and various afflictions (*kleśa*)—to sever these for all sentient beings so that they are exhausted without remainder is what constitutes killing.
This clarifies that one attains mastery over the dharma-gate of death; it is a manifestation produced by the Buddha, not the actual killing of all sentient beings.
The initial syllable *ma* serves as the seed-syllable.
Next is the mantra of the Night Goddess (Rātridevatā). She is the consort of Yama.

*Kāpilālī* (the initial *kā* is drawn out) means "Black" (*kṛṣṇa*). *Tirye* means "night. This mantra is taught because the syllable *kā* serves as its essence; since there is much terror and various afflictions within the darkness of night, this mantra is spoken in order to eliminate the fears, obscurations, defilements, and so forth of the long night within the darkness of ignorance.
Next are the Seven Mothers of King Yama.
There are seven sisters, and according to other scriptures, these Seven Mothers all employ their original names as mantras.
Herein, the general mantra is set forth as follows.

*Matri-piya*. *Matri* has the sense of "equal" (*sama*), which signifies "not one, but many," referring here to the seven sisters and so forth. Taking the initial syllable *ma* as the seed-syllable (*bīja*) signifies the meaning of "non-self" (*anātman*).
Next is Śakra-devānām-indra.
"Śakrāya" is his name; "Śakra" signifies "one of a hundred merits.

Because he cultivated merit one hundred times during his causal stage—specifically by performing a great, unrestricted *pūjā* assembly (*mahā-amogha-dāna*) one hundred times to universally bestow gifts upon sentient beings—he attained this superior birth.
The first syllable of the name is taken as the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and it is based on this that the name was established.
This signifies "stopping" (*śama*), meaning to bring all obstacles to rest.
Once the obstacles have been stilled, one's merit increases; *kāra* signifies "increasing" or "progressing."
Furthermore, the entry into *śamatha* is itself *śamatha*.
