Because one constantly benefits all devas with profound words, the mind constitutes the mantra.
It is also born through the Buddha’s transformative power.
Next is the mantra of the Nāga King Varuṇa.
He is a nāga of the great ocean, and all nāga kings share this same mantra.
*Āp* (the retroflex *ph* is pronounced as *f*) means "water"; *pati* means "lord. Because he attains mastery over the waters, he is named the Lord of Water (*Varuṇa*).
The initial syllable *A* serves as the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
Next is the Brahmā-mantra;
for the purpose of accomplishing that Matrix of Great Compassion (*Mahākaruṇā-garbha*), it is also as described above.
*Puraja* means "all beings" (*sarvasattva*); *īśvara* means "lord. Thus, he is the Lord of all beings.
Because all sentient beings originate from Brahmā, he is called the Lord of all beings, for he is able to produce all sentient beings.
The syllable *pra* serves as the seed-syllable (*bīja*).

*Pra* signifies the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), while *ra* signifies obscurations and defilements. Within the ultimate truth, there is neither obstruction nor non-obstruction; all noble ones (*ārya*) arise from this, and thus it is the Lord of Birth (*janmin*).
This is also a transformation body of the Buddha.
It is the mantra of the Heavenly Son for the following day:
*A-bha-va-sva-bhā-vā-t-ma-yo-h*. Here, the initial letter *A* serves as the seed syllable, which signifies "primordial non-arising."
To personally realize this principle and transmit it to others is precisely the meaning of constantly benefiting sentient beings, just like that sun.
The people of the world say that the sun constantly benefits sentient beings.
Next is the mantra of Candramas-tathāgata.
"Candra" is the name for the moon; it takes the first syllable as its essence.
If one does not die, then one likewise does not arise [in rebirth].
That which is neither born nor dies is called "ambrosia" (amṛta).
Because the moon can eliminate the feverish afflictions of poison, worldly people regard it as being like ambrosia;
therefore, they have given it this name.
Among all the flavors of ambrosia (*amṛta*), none surpasses the Samādhi of the Pure Moon.
Next are the mantras of the various nāgas.
The preceding [mantra] was for the Nāga Kings; this one is for all nāgas and is universally applicable.
*Me-ka-yun-ya-shan-ni* means "eating clouds. This is explained as "consuming the clouds.
These are the darknesses, which are the defilements and obstructions of all sentient beings.
Because he can consume all such obstructions and thereby attain mastery, this is used as his name.
Taking the initial syllable *mi* as its essence, it signifies "I," yet there is no self.
Next is the mantra of the two gate-keeping nāga kings, Nanda and Upananda.
It is difficult to take only the initial character of the name *Nanda* as its essential body;

this is the meaning of "contemplation" (*guan*). That is, having contemplated and transcended contemplation, one abides in the Middle Way; having attained self-illumination, one benefits sentient beings. As for the sound and force of the characters *Na*, *Da*, *Yu*, and *Ba*: the character *U* (in *Upa*) signifies "transcending. One transcends all phenomena and the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), abiding in the most supreme state, and thereby protects and sustains the world; thus, this is how the name is formed.
The above concludes the retinue of Śākyamuni.

They all abide in the *ratisthita-samādhi* (Treasure-Abiding Samādhi) and, through the emanations of the Buddha, they proclaim mantras for the sake of accomplishing the Great Compassion Treasury (*mahākaruṇā-garbha*).

Regarding the statement that "at that time, Vairocana Buddha himself taught the Mantra Consort, the Mother of all Bodhisattvas, for the sake of the joy of the *asādhya-siddhi* (unfailing accomplishment) of his own teaching-tradition": "his own teaching-tradition" refers to the teaching of the Dharma-Buddha’s self-realization, which is the secret teaching of equality.
In this regard, all those who practice are entirely not empty; "not empty" carries the meaning of being not in vain.
According to their respective capacities, they all tend toward the principle of the Dharmakāya and are thus identical to those Buddhas; therefore, it is said to be "not empty."
As the aforementioned Bodhisattvas have each spoken mantras, desiring to attract practitioners of a similar kind so that if they practice, they will be identical to me;
now the Dharma-Buddha himself explains the mantra of the Consort. If there are practitioners, they shall arise from the Eye of Space as the Dharmakāya, no different from me.
Gaganā takes its first syllable as the heart-mantra. *Ga* signifies the meaning of being without coming or going.
Furthermore, *gaganā* is emptiness, namely the Great Emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*) of all Buddhas. *Pra* is aspiration; *lakṣa* is characteristic; and *nu* is Great Emptiness.
This vow is supreme; it is identical to space, characterized by a single mark, pure, and boundless, and is thus beyond conceptual differentiation—*gagaṇa-śūnyam*, *samam*, etc.
As stated above, these great vows have the characteristic of space; they are equal to space. *Svabhāva* means "in all places," and *anupama* means "beyond compare.
This signifies that these empty vows of space pervade all places, and there is nothing whatsoever that can be compared to them as an equal.

Above the heart is the syllable *A*, connected to *Vijaya* (Victory), which is indestructible (*abhedyam*). From this arises *Jvalara*, meaning "resplendent light. Thus, it is that which is produced from the indestructible.
By abiding in the practice that is neither departing nor arriving, one achieves great majestic radiance beyond compare;

*namo*, I take refuge. Because one abides in this Dharma, I take refuge; *amoghaṃ*, the non-empty. That which is taken as refuge—I take refuge in the head of mantras, taking refuge in all Buddhas universally. This is because the name "all" itself is already universal.
If one were to point to all Buddhas in the eastern direction alone, they would not encompass those of the ten directions.
To distinguish this limited "all" from the universal, it is said that [the light] pervades all Buddhas.
He has set this aside.
The *Ākāśanetra*, the Mother of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, is hereby concluded.
At that time, for the sake of pacifying all obstructors, the Buddha further entered the samādhi named "Fire-Arising" and proclaimed this Great Mantra for Subduing Obstructors.

This possesses majestic power capable of removing all manner of obstacles and difficulties for those who practice true mantras; even when the Buddha was at the Tree of Enlightenment, it was by means of this mantra that all the demonic armies were dispersed and destroyed—how much more so, then, the various obstacles of the mundane world!
Furthermore, these hindrances are briefly of two types:
first, internal hindrances, which arise from one's own mind and are so numerous that they cannot be described in detail;
second, external hindrances, which arise from external matters and are likewise very many.
All [these] can be utterly destroyed. *Canda* means extremely evil;

it refers to that which is even more violent than the most violent evils. *Mahā-ruṣṇa* means great wrath. *Sphoṭaya* means to shatter. *Hūṃ* signifies terror. *Tarakā* means firmness. *Haṃ Phaṭ*—the latter two syllables serve as the seed-mantra (*bīja*), through which all the meanings of these phrases are accomplished.
Regarding "initially battling *ca*": "battle" (*yuddha*) carries the meaning of death; entering the *a*-gate signifies that, fundamentally, there is neither birth nor death.
*Ca* carries the meaning of "battle"; by means of this sovereign of the great power of no-birth-and-death, one battles against the four māras.
Next, *ma* has the meaning of "self"; entering the gate of the syllable *a*, there is no-self, which is also emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
*Ha* has the meaning of "joy" and is also "practice.
Regarding *lu-se*: the presence of the syllable *ra* signifies defilement and obstruction; the presence of the sound *u* signifies *samādhi*, which is precisely what is called *śamatha*.
*Na* signifies emptiness; the fifth syllable is the Great Emptiness Samādhi (*mahā-śūnyatā-samādhi*).
*Sa* signifies firmness, and *pha* signifies phenomena (*dharma*), for one thoroughly understands that the world is like a mass of foam and is thus easily broken and destroyed.
Beside it is the dot of the letter A, which signifies "action" (karma).
*Ṭha* has the meaning of "struggle"; it is able to oppose obstacles and fears so as to shatter them.
It also has the meaning of "vehicle" (yāna).
HŪṂ is the samādhi of the Great Space-farer, as explained above.
*Tat* is suchness (*tathatā*); *ra* is stainlessness; *ka* is "to act," meaning that all phenomena are without action (*akṛta*).
The syllable *haṃ* signifies "action" (*kriyā*). Furthermore, there is the sound *a*, which represents the Vajra-samādhi that terrifies demonic obstacles.
The nasal dot (*bindu*) is the Great Emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*); by means of this Great Emptiness, which moves through immobility, one greatly terrifies all demonic obstacles.
The syllable *vaṃ* signifies "self" (*ātman*); by entering the gate of the syllable *a*, there is no self.
Furthermore, one uses this samādhi of the great emptiness of non-self to terrify all Māras; for this syllable also contains the sound of *a* along with the bindu.
The four syllables *hā lu haṃ ca* all contain the sound *a*, which signifies the repeated terrifying of Māras and the extreme subduing of both internal and external obstacles.
This concludes the mantra of the Honored One Acala.
Next is the mantra of Trailokyavijaya Vidyārāja.
All of these were produced by Vairocana Tathāgata while abiding in the Samādhi of Observing the Support of the High Peak of the Dharma Banner, as explained in the first "Introductory Chapter."

The Tathāgata has taught that these two vidyās are both the samādhi of the Dharma-Buddha; they are intended to cause practitioners, from their initial generation of the bodhicitta, to guard, increase, and bring to fruition the attainment of the Buddha-fruit, ensuring they never regress or fall into heterodox paths. This is none other than Acala Vidyārāja.
In order to subdue those sentient beings in the world who are difficult to tame, he is none other than the Vidyārāja Trailokyavijaya.
This shall now be explained in sequence.
As for "the three worlds" (trailokya), "world" refers to greed, hatred, and delusion; to subdue these three poisons is called "subduing the three worlds."
Furthermore, because of past greed, one now receives this body as the retribution for that greed; subsequently, one generates greedy karma and undergoes future retribution.
This applies to all three poisons, and thus it is called Trailokyavijaya (Conqueror of the Three Worlds).

Furthermore, the three periods of time are called the three realms. This refers to the Tathāgata Vairocana, who, beginning from the Summit of Existence (*bhavāgra*) down to the lower planes, sequentially transformed each celestial abode from above downward, manifesting immeasurable retinues and great lords of the heavens.
Now he surpasses those gods by hundreds of thousands of millions of times; they have never experienced such terror. "What other sentient being could possibly surpass me?
Thinking thus, [the Buddha] eventually subdued him through the Dharma, and he descended step by step.
Because he is able to subjugate the lords of the three worlds, he is named the Vidyārāja Trailokyavijaya.
"Ha ha ha ha" signifies practice and signifies joy.
These three practices are precisely the practices of those who follow the three vehicles.

These modes of conduct—these three modes of conduct—are from the very beginning unborn; because they are unborn from the beginning, they transcend these three modes of conduct, and this is the conduct of the Buddha. *Viṣamaye*: this means "how marvelous! or "how extraordinary!"

As the Buddha has constantly taught: one counteracts hatred with loving-kindness, greed with non-greed, and false views with right view. Now, however, to eliminate hatred by means of great wrath, and to eliminate all greed by means of great greed—this is most difficult to understand and difficult to believe; therefore, it is said, "How strange! *Sarvatathāgata* refers to all Buddhas; *viṣaya* refers to the realm; *sambhava* refers to arising. That is to say, it arises from the realm of all Buddhas.
The "Buddha-realm" refers to the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.

Because he arises from this true nature, he is titled Trailokyavijaya. *Trailokya* means the three times (the three worlds); *vijaya* signifies victory over them; *hūṃ* has the same meaning as explained above; and *jaḥ* signifies summoning and awakening.

If one recites this, it can enter the minds of all sentient beings universally and awaken them so that their obstructions are exhausted, becoming equal to a Buddha of the Dharmakāya. Furthermore, this mantra takes the syllable *ḍre* as its essence; the multiple sounds above it signify the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness).
*Ra* represents defilement and obstruction.

The presence of the sound *i* signifies samādhi; because the essence of suchness (*tathatā*) is fundamentally unarisen, and because it is unarisen, even these defilements and obstructions are themselves fundamentally unarisen.
By practicing in accordance with this principle, one becomes fully endowed with both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), and is thus able to subdue the three periods of time.
Next is the mantra of the Śrāvaka:

*Hedu* (cause), *pratītya* (condition), *abhijātāḥ* (born), *karma* (action), *niścitāḥ* (determined), *hūṃ* (fearful obstacle). The general explanation states: "Born apart from causes and conditions."
Birth arises from karma; thus, freedom from birth arises from freedom from karma.
The initial *he* sound signifies "conditioned formations" (*saṃskāra*) and "joy," which refers to the practice of the Śrāvaka.
The *i* sound of *samādhi* refers to the meditative concentration of the Śrāvaka. Next, the syllable *du* has many sounds, which refers to the *tathatā* (suchness) entered by the Śrāvaka.

Furthermore, there is the sound "U," which is the samādhi; next, the sound "Pa" refers to the ultimate truth (paramārtha) perceived by the śrāvakas. Next, the letter "Ra" refers to the six sense objects (ṣaḍviṣaya) confronted by the Hīnayāna. The syllable "Ti" has the meaning of "vehicle" (yāna), which is precisely the meaning of the vehicle ridden by the śrāvakas. The syllable "Vi" contains the sound "Va," which signifies "bondage" (bandha).
The sound "i" refers to samādhi; "ke-ta-li" and the remainder are to be explained extensively by analogy.
The meaning of "fearing obstacles" is as previously stated, with the only difference being that this pertains to the practice of the śrāvakas.
This is the power of the great compassionate vow of the Dharma-Buddha; for the benefit of sentient beings, he manifests within samādhi the mantras of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
If there are sentient beings who should enter the Way by means of this dharma, he causes them to enter the Treasury of Great Compassion through this gate.
Next is the mantra of the Pratyekabuddha.
*Va* signifies the severance of the path of speech; it refers to the aforementioned realization by the Pratyekabuddha of the ultimate realm beyond verbal expression.
Having attained realization from within this, one further benefits sentient beings by means of this Dharma.
Having personally mastered it, one likewise benefits others through this Dharma, as previously described for the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, who take the phrasing of the Dharma as their mantra.
Now, as for the single syllable, this is the essential core of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Because it is the dwelling place where that ultimate practice is realized, a single syllable is employed.
Next are the heart-mantras (*hṛdaya-mantra*) of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

*Sarvabuddha* means all Buddhas; *bodhisattva* means a bodhisattva; *hṛdaya* means heart; *praveśaya* means "enter. This is the general explanation: it means "enter the hearts of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. *Namaḥ* means "homage"; *sarvavidhe* means "granting the boon," which refers to granting the boon of the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
*Sat* has the meaning of "solidity," yet it is that which can leave behind all solidities; it leaves behind what is not solid. *Upara* means "stain" (*rajas*), and *va* below means "bondage.
*Vi* signifies the severance of the path of speech, and it also refers to *samādhi*.
"Looking at this, it has the meaning of 'bestowing.
The sound *iti* refers to samādhi.
Because one is already self-sufficient, one then bestows it upon others."
Because one has personally attained the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), one is able to bestow this vow upon others.
This is precisely the heart-mind of all Buddhas.
The syllable *Ī* (formed by the combination of two characters) serves as its seed-syllable.

This is connected with the syllable *ā* in the preceding phrase; it is precisely this syllable *ā* that serves as the seed-syllable (*bīja*), which signifies the meaning of "primordially unborn" (*mūla-anutpanna*).
Next are the heart-mantras (*hṛdaya-mantra*) of Viśvadeva and the other deities.
*Lo-ka-lo-ka* means "the world," which carries the sense of darkness— that is, ignorance (*avidyā*). On the side of each of these characters,
there is the sound *a*, which signifies "primordial non-existence" (*mūla-abhāva*).
The absence of darkness is true illumination.
*Aruka* is the illuminator, which is *kāra*, meaning "to act";
that is to say, it has the sense of "shining."
It is the creation of light, by means of the signs of light.
Manifesting these bodies of the eight classes of beings and others universally, it dispels their darkness and causes them to engage in luminous conduct.

It creates this light to illuminate the world. *Sarva-deva* (all gods), *nāga*, *yakṣa*, *gandharva*, *asura*, *kinnara*, *mahoraga*, and so forth—these various classes are gathered. *Hr̥daya* (heart), *japa* (recitation), *kāya* (body), and *grahaṇa* (seizing). (Note: The Sanskrit terms provided in the source text have been transliterated using IAST diacritics as requested.)
This refers to causing the eight classes [of spirits] and others to act with a focused mind; "Vicitrā-kṛti" means various activities.
It also carries the sense of "skillful form," meaning the manifestation of all desirable bodies according to the specific type [of being], which is termed "skillful form."

It also carries the meaning of "variegated colors," for by means of various practices and various variegated dharma-gates, it dispels the darkness of the world; thus, it signifies that which is peerless among all illuminations. Its seed syllable is the initial letter *Lu*.
Next are the mantras of all Buddhas: *Sarvatathāgata-vimati-cchedana-dharmadhātu*. *Sarva* means "all. *Vimati* means "lack of wisdom";

because of this lack of wisdom, it is termed "doubt," and this term is correctly explained as doubt. *Cchedana* means "removal"; just as a person discards filth, this is called "removal" or "discarding. *Dharmadhātu* refers to the "Dharma-realm."
This means that by eliminating all lack of wisdom, one causes all beings to abide in the *dharmadhātu*; "Nirja" refers to birth.

This syllable "Ni" is the Great Emptiness Samādhi (*mahāśūnyatā-samādhi*); that which arises from this is "birth from the *dharmadhātu*. The three syllables "Saṃ Saṃ Ha" are all seed-syllables (*bīja*).
*Sat* has the meaning of "firmness," just as removing this firmness constitutes the most supreme birth.
*Bindu* (the dot) signifies entering into samādhi;
it is like the entry into nirvāṇa by the followers of the Two Vehicles—this is precisely the meaning of firmness.
Furthermore, if there were anything solid, it would be a characteristic of arising and abiding.
All moving phenomena are inherently unstable; by utterly eliminating them, one realizes the meaning of the profound samādhi of emptiness.
"Hā" is this very practice, namely the mantra for guarding the sequence of the Tathāgata’s conduct.

It is "untransgressible" (*avilanghya*), which carries the sense of being difficult to maintain—that is, the meaning of being upheld by power—and it is also unobservable through mere observation. Furthermore, it has the sense of being difficult to subdue; those who respectfully follow the Buddha’s teachings always remain on the right side of the inner gate, and are thus called "Untransgressible Messengers" (*Avinivartanīya-dūta*). No one may overstep the power of the Buddhas’ *samaya*.
One receives and practices the Vajra Precepts, not daring to transgress them in any way.

It is also called "The One Who Cannot Be Gazed Upon," because those who uphold these teachings are as fierce and blazing as hundreds of thousands of suns; no one dares to look upon them, just as a newborn infant cannot bear to look up at the solar disc. For this reason, it is so named.
He is always at the inner gate of the Buddha; because he acts according to whatever instructions he is given, he is called "one who follows the teaching" (ājñākaraḥ).
*Dāsa* is his name, which carries the meaning of "one who cannot look beyond [his master's command]."
*Ḍa* is the *dharmadhātu*; *ra* with the sound of *la* is stainless.
*Śa* is *śamatha*. *Mahā-ruṣṇa* means "great wrathful one. *Khāda* means "to eat," referring to devouring all delusive appearances and afflictions.
Taking the syllable *kha* as the seed-syllable (*bīja*), all subsequent syllables serve to explain it; that is, the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

*Dha* has the meaning of "giving" (*dāna*) and also the meaning of "vehicle" (*yāna*). *Sarvatathāgata* refers to all Tathāgatas. *Āṃ* is pronounced with a long vowel and signifies a command (*ājñā*). When combined with the preceding syllable *a*, it forms *ā-klṛ*, which means "to cause to act"; thus, it means to cause [them] to carry out the commands of the Tathāgatas.
Acting in accordance with the instructions without contradiction, one may contemplate and receive the meaning of the command. Next is the mantra for the gatekeepers facing each other:

*Hī* (summons), *Mahā-vajra* (the great vajra), *Canda* (greatly wrathful and violent)—this carries the sense of extreme fury—*Abhimukha* (facing toward), following the previous [gatekeeper] *Sarlhaṇa* (seizing) and *Khāda* (eating/consuming).

Furthermore, *kha* is used as the seed syllable; *kiṃ jīrāye* means "why [do you] not hasten?"; *samaya* is explained as before; *maṇusmara* means "to remember," specifically to remember the *samaya*.

Because his wrath is so extreme that he cannot be looked upon or scrutinized, and because he stands in direct opposition [to all defilements], this is the origin of his name. Carrying out the commands of all Buddhas, he devours all sentient beings who cling to signs by means of the emptiness of the unattainable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*). To subdue those who are difficult to transform and to leave none remaining is the very meaning of "Great Wrathful One" (*Mahākrodha*).
Next is the mantra for binding the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*).

As the Buddha has taught, there are further immeasurable vidyādharas; fearing that other mantra-holders and the like might, due to the absence of such protective binding, disrupt the ritual proceedings or harm the practitioner, this method of binding the boundary is established.
Because of the establishment of the boundary, even the vidyādharas cannot destroy it.
It is like when bhikṣus establish a boundary for performing ritual acts; although a bhikṣu outside the boundary performs the rite, he cannot obstruct or break it.
"Universally pervading all directions.

*Sarvatrānugate* means "in all places and locations," signifying that one must perform the *pata-bandha* (boundary-binding) throughout the ten directions; the first phrase constitutes the binding, while the second phrase constitutes the boundary.

The meaning of this is that it refers to the boundary (*sīmā*) established in all directions and locations. *Mahāsamaya* means the Great Pledge (*mahāsamaya*). It is by means of this Great Pledge that the various boundaries are bound; *nīrājati* means "arising from," which refers to arising from the Great Pledge. *Smaraṇa* (pronounced with the retroflex *ṇ*: *smaraṇa*) means "recollection" or "mindfulness."

This refers to recollecting all the Buddha's teachings. *Abhāṭīha* means that there is nothing capable of harming it; it is also called "unobstructed," and it is likewise "incapable of being destroyed."
Because of the boundary (sīmā), there is nothing that can destroy it. *Dha-kadha-ka* means "light-power" (*prabhāva*); because of this light-power, the boundary is established.
*Dha* is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
*Ka* means "to act."

It is said that the essence of the *dharmadhātu* is free from all conditioned activity; being free from activity is itself the *dharmadhātu*. *Cchra cchra ccha* has the meaning of cessation, which refers to birth, cessation, and transition.
"La" (羅) signifies defilement and obstruction.
"Ju" (句), pronounced in the level tone, signifies pervasive movement throughout the ten directions;
it is also movement, which refers to coming and going.
To weigh it again is the meaning of "extreme arrival"; this is "urgent arrival. *Paṇḍa paṇḍa* explains the phrase as having the meaning of "conclusion.
The upper part has the meaning of "capacity," while the lower part is "emptiness."

Just as nothing can corrupt or destroy that which is equal to space, because of this *dhāraṇī* boundary (*sīmābandha*), it cannot be destroyed. *Nāśa* (upper tone), ten; *diśām*, the directions; that is, the binding of the ten directions. *Sarvatathāgata*, all Buddhas; *anu-jñāta*, authorized.

This is the teaching of all Buddhas; "purva" (previously) refers to that which was previously contemplated and causes one to remember it; "prāvara" (pravarā) is what has been realized; "dharma" is the Dharma, specifically the Dharma realized by all Buddhas; "lābha" (labhate) means realization or attainment; and "vijeṣe" means invincibility.

Among all obstacles, he is supreme; that is, the Bhagavat, who cannot be defeated or destroyed—this is the Lord of Mantras. This praises the virtues of the World-Honored One. *Vikule* means "to remove," for he is able to eliminate defilements.

The initial exhortation to "remove" is also an exhortation to mindfulness that effects the removal of the stains of conceptual characteristics prior to the *vikuṭi* (the state of non-conceptualization); it is precisely "not to act," which is precisely "removal."

The latter phrase removes the defilement of conceptual characteristics; this is the removal of all obstacles, the seed-syllable *hreḥ*, and the meaning of *ru* (long-drawn) and *pṛ* is "palace" and "abode."

By means of the true Dharma, one eliminates the marks of defilement; this is precisely the palace wherein all Buddhas dwell. To cause it to be identical with this realm, one further refines the characters to be exceedingly subtle and radiant, using only the character "Lì" (隷) from the final phrase as the seed-syllable.
"Ra" is the characteristic; adding the sound "yi" (i) to it constitutes samādhi, which possesses all characteristics while remaining detached from all characteristics.
This is the essential nature and characteristic of the realm.
The following explains the seed-syllable (*bīja-akṣara*): it is called a "seed" because a single syllable can give rise to many [qualities].
It is the seed of evil *bodhi*.
Since all practitioners of recitation possess this mind that aspires for unsurpassed *bodhi*, this syllable is explained first.
From this, all dharmas arise; that is, it is the bodhicitta.
"A" (阿) is the seed for cultivating the practices of enlightenment (*bodhicaryā*), because it brings about the perfection of merit and wisdom. "Am" (暗) is the seed of enlightenment.

The preceding character is *bodhicitta*; when a dot (*bindu*) is added above it, it becomes Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*). Realizing this Great Emptiness is the attainment of *bodhi*. *Aḥ* is the seed-syllable of *nirvāṇa*. When there are two dots on either side, they are both pronounced with urgency; this is the sound *ha*, which carries the meaning of "expelling. Expelling all defilements is entry into *nirvāṇa*. *Ha* (in the departing tone) is Trailokyavijaya.
The syllable *ha* signifies "activity" (*saṃskāra*), while adding the sound *a* signifies "the ultimate activity.

By means of this, one dispels all activities; thus, it is the non-performance of all activities, which constitutes the sense of "dispelling. Because of this, one is able to subdue the three worlds. *Han* signifies the unmoving Lord.
The syllable *ha* represents activity; the sound *a* also represents activity; the bindu is the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*).
By abiding in this state, one is able to subdue all things and acts as a great protector for the bodhicitta. *Ā* is the removal of obscurations (*sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin*).
The syllable *A* is an obstruction; when there are two dots (*bindu*) beside it, it signifies its removal. This is the meaning of "removing the obstructions" (*Ārya*).

*Sva* refers to Avalokiteśvara. *Sva* represents the various outflows (*āsrava*); with two dots beside it, it becomes *Ha*. Because he removes the perception of outflows through the perception of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), he is "Self-Mastering" (*Īśvara*). *Bha* refers to Vajrapāṇi.
The meaning of "bondage" (ba) is that it has two dots on its sides, which signify the removal of all bonds.
This is the seed-syllable of Vajra. "Maṃ" refers to Mañjuśrī. Its fundamental essence is emptiness;
with another dot above it, it is further emptiness, namely the "Great Emptiness" (mahā-śūnyatā).

Transcending the eighteen kinds of emptiness is called the Great Emptiness; abiding in the stage of emptiness is called the Great Emptiness, which is precisely the Great Prajñā. It is the adornment of the Eye of Space.

*Ga* signifies coming and going; since phenomena that come and go are identical to the great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*), a dot is added. *Raṃ*: all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas emerge from within this, which is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

*Ra* is defilement; the dot above it signifies being free from defilement and identical to the great emptiness—this is the meaning of the *dharmadhātu*. *Khaṃ* is the seed-syllable of Great Diligence (*mahāvīrya*).
Because the Buddha sat at the site of enlightenment and subdued all Māras, all devas and humans call him Mahāvīra; he is Vairocana.

*Kha* signifies emptiness (*śūnyatā*); the nasal dot (*bindu*) above it is "Great Emptiness" (*mahāśūnyatā*), which purifies all emptinesses through Great Emptiness. *Hrīḥ* is the Bodhisattva Jalaśvara.
Because he arises from water, he is named "Water-Sovereign" (*jala-īśvara*); this is the name of the Bodhisattva.
It is contained within the *Mahāmūla*; however, the specific locations for placement are not mentioned here in this maṇḍala arrangement and should be examined in detail.
"Ja" (ja) has the meaning of "birth"; it signifies the removal of all arising and ceasing, becoming equal to the great void (*mahāśūnyatā*). "Tandara" refers to the Honored One (*bhaṭṭāraka*).
For the most part, this is *tathatā* (suchness); the nature of suchness is identical to the great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*). *Bhrī-vijayā*:

*bha* refers to the three realms of existence (*tri-bhava*), and *ri* refers to *samādhi*; thus, it signifies attaining mastery within the three realms of existence. The two dots on the side signify the removal of the three realms of existence. *Saṃ* signifies the attainment of great power (*mahā-bala*).

The syllable *sa* represents all outflows (*āsrava*), which is identical to the seed-syllable of Avalokiteśvara; however, with a bindu above it, it signifies that these outflows are identical to the Great Emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*). The syllable *bhaṃ* occupies its own place.
She is the Mother of the Avalokiteśvara family.
*Bhā* is the essence of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), like space. *Haṃ* signifies action;
when joined with *mahā-śūnya*, it refers to the practice of Great Emptiness. *Yamāntakṣaya* is the consort (*vidyārājñī*) of the Lotus family.

This also carries the meaning of "vehicle" (*yāna*). The dot above indicates that this vehicle is pure and identical to the great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*). It accords with the seed-syllable of Bodhisattva Ratnakoṭi;
like Mahāsthāmaprāpta, it takes the "jewel-place" as its meditative concentration.
Because their hands are made of jewels, jewels are produced from them.
This also carries the sense of permanence, as well as the sense of action. [This is] the Bodhisattva Radiant Net of Beards.
The *maṇḍala* of Mañjuśrī’s retinue is explained in the same manner as before. *Bha*: Śākyamuni. *Bha* signifies the three realms of existence (*tribhava*);

the two dots (*bindu*) on its side signify the meaning of dispelling the three realms of existence. *Hūṃ ṭa laṃ ha*: *Ha* is activity; *laṃ* is samādhi; the dot above is Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*). *Laṃ ṭa ra*: *Ṭa* is the enemy to be battled; *ra* is defilement; the sound *u* on its side is samādhi; the dot above is Great Emptiness. These are the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the three Buddha-Uṣṇīṣas, which are to be assigned in sequence as before.
*Nei* (隣) is the white parasol (*sitātapatra*).
*Ra* (羅) is the sign; the dot above it is the same as *Dàkōng* (大空). *Shànshè* (苫社) is an obstruction; it carries the meaning of facing an enemy.

All obstructive phenomena (*sapratigha-dharma*) are identical to the Great Emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*); there is neither superior nor inferior. *Siṃ* (pronounced with a retroflex *ṣ*), meaning "most victorious," is the *Uṣṇīṣa*. *Sa* signifies "solidity";

being free from solidity yet not non-solid is the Great Emptiness, and it also carries the meaning of *samādhi*. *Tad* (a diphthong) signifies "suchness" (*tathatā*). *Ra* signifies "defilement," and it also carries the meanings of *samādhi* and Great Emptiness; this is the mass of fire. *Hraḥ* (a conjunct): *Ha* is "activity," *Ra* is "defilement," *U* is *samādhi*, and the dot (*bindu*) is Great Emptiness. These are the seed-syllables of the Five Buddha-Uṣṇīṣas, beginning with the *Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin* Uṣṇīṣa on the right.
*Dāṃ* contains both the "half-included" and the "fully included," which is suchness (*tathatā*).

Above it is emptiness; since suchness cannot be apprehended, it is identical to the great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*). *Hūṃ* is practice; entering the letter *A*, one practices non-practice, which is again emptiness. *Mi* is entry into the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), yet it is apart from the ultimate truth. *Cī* is practice, yet it is apart from practice. *Nī* is all vehicles (*yāna*).

"Immediately mounting the vehicle-less vehicle, its essence is identical to emptiness. These five characters are the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the Worldly Vidyārājñī; although they are emanations of the Buddha, they resemble those of the world, namely the gods and so forth.
From among all the vidyā-vidyās (consorts) that exist everywhere, take whichever one you choose. *Hūṃ* is the seed-syllable of the Samādhi of the Invincible (*Ajita*).

*Mī* is the seed-syllable of the Earth Goddess (*Pṛthivī-devī*). *Ki* is the Samādhi of Action (*Karma*). *Li* is the Samādhi of the Signless (*Animitta*). *Keśinī* is the messenger of Mañjuśrī; she is so named because she is exquisite and beautiful due to the knotting of her hair. *Ni* is Emptiness (*Śūnyatā*). *Li* is the Bestower (*Dātṛ*), which is the sign of meditative concentration (*Samādhi-nimitta*).
*Tā* is giving (*dāna*).

It is that which can fulfill all vows within the signless (*animitta*); this is *upakeśanī*. *Śūnyatā-dharmamudrā-lakṣaṇa*: as previously stated, this messenger of Mañjuśrī is named *Citra*. *Ma* means emptiness; it is the self (*ātman*).
The lower *la* (ra) is the sign (*nimitta*); because signs still exist, there is a self (*ātman*), and because one is free from signs, there is no self.
This is also the concentration (*samādhi*) of Mañjuśrī.

It is the practice of "binding joy" (*pramuditā-caryā*). Treading upon the signs is the wealth and wisdom of the messenger of Mañjuśrī; that is to say, it is that which can fulfill all vows and cause all to rejoice.
Furthermore, there is another messenger named Akāśani, who is the messenger for summoning and seizing objects.
A few seed-syllables from the sūtra have not yet been obtained.
The above are the five messengers of Mañjuśrī.
Each messenger has one attendant; they share the same seed-syllable and are identical to the messengers.
Next is the Bodhisattva Dharanimdhara.

He rebukes those who find it difficult to practice and depart from emptiness, as well as the Great Emptiness—namely, the nectar of the Dharma. This summary phrase signifies joy, meaning the sense of exultation and leaping for gladness.
Next is the gift of fearlessness (*sarvābhaya-dāna*).
Regarding *rasa-na-ka*, it is as explained above.

Because of the meaning of these syllables, there is fear; however, if one enters the gateway of the syllable *A*, all fears can be eliminated. This is the summary statement: its flavor (*rasa*) is such that the flavor of the unsurpassed, true Dharma fulfills all aspirations.
Next, it eliminates all evil destinies.

*Dharmadhātuvibhavana*—the compound *vibhavana* here has the meaning of "shattering," like a person holding an object in their hand and striking another object until it breaks. Subsequently, it is named from its compassionate wisdom that takes pity upon all beings.

"Mi-ba (subtle bond), samādhi, and the sound 'i'—these are the comprehensive terms for the preceding [sections], such as *dhyāna*, *prīti*, *sukha*, and *dhṛti*. Through various skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they cause sentient beings to rejoice and reach this state."
The meaning of growth and accumulation is that the seed of a Bodhisattva arises from great compassion (*maitrī*).
This compassion is supreme, vast, and incomparable; it is from within this compassion that [the Bodhisattva] is born.

"Vāhana" (vehicle) also carries the meaning of coming and going; being free from coming and going, it is identical with the great emptiness. *Yam* is the seed-syllable of the Bodhisattva Mahākāruṇika.
Because he envelops his own mind with great compassion, he is so named. It signifies the Bodhisattva Sarvaduḥkhapraśamana (the One Who Eliminates All Torment).
To be able to remove the feverish affliction of the three poisons is the meaning of the ultimate samādhi.
*U* also signifies the meaning of the ultimate samādhi. *U* refers to this Bodhisattva of inconceivable wisdom.
By means of inconceivable wisdom, one eliminates the absence of wisdom.
As for giving (*dāna*), because one possesses it oneself, one is able to bestow wisdom upon others. This is *śamatha*.
Furthermore, he is the Bodhisattva Ratnasambhava of Great Emptiness; because he is able to give birth to all the jewels of the Dharma, he is named the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi (Jewel-in-Hand).
Just as when the cintāmaṇi jewel is held in one’s hand, it can fulfill the wishes of all people, so too is this Bodhisattva; thus he receives his name. "Yan" (儼):
the fifth character is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and furthermore, it is the Great Emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*). "Xian" (噞) refers to this Earth-Holding One (*Dharanimdhara*).

Just as the great earth sustains all things and the Buddha-ground sustains sentient beings, so too is this Bodhisattva; by the meaning of this word, he sustains all. "Hn" (髯) is the letter *ñ*, and it is also the fifth letter.

Furthermore, the original version of the *Mahāśūnyatā-sūtra* lacks the name of the Bodhisattva; upon examining the preceding section, it largely concerns the meaning of how [phenomena] are like a mass of foam and lack solidity.
One realizes that the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas are thus, being identical to great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*).
This is the seed-syllable of the Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta.
*Nan* is the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati.
"Emptiness" (*śūnya*) is further "emptiness," which is the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati; within emptiness is the cessation of defilements. *Lin* is the Bodhisattva Gaganamati.
Just as space is boundless and unobstructed, so too is the wisdom of this bodhisattva. It encompasses space and is stainless.
This wisdom is pure and stainless like space; its practice is rooted in space, and once that practice is perfected, it becomes identical to space. Space-like suchness-wisdom has arrived.

*Ghu* means *skad cig ma* (momentary), which refers to going to achieve perfect enlightenment and reaching suchness (*tathatā*). *Ra* is the pure wisdom of the *buddha*-nature; it is the wisdom of the mind that purifies the stains of emptiness. *Dhiḥ* is the wisdom of conduct; one should always benefit sentient beings with this wisdom. *Hūṃ* is peaceful wisdom.
This wisdom is called "eternally abiding" because it benefits sentient beings; the phrase [in the text] means "fearlessness.
This wisdom is "securely established," like the Samādhi of the Vajra Mountain.

Regarding the four syllables *dhi*, *dharmadhātu*, *śrī*, *jñāna-vimala-hūṃ*, *caryā-śūnyatā-bharaṇa-vimala-śūnya*: all those who follow the teachings agree upon these; one may take any single one of them as required.

The two syllables *ca* and *sa*, together with the two dots (*bindu*), signify terror; the *ra* dot causes the removal of battle, and causing that [terror] is the great victory. Like Yama, he is stainless and reaches all vehicles; the sword severs both the created and the uncreated.
By what means is one liberated?
It is because their essence is the Great Emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*).

Take any single seed-syllable; [the text is missing] the third right-hand sixth character from this many [syllables], which are the seed-syllables of Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields. By employing any one of these syllables, they may be used universally.

In all mantras, one may take any syllable from the beginning, middle, or end to serve as the seed-syllable (*bīja*); this is permissible as long as one observes and selects a syllable that captures the essential core.
Next is the mantra of the Śuddhāvāsa devas.
Manu-ra means "joy of mind"; because one experiences various pleasures, dharma-sambhava (the arising of the Dharma) occurs.
This is born from the transformation of the Buddha; it has no connection with the worldly heavens.

"Defilement" (mala) refers to that which arises from phenomena; "anuśaya" has three types, and these three are also seeds—this is the explanation of Kātyāyanīputra. Taken together with the preceding, it means "according to what is taught."

Arising in accordance with those dharmas, one preaches the Dharma for sentient beings by means of the dharma of liberation. The three seeds are likewise seeds; whether firm or non-firm, they are all detached, their essence being identical to emptiness. Because it brings about ultimate emptiness, the syllable *huṃ* follows the *rākṣasa-mantra*.
One employs those very vernacular sounds as mantras.
*Kharaṇi*—these three syllables constitute the seed-mantra (*bīja*). Within it are two *ka*s and two *ra*s, which signify the ability to consume all karmic defilements.
The second is the syllable *yi*, which is samādhi.
"Repetition" means "repeated purification.
Next is the mantra of Ḍākinī.
This is a worldly magical art possessed by those who practice it; it is also a sovereign incantation that enables one to know when a person’s life is about to end, knowing it six months in advance.
Having known this, he immediately performed the rite and took that heart-meat to eat it. Why was this so?
Within the human body there is bile, which is called "human bile," just as cattle have bile.

If one obtains this food, one can achieve supreme accomplishment: one may travel throughout the four quarters in a single day, accomplish whatever one desires at will, and is also able to treat various ailments of people.
Those who harbor resentment treat them with sorcery to inflict extreme suffering and illness.
However, their methods do not permit killing; they must rely on their own calculated arts.
When a person is about to die, they know it six months in advance; having known this, they take the person's heart through their art.

Although their hearts are extracted, there is a magical artifice by which other substances must be used as substitutes; thus, the person's life does not end until the time for death arrives, at which point [the heart] finally perishes.
The "Great One" (Mahā) is the Great Sovereign among yakṣas; in the terminology of worldly people, it refers to the ultimate greatness, belonging to Mahākāla, the so-called Great Black Deity.
Vairocana, wishing to eliminate those [obstacles] by means of the Dharma-gate for subduing the three periods of time, manifested as the Great Black Deity (*Mahākāla*).

Transcending those immeasurable manifestations, he smeared his body with ash and, in the midst of a wilderness, summoned through esoteric arts all the *ḍākinīs* who have accomplished the vehicles of all dharmas and move unhindered through the air or across water;
he then rebuked them, saying: "Because you constantly devour human beings, I shall now likewise devour you."
He immediately swallowed and devoured it; however, he did not cause him to die, but having subdued him, released him, ensuring that he would completely cease eating meat.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have now survived by eating all kinds of meat."
"How shall you now save yourself?
The Buddha said,
"I permit you to eat the hearts of dead men."
He said: "When a person is about to die, the various great yakṣas know that their life has ended and vie with one another to eat them.
How could I possibly obtain one?"
The Buddha said:
"I shall teach you the mantra-dharmas and mudrās; if you do not die within six months, you will be able to understand them.
Once you have understood them, protect yourself with these dharmas so that others may not cause you fear or harm; until the time of your life's end, you are permitted to take food."
Thus, by gradually leading them so that they may enter the Way, there is this mantra.
*Hāri* (the syllable *ha*) signifies the practice of concentration; *li* signifies the removal of defilement—that is, the removal of the defilement of those heterodox arts.
Next is the mantra of the Yakṣiṇī: *Aṃkule*. The meaning of "Yakṣa" is one who can devour the world and consume the impurities of all karmas and other evils;

it is the vehicle (*yāna*) of the Yakṣa. Regarding the mantra: *Aṃ* is as above; *kule* means "speech-determination"; *yāna* means "vehicle"; *dharmadhātu* means "the realm of phenomena"; *vimala-samādhi-pada-artha* means "the meaning of the phrase of the stainless meditative concentration.
It says: "That which holds the Yakṣa’s vidyā is the mind"; this mantra is composed using that specific regional dialect.
Next, the mantra of the Piśācas translates as "extreme suffering"; these beings are mostly hungry ghosts (preta).

This is compared to the definitive meaning of the First Principle (*paramārtha*); "death" is compared to the definitive meaning of the ultimate extinction (*paramārtha-nirodha*). Furthermore, this is also performed according to local dialects.
Next is the mantra of the Bhūtas;
these belong to the class of yakṣas:
*Oṃ khaṃ īḍiṃ ṭaṃ ṭaṃ maṃ me kaṃ saṃ naṃ khaṃ ṭaṃ*. Next is the mantra of the asuras.
Each of these serves as a seed-syllable; take whichever one you prefer. *Rakṣa rakṣa* (repeated) means "protect, protect.

*Dharmadhātu-abaddha-gagana-vat* means "unbound within the realm of phenomena, like space. *Māra-māra* means "like space, [where] the path of speech is cut off," referring to being free from all defilements. Within this phrase, there are words regarding desire and hatred; it is spoken for the purpose of removing those many desires and hatreds.

Next is Mahoraga; likewise, one takes whichever seed-syllable from among them is appropriate—*ṣṭra* for coming and going, *ra* for defilement, and *laṃ* for characteristics—meaning the characteristics of the bonds of birth and death, *ṣṭra-ba-ra-ka-laṃ*. Next is the mantra of Kinnara.

*Hā kha ga ra saṃ kaṭe*: this is what is called "my retribution," which is difficult to empty; furthermore, it is the emptiness of the preceding phrase. *Mī va dhi hā saṃ kaṭe na*: like the upper and lower phrases, the meaning of this phrase is that the upper phrase is joy, while the lower phrase has the meaning of bestowing joy upon others.
Because it is able to eliminate the grasping at a self, it is firm and realizes the great emptiness; therefore, one rejoices immeasurably.
Having attained it for oneself, one is also able to bestow it upon others.
The mantras of these various deities are each their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*).

*Eka-cakra-gati-pratibimba*: Beside this is the sound *ā*, which signifies movement. *Paramārtha-laṃ-rajas-tad-mahāśūnya*: "Dust" (*rajas*) is the Great Emptiness; "that" (*tat*) is non-self (*anātman*), which is also the Great Emptiness; "bow" (*dhanus*) is emptiness within emptiness. The sound *i* is emptiness within emptiness. *Yamini-śūra-saṃsthita-svāhā*. As above. The distinct characteristics of these various mantras are hereby concluded.

Next, regarding Vairocana’s teaching on the heart of mantras: within each of the aforementioned mantras, there are root mantras, heart mantras, and secondary heart mantras; such as these are immeasurable, boundless, and beyond calculation. Now, to speak of the heart of all mantras in general, it is precisely this syllable *A*.

This is the meaning of the fundamental non-arising of all phenomena: if one is apart from the sound "A," there are no other syllables; it is thus the mother of all syllables and the source from which all mantras arise.

This means that all dharma-gates and bodhisattvas alike arise from the self-realized mind of Vairocana’s own essence; desiring to benefit sentient beings, they manifest these functional capacities through the power of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). In reality, their essence is unborn, identical to the dharma-body of the letter A.
This syllable is the most supreme and wondrous among all mantras; therefore, practitioners of mantra should always uphold it in this manner.
For this reason, all mantras abide in the letter A; because they abide therein, when recited, they are immediately brought forth.
The above concludes the *Samanta-mantra-nidhāna*.
The mantras herein are applicable universally; those in the subsequent sections of the Dharma are each specific practices.

5. The Chapter on Mundane Accomplishments (10). The fifth chapter, the Mundane Accomplishments, states in the third sūtra: "At that time, the Blessed One again addressed the Lord of Secrets, Vajrapāṇi, saying:"
"Listen attentively, listen attentively": since he had previously questioned the Buddha, this is spoken as a summary of that prior response; thus, it is not a teaching given without being asked.

Regarding the teachings of the mantra-dharmas, "accomplishing that fruit" means that a practitioner of mantras, in accordance with the dharma-teachings, practices the dharmic conduct by relying on the correct instructions; when this practice is successfully perfected, one attains the fruit of *siddhi*.
The Buddha’s intention was this:

if there are sentient beings who wish to achieve the great fruits described above, they must first practice according to the sequence of this chapter; for this is the very place where one first sets out upon the path.
"Each syllable should correspond [to its meaning], and each phrase is likewise.
One should perform mental visualization while reciting, dwelling well for one *lakṣa*.

The first syllable is the bodhicitta. This means that as each individual syllable above possesses its own syllabic meaning, entering the gate of reality from this syllable constitutes the syllable of the mantra.
Furthermore, when these syllables combine to form a phrase, there is a meaning to that phrase; this phrase precisely elucidates the essence of the true nature (*dharmatā*).
Therefore, a practitioner of the mantra path must ensure that each syllable corresponds [to its meaning] and each phrase corresponds [to its meaning].

One may dwell upon the seed-syllable of the mind, or visualize the mantra as forming a wheel-like image, or like a garland, or like a string of pearls—luminous, pure, and stainless—revolving in continuous succession without interruption.
Having thus brought it clearly before one's mind, one should visualize this mantra-wheel as pure and bright as clarified milk, flowing forth in succession without interruption.

Entering through the mouth, it flows from above downward, sprinkling the lower parts; head and tail joined together, it is drawn into this interior, permeating the body and mind and bathing the limbs.
By means of these causes and conditions, one can cause all obstacles of body and mind for the practitioner to become completely purified.
That which is called "one lakṣa" is an esoteric term; it is a distinct meaning in the Sanskrit sound, namely, the sense of "one vision."

Cause the mind to abide upon this object with single-pointed focus and without distraction; let each syllable correspond [to the next] and each phrase likewise correspond. Visualize each individual syllable as being bright, pure, and transparent like a polished mani-jewel; each syllable is further clearly manifest, pervaded by a garland of light that flows in uninterrupted succession, pouring into the mind like the sprinkling of nectar.

When one is thus focused on a single object, even if various obstacles should arise—such as manifesting forms of great terror that would drive those with distracted minds to madness—or producing a great sound capable of shattering even the king of mountains; [the practitioner remains undisturbed].

When such circumstances arise, the practitioner abides in the truly vigorous bodhicitta; with a single object of focus, unmoving and free from grasping or rejecting, it is therefore called "abiding in the single view."
If one does not act in this way, even if one recites a full ten million *lakṣas* over the course of a hundred years, one will still not achieve accomplishment, let alone a single *lakṣa*.

Furthermore, these syllables are themselves the bodhicitta; since each individual syllable is an entrance into the gate of the true nature of reality (dharmatā), they all attain the essence of the dharma-dhātu.
Regarding what is called "syllable" (字), in Sanskrit it is *akṣara*. *A* has the meaning of "indestructible," which is precisely the pure bodhicitta.
This practice gate exists for the sake of the pure bodhicitta.
If impurities are not removed, the samādhi of the tutelary deity cannot manifest; therefore, the practitioner causes each individual syllable to correspond with the pure bodhicitta.

Regarding the phrase, "The second is called sound; taking the perception of the phrases as the deity, one should perform it in its own place": one should further visualize the sounds of the mantra syllables and phrases as a continuous, uninterrupted cycle in their proper sequence, as previously described. Each individual sound should be clearly manifest, like the successive, unbroken resonance of a bell, a gong, or the wind and Brahma-sounds, entering the body and pervading its interior.
By means of these causes and conditions, one is able to sweep away the defilements and turbidity of body and mind, just as all dust is completely cleared when a fire breaks out.

One should also maintain the mind in a state of single-pointed concentration, dwelling well therein without distraction; even if various objects of perception arise, they should be treated as previously described.
Furthermore, regarding the meaning within the phrase: it is the very essence of the deity.
First, one visualizes the deity clearly; next, one contemplates oneself as being identical to the deity, making both the internal and external aspects manifest and clear.

The visualization of the syllable-mantra is the body of the mantra; the visualization of the sound-mantra is the lord of the mantra; the visualization of the meaning of the phrase is the essence of the mantra, which is the heart of the mantra.
A "phrase" (*pada*) is the destination to which the intended meaning converges; it is the very heart-mind of the Honored One.

When the three matters of body, speech, and mind are pure—being equal and purified—it is as if one possesses clear vision within, perceives a pure object without, and is free from the obscuration of darkness; because these three matters are equal, [the reality] appears clearly before one.
Because these three things are equal, body, speech, and mind all abide in a single vision.
When all conditions are complete, there is the joy of accomplishment.
Since these three things are equal, one clearly perceives the Honored One; therefore, one should perform [the practice] in one's own place.
Furthermore, one observes that one's own body is likewise identical to that of the deity; because these three things are equal, this is called mundane accomplishment (*laukika-siddhi*).

At that time, the deity and the various bodhisattvas appear according to one’s visualization, arrive according to one’s recollection, and respond according to one’s inquiry. Thereafter, one enters the practice of training in supramundane mantra (*lokottara-mantra*).
If one does not do so, one will merely waste their efforts without any benefit.
"The third line should be known as the supreme phrase of all Buddhas.

The practitioner contemplates abiding therein, within an extremely perfect and pure lunar disc; therein, with sincere visualization, one imagines the various syllables in their proper sequence. Next, one should contemplate the Buddha, which is to say, one contemplates the *iṣṭadevatā* (the chosen deity).
According to whatever action one intends to perform, there are corresponding categories of dharma-gates.

For example, just as with form, there are white, yellow, red, and so forth; likewise, there are the forms of sitting, standing, and hand-seals (mudrās). One should intensely visualize these according to the specific action one wishes to accomplish.
If one wishes to pacify the mind and extinguish calamities, one should visualize the form of the Pacification deity.
Once this has been accomplished with clarity and unimpeded mastery, one further contemplates a lunar disc that is perfectly round, bright, and pure.
One contemplates the wheel of syllables within this luminous and pure heart-mind, achieving it as previously described; this is the meaning of the purified bodhicitta.
Through the equal purification of the three karmas, one is able to perceive the forms of all Buddhas.
The pure bodhicitta, in conjunction with the samādhi of buddha-remembrance, is clear and unimpeded; it is understood solely by oneself alone, and is not seen by others.

Regarding the phrase "to contemplate with sincere clarity within," it means to observe the perfect and luminous Honored One and the seed-syllable, perceiving them with such distinct clarity that there is no obscurity; this is called "perceiving with distinct clarity."

Regarding the statement, "Place the syllables and phrases therein and contemplate purifying one's life," this means that as previously described, one first contemplates the syllables, contemplates the sounds, contemplates the deity, or further inquires regarding the removal of phrases, and only thereafter contemplates the Buddha.

The Buddha is the very essence of the Honored One (the deity). Contemplating them according to whatever conditions they possess, one sees that they are all the Universal Gate body of the Buddha; thus, there are no differing characteristics, and they are all equally named "Buddha."
First, one performs these three kinds of contemplations; when they are fully integrated, they together constitute the seed. Because it is a seed, one will inevitably obtain the fruit.
Next, one contemplates the Honored One (the deity) in order to bring that fruit to fruition.

Just as one who possesses seeds plants them in fertile soil and nurtures them through skillful means to bring them to fruition, it is said that these are "perfected seeds. Since they have already become the fruit of the wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), one contemplates the Buddha.

When the practitioner first contemplates, they may suddenly and momentarily attain correspondence with it, like a flash of lightning that briefly illuminates the path; at that time, one should not give rise to attachment. Why is this so?

For example, there was once a disciple of an ācārya in the West who, while practicing this meditation, suddenly experienced a brief state of resonance. Consequently, his mind became conceited, and he spoke of it to other fellow students.
He then said: "One who perceives the Dharma is one who has realized the fruit.
Now, as for the fruit of mantra, it is the possession of the wisdom of all modes."
"I composed a verse yesterday; are you able to understand it?
If you cannot even grasp this mundane matter, you should know that the realm of the Buddhas is not yet accessible to you."

The reason for explaining this matter is that when a person clearly perceives the characters, because they are in accord with the Dharma, there will necessarily be a transformation within their body and mind.
Those who were previously dull-witted have now attained *dhāraṇī*, such that upon hearing a single phrase, they penetrate immeasurable meanings and can explain them without end.
How much less, then, would those moved by faults such as self-conceit (*māna*) give rise to a mind of arrogance and attachment?
Therefore, the practitioner should abandon such attachment to dharmas so as not to cause their own regression.

Furthermore, when the practitioner contemplates the *iṣṭadevatā*, if the image suddenly appears and then vanishes, they should not indulge in relishing it or become attached to it, nor should they give rise to regret; rather, they should practice with single-mindedness, for after a long time, it will naturally become clearly manifest.

When one beholds the Honored One, all that is conceived is spontaneously accomplished; the circular halo, the lunar disc, the seed-syllables, and so forth, appear clearly and transparently according to one's thought.
If one sees the letters, there are flames of light outside each letter, as brilliant and pure as a blazing fire, beyond compare.
Or, as previously described, they may appear as wheels of letters, which likewise possess radiance upon them that is accomplished according to one's intention.

Continuing thus, he contemplates this perfect luminosity, making it small when he wishes to urinate and large when he wishes to defecate, until it pervades everywhere throughout the Buddha-fields of the ten directions.

Or, if they wish to behold the infinite and innumerable forms, colors, and speech of the Buddhas of the ten directions, as well as the secret treasuries they expound and their miraculous manifestations, they shall all see them clearly.

For example, it is like a skilled goldsmith who obtains fine, genuine gold—purified by a hundred refinements, supple, and stainless—which can be fashioned into anything according to his will or intention, without any obstruction.
This is called the fruit of recitation.

Furthermore, as for what is known as inhalation and exhalation, it is like the breath of worldly people: entering the body and then exiting, and having exited, entering again, without interruption or gap.

This entry into contemplation and the vision of the wheel of syllables as perfectly radiant is likewise so: from the heart of the Honored One, it flows into one’s own body moment by moment like inhalation; then, from within one’s own granted body and mind, it flows out moment by moment to enter the heart of the Honored One, with moments of mind following one another without interval like exhalation.
Thus, moment by moment, this cycle revolves without end; it is precisely the inhalation and exhalation of the practitioner of mantras.
As these inhalations and exhalations flow through the body and mind, they purify all defilements, gradually bringing about the purification of the sense faculties.

Furthermore, one should observe the colors of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) within the wheel of syllables (*akṣaracakra*) according to the specific rite: for instance, white for pacifying rites, blue-black for subjugating rites, and so forth; these may be understood by analogy.
By practicing in this manner, one can likewise accomplish all tasks in accordance with one's intentions.
Furthermore, as it is said in the Sūtra: "Life is what is called wind; wind is perception (saṃjñā); perception is mindfulness (smṛti).
Although the perception of the breath—the life-faculty—may be pure and subtle, it is nonetheless produced by the wind of perception and must likewise be purified.

Regarding what was said—that after those [impurities] have been purified, one performs the preliminary recitation method—the syllable *A* refers to the fact that all seed-syllables arise from the syllable *A*.

If one contemplates the characteristic of the seed-syllable itself, one does not contemplate "A"; if one contemplates both simultaneously, there would be two characteristics. Therefore, one contemplates only the syllable "A" as the seed of all things, because no phenomenon transcends the gateway of the syllable "A."
This refers to first observing the specific characteristics of the seeds,
and then, upon reaching this point, one must enter the gateway of the letter A for each and every one.
If one enters the gateway of the letter A, one immediately perceives the fundamental principle of the unborn nature.
Having seen this, their three karmas immediately become all-pervasive.
By means of physical mastery (*ṛddhi*), they universally perceive form-bodies (*rūpakāya*), manifesting to all beings according to their kind those bodies that each finds pleasing to behold.

Because of his mastery over speech, he is able to reach all Buddha-fields in the ten directions with a single voice, and can also universally respond to the diverse linguistic expressions of all sentient beings.

Because of his mastery over the mind, there is not a single movement of the minds of all sentient beings or a single conceptual proliferation of their minds that he does not clearly know; he is also able to know the secret matters of all Tathāgatas.
This is precisely the ultimate purification of the six sense faculties and the attainment of the wisdom of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).

A practitioner cultivating the path of mantra and conduct should first perform service for one month through recitation; that is to say, during this month, they should first perform the visualizations as described above.
Furthermore, as for the esoteric interpretation: the twelve months of a year complete the cycle, returning once more to the primordial limit to attain its original source.
This is also like the twelve stages of a Bodhisattva, which are the wondrous awakening of the ten abodes and so forth.
Just as there are twelve months, one obtains the portion of one month therein; this is precisely entering the first stage (prathama-bhūmi).

Each and every phrase or syllable, or the principal deity and so forth, is realized according to each respective truth (satya) such that accomplishment is attained without obstruction or defilement; therefore, it is said that "each and every phrase is in correspondence."

Regarding "the preliminary skillful means of the practitioner": when practicing contemplation in this manner, if one offers a single flower to the Buddha and dedicates the merit with a sincere heart, one should vow that through this, one may attain thorough understanding and liberation within each and every phrase.

Furthermore, as for the flowers mentioned below, they pervade all lands throughout the ten directions and universally perform the work of a Buddha; at that time, they are accomplished as soon as one thinks of them.
This applies even to matters such as incense and food, each being explained extensively in this same manner.

Should there be a great drought among the heavens, or various kinds of calamities and afflictions, at that time the practitioner should offer a single flower, vowing to cause this drought to be removed and for a great rain to descend, or vowing for all afflictions to naturally subside; there shall be nothing that is not accomplished in accordance with the occasion.

Furthermore, one should dedicate each of these individual merits toward Bodhi and bestow them universally upon all sentient beings; if even such great vows for Bodhi are destined to be fulfilled, how much more so other matters?
What was previously referred to as "one month" means that the mind is in union with a single object.

Regarding "thoroughly penetrating each and every syllable," this refers to the previous visualization of the wheel of letters, the wheel of sounds, and the seed-syllables of the deity; when each of these appears clearly before one without error, it is called "thoroughly penetrating each and every syllable."

First, one visualizes the Buddha until accomplishment is attained; then, one perceives the perfect luminosity (*pariśuddha-āloka*), whereby the realization of any single aspect brings the others to completion.

That is to say, when the visualization of the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity) becomes clear, the characteristics of the perfect luminosity, the syllable-wheel (*akṣara-cakra*), and so forth, are spontaneously accomplished.

This "moon" is precisely the Samādhi of the Moon Metaphor; because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is cool and refreshing, it is able to manifest universally within the waters of the minds of sentient beings. It is not like the moon of the mundane world; rather, the mind is merely borrowed as a metaphor.

It is sufficient that one [method] be established, for the others will then be established of themselves; however, the reason for explaining them all in detail is that each has its specific application in the subsequent sections, and thus it is necessary to clarify fully the methods and functions of contemplating the moon.
"The Buddhas of great renown have taught that one should first uphold this" refers to the initial accomplishment of the seed-syllable.

"Next, one should offer whatever is available, such as unguents and flowers," means that one can take a single flower and pervade the entire Dharma-realm; furthermore, through the causal conditions of the power of aspiration, one can eliminate the various sufferings and afflictions of sentient beings, as is constantly explained in the *Samantamukha* (Universal Gate) chapter.
How could a single flower be capable of accomplishing such power and vows?

Regarding the phrase "in order to achieve perfect enlightenment, one dedicates [merit] toward one's own bodhi," one should know that this is the sovereign power and function of the clear and pure manifestation of the seed of bodhi within one's own mind.
Next, it says that herein the profound meaning of two characters is explained: "In this way, for two months, one should be fearless regarding the mantra," which refers to the attainment of *siddhi*.
This present stage is the "Great Application," which is the second month.
The first month refers to the formation of the seed-syllable (*bīja*), while the second month refers to the formation of the state (*pada*).
Once this month is completed, if one becomes a worldly practitioner, they enter the stage of recitation; if one becomes a worldly teacher, this constitutes the initial month of recitation.

In the following month, one attains accomplishment within worldly dharmas; that is to say, by means of various medicinal substances perfected through the Dharma, one attains the power of hearing and retention such that what is heard once is never forgotten, and even powers, supernatural penetrations, clarities, and practices are all successfully accomplished, thereby attaining mastery over the great void.
If explained according to the supramundane meaning, this means that at the very moment of accomplishment, one is able to fulfill all aspirations.

Regarding the phrase "mountain peak and cow pen," as for the contemplative meaning: when performing the rite of accomplishment, it is like being upon a mountain; that is, one accords with the mountain of the Middle Way, such that every single matter accords with principle.
This refers to the immovable "Mountain Name," which is none other than the Great Bodhicitta.
Because it is the most ultimate point of this bodhicitta, it is called a "mountain peak.
It is like a person ascending a mountain; looking down from there, one perceives all things with complete clarity.
This Mountain of Dharma-nature is likewise; looking downward, one contemplates the dharma-realm’s perfect illumination and non-obstruction.
As for the "cow-pen," the cow is produced from the five purities; it can repel filth and remove obstacles, thereby accomplishing matters of purity.
Because it is nourished by the pure ox, the fine grass grows lushly and naturally.

This cow-pen of the bodhicitta is likewise: it can prevent the faults of discursive thought and discrimination, purifying the ground of the mind; when sprinkled with the water of great compassion upon this level ground, the merit that arises grows spontaneously.
The meaning of the two rivers has already been explained above.
As for the two rivers: that which flows and pours forth without ceasing is the stream of birth and death;
furthermore, that which is the quiescence of mind-moment after mind as it tends toward the great ocean of *dharmatā* is the supramundane stream.
Within this interval, it is the state of abiding in the sublime Middle Way, wherein one is capable of accomplishing the sublime siddhi.
As for the "four paths," this refers to the path of the Four Noble Truths.
"The single room" refers to the removal of all objective distinctions and abiding in the practice of suchness; this constitutes the room.
"The room of the Great Deity" refers to the room of nirvāṇa, by which the sovereign power of awakening is accomplished.
If one does not enter such a great celestial palace, how could one possibly achieve sovereign power?
As for the maṇḍala, its meaning is as explained above.
Its four corners form the shape of a three-pronged vajra, joined together on all sides; this is called the Vajra Palace.

If this is explained as a secret teaching, it is the great wisdom that none can destroy; for by means of that adamantine sublime wisdom, one binds the adamantine realm and protects the bodhicitta, thereby accomplishing all that is to be done.
Regarding "performing protection," this refers to protecting all matters by means of the Vajratuṇḍa of the Three Times and Acala.

To explain it according to principle: this Vajratuṇḍa of the Three Times and King Acala is none other than the Great Bodhicitta; it is capable of protecting all sentient beings and causing their roots of goodness to be accomplished with mastery.

That which is accomplished through the power of medicinal substances refers to the successful preparation of materials such as *vaidūrya* (azurite), *sarpis* (clarified butter), and *gorocanā* (bezoar), as explained in other passages.
That which is explained in terms of principle refers to the accomplishment of body, speech, and mind.
This refers to the manifestation of the "Swift Display of the Treasury of Inexhaustible Adornments of the Three Karmas," which brings to fruition all sentient beings within the *dharmadhātu*.

It is the nature of the Buddha-dharma that one first achieves accomplishment through phenomenal activities, and subsequently observes them with the great emptiness of pure wisdom; this is what constitutes supramundane accomplishment.
When the medicine and the mind achieve accomplishment, there are superior, middling, and inferior signs: sunrise is superior, midnight is middling, and the first watch of the night is inferior.
At this time, there are signs; one should know that according to the specific circumstances, these constitute the superior, middling, or inferior attainment.
The first watch of the night signifies the initial entry into what has not yet been realized.
Midnight signifies the meaning of bodhicitta; it refers to departing from darkness and turning toward light, yet it is not yet the Great Illumination itself.
The rising of the sun represents the aspect of fulfillment, like the Great Sun universally illuminating the world.

During this time, there may be the sound of *hūṃ*, or the sounds of various drums, or the shaking of the great earth; or one may hear wondrous sounds and various sublime signs that people delight to hear and which gladden the mind, whether occurring in the air or within the maṇḍala.
If these signs appear, one should know that this is the accomplishment of worldly *siddhi*.
To explain it according to principle, the fruit is attained at the point where each and every dharma accords; that is to say, the fruits of the Three Vehicles.

Or they turn the wheel of Dharma and attain great power, even to the extent of having a lifespan of countless years; they advance victoriously, roaming through space with pure eyes that shine brightly, possessing pure and unobstructed comprehension, a pure mind of universal knowledge, and a divine ear.
The above concludes the Chapter on Accomplishing the Worldly [Realms].

The Record of the Śramaṇa Aśvaghoṣa Ācārya, Part 6:
Chapter Six, "The Manifestation of Siddhi" (11–12). Chapter Six: The Manifestation of Siddhi.

"At that time, the World-Honored One again surveyed the great assembly; desiring to fulfill all vows, he further proclaimed the Dharma-phrases of the Perfect Wisdom of the Decisive Knowledge of the Immeasurable Gateways of the Three Times. This indicates that his observation of the great assembly was not without cause or condition.

First, one should observe those sentient beings with the Buddha-mind, examining their various types, characteristics, and essential natures to determine what Dharma they are capable of receiving and which kind of teaching would bring them benefit.
Having observed in this way, one should know that they will thereby attain realization and entry into each respective Dharma-gate.
It is for the purpose of explaining this that one first observes the capacities of the audience.

The "gateways of immeasurable, determinate wisdom regarding the three periods of time" refers to the gateways of immeasurable and unimpeded wisdom within a single thought-moment across the three periods of time.

The Buddha, through various skillful means, has preached this sublime Dharma; all sentient beings each attain certainty according to the gateway of wisdom appropriate to them. Since these gateways are immeasurable, it is called the "immeasurable gateways."
