The Buddhas, the ācāryas, and their companions each have their respective numerical proportions and methods;
one should inquire further about these.

Regarding the statement, "That which is accomplished through mantras is called siddhi": if one attains such an accomplishment, it is termed "accomplishment with conceptual differentiation" (savikalpa-siddhi).
Because these matters such as medicinal substances are still dharmas characterized by conceptualization, they are called "accomplishment with conceptualization.

Regarding the phrase "by means of conceptualizing medicinal substances, one accomplishes non-conceptuality," it means that through the cause of conceptualization, one attains the accomplishment of non-conceptuality.
This refers to the fact that conceptual discrimination serves as the cause.

Regarding the attainment of the fruit of non-conceptualization based upon this conceptual discrimination: although the fruit—which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), signless (*animitta*), inconceivable (*acintya*), and untainted (*anāsrava*)—is not produced by causes, it nonetheless takes conceptual discrimination as its cause and thereby brings about this fruit of non-attainment and the unconditioned.

“Lord of Secrets! All the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas currently residing in all worlds have attained mastery in the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*). Those Tathāgatas know that the intrinsic nature of all conceptualization is empty; yet, by the power of the perfection of skillful means, they manifest the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) through the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).”

"Successively corresponding with one another, they manifest throughout the entire dharma-realm for the sake of sentient beings" means that while this is an unconditioned fruit, it can be accomplished through conditioned skillful means; this is inconceivable.
The Buddhas of the three periods—present, future, and past—all preach this Dharma as one because they have thoroughly mastered the *pāramitā* of skillful means (*upāya*).
By citing the Buddhas of the three periods, it is intended to clarify that they all enter [to this realization] by means of this same method.
Although these conditioned expedient means are established, one realizes that the very nature of these discriminated phenomena is eternally empty.

Such phenomena arising through causes and conditions are free from arising and ceasing, annihilation and permanence, identity and difference, and coming and going; they are merely like illusions and transformations, no different from the Middle Way.
If one seeks a separate, unconditioned entity apart from this [conditioned world], it cannot be found; for the nature of the unconditioned is not different from the conditioned.
Because one thoroughly understands such profound dependent origination, one is able to realize that these very conditioned phenomena constitute the fruit of the unconditioned.

Therefore, by the power of skillful means, all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, although they have realized the dharma-realm, are able to manifest from this unconditioned and uncreated essence of fruition the various conditioned retinues.

Just as the Tathāgata Vairocana, through the power of his empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), manifests the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) by means of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) within this self-realized virtue—wherein the fundamental nature is itself non-active, yet it is precisely through activity that the unconditioned can be accomplished.

Regarding "successive correspondence": before one has performed the recitation, one's nature is fundamentally impure; through the practice of recitation, it becomes pure, enabling one to deliver sentient beings.

Thus, while manifesting an impure body, one further acts as a causal condition for the purification of others; this is called "mutual correspondence," which serves to demonstrate that conditioned phenomena arise from the unconditioned.

Therefore, ten world-microdust numbers of Vajra Bodhisattvas manifest, each one guiding and receiving sentient beings through the gateway of mantras, causing them all to attain the fruit of the unconditioned. This is it.
By these skillful means, they pervade the entire dharma-realm, universally responding to all sentient beings to enable them to attain benefit and profit.

"They cause [beings] to see the Dharma and dwell in peace and happiness, giving rise to a heart of joy; or they cause them to obtain long life and delightfully sport in the five desires, enjoying themselves as offerings made to the Buddha, the World-Honored One."

"Realizing such phrases, which cannot be believed by any worldly person, the Tathāgata, seeing this benefit, speaks with a joyful mind these rules for the sequence of the path of the Bodhisattva’s mantra practice" means that all Tathāgatas, through skillful means, do not abandon sentient beings from the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*) by means of their power of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*); they manifest the cultivation of various practices according to sentient beings, or cause them to see the Dharma abiding in the practice of peace and bliss, thereby giving rise to a joyful mind—this is the first stage of the joy of the Dharma (*dharmaprīti*).
Some attain long life, meaning they shall constantly behold the appearance of Buddhas throughout incalculable kalpas.
Some attain pure and excellent fivefold desires with which to enjoy themselves, and are furthermore able to make offerings to all Tathāgatas.
Those who lack skillful means cannot believe this matter.
They will think: "The essence of the mantra is identical to the dharma-realm—unconditioned and uncreated; how could it possibly accomplish such a thing?"
If such a thing were produced, it would be a conceptualization based on signs; how, then, could this be consistent with reason?
For this reason, [the Buddha] censured it.
To say that the Buddha’s words herein contain secrets difficult to understand is the claim of those lacking skillful means; therefore, they are unable to comprehend them.
However, within this context, mastery over the mind is spoken of as longevity; such a lifespan is precisely the life-force of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-life.

As for the "five desires," they refer to the four immeasurables and the bodhicitta; all noble ones delight in these phenomena of the present life and thereby make offerings to the Tathāgata—this is the true Dharma-offering to the Dharmakāya Buddha.

If a practitioner, relying on the Buddha’s skillful means of profound dependent origination, attains the accomplishment of worldly dharmas, and then contemplates their intrinsic emptiness therein, this is the accomplishment of the unconditioned.
Such an inconceivable dharma as this cannot be believed by ordinary beings themselves.

Nevertheless, because the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and Bodhisattvas perceive its beneficial significance, they have taught this path of the sequential stages of mantra practice; it must not be slandered as being non-existent.

"Why is this? That which could not be attained through the diligent cultivation of various ascetic practices over immeasurable kalpas is obtained by Bodhisattvas who practice the path of the mantra-gate in this very life. Thus, while other Bodhisattvas, for the sake of seeking the unsurpassed path, perform difficult and painful practices as if their heads were on fire, yet fail to attain such accomplishment even after immeasurable kalpas, [the mantra-practitioner succeeds].
If this practitioner of mantra-vidyā possesses skillful means, they may achieve the accomplishment of the holy ones.

Because they understand the meaning of the ten similes of profound dependent origination, they employ mantras and other methods to bring about various accomplishments without attachment; thus, they do not differ from the subtle and swift nature of such dharmas.
"Furthermore, O Lord of Mysteries!

A bodhisattva practicing the bodhisattva path through the gateway of mantras who thus performs the accomplishment (*sādhana*) by holding three *lakṣas* [of recitations] of such things as the *ketu-khaḍga*, the parasol, the sandals, the *cintāmaṇi*, the *añjana* medicine, and the *vairocana* [ointment], shall likewise attain *siddhi*. This next passage clarifies the medicinal substances to be accomplished.

That is to say, as previously mentioned, after first performing one hundred thousand recitations and then two months of further recitation, one constructs a maṇḍala; within it, one places the object thus produced and performs the recitation, completing the rite only after another hundred thousand recitations.
The positions of the deities in this maṇḍala are identical to those in the Great Compassion Womb (Mahākaruṇā-garbha), and therefore they are not described here.
One should simply place the object to be accomplished in the center and position the Tathāgata Vairocana in the cardinal and intermediate directions; this is certain. Thus it is asked.
The banner has a bamboo shaft wrapped in clean silk cloth, extending downward for one zhang or more; it is shaped like a pennant with tiered forms at the top, upon which a *vajra* is placed.
However, knives are made with tempered steel and bone handles.
Umbrellas are categorized as superior, middling, and inferior, being made of gold, silver, or peacock feathers respectively.

Footwear is made of leather; first, it is washed with various substances until it is utterly clean and odorless, then treated with medicinal preparations until it cannot be burned by fire and becomes intensely fragrant, only then is it fit for use.
One should take pure and excellent jewels as desired and place them atop the banner.
Eye medicine is prepared using *añjana*; there are two kinds of this *añjana*:
one is extremely light and rises against the current when placed in water. [The other is] ... (further inquiry).
Regarding cow bezoar, there are furthermore immeasurable medicinal substances—namely azurite, cinnabar, realgar, orpiment, and so forth—all of which can be accomplished.
Moreover, immeasurable objects such as the vajra and others may also be accomplished.
The *Mahāmūla-tantra* fully explains the methods and procedures, and the *Susiddhi-tantra* likewise possesses a systematic sequence.
Just as one can walk upon shoes once they have been completed, so too may one ride them to travel through Buddha-fields without obstruction.

As for the accomplishment of eye salves and the like, one immediately beholds the Buddha-fields of the ten directions and is able to travel through those Buddha-fields of the ten directions by soaring through the air.
The rest is understandable.

Furthermore, if one draws various forms of birds and beasts and, having selected any one of them, performs the ritual procedure, one will be capable of traveling at will to the Buddha-fields of the ten directions.
Alternatively, one may empower a boy or girl with the Dharma so that they achieve accomplishment as attendants; such a person will then travel to the lands of the ten directions.
In the west, there was one person who attained accomplishment and led five hundred people to ascend into the air and depart, their destination unknown.
When this rite is accomplished, one becomes a vidyādhara.
This object can be produced according to one's heart's desire.
Furthermore, while reciting the mantra, one attains the meditative state (viṣaya) that enables the creation of such and such objects.
Alternatively, one may accomplish this by directing the mind to create these objects, and it will likewise be achieved.
As the Sūtra says: "O Lord of Secrets!

If a son or daughter of good family possesses skillful means, whatever they seek to accomplish according to their desire, they shall achieve it through mastery over their own mind. What the world cannot believe, that person attains; such a person is called an achiever (*siddha*).

One can attain all things that are otherwise unbelievable and marvelous; therefore, it is said that if sons and daughters of good family possess the skillful means and desire to seek what they wish for, they will achieve accomplishment solely through the mastery of their own minds. In this way alone is success attained.

Regarding the statement that "his own mind is sovereign" and that "only in this way is accomplishment achieved," this means that whatever one desires according to one's will is accomplished simply through the transformation of the mind alone.
"Only" (kevala) signifies that one employs only one's own mind, without depending on any other conditions.
"Only" (*kevalam*) also carries the sense of "momentarily"; it means that as soon as the mind forms the thought, [the goal] is accomplished. "O Lord of Secrets!

Regarding those who desire the causes and effects [of worldly pleasures], the secret dharma—the characteristics of the mantras of all mantras—is not something that can be known by those foolish persons. This refers to if a person, within this practice of mantra (*mantracaryā*), should form such a thought:
"I am now performing such causes and shall obtain such results"—
know that this is not a correct teaching, but is merely the false conceptualization of a fool.

Why is this? There are certain non-Buddhists who claim that all phenomena arise from a self; thus, if [the self] is pleased with such sovereignty, it bestows [results], and if it is not pleased, it does not bestow them.
People such as these cannot understand this Way.

According to [the principle of] "should," all things would arise from causes; if they arise from causes, then those causes must possess a nature (*svabhāva*). If there were an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), one would fall into the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*).
How can a permanent dharma give rise to anything?
If the cause perishes and the effect arises, it would be a dharma of annihilation; how then could it give rise to anything?
As the Sūtra says: "When it is said that the cause is not an agent, its effect does not arise. The intent of this is to clarify that the cause is empty of inherent existence.
Since causes themselves are empty, how can there be effects?
Therefore, this is extensively refuted in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
One should know that these causes, when examined with wisdom, cannot even have their origin found.
This cause lacks a basis; that which lacks a basis is inherently unborn. How can a cause that is inherently unborn produce an effect?
Therefore, the effect is likewise inherently unborn.
The Sūtra states: "If this cause is itself empty, how can there be a fruit? This means to clarify that the cause is not substantially real.
Since the cause is not ultimately real, it can never produce a real fruit; one should know, therefore, that the fruit is fundamentally unarisen.
Furthermore, since the nature of causes is empty and quiescent, one should know that the characteristics of effects are likewise so.

To speak of there being causes and effects within such dependently originated phenomena is merely a construction of false imagination (*parikalpita*); it falls into the extremes of nihilism or eternalism, or identity or difference, and does not enter the Middle Way.
Therefore, it is realized that such mantras, being eternally free from causes and karma, are themselves the *dharmadhātu* and the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*).

As the Sūtra states: "One should know that the fruit of mantra is entirely free from causes and karma. This clarifies that because causes are phenomena produced through volitional action (*abhisamskāra*), and since the cause involves action, one should know that the fruit likewise involves what is produced.
Since there is that which is produced, how can it be established as reality?
One should know that the fruit is distinct from its causes and karmic actions.

As the Sūtra says: "Even the bodily realization of contact with the signless samādhi"—this refers to the fact that such characteristics of cause and effect exist only through deluded conceptualization.
The fundamental nature of correct observation is non-abiding; because it is non-abiding, the essence of the fruit does not arise, which is identical to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Therefore, if a practitioner should think:
"I shall recite mantras and cultivate the practice of mantra, and thereby attain the realization of the fruit."
"This is merely self-deception.

If these true mantras arise from conditions, they are in reality without action; from the very beginning, they are fundamentally the Dharma-realm—without birth or extinction, neither pure nor defiled."
Since the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is thus, how can it be accomplished?

As the Sūtra says, "The practitioner of mantras shall attain *siddhi*, for it arises from the mind," one should know that the practitioner of mantra-rites merely purifies their own mind through skillful means.
If one’s three karmas are pure, one will naturally attain clarity within this state and achieve self-awakening.

It is like a person who, while dreaming, practices the various six perfections and purifies buddha-fields; yet upon waking, no signs of having achieved results are seen—there is only the myriad practices of cause and effect within the mind of a single moment of ignorance.

Furthermore, it is like a treasure trove within a dark room: if one employs skillful means to light a bright lamp, although the causes and conditions that produce and extinguish it cannot be found upon analysis—being fundamentally identical to emptiness—the Dharma nevertheless arises spontaneously. By means of the clarity of the mind regarding these causes and conditions, one perceives the treasure trove; yet this treasure trove is not produced by those skillful means.

Those who cultivate the practice of mantra are fundamentally seeking to eliminate delusion and karma; they should realize within their own being that the dharma-realm is devoid of arising and ceasing, pure and yet not defiled, and free from all conceptual discrimination, knowing that the essence of this mantra is itself the essence of the dharma-realm.

If one realizes that the essence of the mantra is identical to the Dharma-realm and equal to great emptiness, one will naturally attain the signless samādhi; therefore, the siddhis will manifest before one, and one should give rise to such faith and understanding.
Next, "At that time, Vajrapāṇi again addressed the Buddha, saying:
'World-Honored One!

We pray that you will further explain the phrases of Perfect Enlightenment and the phrases for the accomplishment of siddhi. This refers to what was explained above: how a single syllable can give rise to four syllables, even unto pervading the entire Dharma-realm; this is precisely the phrase of the Buddha’s Mind.
Now, I shall explain the method for accomplishment herein.

"When these sons and daughters of good family behold this Dharma, their minds attain joy, they dwell in peaceful bliss, and they do not harm the Dharma-realm"—this refers to those who practice awakening in accordance with this [Dharma]; if they achieve accomplishment, it is called "seeing the Dharma."
"Accomplishment" refers to attaining the vision of the truths (*dṛṣṭadharma*) in this very life.

Those who have seen the Dharma, upon hearing the Buddha teach this method of accomplishment, will surely experience profound joy in the Dharma (*dharmaprīti*), abide in the practice of peace and happiness, and dwell in the bliss of the present life; therefore, they inquire about it.
"Not harming the dharma-realm" means that within this dharma-realm there is nothing that can be obstructed.

Even when experiencing various worldly pleasures, those worldly pleasures are themselves the dharma-realm; one never, because of them, obstructs or harms the dharma-realm, and thus it is "not harming."
"For what reason?
World-Honored One!
The dharma-realm is that which all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas declare to be the inconceivable realm."
Therefore, World-Honored One!

For those bodhisattvas who practice the bodhisattva path through the gateway of mantras and attain this "penetration of the dharma-realm that cannot be divided or destroyed," these four characters are ultimately perfected and do not conflict with the dharma-realm.
These four phrases are all the Buddha-mind; how could the Buddha-mind obstruct the dharma-realm?
One who abides in this accomplishment is non-dual and undifferentiated from the dharma-realm; therefore, there is no obstruction.
This siddhi and that dharmadhātu are entirely without mutual obstruction.
Why is this? Because the dharmadhātu is inconceivable.
Therefore, although immeasurable Buddhas attain the Way and achieve fulfillment, the dharma-realm does not increase;
although immeasurable sentient beings are brought to extinction, the dharma-realm does not decrease.
Even if sentient beings advance toward excellence, there is no addition; even if they destroy their afflictions, there is no subtraction.
It is also because the nature of the inconceivable realm is identical to a vajra and cannot be destroyed.
If there were obstructions, there would be "this" and "that"; where there is "this" and "that," there can be destruction.
Since there is currently no obstruction, it cannot be destroyed.
One should know that this indestructibility also carries the meaning of being indivisible.
That is to say, various gateways and various mundane and supramundane phenomena are of one single dharma-realm; they cannot be analyzed or divided so as to become separate entities.
If a practitioner can thus penetrate this, it is the attainment of the realization of the Dharma.
The World-Honored One addressed Vajrapāṇi, Lord of Secrets, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, Lord of Secrets!"

Regarding the phrase, "It is well that you have again been able to ask the Tathāgata about such a meaning," this clarifies that the Vajradhara Lord of Secrets is praised once more because he has raised such a question out of compassion for those of the future who practice the path of mantra and conduct.
"Listen attentively, reflect upon it well, and I shall now expound it"—this statement is spoken by the Teacher to the entire assembly, meaning:
"Listen attentively, reflect upon it well, and I shall explain such matters for you."
When the Lord of Secrets said,
“So be it, World-Honored One!
I wish and desire to hear [it],” he reiterated that the Tathāgata’s compassion is all-pervasive, and having affirmed this inquiry, he proceeded to provide the explanation.
"The Buddha told Guhyapati:
'Accomplishment is performed by means of the letter-gateway A'—this refers to the method of accomplishment within the phrase of Perfect Enlightenment."

Regarding the phrase "whether in a monastery residence, within a mountain cave, or in a pure chamber," the preferred locations according to one's inclination and their secret interpretation have already been set forth above.
"Spread the letter A throughout all limbs and perform three lakṣas of recitation" means that one should mentally project this letter A.

Starting from the crown of the head and the eyes, ears, and so forth, until it pervades all internal and external parts of the body, one accomplishes the rite by reciting this letter three lakṣas of times.
Furthermore, it is said:
the deity, the seed-syllable, and the *maṇḍala* (perfect luminosity) constitute the triad.
The syllable resides within the *maṇḍala*, and the *maṇḍala* rests upon the heart of the deity; when one of these is visualized as perfected, all three are spontaneously accomplished.
Because these take those three objects as their focus, they are called the three *lakṣas*.
*Lakṣa* has the meaning of "vision.
Having recited these three *lakṣas*, one reaches the fifteenth day of the waxing moon, which is the full moon; there, one completes the recitation of the three *lakṣas* according to the text.
"Next, on the full moon, one should offer everything one possesses as an act of worship" means that one constructs the maṇḍala for accomplishment on the fifteenth day of the waxing moon.
When performing this rite, one should offer all that one possesses as an offering to the Triple Gem; this constitutes the rite of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
While performing the rite of accomplishment, one should also recite these syllables; the secret exposition is as previously explained.
"When performing this rite, Bodhisattvas such as Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, and Vajrapāṇi, or other noble deities, may appear before you, touch your head with their hands, and exclaim:
'Excellent, O practitioner!'"
This commentary explains:
"Or other vajras" means that this cannot be fixed as a single standard; whichever deity arrives serves for the sake of accomplishment.
Nevertheless, when they are seen, they are also described in terms of superior, middling, and inferior signs.
If one sees [the deity] clearly and distinctly, no different from being face-to-face, it is the highest accomplishment;
if one merely hears the voice appearing before them to provide instruction, benefit, and joy, it is the middling accomplishment;
if one sees [them] in a dream and so forth, it is the lowest accomplishment.

Furthermore, when one perceives differences such as clarity or obscurity in the vision, one knows that there are obstructions or an absence thereof; this esoteric teaching is to be grasped through the mind.

Thus, when the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity) and others manifest before one and bestow their grace, one "should prostrate and pay homage, and offer *argha* water. This refers to the water of incense and flowers, to which the five jewels, grains, and so forth have been added, as described above.
“Immediately, one attains the samādhi of the non-forgetfulness of the bodhicitta.
Because the practitioner has attained this samādhi, their body and mind both attain pliancy; pliancy refers to the removal of defilements and hindrances.

Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, by reciting and practicing with such physical and mental pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), one shall accordingly attain purity of mind and purity of body," this means that through the application of this very pliancy in the cultivation of mindfulness and the intensive retention of recitation, the five faculties, beginning with the body, become pure.
As stated in the "Chapter on the Six Faculties," all myriad phenomena are seen, and one is able to know the Buddha-mind and so forth.
Because body and mind are pure, one attains birth according to [one's intent]; the mind-made body (manomaya-kāya) arises in accordance with thought.
"Taking rebirth as the cause and recitation as the purification, one immediately attains the purity of body and mind associated with that rebirth.

Regarding the statement, "If one places it upon the ear and maintains it, one shall attain purity of the auditory faculty," this explains that if a practitioner desires purity of the auditory faculty, they should visualize the letter *A* spread across their auditory faculty and then perform recitation; thus, they immediately attain purity of the auditory faculty and the power of hearing and retaining without forgetting. They will be able to hear the teachings spoken by the Buddhas of the ten directions, as well as the sounds of devas and others, just as described in the *Lotus Sūtra*.
The Sūtra states: "By means of the gateway of the letter A, one performs inhalation and exhalation, contemplating it during the three periods [of the day].

At that time, the practitioner is able to maintain the recitation, and their lifespan will endure for long kalpas. This clarifies that the letter A is the gateway of the bodhicitta, which is neither arising nor ceasing.

If one wishes to dwell for a long duration of life, one should contemplate the syllable *A* as being identical to the inhalation and exhalation; that is, one should take this syllable as the inhalation and exhalation, ensuring that the breaths are distinct and uninterrupted.
If one who has a short lifespan contemplates in this manner, reflecting upon it three times each day, they will immediately attain a long life.
Regarding the "secret teaching," the syllables, the phrases, and the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity) constitute the three times.
If one wishes to subdue all poisons, one should visualize this letter A, either upon oneself or another, as being within the body.

If one is like a sovereign, one should visualize this letter at the location where the poison resides; it gradually pervades the parts of the body and drives the poison downward. As the poison gradually descends, the letter follows it; once it has been completely expelled, the poison is eliminated.
There are two kinds of poison:
first, the poison of material substances;
second, the poison of sentient beings, which refers to the venom of dragons, snakes, and the like.
Regarding the "secret teaching," "poison" refers to the three poisons.
When the three poisons are rampant and one wishes to eliminate them, one should proceed as previously described, meaning to pursue them until they are completely exhausted.
As for the phrase "wishing to be loved and respected by kings and others," this means that one employs the letter-gateway *a-ha* to transform those who are to be saved.
That is to say, if one wishes to cause others to feel affection and to take refuge [in oneself], one should visualize the syllable *A* as one's own body and the syllable *Ha* as the other's body.

One visualizes holding a conch (*śaṅkha*) with one's own body, and further visualizes holding a lotus flower with that [other] body. As the two look at each other, they recite this syllable *A* within their minds.
Even if they are angry or arrogant, they will likewise be subdued by their own loving heart.

As for the secret teaching: if one wishes to subdue their mind, one should visualize oneself as the syllable *A*, visualize the heart as the syllable *Ha*, and imagine a lotus at the heart and a conch (*śaṅkha*) in the hand; by causing these to accord with one another, one is able to subdue them.
Even those who are entirely difficult to subdue can be subdued; this refers to the primary afflictions (*kleśa*) and their secondary derivatives (*upakleśa*).
The Buddha further addressed Vajrapāṇi:

"The Tathāgatas possess a mind-born [being] named 'Acting Out Playful Movements' (*karmakrīḍānartaka*), which arises from the mental karma of the Buddha's heart. It performs various playful movements and manifests various types of dramatic dance-like appearances."
This refers to the Universal Manifestation Body (sarvarūpasaṃdarśana-kāya), which assumes the forms of the six realms of existence according to their respective types.
"Dance" refers to various miraculous transformations and illusory feats; as these manifest according to specific circumstances, their varieties are so numerous that they cannot be fully described.

The four elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—sustain and maintain this body, manifesting both its internal and external environments and their inhabitants. Nevertheless, this is the Mind-King abiding in a manner identical to space; for space is eternally unmoving yet contains and accommodates all things.
Therefore, it arises solely from the mental karma of the Buddha; it exists in accordance with the mind, its essence is identical to emptiness, and it cannot be grasped.

"Seeing" refers to the various appearances of dance and play, while "not seeing" refers to the principle of *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, "seeing" refers to the fruits of the mundane world, while "not seeing" refers to the fruit of *bodhi*.
These types are immeasurable; therefore, they are called "vast.

Furthermore, one sees them practicing various Dharma-gates of the Three Vehicles, fulfilling their respective aspirations; this is precisely the ability to manifest all manner of visible and invisible phenomena.

Even for the numerous jewels of dharma-gates such as meditative concentration and wisdom that they may seek and pray for, [the Buddha] manifests them according to their respective types and bestows them upon them.
It is just like the sovereign wish-fulfilling jewel, which grants everything according to whatever the mind desires.

"Samāhita" means meditative equipoise (*samāhita*); it refers to the arising of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth while in equipoise, not merely the state of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
"Then, after Vairocana Buddha had observed the entire great assembly, he addressed the Lord of Secrets, Vajrapāṇi, as explained above."
"Vajrapāṇi performs the dance; all things are accomplished as the vast fruit of creation and destruction, bestowing everything directly. Here, "dance" refers to play.

Furthermore, he universally manifests form-bodies (*rūpakāya*) to skillfully bring about results according to the various types of beings, manifesting in diverse responses. These are not real, but are merely like illusions; therefore, it is called the "Dance of the Tathāgata."
It is like a dancer who can delight the hearts of the multitude; though their various understandings differ, he causes them all to find joy in their hearts.
The Buddha is also like this: he is not produced by the matter of the four elements, but arises in accordance with the Buddha’s own mind.
Arising from the mind and ceasing within the mind, though it is an eternal dharma, it is able to arise and cease in accordance with conditions.
Because this emergence and disappearance follow conditions, they are called the fruits of arising and ceasing; that is to say, formation and destruction.
These traces pervade the entire dharma-realm, being vast and boundless; thus they are called "vast.
Once manifested, they subsequently cease; thus they are called "formation and destruction.
Regarding this vast formation and destruction, this very formation carries the meaning of transformation, and therefore there is destruction.

However, this process of formation and destruction is precisely the wondrous response of the Tathāgata; it arises from the Dharma-realm through the resonance of sentient beings' capacities. Although it arises, it does not arise; although it perishes, it does not perish. It is identical to an illusion, for it is not different from the Dharma-realm.
Because its performance is not real, it is called "dancing.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time perform this dance.

Regarding "intimately bestowing upon all": I personally received this Dharma from the Buddhas of the past, and now I again personally bestow it upon you; therefore, it is said that it is "intimately bestowed upon all."
Regarding the term "intimate" (*sākṣāt*): it means that one is intimately able to manifest and bestow the fruits of all one's aspirations;

this is the correct meaning. Regarding the phrase "first performing the true aspect": as previously observed, one contemplates the seed-syllable mantra and the deity. By contemplating and beholding the deity, and having beheld them, one immediately transforms one's own body into the deity. These states are mutually identical and do not obstruct one another; this is precisely seeing the fruit of the Vajra, which is the bodhicitta. Therefore, it is called "first performing the true aspect."
To abide in this successive order means that the mind dwells securely based upon what was previously contemplated;
it is because one has already perceived the true reality, which is the letter A.
The Sūtra states, "Just as previously correctly contemplated," which means to recollect and maintain the dharmas through contemplation as described in the preceding text.
One forms the letter A for oneself, adding a dot to make it wide; all is yellow and extremely pleasing to the mind.
Within the four-cornered vajra-mark, one should contemplate the syllable *ra*, which is the light of all Buddhas in every respect.

Regarding what is said here concerning the self-nature of all these Buddhas: one should visualize the syllable *a* as being deep yellow in color, with a form that is upright, majestic, and pleasing to the mind, situated within one’s own heart.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the sūtra says that adding points makes it broad" (*bīja*): this means placing dots upon the syllable; "increasing" is synonymous with "broadening.

One constructs a four-cornered vajra railing around the exterior of the syllable; this railing is identical to a three-pronged vajra, with the prongs interlacing one another, and the syllable is placed within it.

Having visualized this syllable A, one immediately transforms this syllable into the form of the Vairocana Honzon; that is, one's own body manifests as an image identical to the Honzon, and this image is formed precisely according to the fundamental mudrā.

This Buddha’s entire body is radiant; he is the Buddha of the true mark perceived within the mind of bodhi, like seeing the image of pure gold within clear lapis lazuli, and is not the same as the deluded thoughts within other mental factors.
One should know that such a vision is precisely the vision of the Buddha who is the true reality of the mind.
If one who accomplishes this is free from doubt and anxiety, they will be able to universally bring great benefit to all sentient beings.
The Sūtra says, "That which is vast and marvelous" refers to being like an illusory person, meaning there are various extraordinary occurrences.

It is like the great Bodhisattvas who, according to their own inclinations, perform deeds to benefit sentient beings; like illusions, mirages, or the moon reflected in water, they respond to the myriad categories of beings, and all things are thereby accomplished.
This is the phrase of the Tathāgata’s illusion-like samādhi.

If one can practice in this way, the evil karma accumulated since beginningless birth, the fruits of oppression within the three realms of existence, and even the grave karma of the Avīci hell, shall be extinguished in this very life; how much more so for other [lesser karmas].
To state it briefly: the various sufferings of the three realms of existence and their karmic fruits are all extinguished. Why is this?
Because the practitioner, by abiding in the stage of *samāhita*, contemplates suchness (*tathatā*) and thereby becomes free from suffering.
The Sūtra states: "If one contemplates that mind, it is the unsurpassed bodhicitta. This refers to the contemplative practitioner contemplating the unsurpassed bodhicitta within their own mind.
What is called "mind" is precisely the unsurpassed Great Bodhicitta.
If one abides in this contemplation, one is able to purify the actions of body, speech, and mind.
Because one is able to purify these actions, one becomes detached from both pure and impure karma.
The commentary states:
"There is such karma that arises, which neither purity nor impurity can defile.
The Sūtra speaks of "karma of the future," meaning the karma for producing this pure mind in a future life.
None of these fruits can defile it.
Why? Because it is always in accord with principle.
For example, although a lotus flower grows from within the mud, it is not defiled by it.
In this same way, the practitioner is identical to all Buddhas.
Why is this? Because it is able to give birth to all Tathāgatas;
this is none other than the Buddha, the Honored One among benevolent beings.
The meaning is this:
if one merely contemplates the bodhicitta, one already attains the fruit of the Tathāgata; how much more so when the body manifests realization and becomes a Buddha.

Furthermore, at that time, Vairocana Tathāgata again dwelt in the *vajra-līlā-samādhi* of subduing the four māras; having subdued the four māras and liberated the six realms of existence, he spoke the vajra syllables that fulfill all-knowledge wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to subdue the four māras;
it can eliminate the afflictions, karma, and suffering of the six destinies and bestow the bliss of liberation; furthermore, it can fulfill all the aspirations of both ordinary beings and sages.
The Buddha, abiding in this samādhi, expounded the meaning of the Vajra-phrase mantra; these five syllables are the mantra-phrase for subduing the four māras.
"A" is activity, namely the activity of primordial non-arising.
The two dots on the side signify the meaning of purification; by this meaning, one can subdue the four māras and eliminate all suffering.
"Taste" (rasa) signifies bondage; adding a stroke above it constitutes the samādhi of non-liberation, which is the inconceivable liberation.
*Ra* signifies the purification of the six sense faculties; because the six sense faculties are purified, there are no sensory objects (*viṣaya*).
The meaning of *ha* has already been explained above, and the meaning of *kha* also has its explanation in the section above.
Furthermore, the syllable HŪṂ has three meanings, which are the three liberations of the Tathāgata.
Because one practices to eliminate obstacles, one abides in the Great Emptiness through these three liberations.
The "deficiency" refers to the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*).

When the Buddha spoke this mantra, Vajrapāṇi, Samantabhadra, and others attained the unprecedented opening of their eyes as described above, and they prostrated themselves before the All-Knowing One (*sarvajña*). Thus they spoke: "The All-Knowing One is the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena; that is to say, the Tathāgatas."
"All" (*sarva*) refers herein to the Sanskrit term meaning "without deficiency," which carries the sense of a treasury.
It is said that these five syllables constitute the treasury, capable of fulfilling all forms of wealth.
"All Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Saviors of the World"—this refers to all these Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Saviors of the World.
"Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas who have destroyed [defilements]"—this praises the virtues of the Śrāvakas, meaning they have destroyed the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and so forth.
Another interpretation states:
*sura* means "one who harms afflictions.

Regarding the phrase "capable of traversing all grounds and manifesting various supernatural powers," "wealth" refers to the Dharma-treasure of the Tathāgata, which is never exhausted even when bestowed upon all sentient beings.
Such an inexhaustible treasury of great wisdom is therefore called "the one possessed of abundant wealth.

Because the wealth of the Dharma enables one to bestow upon all, this gateway of mantras is taught; from the Buddhas above down to the śrāvakas below, there are none who do not rely on these words to perform various miraculous transformations and benefit all beings.
Therefore, it is said that various supernatural powers (ṛddhibala) manifest according to the stages of practice traversed.
"Stages of practice" refers to wherever one travels; as the verse says: "Searching through lands, mountains, and forests, there is none equal."

Regarding the statement, "He attains supreme wisdom; the Buddha-wisdom is supreme wisdom," this refers not merely to supernatural powers alone; rather, by virtue of these words, all noble sages attain wisdom, even unto the attainment of the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).

However, the wisdom of the two vehicles is also termed "unsurpassed" in comparison to the mundane world; it is for this reason that the Buddha’s unsurpassed nature is clarified here once more, and thus it is stated again.
Having first offered praise, he subsequently requested the teaching of these five characters concerning the Buddha, which are then explained in detail in successive order.
Regarding the various types such as the visualization of the letter *bu* (*布*) and so forth that were not previously mentioned, these are all now requested to be explained herein.

Concerning the formation of the letters *bu*, *xiang* (*想*), and *shang*, *zhong*, *xia* (upper, middle, lower), as well as the distinctions in their colors, functions, and various skillful means, we request the Buddha to expound upon them extensively.
To achieve, advance toward, and practice this Dharma through various gateways is called "teaching.
To request that he himself explain this teaching means to entreat the Buddha to personally expound it.

If the Buddha were to explain this Dharma extensively, those who practice the supreme mantra path of the Mahāyāna would come to see the Dharma; and those who have already seen it would likewise all rejoice.
"Seeing the Dharma" refers to its realization.
"One should abide therein" means that having seen it for oneself, one further imparts it to all sentient beings.
Because by seeing this matter both self and others obtain the supreme benefit of the Dharma, he requests the Buddha to explain it extensively.
This sutra consists of three thousand five hundred verses, which explain the meaning of these five characters.
*Samādhi* (三摩醯多) correctly signifies the sense of dwelling the mind upon a single object.
The Buddha, wishing to proclaim the vajra-words so that the entire assembly might dwell within the state of a single mind and listen,
first desired to establish the method for accomplishing this vajra-mantra by having them construct a vajra-seat.
Just as when the Buddha first desired to attain enlightenment, he was at the Vajrāsana site;
even after removing this seat, there would be no other seat capable of surpassing it in excellence.
At that time, the Great Vajra extended from the earth to the very limits of the earth.
This empowerment of the lower body at the limit of the earth was intended to explain the letter A.
Its meaning is as follows:
This syllable is most excellent; it is the foremost of all syllables.
As for "empowerment" (adhiṣṭhāna), because he now wishes to expound this Dharma, he first empowers his own body.
Next, one contemplates the lower body; that is, one visualizes everything from one's own navel downward as being composed entirely of pure vajra.
This has both internal and external aspects. The internal refers to what was described above;
the external refers to visualizing oneself seated within a square vajra mandala, the layout and railings of which have already been described above.
That which is named Mahendra is the most adamantine among adamants; it can shatter adamant, yet adamant cannot shatter it.
Furthermore, it is an intense yellow, like the color of purple-polished gold.
One should contemplate the syllable *A* as being this [color], which is called the Vajra-wheel.
Contemplating all things within this seat is the seat of yoga; this is the place where those who practice according to principle sit.
This refers to contemplating all things; that is to say, all matters are contemplated and enacted within this [state].
Because the matters are numerous, they are called "all.
Thus ends the first explanation of the letter A as the seat.
Next, the long vowel *ā* is explained; this is the first life-force (*prāṇa*) of *a*.
Because it can sustain all syllables, it is called "life.
If the syllable *a* did not exist, no other syllables would arise; therefore, it is the primary life-force.

This is the phrase for summoning. If one contemplates this syllable as being able to summon, the long *ā* is itself practice (*caryā*). If one touches the syllable *ā*, it draws forth the practice of all Buddhas; therefore, it is called "summoning."
To "summon" (*saṃgraha*) all internal and external phenomena means to summon them so that they are brought under one's own control for the purpose of being utilized with mastery.
This gateway of the letter *A* is able to summon all the merits of the Tathāgatas and cause them to return to one's own person, and it is also able to fulfill all practices.
Next, the syllable *Aṃ* is explained: if one visualizes this syllable, it can gather and eliminate all poisons, diseases, and other obstacles;
it can gather and remove all internal and external hindrances.
Internal obstacles refer to various factors that obstruct the Path; as long as they are present, this [power] can eliminate them all.
External obstacles refer to all external objects acting as obstructions; these too it can entirely remove.
Furthermore, it eliminates all poisons and diseases; "diseases" refers to those of various kinds, all of which it can remove.
Moreover, as for its power to eliminate, even in cases of losing one's mind, it can rescue them and cause them to regain their original state of mind.
Furthermore, by means of this syllable, one can concentrate the mind on a single object and swiftly attain correspondence with samādhi.
If one visualizes this syllable, one obtains the aforementioned merits.
Regarding the phrase "one who can grant all," "granting" refers to fulfilling one's wishes and bestowing the fruit of siddhi.
If the practitioner, for one month, binds the Vajra-Wisdom Mudrā and recites the syllable *Aṃ*,
performing this three times daily throughout that month, the entire city of ignorance shall be destroyed.
All sentient beings are entangled by ignorance; the four enclosures are as solid and firm as a fortified city, impossible to destroy, yet through this gateway of letters, they can be destroyed.
"Attaining immovable firmness" means that one cannot be destroyed by gods, humans, asuras, and so forth.
Whenever one wishes to perform any act of augmentation, one always sits upon this seat.
"Augmentation" (*vṛddhi*) is also called "fulfillment," meaning that it can fulfill all aspirations.
If explained esoterically, "one month" refers to "one vision.
If one attains this vision of the Dharma, one enters the first stage (*bhūmi*), whereby all samādhis, dhāraṇīs, and the various stages are spontaneously augmented.
When one wishes to perform this rite of augmentation, the practitioner, within this vajra maṇḍala, should visualize the Buddha abiding in a samādhi-body of true golden color.
"Radiant flame" (*jvālā*) carries the meaning of majestic splendor (*tejas*).
That which possesses majestic splendor is simultaneously the elucidation of the meaning of the Honored One (*devatā*);
such is the Sanskrit sound. This refers to the encircling flames with hair forming a crown; this is the Great Indra (*Mahendra*).
This solidity of the great vajra is the meaning of the Buddha’s wisdom;
it can shatter all that cannot be removed by others.
Visualize this Buddha within the square vajra maṇḍala, and one may accomplish all siddhis at will.
Regarding the scriptural passage "Vajra, Lotus, and so forth," it means that all such matters should be performed within this wheel.
If one seeks to accomplish the Vajra-dharma, one should fashion a five-pronged [vajra] out of pure gold, place it within the maṇḍala, and perform consecration.
The superior, middling, and inferior accomplishments regarding the conch-shell and other implements are also as described above; that is to say, one should in all cases recite this syllable AṂ.
If one wishes to accomplish the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa, one should fashion the uṣṇīṣa out of pure gold and apply this rite.
If it is successfully accomplished, it is identical to the body of the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana.
Alternatively, one need not employ separate substances; simply visualize yourself with sovereign mastery as the Buddha-body and empower it. If it is accomplished, it is identical to the Buddha-body.
If one performs the Vajra-sādhana, the practitioner who maintains the recitation becomes identical to the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi.
As for the Lotus: having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus and so forth out of gold, if one performs the recitation therein and achieves success, one becomes identical to Avalokiteśvara.
Regarding the sword, there is a specific method for its formation; once it is accomplished, one becomes identical to the youth Mañjuśrī.
Regarding the goose, if the ritual procedure is accomplished, one’s own body is transformed into the body of Brahmā.

Regarding the accomplishment of external wealth—whether it be gold, or earth and earth referring to hidden treasures (*nidhi*), or wish-fulfilling jewels (*cintāmaṇi*) and the like—all those things associated with increase (*puṣṭi*) are to be accomplished using this method; it contains methods of the superior, middling, and inferior grades.
Regarding the statement "the contemplation of Mahendra," it refers to contemplating within the golden wheel.
*The Commentary on the Mahāvairocana Sūtra*, Fascicle Eleven;
*The Commentary on the Mahāvairocana Sūtra*, Fascicle Twelve.
The Remainder of the Sixth Chapter, "The Appearance of Siddhi," from the *Record of the Śramaṇa Acala-ācārya*.

Furthermore, regarding the methods of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), such as those previously mentioned for the empowerment of the winds and so forth, the application of the seven points and other rites has not yet been fully exhausted; these shall now be explained in their entirety herein.
Whatever acts as an obstacle to the path, all are rendered immovable by means of this method.
Regarding "all as a single object," it means causing the mind to abide in its entirety as the very essence.

To perform this rite, first visualize Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, with eight peaks; that is, imagine mountain peaks surrounding it on all four sides. Upon these eight peaks, visualize lotus flowers, and upon each flower, visualize a three-pronged vajra with its prongs pointing upward.
The Sūtra states, "Place it upon his crown," which refers to the upper end of the vajra.
Looking upward, one should visualize the letter A above it, surrounded by blazing light and flames.
Having visualized in this manner, all obstacles will be gathered and eliminated.
In this way, one gathers that [mind] and causes it to abide in a single object so that it cannot be moved.
This is not merely "Immovable Honored One" (Acala), but rather the sense of being firmly established; it means practicing the path with mastery and according to one's will, without obstruction.

Furthermore, regarding the methods for accomplishing medicinal substances: whenever one wishes to accomplish such things as these, there are complete sequential ritual applications; here, however, I have merely briefly clarified the general principles.
When preparing medicine, add the mantra one hundred times; generally, whenever "one hundred" is mentioned, it means adding eight times more.
Having recited it, one may drink it oneself or give it to others; it can eliminate all illnesses, even those resulting from past karma.
Generally, all matters of augmentation correspond with the yellow color of Vajra.
Next, the gateway of the syllable *va* is explained; this is the aforementioned syllable *va* (𑖠), first clarifying its essential form and subsequently including the stroke of samādhi.
Regarding this visualization: one should conceive of this syllable as being purely white, as brilliant and pure as a snow mountain or cow’s milk.
First, one visualizes a white lotus flower above the navel, imagining it to be extremely white and radiant; upon this white flower sits the syllable *bā*, which is entirely white in color.
Once this has been accomplished, one immediately transforms these syllables into the form of the deity.
This is the foremost among all rites for pacifying calamities (*śāntika*).
The Buddha-deity likewise assumes a tranquil form, abiding in meditative absorption with an utterly serene demeanor.
It is of incomparable pure white, like the moonlight of an autumn night.
That maṇḍala should be made perfectly circular, fashioned like nine successive lunar discs, and one should abide within it in the manner of a fine, drifting mist of white clouds.
When this rite is accomplished, all the fevers of affliction and the like are entirely pacified.
Whatever rites correspond to the pacification of calamities (*śāntika*) are all performed within this context.

Regarding "the milk and the pearl garland being identical": one should visualize that from within these syllables, a stream of milk flows forth as described above, continuous and unceasing, like white pearls descending and pouring into one's heart.
Whether visualizing it for oneself or another, if one imagines this being poured, all internal and external fevers and afflictions will be eliminated without exception.

Alternatively, one may visualize it as the moon or as crystal; as the light of the pure moon flows forth everywhere, whatever ailments of fever and affliction exist, they are all removed by this infusion.
All *śāntika* rites are associated with the color white; they are performed herein.
The preceding syllable *A* is the Vajra Maṇḍala, while this syllable *Va* is called the Water Maṇḍala.
The earth element of vajra is yellow; the water element is white;
the fire element is red; the wind element is black;
and space has no fixed form, yet manifests in various ways.
Emerging from the maṇḍala of the massed mists of the lunar disc, it flows forth like milk, capable of removing all feverish afflictions.
That is to say, the internal and external obstructions are themselves the obstruction of heat; this [emanation] is able to remove them all.
"Exemption and liberation" refers to being freed from these sufferings and afflictions.
Thus, by binding the object of focus to a single point, one accomplishes [the appearance of] ghee, milk, a pearl necklace, a lotus root, crystal, or curd, or water.

Such objects as these are numerous; whatever one wishes to accomplish according to one's heart's desire will all be achieved provided it accords with the *Śāntikarman* (the rite for pacifying calamities).
Whether seeking a long life to endure for immeasurable time, or manifesting various bodies with exquisite, wondrous, and extraordinary marks—[all shall be attained].
Some say that "supreme" refers to being supreme among those who are loved and respected, causing one to be loved and respected by others.
Whether seeking the power of hearing and retaining [the teachings], or seeking intelligence, or seeking wisdom and the cessation of all illnesses—all such things shall be accomplished.
If this syllable *bha* is provided with a bindu, it swiftly accomplishes the removal of illnesses and all internal and external poisons.
This is the peaceful and auspicious maṇḍala.
However, because it subsumes and excludes immeasurable matters, the word "etc. is used.
Next, the *Rā*-syllable Maṇḍala for the Removal of Obstacles is explained; among all methods for removing obstacles, this is the foremost, most authentic teaching.
This syllable RA is the reddest among the red, the fire among fires, and the burner among burners.

Because it can incinerate and extinguish the various afflictions, karmas, and sufferings—even those of one who has currently committed the five crimes of immediate retribution—if one cultivates this gateway of syllables, it can purify and eliminate them without remainder.
Once the transgressions have been extinguished, various wholesome merits will arise.
This gateway of syllables functions in conjunction with Acala-vajrapāṇi; indeed, the phrase of Acala-vajrapāṇi is capable of accomplishing all matters of the three categories.
Regarding this method: first, as described above, one abides with the mind on a single object and visualizes a triangular maṇḍala that is intensely red, making it exceedingly pleasing to the mind.
This "pleasing concentration" refers to making it vivid and exquisitely well-ordered.
Furthermore, "Delighting the Mind" (*Ratimanī*) refers to performing this with the mind; this is the secret instruction.
One should fashion a garland of flames all around, visualizing the form of blazing fire and light-flames, and contemplate the syllable *ra* in the center.
Once accomplished, one transforms into Acala Vidyārāja, manifesting a serene form that is neither wrathful nor smiling; his appearance is tranquil. Furthermore, it is said:
first visualize Acala Vidyārāja, and upon his heart, create a triangle. Within it is the syllable *ra*; once the syllable is formed, it transforms back into Acala Vidyārāja.

Because obstacles are removed, transgressions are extinguished; because [the mind] is tranquil, calamities are stilled—this is precisely the meaning of the extinction of transgressions and the arising of merit.
"Next, this accomplishment is for the sake of this object" refers to this triangular mandala.
As for Aṅgāraka, he is a retainer of the Sun; indeed, all eight planetary deities (navagraha) are termed "retainers" (graha).
All these retainers, such as the Sun and others, as well as Agni and the other deities, reside together in the southeast corner; their ritual procedures are largely identical.
This means that when fire is required for use, or when fire is transformed to become cold and so forth, all such actions are performed within this [state].
However, the secret intention is that because this is the day of action, it is the fire of wisdom (*jñānāgni*).
The sun is also the Sun of Wisdom (*prajñā-sūrya*).

As for "gathering" (*saṃgraha*), it means gathering those who follow unwholesome dharmas and are difficult to tame, causing them all to become supple, compliant, and disciplined. According to the principles of interpretation, the twenty-eighth and twelfth lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) correspond to the same positions as the moon and water.
In this context, "subduing wicked people" refers to those who are able to subdue their afflictions (*kleśa*) and attain mastery.
Furthermore, regarding "arousing resentment," it means being able to cause both oneself and others to achieve accomplishment, such as by arousing resentment in those enemies and so forth.
"Causing the withered branches to waste away" means that it can cause that body to become parched and devoid of any functional capacity.
Since all parts of the body have the three poisons as their fundamental essence, it causes them to be completely consumed and exhausted without remainder.
Speaking in terms of external signs, "drying up" refers to such acts as exhausting dragon pools and the like.
All activities involving subjugation performed by any agent whatsoever are carried out within this context.
Nevertheless, all of these are in accord with compassion, for the purpose of subduing and properly training them so that they may become causes and conditions for attaining the Buddha-way.
The first true reality of the syllable HA is this wind maṇḍala.
The nature of wind is that which increases [the power of] action.
That which is born of wind refers to all matters involving the functional application of wind; these are all produced within this maṇḍala.
It is also that which gives rise to these various activities.
All phenomena are capable of being consumed and transformed in infinite ways; the functions of these characters and things are likewise so.
This means that through karma and other causes, all various matters of growth and flourishing attain mastery.
If one places a bindu (dot) above, one is able to destroy all such matters as causes, karma, and so forth.
As for the method: first, visualize the deity; upon the forehead, joining the eyebrows, form a crescent moon shape, and within it, place the syllable [𑖮].
First, visualize it as being formed externally, and then transform it into one's own body.
This half-moon possesses an image of great majesty and radiant light; black flames issue forth from all sides, manifesting the sign of being stirred by the wind.
"Evil" refers to its image being formed in an extremely wrathful shape.
It is said that this is merely the deity of the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) and not Trailokyavijaya.
Its image is also deep blue in color, which belongs to the black category.
If one performs this accomplishment, one can bring about various benefits for all sentient beings.
As for the subsequent accomplishment, it refers to performing [the rite] with the items listed below in the wind; thus, one’s own present body will be able to achieve success.
This refers to ascending into the void through the supernormal power of psychic transformation, as well as the divine eye, the divine ear, and the disappearance of the body.
"Opening" refers to opening the palaces of the asuras and so forth.
What is referred to below as "recollection" (nian) is simply the application of the mind.
These five characters all constitute the mental construction of the accomplishment mandala.
Furthermore, one may construct the mandala through ritual methods while contemplating the mind so that it accords with them.
If one practices the supernormal powers by constructing a mandala according to the characteristics of the ritual objects, one should likewise perform it while seated within that [mandala].
If lotus roots and so forth are also placed within the mandala for the practice, one should visualize white milk flowing and filling its interior.
In the past, when the Buddha sat beneath the Bodhi tree, he subdued the immeasurable hosts of Māra’s armies by means of this gateway of letters.
If a practitioner can train and practice according to the Dharma, before long they will become equal to the Tathāgata, able to subdue those armies in their very own body.
The one of great renown is precisely that subduer of Māra.
Next, from the gateway of the syllable *ha*, the syllable *kha* is manifested.
*Ha* signifies the meaning of "cause"; because there is a cause, there is the characteristic of receiving the fruit according to karma.
However, within this ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the gateway of the syllable *ha* is fundamentally unborn; because it is unborn, a cause cannot be apprehended.
If even this cause is fundamentally unborn from the beginning, how much more so could there be karma and its fruit therein?
When observing in this manner, the phenomena of causes—karma—and their effects are stilled, and all are found to be ungraspable.
If one can observe in this way, one is identical to the Tathāgata sitting beneath the Bodhi tree and subduing Māra.
Because these causes and so forth cannot be apprehended, their characteristic is like empty space; it is empty and yet further empty.
When the Great Virtuous World-Honored One speaks of that "form," he is speaking of the form of empty space.
If a dot is added above [the letter *ka*], one enters the gateway of the syllable *kha*.
This gateway of the syllable *kha* describes the Honored One as "Honored," meaning the most honored among the honored, which is Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*).
If one wishes to accomplish all ritual vessels, they shall all be accomplished.
Their names and varieties are immeasurable and cannot be fully recounted.
This maṇḍala possesses no characteristics such as square, circular, or semi-circular; one should know that while space is signless, it is capable of accomplishing signs.
This mandala is made of various colors; it manifests various colored forms within emptiness.
It is performed by means of the Wisdom Sword mudrā together with others, meaning that one achieves accomplishment while simultaneously protecting the rite with the Sword mudrā.
If one makes a blade, it should be made of bīṇḍi iron;
the cord should be made of thread or lotus fibers;
and the wheel should be made either of gold or of bīṇḍi iron.
The place of benefit is located below and is named Nalaccha; this is called Mūrkhaṇḍa. These vessels are extremely numerous and cannot be recorded in full; they exist separately.
For any of the aforementioned vessels, perform whichever task is required and accomplish it by using this syllable *khaṃ*.
If one attains the superior, middling, or inferior accomplishments, employ them according to the specific purpose.
Until such attainment is reached, one maintains this [mantra] while traveling through the various Buddha-fields; such a person is called a Vidyādhara-siddha.
Next, the meaning of the five syllables will be explained in further detail.
If one abides in this principle and acts in accordance with all phenomena, one will be able to accomplish all tasks.
Therefore, the Buddha, observing the great assembly, addressed Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"This is the mantra-bodhisattva practicing the bodhisattva path; the letter A is its original color, wherein all things internal and external are relinquished."
"One who attains the meaning of all phrases" is one who attains correspondence with the fundamental essence and color of the letter A.
This essence is fundamentally unarisen, identical to the body of the adamantine true mark (*dharmatā*).
If one accords with these characteristics, one is able to relinquish all phenomena, regarding the coarse and the sublime as equal.
Just as one views clay and gold with equanimity, because one dwells well in the contemplation of equality, one completely leaves behind all three poisons and sinful karma.

If one acts in this way, one shall attain a pure mind; having attained this purity, one becomes equal to the Buddhas, the Honored Munis, capable of universally benefiting all sentient beings, transcending the commission of offenses and remaining free from all faults and afflictions.
Next, the gateway of the syllable VA is explained.
If one can correspond with this and understand all phenomena, it is precisely the sequential method of mantras; thus, one will be able to perform deeds of great benefit for all sentient beings.
First, one should contemplate this syllable as described above: it is white like snow or milk, flowing into the heart.
If it flows until it fills the entire body, both internally and externally are purified; all who behold it will then become identical with the Buddha-body.
Furthermore, it flows forth from his body, pervading the bodies of all sentient beings and making them utterly pure and full; it then flows further to fill the great earth.
It should be understood that, within the secret interpretation, this is the water of great compassion.

Because it observes the extreme heat and affliction of the world, it benefits them; whether by being drunk or touched, it can eliminate various ailments and possesses the power to lead one certainly to unsurpassed bodhi—this water thus manifests as identical to nectar (*amṛta*).
Whether manifest or secret, both interpretations possess mundane and supramundane utility.
"Without doubt" means that one should give rise to definitive faith and not harbor any uncertainty.
Next, the letter-gateway *ra* with a dot (*bindu*) is explained.

One should contemplate it as before: all is quiescent, yet there is a brilliant radiance like a wheel of fire, surrounded by light; both internally and externally, everything is entirely of this color.

Flowing outward, it even illuminates the bodies of others, causing this light to gradually expand until it pervades the entire Dharma-realm; it can eliminate all manner of evil deeds of sentient beings, fulfilling their desires and inclinations as they wish, and it can also manifest various supernatural transformations.

Next, the practitioner places the syllable RA above the navel and the syllable VA at the center of the navel; both manifest miraculous transformations, such that fire arises from RA and water arises from VA, thereby eliminating ailments such as cold and heat.
Even the heat of the eight great hot hells can be cooled and extinguished by means of the syllable *va*;
the cold of the eight cold hells can be warmed and extinguished by means of the syllable *ra*.
Next, one should again place the letter *ra* and others below, and place the letter *ha* atop the banner; this can eliminate all sins and sufferings of oneself and others.
Furthermore, as above, one should form the Great Vajra Wheel; this is the most adamantine among the adamantine.
Within that Great Vajra Indra-wheel, one forms the two syllables "A" and "Va" together; originating from the direction of the Dragon (the West), this is able to subdue all things.

Wind can pervade all places, either opening or destroying; "opening" refers to opening the palaces of the asuras and all obstructive material objects, while "destroying" refers to crushing and breaking them apart.
It is formed by various mixed colors resulting from internal and external karmic causes, and all are capable of being opened and destroyed.
The *rūpa-maṇḍala* refers to that which relies on its original color; this is precisely the wind altar (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) previously described.

Regarding "the mind touching by friction": this means visualizing these characters within the perfect luminosity as being situated in the center of the heart, which enables the mental faculty (*manas*) to attain purity—this is what is meant in the *Lotus Sūtra* by the "purity of the mental faculty."

While walking in meditation (caṅkrama), one should recite it and contemplate these syllables while forming the thought of levitation; thus, one can lift the entire body to ascend into the air and manifest various supernormal powers (ṛddhi).

Alternatively, while sitting, one contemplates that the letter A resides within the faculty of hearing; as this letter enters and exits with the perception of sound, one immediately attains the supernormal power of the divine ear-faculty.

Some say that any single character may be used according to the specific application, while others suggest this particular passage refers to the application of the letter *A*; further inquiry is required.

As for the "body born of mind" (*manomaya-kāya*), this is stated by way of summary: it means that whatever one desires is accomplished at will, such as when the mind-born body reaches the ten directions upon a mere thought.

One should know that the Tathāgata possesses such sovereign skillful means that, within the practice of signlessness and the departure from signs, he can universally manifest form-bodies to accomplish all buddha-works.
The moment one begins to recite it, it can destroy all seeds of birth and death and accomplish the seeds of bodhi.
"Transforming" (zhuǎn) refers to the act of transforming through recitation.
If a practitioner can cultivate in this manner, all Buddhas will constantly appear before that person, following them like a shadow follows the body and fulfilling their aspirations.

Once the practitioner has fulfilled their aspirations, they will then be able to never abandon any sentient beings; likewise, [the Buddhas] will constantly appear before them, fulfilling their aspirations and causing them to attain the joy of the Dharma.
Therefore, it is said that they are identical to reflections, conforming to all places and to all sentient beings.

Why is this so? Because these Tathāgatas abide in the stage of the threefold equality, free from conceptual proliferation and discrimination; furthermore, they have transcended all marks of the objective sphere of the mind, and are likewise detached from time, direction, and the performance of deeds.
"Time" refers to the time of arising and ceasing within the three periods.
"Direction" refers to spatial location.
"Action" refers to various karmic activities.

Although it manifests myriad forms, there is nothing that is manifested; it is identical to the ten metaphors because both phenomena and non-phenomena are utterly transcended. Since it thus attains such an inexhaustible treasury of adornment, it is able to universally respond to all sentient beings.
Therefore, the practitioner should diligently seek the supreme siddhi of this mantra practice, namely the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
One should know that among all accomplishments, it stands at the very pinnacle; it is peerless and beyond compare.
Since this omniscience arises from the practice of mantra, one should diligently study it.
Here ends the Chapter on Attaining Siddhi.
Chapter Seven: The Chapter on Accomplishing Siddhi. At that time, the Holder of the Vajra, Śrī-Rare-Flower-Blossomed-Eyed One, is the secret wisdom of the Tathāgata Vajropama.
The Vajra has no dharma that can destroy it, yet it is able to destroy all things.
This wisdom is likewise: it cannot be destroyed by anything, yet it can shatter all that is capable of destroying or is difficult to destroy—namely, the roots of the three poisons.

Furthermore, the body of this Bodhisattva is itself the substance of vajra; and since all Buddhas of the ten directions collectively bestow the Tathāgata’s Vajra-Wisdom Seal (vajrajñānamudrā) into his hand, he is therefore named Vajradhara.
"Śrī" (Auspiciousness) praises the virtues of the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi.
To be fully endowed with all excellent merits and qualities without deficiency is the meaning of "śrī.

At that time, having heard the aforementioned profound, rare, and extraordinary Dharma of the Buddhas, that Bodhisattva gave rise to a sense of wonder; his eyes blossomed wide, and he gazed at the Buddha with single-minded focus without a moment’s distraction, just as he first gave rise to the Four Great Vows.
Furthermore, just as a worldly lotus flower gradually grows, yet cannot blossom and flourish unless it honors the light of the sun and moon and the proper seasons, so too it is with the Bodhisattva:
although they possess the secret treasury of the Tathāgata’s merits—the true mark of bodhicitta—it will not open and unfold unless they honor the fierce sunlight of the Buddhas’ equal great wisdom.

Because this Bodhisattva has now perfectly attained this true knowledge and vision of the wondrous Lotus Flower Throne of the Dharma, he again questions the Buddha, desiring to propagate widely this Dharma of the Mind-Ground and bestow it upon all sentient beings, so that they too may attain such blossoming.

Furthermore, as previously stated, this is the gateway of the letter A, the adamantine nature of the Tathāgata; it is the gateway to the eternally abiding sublime principle, wherein the treasury of merit is complete and without deficiency.
Turning the vajra scepter has a subtle significance: it means wishing to turn this unimpeded secret wisdom into the minds of all sentient beings.

Why is this so? Because such a dharma of self-realized quiescence is subtle, pure, and unsurpassed; yet sentient beings do not awaken to it themselves. For this reason, within the secret treasure-trove of immeasurable Buddhas, they undergo immeasurable terrors and suffering.
It is because of this matter that he gives rise to great compassion, desiring to turn forth this wisdom so that all may cause the eye of the mind to blossom.
As for the "faint emission of firelight," fire is a metaphor for the *prajñāpāramitā*; it cannot be touched from any side because it is not to be grasped.
Furthermore, its essential nature is stainless; it can incinerate all the defilements of afflictions and delusions, leaving nothing behind, just like the fire at the end of an eon.

As for "universally illuminating the Buddha-fields," it means that by means of this light of wisdom, one universally shines upon all those with karmic affinity within the infinite Dharma-realm who are ready to be saved, appearing before each of them without exception. Manifesting bodies that are pleasing to behold according to their capacities, one preaches the Dharma so that all may enter this gate of the letter A.
The various Buddha-fields are, that is to say, the worlds without remainder. I privately maintain that this world is precisely the land of the pure mind, the indestructible vajra realm.
"Uttering a wondrous and beautiful sound to praise the Muni, the Sovereign of Dharma" means that he uttered a subtle and sublime voice to question the Tathāgata.
Regarding "the Sovereign of All Dharmas": just as a worldly elder who is fully endowed with wealth has no lack or deficiency and can thus accomplish whatever he desires at will, so too is the Buddha.

The Tathāgata is likewise; as the sovereign of all dharmas, he is fully endowed with all the riches of the Dharma. Therefore, he is able to accomplish the inconceivable Great Matter, accomplishing everything.
