This does not merely pervade the realm of the Tathāgata, but also pervades the realms of all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; even those who have only recently resolved to attain enlightenment, provided they can practice this vidyārājñī conduct, will likewise enter the realm of the Tathāgata.
"Namaḥ sarvatathāgatebhyaḥ" means taking refuge in all Tathāgatas and so forth.
Since the Tathāgatas arise [in manifold ways], they are not one; because they are not one, they are called "all" (or "etc.").
*Sarvamukhāye*: "To all those who have the Buddhas as their foremost object of regard," it is further asked. *Asame*: "The peerless."
Because it arises from the realm of all Tathāgatas, it is peerless.
Furthermore, according to the esoteric interpretation, the syllable *A* herein is the very body of the Buddha; the three delusions are "equality."
To be equal to all Buddhas is to be equal to the essence of the letter A.
"Prami" is translated as "foremost"; because it is without equal, it is the foremost, and there is nothing superior to it.
Regarding the secret interpretation: this syllable *bha* is itself the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Because the aforementioned syllable *a* is identical to the essence of all Tathāgatas, it is the ultimate truth and is equal to the Tathāgata.
The Ācārya is immovable; because of the syllable *A*, he is identical to the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
That which is ultimate is where the path of language ceases and the movements of the mind are stilled;
therefore, it cannot be destroyed nor can it be turned back. *Gagaṇī* is empty; because of its immovability, it is identical to space.
Its nature is buoyant, vast, and immeasurable, beyond conceptual differentiation.
*Samāra* (sa-ma-ra) means "to seek and contemplate"; that is, to seek and contemplate the meaning of the syllable A.
This signifies the sense of contemplating this meaning at all times and in all moments, without interruption. *Sarvatara*.
*Nu-ke-ti* means "pervasive arrival. Because one constantly contemplates this meaning, one is able to reach all places;

it does not merely mean reaching all Buddhas, but also pervading all places, including those of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and even those who have first resolved to attain enlightenment (*prathamacittotpādika*). *Svāhā svāḥ*: *svāhā* is the root.
Furthermore, it asks the awakened Buddhas to cause them to remember their original vows.

Since the Tathāgatas established such definitive great vows in the past, all practitioners who cultivate these mantra practices (vidyā-mantra-caryā) should establish themselves accordingly, so that their aspirations may be swiftly fulfilled.
Because I now practice in this manner, I awaken all Buddhas, who should then remember their original vows.
Next is the method for preparing the pigments:

one pays homage to the Buddha and Prajñāpāramitā and recites this vidyā-queen eight times. Regarding the reciter, it means that when one intends to paint an image of the Tathāgata’s true form, one must first read and recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and perform reverent offerings; this is precisely the meaning of paying homage.
Whenever adjusting the colors, one must act in this manner.
Furthermore, one should visualize the classes of letters within those colors—such as the letter A (A-kāra) and so forth—and recite these letters either a hundred or a thousand times.
Furthermore, recite the vidyā-queen eight times.
Once the master has adjusted the colors, he rises from meditative absorption, circumambulates, and enters within, focusing his thoughts upon the disciple.
Through the power of great compassion, the master himself then forms the vajra and the letter-seals.

Emerging from meditative absorption, he circumambulates the maṇḍala and generates a mind of great compassion; having empowered the disciple with this power of great compassion, the ācārya performs the empowerment of Karmavajrasattva.

Regarding the phrase "the *vajra* of the boon-granting [mudrā] of the syllable Vāṃ and so forth," because this ācārya is empowered by the Tathāgata and by the syllable A, he is himself Vairocana Tathāgata; for it is not appropriate that the Tathāgata himself should perform the activity of accomplishment (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna*).
The syllable *vaṃ*, together with the Wish-Fulfilling Auspicious Vajra, is Mañjuśrī.
The subsequent seed-syllable is the letter *ma*, which is the bindu of emptiness; it is simply the letter *va* with the addition of the bindu to form *ma*.

Furthermore, one should empower [the image] with the syllable *vaṃ* to manifest it as the body of Vajrasattva and then paint the various figures; at the time of doing so, one should visualize [it] as being identical to one's own body, as described above.
Furthermore, one should recite this syllable *vaṃ* one hundred or one thousand times, and so forth.

Having drawn the Maṇḍala of the Arising of the Great Compassion Treasury, the Master—having thus performed self-consecration while remaining composed within the inner maṇḍala—arises calmly and enters the central platform. There, he gradually applies the various pigments to fashion the image of Vairocana.

The original form of the image sits upon a seat of white lotus flowers; it wears a crown made of hair without added ornamentation, uses extremely fine silk for the lower garment, and further employs the finest gauze and light muslin for the upper robe, so that the flesh-colored skin shines through from within.
His body is the color of Jambū-nada gold; that which is the deepest gold is of such extreme brilliance and purity.
From his entire body, rays of light and flames arise, merging together to form a continuous garland of interlocking rings that covers his whole body.

The reason why this form of the Buddha must be fashioned within the maṇḍala is that it is intended to cause the disciples to swiftly give rise to supreme aspirations, and through the power of empowerment (adhiṣṭhāna), to bring to fulfillment the body of omniscience; therefore, it must first be constructed and established.
Furthermore, there are superior, middling, and inferior methods for constructing the mandala.

If a disciple possesses abundant wealth and resources and is capable of making extensive preparations, the master should construct a mandala using painted colors and images, in order to demonstrate the physical forms and hand-seals (mudrās) of the tutelary deity.
If one lacks the necessary resources yet proceeds to construct a letter-maṇḍala, one commits the offense of concealing the secret dharma.

However, if one observes that the disciple’s mind is extremely earnest—even to the point of being willing to sacrifice their own body and life to serve the teacher—how could they possibly harbor any stinginess? Nevertheless, for those who lack the requisite means, it is permitted to construct a letter-maṇḍala; in this case, one simply draws the letter *A* at the place where the Buddha would normally be installed, for this is the very embodiment of the Tathāgata.
Having completed the placement of the letter *A*, one should place the letter *A* with the great empty dot (*bindu*) directly to the east of the outer enclosure of the central terrace.
Furthermore, one should place the letter *Ga* in the northeast, the direction of Īśāna; this letter *Ga* is the Eye of Space (*ākāśanetra*) and is the mother of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Next, in the southeast direction (the fire quadrant), place the Cintāmaṇi seal of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, or alternatively, the syllable *ja*.
In the north, place the syllable *sa*, representing Avalokiteśvara and Maitreya, together with the Bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa who are bound for Buddhahood in their next birth as their retinue.
In the south are Vajrapāṇi and others; they may appear in bodily form or as mudrās, such as the three-pronged vajra or the syllable *ba*.
Furthermore, the placement of these syllables within this [mandala] may differ from the orientation used for the previous mandala.
Questioning him, he again [explained] the three types of abandonment regarding those respective states.

As for all the drawings of the seals (*mudrā*) of the Vajradharas, or those syllables, there are many instances of the three abandonments; these are also explained as before, not differing from the *hūṃ* syllable formed by the seal of the syllable.

Next is the direction of the Rākṣasas, the southwest. Below Vairocana, one should paint the Honored One Acala, seated upon a rock, holding a sword and a noose, with a wreath of flames enveloping his entire body, who strikes down all those who create obstacles.
Alternatively, one may simply form the mudrās; the upper mudrās refer to the noose and the sword. Alternatively, one may form the syllables, which are *haṃ*.

Next, in the northwest—the direction of Wind—one should manifest Trailokyavijaya, the supreme subduer of all obstructors. His head has the appearance of blazing flames; he assumes the form of a great wrathful deity like Yama, black in color, who causes even those who are already terrified and fearsome to become utterly terrified. One should thus manifest this most formidable form.

In his hand he turns the *vajra*; this is the three-pronged golden *vajra* mudrā. This represents meditative concentration (*samādhi*), or alternatively, it may simply be represented by the syllable "Hā.
Next, one should draw the four great protective knots at the four directions.
In the east, one should paint the deity named Abhayāṅkuśī; her body is golden in color and she wears white garments. Her face has a slight expression of wrath, and she holds a staff in her hand.
If only the mudrā is to be placed there, one should simply draw the seal of the staff, or alternatively, place the syllable *vaḥ*.
In the north is Mahāpālaka, the Great Protector who destroys all fears; he is white in color, holds a sword in his right hand, and wears white garments and radiance.
If one forms the mudrā, simply draw the shape of a sword; if using a seed syllable, it is the letter *pha*.
He is a great protector of the western direction who is difficult to subdue, and there is no one capable of overcoming him; thus he is named accordingly.
His body is the color of the *aśoka* flower—like the deep purple of the hollyhock flower found here—and the garment he wears is also red, though slightly paler than the hue of his body.
His face bears a smile, situated within a circular halo.
Regarding the manner in which he contemplates the great assembly, this refers to the congregations from the four directions.
As for the mudrā, one simply forms the *kartṛ* (knife) mudrā; as for the syllable, it is called the *sraḥ* syllable.
The "Great Protection of the Southern Vajra Invincible" is so named because it is like a vajra, having nothing superior to it.
Furthermore, "Vajra" is an alternative name for Śakra, Lord of Devas; however, the power of this Great Protection exceeds even that appearance, and thus it is so named.
His body is black in color, with a wrathful form and knitted brows; his garment is also black, though slightly lighter than the hue of his body and face.
He has a topknot of hair on his head, which emits flames from his own body, and he holds a staff in his hand.
If one merely draws the mudrās, one may likewise simply place the staffs; the syllables are written as the character *chan* (懺).
Regarding the four great protectors mentioned above, it is necessary to place their retinues alongside them; these retinues are their attendants, all seated upon white lotus flowers.
The mantra-holder should arrange and install [the deities] in this manner.

Next, one proceeds outward to the third enclosure and draws the Muni King of the Śākya clan, wearing the saṃghāṭī robe and endowed with the thirty-two marks, who bestows fearlessness upon all sentient beings by benefiting them through the Dharma so that they all attain fearlessness.

As for the mudrās, one should place them upon the alms bowl, the *kāṣāya*, and so forth—referring to items such as the mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*). If expressed in syllables, it is formed with the letter *va*.
This is the most excellent, meaning the supreme secret significance.

Next, regarding the outer maṇḍala, for those who have set out with the bodhicitta empowered by the intrinsic nature of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-svabhāva-adhiṣṭhita-bodhicitta*), one performs the visualization of the intrinsic nature of the dharma-realm.
The dharma-realm is the body of the Tathāgata; one visualizes one’s own body as being identical to the body of the dharma-realm of all Buddha-dharmas.

By means of this empowerment, one abides in the bodhicitta; this "setting forth" (prasthāna) carries the meanings of "orientation," "arrival," and "practice. Furthermore, this section shall now be further questioned.

Regarding the abandonment of those three stages, one performs three prostrations to the Buddha Vairocana and recollects him as previously described for the adjustment of colors; that is to say, having placed Śākyamuni, one next proceeds to the second courtyard to pay homage to Vairocana, just as before—referring to the method of painting within the colors—and asks further.
In the east is the Vajra of Bestowing Boons (Varada-vajra), in the form of a youth—this being another name for Mañjuśrī—who holds a blue lotus in his left hand with a vajra placed upon it.

Adorning their bodies with every kind of necklace and ornament, they wore exquisite, fine silk as lower garments and extremely delicate gauze as upper robes; these were so fine that the color of their skin shone through the lower garments.
The body is the color of *uraga* gold, and upon the head are five topknots (*pañca-śikhā*).
As for that mudrā, one simply draws a blue lotus, with a vajra placed upon the flower.
If it is to be represented by a syllable, it is the syllable *VAM*.
To the right and north of Mañjuśrī, one should place the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha, with all his limbs perfectly complete; his left hand holds a jeweled net, and his right hand holds a hook.
If one merely places the seal, it may be either a painted seal or a hook.
As for the "syllable," this refers to the colored syllable; by merely placing this seal, the requirement is fulfilled.
In the south, one should paint the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, with golden hair and a crown, but no necklaces or ornaments. His left hand holds a cintāmaṇi jewel atop a lotus flower.
If one forms only the mudrā, there is a maṇi jewel placed upon a lotus.
Alternatively, if one forms only the syllable, it refers to the syllable *Aḥ*.

In the north, one should depict Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, whose color is like that of the *pāṭalī* flower. This flower grows in the west; its color is like that of millet, and its calyx is like a grain ear, being exceedingly fragrant.
This Bodhisattva holds a lotus flower in his hand, and his body is adorned with various necklaces and ornaments.
If one merely forms the mudrā, one simply places a lotus flower there.
If one places a syllable, it is the letter *ī*.

The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha from the western quarter likewise adorns his body with various necklaces; his body is white in color, and he wears white garments, yet the color of these white garments is so pale that it makes his body appear flesh-colored, differing slightly from its true hue.
The body possesses blazing flames and holds a great sword.
To form that mudrā, one simply draws a great sword.
If one merely places the seed-syllable, it is formed as a long *ī*.
However, there are still many positions lacking within this mandala; thus, the statement that it has been "completed" also indicates the mutual manifestation of the upper and lower realms.
At the time of completion, the Ācārya first sits outside the gate, abiding in the *dharmadhātu* while maintaining the *bodhicitta*.
The Sanskrit text says: "Next, the reciter abides in the dharmadhātu, [realizing] 'I am of the very nature of the dharmadhātu.
Abiding in the bodhicitta—this bodhicitta is itself the nature of the dharmadhātu."
Facing east, one forms the Vajra-seal mandala with its gate opening to the west; therefore, the Master faces east.
Once the mandala is completed, one should sit facing east within the mandala and contemplate oneself as being identical to the Buddha, for the Buddha is the very essence of the Dharmadhātu.
Having become identical with all Buddhas, one then performs the activities for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
Regarding the "Vajra of Action," this refers to the various Vajras of Action, which is precisely the three-pronged *viśvavajra* mudrā.
Generally speaking, when one speaks of performing the *vajra* [mudrās], one performs all the *akṣara-kāya-mudrās*; the same applies to performing the Buddha [mudrās].
Fearing prolixity, I shall not state each one in detail.
Regarding the subsequent offering made with earnest diligence: the practitioner who observes the precepts should perform it with careful heedfulness, not forgetting the proper sequence.
The Sanskrit text states: "One should form the Vajra-mudrā, then perform the Vajra-activities, and offer with earnest diligence."

Regarding the phrase "manifesting the samaya of all Buddhas, the Saviors of the World, and further manifesting the mudrā-samayas and so forth," the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) is used because the samaya-mudrās are numerous.
For making offerings, performing the Buddha-activities, and so forth, one should recite the samaya-mantra three times; this is because it is extensively used for various ritual actions.
By performing this rite, through the mind directed toward whatever task is being performed, one is able to pervade all directions and awaken all Tathāgatas.
By virtue of the Buddha’s original vow, they are all awakened and empowered.
First, one contemplates pervasively throughout all places; that is, one directs the mind universally toward all the deities according to their respective positions within the maṇḍala.
If one is a practitioner of the profound path, this refers to the samaya that reveals the respective positions of all the deities within the maṇḍala.
Next, regarding the summoning of the disciple to maintain ritual purity: the disciple is already standing outside the gate, and he is summoned from there.
One may accomplish all tasks by invoking the various honored dharmas using the mantra for accomplishing all matters through two types of messengers;
alternatively, if one possesses the most swift wisdom, it is also possible to invoke them individually using their respective root mantras and mudrās.
Have them stand near the gate facing the altar;
furthermore, they should first be instructed to purify themselves according to the Dharma.
This is precisely the invitation to the Honored One.
Next, the procedures from the binding of the boundary (*sīmābandha*) up to the dismissal (*visarjana*) are all contained within the ritual of offering; they may be applied accordingly.
Once the protection has been established, one bestows the Three Refuges (*triśaraṇa*); these three refuges are what is called the "Dharma of Seals" (*mudrā-dharma*).
First, seal the body; next, seal the various parts of the body with the Dharma Wheel Seal; next, there is one seal which shall be explained below.
First, apply the seal to the crown of the head; next, apply the seal to the limbs; these are referred to above as the "Vajra Sentient Beings."
By means of these three seals, one abides in the bodhicitta.

When performing the Dharmadhātu-dharmacakra-mudrā, the instruction that "one should single-mindedly manifest oneself as the essence" means that when the practitioner directs the mind to form this dharmadhātu, they should contemplate their own body as being identical to the dharmadhātu.
When forming the mudrā, it is identical to the essential nature of that seal.
First, one forms the Dharmadhātu-svabhāva-mudrā, followed by the Dharma-cakra-mudrā.
One first visualizes the letter *A* within the disciple’s topknot, and then seals them with the Dharmadhātu-svabhāva-mudrā, pressing down with the seal while reciting the mantra three or seven times.

Next, one should cover his face with a cloth; the master should then give rise to a mind of great compassion and take pity upon him, for the purpose of enabling him to forever cross over birth and death and open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
At that time, the disciple should likewise personally make a supreme and unsurpassed vow.
This is for the sake of accomplishing the perfection of bodhi through the Amoghapāśa [Amoghakara] rite.

That is to say, because that disciple desires to swiftly perfect unsurpassed bodhi, they should—according to their superior, middling, or inferior capacity—prepare whatever offerings they possess for the Buddhas and deities, such as by holding and presenting precious flowers and the like.
At that time, because the teacher wished to cause his disciples to perform the protective rite (*rakṣā*), he instructed them with whispered words—namely, to cause them to abide in the bodhicitta.
There is a separate passage explaining this.

Once they have generated the bodhicitta and remain with single-minded devotion and reverence, the master himself forms a mudrā and places it upon their crown; he then asks, "What mudrā is this? and subsequently instructs them to cast a flower.
One should record in which deity’s position that person has fallen.

Within the body of a single presiding deity, there are further distinctions of superior, middling, inferior, left, and right; according to the specific place where they have fallen, one should bestow upon them the corresponding mudrā and mantra.
"Disciples, because you have thus performed the samaya according to the Dharma teachings, I shall grant everything and ask further questions.

At that time, the Virtuous Vajradhara again asked this Buddha regarding the method of empowerment: "I pray that the Buddha will himself explain it," which is a request for the Buddha to speak it himself.
At that time, the Buddha, abiding within the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, addressed Vajrapāṇi:
"Listen attentively and with a single mind.
I shall expound this Dharma so that practitioners may attain mastery within it—namely, the attainment of the supreme and exalted teaching."
This "mastery" (vaśitā) also carries the sense of "attaining quickly," as well as the sense of "sovereignty.
This meaning differs from the sense of "mastery" previously mentioned regarding the possession of abundant wealth.

When I speak of the teachings on all phenomena, that which is called "supreme mastery and gathering" means that when the mind possesses aspiration and seeking, it is able to gather everything through mastery so that its wishes are fulfilled.

Just as one who possesses sovereign power over a single kingdom will surely achieve whatever they undertake, so too does the Ācārya, through the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s original form and intent, perform those mudrās. According to the superior, middling, or inferior rites, he may manifest as a Tathāgata or as the Lotus or Vajra families; following the specific maṇḍala presided over by each, he assumes that form and bestows the consecration.
The empowerment of the Tathāgata’s original form means that the ācārya empowers his own body with the nature of the Tathāgata; this nature of the Tathāgata is the fundamental essence.

Alternatively, one may employ those mudrās, meaning to empower with the mudrās while visualizing one's own body such that the letter A pervades all its limbs; this letter A is the essential nature of the Dharma-realm.
Because of this adornment, one becomes identical to the body of a Buddha; only then may one address others as "disciples.
If one is an ācārya who has attained meditative concentration or has already achieved realization of the Dharma, whatever he undertakes will be spontaneously accomplished.

If one is unable to do so, one should perform it by means of mudrās and visualization. Next, the disciple is led toward the Great Flower King Maṇḍala—which refers to the location of the preliminary consecration maṇḍala situated outside the main altar.

Regarding "the great vase empowered by the four great bodhisattvas made of the four jewels," this refers to the vase empowered by the four great bodhisattvas of the central platform, which is adorned with the jewels of the bodhisattvas.
Next, one should perform the mudrā for generating all limbs and consecrate it upon the crown of the disciple’s head.
Whenever performing an empowerment, one should form this mudrā; having bound it, one takes the flask to perform the consecration.

If one does not employ this seal, the ritual procedures will be incomplete, causing the disciple to be unable to abide in the bodhicitta; they will then regress, which is no different from sprinkling scented water into empty space.

Furthermore, prior to the empowerment, one should visualize the syllable *Aṃ* at the fontanelle (the "cross-seam") on the crown of the disciple’s head; one should intensely visualize the syllable *A* within his heart, and also visualize the syllable *A* upon his chest. Alternatively, one may simply visualize the syllable *A* pervading all locations.

Regarding "one with golden-hued light and a hair-crown seated upon a white lotus": this means one should visualize a fully blossomed white lotus within the heart of that disciple, with Vairocana Tathāgata seated upon it, and then perform the consecration.
The Sūtra states: "O Benevolent One, you are none other than Vairocana Tathāgata.

If one is consecrated by means of this Dharma, it is equivalent to being consecrated with the water of the Dharma by all the Buddhas of the ten directions and being invested with the rank of Dharma King."
If it were otherwise, it would be merely pouring water in vain, accomplishing nothing at all.

Chapter Nine: The Secret Seals (13–14) Regarding the passage, "At that time, Vairocana Buddha surveyed the great assembly": since the Buddha had already briefly explained the ritual for empowerment (*abhiṣeka*), he was about to further expound upon it; therefore, his surveying of the great assembly—equal in number to the atoms within ten buddha-fields—is not without cause or condition.
This refers to the teaching of the seal (*mudrā*) of the Tathāgata’s body-mystery.

Next, he addressed Vajrapāṇi: "There is a seal called 'Identical to the Adornments of the Tathāgata' and 'Identical to the Banner of the Dharmadhātu-Access. It is said that because all Buddhas take this as their adornment, they attain the body of the Tathāgata’s dharmadhātu."
If there are sentient beings who practice this dharma, by virtue of the empowerment of this seal (*mudrā*), they likewise become identical to the Tathāgata’s body of the *dharmadhātu*.
This seal is the emblem of the *dharmadhātu*; because it marks the essence of the *dharmadhātu*, it is called the Banner of the *Dharmadhātu*.

Because all Buddhas adorn their bodies by means of this, they establish this banner of the supreme, unsurpassed Great Bodhi within all great assemblies; they are thus able to cause those among the eight classes of beings who are evil and heterodox to depart from afar, while causing those of a nature possessing roots of goodness to draw near, receive the teachings, and practice them.
"Listen attentively and apply your minds with great care; I shall now proclaim it.
Regarding the two phrases, "The World-Honored One, now is precisely the right time; the Buddha, now is precisely the right time," these words carry a specific meaning.

When he first spoke the word "kāla" (time), his intention was this: "Now these fourfold assemblies are devoid of branches and leaves; they are purely authentic and capable of receiving the Great Dharma. The Tathāgata speaks in accordance with their capacity, and now is precisely that time."
Next, at the time of the *samaya*, that is, at the time of division;
now is precisely the time, the time for preaching the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One abided in the *samādhi* of the Harmless Body-Power; for the sake of fulfilling this vow, the Buddha again entered *samādhi*.
This is precisely the Tathāgata’s power of mastery over his immeasurable bodies; therefore, none can harm him.
Abiding in this samādhi, he utters the mantra of the Threefold Knowledge (vidyā), a knowledge named "Unobstructed, Unharmable, and Unequaled Power."
By means of this samaya, those who are practitioners are permitted to hear and enter the True Dharma.
If one does not perform it, they are not permitted to enter the maṇḍala, nor are they permitted to hear the secret teachings.

If one cultivates this vidyā, one is able to attain purity of body and purity of speech; with all aspirations fulfilled, one realizes the three bodies (trikāya), and is therefore called the Three Vidyās.
As for the "three powers," they refer to the power of the three times, or alternatively, the power of the three equalities.
The "unequaled powers" refer precisely to these three powers.
Their illumination shall be explained next. *Namaḥ samantabuddhānām*.

*Asame* means "unequaled"; *tatsame* means "equal thereto"; *samaye* means "in the samaya" (or "oath"); *svāhā* means "to awaken. Regarding *asame*: this clarifies that taking the letter *A* as the foremost is identical to the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of all Buddhas—being signless and free from signs. One should know that this dharma-body is without equal comparison.

The third "mystery" refers to the three bodies of the Buddha—namely, the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body—which are unified as a single body to teach and transform sentient beings.
Furthermore, their essence is identical to the gateway of the letter A; being without marks and transcending all marks, they are said to be "equal."
*Samaya* means that which is not to be transgressed.
This is the peerless *trisamaya*, as proclaimed by all the Tathāgatas.
When the Buddha abides in samādhi, he speaks this vidyā of harmlessness and peerless power; by means of this vidyā, one is able to enter the *samaya*.
This samaya is itself a vow, like a royal decree; it is the fundamental vow that the Buddhas of the three periods of time have made.
This dharma-gate is difficult to believe, difficult to enter, and difficult to hear, because such a dharma is not easily encountered.
For this reason, the Buddhas of the three periods of time have all spoken this mantra; by being empowered through this samaya mantra, one attains entry, hearing, and the practice of this dharma.
The instructions of the Honored One must not be transgressed; if one does not hear them, one shall neither be able to enter nor be able to hear.
*Saha* has the meaning of "to awaken"; by means of this mantra, all Buddhas are awakened.
When this vidyā is spoken, all Buddhas are awakened and arise, bestowing their empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) upon the practitioner.
By the power of this vidyā, one is able to fulfill all the stages (*bhūmi*) and enable the practitioner to attain the three dharmas in the present life.

It is said that there are three factors for achieving accomplishment: the power of the deity, the mantra, and the mudrā; through these three dharmas, one attains accomplishment within the realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*).
Next, the characteristics of the hand seals (*mudrā*) are explained.

Regarding the phrase "not transgressing the three dharmas of the boundary-sphere" (*dharmadhātu*): this sphere is the fruit of establishing the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), not the *sthāpana* (the formal act of establishment).
One is said to "not transgress" because one proceeds within the middle of the path of the boundary.
Now, herein first the names and characteristics of the twelve kinds of *añjali* (palms-joined gestures) are explained.
For all mudrā rites, these twelve are of the utmost importance and should be clearly committed to memory.

First: join the palms so that they meet firmly at the center; let the tips of the ten fingers be slightly separated and opened a little. This is called the *niṅa-tsa-wi-na* upper-joined *añjali*, and it is known as the "firmly joined heart-palms."

Second, next, with the ten fingernails aligned and even, join the tips of the fingers while the centers of the palms remain slightly apart; this is called the *tripuṭaka* añjali, also known as the hollow-palmed añjali.

Third, next, join the tips of the ten fingers together so that they are even; however, leave the palms hollowed so that they form a slight dome. This is called the *kuṭmalāñjali* (the "unopened lotus" mudrā). It is translated here as "like an unopened lotus."

Fourth, next, join the two middle fingers to touch at their tips, while slightly spreading the remaining fingers; this is called the *pūrṇa* (pronounced *shou* with a reversed *han*) *añjali*, and it is known as the "first-blossomed lotus."

Fifth, next, again turn both palms upward so they are side by side, placing them together facing upwards and spreading them evenly; this is called *ut-tāna*, which here [in Chinese] is translated as "exposed" (*lu*).

Sixth, next, again raise both palms together as before; however, let the fingers meet and slightly bend them together in the manner of a person cupping water, but do not bend them too much. This is called the *ādarśa* (or *ādhāra*) añjali, which translates as "holding water."

Seventh, next, one should again interlace the ten fingertips, placing each right finger over its corresponding left finger, like the *vajra-añjali*. This is called the "homage *añjali*"; in Sanskrit, it is named *praṇāmāñjali*.

Eighth: Next, again place the right hand over the left with the palms facing upward, interlacing the tips of the ten fingers, and likewise placing each finger of the right hand over a corresponding finger of the left hand; this is called the *mukhara-muṣṭi* (or *mukhara*) *añjali*, which in Chinese is translated as the "inverted-interlocking *añjali*."

Ninth: Next, again with the right hand turned upward over the left hand, and the left hand placed face down beneath the right hand, slightly resembling the manner of hands joined by one sitting in meditation; this is called the *vimalaricita* (reversed) *añjali*, which means the palms are joined with the backs facing each other.

For the tenth, turn both palms upward and join the tips of the middle fingers of both hands while keeping them facing up; this is called the *Tathāgata-saṃpuṭa-mudrā*, also known as the *tiryak-stambha-aṅgulī-saṃpuṭa-mudrā*.

Eleventh: Next, again cover both palms with the hands and join the middle fingers of both hands together; this is called the *adharā* añjali, which here is translated as the "downward-facing covered-hand añjali."

Twelfth: Next, again place both hands together with palms facing downward, join the two thumbs side by side, and extend the tips of the ten fingers outward; this is also known by the same name, and is called the "inverted-hand joined-palms" (fùshǒu hézhǎng).

Now, as for this samaya-mudrā: first join the three *puṭa* palms; initially keeping the hands at a distance, gradually bring them closer until they touch, leaving a slight space within the palms—this is it.

Place the two index fingers side-by-side and extend them straight upward; do not let them sag too low or lean too far to either side, ensuring that the two index fingers point directly up. Among the five fingers, the little finger is designated as Earth, the ring finger as Water, the middle finger as Fire, the index finger as Wind, and the thumb as Space.
The left hand represents concentration (*samādhi*) and the right hand represents wisdom (*prajñā*).
Alternatively, one may designate the little finger of the left hand as the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), counting upward from there, with the index finger representing concentration.
The little finger of the right hand represents the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā); counting upward from there, the index finger represents the Perfection of Knowledge (Jñānapāramitā).
This is the Samaya-mudrā; when first practicing and performing various virtuous deeds, if one does not first perform this, it is not appropriate to engage in any dharmas.
It is not enough merely to perform this; one must also recite the aforementioned mantra. As for the ritual procedure:

first, place the Samaya-mudrā upon the crown of the head and recite the aforementioned mantra once. Then, place the mudrā on the right shoulder, next on the left shoulder, next on the heart, and finally on the throat. At each placement, recite the vidyā-mantra once. Thus, by reciting it five times, the mudrā is applied to the five locations.
What, then, are the merits of this mantra?

By means of this mantra, one can eliminate past obstacles and purify oneself; because the body is purified, external obstacles are likewise purified; and because external obstacles are purified, no obstacles whatsoever can enter. This constitutes great protection.
Because of this inconceivable protection, merit increases spontaneously and transgressions are naturally eliminated; the Buddhas provide awakening, fulfilling all one's aspirations.
Furthermore, the mantra for generating the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is as follows:
Namo samantabuddhānām | dharmadhātu-svabhāvātmaka hūṃ | Dharmadhātu is the nature of phenomena; that which is the Dharma-realm is the very body of the Buddha.
The subsequent phrase, "I am," means that "I" is precisely the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Furthermore, although this practitioner may not yet have realized the true nature of their own essence, by merely forming this seal and reciting the mantra, they likewise realize an identity with the Dharma-realm.

For this mudrā, place the two middle fingers (the *śūnyatā* fingers) within the palms. Form fists by pressing the three fingers of earth, water, and fire with both hands. Straighten the two wind fingers and hold them upright; form separate fists with each hand and keep the wind fingers erect. First, extend the two [thumb] fingers together at the chest, then rotate them inward. Guide the two fingers from both sides of the crown toward the left and right cheeks and neck respectively, drawing them inward and slightly downward.

This means: first, extend the fingers vertically; then slightly tilt the fingertips downward and turn the backs of the fingers inward, gradually bringing the fingertips closer to the lower part of the head and cheeks; finally, when reaching the heart, disperse the hands.
In all recitations of mantras and the performance of mudrās, it is likened to two oxen plowing together;

they must advance side by side and not one before the other. Next, perform another mudrā: first, join the palms with the backs of the hands facing outward. Hook the two ring fingers (the earth-fingers) with their backs turned toward each other, placing the right over the left. Then, likewise hook the remaining three fingers—water, fire, and wind—in succession with their backs turned. Finally, interlace the two thumbs within the palms so that they press against each other.
This is the Seal of Turning the Wheel of Dharma.
By forming this seal, one’s body and mind are purified, enabling one to directly behold the Buddhas of the ten directions turning the wheel of Dharma.
The mantra is: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ vajra-tama hūṃ*. This mantra has already been explained above; it should be further verified.

Next, regarding the formation of the sword mudrā: the sword is a metaphor for sharp wisdom, and its meaning lies in its ability to sever and eliminate—that is, to remove the mountain peaks of evil views.

Just as the peaks of a great mountain are exceedingly numerous and disordered, so too are the afflictions (*kleśa*); now, by forming this sword mudrā, one acts according to what was explained above through the power of this seal.
Then, bend the two wind-fingers so that their tips touch each other, and place the two space-fingers side-by-side to press and pinch them, forming the shape of a great sword. This is it.
The mantra is as follows:
*Namo samantabuddhānām*, and so forth.
The stainless manifestation of the Great Sword severs innate views of selfhood; faith and understanding in the Tathāgata arise, and the dharma of non-attachment arises.
This mantra is recited in its Sanskrit pronunciation.
Within the sūtra, its meaning has already been fully annotated as explained above.
This mantra takes the initial syllable *ma* as its heart, which signifies the meaning of "I."
Furthermore, these five dots of emptiness signify the meaning of pervading all places.
The intention here is precisely to destroy this view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
One should know that this Sword Mudrā is the Great Wisdom of all Buddhas, for it is able to sever all views.
By severing the roots of affliction with the sword, the stainless Dharma immediately manifests.
The category of views regarding a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) that arises simultaneously [with consciousness] is precisely what constitutes defilement.
Now that these defilements have been severed, there is immediate cessation.

While the afflictions have not yet ceased, there is a further superior dharma: namely, having removed these defilements, one should give rise to faith and understanding toward the Tathāgata, understanding this meaning just as it was understood at the beginning.
What is this dharma called "faith and understanding toward the Tathāgata"?
This refers to the roots of goodness such as non-attachment; for this reason, the syllable *ha* arises next.

Within this, the syllable *ha* serves as the cause, and in order to eliminate this cause, there is a long vowel mark (*ā*) attached to its side, which signifies that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen.
Below is the letter *u*, which constitutes the *samādhi*; above it is a dot (*bindu*), representing the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*).
One who recites this can cause the practitioner to fulfill the three kinds of bodies; because there are three meanings within this syllable, it is the manifestation of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
The Tripitaka Master said:

"In the Western Regions, the methods of mudrās are especially secret; when performing them, one must be extremely reverent, ensuring they take place within a sacred chamber or in a place that is empty, quiet, and clean."

When bathing and adorning the body, if one is unable to bathe every single limb, one must at least wash the hands and rinse the mouth; only then may one apply scented unguents to the hands and perform the rite.
Furthermore, while performing [the rite], one must maintain proper deportment, such as sitting in the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
Otherwise, one incurs offense, which will prevent the Dharma from being swiftly accomplished.
Immediately thereafter, perform the *śrīvatsa-śaṅkha-mudrā*.

First, perform the *añjali* mudrā in mid-air as before; bend the two *ākāśa* fingers (thumbs) and press down upon them with the two *vāyu* fingers (index fingers) so that they take the shape of a conch (*śaṅkha*).
Having formed the seal, bring it close to the mouth and blow into it according to the method for blowing a conch shell.
This is the Auspicious Dharma Conch Seal that Fulfills All Wishes.
By forming this seal, all virtuous aspirations are fulfilled, and one proclaims the Great Dharma so that it may be heard and known throughout the ten directions.
This is the seal of tranquil nirvāṇa.
Its mantra’s homage is the same as before:
*sarvatathāgata*. This is the heart of the mantra: *dharmāḥ sarve ’nutpannāḥ* (all phenomena are originally unarisen).
Above this, there is yet another point, which is the Great Emptiness pervading all places.
This is the essential nature of the Great Quiescent Nirvana; all myriad virtues are tranquil therein, pervading every place.
Next is the Vajra-Abhedyāsana. Regarding the mudrā ritual:

first, the two middle fingers and the two ring fingers are placed side by side; the remaining fingers are extended and spread like an opened lotus flower. As the sūtra states, they should be shaped like a bell (*ghaṇṭā*).

Next, one changes this by interlocking the earth and space fingers; the six middle fingers remain extended side-by-side as before, while the fire and wind fingers are joined together, and the water finger is held single—this is it.
This is the Lotus Seat, also known as the Vajra Seat.
Because all Buddhas are able to arise by sitting upon this seat, and because all Buddhas pass through this seat, it is called the Auspicious Seat; thus, it is named the Indestructible Vajra Seat.
The mantra’s homage is as before.
􈅺 This is the heart of the mantra.
This extended letter A constitutes the practice (*caryā*), while the two dots at its side constitute samādhi.
In order to make this dharma firm and stable, there is subsequently the "dot" (bindu).
Now, there are four methods for forming the fist:
the first is the ordinary method of forming the fist, with the thumb held upright; this is the first.
Next, place the empty fingers within the palms and clench them into fists; this is called the Vajra Fist, the second.

Interlace both hands to form fists, causing the ten fingers to appear on the outside; this is called the "Fingers-Appear-on-the-Outside" Fist, the third. [In this case,] the right fingers are placed over the left.

Next, interlace the ten fingers so that all the tips of the ten fingers are placed within the palms; this is called the "two-fisted mudrā," the fourth, in which the right hand is likewise placed over the left.
Next, perform the Vajra-mudrā:

bend both ring fingers (salīla) toward the palms; join the backs of the middle fingers (tarjanī) with the tips of the index fingers (agraṅgulī) without touching them; this is the Vajra-mudrā. The two thumbs (aṅguṣṭha) are held side by side and upright.
By means of this vajra-mudrā, one can destroy the city of ignorance; nothing else can destroy it.
Its mantra’s *namas* (homage) is as before. The essence of the spell consists solely of the syllable *HŪṂ*; its meaning is to be understood as explained above.

Next is the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa mudrā. First, form a fist with the fingers pointing inward; then extend the two middle fingers so they are side by side. Next, place the two ring fingers (vāyu) upon the backs of the middle fingers and bend the two thumbs (ākāśa) so they are side by side. This is it. Regarding "the fingers pointing inward," this means the tips of the fingers are directed inward.
This great seal is named Buddha-uṣṇīṣa; when one binds this dharma-seal, one is immediately identical to the Tathāgata.
"Identical to the Tathāgata" means that by forming this seal, one becomes one with the bodies of all Buddhas.
This is a mantra, and it also possesses the meaning of samādhi and liberation.
The former is the cause and the latter is the fruit.
The cause is the practice of the Tathāgata, and the fruit is the Buddha himself; these should be added above the crown of the head.
Ask further.
Next is the Seal of the Tathāgata’s Majestic Mark:
form a fist with the hand of wisdom (the right hand), extending the thumb, and place it between the eyebrows; this is it.
By forming this mudrā, one becomes identical to the Tathāgata, fully endowed with the marks of majesty.
Its mantra for taking refuge is as before:
*Jñā* (the syllable of wisdom), *Hetu* (the cause), and *Utpāda* (arising). By means of this practice of non-arising, one purifies all causes.
*Ja* signifies that birth cannot be found. Next, perform the Seal of the Tathāgata’s Almsbowl (*pātra-mudrā*).

With the left hand, take hold of two corners of the robe: the corner near the tip of the wrist and the corner that rests upon the shoulder. Wrap them around the arm and bring them back into the hand so that the two corners resemble a pair of ears. Then, with both hands placed one over the other, let the right hand be placed above the left like the hands in the *dhyāna-mudrā*. Draw them upward until they are level with the navel, slightly bending them into the shape of supporting a bowl with cupped hands; this is it.

To perform this is equivalent to the Tathāgata himself wearing this kāṣāya; it is the ritual of the insignia of all Buddhas, and it can also cause all sentient beings who are not yet vessels for the Dharma to become fit vessels for the Dharma.
The mantra’s homage is as before.
*Bha* has the meaning of "existence," namely the three realms of existence (*tribhava*).
Because they are fundamentally unborn, one is detached from the three realms of existence; the three realms of existence are originally unobtainable.
Transcending these three realms of existence (*tribhava*), one attains the true existence of the Tathāgata, which is the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas.
Next, perform the mudrā of granting fearlessness (*abhaya-hasta*).

With the left hand as before, hold the two corners of the robe and extend them to the level of the navel; the right hand has its fingers pointing upward and extended outward, like the gesture of spreading out an object. This is the same as the Śākyamuni mudrā described in the *Yogatantra*.
If one forms this seal, it can eliminate the various fears of all sentient beings; love and hatred will immediately cease, and it shall also remove their various great terrors of the future.
The *namas* (homage) of this mantra is as before.
*Sarvathā śānta śānta śāmya śāmya naśya*, which means "to remove fear. *Sarva-* has the sense of "universal," meaning "pervading all places."
Among all skillful means, this is the most supreme; it can overcome them all.

First, it abandons the afflictions of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), and next, it abandons the afflictions of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*); thus it is stated twice, meaning it is the most supreme among the supreme.
For this reason, the Tathāgata is able to pervade all places and universally eliminate all fears and afflictions.
Next is the Tathāgata’s Seal of the Fulfillment of Vows:
the left hand also holds the corner of the robe and spreads it as before; the right hand is extended outward and hangs downward, like the seal of Ratnasambhava Buddha in the *Yoga* [Tantras].
When forming this mudrā, by the power of the Tathāgata, all Buddhas fulfill their aspirations and all attain accomplishment.
The mantra for taking refuge is as before.
*Varadāya vajrātmake*: "O you who possess the vajra-nature, grant [me] the vajra-body. It also means: "Grant me the body of great vows.
It also refers to the body and mind; the meaning is: "May all Buddhas grant me the vajra-body," which is also the granting of the body of great vows.
This is the seal for fulfilling one's wishes.
Next is the seal for terrifying all obstructors:
form a fist with the right hand, extend the thumb, and raise the index finger (vāyu-aṅguli), placing it at the space between the eyebrows, with the tip of the finger pressing against that point.
Regarding "equipoise" (*samāhita*): it refers to assuming the form of Vajucī with a face like that of a wrathful deity, while the mind dwells one-pointedly without wavering.

This Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) of all Buddhas can manifest the power of the Tathāgata’s formidable majesty to terrify all obstructors and bring them under subjugation; it can also fulfill the aspirations of all sentient beings.
When the practitioner binds this seal, there are no obstructors who do not flee in the four directions; even the hosts of the celestial Māra armies of great power naturally retreat and disperse.
When the Tathāgata realized the path to Bodhi, he was able to subdue all Māras by means of this seal.
The mantra for taking refuge is as before:

*Mahābali* (Great Power), *Vajri* (Holder of the Vajra), *Daśabala* (Ten Powers), *Dhava* (Support), *Vidyā* (Knowledge), *Mahāmaitrī* (Great Compassion), *Jaya* (Victory). This mantra is the great power of all Buddhas.
What is this "great power"? It is precisely the ten powers (*daśabala*) of the Tathāgata, the greatest sovereignty among all powers.
How does the Tathāgata attain these ten powers?
This means that these ten powers are obtained from Great Compassion; therefore, it is said that these powers are born from Great Compassion.
Next is the Buddha-Eye Seal (*buddhacakṣur-mudrā*).

First, form a fist, then press the space-finger (*ākāśāṅguli*) down upon the wind and earth fingers (*vāyu* and *pṛthivī*), bending those fingers so that the tip of the space-finger presses upon their nails. Then extend the water and fire fingers (*ap* and *tejas*). Perform this with the right hand.
Having performed this, one uses these two fingers to support the eyes, first applying them to the right eye and then to the left.
By means of this secret expedient, one can purify the visual faculty, achieve the Buddha-eye, and perceive the profound and secret realm of the Tathāgata.
The mantra for taking refuge is as before:
*Gagana-kāra-ya-vā-ra-ya-karuṇā-maye-tatāgata-cakṣuṣe*. Although the sky is signless and unobstructed, it cannot accomplish great deeds.
Now, although this emptiness of the Tathāgata has no basis, it is able to accomplish all supreme and sublime matters; it surpasses that [ordinary] space and cannot be equaled by it.
The essence of great compassion is the eye of the Tathāgata.
This eye arises from great compassion and can, in turn, give rise to great compassion—this is further explained.
Next is the Tathāgata’s Pāśa-mudrā (Lasso Seal).

First, form fists with both hands, the ten fingers pointing inward. Then, extend the two index fingers (vāyu-aṅguli), pressing their tips against one another and bending them so they join in the shape of a circle.
As for the two middle fingers (ākāśa-aṅguli), the right is placed over the left, and both are tucked into the palms; this is it.
This mudrā can bind all those who commit evil and can also destroy them, causing their various evils to cease.
The mantra for taking refuge is as before.
The syllable *he* (係) herein is the causal factor (*hetu*), which also carries the meaning of *samādhi*.
This *he* is a vocative sound, signifying the invocation of this cause for attaining Buddhahood.
This cause, because it is originally unarisen (*an-utpanna*), is free from cause and effect; thus, it causes this cause to be pure, and further purifies it. *Mahā-pāśa* means "great noose.

This cause, which is free from characteristics, because it is originally unarisen, is free from the characteristics of cause and effect; it causes this cause to be pure, and that which further purifies it is called *mahā-pāśa-vilupta*. *Svādhārīya* means "like space"; it signifies that this great noose is vast and universal like space, pervading everywhere without exception. *Sattva-dhātu* asks: what does this noose, being so vast and universal, do?

This means that among sentient beings, one upholds [the Dharma] in order to eliminate delusion—*phaimukhaka* meaning delusion, and *prahāṇa* meaning the eradication of delusion—and to give rise to faith and understanding in the *tathāgata*, the Thus-Come One; it is also the manifestation of the original vows of all Buddhas.
"When all Buddhas practiced the bodhisattva path, they at that time fully delivered all sentient beings from great evil.

Now, by means of this cause, the fruit must necessarily be accomplished; let this delusion be removed so that they may reach the ultimate state of Buddhahood and constantly perform the work of a Buddha. Furthermore, from what does this lasso arise?
This means it arises from the faith and resolve (*adhimukti*) toward the Tathāgata.
The meaning of "faith and resolve" has already been explained at the beginning of this sutra scroll.

By the power of this faith and resolve, the Tathāgata manifests various types of forms through the universal gate (*samantamukha*): sometimes performing great wrathful deeds, and sometimes acting as a *vidyādhara* ṛṣi endowed with great majestic power, subduing and gathering in immeasurable sentient beings so that they all may attain the sublime fruit of the Tathāgata. This is precisely the meaning of the "Great Rope" (*mahāpāśa*) being vast and universal, coextensive with the realm of sentient beings.
Next, perform the Tathāgata Hook Seal (*vajrāṅkuśa-mudrā*).

First, with the left hand, press the tips of the four fingers except the thumb together so that they form a ring-like shape. Then, insert the three fingers of the right hand into the ring. Place the right thumb over the outside of the left thumb and bend it into the palm to grasp the three fingers of the right hand, making them also form a ring-like shape. Extend the right wind-finger (the index finger) and slightly bend its third joint so that it takes the form of a hook; this is it.

By forming this hook-seal (*ākarṣaṇa-mudrā*), one can summon all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions to assemble at the site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*). It can also fulfill the stages of the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*); how much more so would those of the eight classes of beings who have not yet given rise to a wholesome mind not come?

ĀRYĀ-SARVATRA-PRAHĪTA means "unobstructed in all respects" and refers to that which is free from all harm. TATHĀGATA-AṄKUŚA-BODHI-CARĪ means "the conduct for enlightenment, the hook of the Tathāgata. PARIPŪRAYA SVĀHĀ means "nirvāṇa," which signifies fulfillment. Regarding the practitioner herein: it is by means of this practice that one is able to summon the great ocean of merit of all Buddhas.
Just as a worldly hook has a specific location and position and cannot summon things everywhere, the hook of the Tathāgata is not like this;
it reaches all beings without exception and can even summon the fruit of Great Bodhi.
To state it briefly: this fulfills all the merits of the Tathāgatas and universally summons all sentient beings so that they too may attain this path.

Therefore, the subsequent phrase says, "pervading all harms," where "harm" refers to the hooking and seizing of what remains. By pervasively harming all those who are undisciplined, one causes them all to incline toward the practice of bodhi and to attain fulfillment.
Next is the Tathāgata Heart Seal.
The ritual procedures are all performed according to the previous method, with the sole addition of extending the fire fingers (the middle fingers).
These two extended fingers must both have their third joints bent.
The mantra’s homage is as before.
*Namo* (the syllable *na* with the *u* vowel and the *ma* bindu) signifies wisdom; this is the wisdom of all Buddhas. This wisdom is not obtained from another; it arises from the Buddha-mind itself.
Next is the Tathāgata Navel Mudrā.
This is also based on the previous [mudrā], with the addition of extending the water-finger (the ring finger); in all cases where three fingers are extended, their third joints are also bent.
The mantra for taking refuge is as above.
*Amṛtodgata-madhu-udbhava*. "Amṛta" (ambrosia) is a specific name for wisdom-wisdom (*jñāna-jñāna*). It can eliminate the feverish afflictions of body and mind;
having attained it, one partakes of it and becomes neither old nor dead. Thus, it may be used as a metaphor for the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Now, by means of this wisdom, one removes the feverish afflictions of all sentient beings and causes them to attain a body of eternal life.
This flavor of ambrosia also arises from the Buddha-mind.
Next is the Tathāgata Waist Seal (*kaṭy-mudrā*).
This is formed in the same manner as the Tathāgata Hook (*aṅkuśa*), with the exception that the wind fingers (*vāyu-aṅgulī*) are tucked inward while the water fingers (*toya-aṅgulī*) are extended.
These water fingers need not bend their third joints; this refers to the water finger of the right hand.
The mantra for taking refuge is as before:
*tathāgata-rūpam eva bhavati*. One should know that this wisdom-seal (*jñāna-mudrā*) is indeed born from the Tathāgata.

In general, when sealing a mantra, one always recites its meaning for oneself; others should all follow this principle. Next is the Tathāgatagarbha Seal. First, form the *tripuṭa* (three-fold) hollow-palmed *añjali*:

the water and wind fingers (the index and ring fingers) are both bent into the palms, with the tips of the fingers meeting and facing each other. The fire fingers (middle fingers) of both hands are extended straight, with their tips joined together. The two space fingers (thumbs) are placed side by side and pressed down upon the wind fingers. The earth fingers (little fingers) of both hands are also extended, but without the tips touching, they are slightly bent and made curved; this is it.
"Rara rala" signifies the meaning of being stainless; the dot above represents the Great Emptiness Samādhi (*mahāśūnyatā-samādhi*).
First, it removes the obstacles of ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles; second, it abides in the emptiness that is the nectar of the Tathāgata.

The two dots beside the next two characters signify the meaning of "purifying and removing": the first removes the defilements of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), and the second removes the defilements of those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
Next, perform the seal of the Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā-mudrā*).

Following the previous method for the Tathāgata Hook Seal (*tathāgata-aṅkuśa-mudrā*), simply raise the water-fingers of both hands and extend them straight upward; this is it. Furthermore, when questioned about it, [the practitioner] was not clear.

Regarding the "great boundary" (*mahā-sīmā*) herein: it refers to the period from the initial generation of the great bodhicitta until the attainment of Buddhahood; during this interval, one does not allow for interruption, nor does one undergo further birth and death or regress from bodhi—this is the meaning of the "great boundary."
The mantra begins with "Homage" (*namas*) as before. *Lī* signifies the mark of detachment;

*tri* and *lū* are the sounds of the two wheels, each mounted upon its respective sign. *Bhu* signifies the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), for the ultimate truth is unattainable. *Li* signifies freedom from defilement; *mi* signifies freedom from bondage. *Ku-ku* (the sound *ku-ku*) signifies "to act"; *lī* signifies the mark of detachment. All of these are samādhis.
The Tathāgata adorns himself with these various samādhis, beyond which nothing superior exists; this is the great boundary of all Buddhas.
Next, perform the Great Protection Seal (Mahārakṣā-mudrā).

Following the previous Tathāgatagarbha mudrā, extend the two water-fingers (ring fingers) so that their tips touch like a mountain peak; likewise, the tips of the two fire-fingers (middle fingers) should also touch but be slightly bent, resembling the shape of a lotus ring.
Furthermore, open the two fingers of emptiness; it is at a distance of two inches [from the tips] that this is located.

The mantra is as follows: *Sarvatathāgatebhyo namaḥ* (Homage to all Tathāgatas); *Sarvabhayavigatebhyo namaḥ* (To those who have removed all fears and obstacles), which is also an expression of praise and homage to the Buddhas; *Viśvamukhebhyaḥ* (To those with manifold gates), which also carries the meaning of "skillful," referring to the Buddhas' skillful manifestation of various gates of merit; *Savatha* (Pervasive), meaning at all times, in all places, and in all directions; *Haṃ Khaḥ*—*Haṃ* signifies "cause" (*hetu*), while *Kha* signifies "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*); the nasal dot (*bindu*) is also emptiness, by means of which one purifies all causes through emptiness.
Furthermore, as for "emptiness," this emptiness is itself empty. *Rakṣa* means protection;

it protects not only those of the two vehicles, but also all Buddhas. Because of this, the Buddhas do not abandon sentient beings, constantly performing the work of a Buddha without rest, and do not abide in [mere] quiescence. *Mahā-male*. Great!
"Power" (*bala*) refers to the ten powers of the Tathāgata. *Sarvatathāgata* means "Tathāgata";
*buddhyanirjāta* means "born from the merit of the Tathāgata," signifying that these powers arise from the Tathāgata’s virtues. *Hūṃ hūṃ*:
the first [syllable] signifies the terror of obstacles; the second is for the purpose of fulfilling Buddhahood.

Because these are the three virtues, they are spoken of repeatedly; "tāṭa tāṭa" means to utterly terrify and to subdue, subduing both internal and external obstacles, and furthermore, because it constitutes the Buddha-body (dharmakāya), it is stated twice.
"apratihate" means non-harming; it signifies the meaning of being without obstruction. This is called "Non-... [The text ends here].
The Great Protector Endurance (Kṣānti-mahārakṣa).
Because his majestic radiance is so fierce and intense, it is like a newborn infant who cannot endure the light of the scorching sun.
It is just so with this [protector]: no one at all can endure him or dare to eclipse or surpass him; therefore, he is named the Great Protector Endurance.
This is the mudrā for the practitioner of the mantra of protection.
Next is the Tathāgata Universal Radiance (Samantaprabhā) mudrā:

join the two space-fingers (thumb and index finger) together and bend them into the palm; extend the two wind-fingers (middle fingers) straight up so that they do not touch each other, keeping them both upright; join the tips of the two fire-fingers (ring fingers), spacing their joints slightly apart in the shape of a bell; the remaining fingers are as before—this is it.
The mantra is as follows: *jīvāravāra*. "Jīva" means birth; "ra" means binding; "vā" means characteristic.

The side [syllable] has the vowel *a* with a bindu, which is identical in meaning to non-arising; thus, it is the non-arising of characteristics. "Maliṇi-ma" refers to the self (*ātman*). There is a long vowel *ā*, and "li" signifies perception (*saṃjñā*). The meaning of perception is contemplation (*vipaśyanā*); it is the departure from existence through the contemplation of non-existence. "Tathāgata" refers to the light of the Tathāgata; this light of the Tathāgata arises from meanings such as the absence of characteristics and the absence of contemplation. Next is the Seal of the Tathāgata’s Armor.
Form the *tripuṭa* añjali; place the two *vāyu* fingers (the index fingers) alongside the backs of the middle fingers and extend them parallel—this is it.
The mantra for this is omitted; consult the original text further.
The Tathāgata’s tongue mudrā is also omitted; consult the original manuscript.
The mantra of the Tathāgata’s tongue is as follows:
Homage is as before.

*Tathāgata* [is composed of]: *tathā* (thus), *āgata* (come); *svākhyāta* (well-proclaimed); *svalakṣaṇa* (own-characteristic); *dharma* (phenomenon); *pratisiddha* (established). Thus, a *Tathāgata* is one who has come in accordance with reality (*yathābhūtam*).
Just as the tongue of the Tathāgata always utters words that are such-as-they-are, not deceptive, and not otherwise, it abides eternally by virtue of such truth.
Next is the Seal of the Gate of the Tathāgata’s Speech.

Following the previous mudrā, form the *tri-puṭa* (three-fold) *añjali*: join the tips of the water-fingers (*salila*) and wind-fingers (*vāyu*) within the palms, pressing them down with the two space-fingers (*ākāśa*) side by side; then align the two earth-fingers (*pṛthivī*) and two fire-fingers (*tejas*) straight, their tips touching each other like the shape of a bee. This is it.
The mantra’s invocation is as before.

*Mahā-vāk-trā* (the second syllable is a conjunct) is the speech; *viśvaya* means various skillful wisdoms; *mahā-dhaye* means great and vast. This signifies that this speech is produced from the Tathāgata’s immeasurable gateways of skillful wisdom, and this wisdom is vast and immeasurable.
Next is the Tathāgata’s Tooth Seal:
form the *tripuṭa* (three-fold) añjali, bend the two *vāyu* fingers (index fingers) into the palms so that the backs of their joints are aligned.

The mantra begins with *namas* as before. *Tathāgata-śāstṛ-jaya-rasāgra*, "the supreme flavor of the Victor, the Teacher of the Tathāgatas. Because it is the flavor among flavors, it is stated twice; this refers to the Dharma-flavor of the Tathāgata. *Agra* (the word *agra*) connects with the preceding phrase; since the preceding phrase lacked the vowel *a*, it is joined with *a*, signifying "supreme" or "preeminent," meaning the supreme flavor. *Saprabhoga*.
*Labdha-tathāgata-viṣaya-sambhava*, meaning that this supreme flavor arises from the realm (*viṣaya*) of the Tathāgata; next is the Seal of the Four Eloquences of the Tathāgata.
Form the *tripuṭa* añjali: bend the two wind-fingers (*vāyu-aṅguli*) inward so that they rest upon the backs of the two fire-fingers (*tejas-aṅguli*), ensuring their tips do not touch one another;

this is it. By means of this seal, the Tathāgata dwells among the assembly without fear and expounds the True Dharma for others; even within a single syllable, he contains infinite meanings, and such eloquence is inexhaustible.

The mantra begins with the homage as before: *A-kṣi-ṇya* (the two syllables combined) means "inconceivable"; *anupama* (two syllables combined) means "extraordinary"; *arvāṅga* (the division of the word) also means "extraordinary"; *vāk-samanta* means "pervasive," for when the Buddha preaches the Dharma with a single voice, it reaches the presence of all sentient beings, and wherever it reaches, each individual thinks, "The Buddha is using my own voice to preach the Dharma to me. *Viśuddha* means "pure"; *sarva-ruta* refers to "all sounds and voices."

Because the speech uttered is free from the faults of verbal karma such as coarseness and harshness, being subtle, pure, and pleasant for others to hear, it is called "pure vocal sound. Next is the Seal of the Tathāgata’s Ten Powers.
Bend the index fingers of both hands so that their tips meet at the palms, joining them together; the remaining fingers form the *tripuṭa* (three-fold) joined palms.
The mantra for taking refuge is as before.
*Hūṃ* represents the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
*Ma* is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The bindu is samādhi. *Ja* has the meaning of "birth" and also signifies "summoning.
Furthermore, it is asked how one attains summoning.
This seal can uphold the ten powers (*daśabala*) of the Tathāgata.
These three characters are combined at the end of the phrase; as in the *Mahāsūtra*, "dha" is inserted into "śavalan-ga," which refers to the constituent parts of the ten powers.

The syllable *laṃ* above represents the ten powers (*daśabala*). This very syllable *laṃ*, when joined with the long vowel *ā* and the letter *ga*, constitutes the "body-part" (*aṅga*), which means "to hold" (*dhāraṇa*). That is to say, by the power of this wisdom-seal (*jñānamudrā*), one is able to uphold the constituent parts of the Tathāgata’s ten powers.
Next is the Seal of the Tathāgata’s Mindfulness (Tathāgata-smṛtyupasthāna-mudrā).
Form three *puṭas*, all like unopened lotuses, with the palms joined at the height of the crown of the head (*paramākāśa*).
Furthermore, consult the preceding text to ensure there is no error. It is formed by joining the two thumbs and two index fingers (*vāyu*) and pressing them together; this is it.
As for the method of forming the mudrā: one should cause the nails of the four fingers to touch the ears.
The mantra for taking refuge is as before:

*Tathāgata-smiti* (the mindfulness of the Tathāgata), *sattvārtha-karoti* (he acts for the benefit of sentient beings), *ākāśa-sama* (equal to space). This means that this mindfulness is equal to space and immeasurable; yet, because space itself cannot serve as a comparison, it is further described as "unequaled" (*asama*).
Why is this so? Because the nature of space is non-existent, it cannot bring about great benefit for all sentient beings.
Next is the Seal of the Equal Enlightenment of All Dharmas.
Form the *tripuṭa* añjali gesture by joining the two water fingers and the two space fingers and pressing them together;

this is it. The mantra for taking refuge is as before: *sarvadharma-samanta*, meaning "all phenomena are equal"; *prāpta*, meaning "attained," referring to the attainment of all equality; *tathāgata*, the Tathāgata (the term *tathāgata* has the correct meaning of "Thus-Gone"); *anugata*, "following" or "conforming," meaning following all Tathāgatas; and "having attained that same such awakening. Next is the Samantabhadra Seal of the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel.
He is named Samantabhadra because all three of this bodhisattva’s modes of action (trikarma) are universally virtuous and good, and he is thus praised by all buddhas and bodhisattvas.
To form this mudrā, make three *puṭas*: rotate the two *vāyu* fingers (the index fingers) behind the joints of the two *tejas* fingers (the middle fingers), making them round;
the rest is as usual.
The mantra begins with *namas* as before.

*Samantānugata* means "pervading all equally. *Vairocana* means "stainless" and "dustless. *Dharmadhātu* means "born from the Dharma," signifying that this stainlessness arises from the Dharma. *Mahā-mahā* is a reduplication for emphasis, similar to saying "the God among gods."

The various bodhisattvas make offerings to the Buddha, and the Buddha in turn makes offerings to Samantabhadra; this is because the body of Samantabhadra is equal to the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
This is thus the greatest among the great and the supreme offering among all offerings; therefore, the seal of Maitreya is mentioned again in succession.

Form the *tripuṭa* mudrā, bend the two ring fingers so that their tips reach beneath the base of the middle fingers, join the two little fingers together and press them down, and let the remaining fingers be as usual.
This mudrā is like the shape of a stūpa because it upholds the Dharma-body stūpas of all Tathāgatas, just as Avalokiteśvara upholds the Buddha’s body.
The mantra for taking refuge is as before.
*Āśīdan* is translated as *Ajita*; this is his name.

Its meaning is "unconquerable," signifying that he cannot be surpassed by any afflictions of craving or views, nor even by those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). *Jaya* means "victory."
"To attain victory over those who are invincible" means: *sarvasattvāḥ* refers to all sentient beings; *āśayaḥ* refers to their nature; *nuktaḥ* refers to knowing the arising of their minds.
"Arising" (utpāda) has the meaning of "knowing," which refers to knowing the nature of all sentient beings.
Regarding the syllable, the Ācārya says:
"This is the seed-syllable of Maitreya. Next is the seal of Ākāśagarbha.
With an open mind, join the palms; this is done by placing the two index fingers side-by-side and bending them into the palms.

The mantra for taking refuge is as before: *ākāśa* (space), *samanta* (all-pervading), etc.; *sama* means "equal to," as in "equal to space. *nugata* means "attained" (*prāpti*), which corresponds to the previously mentioned sense of "knowing" (*jñāna*) and "arising" (*utpatti*). *vicitra* means "various"; *ambara* means "garment"; *dhara* means "wearing"—that is, wearing various garments. (Note: *Ambara* is derived from *am*, the bindu, added above the letter *ka* to form *kama*, which becomes *kala*; *ra* combined with *vicitra* signifies "various," and *ambara* signifies "clothing.")

Just as space is formless yet can manifest various forms, so too is this Bodhisattva; like space, he is able to fulfill all manner of vows and manifest various forms to benefit sentient beings. Next is the seal of the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin.

Form the *tripuṭa* añjali; bend the earth and water fingers (the thumbs and ring fingers) into the palms, while the remaining [fingers] are as usual, with the nails of the earth and water fingers pressed together.
The mantra for taking refuge is as before.
*Asattva* (阿薩埵) is composed of *a*, which has the meaning of "removing," and *sattva*, which has the meaning of "benefiting";
that is to say, it means benefiting sentient beings. *Pryotkṛta-taraṃ taraṃ raṃ raṃ* has the meaning of "removing."
This also serves to manifest their virtuous nature.
Regarding what was mentioned above as "removing attachments," what is it that is removed?
It refers to the removal of the four defilements.

The defilement of craving and views of ordinary beings is the first; the defilement of śrāvakas is the second; the defilement of pratyekabuddhas is the third; and the defilement of bodhisattvas is the fourth.
It is for the sake of removing the defilements of sentient beings that one enters the stage of a śrāvaka.
Because one removes the defilements of the śrāvakas, one enters the stage of the pratyekabuddha.
Continuing in this manner until one removes the defilements of the bodhisattvas, one enters the stage of purity. Next is the mudrā of Avalokiteśvara:

first, form the *utkṣipta-karapuṭa* (opened palms); join the tips of the thumbs and the ring fingers, while the remaining six fingers are spread apart; the fire and wind fingers (middle and index fingers) are all placed side by side, and the water finger (pinky) stands alone—this is it.

*Sarvatathāgata* refers to all Tathāgatas; *avalokita* means "observed" or "contemplated," signifying the contemplation of the Tathāgatas. *Kāruṇika* means "compassionate," indicating that great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is its essence; it signifies that both body and mind, internally and externally, are entirely composed of the body of compassion. *Rara ra* refers to the three defilements; *hūṃ jaya*. (Hūṃ signifies victory.)
This syllable *hūṃ* refers to the three: practice (*caryā*), liberation (*vimukti*), and great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*).

*Ja* has the meaning of "arising," referring to phenomena produced from conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharma*). Regarding the phrase "the Tathāgata’s contemplation" herein: it means that although a bodhisattva has not yet attained Buddhahood, their vision is equal to that of a Buddha; because they perceive the nature of the aggregates (*skandha-svabhāva*), they receive the name "contemplation."

Taking compassion alone as its essence, this compassion arises from the departure from the three poisons; by attaining the three wholesome roots such as non-attachment, it brings about the three liberations, and thus there are the three syllables *ra*.
Next is the mudrā of Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
Form the *tripuṭa* (three-fold) *añjali*, bend the ten fingers so they support one another to form a perfect circle, like an unopened lotus.
This unopened lotus is the precious casket of the Tathāgata, for it is as if it were already blossomed and then closed again.
Regarding the mantra:

*Jana* signifies birth; *sa* signifies equalizing wisdom (*samatājñāna*). Furthermore, one asks the Lord of the World, and moreover transcends the birth of a bodhisattva, abiding within the midst of equalizing wisdom.
Next is the mudrā of Bodhisattva Tārā:

first, form fists by interlacing the fingers with the palms facing inward; then, extend the two index fingers (vāyu-aṅgulī) so that their tips meet like a needle, and place the two little fingers (ākāśa-aṅgulī) side-by-side, extended and pressed down. This is it.
The mantra is: *Tāre hupe tārini* (the syllable *tārini* is pronounced with a rising tone), which means "O Savior.

Just as one ferries people across a great river and places them upon the further shore, *kāruṇya-utpāda* means "arising from compassion"; for by this, the Bodhisattva arises from compassion and likewise ferries sentient beings to the state of compassion. Next is the Vajrakuśa mudrā.
As before, form fists facing inward with palms joined; likewise, extend both index fingers upright, but let them overlap slightly, with the right finger pressing down upon the left. This is it.
