Its form and configuration are largely the same as those of the Tārā [mantra], differing only in that the fingers are slightly offset.
The mantra is:
*sarvabhaya* (all fears), *tārasaṇi* (also meaning "fearsome protector").
Among all terrors, one further terrifies them with terror to cause them to retreat and disperse.

Just as one sees those who are unsubdued, one further subdues them with fierce and formidable power so that they may not commit further wrongs. *Hūṃ* has the three meanings as explained above; *phaṭ* means "to destroy," causing those various terrors to retreat and disperse. This mantra of the Vidyārājñī Jāṅgulī is like a mother among all recitations; her efficacy is most supreme.
Next is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Śvetaketu:

bend both ring fingers (water-fingers) into the palms; likewise, join the two index fingers (space-fingers) together by bending them so that they touch, while the remaining fingers form a *tripuṭa* joined-palms gesture.

The mantra: *Tathāgataviṣayaja-sambhava-padma-mālī*. This means: "Born from the realm (*viṣaya*) of the Tathāgata," indicating that [the deity] arises from the realm of the Tathāgata; and "Padma-mālī," meaning one who possesses a garland (*mālā*) of lotuses (*padma*) as an ornament for the body.
This is that which can give birth to all Buddhas and their Buddha-merits as adornments, thereby adorning the *dharmakāya*. Next is the Horse-Head Seal (*Hayamukha-mudrā*):

form three *puṭa*s; bend the two ring fingers (*vāyu-aṅguli*) so that their nails meet, and place them below the base of the space finger (*ākāśāṅguli*), pinching a space about the size of a grain of barley so that they do not touch one another.
The second mudrā is formed by joining both index fingers together and slightly raising their tips.

The mantra is *khādaya khāda*, which means "consume all obstacles"; *pātaya* means "crush"; and *sphoṭaya svāhā* means "strike these obstacles and scatter them in the four directions. Next is the mudrā of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva.

Form a fist by joining the palms with the fingers interlaced toward the inside; extend the earth and water fingers so that their tips meet like a mountain peak or a blade, and hold the two space fingers straight, side-by-side, and upright.
The mantra:
*Ha ha ha*. These three syllables represent the causes [of the three vehicles], namely those of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.

Generally, all the mantras herein proclaim the virtues of their respective deities; this one specifically proclaims the virtues of the dhāraṇī of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva. *Sudhanu* means "wondrous body."
Because the inner body is utterly pure, it is called the "wondrous body," which is the *dharmakāya*. *Svāhā*. As for the yogin’s abiding, this refers to the practitioner forming such a mudrā.
Next is the mudrā of the noble Mañjuśrī.

First form the *tripuṭa* (three-fingered) gesture: with the two fire fingers (*anāmikā*) inverted to press against the backs of the two water fingers (*madhyamā*), bend the two wind fingers (*tarjanī*) so that their tips touch the tips of the space fingers (*aṅguṣṭha*). This is it.
Regarding the mantra:

the sound *ha* herein is the cause; it signifies being free from the two causes, which is to say, transcending the realms of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). It is also the sound of invocation for Kumāra-kumāra.
It destroys all Māras and is also named Kumāra-vimukti (the liberation of Kumāra). *Bhūtārtha* means the path;
it asks where one dwells, namely, dwelling on the path of liberation. *Smara-smara-pratirāja*: *smara* means mindfulness, and *pratirāja* refers to that which was formerly vowed.
Now I recall my former vow.

The Venerable One’s former vow was to ferry all sentient beings across [to liberation] and to bring them to a state no different from my own; therefore, I shall now remember that ancient oath. Next is the Seal of the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha.

Form a fist with the left hand, extend the vāyu-finger (the index finger), slightly bending its third joint so that it forms a hook-like shape; press the space-finger (the thumb) vertically against the agni-finger (the middle finger)—this is it.
"Kai-kai-kumara. This is as explained previously. "Māyā-ghata-māyā": *māyā* means illusion;

*ghata* means to know, meaning one knows all phenomena (*dharma*) to be like an illusion. *Svabhāva*: nature. *Vasitātmanā*: by means of mastery. Because one thoroughly understands that all phenomena are like illusions, one abides within the true nature and fundamental essence of all phenomena. Next is the Seal of Stainless Light (*vimalaprabhā-mudrā*).

Extend the fingers of the left hand and slightly bend all of them at the third joint; this is it. The space between the fingers should also be kept narrow, with the thumbs held upright alongside the little fingers, appearing as if they were slightly bent.

The mantra: *he he kumāra* (O Youthful One), as before; *vicitra-caryā* (various practices), meaning various modes of conduct; *kumāra* refers to the original vow to manifest bodies through the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*) in various forms to benefit all beings by means of various practices—manifesting either as a youth, or as a person in the prime of life, or as an elderly person; *manusmara* (remember) the vows previously made.
The Noble One formerly made this vow before the Buddha: "May this vow be remembered. Next follows the seal of the secondary wife, Ni-in (Nīlā).
First, form a fist with the right hand, extend the index and ring fingers so they are joined and held straight upright; the middle finger is also held upright and aligned with them.

The mantra: *Kye kye*, as before, is the invocation by Kumārajīva in a female voice; it is also the samādhi of Mañjuśrī. *Na* (pronounced with the *nu* and *gan* tones) means "to grant a boon"; *samyak-sambodhi* means "the original vow."
"Venerable One, the supreme vow you obtained from Mañjuśrī, and the sublime vow you originally made, please bestow that upon me as well," she said next to the nun Upakeśinī.

First, form a fist with the right hand and extend the fire-finger (the index finger) straight; the thumb is also held upright as usual, while the fist is directed outward, with only the middle finger extended.
The mantra is *Vidyādhara-ajñāna-jña*. The final syllable of the preceding phrase is the sound *a*, which connects to this as *ajñāna* (ignorance).

This means that by piercing ignorance with sublime wisdom (*prajñā*), one attains the true nature of reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). *Kumārī* refers to a young girl; it is also a name for samādhi, addressed here using the feminine form. Next is the Earth Wisdom Banner Seal (*Pṛthivī-prajñā-dhvaja-mudrā*).
First, form a fist with the left hand such that the thumb is also on the outside, and extend the index and middle fingers;

this is it. It relates to *asmarana* (recollection), *jñāna* (wisdom); it means one should recollect this wisdom. *Ketu* is the banner; because of this banner of sublime wisdom, all Māras are crushed. Now one should recollect, so that I too may become thus. Next is the mudrā for summoning and inviting.
The five bodhisattvas mentioned above are all messengers of Mañjuśrī.

Their right hands form fists with the thumb positioned on the outside; the ring finger (vāyu-aṅguli) is bent into a circular hook shape, such that it does not quite touch the tip of the space finger (ākāśa-aṅguli). This is precisely how they are formed.

The mantra: *Ākarṣaya*—this means summoning, inviting, or gathering; it all carries the sense of hooking [the deity] and bringing them here. *Svāhā*—*kuru* means "to do" or "to perform"; everything such as taking and giving is included herein.

This means that all matters summoned by the Venerable Mañjuśrī should be performed accordingly; "Āraṅkumāra" refers to the body of this noble being. Next, the various "command-followers" (ājñākārin) are also followers of Mañjuśrī's commands, though they differ slightly from the messengers (dūta).

First, form the inward-turned interlaced palms into fists; then extend the tips of the two wind fingers (index fingers) so they touch, bending them at the third joint, while the two space fingers (thumbs) are also held upright and side by side.

The mantra: *Āḥ* (the *ā* with a dot beside it signifies the form of wrath); *Samayajñe*, which means "fulfilling the vow. It is a marvelous matter that nothing remains unaccomplished; it is able to cause all rare and extraordinary matters to be fully realized.
The sound "Ye" refers to this very Honored One. Next is the Bodhisattva Kāntigarbha (憍都褐羅). This name signifies "removing doubt" or, alternatively, "removing defilement.

For instance, when a great multitude encounters matters of doubt or wonder that they cannot resolve, this Bodhisattva goes to their location and cuts through their web of uncertainty. Because he acts as a friend who does not need to be requested and constantly severs the doubts and delusions of all sentient beings, he is named accordingly.

For this mudrā, form fists with the hands crossed inward and join the palms; extend the two fire-fingers (index fingers) so that their tips touch, bending them at the third joint. This is it. The two space-fingers (little fingers) remain as usual, extended outward and upright.
*Vimati* means lack of wisdom, which refers to that which is not understood. *Vicaya* means cutting off;
it cuts off ignorance and causes wisdom to arise, and it also carries the meaning of decisive resolution.
Furthermore, it carries the meaning of severing and destroying, just like the meaning of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. It is the seal of the Bodhisattva Abhayadāna (Bestower of Fearlessness).
One forms the hand gesture of bestowing fearlessness; as in the yoga of the Śākyamuni seal, one extends the arm upward, turning the palm outward—this is it.
This mudrā demonstrates the practice of the five dharmas: earth represents faith, water represents diligence, fire represents mindfulness, wind represents concentration, and space represents wisdom.
While all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas teach the Dharma through body and speech, this mudrā now symbolizes these five faculties and powers.
The mantra is *abhayaṃ dadāmi*, which means "I bestow fearlessness.
By what dharma does one bestow fearlessness?

This means that by abiding in the gateway of the letter A, one is free from all arising; the Venerable One’s vows have already been fulfilled, whereas we have not yet attained them—may you grant this to me and to all sentient beings.
Next is the seal for eliminating the evil realms (*durgati*).
It is as follows: extend the hands as before with the palms facing upward, and raise them upward;
this is it. The mantra:
*Abhava-dharana-jya-sattva-dhatu*. Regarding this meaning: because all sentient beings have, since beginningless time, been subject to ignorance, they constantly dwell within the three evil realms.
Now that the Noble One has already attained these five powers, we pray that you will lift us up so that we may attain pure transcendence. Why is this?
Because the Venerable One is already able to pull yourself out, you shall likewise lift the entire realm of sentient beings.
Next is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Saṃtrāsanarakṣaṇa (Protector Who Guards from Fear).
As before, extend the hand and place it at the heart; one should turn the palm toward the body to cover one's own heart, with the thumb slightly raised upward.

The mantra signifies "separation from causes," and it also carries the meaning of "summoning" and "awakening. *Mahā-mahā* means the greatest among the great, the most venerable among the venerable. *Sammala-pratītya* refers to the original vow.
The Original Vow removes all suffering; because it removes suffering, it is called "protection.
Now, by calling upon that name, one causes [the Buddha] to remember his original vow and protect all beings. Next is the Seal of the Bodhisattva Mahāmaitrīsaṃbhava.

As before, with the hand in the gesture of fearless giving (*abhaya-mudrā*), join the index finger and the ring finger so that they resemble a person holding a flower; the remaining three fingers are held upright and pointing upward—this is it.
The mantra is:
*sarvasattvānāṃ hṛdaye jāta*. This means that this compassion arises from one's own mind and is not obtained from another; therefore, it is called "Great Compassion" (*mahāmaitrī*).

This means that it arises from the mind of intrinsic purity and does not arise from the mind of the great elements; therefore, it is called "arising from one's own mind. Next is the seal of the Bodhisattva Karuṇācintin (Compassionate Thought).
As before, extend the hands with palms downward to cover the heart, then bend the middle fingers so they touch the heart; this is it.
The mantra:
*Karuṇāye malu kṣaṃte niyate*. This means: "O Honored One, by virtue of your original vow to eliminate all suffering, please now turn your mindfulness toward us."
However, although this bodhisattva is named "the Compassionate One" (*karuṇā-manas*), his intention is not yet fully perfected.
This intention means that this bodhisattva is bound by compassion.

Just as a person who is held captive by another cannot attain autonomy, so too this bodhisattva’s body and mind are bound by compassion; because he is sustained by compassion, he does not attain autonomy.
Furthermore, just as a person who is a servant to a king lacks autonomy, so too is this bodhisattva: he is constantly led by compassion and lacks autonomy.
For this reason, he should simply remain mindful of his original vow to save all sentient beings.
Next is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Sarvaparidāhapraśamana.

It is formed by making the hand of granting boons (*varadamudrā*); that is, extend the right hand with the palm facing upward and let it hang down, as in the *ratnasambhava-buddhamudrā* in the Yoga system.

The mantra means "vara" (bestowal), which is the granting of boons; by means of the dharma that is free from causes, it fulfills the wishes of all sentient beings. "Varapratāpta" means that one has first attained [the boon].
If one has not first attained what was wished for, how could one bestow it upon others?

It is because one has first attained all that was wished for and brought them to complete fulfillment within oneself; now, recollecting one's original vows, one gives to all sentient beings so that they may eliminate all their burning afflictions.

Why is this? Venerable One, you originally established a vow with the resolve to seek the Buddha-way; now that you have attained it, you ought to remember your original vow to extensively deliver all sentient beings, causing them all to enter the sequence of the Buddha-way through the Seal of the Bodhisattva of Inconceivable Wisdom.

With the hand of granting fearlessness, the fingers of space and wind are pressed together in the shape of grasping a jewel; this hand should be tilted slightly, as if one were about to join the fingers to grasp a jewel.
The jewel points upward.
Furthermore, the tips of the middle fingers are slightly separated and turned inward, while the other two fingers are held upright.

*Sarva-āśā-pāripūrakam* means "the fulfillment of all aspirations," signifying that it causes the various supreme vows of all sentient beings to be fulfilled, like a wish-fulfilling jewel. Next is the Banner Seal of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva.

First, form the inward-pointing crossed-fist mudrā; extend the two fire-fingers (index fingers) and hold them upright, ensuring their tips are about one cun apart from each other—this is it. The two space-fingers (thumbs) are held side by side and upright as usual.
To calculate it, observing this banner, this seal is like a banner.
The mantra:
*ha ha ha*—the three causes are as above; *veśamala*—it is marvelous.
All sentient beings are constantly afflicted by the notion of a self; if one cuts off this thought, the notion of a self is immediately eliminated.
This is rare, and it also carries the sense of being extraordinary. Next is the seal of the Bodhisattva Ratnasthāna.

Forming a fist with the right hand such that the thumb is on the outside, then extending the index, middle, and ring fingers (the earth, water, and fire fingers) so they stand side by side—this is it.

It is as described above: *mahā-mahā*, "Great within the Great. As for why it is named "Jewel Source" (*ratnākara*): just as jewels arise from the ocean, because [the mudrā] arises from that source, it is called the Jewel Source.
Just as jewels exist within the ocean and are named for their origin there, next is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi.
Form a fist with the right hand, press the fingers down with the thumb, extend the index finger straight, and hold the middle finger upright; this is it.
The mantra: *Ratna-udbhava*. This means "arising from jewels"; it signifies that this Noble One is born from jewels.
From what jewel does it arise? It arises from the jewel of the bodhicitta. Next is the earth-holding mudrā:

form the palms by crossing the backs of the two hands; the right hand is turned upward and the left downward, with the fingertips pressed together and the thumbs and little fingers entwined. That is to say, the thumbs and little fingers of the left hand point upward, while the thumbs and little fingers of the right hand point downward, clamping them together. This is it.
Mantra is the ground of dhāraṇī.
It is so named because the ground is able to support all things; "dhāra" means to hold.
Because it upholds the stages of all Buddhas and bears the burden of sentient beings, it is called a "stage" (*bhūmi*);
it also causes all sentient beings to attain the name of this stage. Next is the seal of the Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta.
First, form the outward-facing crossed-fist mudrā. Extend the two fire fingers (index fingers) so that their tips touch one another, and keep both the thumbs and little fingers straight and parallel.
Bend the two wind fingers (middle fingers) back against the backs of the middle fingers, ensuring they do not touch them; this forms the five-pronged vajra. This is it.
The mantra is:
*Ratna-anīta-janma* (meaning "born from the jewels of all Tathāgatas"). Next is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati.
It is just like the form of the previous five-pronged [vajra]: cause all the fingertips to join together;

this is it. The mantra: *Vajrasamaya*. It arises from the vajra, and it also arises from the indestructible wisdom-seal (*jñānamudrā*) of the vajra; therefore, it is named as such. Next is the seal of the Bodhisattva Gaganāmala.
Form three *puṭas* by pressing the tips of the space-fingers (*ākāśa-aṅguli*) together so that they meet; this is identical to the Tathāgata-khaḍga-mudrā.
The mantra is:
*Gagana ānanda amita yuga-vajra-gati*. Because his practice is immeasurable and identical to space, he is so named. Next is the Ākāśaprajñā-mudrā.
The mudrā is the same as the previously described Wheel of Dharma mudrā.
The mantra is *cakravarti-vartaya*. This means that the Noble One, having first attained this Wheel of Dharma, now turns this Wheel of Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
Next is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Viśuddhimati:

form three *puṭas*; bend both thumbs (*aṅguṣṭha*) double and insert them into the palms; press them upon the backs of the two index fingers (*tarjanī*) with the two ring fingers (*anāmikā*); curve the joints of the index fingers so that their nails face each other—this is it.

*Dharma* means "Dharma"; *svabhāva* means "birth. This signifies that this Bodhisattva has attained mastery equal to the realm of a Buddha and is born from the Dharma; therefore, he is named Dharmasambhava ("Born of the Dharma").
This means that it arises from the dharma of intrinsic purity.
Next is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara’s Wisdom.
It is identical to the Lotus Mudrā of Avalokiteśvara: the thumb and ring finger are joined at their tips, while the other six fingers are opened and spread like a lotus blossom as described above.
The mantra: *Padma* means "lotus," which is the *ālaya-garbha*; the *garbha* is the bodhicitta.
It arises from that womb-treasury (*garbha*). Next is the Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa (also called Prajñāvihārin), who is even more discerning.

Form the inward-facing crossed-fist *añjali* mudrā; extend the two *vāyu* fingers (index fingers) and hold them upright, their tips slightly apart and not touching one another—this is it. The two *ākāśa* fingers (thumbs) are likewise held side by side and upright.
The mudrā is similar to that of Bodhisattva Tārā, differing only in being slightly opened; inquire further regarding this.
The mantra is:
*jñānaja upāyaja*. It arises from wisdom, and next follows Vajradhara.

Form the five-pronged mudrā as previously described; it is constituted by the two *vāyu* (ring) fingers being positioned one barley-corn’s distance from the upper joints of the *tejas* (middle) fingers.
The mantra is *Śmaśāna*.
The syllable *śaṃ* has a *cha*-sound, which signifies birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); that is to say, it means to transcend birth-and-death.
The "nāga" above signifies the Great Emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*); it means that this cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) is identical to the Great Emptiness.
"Tā" has the meaning of an adversary.
Just as one departs from birth and death and becomes equal to the Great Emptiness, there is consequently no one who can act as an opposing adversary.
Regarding the meaning of the words: *caṇḍa* means "violent and evil," and *mahāroṣaṇa* means "great wrath.

As stated above, there is no one who can oppose him; this is why he is called "wrathful. *HŪṂ* is drawn out in a long sound, which is identical to the three gates of liberation explained previously. By means of the aforementioned methods, he terrifies sentient beings, causing them to leave birth and death and attain the three liberations.
Next is the Māmakī mudrā.

It is like the five-pronged vajra described previously; however, both the two space-fingers (index fingers) and the two earth-fingers (little fingers) are inserted into the palms, with the right pressing down upon the left. This is no different from the previous inward-pointing crossed palms (*añjali*), except that the fire-fingers (middle fingers) and wind-fingers (ring fingers) are positioned like a vajra—this is the Vajra Mother.

*Ṭalita ṭalita*: here, the multiplicity of sounds is itself the state of evenness, identical to suchness (*tathatā*) and the principle of reality; this is samādhi, and it is the relinquishing of the conceit of "I."
Abiding in this suchness (*tathatā*), all pride (*māna*) naturally ceases to exist.
To speak of it again is to express the ultimate meaning and intent; "sa" means supreme (*parama*).

This means that by means of the dharma of suchness and selflessness, one subdues all obstacles and difficulties, causing them to submit out of fear; this is the meaning of "victory in battle. Next is Vajraśaṅkha, which is the vajra chain—the chain of great wisdom.
As previously described, this is the Dharmacakra-mudrā (Wheel-Turning Seal).

Using the fingers representing earth, water, fire, and wind, rotate them downward and inward; at the level of the chest, extend the two *ākāśa* (space) fingers outward, ensuring that the right *ākāśa* finger presses down upon the left as they hook together.
The mantra:
*HŪṂ*, recited three times as before, followed by *PAÑTĀ PAÑTĀ VAYA*.

This means to be freed from the two kinds of bonds, namely the bonds of afflictions (*kleśa*) and the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*). *MUTTHĀYA MUTTHĀYA* is like a strong man seizing and binding a powerless person, twisting them until they reach the neck, causing their limbs to be broken apart.

Causing the two obstructions to be shattered is likewise thus; therefore, this is the meaning of Vajravidāraṇa. *Dhā* means birth, arising from Great Wisdom (*mahājñāna*). *Sarvatrā* means in all places. *Pratihata* means there is nothing that can harm [it]. Next is the wrathful mudrā of the Vajracandrakala.
This vajra was born from the ūrṇā-kośa (tuft of hair) on the Buddha’s forehead; thus it is named after that mark.
Because the ūrṇā-kośa is luminous and pure like the full moon, it is called the "Moon-Mark" (Candraka).

As with the previous five-pronged vajra mudrā, bend the two *vāyu* fingers like hooks to pinch the two *ākāśa* fingers; cause them to be slightly bent so that they do not touch one another—this is it, which differs from the previous [mudrā].
Hrīḥ, the cause of stainlessness, with a bindu [dot] attached, signifying extreme wrath; Hūṃ, recited three times; Phaṭ, because it causes extreme removal. Next is the Vajrasūcī-mudrā.

Form the fists with the hands crossed toward the interior; extend the two wind-fingers (index fingers) so that their tips touch like needles, and bend both space-fingers (thumbs) together into the palms.

The mantra: *Sarvadharmanirvedhani vajrasūcī*. "Sarvadharma" means all phenomena; "nirvedhani" means piercing, signifying that one pierces through all phenomena with the needle of vajra-wisdom; "vajrasūcī" means the vajra-needle.
With what object is it pierced?

It is with the diamond wisdom needle (*vajrajñānasūcī*). *Varade* means "granting boons"; because of the power of previous vows, one now attains this boon, and shall likewise cause all sentient beings to reach the source of all phenomena. Next is the mudrā of the diamond ground (*vajrabhūmiparigraha*).

Form fists by crossing the hands inward; extend both thumbs side-by-side to form the fists. Bring both elbows close together and raise them slightly upward to resemble the shape of a mallet. Lift [the right hand] toward the right side, as if intending to strike in anger.
Mantra: *Saptatha sañja*.
With the hammer of vajra-wisdom, strike the bonds of the three poisons, causing them to disperse, divide, and be destroyed. *Svāhā* (pronounced with the high tone).
Who is able to perform this rite?
It is one born from Vajra who is able to do so. Next is the Vajra Mudrā of Durjayā (Invincible).

Form a fist with the right hand and extend the index finger (*tarjanī*) upright against the heart; form a fist with the left hand with the thumb on the outside and extend the arm straight, holding the fist slightly high so that it is level with the head.
It is so named because all Māras cannot disturb or confound it; thus it attains this name.
The mantra: *Dūḍariṣa*, meaning "difficult to overcome" or "subduing"; *Mahāroṣaṇa*, meaning "Great Wrath."
By what dharma does one subdue the hosts of Māras?

It is through the Great Wrathful One, Khāḍaya, who devours all afflictions, obstructions, and fetters (*sarvātathāgatājñayā kuru*). This means that by honoring the teachings of all the Tathāgatas, one should act in accordance with their instructions; next, one faces the Vajra.
It is so named because it faces Yūyudhāna across the gate.
Its mudrā is as described above, with the sole difference that the right hand is reversed to the left.

It corresponds to the aforementioned Abhimukha facing one another. *Mahā-pracaṇḍa* means "extremely fierce"; *khādya* means "to eat"; *kiṃjila* means "why not quickly?"; *samaya* means "original vow"; and *manuṣyamāra* means "to remember."

Based upon the samaya vow made before all Tathāgatas to consume all afflictions, why do you not now recall your original aspiration and act upon it with haste? Next, perform the Buddha-bowl mudrā as before.
This is the *bowl-mudrā* of Śākyamuni Buddha. The mantra is: *sarva-kleśa-niḥsūdana-kuja*.

"All afflictions" (*sarva-kleśa*) refers to all defilements. "Nih-sūdani-kuja" means to strike directly downward with a sharp mattock until reaching the very bottom. "Sarva-dharma-prapatti" means to attain mastery over all phenomena (*dharma*). "Gagana-samam" means equal to space; because one attains mastery over all phenomena, one is equal to space, and by means of this dharma, one excavates the afflictions. Next, perform the *ūrṇā-kośa-mudrā* (the hair-tuft seal) as before.
This is the Śākyamuni-vaṃśa-mudrā.
Next, with the five fingers of the right hand, clench them together and place them upon the crown of the head; this is the Sarvabuddha-uṣṇīṣa-mudrā.
The mantra is: *Vaṃ vaṃ vaṃ*.

The sound *vaṃ* signifies that both the bonds of afflictive emotions (*kleśa*) and the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are made entirely like space. *Hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ*: one becomes detached from the three causes, attains the three emptinesses, and realizes samādhi. Next, form a fist with the left hand, extend the wind-finger (index finger) and fire-finger (middle finger), and press the earth-finger (ring finger) and water-finger (pinky) down; the nails serve as the scabbard for the sword.
The right hand is likewise formed into a sword and inserted into the scabbard;
this is the seal of Acala. The hand holding the scabbard is palm upward, while the hand holding the sword is palm downward.
The Trailokyavijaya mudrā is as previously explained regarding the five-pronged vajra.
Next is the Buddhalocanā mudrā.

Form the *tripuṭa* seal: double-bend the earth and water fingers, placing them within the palms; extend the two fire fingers upright so they are like needles; and rotate the two wind fingers to press upon the third joints of the two fire fingers, making them resemble the shape of eyes.
Place both hands side by side with the fingers extended upward and slightly bent, positioning them beneath the second fingers so that the tips of the fingers form the shape of upright eyes;
this is the *samādhi* mudrā.
The placement of the hands and fingers is as in the method of joining the palms inwardly; as previously described, this is called the Buddha-mother Seal (Buddhamātṛ-mudrā).
Herein, it is called the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa Seal, and is also known as the Buddha-and-Bodhisattva-mother Seal.
Next is the mudrā of the Sitātapatra Buddha-uṣṇīṣa.
Extend the left hand with the fingertips separated by about one inch to form the parasol.

Form a fist with the right hand and extend the index finger (vāyu-aṅguli) vertically to serve as the handle; this is done by resting the handle against the center of the palm of the left hand. Regarding the term "forming a fist," the thumb is always positioned on the outside; all other instances follow this convention.
The mantra is as before.
Next, perform the Seal of the Victorious Uṣṇīṣa; it is the same as the previous Sword Seal.
That is to say: form three *puṭas*, join the fire-fingers (middle fingers) upright, and interlace the wind-finger (ring finger) and space-finger (pinky). This is it.
Next is the Most Victorious Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa;
it is the same as the Dharma-Wheel Seal described previously.
Next is the Karma-Removing Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa; it is the same as the Hook Seal described previously.

This refers to forming the inward-facing interlaced palms (*añjali-mudrā*); then, bend the ring finger (*vāyu-aṅguli*) of the right hand into the shape of a hook, and likewise twist the two little fingers (*ākāśa-aṅguli*) of the right hand over and press them against the left.
Now, for the single-hand version: form a fist with the right hand, and extend the ring finger upright, slightly bending its upper joint.
Next is the mudrā of the Fire-Cluster Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa; it is the same as the previous Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa mudrā.
The mudrā of the Extensively-Arising Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa is like the previous five-pronged vajra mudrā.
Next is the Arising Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa; perform the lotus mudrā, which is the same as the previous Avalokiteśvara mudrā.

For the *Aparimitaghoṣa-uṣṇīṣa*, perform the conch-shell mudrā (*śaṅkha-mudrā*) as previously described—that is, the *tripuṭa*—by bending both thumbs and pressing them together with the two ring fingers.
Next is the Seal of the Ūrṇā-kośa (the Tuft of Hair).
Form a fist with the right hand and press the wind-finger (the index finger) against the space between the eyebrows; this is called the Cintāmaṇi, and it is the seal of the ūrṇā-kośa.
The Buddha-eye mudrā is formed as previously described for the Buddha-mother mudrā.

The slight difference therein is that the ring fingers are opened so that the backs of the index fingers are separated by about the distance of a grain of barley, such that they resemble the form of a five-pronged vajra.
Next is the mudrā of the Invincible Vidyārāja:

With the right hand, form the lotus-holding mudrā by joining the tips of the wind and space fingers; the fire finger is bent downward into the center, while the earth and water fingers are held upright. Then, extend the left hand straight upward with the five fingers facing outward and slightly cupped, the fingertips spread apart; hold this hand slightly above the head. This is it.
The formation is as before: *Bhṛkuṭī*. Next, form the inner crossed-fist (*antara-vicita-muṣṭi*):
join the two empty fingers (the index fingers) side by side to form a fist, then separate them as far as possible and bend them so that their joints are like hooks.
This is called the "mouth-form," which is the mudrā of the invincible Vidyārājñī.

Next, extend the right hand and rest it against the right cheek, tilting the head slightly toward the hand with a small distance between them; this is the mudrā of the Śuddhāvāsakāyika gods, which is the hand of contemplation, also known as the mudrā of Maheśvara.
Next, as before, for Īśvara, extend the right palm; slightly bend the head of the middle finger toward the inside, making it form a slight "V" shape together with the index finger.
This is the seal of the Devaputra Viśvapuṣpa; place the hand at the side of the chest.
Next, release the seal of the Devaputra.

Next, as before, extend the right palm and join the fingers of the wind and space elements (the ring finger and the little finger) together in the shape of holding a flower; this is the seal of the Manasija Devaputra. The remaining three fingers are kept together and aligned.
The above are all the mudrās of the Śuddhāvāsa devaputras.
Next is the mudrā of the Bhūmideva.

First, join the palms with the tips of the ten fingers together; bend and press them against one another to form a circle, and tuck the index fingers (śūnyāṅguli) into the palms. Its shape is like a water jar (kumbha); this is it.
Next, perform the gesture of granting fearlessness as before, but bend the ring fingers so they meet within the palms; this is the mudrā for summoning the Fire Deity (*Agnideva*).

Next, with both hands, join the tips of the space and water fingers (the thumbs and ring fingers), while the remaining fingers are held straight, covering both ears; this is the mudrā of the Universal Sound Deity (*Viśvavasu*).
One covers both ears with the tips of the fire and wind fingers.
This [gesture] should originally precede the earth and water fingers; it is said that its sound allows all the assembly to know [the teaching], and it also pertains to the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven.
Together with the seals of the Śuddhāvāsa deities, these constitute the five heavens.
Forming the mudrā of granting fearlessness (*abhaya-hasta*), one presses the second joint of the ring finger against the earth; this is the seal of all the ṛṣis.
From here below, this corresponds to the second sequence listed in the Sūtra; this is the mudrā of the Universal Seer (Viśvadeva).
First, pinch the second joint of the little finger with the thumb, while the other three fingers are held upright and parallel.

In their respective order: first, extend the index fingers; next, extend the middle fingers; next, the ring fingers, keeping them slightly apart from the thumbs; and finally, relax and spread all five fingers.
These are the five great earth immortals (mahābhūmika-ṛṣi),
according to their sequence in the sūtra.
Next is the seal of Yama.

Form three *puṭas*: bend the two *vāyu* fingers and the two *pṛthivī* fingers into the palm so that their tips meet; press the backs of the joints of the two *vāyu* fingers with the two *ākāśa* fingers at the second and third intervals; slightly bend the tips of the *ākāśa* fingers so they touch; and place the two *ākāśa* fingers against the *tejas* fingers—this is the *Tantuka-mudrā*.
Commentary on the Mahāvairocana-abhisambodhi Sūtra, Scroll Thirteen.
Commentary on the Mahāvairocana-abhisambodhi Sūtra, Scroll Fourteen.
Recorded by the Śramaṇa Aśāri Yixing.
The Ninth Chapter on Mudrās, Part Two:
Next, extend the right hand with the fingers spread like the shape of a bell and let it hang downward; this is the mudrā of Yama’s Queen.

Next, with the left hand, clench the earth and water fingers into the palm, extend the fire and wind fingers side by side, and form the space finger into a fist as is customary; this is the mudrā of Rātridevī.
This is the seal of the Queen of King Yama.
Next, perform the hand gesture as before, but bend the index finger and press its second joint with the tip of the thumb; this is the seal of the Queen of Raudra.
The seal of the Sovereign Queen of Heaven (Īśvarī) is further questioned.

Next, with the left hand in the form of holding a lotus flower, this is the seal of the Brahmā Queen; it is said that one extends the palm, joins the thumb and ring finger at the middle finger, and bends the middle finger inward against the palm—as shown straightened in the diagram. Since Brahmā is free from desire and his body is contrary to those of ordinary humans, why is he called a "Queen"?
This is the mudrā of the Consort of the Brahma King; "consort" (*mahiṣī*) is the meaning of the term.

Next, extend the left hand, bend the earth and water fingers (the little finger and ring finger) into the palm, turn the wind finger (the middle finger) to press against the back of the fire finger (the index finger), and slightly hook the space finger (the thumb). This is the *Kāmarūpī-lakṣmī* mudrā; *lakṣmī* refers to a vessel. The illustration is as follows.
This is Kārttikeya, the son of Maheśvara, and Kumārī is the name of his consort.

Next, extend the three fingers of earth, water, and fire of the left hand so that they are each spread apart, and press the wind finger against the space finger; this is the mudrā of Nārāyaṇī’s queen. Holding the flower mudrā to cover the chest, this mudrā is now turned outward.
Next, form a fist with the left hand and extend the index finger straight upward; this is the mudrā for Yama, the Seven Mothers, and others. It is used universally for all seven mothers.
Next, extend the left hand and bend it into the shape of supporting a skull, holding it upward against the chest; this is the *Cāmuṇḍā* mudrā.

With the left hand, place the thumb upon the earth and water fingers (the little finger and ring finger), and extend the fire and wind fingers (the middle finger and index finger) together and upright; this is the *Nairṛti-khaḍga* mudrā.

Next, extend the left hand alone and relax it; this is like the previously described Dharmacakra-mudrā, with the exception that one uses only a single hand without interlocking the fingers. This is the mudrā of the deity Nārāyaṇa.
Next, extend and spread the ten fingers and cover them, then interlace the two thumbs; this is the seal of all nāgas.
Thereupon, place the right hand over the left; this is Nanda-nāga.
Turning the left [hand] over the right constitutes the small Nanda seal.
As previously described for the nine-headed nāga seal, extending the four fingers straight and dividing them like feathers forms the garuḍa seal.
Generally, most terrestrial mudrās are performed with one hand.

Next, extend the left hand vertically so that the fingertips do not touch one another; then, pinch the space between them—that is, pinch the small fingernail. This is the Saṃkara-mudrā, also known as the Aṣṭabhairava-mudrā.
As with the previous seal, join the three fingers together;
this is the Umā seal, which belongs to the consort of Śaṅkara.
The two mudrās are similar;
in the former, the index fingers are slightly bent,
whereas here they are extended straight upward and spread apart.
The left hand forms the half-lotus mudrā;
it is the same as the method for forming the Avalokiteśvara mudrā,
with this difference.
It is performed with only one hand;
this is the Brahmā-mudrā.
Next, display the open palms joined together.
Then, bend the tips of the two wind fingers and press them against the third phalanges on the backs of the fire fingers,
so that they meet with the tips of the two water fingers.
The second water-finger is also on the back of the third joint of the middle finger.
The seal of the Moon Deity is exactly like that of Brahmā, without any difference.
The only difference is that one should visualize it as being white.
Next, join the palms and bend the *vāyu* (ring) and *pṛthivī* (little finger) fingers into the palm so they meet.
Then, make the *tejas* (middle) and *ap* (index) fingers round and bend them like a bow; this is the *Rudra-śakti-mudrā*.
Regarding the wind seal (*vāyu-mudrā*) being as before: one must extend the left hand with the side of the palm facing outward and bend the earth and water fingers;

this is the wind-banner seal (*vāyu-dhvaja-mudrā*). First, turn the left hand upward at the navel in the manner of holding a lute; with the right hand, join the wind and space fingers while extending the others loosely. Move it toward the body in the manner of plucking a string; this is the seal of the goddess Gītamati.
This includes the gandharvas and others; this is the Queen of Heaven, also said to be of the gandharva class.

Next, as for the previous noose mudrā: it is formed by making an inner-interlaced fist, extending the vāyu-finger (the index finger), hooking it, and pressing the tips together. However, this is performed with the left hand; it is the mudrā of the nāga king Vāsuki.

Next, with the left hand, form the mudrā of the Music Deity; in the diagram, the right hand bends the *vāyu-aṅguli* (ring finger) and places it upon the nail of the thumb, while the remaining fingers are all extended and spread out, covering the top of the left hand. This is the *asura-mudrā*.
The mantra is as follows:
*gara-lodhyanga*. "Gara" means "conduct," because conduct is unattainable.
"La" signifies "stainlessness."
"Lo" (邏) signifies the departure from marks.
"Yan" (演) signifies non-attainment.
The dot above it represents the Great Emptiness.
The Gandharva forms the inner fist with the thumbs tucked inside, extending both index fingers so that their tips touch; this is the samaya of this family.
As for the karma-mudrā, it is performed singly: place the thumb upon the nail of the third finger and extend the index finger straight; this is the Gandharva mudrā.
The mantra says:
*Pehi* (enter), *viśuddha* (pure), *sarvaruta* (all sounds), *vāhini* (emerging). The meaning is: "Emerge with pure sound."

These are all worldly samādhis. Next, form a fist with the left hand, bending the wind-finger (index finger) like a hook so that it barely touches the tip of the space-finger (thumb); this is the seal of all yakṣas, which may also be formed by joining both hands together.

The mantra is: *Yakṣa yakṣi*. "Yakṣa" means "vehicle"; "yakṣī" has the meaning of "one who devours. "Iśvara" means "sovereign"; because she attains sovereignty over all afflictions that are consumed [as food], this is her name. Next, with the left hand, press the tip of the thumb nail with the empty finger (the little finger), extend the water and fire fingers (ring and middle fingers), and press the knuckle of the thumb with the wind finger (index finger). This is the seal (*mudrā*) of all Yakṣiṇīs; it may also be formed by combining [the hands].
The mantra is: *yakṣa-vidyādhara*. It means "the vidyādhara (holder of knowledge) who is a yakṣa.
The phrase thus reads: "The Yakṣa Vidyādhara."

This also carries the meaning of "binding," referring to the consumption of this binding. Next, with the left hand, press the three fingernails with the index finger (the *khaṭikā*), then simply extend the middle finger; this is the seal (*mudrā*) of all *piśācas*. Alternatively, it may also be performed by merely forming a fist and extending the middle finger.
The mantra is: *Vijaye vijaye gati gati*.
Because the ultimate goal (*paramārtha-gati*) is unattainable, the next mudrā follows the previous one with the middle finger slightly bent; this is the seal of the *Vijayā* goddess.
The mantra says: *Vijī vijī*.
"Vi" is the meaning of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); "jī" is the meaning of being detached from birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Because one knows the ultimate truth, one is detached from birth and death.

The "repeated calling" refers to the utterance that one is completely detached from birth and death. Next, join the two hands in *añjali*; with the two index fingers (*tarjanī*) also aligned, extend them to their full length so that they are separated from the other fingers. This is the *Gṛhṇa* mudrā. This is a distinct realm of existence; it is neither human nor ghostly, yet it can terrify people. It is this which is possessed by non-humans.
This is not the case here; rather, it is the *yōd* (conjunction).
If it is near a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), one should take the nine planets (*navagraha*) as the definitive standard.
The mantra is:

*Kṛ* signifies action, defilement, and cause; *svāra* signifies sovereignty; *prabodha* signifies awakening; *ruci* signifies light, because it is the light of the various luminaries (*jyotis*); and *ma* signifies the meaning of essence (*dhātu*).

One attains mastery within the nature [of reality], and one attains mastery in calling forth those names and phrases herein. Next, first perform the *tripuṭa* (three-fingered) mudrā: cross the two fire fingers and the two space fingers, with the right hand pressing down upon the left; this is the seal of all constellations (*nakṣatra*).
The mantra says: *Nakṣatrarājasaṃpūjita*.

"Saṃ" (in *saṃpūjita*) means sound; "pūjita" means food, thus it means "the food of all sounds. "Na" has the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*); "kṣaya" has the meaning of exhaustion, thus it means "all is completely eliminated."
*Tara* has the same meaning as previously explained regarding "defilement" (*mala*) and so forth;
according to this principle, it refers to consuming all obstructive defilements.
It is precisely by means of this pure sound that one causes it to be universally disseminated—namely, the "stainless sound" (*vimala-śabda*).
All the mantras described above are spoken according to their meaning to extol the actual virtues of those [deities], awakening them and causing them to rejoice.

Next, perform the *tripuṭa* mudrā: bend both ring fingers (the water-fingers) into the palms while the other fingers remain as usual; this universal "ancient seal" (*sarvapūrvamudrā*) is the *rākṣasa* seal.
Regarding all the mudrās of the terrestrial deva classes described above, they may be formed with both hands or with a single hand.

If, due to circumstances such as recitation or other duties, one lacks the leisure to bind them with both hands, it is sufficient to form them with the left hand alone. As for the "left hand" mentioned in the preceding sutra, where the illustration shows both hands, this [single-hand method] should be employed.
The mantra is as follows:
*Rākṣasa* means "this is defilement. The dot beside it is the sound *a*, which signifies "practice.
*Kṣa* means "treading through space," and *Tiṣya-da* refers to the King, pointing to his virtue.

Having caused them to hear this, they shall rejoice, and the wishes of all sentient beings shall be fulfilled. Next, extend the left hand to cover the mouth and touch the tongue to the palm; this is the Ḍākinī mudrā.
The syllable *Hrīḥ* signifies "free from causes" and "stainless"; the *ā* vowel above indicates *samādhi*, while the dot (*bindu*) on the side indicates wrath.
The syllable *Haḥ* signifies "cause," and the dot above it likewise indicates wrath.

These are the principal ones; as for the various mudrās mentioned above, they extend down to Tākinī as the last. If one were to exhaustively enumerate their categories and retinues, their types would be boundless, as is analyzed in the Great Root Text consisting of one hundred thousand verses.
What is explained in this chapter is merely a brief enumeration of its principal points; it is like grasping the main ropes and the eyes of a net, whereby all the meshes of the net are raised.
O Lord of Secrets!

Regarding these "marks of the Bodhisattva born from the Buddha’s faith and understanding," the Tathāgata has already realized the equal dharma-realm; yet, by the power of his original vows and great compassion, and through the empowerment of his spiritual authority (*adhiṣṭhāna*), he manifests this gateway of the secret body of skillful means so that all sentient beings may attain faith and understanding and together enter the ground of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*).
Therefore, one should know that such mudrās as these arise from the Buddha’s faith and understanding.
One should know that such mudrās as these are the insignia of all bodhisattvas.
This means that by means of these expedient methods, the Tathāgata’s virtue of internal realization is demonstrated;

hence, it is called "marking" (*mudrā*). Just as there are many seals, even the movements and stillnesses of one's physical limbs are all seals. If an ācārya clearly understands yoga and deeply penetrates the secret intent, being able to purify the bodhicitta, then because his mind is pure and he has mastered the secret dharma, whatever he does is for the benefit and subduing of sentient beings. Whatever he performs is in accordance with the majestic deportment of the Buddha; therefore, every movement and action of the body is not something that is not a seal.
"How much less is it merely physical action?
Even all speech whatsoever is likewise mantra. For this reason, O Lord of Secrets!"

"A Bodhisattva practicing through the gateway of mantras, having already generated the bodhicitta, should abide in the stage of a Buddha to construct the maṇḍala. If it is claimed that all Bodhisattvas practicing mantras in this present degenerate age equally transgress the samaya and will certainly fall into the evil realms, it means that those Bodhisattvas practicing mantras in this present degenerate age who have already generated the Great Mind should abide in the stage of a Buddha, and only thereafter construct and establish the maṇḍala.
If one performs the act of giving (*dāna*) otherwise than this, it constitutes slandering the Buddha.
Therefore, regarding what has been explained above, the *ācārya* should understand those methods of mudrās, mantras, and so forth, and become thoroughly proficient in each of their ritual procedures.

Furthermore, one should long cultivate the practice of yoga, purifying the actions of body, speech, and mind, and thoroughly realizing the practice of the dharma-gate of the equality of these three karmas. Because of the empowerment conferred by this yoga, as well as by mantras and bodily mudrās, one becomes identical in essence with the bodies of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, attaining a status equal to that of a Buddha.

Because this samādhi accords with reality such that principle and practice do not conflict, one establishes the circular maṇḍala, as well as its location, colors, forms, and so forth; since each of these accords with principle without error and one skillfully knows their sequence, you should know that one will certainly obtain great benefit without fail.
If one does not do so, one incurs the offense of transgressing the *samaya*.
*Samaya* refers to one’s own solemn vow.

It is the original vow established by all Tathāgatas, intended to universally open the Buddha's knowledge and vision for all sentient beings and cause them all to become like myself; it is for this purpose, through skillful means, that this Dharma has been established.
Therefore, just as the commands of a great worldly king cannot be transgressed— those who do so will surely incur severe reprimand—
one should act in accordance with the bodhicitta, abiding in the stage of a Buddha while doing so.

If there are those who do not comply with the teachings, they will merely waste their efforts and squander their time; in the end, they will achieve nothing and only incur blame and fault without any benefit.
Therefore, practitioners should carefully seek out the sutras and the Dharma, and further consult enlightened masters for instruction, lest they bring about their own ruin.
The extensive explanation of the Chapter on Seals (Mudrā-paṭala) is hereby concluded.

10. The Tenth Chapter: The Wheel of Syllables (Akṣara-cakra-paṭala). Next, the Wheel of Syllables is elucidated. The Buddha again addressed Vajrapāṇi: "As for what was previously asked by Vajrapāṇi, the Buddha has already answered it in successive order."
Regarding what was not fully explained in the preceding text, it shall now be further elucidated; therefore, I inform you that you must listen attentively.

There is a dharma-gate named "Pervading All Places. When a bodhisattva dwells in the position of the seed-syllable (*akṣara*), all their activities attain accomplishment; this very wheel-of-syllables (*akṣara-cakra*) dharma-gate is the dharma-gate that pervades all places.

If a bodhisattva abides in this Dharma-gate of the Syllable Wheel, from the initial generation of the sublime mind of enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood, all various activities for one's own benefit and the benefit of others performed during that interval shall, by entering this Dharma-gate, be fully accomplished without any hindrance.
Furthermore, the meaning of what was stated above—that the ācārya abides on the stage of Buddhahood—is still not fully understood; it refers precisely to these syllable-gates (akṣara).

The initial syllable *A* is the very mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*). If one contemplates this syllable and attains resonance with it, one is identical to the essence of the Dharma-body of Vairocana.

That is to say, one contemplates this wheel of the syllable A as being surrounded by light like the eye of a peacock’s tail; the practitioner abides within it, which is to say, he abides in the state of Buddhahood. Thus he asked again.
This wheel of syllables should be made in three tiers; the syllable A is placed in the center, while the remaining attendant syllables are positioned on the outside—this is further explained below.
Furthermore, this A has five varieties: short A, long Ā, *aṃ*, *aḥ*, and long *āḥ*.

Furthermore, at the beginning of each syllable-wheel, there is first the heart-mantra of the threefold refuge in the Three Jewels, namely the syllables A, SA, and VA; these three syllables manifest the meaning of the three families.
The syllable A belongs to the Tathāgata family, the syllable Sa belongs to the Lotus family, and the syllable Va belongs to the Vajra family.
Each of these three families revolves according to the wheel of the five syllables, corresponding to their respective meanings.
Preface: Regarding the term "maṇḍala," what is now called a "wheel" (cakra) carries the same meaning as maṇḍala.
In the aforementioned ritual for the altar, the central deity is Mahāvairocana Tathāgata; this is identical to the letter A within this [maṇḍala].
On the northern side, one places the Lotus Family and its retinue all together; this is the letter *sa* within this [mantra].
On the southern side, one places Vajrapāṇi and his retinue; this is the letter *va* within this [mantra].
Now, from the letter *A*, four further letters are generated; these are the petals of the Great Compassion Womb (Mahākaruṇā-garbha).
Because many letters are transformed and produced from the single letter *Va*, it is called a "wheel" (*cakra*).

The first letter, A, is the essence of bodhicitta. Following it are the five sounds Ka, Kha, Ga, Gha, and Ṅa; from these, one takes the four letters excluding the fifth (Ṅa). Next, one takes Ya, Ra, and so on, up to Kṣa; all of these are masculine sounds and are entirely included within the wheel of the letter A.
The practitioner, having already resolved upon the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta), should advance in the cultivation of the practices of the Tathāgata;
therefore, the wheel of the syllable Ā is explained next. As for these practices, their three components consist of the three syllables A, Śa, and Va.
Next, from the letter *ka* up to *kṣa*, all likewise have a dot added to their side corners; these constitute the wheel of syllables for the long vowels.
Since one has already perfected the conduct of the Tathāgata, one then attains *bodhi*; therefore, the wheel of syllables for the letters *ma*, *ra*, *saṃ*, and *vaṃ* is explained next.
These are the three families (*trikula*).

This letter *A* has a dot (*bindu*) above it, which signifies the meaning of "Great Emptiness" (*mahāśūnyatā*); just as this bodhicitta is free from all characteristics, it is named the Buddhas—this is the realization of bodhi.
Next, from the letter *ka* up to *kṣa*, each is provided with a dot above to form the wheel of syllables beginning with *aṃ*.
Having already attained awakening, where does one go?
It is said to be Great Nirvāṇa; therefore, within this context, the wheels of syllables such as *aḥ*, *so*, and *mo* are explained.
There are three families.
From *ka* through *kṣa*, all have two dots added to their sides; these are the wheel of nirvāṇa.
The single character *aḥ*, with its long vowel sound, is the wheel of skillful means; therefore, it is absent from the center.
This is the wheel of Śākyamuni Buddha; because the Karma family pervades all wheels, there is no separate maṇḍala.

The Yoga [Tantra] states thus: "Generally, the wheel of syllables is divided into three parts: first, the syllable A constitutes one part; next, from Ka through the twentieth syllable [Ma] constitutes the second part; and next, from Ya through Ha constitutes the third part."
The character *kṣa* is omitted because this character is already duplicated; that is to say, it is duplicated because it contains both the sounds *ka* and *sa*.
All those above are characters representing wisdom (*prajñā*).
Next, there are eight syllables: *i* (with the vowel sign), *ī*, *u* (with the vowel sign), *ū*, *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au*.
By adding these eight syllables, one accomplishes samādhi; they are all sounds of samādhi.
It also revolves perpetually along with the five wheels; its meaning may be understood accordingly.

Next, there are the syllables *o*, *ka*, *ko*, *ja*, *re*, *ka*, *ṭa*, *na* (with the initial nasal), and *mo mo ka*; these characters pervade all places, meaning they pervade both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Furthermore, these five syllables also rotate according to the five wheels; that is to say, by adding a side dot, or an upper circular dot, or two side dots, and so forth—these five variations all constitute the five syllables.
What is called the "wheel of syllables" (akṣaracakra) refers to the production of various syllables from this revolving wheel.

"Wheel" has the meaning of "production. For example, from the single syllable A, four syllables are produced: A is the bodhicitta; Ā is practice; AṂ is the attainment of bodhi; AḤ is great quiescent nirvāṇa; and ĀḤ is skillful means.
Just as it is with the letter *a*, one should know that the letter *ka* likewise consists of five letters; this applies similarly to all twenty letters, including *kha* and the others.

Next, there are twelve letters: namely, *i* (with the vowel sign above), *ī*, *u*, *ū*, *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *lṛ*, *l̥*, *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au*. These twelve letters are identical to the dots placed above the letters, which signify *samādhi*.
The characters *yang*, *ruǎng*, *ná*, *nǎng*, and *mǎng* also possess five dots, which are identical to the dot atop the aforementioned [characters].
The eight characters *qí*, *yě*, *luó*, and so forth, possess two dots at their side, which signify the meaning of "removal."
One should know that this wheel of syllables pervades all mantras.
If one sees the syllable A, one should know it signifies the meaning of the bodhicitta.
If one sees the long Ā, one should know it signifies the cultivation of the Tathāgata’s conduct.
If one sees the syllable *aṃ*, one should know that one will achieve perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
If one sees the syllable *aḥ*, one should know that one will realize great *nirvāṇa*.
If one sees the long syllable *āḥ*, one should know that this is the power of skillful means (*upāya-bala*).
If one sees the twenty letters beginning with *ka*, they should also be expounded according to their respective categories of meaning.
One should know that all these letters are wisdom (*prajñā*).

If one sees the eight letters beginning with *ra*, one should know they are identical to the side-dot (*anusvāra*), which likewise corresponds to its category; that is to say, *ra* signifies "stainless" (*vimala*) and so forth.
If one sees the character *ī*, it immediately manifests samādhi.
If one sees the five characters beginning with *ā*, one should know that these are the points (*bindu*) of Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*).
Great Emptiness is free from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*); this is precisely the meaning of attaining Buddhahood.

If a practitioner thus realizes and penetrates this, they are able to enter the meaning of all dhāraṇīs and revolve within them without obstruction; therefore, it is called the "Wheel of Syllables" (akṣaracakra).
Thus, O Lord of Secrets!

This is the sequence of abiding in the true mantra path of the gateways of the syllables (*akṣara-mārga-dvāra-kuśala-dharma-mantra-yāna*). Regarding the Bodhisattva’s dance of the path of the *Samyaksaṃbuddha*, empowered by the spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of all Buddhas, the Sūtra says "thus," which refers to the aforementioned wheel of syllables (*akṣara-cakra*).
The samādhi, wisdom, emptiness, and so forth described above are precisely the gateways to the Buddha-way, by which one can achieve the path of perfect enlightenment.

If one thoroughly understands the meaning of these words, one will be able to abide in the path of mantra; therein, one will also fully comprehend the sequential rules, the signs of realization and entry, and the distinctions between the stages, thereby attaining clear mastery over both the open and the obstructed paths without any doubt or stagnation.
However, these *siddham* syllables are constantly practiced even by worldly children; how could they suddenly accomplish such a task?

Nevertheless, all these letters were emanated from the Tathāgata’s internally realized essence through the power of his sustaining grace (*adhiṣṭhāna*); therefore, they possess this inconceivable activity and function.
If a person clearly understands the underlying intent and the skillful means herein, they have realized the path to the three types of enlightenment (*trividha-bodhi*).

One who is well-versed in such realization is said to penetrate the faculties, dispositions, and inclinations of all sentient beings; they are able to fully comprehend such infinite and boundless matters as which dharma will enable them to enter the path and through which gate they shall attain awakening.
Yet, in accordance with sentient beings, he bestows the sublime Dharma upon them, causing them all to reach the stage of the Tathāgata.

As for his dancing, it is like the dancing of worldly people; amidst the great assembly, he performs various physical actions—bending, stretching, bowing, and looking up—and produces various subtle, exquisite, and skillful melodies, in accord with what sentient beings desire and delight in.

That great assembly may be made joyful, or moved to sorrowful reflection, or struck with terror; through the skillful means arising from his body and speech, he causes the benefits to sentient beings to differ according to their needs, for he well understands when to advance or withdraw and is able to accord with the minds of sentient beings.

The Bodhisattva is likewise: manifesting various modes of deportment, there are none that do not constitute mudrās; uttering various sublime sounds of Dharma, all are mantras; responding perfectly and without restriction, all bring about great benefit; therefore, it is called the "Bodhisattva Dance."

The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time all speak thus—what they have spoken, what they now speak, and what they shall speak—is this gateway of syllables, the mantra-purified path. The paths of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions and three periods are identical; all manifest such universal form-bodies (vairocana-kāya) and reveal the Buddha-way through various gateways, just as a dancer follows the sentiments of the audience with their performance.

Being without the distinction of self and other, I have observed with the Buddha-eye all Buddha-fields throughout the three periods of time and found them all teaching this same gateway; all Buddhas are no different from me.
All Buddhas and those Tathāgatas likewise speak no differently; therefore, it is said that there is neither "that" nor "self.
This is the teaching of all Buddhas, and one should practice it in this manner.
If it were otherwise, the skillful means would not be complete.
For this reason, the Tathāgata established that meaning and addressed Vajrapāṇi.
If one addresses Vajrapāṇi, it should be known that this is to address the entire great assembly.

That is to say, if those bodhisattvas of mantra practice wish to swiftly attain the Dharma of the ancient Buddhas, they should study and train in this dharma-gate that pervades all places, listening to it with a diligent mind, contemplating it, and practicing it.
For this reason, one may be able to, within a single lifetime, delight sentient beings through the various dances, plays, and songs of all the Tathāgatas.

Regarding the "addition of the beginning, middle, and end": the five letters beginning with *a* constitute the beginning; the twenty letters beginning with *ka* constitute the middle; and the eight letters beginning with *ra*, all of which possess the side-dot (*anusvāra*), constitute the end. These letters all serve to assist in establishing the meaning of the words; therefore, they are the final portion.
All syllables such as ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, and so forth, belong to the gateway of the letter A.

The letter A is the bodhicitta. Regarding the addition of the initial, middle, and final [vowels] therein: for example, while the letter A alone is the bodhicitta, if a stroke is added to its corner, it becomes "practice" (caryā); this is the bodhicitta together with practice.
If a dot is added above [the letter A], it signifies that the bodhicitta, together with the great emptiness, is free from all marks and thus constitutes enlightenment (bodhi).
If two dots are added beside the letter A, it signifies that the bodhicitta, together with the removal of all obstacles, attains nirvana.
All others follow this pattern, adding them successively; it should be understood that they may consist of one, two, or three meanings.

There are instances where, although there is no dot above the letter *a*, the subsequent letter is a doubled (conjunct) character containing sounds such as *ya*, *ra*, *ṇa*, *na*, or *ma*; when these are joined with the preceding [letter], they constitute the syllable *aṃ*.
Why is this so? These [vowels] such as *i* (仰) and others are points (*bindu*); when they are added to the preceding [consonants], the letter *a* becomes the sound *am*.

Alternatively, the letter *a* may be without a point, and following it there are duplicated letters such as *ya* (也). For example, the four duplicated letters *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, and *gha* are used as points for the letter *i* (*i*).
In the syllable *cha-cha-ja*, the letter *ja* is used with the nasal dot (*bindu*) as the vowel *a*.
Others imitate this.
By prefixing the sounds *ra* and so forth to the preceding [syllable], the syllable *aḥ* is formed.
Why is this so? The letter *ra* and others all possess two side dots; now, by connecting these with the preceding [vowel], the letter *a* becomes the sound *aḥ*. Please inquire further into this.

Indeed, the essence of the Dharma is wordless and transcends all conceptual discrimination and frivolous discourse (*prapañca*). Furthermore, because all Tathāgatas, through the power of their sovereign empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), have formed this wheel of syllables, it is able to perform the deeds of a Tathāgata and benefit all classes of beings.

*Ka ca ṭa ta pa*, the chapter on Samādhi, the realization of the practice of the Bodhicitta, the Buddha’s acceptance and bestowal, as well as Nirvāṇa—these, along with the addition of the phonemes and so forth, constitute the Mantra teachings; that which possesses [these] at the beginning, middle, and end is the sūtra text. The explanation of the text is now complete.

One who knows this and recites according to their inclination must apply each and every word with resolute intent and awareness, and should bestow it upon those who possess the unsurpassed excellence of the words.
To know in this way is precisely what is called a specific designation for the wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
If a practitioner thus understands the meaning of the wheel of syllables (*akṣaracakra*), they will be able to achieve all that they desire.
To state it briefly, "everything is accomplished according to one's wish" means accomplishing all the activities of the Tathāgata.
If one accomplishes this, they are identical to the Dharma King, attaining sovereign mastery over all dharmas.
Furthermore, in accordance with their original vows, they are able to open up pure knowledge and vision for all sentient beings, enabling them to attain the wisdom of a Buddha.

Who attains this benefit? It is those who, possessing the proper conditions, maintain the recitation in accordance with the principle; therefore, it is next stated that "it is the one who performs the recitation.
Who attains this definitive intention?
This means that a person of wisdom,

by virtue of skillfully awakening to, understanding, and knowing the meaning of the wheel of syllables (*akṣaracakra*), will— by practicing in accordance with each individual gateway of the syllables beginning with 'A'— certainly and completely attain the fruit of Bodhi.
Do not give rise to doubt.
What dharma is realized herein? It is as follows:
the letter A is the bodhicitta; adding a dot (bindu) is the bodhisattva practice; and adding it to the Great Emptiness (mahāśūnyatā) is the attainment of Buddhahood.
If the bodhicitta is pure and all obscurations are removed, that itself is Great Parinirvāṇa; there is no other meaning.
To thus penetrate and fully understand each of these points is to receive the unsurpassed and most excellent phrase; this unsurpassed phrase is the very attainment of Bodhi.

This unsurpassed bodhicitta is the spontaneous wisdom of all Buddhas; in truth, there is no one who can bestow it upon another. Rather, when a practitioner is fully endowed with skillful means and thoroughly understands the meaning of the wheel of syllables (*akṣaracakra*), they obtain it spontaneously—this is what constitutes the bestowing of unsurpassed bodhi.

In this way, the wheel of syllables revolves as a single wheel; one should know that the practitioner who maintains the recitation is ever-illuminating the world, like the World-Honored One Vairocana.
As for its revolving, it is like a worldly wheel: when it rotates, one cannot know the point where it ends or begins; it has no boundaries and is inexhaustible.

It should be known that each and every wheel of syllables is likewise so: from the letter *A*, all other syllables revolve and are produced. This wheel of syllables pervades the names of all mantras; it revolves as a dhāraṇī without limit, its source being inexhaustible, pervading all places—it is the hundred-thousand-myriad-billion-fold Revolving Dhāraṇī.
If a practitioner can thus understand the meaning of the wheel of syllables (*akṣaracakra*), they will be able to illuminate the world with this ever-luminous light.
This ever-abiding luminosity is the very body of the Tathāgata Vairocana; by being identical to that Vairocana, one turns the wheel of Dharma.

Within this, the ever-luminous is precisely the great sun of wisdom; this sun is the essence of the letter "A" of the bodhicitta, which is unarisen, unconditioned, and immutable, not produced by any causal formation.
Such wisdom of the eternally abiding true reality is therefore called "Ever-Brilliant.
If a practitioner exerts diligent effort and cultivates for a long time without laxity or retreat, they will certainly attain it.

However, the aforementioned methods and applications for the mandala ritual—including the scattering of flowers, the conferral of empowerment, and even the presentation of a clear mirror, which is like using a golden scalpel to clear away cataracts from the eyes—all these serve those who have newly resolved to attain bodhicitta; through the sequential application of skillful means and empowerment, they bring about firmness in that resolve and act as the gradual stages for entering the Buddha-dharma.
However, the secret intent herein lies in the wheel of syllables (*akṣaracakra*). Why is this so?

If a practitioner acts as an ācārya for others and wishes to construct a maṇḍala, they must first abide in the station of the World-Honored One; that is, by synthesizing and assembling these various gates of syllables (*akṣaramukha*) to form a body, one’s own body becomes identical to that of the Buddha.
This means that when a yoga-ācārya achieves accomplishment through contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), whatever he performs according to his intention is spontaneously fulfilled.
Because he clearly perceives this wheel of syllables pervading all parts of his body, he is identical to a Buddha and occupies the same station as a Buddha.
However, when arranging the characters, one should divide them into four parts; these constitute the four-layered maṇḍala.
The head is the first part, which is the position of the letter A as the bodhicitta.
From *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, and *ṅa*, up to *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha*, all those which are primary sounds belong to the bodhicitta.

One should contemplate the syllable *ka* at the location of the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows of the practitioner; from *kha* downwards, one should rotate to the right following the path of the sun, arranging them in succession for one full circuit so that they join together in a continuous circle.

Next, from the throat downward is the second division, which belongs to the gateway of the long letter Ā; it also connects vertically with the white *hrīḥ* at the center, extending to the right in a single continuous circuit—this is the practice of Bodhi.

Next, from the heart downward constitutes the third section, which belongs to the gateway of the syllable *Aṃ*; from above the heart, one arranges the syllable *Khaṃ*, proceeding clockwise for one full circuit to join them.

Next, from the navel downward belongs the syllable-gateway *A*, which is the Great Nirvāṇa; within this, one also places the syllable *Ka-ja* (Kha), which is joined by circling once clockwise in succession.

The head is the upper portion; the throat and heart are the middle portion; and the navel is the lower portion. [My private opinion is that] generating the bodhicitta is the beginning, the practice and its fruit are the middle, and great quiescence is the end.
The fifth syllable, AḤ, pervades all places; whatever one intends to do is accomplished.
This exists outside the body, like the light of a Buddha’s body which functions according to one's will, and does not occupy a position for arranging syllables within the body.
The syllable *Aṃ* is likewise identical to *Aḥ*.

Once the Master has thus accomplished the body [of the deity], he should likewise arrange the maṇḍala accordingly; he should also instruct the disciple to perform it in this same manner. When these three matters are all accomplished, this is the secret maṇḍala.

If one does not comprehend the underlying intent herein, then even if one acts based on the aforementioned phenomena and dharmas, it cannot be called acting skillfully; one will merely waste effort and achieve nothing.

Furthermore, this method of arranging the syllables constitutes a secret maṇḍala; it may only be transmitted through the intention of the master to those who have long practiced the conduct of true illumination (*vidyā*) and are worthy of receiving the transmission. It cannot be recorded in writing; therefore, the teacher transmits it orally, as it is not explained in the sūtras, which merely state that it is "like the revolving wheel of Vairocana."

Furthermore, the practitioner must know the colors of the various syllables: namely, the initial letter *A* and the twenty-five letters beginning with *Ka*, as well as from *Ya-ra* up to the letter *Ha*, all of which belong to *A* and are made yellow, which is the color of the Vajra.
The second letter A transforms into a yellowish-white color, which is what is called the color of tranquility.
The essence of the letter A is yellow and samādhi is white; because these two colors merge, it is yellowish-white.
The third addition, the dot upon the head, is also yellowish-white;
this signifies "darkness. The letter *A* is yellow, and the large circle is white; thus, it is yellowish-white.
Next, the fourth, the syllable *E*, transforms into yellow-black; the letter *A* is yellow, and the two dots, which are the color of *nirvāṇa*, are black; thus, it is yellow-black.

Furthermore, the two dots signify the meaning of subjugation; just as *nirvāṇa* destroys, annihilates, and crushes all obstructive phenomena, so too does this [mantra], and thus the two dots are made black.
Regarding the fifth syllable, *Aḥ*: the body of the letter *A* is yellow; the dot above is white, and the side-stroke is black. One should know that this represents various mixed colors.
In laying out the maṇḍala, it is likewise arranged in three tiers; the first tier consists of the letters from *ka* to *ha*, which encircle the innermost layer and is called the Vajra-wheel.
This Vajra-wheel sustains all phenomena, just as the vajra-wheel of the world sustains the world; it is the practitioner’s initial wheel of bodhicitta.
This means that in order to make the bodhicitta firm and stable, one first performs the inner heavy [recitation].
Next is the second wheel, which refers to Ā and Am; these two wheels of the long Ā and Am are both of the middle division.

If the syllable KA is used for the wheel, then the wheel of the syllable KHA need not be employed. [The author] privately comments: KA is the cause for the practitioner, while KHA is the realization, which is the fruit.
Next, for the third wheel, the wheel of the syllable AṂ is used; it is also arranged as above in accordance with the middle [wheel], so that they form a continuous circle.
The twelve syllables beginning with *I* are scattered on the outside like blazing flames;
this is the meaning of the three turnings of the Wheel of Dharma.
Once they have been thus arranged, the practitioner becomes the body of a Vidyādhara, no different from being empowered by the spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of Mahāvairocana Tathāgata.
This wheel is also called the Wheel of Causes and Conditions (*hetupratyaya-cakra*).
The master, the disciple, and the maṇḍala together constitute such a secret wheel.
Furthermore, these various syllables are themselves the wheel of mantra; thus, there are four kinds of wheels in total.
