Furthermore, as for the "wheel of syllables" (akṣaracakra), in the Sanskrit language it is called the *akṣara-cakra*. *Akṣara* has the meaning of "immovable"; that which is immovable is precisely the syllable A, the bodhicitta.

Just as Vairocana abides in the essential nature of the bodhicitta, manifesting various universal gateways for the benefit of all beings, and displaying various transformations that are immeasurable and boundless.
Although its manifestations thus descend infinitely, it is truly able to abide eternally and immovably, without any sign of arising or ceasing.
It is like a wheel which, though it revolves without end, never wavers at its hub; because it is immovable, it can govern all movement without exhaustion.

This letter A is also like this: because it is unborn, it is without movement or regression; yet it gives rise to all the wheels of letters, revolving without end. Therefore, it is called the Immovable Wheel.

If a practitioner can thoroughly comprehend such an immovable wheel and manifest the various vidyās, then by its very nature, whatever is manifested by the body is none other than a mudrā, and whatever is spoken by the mouth is entirely a mantra.
All those who see, hear, touch, or know [this] will certainly attain the benefits and merits realized in unsurpassed bodhi; this is truly not in vain.
If one can act in this way, one is identical to Vairocana in performing buddha-work, constantly illuminating the world.
Whenever a practitioner recites, they should visualize either a wheel of syllables (*akṣaracakra*) or a wheel of phrases (*padacakra*).

Regarding the wheel of phrases: one visualizes a luminous orb upon the heart of the deity, within which the syllables of the mantra are arranged as a wheel in continuous succession, causing them to appear clearly before one.

While reciting, one should visualize this syllable as being like white milk, flowing down in succession into the practitioner’s mouth or onto the crown of their head, continuing without interruption until it completely fills the body and even its limbs.
The seed-syllable within that luminous orb is always clearly manifest, like a constant flowing stream that never exhausts itself.
When one becomes utterly weary from such recitation, one should simply abide in a state of mental stillness; this refers to contemplating the seed-syllable.
The method for this visualization has already been fully explained above.
Once one has perceived the seed-syllable (*bīja*), one then perceives the *iṣṭadevatā* (the chosen deity) arising from within that seed-syllable.
Once this has been accomplished, one is able to pervasively establish the wheel of syllables (*akṣaracakra*) to form the body of a Vidyādhara, and only then is one fit to perform various activities.

Thus, the syllable *A* signifies immovability and is the essence of the vajra; whenever one wishes to make an undertaking firm and unshakable, or to ensure that the bodhicitta of oneself or others remains unshakeable, one should apply the syllable *A*.
All other syllables are likewise to be applied according to their respective functions and characteristics.

**Chapter Eleven: The Secret Maṇḍala** At that time, the World-Honored One Vairocana again entered the samādhi called "The Manifest Realization of the Tathāgata’s Eye-Pervading All Dharmadhātus, the Vigorous Array of the Dharmadhātu-Treasury, the Equal Adornment Treasury. This was because he manifested the inexhaustible adornments of the dharmadhātu and fulfilled his original vow to deliver the entire realm of sentient beings without exception through this gateway of mantra practice (*mantrayāna*). Having already concluded the preceding "Chapter on the Syllable-Wheels," the following "Chapter on the Secret Maṇḍala" is now explained.

Because it is secret, whatever is spoken therein is all the power of the Tathāgata’s sustaining grace (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and thus cannot be fully expressed; for this reason, it is titled "The Chapter on the Wheel of Syllables Sustained by Power. All other chapters are to be explained in this same manner.
Having finished explaining the "Chapter on the Wheel of Syllables," he next enters samādhi in order to accomplish this wheel of syllables.
What is stated in the sūtra here is the name of the samādhi from which he emerges.
The "entire dharma-realm" refers precisely to the signless dharma-realm.
Because it is already this signless dharma-realm, one contemplates such a dharma-realm by means of the Buddha-eye and other [perceptual faculties].

Furthermore, as for the secret interpretation: the aforementioned wheel of syllables is the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) of all Buddhas; it is with the Buddha-eye that one contemplates this dharma-realm.
One should know that this contemplation by the Buddha-eye is itself the power of the Tathāgata’s empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*); apart from such empowerment, it cannot be explained.
Regarding the "Dharmadhātugarbha" (Treasury of the Dharma-realm), this term "garbha" in its Sanskrit original is *kośa*, which means a sheath.
Just as a sword in the world resides within a sheath, so too does this treasury; therefore, it is translated according to this meaning.
Therefore, what is here called the "Dharmadhātu-garbha" (Dharma-realm treasury) is precisely the place from which the Tathāgatas emerge; that is to say, all Tathāgatas abide within it.
"Vikrīḍita" (exuberant play) carries the meaning of flowing forth and the meaning of overflowing.

It is like a lion king dwelling unmoving within a deep cave; at times he emerges from his lair, stretches, and rouses himself. This is because while his body was originally motionless, it now moves by departing from its usual place.

The Buddha is likewise; dwelling within such a profound and secret treasury, it cannot be manifested unless sustained by the Tathāgata’s power of empowerment. It is subtle, tranquil, and absolute, and thus cannot otherwise be shown.
Now, manifesting inexhaustible varieties of forms, sounds, and actions of body, speech, and mind that pervade the entire Dharma-realm—this is the "exertion" (*visphurana*) of all Buddhas.
Manifesting the Tathāgata’s treasury of equal adornments—this is the "Womb-treasury" (*garbha-kośa*).

Furthermore, upon entering this Dharma-gate, the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas of the ten directions and three periods of time are entirely equal and equal; as the Way of every Buddha is the same, it is therefore called "equality."
"Adornment" (yán) refers to the adornment of one's body; that is, using the infinite gateways of the Buddha-way to adorn the Dharma-body in order to deliver sentient beings.
It is precisely because the Dharma-body is adorned by the equal Dharma-realm that it is called "adornment" (yan).
It is just as in the world, where a place occupied by a great army is said to be "adorned" by the presence of a great banner.
This samādhi is likewise; it is so named because this samādhi can manifest the secret matters of the Tathāgata.

Herein, "treasury" (kośa) is called *ga-ha* in the Sanskrit language, which signifies the inexhaustible flow of adornments, manifesting with such vigor that they can never be exhausted, just like a great treasury of jewels.
This treasury of the equal dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is precisely the meaning of the Tathāgata-garbha.
Because the adornments of the dharma-realm are inexhaustible—just as the revolving wheel of syllables is inexhaustible—it is called the "Inexhaustible Treasury."
For what reason does the Tathāgata abide in this samādhi?
It is certainly not without cause or condition; it is precisely for the purpose of revealing the profound and essential mysteries of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, the subsequent scripture states: "By means of this gateway of mantras, one delivers the realms of sentient beings without exception, thereby fulfilling one's original vow.
When the Buddha was practicing the bodhisattva path in his former lives, he established a great vow to cause all sentient beings to enter together into the treasury of the Tathāgata’s dharma-realm.
Now my aspirations are fulfilled; through great compassion, I manifest with vigorous power to deliver sentient beings.
Just as the Adornment-Treasury of the Dharma Realm is inexhaustible, so too is the realm of sentient beings inexhaustible.

Now, wishing to universally benefit all through the gateway of mantra practice with impartiality, so that everyone may open up pure knowledge and vision to ultimate completion without remainder—this is the fulfillment of one's vow; hence it is said, "fulfilling the original vow."
Furthermore, because the ritual procedures have not yet been accomplished and remain unperfected, practitioners of the true mantra-conduct cannot swiftly attain the Unsurpassed Way.
Now, in order to definitively resolve these matters so that they may all be made manifest, he enters this samādhi.
Next, regarding "abiding in meditative concentration," this refers to the Buddha dwelling in *samādhi* and manifesting rare and wondrous deeds to universally benefit all sentient beings.
Within this concentration, what kind of rare and wondrous deeds does he manifest?

That is to say, there are no remaining realms of sentient beings, such as the gates of sound and so forth; according to the accomplishment of their mental karma, they receive the sounds of physical forms and appearances as various fruits of retribution, and they preach various dharmas according to the thoughts of others, causing all sentient beings to rejoice.

Regarding "the bodies emerging from all pores, equal to the dharma-realm, increase": this sound, which is the Brahma-voice, is also a roar; it is like the thunderous roar produced by a great dragon appearing, which everyone hears and which pervades everywhere without exception.

The roar of the Tathāgata is likewise: it pervades the entire realm of sentient beings without exception, and its immeasurable sound is heard everywhere; unlike that of a worldly dragon, which is limited in scope.

Within the realm of sentient beings, there are superior, middling, and inferior grades; according to whatever karma one performs, one obtains its corresponding retribution. Therefore, it is said that "birth through karma is accomplished.
This is like a person who receives food but has not yet eaten it: as long as it has not been consumed, it cannot yet be called "receiving";
only after one has accepted and eaten it can it be called "receiving that offering of food."

Now, the experience of the ripening of karmic results is likewise: each receives its fruit in accordance with its prior cause. The distinctions in shape, manifestation, and color are ten thousandfold and diverse; the sounds and explanations differ, and the inclinations and convictions of the mind are each again distinct.

With a single, sublime voice of equanimity, the Buddha accords with each and every mind according to their aspirations, employing their respective languages to instruct and awaken them. He rouses their thoughts and awareness, using skillful means to guide and inspire them so that all attain joy; this is a marvelous omen unprecedented within samādhi.

Regarding the various types mentioned herein, according to the principles of phonetics (*śabdavidyā*), even if three sounds combine to express a single meaning, if that meaning is not yet complete, an additional syllable is added to fulfill it.
If four phonemes together express a single meaning, and the meaning is already complete with three phonemes, then one character is removed.
In this manner, additions and subtractions are made as appropriate.

Now, it is likewise here: by means of the single gateway of the letter A, all meanings are fully encompassed, and there is nothing regarding phenomena that is not perfectly complete; therefore, this is called "expounding," which is not the same as the expounding of spoken Dharma.
The Brahma-voice was different, so he questioned him further.
As for that which emerges from the body of the increased Dharma-realm: the ultimate quiescence of the equal Dharma-realm possesses no characteristics of entering or exiting.
By virtue of the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*), inexhaustible physical bodies emerge.

That is to say, from each and every pore of the Buddha, there appear roaring sounds as previously described, and various forms likewise manifest; therefore, it is called the "Body that Increases throughout the Dharma Realm."
In truth, that which arises from conditions possesses the nature of non-arising; such a true mark is identical to the essence of the Dharma-realm—how could there be any increase, birth, or cessation?
Although it is a phenomenon of dependent origination, its essence is eternally like its true appearance.

Nevertheless, through the power of the Tathāgata’s empowerment, a roaring sound issues from each and every pore—whether in gentle words or harsh speech, whether profound or shallow—responding to the mental capacities of those beings, just as the tide of the great ocean never exceeds its constant limit.

His body is likewise: sometimes large, sometimes small, or appearing in wrathful forms; sometimes practicing the six perfections, or subduing through majestic power. Though these manifestations differ in myriad ways, there is no error in the sentient beings he delivers.
Previously, the wheel of syllables was shown; now, forms and sounds manifest from within the wheel of the Dharma-realm.

Having emerged into space, they are equal to the single sound of the Dharma-realm throughout all worlds, expressing the verse on the birth of the Tathāgata. Just as space has no boundaries, so too is this sound; it is identical to space.
"Manifestation" (*vijñapti*) means making known; it refers to the verbal manifest karma of the Tathāgata.
That is to say, it manifests [the truth] to all sentient beings, causing them all to realize the equal dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
By means of this wondrous sound, the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is manifested; therefore, it is said that the dharma-realm is the mind.
This single sound is the gate of the letter A, revolving without end, equal to space and filling the dharma-realm.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time are born from such sublime verses; therefore, it is called "the birth of the Tathāgata.

Now, the Buddha speaks these sublime verses through this gateway of a single sound, causing all worlds without exception to hear and know them equally, each attaining understanding according to their kind; hence, this is the name by which it is known.
The wheel of syllables described above is intended to manifest the merits of the Tathāgata.

Therefore, from every single pore, the Buddha emits sublime sounds that pervade this world-system, proclaiming the profound meaning of these wheels of syllables; that is to say, the verses capable of giving birth to all Buddhas.
If there are sentient beings who understand the meaning of such a wheel of syllables, they immediately realize Bodhi; therefore, it is said that all Buddhas are born from this.

However, the Dharma-body of all Buddhas is free from arising and ceasing. If a Tathāgata were subject to birth, he would be attached to signs (*nimitta*); now, those who are attached to signs cannot even escape birth and death, much less achieve Great Bodhi.
What is here called "arising" is an arising that is truly free from all characteristics.

While the pure *dharmakāya* is devoid of all marks, the Buddha, through the power of his *adhiṣṭhāna*, employs this wheel of syllables to reveal the secret, internally realized virtues of the Tathāgata.
Because they are sustained by the sovereign spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Buddha, through this expedient means of signs, one is able to give rise to the sign of signlessness.

Just as when one has not yet awakened to realization, one gradually attains thorough understanding and observation of the gateway of the letter *A* by means of this wheel of syllables as an expedient.
Because one enters the gateway of the letter A, one is able to attain the ultimate, sovereign Dharma-body.
As the verse says:

"Taking birth in forms according to their kind, while the Dharma abides in the characteristics of all phenomena"—this means that by entering the gateway of the letter A, one is precisely the equal Dharma-body.

Because of this formless Dharma-body, one is able to manifest universally in form-bodies according to conditions and responses; assuming various types of forms according to those beings, one reveals the wisdom of the Tathāgata by means of a body that is pleasing for all to behold.
The verse says:

"All Buddhas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas, as well as the world-saving bodhisattvas who advance with valor like the Buddhas themselves, do so because of this unsurpassed, signless body. All Buddhas are born from this; not only are all Buddhas born from this, but all the various stages of practice for śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, up to the stage of the 'one-life-to-enlightenment' (ekajātipratibaddha), are all born from the principle of this letter A."

Not only do all the fruits of the noble and sagely beings arise thereby, but even the various distinctions and successive developments of the entire world of sentient beings and the physical world of the vessel are likewise produced from the meaning of this syllable *A*.
Therefore, those who are born herein are briefly of three types:
those of superior birth refer to the resultant essence of the Tathāgata’s truly pure *dharmakāya*, which is eternally abiding;
next are the various Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and followers of the two vehicles, who, wherever they may be, eliminate their respective hindrances.
Regarding the arising of the inferior grade, both sentient beings and the vessel-world (the physical environment) are likewise established through this dharma-gate.
Although phenomena such as arising and abiding are said to be eternal, what is taught here is not the same as the views of permanence and annihilation held by non-Buddhists.
Although all phenomena arise from causes, those causes are without marks;
although they arise from conditions, these conditions are without marks.
Although they arise through conditions, phenomena are fundamentally unarisen.
Although it arises and ceases according to conditions, it lacks the characteristics of birth and abiding.
Therefore, it is eternal; this is not the same as the views of the non-Buddhists, who speak of the eternity of arising and ceasing.
The verse says:

"One who possesses both wisdom and skillful means, and is free from lack of wisdom and doubt, thoroughly understands the wheel of the letter A—the essence of all phenomena as ultimately empty and non-existent, quiescent, signless, and fundamentally unborn; this is wisdom."
Mantras, bodily mudrās, yoga, and so forth, which enable one to perform great benefit and enter the wisdom of the Buddha, are the skillful means (*upāya*).

If one relies on skillful means without wisdom, or possesses wisdom alone without skillful means, one will ultimately be unable to accomplish the inconceivable, spontaneous activity (*anābhoga-pravṛtti*).
It requires the fulfillment of both skillful means (*upāya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*); through skillful means, one gains entry into the secret treasury of the wheel of syllables (*akṣaracakra*).
As for those who are devoid of wisdom and free from doubt: if one is separated from these two dharmas, it should be known that such a person is one lacking wisdom.
Due to a lack of wisdom, one will give rise to doubt in every situation and be unable to advance.
Furthermore, if a practitioner possesses both wisdom and skillful means, they will naturally be free from a lack of wisdom and will not give rise to false doubts.
The verse says:
"Regarding this path taught by all Buddhas"—this means that it is not only I who speak thus; for all the Samyaksaṃbuddhas speak in this same way, without any difference.

Because the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time have all attained this same path, there is no distinction between them; it is of a single characteristic and a single flavor, with no differing teachings.

At that time, the body of the Tathāgata arises from the *dharmadhātu*, manifesting itself throughout the entire *dharmadhātu*. The clouds of emanations fill the heart of Vairocana’s sovereign mastery, and as Buddhas are born and pass through one another within every pore, the "body arising from the *dharmadhātu*" mentioned therein is precisely the *dharmakāya* of Vairocana.
Because it arises from the true reality of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), it is called "born of the dharma-realm.
Regarding the phrase "the manifestation of the body of all dharma-realms," "manifestation" means that which enables all beings to fully know and see.
This means that within the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), clouds of the Tathāgata’s own manifested bodies pervade everywhere.
That is to say, the Tathāgata’s manifest body—the *saṃdarśana-rūpakāya*—appears universally, just as those great clouds pervade the realm of phenomena.
"Cloud" signifies the sense of pervading.
This means that the clouds of these transformation bodies pervade the entire Dharma-realm, extending throughout the worlds of the ten directions in immeasurable quantity.

Regarding the phrase "mastery of mind" (*citta-vaśitā*) here, it is translated according to its meaning; the correct interpretation states "as soon as the mind [is withdrawn]" (*citta-mātra*). This means that at the very moment one withdraws the thought, one is able to become thus vast and pervasive without requiring further effort; this is precisely what is meant by attaining mastery over the mind.

Regarding "the Buddhas born from within all the pores mutually sustaining one another through empowerment": it is because as soon as the Tathāgata enters samādhi, such universally wondrous events are manifested instantaneously; this is precisely the power of the Tathāgata’s sustaining empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
"Successively transforming and pervading" means mutual interpenetration.

From the pores of the Buddha’s body, the Tathāgata’s own bodies flow forth, successively entering one another; each individual body manifests the aforementioned supernatural powers, transforming again and again without end.
These meanings shall be explained in further detail.

Regarding "successive empowerment" (*anuparivartana-adhiṣṭhāna*): this refers to being empowered by the sovereign spiritual power (*vibhutva-ṛddhi*) of the Buddha; it is precisely the empowerment of the aforementioned wheel of syllables (*akṣara-cakra*) which is the nature of the *dharmadhātu*.

From each and every pore of the Buddha’s own body, various clouds of bodies emerge; according to their upper, middle, and lower parts—namely, the head is the inner womb, the area above the heart is the first court, the area above the navel is the second court, and the area below the navel is the third court.

These correspond to the four positions on the previously described circular altar; according to their respective left, right, front, back, upper, middle, and lower divisions, they manifest as the bodies of the principal deities, each emerging from its own position to perform buddha-activities within the world-systems.
From each and every body, they emerge in succession to perform the various deeds of the Buddhas;

thus it is called "succession" (*kṣepa*). At that time, Vajrapāṇi also understood the Buddha’s intention: "Now the World-Honored One manifests this rare and unprecedented event; it cannot be without cause or condition. He will surely further expound the profound and secret Dharma—namely, he will certainly explain whatever remains unresolved or omitted from what has been taught above. With sincere hearts full of longing and veneration, they remained there.
Therefore, the Buddha spoke again:
"Lord of Mysteries!
There is the construction of a maṇḍala, the arrangement of the positions of the deities along with their seed-syllables as markers."

"Listen attentively; well done! Attend with excellent mental focus, and I shall speak for you. At that time, after the Buddha had manifested the aforementioned stages for the Vajradhara and others, and those deities had performed their various buddha-activities, they returned from their original positions and entered the body of Vairocana Tathāgata. Their sequence and order were no different from when they emerged; thus, that sūtra states, "They re-entered the Palace of the Dharmadhātu."

Regarding the seeds of the venerable states: all these venerable ones are the virtues internally realized by the Tathāgata; each one individually represents the profound orientation of the dharmadhātu manifested by the Tathāgata.

Now, if there is an ācārya who wishes to construct a maṇḍala, he should first abide in this yoga. Just as [the deities] emerged from each successive position of the Buddha’s body, having visualized them according to their respective forms and colors, one should create a luminous orb upon their hearts and visualize their seed-syllables within those luminous orbs. Only after thus establishing each one individually is the ritual procedure completed.
If it were not thus, one would ultimately be unable to empower and establish those disciples, nor would one attain the title of *ācārya*.
As previously stated, once the seeds of affliction have been severed, the seeds of the nature of the *dharmadhātu* arise next; these are the seeds of equality for all sentient beings.
This seed-nature of the equal dharma-realm is that which grows from the ground of the Tathāgata’s omniscience.

Just as the various kinds of grasses and trees in the world, each distinct according to its own nature and portion, all grow depending upon the great earth—with their roots, stems, branches, and leaves being diverse, and their growth, size, and natures differing—yet all are of the nature of the great earth and arise from it.

Although they ultimately all return to the earth, they grow and flourish due to the convergence of causes and conditions; yet in reality, they possess no intrinsic nature, being neither born nor arisen.
If sentient beings have already been established with such seeds, they are identical to the stage of the Tathāgata.
Because these seeds arise from the nature of the dharmadhātu and are able to produce the dharmadhātu, they are called "seeds produced from the dharmadhātu."
That which arises from the *dharmadhātu* is precisely the Tathāgata’s essence-body (*svābhāvikakāya*).

As for the "signs," it is like the various distinctions among worldly seeds: even in the case of a small herb seed, one with wisdom observes that although it has not yet grown, they already know the extent of its potential and the limits of its inherent nature.
If one observes that sentient beings practice such and such causal-stage seeds, all are likewise so.

However, these present seeds are the seeds of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*; one should know that this nature will certainly give rise to the Tathāgata’s body of equal dharma-wisdom, and for this reason they are called "signs."
Furthermore, each and every section of this maṇḍala possesses its own seed-syllable (*bīja*), which serves as a marker for the gates of the differentiated *dharmadhātu*.

One should know that each enters into the letter A; by seeing the marker of internal realization, one immediately understands the virtue of the Tathāgata’s internal realization. Therefore, they are called "markers."

Those who emerge from the four successive stages are the very insignia of the Buddha; whether they emerge from the stage of a bodhisattva, or from the stage of the two vehicles, or from the stage of the eight classes of devas and nāgas, one should know that the differences in their respective levels indicate that their seed-syllables (*bīja-akṣara*) are distinct.

When the Buddha had thus addressed the Lord of Secrets, Vajrapāṇi said to the Buddha, "I wish to hear it with joy. This was because he desired to propagate and disseminate [the teaching] for the universal benefit of all sentient beings; he requested the Buddha to expound it for the sake of all future sentient beings and also to benefit the entire great assembly.

Although the methods for the maṇḍala have been explained above, the secret treasury of colors and seed-syllables has not yet been taught; therefore, listen with a single mind as the Buddha is about to expound it.

Next, the Buddha told Āyusman: Whenever an ācārya wishes to establish disciples within the construction of the Great Compassion Womb (Mahākaruṇā-garbha), he should first abide in yoga and contemplate his own body.
From the navel downward, one should visualize a vajra-wheel, yellow in color and firm.
Next, from the navel upward to the heart, one should visualize a water-wheel, white in color.
Next, from the heart upward to the throat, one should visualize a fire-wheel, red in color.
Next, from the throat upward to the crown of the head, one should visualize a wind-wheel, black in color.
Furthermore, the earth mandala is square, the water mandala is circular, the fire mandala is triangular, the wind mandala is semicircular, and the space above is represented as a single point.
These various colors are placed upon the cross-seam at the crown of the head.
○△○□ This is the shape of a wheel, which corresponds exactly to the proportions of the body.

These five positions correspond to the five syllables previously mentioned: the syllable *A* is placed within the square, the syllable *Va* within the circle, the syllable *Ra* within the triangle, the syllable *Haṃ* within the half-moon, and the syllable *Kṣa* within the bindu; these should be further verified in the preceding fascicle.

Once the Master has thus visualized his own body in sequence and empowered it with colors, he further visualizes the placement of seed-syllables; having done so, he next visualizes the ground of the maṇḍala, which he inverts and establishes as follows: at the very top is the vajra-wheel (vajramaṇḍala); beneath the vajra-wheel is the water-wheel (toyamaṇḍala); beneath the water-wheel is the fire-wheel (tejomaṇḍala); beneath the fire-wheel is the wind-wheel (vāyumaṇḍala); and beneath the wind-wheel is the space-wheel (ākāśamaṇḍala).

Why is this so? Because all worlds are supported by the five wheels (*pañcamaṇḍala*). When a world is formed, first wind arises from space; from the wind, fire arises; from the fire, water arises; and from the water, earth arises. This is the sequential order of the establishment of the maṇḍala.
At the time of destruction, the earth mandala is the first to perish, until finally only empty space remains.
This is the sequence of the Master’s own empowerment, which he further explains.
Now, the practitioner’s cultivation of the path is also analogous to this: first one generates faith, next the bodhicitta, and next, up to the great emptiness—this is what he further explains.

Once the ācārya has performed the empowerment in this manner, he should then install the various deities according to their respective positions and contemplate each one through yoga. According to their directions, colors, and forms, he should place a luminous orb (*maṇḍala*) upon the heart of each; within that luminous orb, he should cause the seed-syllable (*bīja-akṣara*) to appear clearly and without obstruction.

One who is able to act in this manner is precisely within the stages of the Maṇḍala of the Matrix of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-garbha-maṇḍala*). This is because it causes all Tathāgatas to collectively bestow their empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and all Honored Ones to assemble together to empower the practitioner and establish the disciple so that they shall ultimately never regress from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*);
otherwise, one would merely expend effort in vain without any benefit.

Furthermore, regarding this seat of yoga, the square golden vajra-wheel is the vajra-seat itself: the square represents pacification (*śānti*), the circle represents enrichment (*puṣṭi*), the triangle represents subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), the half-moon represents summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*), and the bindu represents the accomplishment of all activities (*sarvakarmasiddhi*).
This wheel of space is formed solely through mental attention and not by means of physical form.
When the world is destroyed, it likewise first destroys the earth from the wind-wheel, giving rise to fire; once the fire has ended, the wind follows.
Question him further:
"In this manner, one forms the five wheels; one should know that there are space-wheels both above and below.
Since wind, fire, water, and earth arise from the space-wheel, and since one gradually ascends from the earth-wheel up to the space [wheel], there is space both above and below."

When constructing the maṇḍala, the master should personally contemplate his own body and the ground; he should likewise contemplate the disciples to be initiated in the same manner, establishing them according to the rules of the master’s tradition.
If it were not thus, it would not be called "in accordance with the Dharma.

At that time, Vajrapāṇi—having ascended to the ground of the body, speech, and mind of the Tathāgata Vairocana and contemplating the equality of the Dharmadhātu—is one who can know the secrets of the Tathāgata’s body, speech, and mind; therefore, he is named the Lord of Secrets (Guhyapati).
The Dharma of the Tathāgata’s secret intent can only be fully realized by a Buddha and a Buddha.
As it is with the mind, one should know that the same applies to the body and speech.

That this Bodhisattva is now able to know them as well should be understood as meaning his rank is identical to that of Great Enlightenment; yet, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, he manifests as a Bodhisattva to inspire others.
Among these, the "secrecy of body" refers to the various mudrās; for instance, each deity within the fourfold Great Maṇḍala possesses its own secret seal.

By contemplating these bodily seals, one comes to know the secret virtues manifested by each deity, which exist in infinite varieties according to their respective distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior types.
The mystery of speech (*vāg-guhyaka*) refers to the mantras of all the deities; by hearing these mantras, one immediately comes to know the virtues realized within those deities.

The mystery of mind (*manoguhya*) refers to the visualization of the yoga of the principal deity, which likewise differs according to each of the four directions; by corresponding with this, one enters the secret treasury of the Tathāgata’s mind.

Within this context, the secrets of body, speech, and mind range from the stages of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas down to those of the two vehicles, the devas, and the eight classes of beings, with immeasurable distinctions.
To speak extensively, they differ individually as much as the number of atoms in ten worlds;
yet to speak briefly, the positions indicated in this sutra all represent the secret virtues of the Tathāgata’s body, speech, and mind.
If one can understand this as it truly is, one is identical to the Lord of Secrets (*Guhyapati*).

Now, the Bodhisattva Lord of Secrets, dwelling in the contemplation of the equality of the *dharmadhātu*, for the sake of future sentient beings and to cause all to tear asunder the great net of doubt, spoke this Great King of Mantras before the Buddha.
This may be understood according to the text.
The mantra is as follows:

*Namo samantabuddhānām*—homage to the all-pervading Buddhas; *asamaprabha*—of inexhaustible radiance; *dharmadhātu*—the realm of phenomena; *gati-gata*—having transcended the inexhaustible realm of phenomena.

"Transcending" (*atikrānta*) refers to praising the virtues of the Tathāgata’s secret body, speech, and mind. *Sarvathā* means that at all times and in all places throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, one transcends the inexhaustible *dharmadhātu* and is able to universally benefit all beings through every gate. *Aṃ khaṃ aṃ aḥ*: these four syllables constitute the four wheels.
The first syllable is the earth-vajra-wheel; the second syllable is the water-wheel; the third syllable is the fire-wheel; and the fourth syllable is the wind-wheel. Regarding the syllable *Aṃ*:

its fundamental essence is the Vajradhātu, while its long vowel (*ā*) constitutes its activity (*saṃskāra*), which is the fire-wheel. The dot (*bindu*) above it represents the space-wheel (*ākāśa-cakra*), serving as its adornment.

Next, regarding the syllable *kha* as the water wheel: *kha* signifies emptiness (*śūnya*). Furthermore, there is a long vowel which represents formation (*saṃskāra*), and with the addition of a bindu, it becomes emptiness—that is, the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*).
Next, regarding the syllable *aṃ* as fire: in Sanskrit, *akṣaṇam* is fire.
"Āḥ" is the nature of nirvāṇa;
"Kṛṣṇa" (black) is wind.
Furthermore, space is formless, yet it is able to contain all forms and images.
Now, this syllable *kha* possesses both vowels and consonants, which refers to all forms and images (*rūpa*).
That which is the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*) is likewise like space, endowed with the forms and images of all phenomena; this emptiness is that which accomplishes all tasks.
Therefore, the syllable *khaṃ* can function as water. Furthermore, it is asked:

*saṃ* (earth), *haṃ* (wind), *laṃ* (space), *ṭaṃ* (fire), and *vaṃ* (water). As with the aforementioned syllable *a*, there are four syllables; that is, the long vowel has a dot above and two dots beside it, and the short vowel likewise has a dot above and a dot beside it—these two [types] constitute four.
One should know that these, such as *sa* and so forth, are likewise; all possess four syllables.
Here, only their short vowels are cited, while the two long vowels combined are placed before the short vowels, as explained according to the preceding principle.
*Saṃ*, *sa*, *haṃ*, and *ha* are these [syllables].

Others follow this pattern. Furthermore, to discuss them collectively: the syllable *A* belongs to the Buddha Family (*buddhakula*), *Sa* belongs to the Lotus Family (*padmakula*), and *Va* belongs to the Vajra Family (*vajrakula*). Wind and fire are employed throughout all three families; inquire further on this.

As in the Lotus Family, there are inherently the elements of earth, water, fire, and wind; if for the rite of pacification (*śāntika*), one must use the square vajra-wheel; if for enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), one must use the water-wheel; and if for subjugation (*abhicāruka*), one must use the water-wheel and so forth—employing them according to their respective types.
It should be understood that these five gates of A-sa-ha-ra-va are identical to the aforementioned five-syllable wheel; within each individual wheel, there are naturally four wheels.

For example, within the syllable *va* of the Vajra Family, there are naturally four wheels, which are employed according to their respective types for pacifying (*śāntika*), increasing (*pauṣṭika*), or subjugating (*abhicāruka*).

If one reads other mantras and finds such characters within them according to their respective classes, one should know that they indicate the specific applications for which those mantras are intended; each has its own appropriate domain as its primary governing principle.
This section is not yet clear; I shall ask further about it.
There are three more mantras of the Three Paths:

􈅼􄙈􄙉 is the mantra of this body; 􄮮􄚳 is the mantra of this speech; 􄙈􄙉 is the mantra of this mind. These three mantras of the Three Paths encompass the Dharma-gate of the equality of the Tathāgata’s body, speech, and mind.

However, regarding these three mantras, it is acceptable whether the word *svāhā* is appended or not; the practitioner should observe the expedient means according to their own realization of the meaning.
Furthermore, because this mantra is most supreme, it is designated as a "King.
As stated above, although each [of the other mantras] consists of four syllables, these are contained within it; thus, it is simply called the Twelve-Syllable Mantra King.
Among these, the four wheels each empower the body of the ācārya in accordance with the respective wheels of earth, water, fire, and wind, whereby he attains the function of mastery.
His mantra of body, speech, and mind likewise empowers his own physical, verbal, and mental activities.
Since this matter is not yet clear, ask about it further.

It is also said that while previously this was the method of arranging the characters, here we employ a distinct calculation of combinations; thus, the characters corresponding to the five types of matters encompass their respective functions.

When he had finished speaking thus regarding the Great King of Mantras, Vajrapāṇi asked further questions; at that time, all the Tathāgatas dwelling throughout the worlds of the ten directions extended their right hands, stroked the crown of the Bodhisattva Vajradhara’s head, and praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family!"
O Son of the Buddha!

You have already transcended the stages of body, speech, and mind of Vairocana; you abide in universal equality within the path of Mantra. Desiring to act as the illumination for all bodhisattvas, you have spoken this King of Mantras.
Regarding the touching of the crown of the head mentioned here, it does not mean that the Buddhas of the ten directions extend their hands to this world to touch his head.

Rather, when this Lord of Secrets recites this King of Mantras before the Buddha, by virtue of being the King of Mantras, he speaks it simultaneously with a voice that is equal and all-pervading before every Tathāgata in all worlds throughout the ten directions; therefore, each and every Tathāgata extends his hand to touch his head.
"Transcending" (*vyut*) carries the meaning of "surpassing entry.

For example, when Vairocana sat at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) in the Akaniṣṭha heaven, it was by means of this King of Mantras that he attained the ultimate, equal, and sovereign function of body, speech, and mind.
You have now also attained entry into this stage of the equality of body, speech, and mind, becoming equal to Vairocana.
This is precisely what all Tathāgatas praise as your true virtue.

It is said: "Since you have already attained such a ground of equality, and because you desire to universally benefit all sentient beings through the universal gate, and because you desire to illuminate and remove the darkness of those bodhisattvas who practice the true words and deeds, you shall therefore proclaim this King of Mantras."
The King of Mantras can tear asunder the net of doubt regarding the entire dharma-realm.
Doubt is itself darkness;
to be able to sever all doubts and delusions is precisely to provide illumination.
Why is this? Because this Bhagavān Vairocana, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, while seated upon the Bodhi-maṇḍala, contemplated the twelve-syllable mantra and thereby subdued the four Māras.

Regarding this manifestation of the Dharma-realm flowing forth from the three places to subdue the celestial Māras: it refers to when the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana sat at the site of enlightenment and, observing the Dharma-realm with equanimity, spoke these twelve phrases of the King of Mantras.
By this very power, one is able to subdue the four māras and eliminate their defilements and impurities.
Among these four types of māras, three are formless; these the Buddha had already subdued while he was in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.

Only the celestial Māras possess physical forms; however, because he wishes to make his sovereign power known throughout the world, he further manifests as a vanquisher of the celestial Māras within this land.

As for the "three places," they refer to what was described above: from the upper part of the Buddha’s body, all Tathāgatas emerge; from the middle part, extending from the heart to the navel, all Bodhisattvas emerge; and from the lower part, extending from the navel to the feet, all eight classes of divine beings and others emerge.

All of these are universally manifested from the Tathāgata’s three equal karmas through the Gate of Universal Access; they demonstrate the positions within the Great Maṇḍala Womb Matrix Adornment, which are precisely the mantras and mudrās of the respective deities.
One should know that when the Buddha manifests such deeds from the virtue of his internal realization, at that very moment he universally subdues the four māras without exception.

Now, when an ācārya intends to construct a maṇḍala, he must likewise contemplate himself as identical to Vairocana; thereby attaining sovereign power, he too becomes like that Buddha, capable of subduing the four māras.

Next, the World-Honored One’s body, speech, and mind are equal, attaining a measure identical to space; having attained such body, speech, and mind, he has acquired such wisdom and attained mastery over all phenomena. This refers to the Buddha sitting at the Vajra Seat, who, upon merely recollecting these three mantras of the three paths—namely, the aforementioned mantras of body, speech, and mind—[attains this state].

When one contemplates in this way, one immediately attains the stage of equality of body, speech, and mind; body, speech, and mind are all the essence of the Dharma-realm, boundless like space, and by such power, one subdues the four māras.
Regarding the "three paths" mentioned previously, one interpretation states:
these three mantra-paths are the power of the sovereign equality of body, speech, and mind; they are thus emanated from the Buddha.

By means of these three paths of mantra—body, speech, and mind—the Tathāgata attains transcendence and entry into the ground of the three equalities. Accordingly, he manifests various forms of the Honored Ones (Bhagavats), various mantras, and various mudrās through the Universal Gate for those of superior, middling, and inferior capacities. These are equal to space and have no boundaries; they pervade the entire Dharmadhātu to deliver all sentient beings, ultimately causing them all to likewise attain transcendence and entry into this ground of the three equalities.
The body is endowed with immeasurable merit, just as space cannot be known to have any limit; the same applies to speech and mind.
By contemplating this mantra, one attains such merit as to become equal to the Tathāgata.
Because the three types of karma are inexhaustible, if it is appropriate to save beings through the body, one universally manifests various physical forms;

if it is appropriate to save beings through speech, one universally manifests various languages through the universal gate, guiding and instructing according to what is suitable, so that they may enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
If one were to gauge others by means of their mental faculties, such various forms of spiritual resonance and communication would likewise be inexhaustible.
Not only are the body, speech, and mind limitless and endowed with all merits like space, but one should know that wisdom is also thus limitless, just like space.
If one attains such unimpeded, wondrous wisdom, one thereby gains mastery over all phenomena and becomes equal to the World-Honored One.
What is called "mastery" refers to [attaining control] over all matters that are otherwise not under one's own power.

Because all classes of sentient beings have not yet reached the ultimate purity of the dharma-realm, they are all scorched and confined by karma and afflictions; bound to birth and death, they are unable to attain the power of mastery.

Now, within that great ocean of birth and death, the Tathāgata proclaims the profound and secret essentials of the Tathāgata’s Dharma through various gateways of teaching. For the sake of the single great causal event (*ekamahā-kṛtya-hetu*), he brings them to fulfillment through various skillful means, causing all to reach the stage of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*); this is precisely the meaning of attaining mastery over all phenomena (*sarvadharma-vaśitā*).
By realizing such a Dharma, one attains mastery over this Dharma.
Because of this mastery, one is able to expound it without obstruction, skillfully adapting to the diverse capacities of sentient beings.

That the Tathāgata is able to attain such sovereign function is entirely due to contemplating this Dharma-gate of the twelve-syllable wheel; one should know that this Dharma-gate of the twelve syllables is the very essence and nature of the Dharmadhātu.
At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions, seeing Vajrapāṇi proclaim this mantra, [declared] it to be identical to the path of the Buddhas of antiquity:
"We Tathāgatas of all times have likewise attained the ultimate wondrous body by contemplating these twelve gates of letters; and all future World-Honored Ones shall do the same."
Therefore, with great joy, he stroked the crown of the Bodhisattva’s head and addressed him, saying:

"All Buddhas, because they possess mastery over the Dharma and for the sake of the single great causal event, have taught this Dharma-gate with the equality of body, speech, and mind. You now likewise are able to teach it; this means that you have also realized this Dharma and are equal to the Tathāgata."

Although Vajragarbha has not yet reached the ultimate state of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*), he is nonetheless equal to the World-Honored One of Wondrous Enlightenment; for, through the collective empowerment of the spiritual powers of the Buddhas of the ten directions, he likewise manifests within this great assembly as one who has realized the same reality as the Tathāgata.
If one were apart from the empowerment of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-adhiṣṭhāna*), one would likewise not yet have attained ultimate equality with the Tathāgata.
Therefore, O son of good family!
When it is said that Vairocana’s body, speech, and mind are realized as equal, and all Buddhas know it thus—“knowing” (*jñā*) is a specific name for awakening (*bodhi*).
By knowing the inexhaustible practices of the universal gate of all Tathāgatas, one realizes the three kinds of equality of the Tathāgata.
That is to say, one knows the secret treasury of the Tathāgata’s body, and likewise knows the subtle and secret treasuries of his speech and mind.
If one realizes and knows this Dharma, that person is identical to the Tathāgata.
Having thus finished praising and sealing [the teaching], he further requested the Tathāgata once more. Why was this?
This profound and secret treasury can be thoroughly understood only by Buddha after Buddha; therefore, among all bodhisattvas, none has been able to pose a question.

Now, the Buddhas of the ten directions collectively empower Vajrapāṇi through their spiritual power for the benefit of all sentient beings, and thus, riding upon the spiritual power of all Buddhas, he now questions the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana.
What is being asked here?
Since the profound and secret meanings of the matters previously explained by the mind have not yet been fully set forth, one asks again for their essential core.
The one who has attained all-knowledge is precisely the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana.
The meaning of *bhagavat* is as explained in the section on the six meanings and was previously interpreted.

As for Vairocana, he is like the sun appearing in the world: able to dispel darkness and able to accomplish all the activities of sentient beings, such that there are none among the species born upon the great earth who do not receive benefit.

This natural sun of great wisdom of the true mark (*dharmatā*) is likewise: if there are sentient beings who understand and realize it through self-attestation, it possesses such power that, like a fierce wind blowing away clouds and the appearance of the sun and moon, it brings about great benefit throughout the entire *dharmadhātu*, illuminating the world just as the sunlight does.
The "Lord" (prabhu) is so named because he has attained mastery over all phenomena; thus, he is called the Lord.
Now, the Buddhas have commanded Vajrapāṇi to inquire into these secret matters concerning the mantra-words of this Mahāvairocana Tathāgata.

Regarding the statement that "the superior teaching of one's own doctrine is extensive": it is called "superior" because, through a single syllable dharma-gate, one penetrates all dharmas and realizes the inexhaustible equality of the body, speech, and mind of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
"Teaching rules" (*jiaoze*) is another name for "dharma-rules"; "dharma" carries the meaning of a guiding principle or norm.

By this, it is meant that in the past, when I generated the aspiration for bodhi and unsurpassed bodhi, I proclaimed my teaching of all dharmas and nirvāṇa. Regarding the statement, "As witnessed by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in the worlds of the present," it means that when we were practicing the bodhisattva path in the past, we likewise attained spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*) through this gateway of mantras, and further expounded it thus for the sake of all sentient beings, so that they might all attain great nirvāṇa.
The origins of these words of mine are profoundly deep; even those with minds are unable to pose questions about them, let alone believe and understand them.
Only all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have reached this same Dharma, and they can serve as witnesses that it is ultimately not false.
Since you have now attained the tracks traversed by us, you should further question the Tathāgata.

At that time, the Virtuous One Vajradhara, still holding in his hand the Seal of the Tathāgata’s Wisdom—which is the single flavor of all the various merits of all Buddhas, namely, the flavor of the Tathāgata’s liberation—[spoke thus].
Because that seal of wisdom is identical to that of the Tathāgata, he is said to be "endowed with virtue.

At that time, through the collective empowerment of all the Tathāgatas, that bodhisattva, with great joy, attained profound understanding of the Tathāgata’s words and also came to know the Tathāgata’s mind. Regarding matters previously beyond his reach and which he had been unable to ask, he was now able to inquire freely of the Tathāgata without any doubt or difficulty.
Now, wishing to question the Tathāgata, I first extol the virtues of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) by speaking these verses:
"This Dharma is inexhaustible and lacks intrinsic nature (svabhāva). Here, "exhaustion" refers to having a beginning and an end, or arising and ceasing.
Because there is arising and ceasing, there is the dharma of origination and extinction.
However, the nature of the presently equal dharmadhātu is free from such faults; it has neither beginning nor end.
Because there is neither arising nor ceasing, this is precisely the meaning of inexhaustibility.
"Inexhaustible" is another name for the signless (*animitta*).
Because they are inexhaustible, all phenomena (*dharma*) lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); they are without movement, without change, and have no place of abiding.
Ālaya has the meaning of "dwelling" and the meaning of "receptacle for what is gathered.
Now, within the impartial dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), there is no such characteristic of a receptacle for accumulation; therefore, there is no place of abiding.

If all dharmas are devoid of intrinsic nature, they are without activity; because they are without activity, they are without birth, cessation, retribution, and so forth. Being originally quiescent and characterized by perpetual self-extinction, they are identical to the inconceivable liberation.

Regarding "the Buddhas share the same state": this profoundly deep and quiescent Dharma is beyond the reach of all names and words, and there is nothing else that can serve as a metaphor for it. It can only be illustrated by what the Buddhas themselves have equally realized and known; therefore, it is said that they are identical to perfect enlightenment.
However, if all phenomena were merely ultimate, there would be neither arising nor activity.

To speak of "the ultimate" implies that there are no distinctions or gradations among the various vehicles; thus, the equal stages of all sages would fall into nihilism, and by realizing a realization of reality [in that way], they would be unable to benefit all beings.

Next, it further states that the Buddhas and others, through their compassionate vows, transform the teaching of signlessness to bring about awakening to such signs; because they possess skillful means, they are able to fulfill all aspirations.
This skillful means is precisely the great compassionate vow; by virtue of this great compassionate vow, one is able to transform and further inquire.

Within this signless dharma, there is no one who can speak it and nothing that can be indicated, yet it enables all to attain it and they themselves realize it—know that this is the power of the great skillful means.

This Dharma cannot be taught by anyone; it is realized through awakening that does not depend on another. It is the self-awakened wisdom that requires no teacher, whereby one spontaneously attains the Buddha-way and manifests tranquility at the site of enlightenment, awakening to the true mark of such dharmas.
All of these are verses; they shall be elaborated upon later.

Furthermore, if one were to say that the dharma-realm is inexhaustible and without beginning or end, this would constitute nihilism, and it would be unable to bring about any benefit for sentient beings.
Why is this? Because they have already established a limit for birth and death, yet they remain among those subject to worldly afflictions.

They are the lineage of the Tathāgata; if all things were without arising, without nature, and without a place of abiding, how could they universally respond to the world to perform the various deeds of a Buddha?
However, because bodhisattvas possess two things, they do not fall into the extreme of annihilationism; namely, great compassion and skillful means.
By virtue of these, they are able to bring themselves to awakening.
Regarding the term "spontaneous unfolding" (*prakāśana*) used therein, it refers to the spontaneous unfolding of the bodhicitta.

If one were to represent this through verbal expression, claiming that such spontaneous, teacherless wisdom can be attained by awakening through the instruction of another, such a thing is impossible.

Why is this so? It is because the practitioner, through practicing according to reality, personally awakens to and personally contemplates the inexhaustible Dharma-realm as it truly is; thus they attain such wisdom of the true mark, which is not realized through another.
The meaning of the sutra is that the characteristics of dharmas are thus; hence it says "thus-characterized.

Having attained this dharma of suchness (tathatā), one then uses the skillful means of great compassion to reveal and expound it for sentient beings; yet, in reality, this awakening does not depend on another, nor is it obtained through transmission from another.

It is like a blind man asking what the color of milk is like; upon hearing that the color of milk is like snow, he conceives the notion of coldness; yet upon hearing it is like a crane, he conceives the notion of movement. Even through various metaphors and skillful means of expression, he ultimately cannot understand, merely increasing his mental false imaginings.
Why is this? It is because they themselves lack clear vision.

The ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is likewise; if one does not correctly understand it for oneself, then even if others provide various forms of guidance, there is ultimately no possibility of realization.
If a person does not personally awaken to such a Dharma of internal realization yet speaks of it for others, desiring to cause them to understand, this is likewise impossible. Why is this so?
It is like a person without feet who calls out to a crowd, saying,
"I shall climb Mount Sumeru for you.
One should know that such a person will surely be held in contempt and ridiculed by the wise.

Why is this? If one lacks the capacity for self-reliance, one cannot even ascend to a small portion of the high regions of such a king of mountains as Sumeru, much less be able to ascend its summit for the sake of all beings.
Furthermore, it is like a person who, being unable to cross the waves of the great ocean themselves, says to others:
"I shall ferry you across so that you may reach the other shore.
One should know that such a claim is likewise devoid of any principle of attainment.

The practitioner is also like this: if one has not yet personally awakened to the teacherless wisdom (*asat-svayambhū-jñāna*), yet desires to cause others to hear the Dharma and attain realization, such a principle is necessarily impossible.
At that time, after Vajrapāṇi had praised the Tathāgata with these verses, he next spoke an udāna verse to question the Buddha.

"Udāna" carries the meaning of "comprehensive synthesis"; because the meaning of a single verse synthesizes the infinite dharmadhātu—the phenomena free from characteristics and their immeasurable doctrinal meanings—it is called "synthesis."

Having finished reciting these verses of praise, he reflected that sentient beings of future ages who cultivate the practices of truth and conduct would be unable to swiftly attain unsurpassed bodhi because they might lack certain elements within this Maṇḍala Born of the Great Compassion Treasury; therefore, he sequentially questioned the Buddha regarding the secret and essential expedient means.
Regarding "severing all doubts": if one cannot universally sever the various nets of doubt of sentient beings, one is not called an omniscient person.
It is only by being free from the net of doubt within all phenomena oneself that one is able to sever the nets of doubt in others.
Now that the Buddha has himself severed all nets of doubt, I therefore ask my question, wishing for him to sever my doubts for me.
"Free from feverish affliction" means to have eternally severed the roots of the three poisons.
Now, for the sake of all sentient beings, I ask the Teacher; because he is able to guide one through all dharmas and lead one to the wisdom of a Buddha, he is called the Great Teacher.
Commentary on the Mahāvairocana Sūtra, Fascicle Fourteen Commentary on the Mahāvairocana Sūtra,
Fascicle Fifteen Recorded by the Śramaṇa Acharya Yi-hang (Ichigyō)
The remainder of Chapter Eleven, the Secret Maṇḍala:
Furthermore, the Buddha was questioned in succession by means of verses;
these are now listed here, though the concluding lines of the verses have not yet been joined.
Regarding the maṇḍala, what should be performed first? It is asked: since there are many types of matters concerning the maṇḍala, which one should be performed first?
That is to say, what task should be undertaken initially?
Furthermore, it is also asked: how many kinds of ācāryas are there? Please explain these as well.
How many kinds of disciples are there whom the Great Muni has also taught?
How does one know the characteristics of the ground?
Regarding the inquiry into the qualities of the ground—namely, whether it is good—and the taking of the ground, what are the superior, middling, and inferior accomplishments?
What is the discernment of the ground?
Having discerned it, how does one perform the purification? Why are there only three questions asked again?

Once the purification has been performed, how does one abide? Although the purification has been completed, fearing that one might again be troubled by obstructors, he asks how one may attain stable abiding.
There are only three questions; he asks again: "How does one purify for the sake of a disciple?
May the Buddha explain how many kinds of disciples were mentioned in the previous question.
Now that we have obtained the status of disciples, we ask what the prior matter was."

What are the characteristics of that which has been purified? Herein, there are three matters and three phrases of inquiry: the inquiry concerning the teacher, the inquiry concerning the ground, and the inquiry concerning the disciple.
What protection is employed?

How does one perform the protection of the site? Furthermore, one asks the master how he himself performs the protection of the site, the protection of the ground, and the protection of the disciples—these being the three questions.
How, then, does one perform the consecration (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the site?
The acts of binding, protecting, maintaining, and so forth have many meanings, and three matters are also questioned therein.
What is the initial function? It refers to the maintenance of the ground and the completion of the purification; it concerns the tasks that ought to be performed regarding the maṇḍala.

In this context, there are two kinds of activities to be performed: external activities, which refer to the various matters involved in constructing the mandala; and internal activities, which refer to the various yoga methods such as the master’s own visualization of his own body as the Tathāgata Vairocana and so forth.
By what mantras and other methods is this performed?
Is protection established first, or is purification performed first?
This is a question concerning the sequence of preceding and succeeding actions.
These two matters constitute the function.
Into how many kinds is the cord divided?
Furthermore, how does one measure the ground using the cord, and what is meant by "measuring the ground with the cord" and "joining the cord"?
The boundary is demarcated using thread.
Furthermore, how many kinds of offerings are there?

Regarding flowers, incense, and so forth, there are additionally items such as unguents, lamps, jeweled nets, jeweled pavilions, and jeweled trees; various such articles for presentation and offering should be prepared according to precedent, which is why the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) is used.
The term "etc. refers to the plural number.
Question: What is the method for offering incense and flowers?
Answer: Flowers should be offered; however, since there are various kinds of flowers, the deities to whom they are to be offered also differ accordingly.
What flowers are used for making offerings to the Buddha?
What are used for the Bodhisattvas, devas, and others?
The same applies to incense and other offerings; ask according to the ritual rules.
The offerings of food and so forth have distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior. How is the *homa* performed? Question:
What is the sequence for making offerings to the Buddha and performing the *homa*? Answer:
The arrangement of the ritual rules (*vidhi*) is itself the sequence; this is the general designation.
How should one attend to the seats of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the eight classes of beings? With what should they be seated together? How are offerings presented?

Regarding the teachings, principles, methods, sequences, and rituals: these all involve manifesting forms, colors, and so forth. "Manifest" refers to the various colors of the deities—blue, yellow, red, white, and so on; "form" refers to their postures, such as sitting or standing, and their dimensions; "color" refers to their physical appearance.
These refer to the categories of joyful laughter, wrathful anger, and peaceful abiding.
These are the three questions; please explain them in order.
"Not following the rules" refers to the mudrās of the various deities and one's own seat—that is, the seat for one's own constant recitation—such as a mat of *kuśa* grass and so forth.
"I pray that the Teacher will explain this.
From what source does this mudrā arise?

And for what purpose is it taught? Just as worldly people employ seals so that kings and others may trust them and have no doubt regarding their authenticity or falsity, [what is the function of this mudrā]?"
Now, what is this seal of the Tathāgata?
By what name is this seal known, and how is it that it is called a "seal"? I wish to understand this.
Furthermore, how many types of consecration (*abhiṣeka*) are there? I wish to know and understand them.
How many kinds of samaya are there?
For how long must the practitioner maintain the recitation according to the standards?
And for how many days will the practitioner, who diligently cultivates the gateway of mantras, attain the path of a bodhisattva?
O Omniscient One, we pray that you explain:
at what time should one see the truths—that is, when does one attain the knowledge and vision of reality through the gateway of mantras?
At what time is the meaning realized?
Regarding *siddhi*, there are three questions to be addressed: how many types of *siddhi* are there? When does *siddhi* arise? And what is the timing for the attainment of *siddhi*?
How does one ascend into the great void?
How is it that there are two questions concerning the secret of the body?
And how is it that one attains the body of a celestial being (deva) without discarding this present body?
Once these have been accomplished, how do the various transformations arise? That is to say, all things are attained simply by recollecting them; from where does this arising occur?
Is it from one's own mind?
Is it from another?
Who produces these various transformations?
And from what, in turn, do they arise?

Regarding the sun, moon, fire, directions, the planets, time-periods (*yoga*), and so forth—how are these various inauspicious omens to be dispelled? When the sun and moon undergo transformations into calamities of fire, or when strange portents occur in the various directions.
The "lunar mansions" (nakṣatras) are the twenty-eight constellations, and the "stars" (tārās) are the multitude of stars.
As for those who arise to undergo suffering within birth and death, how can they all be made to eliminate it?
There is no such meaning of elimination.
How does a practitioner always assemble in one place together with all the Buddhas?
How many kinds of homa are there?
Herein, it is asked how many kinds of fire must be used at the time of homa; this is what one wishes to know.
Increasing the majesty within the fire is a method of augmentation.
Furthermore, how many such increases of majesty are there?
They are like the use of flowers and so forth in all places.

Venerable One, regarding the natures of the various classes of honored ones—namely, the forms and essential natures of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the eight classes of beings—one must recognize their fundamental natures, such as wrath, tranquility, or joy; I pray that the Teacher will explain this.
Regarding the remaining worlds and the supramundane fruits: how many are there, and what is their number?

As for "supramundane," this refers to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; as for "mundane," this refers to the eight classes of beings and so forth. When these are accomplished, what are the measures of time, the fruits, and the numbers?
There are six questions.
Furthermore, he asks: "What are the worldly and world-transcending samādhis?
Together with the previously mentioned superior concentrations, there are eight.
Where does the accomplishment of karma reside?
This asks in what location the experience of the fruit of accomplishment resides.
The same applies to that which is not yet accomplished; this asks regarding non-accomplishment.
Furthermore, it was asked: "When can one depart from birth caused by karma and thereby attain liberation?
At that time, Vajragarbha, empowered by the majestic spiritual authority of the Buddhas of the ten directions, spoke these verses to question the Buddha.
Because that Bodhisattva of the Mantra Practice lacked something and his essential methods and skillful means were not yet fully perfected, he answered.
Then the World-Honored One Vairocana, the Omniscient One who is free from all afflictions, having heard the secret and essential matter of his question, praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, O Great-Minded One of Diligent Valor!"
This refers to the "Greatness" throughout all times—the great mind, the great vows, the great practices, and so forth.

Regarding the "Determination of the Arrangement of Honored Positions in the Secret Maṇḍala," this means the definitive establishment and alignment of the seating positions for the various holy beings.

"Secret" refers to the profound and esoteric treasury of the Tathāgata. This essential teaching has been long kept in silence, like the udumbara flower, and is spoken only at rare intervals. It is not bestowed in vain upon those who are unworthy; thus, it differs from the manifest and ordinary teachings.
The maṇḍala possesses manifold virtuous meanings; it is the secret virtue of the Tathāgata.
Such secret virtue is naturally adorned like a lotus flower in full bloom.
The "Determination of the Arrayed Honored Positions" (Peizunwei jue) means the sense of definitive discernment (*viniścaya*).
Thus, regarding this secret treasury of the lotus, it definitively discerns all matters that ought to be performed by distinguishing their various stages and positions.
"Decisive" (ketsu) means to state with certainty.
The root-source of great compassion arises from the fundamental source of great compassion.
That which is the most secret among the unsurpassed Mahāyāna Buddhas refers to this maṇḍala, which is the very root-source of the unsurpassed Mahāyāna.
This bodhicitta has great compassion as its root; it is also like a womb, and is therefore called the "root.

As for "vehicle," it refers to the practices of a mantra-practitioner (mantrayāna-bodhisattva); because it is fully endowed with skillful means, one traverses the great direct path, proceeding without any obstacles until reaching the ultimate reality.
It is like mounting a well-trained and excellent vehicle and traveling along the great direct path to reach the great city.
This is precisely the most supreme and secret essential dharma of all Buddhas.
Were it to be explained in detail, it could not be exhausted even throughout kalpas extending to the end of the future; for now, I shall explain it briefly by means of skillful expedients.
Now, even within a single word, all meanings and flavors are fully contained; therefore, it is called a "concise exposition.
This is the secret matter of the Buddha; since you are able to inquire about it, I shall provide a concise explanation.
Having first praised the Dharma and promised to provide a brief exposition, he then proceeds to answer the questions in their respective order.
The Buddha addressed Vajrapāṇi:
"Listen attentively!"
The Great Power Maṇḍala: the Birth of the Vidyārāja from the Twelve Branches.
Regarding the "Great Power Maṇḍala," this refers first to the preliminary practice. As for what must be performed first:

it is as previously described—the birth from the twelve branches and the phrases of the twelve supports. From these twelve supporting phrases, this Great Power Vidyā is born; it is the essence of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) consisting of twelve phrases. Therefore, one should first perform the rite of the Vidyārāja.

By means of this vidyārāja, one completely encompasses all that exists within both the mundane and supramundane realms; when first constructing the maṇḍala, one should first abide in the samādhi of that vidyārāja.
As for the "King," it is simply Mahāvairocana.
This means that one places the first of the twelve syllables within the heart; by taking this first syllable, one sustains the body, for all mantras are entirely subsumed within it.
If one wishes to construct a maṇḍala, it is essential to first recite [the mantra].

This means that when about to create the maṇḍala, one must first perform the recitation; thereafter, one should abide in yoga, which is precisely the practice of this Vidyārāja in accordance with principle.
Once established in yoga, one should correctly observe: "What is the appropriate task for this present undertaking?
This refers to the five families.

Regarding the specific applications of the five syllables as described above—whether square, circular, triangular, crescent-shaped, or of similar types—what should be done with them upon the upper, middle, and lower mandalas?
"What is the spiritual capacity (*indriya*) of the disciple?
Only when such various matters are all known may one proceed.
However, regarding these various distinctions within the King of Mantras, they are not yet clearly understood; therefore, I ask further.

Furthermore, there are two kinds of those who possess prior knowledge. By virtue of this, a teacher who has realized the Truth (dṛṣṭasatya) is able to perceive all faculties and conditions within such a King of Mantras, attaining unobstructed penetration.
If one is a teacher who has not yet realized the Truth, one must observe according to the instructions and the intended meaning transmitted by the teacher; this, too, is the next best course.
Having thus observed and gained knowledge, one performs whatever actions are appropriate; therefore, this King of Mantras must first be employed.
Once the body has been sustained by the fundamental samādhi, one first understands the path of yoga, and thereafter performs all various activities as desired.

However, to explain this according to the secret teaching: these twelve mantra-kings are themselves the Vajrasamādhi. Because the Bodhisattva necessarily sits at the site of enlightenment and enters the Vajradhātu, he receives the simultaneous empowerment and collective sustaining power (adhiṣṭhāna) of all Buddhas of the ten directions, thereby attaining entry into the rank of a Buddha.
To enter the stage of the Buddha is precisely to achieve the ultimate meaning of the Great Maṇḍala born from the Treasury of Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā-garbha*).

Since Vajrapāṇi has likewise entered this King of Mantras, he too has received the simultaneous empowerment of all Buddhas of the ten directions within this sutra; now, the Treasury of Great Compassion shall be further analyzed and determined.
If it were not so, how could one obtain the empowerment of all Buddhas and attain the station of a Tathāgata Dharma King?
However, since the ritual for constructing a maṇḍala must first require an ācārya, this is answered next.
It should be understood that there are two kinds of masters.

Regarding the status of an ordinary master: they must possess an understanding of mantras, mudrās, and the characteristics of the tutelary deity (iṣṭadevatā), thoroughly comprehending each of these without doubt, and discerning the distinctions between the superior, middling, and inferior methods.
Furthermore, that [teaching] has two divisions; "divisions" means it is twofold:
first, the profound and secret; second, the general and concise.
What is called "profound" refers to the ability to comprehend what is deep and vast.

This refers to one who has attained the practice of samādhi within the mantra vehicle, who thoroughly understands its underlying principles, and who possesses a broad comprehension of the Mahāyāna such that they are worthy of receiving the entrustment.

Herein, "worthy of receiving the entrustment" means one who well knows the appropriate timing, understands the capacities and natures of others, and is capable of bestowing [the teachings] upon them; such a person acts as an uninvited friend, ensuring that others do not lose the causal conditions for the Great Matter.
For those who are not yet capable, one should protect their minds and further instruct, benefit, and gladden them through other profound teachings.
