When the ten mental states of this first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) are perfected, one is immediately able to manifest as many bodies as there are Buddha-lands, as can be known from that same source.

However, the attainment of Buddhahood through a hundred minds is what is taught in the *Ratnaketu-dhāraṇī-sūtra*; it is profoundly deep and subtle, and this sutra has not yet been transmitted to the Eastern lands.
By practicing reality without ceasing, one causes each moment of mind to become pure.
Next, the answer concerns the uninterrupted practice of activities until the mental continuum (*cittasaṃtāna*) becomes pure.
"Purity of the mental continuum" refers to not halting one's functional effort. Such maturation means bringing that which is immature to maturity; thus, one shall attain *siddhi*.
It may also be said that this is "attaining siddhi.
As for when siddhi arises, the Sūtra states: "From life to life and birth to birth, until karma is no longer eliminated, once the fruit has reached maturity, at that time siddhi is accomplished."

"At one time, karma arises and causes [the mantra] to be entrusted to the body; for the practitioner who attains it, the *siddhi* arises according to their will—this is the meaning of the phrase 'in this life and in all future lives.'"
In Sanskrit it is called *saṃtāna*, which refers to consciousness; that is, within the internal mind.

It is just as when sentient beings in the world perform various kinds of karma, and by virtue of this karma they undergo retribution across one, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, or even millions of lifetimes; this karma is never lost, and once it ripens, its retribution is experienced.

Now, the answer to this is that the arising of siddhi is likewise: according to whether the practitioner’s aspiration is superior, middling, or inferior, they shall achieve siddhi by practicing in accordance with the essential requirements of the mantra method.
Because this *vidyā-mantra* resides within the body, it remains constantly within the practitioner’s body throughout every lifetime and successive rebirths.
It is like the fruit of karma: although it arises from a multitude of conditions, it is eternally empty and quiescent, neither existent nor non-existent, yet it neither perishes nor vanishes.
After this siddhi is accomplished, one will receive its fruit in every successive life without fail.
By riding upon the karma of siddhi to receive that fruit, it is called being born into the family of siddhi.
Once one has been born into the family of *siddhi* and continues until the attainment of Buddhahood, it is never lost or destroyed; therefore, it is said that karma cannot eliminate it.
The Sūtra speaks of "ripening," where ripening refers to the fruit itself.
"Causing [the practitioner] to reach maturity" means the sense of experiencing the fruit (*phala*).

"At one time" refers to a single moment; that is, as soon as the practitioner first relies upon the *dhāraṇī* for recitation and attains the meditative state (*viṣaya*), they are permitted to perform the rite of accomplishment (*sādhanavidhi*) and attain *siddhi* within that very same night.
It is produced in a single moment, yet it remains within the body for a long time without being lost or destroyed.
It is like placing poison in milk; even when it has reached the stage of clarified butter (*sarpis*), it is still capable of killing a person.

Just as when a person performs karma for rebirth in heaven and receives its fruit, having attained that celestial retribution, it is obtained immediately upon thought; without applying further effort, it is accomplished simply by thinking of it.

This *siddhi* is likewise: at the time of birth in any life, when that practitioner arises from the wholesome, pure karma they have cultivated, the practitioner subsequently attains *siddhi* arising from their intention. The pure karma and the mind that arises are equal and non-discriminative.
The mind and other factors produced by karma are all accomplished as *siddhi* at that single moment.
Because they are constantly born according to one's will, it is called "born according to will" (*yathābhilaṣita-ja*).

Next, in response to the question "How does one ascend to the realm of space?", it is said: the practitioner, riding upon the power of *siddhi*, wanders through the realm of space with sovereign non-obstruction, just like one who has attained fearlessness within illusory phenomena.
Regarding fearlessness: it refers to being able to fully comprehend the methods and principles of illusory phenomena without doubt or difficulty, thereby accomplishing what one desires.

It is like a magician who creates various realms and manifests them according to people's wishes; yet that magician remains truly unmoved and undergoes no change whatsoever, acting only through the causal conditions of mantras and medicinal herbs to delude the minds of the multitude.
Now, this siddhi is likewise: without discarding this very body, one fully accomplishes siddhi.

The illusion of mantra is like the net of Śakra; it traverses the realm of empty space and wanders through various buddha-fields with manifold sovereignty, yet it never wavers at all. It is simply because of the power of the illusory creation of mantra that such a thing is attained.

This mantra of the illusionist is called the "Indra’s Net" (Śakrābhrajāla). Just as that net displays various appearances in all its phenomena, yet in reality there is not a single substantial entity therein, it is therefore named "Indra’s Net."
This is the mantra of that illusory person in the world;

it is borrowed as a metaphor to illustrate the illusion of supramundane mantras. Furthermore, "net" (jāla) signifies the meaning of being unbroken; if one is caught in a net, it causes people to become deluded and unable to escape on their own.
This net of mantras ensnares the minds of all people; furthermore, because they are deluded and falsely perceive objects, it is called a "net.
Next, regarding the answer concerning the secret of the body being like a city of gandharvas: those who dwell therein possess neither a physical body nor consciousness.
What is the secret of the body?
It refers to those who have attained *siddhi*, who, without discarding this body or this consciousness, are able to keep their bodies secret.

It is like a city of the gandharvas, within which various forms of palaces, people, and objects are perceived; although they appear to exist, they do not truly exist. Yet, while they are not existent, they are not non-existent either, appearing at times and vanishing at others.
This practitioner conceals their body like a city of the gandharvas; it arises solely from a multitude of conditions, being neither real nor unreal, and appearing either hidden or manifest.
Due to the various causes and conditions of mantra practice and contemplation, this body likewise arises and ceases in accordance with those conditions.
Furthermore, it is like being in a dream where one dreams of ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and experiencing the various sublime pleasures of the gods.
It is like a person who, while dreaming, travels through the palaces of the devas; they do not abandon this body, nor do they go to those realms.

In this way, the practitioner of mantras who is "asleep" in yoga abides in the practice of mantra; this body is like a rainbow, and though a kalpa may pass, from the perspective of waking from that dream, it is but a brief moment.

That person does not cast off this body nor travel to that heaven; rather, it is simply through the mind that dwells in the Dharma that such inconceivable matters arise, which cannot be fathomed by the ordinary cognitive consciousness.
Now, those who have accomplished *siddhi* travel through various worlds in this same manner; it is only through the causal conditions of yoga and dreams that such things occur.
Although they accomplish various feats as if they were real and not non-existent, they know them all to be like the ten similes and do not give rise to attachment.
Because the body is purified, there is siddhi, which is like a rainbow.
Mantras are like wish-fulfilling jewels; through the meritorious activity of empowerment, such siddhi arises.
A rainbow appears in the sky; one does not know from whence it arises, yet it can manifest all manner of colors.
A mantra is like a wish-fulfilling jewel, producing various forms according to body, speech, and mind.
As one recollects the emergence of all requisites, they arise without conceptualization, yet arise from non-conceptualization.
Attaining *siddhi* is likewise.
It is also like a rainbow in the sky: its five colors are brilliantly luminous and clearly visible.
Now, observing this matter, does it arise from emptiness?
Or is it produced from the vapors of the earth?
If it arises from emptiness, since emptiness is fundamentally without phenomena, how could such form exist?
If it were produced from the earth, that too would be impossible;
yet such a thing exists and brings joy to the human heart.

One should observe and know that those phenomena are not self-produced, not produced by another, not produced by both together, and not produced without cause, but arise merely through the conjunction of various conditions.
Now, the body of siddhi is likewise; by the power of the merit from reciting mantras, it possesses such inconceivable and manifold supernatural transformations, just like that rainbow.
Furthermore, he again resolves this doubt:
Suppose someone were to ask,
"How can these dharmas of the ritual characteristics of mantras accomplish the true dharma of signless realization of the truths?"
However, this true Dharma is in fact not separate from causes and conditions;
it is precisely the contemplation of this inconceivable realm of the true nature of dependent origination.
It is like a wish-fulfilling jewel atop a banner: it can fulfill the aspirations of all people, reaching the very place where the mind that seeks them desires, according to whatever the heart wishes.
Now, observe this: does it arise from the jewel, or does it arise from the person's mind?
If it emerges from the jewel, why does it not emerge at all times, but only when one awaits the person's heart-felt aspiration?
If it emerged from the human mind, why would the human mind not seek it for itself instead of waiting for the jewel?

One should know that it does not emerge from the jewel, nor does it emerge from the human mind; it is neither produced by both together, nor is it without causes and conditions—it simply exists through their conjunction.

Now, the wondrous and inconceivable supernatural transformations of *siddhi* are likewise so; they are accomplished solely through the conditions of mantra, visualization of the deity, and bodily mudrās.

Because of the mantra, the karma of speech is purified; because of the visualization of the deity, the karma of mind is purified; and because of the mudrā, the karma of body is purified. Through the equality of these three factors, inconceivable activity arises spontaneously.
Nevertheless, it cannot be differentiated, for it is without thought and without conditioned activity.
If that is so, since it is identical to the wish-fulfilling gem, should one not know it to be a phenomenon with characteristics?
To eliminate such a basis for views, the analogy of great empty space is taught.

Just as space is signless and non-conceptual, yet all the various activities of sentient beings—coming and going, advancing and halting—are accomplished by means of space; and just as the various myriad things and all forms and appearances are manifested by means of space, yet the nature of space is eternally non-conceptual and devoid of any characteristic of arising.

The mantra is likewise: its original nature is eternally pure and identical to space; it cannot be defiled by any conditioned phenomena, yet it can also accomplish various activities. Its universal transformations are inconceivable; how, then, could it possess marks?

One should know that among the various phenomena of the world characterized by signs, the grasping of these forms and appearances is called "sign" (*nimitta*); based on this conceptual differentiation, names are established, which are called "name" (*nāman*).
All such phenomena of names and characteristics are identical to the ten similes; they exist only due to causes and conditions.
Because they arise from inversion, it is said that in reality they are without birth and without intrinsic nature, which is identical to the *dharmadhātu* and the nature of *tathatā*.

If one can contemplate in this manner, it is as if they are assembled together in one place with all the Tathāgatas; although such a person may not yet be able to ultimately realize the Buddha-wisdom, their understanding is identical to that of all Buddhas.
Because it accords with the Dharma and is called "identical to all Buddhas," it is precisely being in the same assembly as all Buddhas.
It clarifies that the ten directions are empty; for example, by using space as an analogy, it clarifies that the ten directions are empty.
Free from all conditioned activities, one remains unstained; the mantra practitioner remains unstained by all discriminative activities.
If one observes in this way, one understands that these are merely conceptualizations.
When the mantra-practitioner contemplates this, all Buddhas likewise rejoice in it.
Regarding the two kinds of *homa*: although the characteristics of *homa* were briefly explained previously, they are now further distinguished as internal and external *homa*.

Regarding the two kinds of homa taught by the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings: the first is external homa, which refers to the ritual performance that eliminates obstacles such as the afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*);
the second is internal homa.

This refers to the two kinds of homa taught by the Buddhas, the Honored Ones among two-legged beings: namely, the internal and the external. These pacify all objective realms, the twelve links of dependent origination, and so forth.
However, the external homa serves as a skillful means for the internal homa; it is, in fact, its cause.
An objector says:
"If one now performs this rite of homa and seeks that fruit, it constitutes having expectations; how, then, can the ultimate truth be realized?"
Answer: I now have nothing to seek.
Question:

If that is so, why do you not follow the constant law of *dāna* by giving universally to all who are poor and suffering, instead of pointlessly performing this burning until it is exhausted? What purpose does this serve?
Answer:

However, when ordinary persons practice giving and there is a recipient, they immediately harbor a mind of aspiration—either seeking a return favor or hoping for the fruit of their gift. Due to these causes and conditions, they are unable to counteract the mind of craving.
Because it cannot be cured, one is unable to sever the source of craving and attachment.
For this reason, it cannot serve as the causal condition for internal homa.
Now, burning this offering is precisely for the purpose of severing those faults.
By performing this as a meditative antidote, it serves as the cause for non-attached wisdom and acts as the skillful means of internal homa; therefore, one proceeds in this manner.

Just as one presents these offering substances to the Honored One (Honzon), one should know that the mind of aspiration is likewise no different from these objects; when all things are like fire extinguished once the fuel is exhausted, there is nothing to be grasped and no location whatsoever. Thus, it can serve as the condition for internal homa.

In profound practice, one performs the stage of augmentation, wherein there is an increase in majestic power; it is like when offering flowers: first, one removes all impurities, and then further augments their majestic radiance before making the offering.
Since this is so, the same applies to homa.
The ācārya performs the internal homa;
whereas those of shallow practice perform the external rite, which ultimately serves as the cause for the internal rite.

Furthermore, one must realize the specific characteristics and fundamental natures of the various honored ones—namely, those of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, followers of the Two Vehicles, and celestial deities, categorized as superior, middling, and inferior; these can be known by observing their physical forms, colors, and so forth.
The practice of mantras further possesses various distinctions, which shall now be examined.

If worldly persons practice the cultivation of mantras by relying upon the honored deities of their respective families—such as Maheśvara and others—there are immeasurable varieties, each distinct from the other, which cannot be recorded in full.
The Sūtra merely cites one corner of the matter, taking Maheśvara as its starting point.
Nevertheless, when those practitioners perform their rites of offering, each hopes to attain the fruit of the accomplishment of the tutelary deity (iṣṭadevatā) of their own respective family.
According to the differences in their respective natures and stages, each harbors aspirations to achieve those specific fruits.
Since the mind has limitations, the fruits and so forth are likewise limited.
The measures described in worldly mantras and the like are well known to the world.
Regarding those gods who possess sovereign merit, the mantras and powerful mudrās they have taught all yield results in the present life.

Therefore, when it is said that there are slight differences in their efficacy, it means that these are phenomena subject to arising and ceasing and lack any stable endurance; it does not mean they will be non-existent in future lives.
Regarding the explanation of "measure" (*pramāṇa*): the Buddha taught that those are dharmas with limited measure; such is his teaching.
Nevertheless, this is not the same as the method for the practice of *homa* (fire sacrifice) taught by the Tathāgata.

Because worldly people seek to realize their goals by merely pursuing the fruits of propitiating the original devas and other deities, the Buddha likewise established the supramundane method of homa as an antidote; thus, there exists the mantra-practice of the homa rite.

However, even those who are honored among worldly people, if they have reached the ultimate consummation within that particular dharma, can at most be of the same class as their respective tutelary deity (iṣṭadevatā), but cannot surpass it.

The same applies to those mantras and mudrās; they are taught as mantras, hand gestures, and deities according to the depth of merit planted by each practitioner and their capacity for spiritual power.
According to their respective capacities, they can only achieve the fruit of those specific deities.
Furthermore, they can only achieve fruits of the present life and attain mundane accomplishments; ultimately, they cannot achieve supramundane fruits.
The skillful cultivation of the Tathāgata’s mantras, mudrās, and so forth is not like this; they are never exhausted or destroyed—this is the distinction.
It is like a puddle in a cow's hoofprint: even if it retains water for a time, it will naturally dry up as soon as its momentum is spent.
If a person were to place this water within the great ocean, there would be no principle by which it could ever be exhausted.
Why is this? Because it has merged with the nature of all waters into a single flavor, it cannot be depleted.

It is the same for those who practice the mantra-vidyā of the Tathāgata: from the time they attain Buddhahood until the end of their succession of lives, they shall never exhaust the fruits of this siddhi, and by relying on this power, they shall ultimately attain bodhi.
Why is this? Because one is of the same single flavor as the great ocean of all Tathāgatas.

The supramundane mantras are, from the very beginning, unarisen and unconditioned; they sever all births from karma and, being free from the three faults of body, speech, and mind, one attains Buddhahood.

Regarding the supramundane mantras that are fundamentally uncreated and non-arising: although the world-honored ones—such as Īśvara and Ekaśṛṅga (the "unicorn," which the original text calls "rhinoceros horn" while the treatise calls it "qilin horn")—as well as the mantras of the Buddhas, śrāvakas, and bodhisattvas, exist, I shall now explain their measure.
The mantras spoken by the gods and others are all conditioned phenomena that arise from those deities.
World-transcending mantras transcend the three times; though they arise from conditions, they may also be employed, for they are all [composed of] syllables.

It can be seen that it is not the fruit of seeing; for that which arises from body, speech, and mind is not like this, being neither created by the Tathāgata himself nor created by the Buddhas of antiquity.

That which is called the "fruit" in worldly discourse can endure for all time; yet the fruit of the mantras taught by the Samyaksaṃbuddha exceeds even the number of kalpas. Therefore, one should know that these mantras, mudrās, and so forth, are from the very beginning the inherent nature (*dharmatā*) of the Tathāgata, and are not something produced through volitional effort.
Question:
If it is said that there is no action and no arising, then why do we now see people who, seeking the fruit of *siddhi*, diligently apply skillful means and thereby achieve those fruits?
If there is arising and there is fruit, then there must be an agent; how then could there be no arising?
Answer: This interpretation is not correct.
The nature of mantras and mudrās, as well as those who maintain and recite them, are identical in essence to empty space; the fruits they produce are likewise so.

Through the causal conditions of the equality of these three factors—mantra, mudrā, and the deity—one is able to purify the three obstacles. From this, inconceivable fruits arise; therefore, the magnitude of these inconceivable fruits cannot be grasped.
Just as those mantras and mudrās are equal to space, one should know that this fruit is likewise equal to space.
Even all the mantras belonging to the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas are of that same measure, for they all transcend the three periods of time.
The "three times" refer to the past, the future, and the present.
Because one is free from these three times, one never loses or destroys the fruit of this *siddhi*, ultimately attaining unsurpassed *bodhi*.

Regarding the arising of the fruit through conditions: it means that because various conditions such as mantras, mudrās, and deities are fully assembled, accomplishment is attained; therefore, this measure is the true mark of the Middle Way of equality.
There are two kinds of fruits:
first, those that are visible phenomena, which are attained and accomplished in the present life;

second, those that are not visible phenomena, because as the fruit of retribution for future lives they are forever inexhaustible, such that one receives the fruit life after life, progressing ever further until the attainment of Buddhahood.
However, it is neither manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*), nor form (*rūpa*), nor mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*); it neither exists nor perishes, and it does not decay or vanish.

Nevertheless, through the pure causes and conditions of the actions of body, speech, and mind, one attains this state which is unborn and devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Since there are many such answers above, one should further examine them in light of the original question.

Recorded by the Śramaṇa Acharya Yi-hang.
The eleventh chapter of the Secret Maṇḍala, Part Two:

Next, regarding the answer as to for how long the lifespan of the resultant number [of deities] lasts—it is said that the power of all mantras belonging to the Honored Ones of the world does not exceed one kalpa at most.

That which the Buddha has taught exceeds the duration of one kalpa; that is to say, it exceeds one kalpa and further exceeds another kalpa, continuing thus immeasurably until the attainment of Buddhahood.
Therefore, the siddhis, lifespans, and fruits protected by worldly beings have numerical limits and do not exceed one kalpa.
Now, one does not lose it; its lifespan is inexhaustible, exceeding the measure of a single kalpa.

If explained according to worldly matters, one may simply transcend a certain number of kalpas according to one's capacity, or transcend immeasurable kalpas such that the lifespan is never exhausted; this is also to surpass those gods of the world.
Thus, the phrase "transcending kalpas" is a general expression that includes the indefinite;
yet, speaking in terms of actual lifespan, it exceeds the number of kalpas, and the duration of its retribution is likewise limitless.
Next, regarding the answer concerning samādhi: briefly, there are many types.
Whether it be the samādhis of the Buddhas and their sons, the Great Sages of the Buddhas, or the assembly of the Buddha’s sons, they are pure and free from all conceptualizations.
Having perceptions is called the mundane; for the two vehicles, it is termed "freedom from perception.
If this samādhi is a mundane yoga, it is called "samādhi with signs" (*sanimitta-samādhi*).

Herein, *sama* has the meaning of "equality," and *bhūmi* has the meaning of "wisdom. By means of wisdom, one contemplates that the three aforementioned things are all empty. Because the essence of these three things is empty, they are equalized and unified as one; this is called the ground of samādhi (*samādhi-bhūmi*).

However, the samādhis of both Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are all free from conceptualization and pure. By means of this samādhi, they correctly contemplate that these three things are all equal, without further discrimination; because they are free from all conceptualizations, their fundamental nature is purely white and free from all defilements, and is therefore called "pure."

If there is conceptualization, it refers to all worldly samādhis; that is, practicing according to their respective fruits, one harbors expectations while cultivating causes in anticipation of results. This reaches its limit at the four dhyānas and eight concentrations and cannot go beyond them; therefore, they are not pure.

Although Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have attained purity, they have not yet attained universal purity; because they have not yet fully understood the two obstructions—those of afflictions and those to knowledge—they have not yet reached complete purity.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of worldly samādhi:

first, the view of annihilationism (ucchedadṛṣṭi), and second, the view of eternalism (śāśvatadṛṣṭi). If one holds the view of annihilationism, there is no discrimination; if one holds the view of eternalism, there is a slight degree of discrimination.
Regarding the attainment of results from karma, there is the process of ripening and the time of ripening.
If one attains *siddhi*, one gains mastery over karma and can transform it; thus, one may either undergo the retribution or not.
Because the mind has no intrinsic nature, the nature of the mind is free from cause and effect.
"How could it not? means that it does not exist [as such].
Within the various voids—such as the marks of liberation, the arising of karma, and so forth—the fruition is attained when the maturation of karma is accomplished.

If siddhi is attained, because the karma that should have been performed has been transformed by the mind into non-substantiality, both cause and fruit are transcended, and karma gives rise to liberation.
That "birth is like space" means that worldly samādhis with signs still involve karma; they are practiced in expectation of retribution, and are therefore termed "accomplishment" (siddhi).
Attaining this maturation is called *siddhi*.

If one dedicates this toward the selflessness of the mind by means of the emptiness of this world, then since its essence is signless and equal to the boundless expanse of space, the merit attained is likewise vast.
That which turns back this mind devoid of intrinsic nature is called *citta*.
*Citta* is like a collection adorned with various colors; thus it is named *citta*.
Because it is composed of various colored threads, it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); this is the reason.
Since the primary cause lacks intrinsic nature, one should know that the resulting effect likewise lacks intrinsic nature.
Why is this so? If there were arising due to a cause, then the effect could have arising.
Now, since the cause itself must depend on conditions to be established, it lacks arising and lacks intrinsic nature; one should know, therefore, that arising is unattainable.
Because both cause and effect are thus, one attains liberation from all karma.
Some may say: "If it were so, then there would be neither cause nor effect, and one would fall into the view of nihilism."
This is also not the case.
It is simply that apart from the nature of arising through karma, once one is free from such karmic arising, there is the arising of the Dharma-nature, which is equal to space.

Because space is boundless, one should know that the merits accomplished and the deeds performed for the benefit of sentient beings are likewise boundless and inexhaustible; therefore, it is not subject to cessation.
The above concludes the response to Vajrapāṇi’s questions by means of a brief summary in verse; it is now further explained in prose.

As for the phrase "Furthermore" (*punar-aparam*), it indicates that since the matters previously discussed were not yet fully exhausted, they are continued and clarified once more; hence, it is called "Furthermore."
"Listen attentively": because this Dharma is increasingly profound and contains secret, essential instructions, he strictly enjoins them to listen attentively.
Within this, five matters are briefly explained: namely, the seal (*mudrā*), the color, the honored position, the abiding, and the samādhi.
*Mudrā* refers to hand-seals (*hasta-mudrā*) or pledge-seals (*samaya-mudrā*), which are here redefined as formal shapes.
*Varṇa* refers to the distinct divisions and characteristics of the deity’s form; "placed" refers to shapes such as square, circular, semi-circular, or triangular.
"Venerable seat" (尊位) refers to the respective locations within the maṇḍala where the positions of the holy ones are arranged.

"Abiding" (住) means that the image of the deity is not merely a painted figure; rather, because it is summoned by means of mantras, mudrās, and so forth, it arrives at its original seat, manifests majestic power, and remains there, displaying signs of spiritual efficacy.
Samādhi refers to the ritual manifestations of tranquility, wrath, joy, and so forth, according to the categories of superior, middling, and inferior.

One should invite the deity according to the Dharma, establish the seals (*mudrā*) and forms, and arrange the positions of the honored ones so that their majestic efficacy manifests before one; this constitutes abiding in samādhi within the place where one proceeds and dwells.
The place where one dwells is called a "destiny" (*gati*), specifically referring to the destiny of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
It is necessary to fully understand these five conditions regarding the so-called five destinies; for "destiny" carries the sense of being distinct and separate.
Because there are distinctions based on these five conditions, they are called "five.
By possessing these five, one is able to fully comprehend all maṇḍalas, both mundane and supramundane.

However, these five matters are the dharma of all Buddhas of antiquity who attained supreme perfect enlightenment, as well as the dharma of the Buddhas prior to them who attained *sambodhi*; they are the practice of the Dharma-realm and empty space.

Regarding the "practitioner whose nature is the dharma-realm and the void": this is because, by virtue of having a nature identical to the dharma-realm, they have accomplished the conduct of a Tathāgata.

Thus, the Buddhas—out of their original vow to deliver sentient beings within the realm of no-remainder, and for the sake of benefiting, gladdening, and bringing peace to those bodhisattvas who practice the gateway of mantras—have expounded this; therefore, it should be received with earnest and careful attention.
Vajrapāṇi said: "So it is, World-Honored One!"

“As for the phrase ‘Indeed, we wish to hear,’ this refers to the great assembly of the ten worlds headed by Vajrapāṇi and the ten worlds headed by Samantabhadra; having received the Buddha’s command, they all spoke with one voice, saying: ‘Indeed.’”
“World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it.
For this reason, the Buddha further expounded the secret maṇḍala dharma.

The Buddha said: "There is the maṇḍala of the Perfectly Enlightened One, which places within the secret and the most secret the names such as the 'Unsurpassed Treasury of Great Compassion. If it is identical to the worldly and world-transcending maṇḍalas of the Immeasurable and others, this is the ultimate teaching of the Tathāgata’s Most Perfect Enlightenment."
However, although this "Birth from the Matrix of Great Compassion" has already been explained previously, for what reason is it explained again?
What is the distinction?
Although it was indeed explained before, that was as a secret; there is yet another secret within the secret.
If this dharma is not taught, even the mastery of the preceding dharmas cannot be accomplished; therefore, it is the most essential and secret.
If one understands this, all maṇḍalas in the world may be employed by it, and there is nowhere it cannot enter.
As for the method of its construction: first, one constructs a square maṇḍala; its boundaries are formed by connecting the *karmavajra-jñāna-mudrās* all around to serve as its paths.
It is simply for the sake of stability.
Within the center of the cross, one further forms the Vajra Seal of the Cross; this seal is made as previously described, differing only in that it consists of a cross.
Upon the *vajra* seal of the ten directions, one forms a lotus flower that faces upward and is half-opened, so that the ten directions take on the appearance of a flower.
Upon this flower, one further places an eight-petaled lotus, which corresponds to the positions of the five Buddhas and four Bodhisattvas as previously described.
One should visualize nine points with the mind; that is, one should visualize a point upon each of the pedestal and the eight petals.
These points are the realization of the Great Void (mahāśūnyatā), which signifies the attainment of perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi).
Regarding these eight types of rites and the intermediate ones, one should construct square or circular maṇḍalas and paint the image of the principal deity therein.
For a Buddha, the altar is square; for a Bodhisattva, it is circular.
This is merely for the practitioner to perform for themselves and must not be shown to others.
When performing the ritual, one should sit at the entrance of the maṇḍala and personally perform the rites such as empowerment; only then may one carry out all ritual activities.
This matter is especially secret; one should practice it by holding it in mind, and it must not be expressed in writing.
Furthermore, upon the altar, one should visualize the twelve-syllable King of Mantras as described above, ensuring that each individual character is clearly distinguished and placed upon the mandala.
He asked further:
"Are they placed like a chain?
By what means is their sequence established?"
Furthermore, regarding the statement "placing a seed within the flower," this refers to painting lotus seeds; whether there are ten, or more or fewer, it matters not.

As for the scripture’s mention of "flowing forth," it means that when a person understands this secret dharma, all mundane and supramundane maṇḍalas flow forth from within it; this can be understood according to its corresponding meaning.

Briefly, there are four methods for performing secret rites: first, "activity" (*karma*), which refers to all the various ritual tasks to be performed at the maṇḍala from beginning to end; second, "form" (*mūrti*), which refers to the manifested physical forms of the deities and so forth; third, "siddhi," which refers to the fruit that is accomplished; and fourth, "placement of position" (*sthāpana*), which refers to the arrangement of the deities' locations.
To understand these four dharmas is to penetrate all dharmas that flow forth; furthermore, it is asked:
from this, all the various maṇḍalas that flow forth are entirely based on what is taught in the fundamental teachings.
"Buddha-son" refers to him being addressed; it means Vajrapāṇi.

Furthermore, as for the four bodhisattvas, their positions are as follows: Samantabhadra in the southeast (Xun), Mañjuśrī in the southwest (Kun), Maitreya in the northwest (Qian), and Avalokiteśvara in the northeast (Gen).

In the previous section on the assembly of the *nidāna*, sometimes Avalokiteśvara is replaced by Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, or Mañjuśrī is replaced by Sarvadurgatipariśodhana; while their respective meanings differ, it is permissible to employ either for the ritual recitation, though in this context, Avalokiteśvara is used as the primary figure.
The above concludes the Vairocana Maṇḍala.
Next, regarding the "Primordial Perfectly Enlightened One," this refers to the initial teaching.
It clarifies the maṇḍalas of all Buddhas, which constitute the Buddha Family (Buddhakula).
Construct this Maṇḍala of the Buddha Family by making a circular maṇḍala; its circle is like the moon, white in the center with the color of a conch shell.

Within this circle, first draw a white lotus flower, and upon the flower, entirely three triangles. Within these triangles, make them red, and therein paint the image of a Buddha. As for which Buddha it shall be, ask further.
Encircle the triangle with a vajra-bond as shown in the diagram.
Place dots around the triangle; these dots serve as markers—ask further regarding this.
On the outer rim, create rays of light in the shape of a repelling enemy.
Around the circumference of the circle, place dots; these dots are each the position of a deity.
Ask further:
alternatively, one may place syllables there.
"Light flows forth universally" means that one visualizes light streaming from within the body of the Buddha, gradually spreading outward beyond the triangle.
"The Lord of Mantras" refers to the Principal Deity (iṣṭadevatā), from whose entire body light flows forth.
In the great maṇḍala mentioned previously, there was also a triangular seal (*mudrā*), but its application was different from this one.
The former was merely a seal, whereas here one places either a Buddha image or a seal; thus, the ritual procedure is fully complete in that [former] case as well.
Next is the Lotus Family.
○ [The circle] This statement refers to the preceding item.
That which is painted as identical in both the mundane and supramundane realms may also be called "existent."

It says that there are immeasurable mundane and supramundane maṇḍalas—this is intended to ensure they listen well. [The symbol] has been moved above the vertical line; one should know that this is the initial maṇḍala born of compassion.

Construct a square maṇḍala; within it, draw a conch shell. Upon the conch shell is a lotus flower; upon the lotus flower is a vajra; and upon the vajra is another lotus flower, upon which one places the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
One may place either seals (*mudrā*) or syllables (*akṣara*).
Upon all the seals, one should place seed-syllables (*bīja*), namely upon the conch, the vajra, and the flower.
In the next courtyard, one should place Mahāsthāmaprāpta and the others, making light radiate everywhere; do not harbor any doubts.
One should skillfully establish the fundamental seed-syllables as the seeds.
In the corresponding positions, one should place the seven white auspicious ones (*śrīvatsa*), each having two messengers (*dūta*).
This sūtra merely provides a brief explanation; it is fully recorded within the separate section on the rites of Avalokiteśvara, which should be consulted in detail elsewhere.
The consort (*vidyā*) is the mistress of resources who is able to bestow [wealth] at will upon those who seek it.
One should likewise fashion Mahāsthāmaprāpta and others according to the Dharma.
Having fashioned them as lords who have attained mastery, one holds their distinctive marks and seals.
One should fashion them with exceptional excellence; this is called "fashioning according to the Dharma."
The Horse-Headed One (Hayagrīva) resides within the triangle; it should be joined in its proper place and drawn in the center of the mandala.

As for the other deities, each has its own distinct color, form, and so forth, as well as shapes such as squares, circles, half-moons, and triangles, along with their respective placements—all of which are as described in the extensive version.
What was previously stated regarding the necessity of understanding five matters—namely, form, color, mudrā, the *iṣṭadevatā*, and position—is precisely this point.
For example, when painting a *iṣṭadevatā*, one must consider what colors and physical forms to employ, as each possesses its own specific mudrā.
The former, the Great Compassion Treasury Birth, was the Assembly Altar; now, within this [text], each of the three families has its own distinct [altar].
For instance, the central womb of the Lotus Family altar is the Auspicious Altar, with Avalokiteśvara as its presiding deity.

Leave an empty space outside the womb-shaped enclosure; beyond that empty space is the second seating area, wherein one should place all the deities of the Avalokiteśvara family. All other matters are exactly as prescribed in the ritual for constructing a great maṇḍala; furthermore, the Buddhas of the ten directions should also be placed within that empty space.
Regarding the third seating position, the eight classes of beings and others are also placed there; this may be understood by analogy with what precedes.
Within the triangle, it is like the radiance of the rising sun—meaning the reddish-yellow hue of the sun when it first emerges.
Those who are at the side of the Vidyārāja are at the side of Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
Next, if one constructs the Hayagrīva Maṇḍala, it should be placed within a triangle; for the three outer layers, those maṇḍalas should likewise all be made triangular.
When performing this, Khagarbha (Akāśagarbha) is positioned in the center; one then moves Avalokiteśvara to occupy the place of Śrīghoṣa (Śikhin), while the remaining retinue surrounds him.
All other positions are interchanged accordingly, which may be understood through careful reflection.
Next, regarding the creation of the second maṇḍala: this refers to counting from the Lotus Family (*padmakula*), where the Lotus is the first and the Vajra is the second family.
What I am now proclaiming is well-spoken; it is taught neither before nor after, following a sequential order, and constitutes the second section.
Its maṇḍala is square-shaped and is entirely composed of vajras.
One should encircle it with three-pronged vajras joined together to form a boundary.
Within the enclosure is yellow; in its center is placed a lotus flower, upon which is a vase as white as the moon.

Alternatively, one may encircle it with a vajra-enclosure, or encircle it with other substances; that is, taking the mudrā of whichever deity it corresponds to as the center, one likewise encircles it with that same mudrā.
Above that jar is a great wind, known as the "half-moon" shape.

Within this, it has the appearance of black clouds, like the dense, hanging black clouds during a rainstorm; beneath it, its form is like that of a banner, moving and flowing with the force of a great wind.
During that half-month, it appears like the flames of a great fierce fire in the shape of a triangle; its three corners are also encircled by vajras.
The interior of the triangle is red, like the color of the sun when it first rises.
Within it, place a lotus; the lotus is intensely red, like the color of the great conflagration at the end of an eon—a deep, rich crimson, or perhaps reddish-black.
Upon the lotus, draw a vajra, or else the form of the principal deity, or the five-pronged mudrā, or a seed-syllable. From that vajra, various tongues of flame stream forth.
If one is painting a form, place the seed-syllable upon the heart; this refers to the syllable *HŪṂ*.
If one is painting a mudrā, visualize the syllable *HŪṂ*, recite it while performing the empowerment, and place the syllable upon the mudrā.
"This is your maṇḍala," [the Buddha] said, personally addressing Vajrapāṇi; thus he declared, "This is your maṇḍala.
All Buddhas of antiquity have spoken thus, and I likewise speak it now.

Regarding the statement that "the various vidyārājas each sit according to their original forms and colors," this refers to the vajramātṛs, the vajrasūcī, the vajrapāśa, and so forth—these numerous vajra retinues each appearing according to the specific forms and colors of their respective principal deities; they may be depicted in form, represented by mudrās, or placed as seed-syllables (bīja).
Each follows its respective dharma in sequential correspondence, meaning that they achieve the sublime *siddhi*.
This Vajrapāṇi is installed as the central terrace, while the various classes [of deities] constitute the second enclosure.

All of these refer to the central platform, which transforms into immeasurable altars; those following the former path are placed on the right, while those following the latter path are placed on the left, with the right and left determined according to the gate through which one enters.
Furthermore, I previously mentioned the various alternative names for the many Vajras.
"Sovereign" (*īśvara*) means attaining sovereignty over the Vajra.

Furthermore, regarding this statement "I am the Sovereign who wields the Vajra," in the aforementioned *Mahākaruṇāgarbha-mahāparṣad*, among the various Vajras depicted below Vairocana and between Akṣobhya and Trailokyavijaya, their names had not yet been listed; they are now being enumerated for the first time, which is why it says "furthermore."

This refers to the stainless vajra of space, the vajra wheel, the vajra fang, and the sublime abiding of the surata-vajra; it refers to dwelling together in peace and security. "The great portion of the Renowned Vajra" means the portion of the Great One, which is the very essence of sentient beings of great mind. "Vajra Sharpness" is a term for extreme swiftness and keenness; this mandala is composed entirely of mudrās.

The meaning of the quiescent Vajra is the sense of profound stillness, like the meaning of *nirvāṇa*. It is the name of the Great Vajra; furthermore, there are the names: Blue Vajra, Lotus Vajra, Wide-Eyed Vajra, Holder of the Wondrous Vajra, Vajra of Vajra-Wisdom (named solely after "Vajra"), Non-Abiding Conceptualization Vajra, and Space-Boundless-Walking Vajra. These are the aforementioned names.
Each should be placed within its respective great mandala.
As for these mandalas, whether square or circular, they follow the previous specifications; their colors and shapes are likewise to be arranged accordingly.
The sequence is established according to the names; it proceeds cyclically from beginning to end.
Regarding white, yellow, red, black, and so forth, they follow the order of the text: first is white, then yellow, then red, then black, and then white again—such is the sequence.
Regarding those who were not mentioned, they should be understood by analogy with this example; they should be fashioned according to their respective original classes and forms.

These vajras number as many as the atoms within ten buddha-fields; one should understand that among the assembly listed previously and those mentioned here, there are mutual absences and presences—some being present here but absent in the former list, and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding these mudrās held by the Vajras, whether three prongs or one prong—that is, the needle—these follow the sequence previously established.
First, one forms three prongs, and then proceeds from there in a continuous cycle.
Alternatively, there are two heads; these two heads constitute the five-pronged [vajra].
This seal is made with four corners all around, like four vajras, and in its center is one that resembles a five-pronged [vajra] but remains closed.
"Or Mālā" refers to those who hold the Vajramālā.
These vajras each take their own original name as their mantra; thus, these names are the supreme syllables serving as seed-syllables (*bīja*).
Next, according to the individual syllables and the general rule, place the syllable HŪṂ upon the heart in each case.
As for the mudrā, the general rule is to employ the five-pronged vajra mudrā.

Regarding the fact that both wind and fire are present in the Maṇḍala of Acala: "wind" refers to the half-moon shape, and "fire" refers to the triangle. This means that one draws a triangle within a half-moon altar, and within that triangle, one depicts Acala.
Regarding "in the direction of Nairṛti," this refers to the construction in the southwest of Vairocana.
Alternatively, "the excellence of the three times" refers to its location in the direction of Vāyu; it is distinguished by this, while the rest is the same as Akṣobhya.
The three locations are encircled by vajras, which refers to the "seized mudrās" (*gṛhītamudrā*). These three locations refer to either a form, a seal, or a syllable.

However, if this Maṇḍala of Acala is constructed separately, Acala is placed in the center; Vairocana is in the eastern part of the inner court, while the remaining vajra retinue surrounds them on all sides.
Next, the Maṇḍala of the Buddha-Mother is explained.

Having previously laid out the form of the maṇḍala, one should first know that these are golden in color; however, as only their names were listed previously without distinguishing their forms or mudrās, they are now set forth here.
First, it is said that the maṇḍala is golden in color, with its four sides enclosed by a vajra boundary.
This refers to the supreme form of the Honored One from above; that is to say, from this point forward, he shall explain it.
This maṇḍala of the Mother of Buddhas is the most supreme among all maṇḍalas.
Next, within the maṇḍala, one should draw a yellow lotus with flames; upon the lotus, one should form the seal (mudrā) of the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa.
The mudrā should be in the shape of a Buddha’s uṣṇīṣa, with the crown made high and prominent, and two eyes painted on the sides.
If one forms the image of the Mother of Buddhas (Buddhamātṛ), it should be like the likeness of a celestial maiden (*devī*), with the seed-syllable placed at the heart.
Alternatively, one may simply draw the mudrās as the uṣṇīṣa, or merely write the syllables.
If the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa constitutes the central matrix (garbha), then the various Buddha-eyes and so forth serve as the retinue surrounding it.
The Buddha constantly dwells within flames of fire himself, and therein he scatters the seed-syllable.
This means that this mudrā dwells within the flames, and the seed-syllable is placed in its center; it is precisely this.
Regarding the abandonment of the three positions: this refers to abandoning the three seats and establishing the Buddha-eye.
As previously stated in the section on the Bodhisattva family, "universally spreading the seed-syllables" means to distribute them throughout the maṇḍala.
That which has not yet been explained shall now be further explained.
All bodhisattvas must construct a maṇḍala; they should fashion an image of perfect luminosity, making it exceedingly white and pure.

Within it, a cross-shaped platform was constructed; upon the platform stood a great cintāmaṇi jewel, each bearing a marker like a "bead-receiving" marker, with a wish-fulfilling gem placed at its tip, which emitted extraordinary rays of light.

The principal deity (bimba-bodhisattva) is placed at the center of the ten directions; the other bodhisattvas are arranged in sequence within the inner courtyard, and the eight classes of beings (aṣṭau nāgāḥ) are positioned further outside.
The color of ultimate whiteness is the color of tranquility; one should cause it to be extremely bright, pure, and abide in stillness.
These Bodhisattvas are all capable of granting every aspiration. Next, one constructs the Maṇḍala of the Lion of the Śākyas, which is Śākyamuni himself.

Listen attentively, O Son of the Buddha! One should make it square with vajras on all four sides. This "vajra" is precisely the vajra-circle square altar among the five wheels mentioned above. "All around" (pu) is a term for the four cardinal directions being perfectly aligned. That altar is yellow and should be made exceedingly brilliant and beautiful.
Within it, draw a three-pronged vajra; upon the vajra, place a lotus flower, which is yellow in color; atop the flower, set a bowl, with flames of light emanating from all four sides of the bowl.

If one is to depict the form of a Buddha, one should draw Śākyamuni Buddha holding an alms bowl, surrounded by a vajra-rail; on the right side place the *kāṣāya*, that is, the *saṃghāṭī* robe, and on the left side place the mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*).
Next are the five Buddha-uṣṇīṣas. As for the White Parasol Buddha-uṣṇīṣa, it is placed upon a seat, and the seal is placed upon the seat.
This is done either according to its own family, as in all cases for the Buddha Family;
or according to the ritual purpose, such as the circular shape for pacifying (śāntika) rites.
Draw it as a seal using an umbrella.
For the Vijaya-Uṣṇīṣa, surround it everywhere with a sword; if there is a specific place for its description, follow the text accordingly.
Light flows forth from all sides, like the fiery flames of heated iron—this refers to red flaming light.

The Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Supreme (Jiusheng Foding) uses the wheel as its seal; the Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Obstacle-Dispeller (Chuzhang Foding) uses the hook as its seal for destruction; for the Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Fire-Mass (Huoju Foding), one should paint the form of the Buddha’s uṣṇīṣa-knot, and the Great Being so named is called Vajra; the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Unifying (Huitong Da Foding) uses the vajra as its seal.
The *Abhibhava-buddhoṣṇīṣa* is the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa of Overwhelming Power.

*Gata-buddhoṣṇīṣa* signifies the meaning of "most supreme and honored," as it transcends all; its seal is the lotus. The *Anantaghosa-buddhoṣṇīṣa* uses the conch shell—known as *śaṅkha*—as its symbol; its color and type should be understood as previously described.
The Buddha’s mark of majesty uses the wish-fulfilling jewel as its seal; this is called the Seal Maṇḍala.
This seal-dharma and so forth are used for consecrations, the accomplishment of objects, and other such purposes.
Regarding pacification and the other rites, they follow the transformations of form and color, which are not what is employed here.
For accomplishment, one always contemplates the deity within as having various colors, such as white, yellow, red, and so forth.
The Buddha-eye should be formed in the shape of a *uṣṇīṣa*, with eyes placed on both sides.
The *uṣṇīṣa* of the Buddha is yellow and encircled by a vajra.

The invincible consort (*vidyārājñī*) holds the lotus mudrā: this refers to the empty-space and wind fingers pinching the flower, while the remaining fingers are extended; the finger pinching the flower is held before the heart.
If the deities possess mudrās, they should be placed according to the textual description;
if there is no such description, one should take the mudrā of the presiding deity of their respective family and place it, provided it is within the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
King Aparājita forms the mouth-mudrā upon a black lotus; this refers to painting his face as wrathful, with both fangs protruding upward.
In these various positions, if Śākyamuni is taken as the central figure, then the Buddhoṣṇīṣa and others are arranged in the second court.
If, however, one is selected from among each individual deity to serve as the presiding lord of the maṇḍala, then Śākyamuni is moved to the exterior, and the rest may be understood by analogy.
Furthermore, the mudrās of the Śuddhāvāsa deities will be explained in sequence.
As the Sūtra states regarding the practitioner of the pure realm: "This means taking meditative concentration as one's sustenance and purity as one's practice.
Their mudrās are now listed below in order.

The *cintā-mudrā* (contemplation hand) is formed by slightly bending the index finger toward the palm with the earth and water fingers, while the other three fingers are extended; the *tri-daṇḍa* (triple-staff) is formed by tilting the head slightly to one side, bending the hand inward, and pointing the index finger toward the cheek.
The *śubha-mudrā* (auspicious hand) signifies the granting of fearlessness; it is performed with the left hand, though the right may also be used, as it conveys the sense of being "excellent.
The *hasita-mudrā* (smiling hand) is formed by turning the *cintā-mudrā* forward toward the chest, causing the three fingers to point upward.

For the Flower Hand (*puṣpahasta*), one holds a flower between the wind and space fingers while extending the three [remaining] fingers; these three fingers may either be extended with the palms facing upward or extended vertically—both are acceptable.
As for the Space Palm (*ākāśapāṇi*), one turns the right hand sideways, spreading the fingers in the air.
Regarding the rules for painting: it means that one should paint according to these methods.
These deities may be depicted as smiling, or in a state of contemplation, or granting boons, and so forth; all such forms are permissible.
Next is the seal of the Earth Deity.
Form a precious vase, white and circular in the center; within the vase, insert various jewels, grains, flowers, fruits, and so forth to adorn it, and encircle it with vajras.

Regarding the mudrā for summoning the Fire Deity: one should extend the right hand sideways; the third joint of the index finger (vāyu-aṅguli) is slightly bent, and the upper joint of the middle finger (ākāśa-aṅguli) is also bent toward the palm.
If it is first straight and then bent, this is the ritual for summoning;
if it is first bent and then extended back, this is the ritual for dismissal.
One should surround [the central figure] with the great ṛṣis, such as Kāśyapa and the ṛṣi Gautama, all of whom should be painted in succession within the fire enclosure.
The Fire Court is the triangular altar; its color within is red, hence it is called the Red Court.
Its mudrā is the same as the four Vedic mudrās described by the sages of the five supernatural powers mentioned previously.

This is the secret record of the practitioners of the Brahma-faring (brahmacārin). If those who recite the Vedas see this hand-seal (mudrā), they will know which treatise and which school it belongs to.

As for the Ṛṣi Gautama: while traveling through the sky, two drops fell and defiled the ground; from these grew sugarcane, which was scorched by the sun, giving birth to two sons—one became the Śākya king, and the other, Makkhali, sat in meditative concentration (dhyāna) until ants covered his entire body. Fearing he might harm the ants, he again entered samādhi. As for the Ṛṣi Garga: "Garga" is the name of a mountain, derived from its location. As for the Ṛṣi Vasiṣṭha: this is the one formerly called the Ṛṣi Vasu. As for Aṅgiras: this signifies the meaning of bodily perspiration.

This seer was not born from a womb, but was born from perspiration; thus he received his name. To the south, one should construct a wind altar for King Yama. Upon this altar, one should draw the *daṇḍa* seal or similar seals; one corner of this altar should face the practitioner and one corner should face outward, or it may be arranged according to convenience.
To the right of the King, one draws the deity Rāhu, whose seal is a bell;
if his form is depicted, he holds it.
To the left, one draws the deity Tamas, whose seal is a banner (*dhvaja*); this banner is called *ketu* in Sanskrit, which also means a flag.
Maheśvara, in his wrathful form, forms the śūla-mudrā; this is the śūla. Maheśvara’s consort forms the śakti-mudrā; this is the śakti.
The Great Brahmā consort forms the lotus mudrā, which signifies an unopened lotus.
Nārāyaṇa forms the wheel mudrā.
The Seven Mothers all employ the musta grass mudrā; this is it.
Kubera performs the Skull-Mudrā (kapāla-mudrā) in the direction of Vaiśravaṇa. Regarding this skull:

with the "smiling hand" gesture, one holds it; that is to say, one bends the ring finger and little finger into the palm, while extending the remaining three fingers like the smiling hand gesture, holding the skull as if holding an alms bowl.
The seven mothers and their retinues include the vulture, the jackal, and the *vāśī* bird—which resembles an osprey, is pale yellowish-brown in color, and has a yellow beak; it is a species of hawk.

These birds possess a secret method of bodily preservation; they all reside within the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*), surrounding the Seven Mothers and all other classes belonging to the realm of King Yama, who likewise abide within the wind-circle.
If one holds flowers or obtains these birds and so forth, one should likewise recite the Seven Mother Mantras.
Each of these has its own specific method of recitation; however, as they now enter this maṇḍala assembly, they are all employed here as adornments.
In the northeast direction, one should form the seal of the great sword.
For Nārāyaṇa, one forms the wheel seal as described above.
For Kumāra, the son of Maheśvara, one forms the śakti seal.
The Nanda and Upananda dragon brothers form the cloud seal; within the clouds there is lightning, and further, the form of water, both situated at the side of the altar gate.
Śaṅkara holds the trident seal.
The consort of Śaṃkara forms the *pātrī* seal.
Candradeva forms the white flask together with a lotus.
Sūryadeva forms the chariot seal within a golden wheel, which is the square mandala.
Śaṇmukha and Viśākha form the bow mudrā, which is also within the vajra-wheel.
Beside the bow, there must be Vāyu, the Wind Deity, who forms the wind-banner mudrā.
For the deity Ghoṣa, form the lute mudrā.
For the nāga Vāsuki, form the noose mudrā.
As for the head, construct a circular maṇḍala and surround it with the fundamental seed-syllable.
The "Great Self" (Mahātman) refers here to Vajradhara.

These aforementioned seal-marks are presented in brief; for a detailed exposition, they are fully contained within the ritual manuals (*vidhi*), namely the specific practice methods (*pṛthag-caryā-vidhi*) for each respective mantra.
The above constitutes the ritual procedures for the Śākyavarga class.

Below, the maṇḍala of the Bodhisattvas is explained; this refers to the second tier of the great maṇḍala, the position of the various Bodhisattvas. Regarding the Mañjuśrī-maṇḍala: it is square and surrounded by vajras as previously described when the fire emerged. Within this, one forms a triangle, and within the triangle, one forms the seal of the blue lotus, which is the seed-syllable.
Recite it while visualizing it pervading the interior.
The syllables of the mantra are placed within it; not only are they placed within, but they are also arranged along the four sides.
Along the inner boundaries of the three corners, one should draw small blue lotuses all around to encircle the seal of the great blue lotus.
The reason for forming mudrās is to recognize the meaning, intent, and other aspects of this honored dharma-gate.
One should observe each according to its shape, color, and so forth, thereby recognizing the secret significance.
Taking the seed-syllable according to the Dharma and "seeding" it means to place this syllable as the seed.
Within that, one forms this seal; perform it in the following order.
The "Diligent Hero" (Vīravīra) is Mañjuśrī.
This refers to the blue lotus seed-syllable and so forth, which are to be performed according to the sequence of the ritual.
One contemplates them according to their colors and forms to realize the secret intention.
The youth Jālinīprabha forms the hook-seal (*aṅkuśamudrā*) or, if forming his body, holds a hook.
The youth Ratnamakuṭa holds a jewel as his seal; the youth Vimalaprabha holds an unblossomed blue lotus.
Regarding the "messenger" (dūta) that has been described, this is the messenger spoken of in the Mañjuśrī family; the reciter should know her mudrā according to what is appropriate.
As for "acting in accordance with the dharma," this refers to using a young girl.
The "Wise One" (Jñānin) is Mañjuśrī himself, who may also be named Guṇadhara.
Ketusena has a large sword as his seal; the minor Ketuśūla has a sword as his seal; Citraratha has a staff as his seal; Bhūmimati has a banner as his seal; and Ākarṣaṇa has a hook as his seal.
All of the above are to be performed by the maiden and the various messengers who follow the teachings, universally forming the small-knife mudrā as described in the sūtra and shown in the diagrams.
This knife is shaped like a saw; it is said that "small knife" is not a literal translation.
As described above, all these actions are performed within the square altar using mudrās, which are surrounded by blue lotuses.
The above constitutes the retinue of the Mañjuśrī division in the eastern direction.
If Mañjuśrī is the central figure, the other bodhisattvas form the second tier, and the eight classes of beings form the third tier; others may follow this model.

In the south is the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, whose seal consists of a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*). He also forms a four-sided vajra wheel, within which a triangular mandala is fashioned; this is called the "fire wheel. What has been described here corresponds to the wish-fulfilling gem.
The "Exhauster of Great Diligence" is the seed-syllable, namely the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*).
One should draw a wish-fulfilling gem within a triangle, surrounded by its retinue.
The following Bodhisattvas should all be surrounded by their retinues; one should know their seal-marks (*mudrā*).
Now, the retinues are explained in detail.
Regarding these retinues, they should be depicted within those [mandalas] according to their sequence; this is precisely what constitutes the proper method.
That text contains this character, which is pointed out as follows:
The Bodhisattva Duryodhana (除疑怪菩薩) is Jāṭāmukuṭa (嬌都). His mudrā is the Vajra-mudrā. Regarding the vessel:
in the Yuezhong (越中) dialect, it is called "ping" (瓶). A single-pronged vajra is inserted into the vessel, with half of it remaining inside the vessel.
The Bodhisattva Abhayamdada (Bestower of Fearlessness) should be depicted making the gesture of granting fearlessness (*abhayamudrā*), as explained in the *Yoga* [tantras] for the seal of Śākyamuni.

The Bodhisattva Durgatipariśodhana (Purifier of Evil Destinies) should be painted making the gesture of exertion (*utthāpanamudrā*), which means extending the hand with the palm facing upward and raising it from below toward the top.

The Bodhisattva Jiuyihui (Rescuing Mind Wisdom) forms the Hand of Compassion (*karuṇā-muṣṭi*): placing it at the heart by joining the tips of the water-finger (*tarjanī*) and the space-finger (*anāmikā*) against the chest, while extending and spreading the remaining fingers; the joined fingers point toward the heart.

The Bodhisattva Mahākāruṇika forms the Flower-Holding Seal: the fingers of the empty-hand and wind-hand are joined in the shape of holding a flower; the remaining fingers are extended and held upright.
The Bodhisattva Karuṇāmaya bends the fire-finger toward the heart while extending all other fingers; those who know this call this Bodhisattva by that name.
The Bodhisattva Removing Feverish Torment forms the "Hand Granting Wishes" (varadamudrā): extending the fingers with the palm facing upward and directed downward, it pours forth nectar-water.
Regarding "the fingers and so forth," "and so forth" refers to all the fingers.

The Bodhisattva of Inconceivable Wisdom forms the *cintā-mudrā* (hand of contemplation), which is identical to the hand of the Bodhisattva Cintāmaṇicakra; it is also like the seal of the Pure Abode Devas mentioned previously, representing the possession of inconceivable wisdom.
All of the above are constructed as square altars, placed upon lotus flowers; this refers to the drawing of these hand-seals (*mudrā*) and so forth.
These are all the retinues of Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin; the remaining meanings are as explained in the section on Mañjuśrī.
The mudrā of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva in the north is formed upon a great Indra-wheel.
Within the vajra-wheel, one forms a jewel; that is to say, one first places the seat in the center.
The ground is adorned; upon the ground, lotuses are painted in various colors, and atop each flower, a banner is fashioned, with a jewel placed at the top of the banner.
One does not paint the actual form [of the deity], but merely paints the banner.
If one forms this mudrā, it is of the most supreme color; this refers to its physical form.
This is called the "supreme form," which is a term of praise, signifying that among all mudrās, it is the most excellent, superior, and exquisite.
This Bodhisattva has immeasurable retinues; here, I shall briefly describe their principal leaders.
As for the seal of the Bodhisattva Vajraratna on the left, one should diligently form the seal depicted therein.
The three-pronged vajra rests upon a jewel; however, the mudrā is formed only upon the jeweled ground.
If one were to depict the form, he likewise sits upon a lotus, as in the ritual of Kṣitigarbha.
The Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi forms a single-pronged vajra and places this vajra upon the jewel.
The Bodhisattva Dharaṇīndhara forms a two-headed vajra and places it upon the jewel; within the single prong there are five prongs, its shape being like the previous seal.
The Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta forms the five-pronged vajra seal; when placed upon a jewel, it represents the vajras of the five Buddhas.
The Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati forms the cross-shaped vajra, which is the karma-vajra.

Regarding the statement that "all these are to be placed within that maṇḍala": one should construct a jeweled ground within the square wheel; upon this ground, place jewels, and upon the jewels, place the seals (mudrās).
Next is the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha in the west; he is the presiding lord of the western division within the Mañjuśrī assembly.
One should construct a circular maṇḍala that is bright, pure, and brilliant white, upon which he sits on a white lotus, holding a sword in his hand.
If one does not depict the form of a bodhisattva, one simply places a blade; that blade is extremely sharp, like frost.
Furthermore, "in this manner" means it is thus firm and sharp.
Furthermore, it is firm and surrounded by seed-syllables.
The wise one seeds it with his own seed-syllable; this is the establishment of the fundamental seed-syllable.

Next, list the principal bodhisattvas of the retinue; they should be depicted with their respective mudrās according to the instructions, meaning that all are fashioned in accordance with the teachings and the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Gaganāmala should likewise encircle the central figure, surrounding him with a wheel.
This root [seal] is the self[-seal].
The seal formed as a wheel is the four-pronged sword-wheel; placing the wheel also means encircling it with the self[-seal].
Within the wind mandala is the seal of the Bodhisattva Gaganagañjā; within the wind mandala, one places the conch (*śaṅkha*), which is the half-moon mandala.
The Bodhisattva Viśuddhamati draws the seal of the white lotus and places it within the wind mandala.
Next, the seal of the Bodhisattva Cāritramati is placed within the wind wheel; a conch shell is set therein, and a blue lotus is inserted into the conch.
The seal of Bodhisattva Sthiramati consists of a flower drawn upon the wind-wheel (vāyumaṇḍala), with a vajra placed atop the flower.

Generally, within this Great Maṇḍala of the *Mahākaruṇāgarbha*, there are four bodhisattvas in the single assembly of Mañjuśrī; whichever one is designated as the presiding bodhisattva is placed in the central maṇḍala, while the others are each arranged according to their respective directions in the second court. In the third court, the eight classes of spirits (*aṣṭanikāya*) are placed.

Furthermore, if this refers to the second enclosure within the Great Compassion [Maṇḍala], then even if Avalokiteśvara is taken as the presiding deity of the section, the Vajra family, the Buddha-Usnīṣas, and so forth, would all be arranged according to their respective directions to form the second enclosure; subsequently, one should understand that the third enclosure places the Eight Classes [of Beings], and thus it is unnecessary to include the Bodhisattvas of Mañjuśrī’s assembly.
If it concerns the assembly of Śākyamuni, one should inquire further as previously explained; this constitutes the definitive meaning.
One should further inquire to verify this matter.
The Chapter on the Secret Maṇḍala is concluded.

Chapter Twelve: Entering the Secret Maṇḍala (16). Regarding the "Entering the Secret Maṇḍala Chapter," this refers to the secret treasury of the body, speech, and mind of all Buddhas, which is the exclusive secret of Vajradhara.

At that time, the World-Honored One again expounded the method for entering the secret maṇḍala; it was because the Lord of Secrets was capable of understanding it that the Buddha spoke to him once more.
Furthermore, this Vajradhara is an emanation of Vairocana, intended to illuminate this profound and esoteric Dharma.
There is no one capable of questioning this Dharma; it can only be understood through the mutual inquiry between Buddha and Buddha.

As stated in the lower section of the "Chapter on the Distinction of Accumulations" (*Vibhaṅga-skandha*) in the *Vajraśekhara-sūtra*: after the Buddha had entered samādhi, from within his body there emerged the forms of letters, mudrās, and the bodies of the deities (*devatā*), each emerging from every direction to perform the Buddha-activities—namely, that through these great causal conditions, the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are opened.
Having performed this, he again entered the body of the Tathāgata.

At that time, a voice questioning the Dharma resounded from the air, inquiring after the one hundred and eight names of the Buddha, asking: "What is meant by 'Buddha'? What is meant by 'Samyaksaṃbuddha' (the Perfectly All-Knowing One)? and so forth.
...up to the questions concerning the sixteen great bodhisattvas, mantras, mudrās, and so forth, as explained extensively therein.
At that time, the Buddha himself uttered this praise:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"You are able to ask about such a matter.
He then answered according to each question.
At that time, the great assembly attained what they had never experienced before and thought to themselves:
“Now, questioning the Buddha from within the Buddha-body is like a magical illusion—without action and without birth—and yet it accomplishes the work of a Buddha.
Now this Vajradhara is likewise: born from the Buddha’s seal of vajra-wisdom, he is able to pose questions while upholding the Tathāgata’s seal of vajra-wisdom, and the Buddha answers him.
Fearing that others might not believe him, and considering that it would lack dignity for one to question and answer oneself, he therefore questioned the Buddha’s own body with the Buddha’s own body.
Furthermore, as to why he is named Vajrapāṇi: because he is able to uphold the secret body, secret speech, and secret mind of the Tathāgata, he is thus called the Holder of the Vajra-Wisdom Seal.

Regarding the passage, "At that time, the World-Honored One further proclaimed the method for entering the secret maṇḍala": although the secret maṇḍala of Vajrapāṇi was previously explained, the method for entering the secret [maṇḍala] had not yet been clarified; therefore, it is proclaimed next.

The practitioner who recites mantras must study the secret maṇḍala in its entirety; "the mantra-practitioner should study it everywhere" means that one must understand it in all respects. The ancient secret altar is precisely what the wise person has mastered and penetrated.
Because one is free from all doubt and obstruction, one is called a wise person (*jñānin*).
A wise person completely incinerates all transgressions; for a disciple whose Dharma is thus, the practitioner of recitation is one who has attained accomplishment, namely an *ācārya*.
Regarding that which should be universally studied: only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully know and fully study all dharmas; only one endowed with such virtues may serve as a teacher.
In this present degenerate age, such persons are difficult to find; how, then, could there be those who transmit the Dharma masters?

Nevertheless, although an Ācārya may not yet have attained the level of a Buddha, he should thoroughly understand the essential tenets of this sūtra and clearly comprehend each of its sequential ritual applications. Furthermore, he should skillfully master all the dharmas that accord with this sūtra, as well as the essentials concerning the maṇḍala.

One should cultivate the practice of yoga, becoming thoroughly proficient in discerning the various faculties of sentient beings—whether they are sharp or dull, and whether they possess obstacles or lack them—as well as the mantras, physical forms, and mudrās of the deities; only then may one transmit the Dharma and act as a preceptor for disciples entering the secret maṇḍala.

Why is this so? Because these essential teachings of the Buddhas are extremely profound and difficult to understand; they are collectively guarded and not proclaimed recklessly. For a long time, I have kept these essentials in silence and have not spoken of them hastily.

If a teacher of the末代 (final age) cannot thoroughly understand demonic activities and the sequential stages of the expedient means for entering the Way, yet still teaches others recklessly, they will fail to differentiate between individuals and mislead others by applying inappropriate methods; therefore, it is necessary to study all aspects exhaustively.
That which is called "wisdom" refers precisely to this person who has studied universally.
Because they are able to know what should and should not be given, what should and should not be entered, and various other such matters, it is therefore called wisdom.

If one is not proficient in skillful means, then despite having something to say, one cannot cause others to establish unsurpassed roots of goodness and swiftly enter the rank of all Tathāgatas; instead, one incurs extremely great obstructing dharmas that harm both oneself and others—how can such a person be called wise?
Regarding "burning away the disciple's sins": this refers to the fact that from time immemorial, the disciple has possessed immeasurable and boundless karmic obstacles.
"The disciple’s dharma is thus" means entering the maṇḍala and performing the ritual according to the Dharma.
If these profound obscurations are not eliminated, then because the vessel of the body remains impure and such obstacles persist, it is not appropriate to teach the complete path of all Tathāgatas.
It is just as with the śrāvakas, who possess the thirteen obstacles and so forth, for whom it is improper to bestow the precepts.
