However, within the Mahāyāna there is no sense of permanent severance; rather, to receive a new self once again is precisely what constitutes birth.
If one commits this transgression, one is no longer a bodhisattva, just as a śrāvaka who commits a grave offense is no longer a bhikṣu.

Why is this so? Because these four matters possess a nature that defiles the bodhisattva-dharma and can obstruct all meritorious qualities, preventing them from arising; therefore, even at the cost of one's life, one must not violate them.

Next, the Buddha again provides scriptural evidence, stating that all Buddhas of the past, future, and present have, by means of practicing this precept with wisdom and skillful means, attained the cultivation and study of unsurpassed bodhi and achieved great siddhi.
"Great siddhi" refers to the fruit of sublime practice, namely the attainment of bodhi.
"Being without outflows" refers to the nature-precepts (*dharmatā-śīla*).
The training rules for wisdom that transcend conventional means are also taught for the śrāvakas.
"The great hero among men" refers to the scriptural text.
Its meaning is as follows:

although the Buddha also taught the complete precepts, the four pārājikas, and so forth for the sake of the śrāvakas, he provisionally made this statement because it was intended to encompass that particular class of those with inferior faculties; it is not the ultimate teaching.
Therefore, this precept is devoid of skillful means; it lacks both skillful means and wisdom.
If one can aspire toward the Great Vehicle and further study the sublime precepts, only then can one be fully endowed with the bodhisattva precepts.
The "Great Hero" refers to Vajrapāṇi, whom the Buddha addressed.

Because sentient beings of inferior capacity lack the aspiration for the Mahāyāna, the Buddha wished to lead them into the house of the Elder so that they would not remain long in the impoverished quarters, exhausting themselves in vain without gaining anything; thus, he led them in by means of this method, which was not the Buddha's original intent for appearing in the world.

Therefore, this precept is not the Buddha’s wisdom—the untainted (*anāsrava*) and inconceivable (*acintya*) precept; rather, it is only when one enters the Buddha’s untainted wisdom that it is realized through self-attestation.

Chapter Nineteen: The Arising of the Hundred Syllables (18). Next, Chapter Nineteen: The Arising of the Hundred Syllables. At that time, Vairocana Buddha surveyed the great assembly and taught the *Amoghasiddhi* (Infallible Accomplishment).
At that time, the World-Honored One Vairocana surveyed the great assemblies and proclaimed the teaching of Amogha, which brings about the accomplishment of all things according to one's desires.

He is the Sovereign of Mantras, the King of Mantras, and the Guide of Mantras, endowed with great majestic virtue. Abiding in the three samayas and perfecting the three dharmas, he dwells in this station as if seated upon, lying upon, standing upon, or riding upon a chariot.
With exquisite words, he addressed the powerful Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"O valiant hero! Listen attentively with a single-minded focus."

The Mantra-Master, the Lord of Mantras, immediately entered the Samādhi of Wisdom-Born; then, according to his desire, the Greatly Majestic One—the Sovereign of all Mantras, the King of Mantras, and the Master of Mantras—spoke, having declared that the three samayas were fulfilled.
The above is the scriptural passage.
Although various skillful means of mantras have been explained thus far, they were not yet fully exhaustive; therefore, he speaks further.

To this end, he again observes the great assembly, illuminating their mental capacities and seeing that all within this multitude are truly authentic and capable of serving as vessels for the Dharma, and thus he speaks once more.
Furthermore, he observes them so that, by means of the empowerment of his inconceivable spiritual power, they may attain the power of the Dharma and become capable of hearing this sublime teaching.
The various mantras have already been explained in detail above.
This is the syllable *Aṃ*, the heart of all mantras and the foremost among all mantras; one should know that this is the mantra of the teaching of Amoghasiddhi.

"Non-empty" means that for all sentient beings, whatever they see, hear, touch, or know, nothing passes by in vain; they will all certainly attain unsurpassed bodhi. Therefore, it is called "non-empty."

Furthermore, it is because all those virtuous vows can be fulfilled, even up to the vow for the great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) of sentient beings; just as a great jewel-king atop a high banner satisfies all, it is therefore called "Non-empty" (*Amogha*).
The Sovereign of All Mantras is like the Tathāgata, who is the King of all dharmas and possesses mastery over them;
even so is this mantra, for it has attained mastery over all mantras.
For these reasons, it is further named the King of Mantras and further named the Guide of Mantras.
It is like many people entering the sea who rely upon a guide; until they have made progress and reached their destination, they obtain a great mass of jewels and return to enjoy them.
This King of Mantras is likewise so; he is the guide for all mantras.
The guide of mantras is the savior of the world, for it is said that this mantra is identical to the Buddha.

Furthermore, the great majestic power and the Tathāgata’s sovereign force of secret supernatural powers all arise from this; if a practitioner can practice according to the Dharma, they too will attain such results through this mantra.
Regarding the "three samaya seats," this refers to the three samayas of body, speech, and mind.

While the meaning of the seat—namely, the oral mantra as the body-dharmamudrā and the mind as the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity)—should be further inquired into, for now it is said that this is the vajra-posture (*vajrāsana*).
The perfection of the three dharmas refers to principle, practice, and fruition.
The teaching is that which has been explained above; now, beneath this teaching, these three dharmas are fulfilled to the ultimate limit without remainder.
The Buddha emitted a wondrous voice and addressed Vajrapāṇi:
"I shall now speak this Dharma; you, O mighty hero, listen with single-minded attention. One might ask:
since this was already included in the previously explained Chapter on Mantras, why was it not spoken there, but only spoken now?
This is for the sake of those who, being deluded, search for the literal meaning of the scriptures.
If the Buddha possesses great compassion, why would he not explain it clearly so as not to delude sentient beings?
The answer is:
It is not that I am stingy;

rather, I mean that there are various teachers in the world who, relying on their own sharp faculties and analytical power, explain the characteristics of all phenomena and master the terminology. Yet, out of pride, they do not rely upon a teacher but instead seek out the scriptures on their own, wishing to practice them immediately.
However, this Dharma is subtle and profound; if one does not rely upon an enlightened guide, it can never be perfected.
Furthermore, there is the fear that through reckless practice, one will harm oneself and others.
If the text were concealed or obscured such that they could not reach understanding through their own intellectual power, they would abandon their arrogance and come to rely upon a teacher.
For this reason, and so that the conditions for destroying the Dharma do not arise, it is necessary to proceed in this manner.

When the Buddha was about to expound this mantra-master, he immediately entered the samādhi called Skillful Wisdom-Arising; because this samādhi can give rise to the Tathāgata’s skillful wisdom of the Universal Gate, it was given this name.

Regarding the explanation of the mantra "Hundred Lights Pervasively Illuminating" (*śataraśmiparivāra*): it means that from this single syllable, the light of a hundred dharmas is emitted, flowing forth everywhere.
If this syllable were translated as "pervasive" (*parivāra*), it would likewise not be correct according to its underlying principle.
If one translates it as "emitting light," the meaning of "emitting light" is still not exhaustive; for the most part, it carries the sense of "pervasive emergence.
It is from this that the hundred lights of majestic power emerge.
This is the mantra; first one takes refuge in all Buddhas and then recites it.
O Vajrapāṇi, this mantra is the savior of the world, possessed of great majesty. The Buddha himself is the Muni who is sovereign over all dharmas.

The Buddha told Vajrapāṇi: "All these mantras and mantra-saviors possess great majesty and power; they are indeed the Perfectly Awakened Ones (Samyaksaṃbuddhas), the Munis who have mastery over all phenomena (dharmavaśitā)."

"Shattering the darkness of all ignorance, he appears universally like the orb of the sun; this is the empowerment of my own great Muni-body. He manifests miraculous transformations—where the root text says 'transformation' (*nirmāṇa*), it means 'to perform transformations'—and benefits sentient beings according to their desires, providing them with whatever they wish for. He brings benefit to all sentient beings, even to the point of causing everything to arise in accordance with their thoughts and aspirations; that is, he causes them to attain birth exactly according to what their minds desire and aspire to."

One is able to perform this supreme state of divine transformation; therefore, among all kinds of excellence, among all that is desired, among all desires, and among all matters, there is nothing like seeking this state of perfect enlightenment.

Therefore, one should, in every respect, purify the body and be free from all hindrances; one should constantly and diligently cultivate the phrase for seeking perfect enlightenment according to principle, thereby purifying the body and being free from hindrances.
This means that the practitioner purifies his own body, cultivating practice so as to be free from all hindrances.
"In every way" means practicing within all types of skillful means and forms.
All darkness of ignorance is shattered; the solar orb appears for all to see—this is my own empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

The Great Sage manifests transformations to benefit sentient beings, even causing such beings to give rise to thoughts and generate [realization]. He constantly performs these supreme transformations; therefore, one should diligently practice all various skillful means and, in accordance with reason, act as one who purifies the self.
This concludes the scriptural passage.
This mantra is identical to the Savior, who is the Buddha himself.
He possesses great majesty and virtue, which refers to the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata.
This mantra is the Muni who possesses mastery over all dharmas; it is an alternative name for Vairocana.

This mantra is the light of wisdom and skillful means, capable of destroying all darkness of ignorance, just as when the great sun rises, all obscurity vanishes of its own accord. It is said that it causes all sentient beings to suddenly eliminate the darkness of all ignorance.
You should know that these syllables are empowered by me; they are identical to me and no different from me.
I am the very essence of the Buddha.
By means of this gateway of mantras, I universally manifest form-bodies according to the various types of beings.

Throughout the entire dharma-realm, among all classes of sentient beings, he is able to manifest his body universally and simultaneously according to their various forms that are pleasing to behold, appearing to them in accordance with their mental inclinations.

It is not merely a matter of manifesting the physical body; rather, because his mental vows and thoughts are immeasurable and diverse—even within a single moment—he is able to satisfy all infinite aspirations and desires. Therefore, it is said that "the arousal of thought gives rise to wisdom."
Furthermore, because it gives rise to the capacity for entering the Path, it is called "arousing wisdom.
As for "abiding in the stage," this refers to abiding in this supreme state.
Therefore, one should diligently practice and study these various phrases of skillful means.
If one practices this, one immediately attains the pure self. Herein, the "pure self" is none other than Vairocana.

Now, in the very center of this wheel of syllables (akṣara-cakra), one places this King of Mantras; next, on the outer circle, there are twelve syllables, namely from *i* to *au*, which are the sounds of the twelve samādhis.

Next, on the outer wheel, one arranges the hundred syllables: first the twenty-five beginning with *ka*, then the twenty-five beginning with *ca*, then the twenty-five beginning with *ṭa*, and finally the twenty-five beginning with *ta*.
The five syllables *ca oṃ āḥ haḥ na maḥ* are the bindu of Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*) pervading all places; therefore, they are identical to the *bhrūm*. Furthermore, another explanation states:
these five syllables are arranged in a circular array separately from the twelve syllables outside them.

Furthermore, it was asked: "If one constructs five layers of cloth, the twenty-five characters beginning with 􄑀 constitute the first circle; those beginning with 􄑁 constitute the second circle; those beginning with 􄊂 constitute the third circle; and those beginning with 􄋃 constitute the fourth circle—this is also permissible. This was further questioned, as the underlying meaning had not yet been fully exhausted.
The sequence for arranging these syllables is to proceed clockwise each day.
This next chapter explains the fruits of this King of Mantras.
Chapter Twenty: The Correspondence with the Fruits of the Hundred Syllables (18). Chapter Twenty: The Correspondence with the Fruits of the Hundred Syllables. O Lord of Secrets!
If one attains entry into the stage of the consecration of the great wisdom of perfect enlightenment, one will see for oneself that one abides in the three samaya phrases. Secret Lord!

When one enters this manifestation of the Buddha-activity in the form of the dhāraṇī of the World-Honored One’s consecration of great wisdom, at that time the Buddha, the World-Honored One, dwells before all sentient beings and performs Buddha-activities by proclaiming the three samaya phrases.
At that time, Vairocana addressed the Lord of Mysteries, Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has entered the stage of the empowerment of great wisdom and attained the three samayas, which unify body, speech, and mind into one."
"Abiding in the view of self,
at this time, the Lord of Secrets manifests the buddha-work in the form of the Great Wisdom Initiation Dharani.
This is the aforementioned scripture.
The stage of the empowerment of great wisdom (*mahājñānābhiṣeka-bhūmi*) is precisely the eleventh stage of the Tathāgata.

By abiding in this eleventh stage, one enters the empowerment of great wisdom and is thus able to perform the deeds of a Tathāgata; therefore, this stage of great wisdom is translated as the "Dhāraṇī-body" through which the Buddha-work is accomplished.
By means of this, one is able to perform the Buddha-work for the sake of all sentient beings.
As for the form of the dhāraṇī, it refers to binding together the wheel of mantras to constitute the body; thus, one accomplishes the Universal Gate Body.

By virtue of abiding in this body of dhāraṇī, one manifests before all sentient beings a body that is pleasing to behold and preaches the Dharma appropriate to their capacities without error, thereby entering together with them into the Buddha-wisdom.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having proclaimed the three samaya-words regarding sentient beings, the deeds of all Buddhas, and their respective abidings, remained there.
O Lord of Secrets!
Behold the vast and long divine transformation of the wheel of syllables of my speech, which pervades the gates of universal purity throughout immeasurable worlds.

Such is its nature that it brings joy to all sentient beings; it is the gateway through which the Dharma-realm manifests according to the various capacities of beings, just as the present World-Honored One Śākyamuni, distinct from the realm of empty space, pervades the worlds and diligently performs the Buddha-work.
"Lord of Secrets!

No sentient beings are able to know how the Buddha’s wheel of speech issues forth such sublime sounds, adorned with necklaces and manifesting as the womb-born image of the Buddha, appearing according to the dispositions of sentient beings to bring them joy."
After the Buddha had spoken the above sūtra passage as previously described, he next addressed Vajrapāṇi:
"You should contemplate my wheel of speech; this is precisely the realm of the syllable-wheel of the body of the Buddha-dhāraṇī."

The Buddha, through the empowerment of his supernormal powers, sustained this great assembly so that the realm of the wheel of speech perceived by the Lord of Secrets was not only vast and extensive, but extended everywhere to the gates of purity throughout immeasurable worlds; in accordance with the fundamental nature of all sentient beings, he manifested various gateways to the Dharma-realm for each type of being, causing them to give rise to joy.
Just as the present World-Honored One Śākyamuni pervades the infinite realms of empty space, diligently performing Buddha-work in all lands,
so too does Vajrapāṇi perceive this entire great assembly, and likewise perceives this inconceivable and wondrous state.
Why is this? This body of great wisdom is eternally abiding in quiescence, free from all causes and conditions, and is not an object within the realm of the mind.
Apart from the empowerment sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, it is not within the sphere of experience of any bodhisattva.
Having thus shown it, the Buddha declared:
"You should now behold the extent and breadth of my realm of the syllable-wheel (*akṣara-cakra*), which is immeasurable.
"Length" refers to that which surpasses human reach.
I ask: what does this mean?
Its breadth extends horizontally across the entire realm of sentient beings; as for its length, it reaches vertically to the very limits of the Buddha-realm; therefore, it is called "broad and long."
How can such a vast and long body, which universally responds to all beings, be obtained?
It is manifested from this single-syllable King of Mantras.
By means of a single mantra, one manifests the body of all bodies;
by means of a single mantra’s phonemes, one produces wondrous sounds that pervade the entire Dharma-realm;
and by means of the mind of the single mantra’s deity, one universally reveals the realm of all wisdom.
Śākyamuni is precisely this body of Amoghadarśin, who enters universally into the world to perform the Buddha-work; therefore, that which is shown here is the very body of the Muni.
The Buddha performs the Buddha-work; that is to say, this Śākyamuni emerges from the syllable-wheel of Vairocana, yet they are non-dual and without distinction, both pervading all places.
Because this single syllable is identical to the great void, being primordially unborn, one should know that the body of the hundred syllables is likewise.

The distinction is that the body of the Tathāgata’s three samayas pervades the world and extends throughout the empty space of the ten directions; there is no empty space whatsoever that it does not pervade.
One should know that just as space is immeasurable, so too is the body.
O Lord of Secrets!
No sentient beings are able to know the World-Honored One.
This wheel of speech flows forth, and one should also examine the "Mind and Self" in the *Avataṃsaka*.

The "wondrous sound" refers to the wondrous sound produced by all Buddhas and Perfectly Enlightened Ones; it is the adornment of necklaces arising from the matrix (garbha), which is the form and appearance of the Buddha’s image. This "adornment" means that its characteristics are adorned by means of language.
The form of the Buddha arises from the matrix of the mind; though its breadth and length are boundless, it performs the work of a Buddha.
That which is not known by sentient beings is precisely this wheel of syllables of the Buddha.
Furthermore, this is not within the realm of bodhisattvas; were it not for their supernormal powers (*ṛddhibala*), they would be unable to perceive it.
How then could sentient beings know its benefits?
Among all vocal sounds, the Buddha is supreme; his various adornments are likewise manifold.
To state it briefly, they are adorned with the signless (*animitta*).

From the mind, they manifest bodies that accord with the various classes of beings; because they abide in this Samādhi of Sublime Sound, these bodies appear universally before them, causing each to attain joy, faith, and understanding according to their own fundamental nature.
The place of birth is precisely the realm where one goes and dwells.
As for this subsequently mentioned "womb-treasury (garbha) adorned with subtle sounds," it is called the womb-treasury because it arises from a single syllable.

From this single syllable it arises as the embryo (*garbha*); that which arises following it constitutes the reflected image (*pratibimba*), like a mirror that is perfectly clear and pure facing various forms.

It neither comes to the mirror nor goes away from it; yet, through the harmony of causes and conditions, the image appears vividly. It is neither born nor extinguished, neither identical nor different, neither coming nor going, neither permanent nor discontinuous—it is, in its very essence, inconceivable.

The image of the Tathāgata is likewise: without thought or volitional action, it responds to all, causing them to rejoice according to their respective minds, thereby manifesting the Buddha-activities of appearing in the world.
That is to say, with the vocal sound of a single Buddha, one can produce all Buddha-activities.

If even [a Bodhisattva] in the "Chapter on the Purification of the Six Faculties" can fill the trichiliocosm with a single sublime voice, how much more so for the Tathāgata’s six faculties, which are ultimately perfect and pure?

At that time, the Gate of the Immeasurable Ocean of Worlds is also the realization of Bodhi within the Dharma-realm as explained in the Oral Teachings, wherein one diligently cultivates the practices and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.

This Bodhisattva scatters these flowers upon the ground; from the ocean of the lineage of the Womb-realm (*garbhadhātu*), he receives the gates of purity of various natures, purifies the Buddha-fields, manifests the seat of enlightenment, and dwells amidst the activities of the Buddhas.
This concludes the scriptural passage.
From this "Gate of the Ocean of Immeasurable Worlds through the Empowerment of Great Wisdom," the term "gate" (*mukha*) carries the meaning of the point of entry.
The "Ocean-mouth Seal of Immeasurable Worlds" refers to the gateway through which all streams flow and enter.
By virtue of knowing this gateway to the ocean of immeasurable world-systems, one diligently cultivates bodhi.
Yet this single bodhi is not merely a single bodhi; it is the bodhi that pervades the entire dharma-realm.
Because sentient beings are infinite, the dharma-realm is infinite; now, it is universally brought to fulfillment.

At that time, within the dharma-realm of the gateway to the ocean of infinite worlds, the World-Honored One earnestly exhorted and inspired them to achieve bodhi, so as to fulfill the practices and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva—Samantabhadra being the very merit of the Tathāgata. From this, the practices and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva were brought forth, and through empowerment, signs appeared as described below.
Regarding this "Wondrous Flower Arrayed Ground Womb World":
the phrase "in this" refers to this very Sahā world. "Birth within the ocean of lineages" means the place of birth;

"ocean" signifies being uninterrupted, vast, and manifold. Because various natures are purified, one purifies the Buddha-fields, manifests the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), and performs Buddha-works—meaning that the performance of Buddha-works through empowerment is all-pervasive.
Furthermore, since awakening is already without distinction and enters equally into the Dharma-realm, this is indeed the practice of Great Bodhi.
To set forth with such a resolve is the practice of Samantabhadra.
To give rise to such a vow is precisely the vow of Samantabhadra.
It is for this purpose that a bodhisattva first generates the mind of enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda*).

As for the "flowered ground," it is like thoroughly clearing and sweeping a level plain until it is pure, then scattering upon it various flowers of lovely color, fragrance, taste, and texture, and sitting thereon, surrounded by a dignified and majestic array.
Now, this ground of the heart of the Great Compassion Treasury is also like this.
The "womb" (garbha) is the initial arising; it is precisely the place from which the Tathāgata arises.
Because it is born from the Tathāgata-nature, it arises from the syllable *tathāgata-jāti*.
To arouse the mind in this way is precisely the first stage (bhūmi).
"Ocean" refers to the ocean of the Tathāgata’s lineage;
from this true nature arise all the merits of the Tathāgata.
"Womb" (garbha) means taking this as the fundamental basis.

Through the practices of Samantabhadra and the Tathāgata, from the womb-treasury of the ocean of the Tathāgata-nature, one gradually fulfills all the limbs and members of the six sense organs of all Tathāgatas.

This Universal Gate Body, according to the various differences in the mental activities of sentient beings and their diverse inclinations and natures, purifies their minds through pure and wondrous gates, yet there is no final attainment.
Purifying the mind in this way is itself the adornment of all buddha-lands.
When a practitioner dwells thus on the bodhisattva stages, they are able to universally perceive worlds wherein the Tathāgata manifests his body and sits upon the site of enlightenment.
Furthermore, the wheel of the pure dharma-realm is able to universally know all phrases, which is to say, the attainment of Buddhahood;
it is also able to accord with whatever one desires or delights in.
Thus, their aspirations are fulfilled and do not pass in vain.

Therefore, the subsequent sutra states: "Furthermore, regarding those who seek the phrase 'Perfectly Complete Knower' (Samyaksambuddha), they possess an immeasurable mind of longing, they know the immeasurability of the body, they realize the immeasurability of the body, and they realize the immeasurability of wisdom."
Furthermore, "those who seek joy" refers to those who practice the Bodhisattva path once again;
this is precisely the work of a Buddha.
Because sentient beings see that path, they are inspired to resolve their minds on enlightenment and study the Way.

Furthermore, regarding those who joyfully and diligently seek the phrases of right universal knowledge (*samyak-saṃbodhi*): by knowing that the mind is immeasurable, they know that the body is immeasurable; by knowing that the body is immeasurable, they achieve immeasurable wisdom; by knowing that wisdom is immeasurable, they realize that sentient beings are immeasurable; and by realizing that sentient beings are immeasurable, they realize that space is immeasurable—thus they attain this.
Lord of Secrets!
The mind is immeasurable, attained through the four immeasurables.
Having attained manifest, perfect enlightenment, one knows that sentient beings are immeasurable; knowing that sentient beings are immeasurable, one knows that the realm of space is immeasurable.
"Lord of Secrets!
By means of the immeasurability of the mind, one attains four kinds of immeasurability: namely, the removal of the mind, as well as the body, wisdom, sentient beings, and space."
Having attained the state of supreme perfect enlightenment, possessing the ten powers (*daśabala*), and having subdued the four māras, he utters the lion’s roar, and so forth.

Having perfected the ten powers, subdued the four māras, and [uttered] the fearless lion’s roar—this is the most supreme gateway of a hundred doors of training, the words of wisdom for all heroes, spoken from the heart of all Buddhas.
This is the meaning of the aforementioned scripture.
It signifies that by entering this gateway of the empowerment of great wisdom and abiding in the bodhisattva lineage, one immediately realizes that the mind is immeasurable.
Because one knows that the mind is immeasurable, one knows that all bodies are immeasurable.
Because one knows that bodies are immeasurable, one knows that wisdom is immeasurable.
Because one knows that wisdom is immeasurable, one knows that space is immeasurable.
Why is this so? All phenomena arise from the mind; to thoroughly comprehend this is to realize that phenomena are immeasurable, and thus to know that the body is immeasurable.

The body perceived through dependent origination accords with the capacities of beings, and the wisdom of the gates of liberation arises in response to them; these too are immeasurable, each and every one equal to empty space.
Because the body, wisdom, sentient beings, and space are immeasurable, they are called the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*).
Since these immeasurables arise from the mind, they are named the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa-citta*).

If one attains these four immeasurable minds, that is itself the realization of perfect enlightenment; it is the possession of the ten powers and the subduing of the four māras; and it enables one to roar the fearless lion's roar.

All such matters as these are accomplished by abiding in these four immeasurable minds and dwelling in all supreme dharmic phrases; therefore, it is called the fruit of the *akṣara-siddhi* (the syllable "A").
These one hundred gates are not spoken by me alone; all Buddhas likewise speak them in this same way.
This refers to the aforementioned qualities such as the ten powers (*daśabala*).
"Hero" (*vīra*) refers to the Lord of Secrets (*Guhyapati*).

Thus, regarding these words of the Supreme Awakened One for the valiant practitioner who studies with diligence: concerning the mental states taught by all Buddhas within the hundredfold gates of training, it is because one trains in this mind of the hundredfold gates that one attains Buddhahood.
The above is the "Fruit of the Hundred-Syllable Mantra: The Article of Enjoyment," which refers to the enjoyment [of the practice] corresponding to each individual gate.
*Commentary on the Mahāvairocana Sūtra*, Volume 18; *Commentary on the Mahāvairocana Sūtra*, Volume 19.
The Record of the Śramaṇa Acala-ācārya, Part 21:
The Accomplishment of the Hundred-Syllable Stage (19). Next, the Twenty-first [Chapter]: The Accomplishment of the Hundred-Syllable Stage.
At that time, the Lord of Secrets, Vajrapāṇi, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare, O World-Honored One!
This is stated by the following verse.
The "Mantra Savior" refers to the King of the Hundred Gateways, meaning he is able to give birth to all mantras.
The Mantra Savior knows the origin of all mantras.
How, by whom, and in what place [did they arise]?
O Great Muni, by whom were the mantras produced?
Who spoke this? It was spoken by all these great heroes and by the Giver of Vows.
This concludes the preceding scriptural passage.
At that time, the Lord of Secrets, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, attained what he had never experienced before and addressed him, saying:
"How rare, World-Honored One!
You have spoken this mantra for the sake of those who rescue the world."
The "Savior of the World" (Jagat-trāṇa) is none other than the Buddha.

Just as the Buddha is the great refuge and place of protection for all sentient beings, so too is this mantra; among all mantras, it is equal to the Savior of the World, serving as the place of protection for those various mantras.
Just as the Buddha is the ultimate refuge for all, so too is this mantra; it is the ultimate refuge for all mantras.

Upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching, the Great Sage immediately realized that from a single syllable one can generate the infinite distinctions of the bodies, speech, and minds of mantras, manifesting various forms, preaching various dharmas, and displaying various supernatural transformations according to the dispositions of sentient beings. Thereupon, he asked: "How is this mantra generated?"
Furthermore, who has witnessed this?
Where was it born? Regarding these three questions, even when asked again, they remain uncertain.
The Great Muni praised this.
What are the four points? First, knowing the One; second, who is the knower; third, in what place—referring to the sūtra—and what is attained; fourth, who gives rise to the various mantras.
The previous question asked who could know this; the subsequent question asks who it is that is born.
O Great Hero, this is the Buddha.
May he explain all of this.
This is spoken by those of middle-to-superior capacity.

"May the Omniscient One grant his wishes"—this is a praise of the Buddha’s virtues; because he is able to grant all wishes and fulfill them, he is called the "Grantor of Wishes. Thus, having requested the Buddha to speak, [the verse says]: "The Great Dharma-Sovereign, the Muni, is fulfilled."
When he had spoken thus, the World-Honored One, the Great Dharma-Sovereign Muni, Vairocana Buddha of All-Knowledge, who pervades all worlds, addressed him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, Mahāsattva, virtuous Vajrapāṇi!"

I shall explain everything for you; I shall explain it all to you. This is the secret, most rare, and essential core of all Buddhas, which no outsiders can know. From this arises the mandala born of compassion for the consecration of all Mahāyāna practitioners, and from this arises the consecration of the altar.

"One who is pliant, endowed with virtuous conduct, and always compassionate in benefiting others, observes enlightenment through its conditions; yet that [enlightenment] can never be seen, for it is unattainable to see."
Regarding the phrase "pervading everywhere throughout the entire world":

at that time, the Buddha, wishing to expound this heart-mantra dharma, employed his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) to empower the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) so that these words and sounds were heard everywhere, and he addressed Vajrapāṇi.
Sarvajña Vairocana: "Excellent, excellent, Great Being, Vajrapāṇi of Great Virtue!
You have spoken of my all-secrets, the foremost rarity, the supreme secret of all Buddhas, which is unknown to all the non-Buddhists."
The above is the scriptural passage.
The Buddha praised Vajrapāṇi, saying: "Excellent, excellent, O Great Virtuous One, Holder of the Vajra!
'Great Virtuous One' (Bhadanta) means one who is endowed with ten thousand virtues."

This Dharma is the secret among all secrets of all Tathāgatas; it stands supreme among all secret treasuries. It is collectively guarded and not bestowed upon others recklessly; it is the foremost, most rare, and difficult-to-attain Dharma.
Now, this secret of all dharmas is that which no outsiders can know.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of outsiders:
first, the various worldly outsiders; [and second, the non-worldly outsiders].
The second refers to those non-Buddhists who exist within the Buddha-dharma.

Although they have entered into the Buddha-dharma, they are unable to understand the Tathāgata’s secrets; because their views and mental activities remain outside the true principle, they are likewise called "outsiders."
This Dharma is that which the two kinds of non-Buddhists cannot know.
Within this Buddha-Dharma, "non-Buddhists" refers to those among the followers of the Two Vehicles.

Since the Buddha does not bestow it upon others recklessly, he has long remained silent regarding this essential teaching, waiting for the appropriate capacity before imparting it; who now is worthy to hear this Dharma?
Therefore, it is said next that those who have attained entry into the dharma of the empowerment of the arising of great compassion within the Mahāyāna are the ones with whom this may be shared;
otherwise, it must not be given.
Next, he questioned him again:
"Who shall be introduced to the empowerment, and who must indeed receive it?
If a person’s nature is gentle, upright, and honest, and is endowed with all virtuous conduct—such a person may then be introduced to the rite of empowerment."
Furthermore, there are those who possess constant compassion (*sadā-karuṇā*), and these indeed should be led together into the maṇḍala.

"Constant compassion" refers, for example, to a person whose compassion exists at one time but not at another, or who possesses it in one direction but not in another, or who has it toward those who are dear but not toward those who are enemies.

Now it is not so; one who at all times and in all places constantly possesses a compassionate heart, which is furthermore vast, universal, and impartial—such a person is fit to be led into the consecration.
Having already received empowerment, one is now fit to hear this; it is not like the sutras that are commonly circulated.
Within the verses of this *Lotus Sūtra*, there is also an extensive explanation regarding the exclusion of certain individuals, which may be cited here.
Furthermore, those who possess objective conditions for contemplation (*sālambana-vipaśyanā*) likewise cannot attain hearing this Dharma.

The Buddha-Dharma is free from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and free from all conditions (*pratyaya*); if there are marks and conditions, one does not depart from the views of annihilationism or eternalism, and therefore cannot hear this Dharma.
Now, when we speak of "absence of conditions," does this mean that one negates all phenomena as being utterly non-existent or nothing at all? It is not so.

Although the Buddha-dharma is free from conditions and free from marks, it nevertheless possesses, through skillful means, all virtuous merits, spiritual powers, and inconceivable various realms. Thus, it is within marks that there are no marks, yet within no-marks it possesses all marks; it is within conditions that there are no conditions, yet within no-conditions it possesses all conditions. This does not mean that it is merely empty or simply nothing at all.
The general meaning is this: it refers to those who possess the great practices and great vows of a bodhisattva and have given rise to the Great Mind; to such persons alone may this be expounded.
As for the previous question regarding from what [the teaching] arises, the present answer is that it arises from the Buddha-mind.
The "Teacher" (śāstṛ) is the Buddha.
If one follows the Teacher wherever he dwells, this mantra will possess the power to know that.
The "Great Self within" (adhyātma-mahātman) refers to praising this very mind.
"Arising in accordance with that" means arising from all the constituent parts.
"In accordance with the state of one's own mind, at the place where the Guide resides, an eight-petaled lotus arises from the intellect, most exquisitely adorned."

Within a perfectly full lunar disc, stainless like a mirror, the Mantra-Savior of the World dwells eternally; golden-hued and endowed with blazing rays of light, he destroys poison and abides in samādhi, as difficult to behold as the sun.
All those sentient beings are thus mind-born upon eight-petaled lotuses of supreme beauty; they dwell within full moons like stainless mirrors.
Therein reside the Great Virtuous Ones, the World-Saviors of Mantras, who abide eternally.
Regarding "abiding in the Samādhi of Golden Color Endowed with Radiant Flames," this refers to the fact that this flower pedestal arises from the mind and its mental factors.
That is to say, one contemplates the eight-petaled lotus of one's own mind; this flower does not arise from any other place, but arises directly from the mind.
The mind is itself the flower; they are non-dual and without distinction.

This flower-pedestal is perfectly bright like the moon and pure and stainless like a round mirror. Since there is nothing else in the world that can serve as a metaphor, only the round mirror can be used as an analogy, so that one may grasp the meaning and forget the words.
In reality, however, it exceeds that by hundreds of thousands of millions of times and cannot be compared to it.
Now, within this circle is the Mantra-Savior of the World, endowed with great merit; he is of true golden color, possesses blazing light, and dwells here, remaining tranquil in samādhi.
One should contemplate this single-syllable king of mantras; from this king of mantras, one should then visualize the deity or Mahāvairocana, as described above in the yoga methods.
The explanation has not yet been fully clarified; one should inquire further about it, though the preceding passage provides sufficient material for citation and verification.

"Harm" refers to all afflictions (*kleśa*); by completely eliminating them, his majestic radiance becomes as intense and powerful as the combined light of a hundred thousand suns. It is like a child seven days old who cannot look up at the scorching midday sun, yet can behold its brilliance.
This light is likewise; just as all sentient beings gaze upon the solar disc yet cannot perceive its essential substance, so too is this light of the Buddha.
"Constantly, both internally and externally, it universally pervades and bestows empowerment.
With such an eye of wisdom, one knows the mirror of the mind.
It is also acceptable to interpret this as "the mirror of the heart-mind."

The mantrin, with the eye of wisdom, contemplates this circular mirror; therein one shall see one's own form and color—that is, one sees one's own physical body, which is the mark of tranquil, perfect awakening.
Both the body and the images produced from the body are images produced from that very body.
The upper body is conditioned and with outflows (*sāsrava*), while the lower body is unconditioned (*anāsrava*).
"The mind gives rise to the mind" means that the defiled mind gives rise to the pure mind.
"Constantly producing purity" means that the various karmas of self-action which defile the *ālayavijñāna* are able to produce pure karma.
"Once impure karma is eliminated, pure karma shall manifest.
Once pure karma has manifested, light will arise like lightning, illuminating everywhere.
Next, that light shall appear, radiating a circular glow like a flash of lightning."
Nor does one grasp the meaning of lightning; rather, one grasps the perfection of various mixed-colored lights—the perfect radiance of these various mixed colors.
"The mantra practitioner is able to perform all the deeds of the Buddhas."

Regarding the phrase "one should universally reflect upon both the internal and external with the mind": the mirror is the perfectly luminous central dais; one should know that this mirror is the mind, and one should know that this mirror is one's own heart-mind.
By what skillful means is this observed and known?

It is by the aforementioned skillful means: placing the syllable *raṃ* on the second day and observing the mirror-like mind of the true reality (*dharmatā*) with this eye of wisdom; thus, it becomes clearly manifest before one.
Who is able to observe it?
It is the mantra practitioner.
This practitioner then observes the mirror of the flower pedestal with the light of sublime wisdom from the eye of the syllable *ra*.
First, one practices the external visualization; it appears with perfect clarity. Within this luminous sphere, the Tathāgata, as well as his voice and physical form, are all entirely boundless.
Once this has been clearly understood, one then draws this [visualization] inward to become one's own body.
This means that one regards the body of Vairocana previously visualized—tranquil in meditative absorption and possessing boundless majestic radiance—as one's own body.
One should then cause one's own body to become identical to that Honored One, dwelling in tranquility within the sphere of perfect luminosity, just like that Buddha.
To manifest signs while remaining detached from all signs is called the "true sign. Why is this so?
This lotus arises from the mind;

it means first placing the syllable *ra* upon the eyes and contemplating the mirror of the heart-lotus pedestal. This is external seeing; by means of this external seeing, internal seeing is accomplished, whereby one realizes the mind for oneself.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The wisdom-eye is thus.
For one who recites with the wisdom-eye, they behold their own form and color as a mirror-like reflection—the tranquil marks of a Buddha.
From the conditions that give rise to body after body, the mental consciousness emerges, constantly purifying the various karmas of oneself.
Next, the light and those lightning-flames surround and sustain the mantra-practitioner, performing all the deeds of the Buddhas.
If one perceives them as pure and self, it is also taught that they perform all intentional activities.
The above is the scriptural passage.
As for what is called "arising," it refers to the arising of body, speech, and mind.

One first contemplates the golden color and other attributes of the perfectly luminous Buddha-image; one should know that this arises from the mind. This draws [the practitioner's focus] from the external toward the internal: the body becomes identical to the Buddha’s body-seal (*mudrā*), speech becomes identical to the Buddha’s mantra-voice, and the mind becomes identical to the Buddha’s mind—all such arisings arise from the mind.
By giving rise to this very birth, one is able to purify all karma; therefore, it is said that one "constantly purifies various self-karmas," which means being free from all karma.
If one is free from all karma, one is then named a Buddha.
If one awakens to and knows it in this way, one is then able to universally illumine with a perfect light.
This universal illumination is precisely the performance of Buddha-work.
Adorned by the universal illumination of body, speech, and mind, one shall perform all Buddha-works, becoming identical to Vairocana.
"Who is able to perform this buddha-work?
It refers to those who uphold the mantras.
These were all the Buddha’s answers to Vajrapāṇi concerning the source from which mantras arise.
This means that this mantra arises from the very body, speech, and mind of the practitioner.
If one understands it in this way, then through inner and outer purity, one performs the work of a Buddha.
The Sūtra states that one's own karma is precisely the Buddha-work.

This refers to the universal manifestation of the form-body (rūpakāya), whether appearing in various places to practice the bodhisattva path or manifesting the eight phases of attaining Buddhahood; the deeds of all these previous lives (jātaka) are immeasurable and boundless.
To state it briefly, all of this is the Tathāgata’s own karma.
If one can understand it in this way, that is the attainment of Buddhahood.

For the practitioner of mantras who dwells in the stages prior to the [ten] bhūmis through the successive expedient means of contemplation, this mantra practice constitutes the dependent origination of the body; there is nothing more excellent or distinct from that of a Buddha.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "If the seer becomes purified, so too are hearing and the others.
Thus, the seer, the hearer, the toucher, and the knower all attain purification.
Herein, the character *néng* (能) carries multiple meanings.
"According to one's thoughts and intentions, it can accomplish all tasks.
Next, that light and its lightning-flames surround and sustain the mantra-practitioner, performing all the works of the Buddhas.
If one is pure, I also say that one performs all activities; the same applies to the mental intention (*manasikāra*).
O Lord of Secrets!
For a bodhisattva practicing the conduct of the mantra-gate, such a dependent origination arises within the mind, wherein there is no distinction from the Buddha.
The above is the scriptural passage.
Since the Master’s explanation was not yet clear, you may inquire further and contemplate its meaning, correlating it sequentially with the visualizations.

Regarding the "visualizations" (*pratibimba*) and their "origins" (*nidāna*): this refers to contemplating the eight-petaled flower of the mind; the perfect luminosity upon the flower is like that of a pure mirror.

At first, one does not immediately attain clarity; however, through the skillful means of the wisdom-eye of the syllable *ra*, one gradually attains clarity for oneself, until finally seeing one's own body within a perfect mirror as being identical to all Buddhas.
Such arising of phenomena is precisely that which originates from causes and conditions.
If it arises from conditions, then by contemplating this gate of non-arising, one enters the essential nature of the Dharma-realm.

With the eye of wisdom as the cause and the pure mirror as the object-condition, immeasurable Buddha-activities—such as those corresponding to one's own karma—arise from causes and conditions; yet, in reality, they are not self-arisen, not other-arisen, not co-arisen, and not without cause, as explained in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* and other treatises.
This Dharma is supreme; there is nothing superior to it.
As stated above, all things are devoid of all marks, without opposition, and without objects of cognition. Now, by performing these visualizations and so forth, does this not contradict that?
Just as all letters arise from the letter A, yet at the very moment they arise, their nature is that of primordial non-arising;

so it is here as well. By the power of skillful means, the Buddha performs this practice of yoga within the signless and quiescent Dharma, and speaks of various signs within the signless; these very signs are themselves signless.

What is called "mark" (lakṣaṇa) refers to phenomena produced from conditions; yet in reality, they are neither self-produced nor produced by another. Being free from the eight negations, this is the primary absence of marks (animitta); it is not that one speaks of a separate absence of marks apart from the marks themselves.
If one were to explain this separately, it would be identical to the "annihilationist emptiness" (uccheda-śūnyatā) of outsiders.
However, an objection may be raised:
"In this case, one is meditating upon various states such as the body, speech, and mind of the tutelary deity."
Furthermore, O Lord of Mysteries!
For a bodhisattva practicing through the gateway of mantras, that which arises from the body is called the "arising of the bodily image.
Here, "body" refers to the defiled body, and "image" refers to the pure body.
Regarding this arising, nothing surpasses the Buddha.
This means that among all arisings of images, none is more excellent than that of the Buddha.

Just as the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind are apprehended in this way, their intrinsic nature is empty and exists only as a name; that which is grasped is like space, free from attachment, and arises from causes and karma.
That which is equivalent to a reflected image is a characteristic (*nimitta*); that which is a characteristic is a worldly phenomenon (*laukika-dharma*).
Now, since the Buddha has taught the practice of attaining Buddhahood through mantras, why does he further clarify the dharmas with characteristics belonging to the worldly samādhis?
Therefore, the Buddha next cites an analogy to clarify this:
just as the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and so forth, are comprised of the four great elements, their intrinsic nature is empty, existing as nothing more than mere names.
One should know that what is grasped is identical to empty space and is devoid of anything to be grasped; it is a shadow produced from causal karma—so says the scripture.
The cause is like a mirror and karma is like a body, just as a shadow appears when facing a mirror.

Just as a practitioner first contemplates the external conditions as the bright mirror of the mind and then draws them into one's own body, if self and other are equal and non-dual, this constitutes the accomplishment of yoga.
Taking oneself as the cause and the object of perception as the condition, the image arises through the conjunction of cause and condition.
To understand these causes and conditions is to achieve equal and perfect enlightenment.
Who attains perfect enlightenment?
It is the practitioner of mantras. This meaning is as follows:
just as in the world the five sense faculties and so forth arise from the causal conditions of the four great elements and from karma and the like.
Although it possesses characteristics and arises from conditions, its intrinsic nature is empty; thus, it is identical to the primary dharma of signlessness (*animitta*).

This yoga is likewise: although it appears to have characteristics and arises from conditions, the true nature of that which arises from conditions is the very essence of the *A* syllable, the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). How, then, can one raise the objection that it possesses characteristics?
If one realizes this meaning, one attains perfect enlightenment.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Just as the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are comprised of the four great elements, their intrinsic nature is empty."
Such "emptiness" is merely a name grasped through attachment.
Like space, it is devoid of clinging; it arises from karma like a reflection.
When the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, these things arise in mutual dependence; within this uninterrupted continuity, they proceed like dependent origination.
That arises as a reflected image; therefore, the deity is myself and I am the deity, mutually engendering one another.
The body of the Honored One arises from the body, and the form of the celestial image arises from that.
This is the scriptural passage.
As for what arises from me: when one looks at a bright mirror through the medium of the perfect mirror, the reflection of one's own body appears.
Because the perfect brightness has not been seen, there is no reflection.
When the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, they arise through mutual conditionality, like reflections appearing within a mirror and reflections generating one another.
Within the uninterrupted continuity of causes and conditions, the impure body gives rise to the pure body; thus, their mutual generation proceeds without interruption.
Continuity within the midst of interruption is itself non-interruption.
If it arises from conditions, it arises like a reflection; this clarifies that it is not separate from causes and conditions.
Therefore, the deities are myself, and I am the deity; we mutually inspire one another.
Because they arise from one another, "body arises from body" means that the pure body is produced, and thus the forms of these deities are generated.
"Body arises from body" means that the defiled body gives rise to the pure body; this pure body is precisely the form of the Buddha-Bhagavān, and one should understand it thus.

Once one's own mind and body have been purified, they immediately become identical with that [pure state], arising through mutual interdependence without interruption; therefore, it is said that "dependent origination is the arising of images."

Because the internal and external are mutually dependent, and because they develop and transform through their reciprocal manifestation, the Honored Ones are myself, and I am likewise the Honored Ones; the Buddha is myself, and I am the Buddha.
Regarding "the arising of the body and the arising of the marks": this refers to their arising from one's own body.

Secret Lord, observe that the wisdom of the thorough penetration of the conditions of phenomena arises from oneself; that wisdom thoroughly penetrates the conditions of phenomena, and these two act upon one another, not abiding in the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
What is the secret intention of the "intentionally produced" (manomaya)?
It is that images can produce [cognition].
To penetrate this is the meaning of realizing the fruit; it refers to reaching the destination.
This penetration should be called realization.
Guhyapati, observe this as previously explained through the analogy of a mirror:
when images and reflections appear in the clear mirror of the mind, there is no conceptual discrimination; they arise solely from conditions.
Now, observe this phenomenon: does it arise from the mirror, or does it arise from the face?
Thus seeking for it, one finds no actual location for it.
If it existed because of the mirror, it should exist constantly even when there is no face;
if it existed because of the face, it should likewise not be absent when the mirror is missing.
Since both cases are untenable, we know that it exists only through conditions, yet is in reality ever-empty.
This is the Dharma. By contemplating this Dharma, one attains realized wisdom.
Yet this wisdom is forever free from conceptual proliferation; it cannot be displayed or described in words.

If one does not speak and does not deliver others, one further violates the original vow; thus, from realized wisdom (jñāna), there again arises the condition of dharmas (dharmālambana). From the Buddha’s causal vision of the Dharma, one attains Buddhahood, and having attained Buddhahood, one again preaches the Dharma.
Furthermore, this [mind] is also a phenomenon produced from conditions.
For example, just as with colors such as white, yellow, or red, when the mind acts, it becomes stained by that action and arises; in that same way, the body evolves through its own kind.
The above scriptural passage means this:

The Lord of Secrets contemplates the dharma; the characteristic of the emptiness and quiescence of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is such that, through these causes and conditions, one is able to penetrate it with wisdom.

The Dharma is the dharma that is free from all marks; the Dharma itself is conditions (*pratyaya*). By contemplating this, one enters the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and attains mastery over the Dharma.
If one attains mastery over the Dharma, one attains mastery over conditions; if one attains mastery over conditions, one attains mastery over the Dharma—they mutually give rise to one another.
To understand that all phenomena are empty and quiescent is precisely to realize the nature of phenomena.

Because conceptual discrimination arises, one knows that phenomena are empty and lack the conditions for cognition; yet conditions depend upon phenomena, and phenomena depend upon conditions, arising through mutual conditioning. This is called the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
If phenomena are thus empty of intrinsic nature, how can a vow arise from the mind? O Guhyakādhipati,
according to the sūtras, those [phenomena] do not abide in one another and are empty of intrinsic nature.
How is it that the mind can produce an image?
O Lord of Secrets!
It is, for example, like forming a mental attention toward something white, yellow, or red; this is the illustrative analogy.
It is like when a person’s eyes first see white and it is not yet clear; subsequently, a mind arises to discriminate whether this is an object-condition (*ālambana*) or something else.
There was no such question regarding what lies above this. Vajrapāṇi did not ask because he lacked knowledge; rather, he raised this inquiry for the sake of sentient beings.
If it is as you say, then since that mind arises from the consciousness, who is able to know it?
The Buddha then spoke a simile, just like the white [crane]. Why is this so?
Because it differs from blue, yellow, and so forth, the arising of this understanding from the mind is itself an origination; from the mind, a mind arises.
If even in the mundane world it is thus, one should know that it is likewise for a pure mind to arise from a defiled mind.

Regarding "the mind-born [consciousness] that is stained by attachment": it is like when one sees white, the mind forms the conceptualization of "white"; because of this whiteness, it causes the mind to become white as well.
For example, when a bhikṣu contemplates white, he perceives everything as white.
That which is seen as blue, all is likewise blue.
When one acts, it is by acting upon the white that the intention is fulfilled.
The consciousness-mind arises from the white mind; it does not arise from without.
It is like when a person observes something white, they see everything as white.
As stated in the *Candrapradīpa-samādhi-sūtra*:
"Just as a woman, fondly adorning herself, looks into a mirror and sees her own reflection, and in turn gives rise to attachment."
If a wise person contemplates from where this arises and from where it comes,
examining each aspect one by one, it cannot be found.
Speaking from this perspective, images arise from the mind and in turn defile it.
If one understands that these arise solely from conditions, there will be no attachment.
By means of this, one realizes for oneself that it is from one's own mind that the mind is produced.
The transformation of that "similar class" (*sabhāga*) refers to the body manifesting as such; that is, the maiden herself perceives her own body.

If it is defiled, it is birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); if one recognizes that it arises solely from conditions and lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is nirvāṇa. Therefore, it is called the "transformation of the similar-class body."
The following, beginning with "From within the contemplation of the mind," constitutes the verse. Guhyapati!
Furthermore, just as when one contemplates the maṇḍala within the mind to cure a feverish illness, that sentient being’s fever is immediately dispelled—meaning it occurs in a single kṣaṇa.
Kṣaṇa, Deva, there is no doubt that this word "deva" is not used [in this sense].
It is not that the mind is different from the mantra, nor that the mantra is different from the mind. Why is this?
Because that *maṇḍala* has a single characteristic, "mental attention" (*manasikāra*) consists of contemplating blue, yellow, red, white, and so forth.
Just as when practicing the ten universal bases (*daśa kṛtsnāyatanāni*), when one contemplates the color blue, everything becomes blue; this blue arises solely from the mind.
Through long-term mental attention, the mind is able to produce it; this form manifests in accordance with the mind.
Since the mind can take it as an object, it is able to generate that kind of thing.
"Defilement" (rañjana) has the meaning of "clinging" (upādāna); one should know that it arises from the mind and mental factors (citta-caitasika) and is of the same nature as them.
Since the mind is thus, so too are the body and speech.
Next, he again provides an analogy.
Furthermore, within the *manas* (mind), one may arise and establish a maṇḍala, such as a triangle and so forth, as described above.
For instance, as a skillful means for removing heat, one may construct a circular maṇḍala; within it, there is the syllable *vaṃ* in white, or the seed-syllable with a bindu placed upon its surface.
Other cases may be understood in this same way.
This point is the removal of feverish affliction and constitutes the flavor of ambrosia (*amṛta*).
By performing this rite, one removes the fever by acting from the mind; even in the space of a single *kṣaṇa*, that illness is eliminated, for it arose from the mind.
One should know that the mind is not different from the maṇḍala, and the maṇḍala is not different from the mind, because they possess a single characteristic.
To say that this maṇḍala and the mind are non-dual and without distinction means that this present dharma is likewise to be understood in this way.
Next, the Buddha again provides a simile:
"Just as a magician transforms himself into men, women, and so forth—this refers to the Lord of Mysteries (Guhyapati).
Furthermore, it is like a magician who conjures a man, and that conjured man then further creates another transformation."
"What do you think, Guhyapati? Which of these is superior?"
Vajrapāṇi replied:
"World-Honored One, these two persons are not different from one another. Why is this?"
World-Honored One!
Because they arise from what is unreal,
these two men are empty by their very nature and equal to an illusion.
Thus, O Lord of Mysteries!
"Matter" refers to matters such as *siddhi* (spiritual accomplishment), and "etc. implies a multiplicity.
All matters that arise within the mind are born from the mind; these two are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*), and their lack of differentiation is called non-duality and non-distinction.
From the mind and that which is produced from the mind, both are empty; they are neither two nor distinct.
Furthermore, when one conjured person creates another conjuration, between these two illusions, which one is superior?
What is superior and what is inferior?
What is long and what is short?
What is beautiful and what is ugly?
The sutra asks, "Who is superior? which is to inquire which of these two illusions is more exalted.
The answer states that there is no difference between these two. Why is this?
Because both arise from what is unreal and because both are empty by their very nature,
what difference is there between that which is illusory and that which creates the illusion?
The Buddha said in response:

"You should observe this dharma: just as the circular mirror and other such objects arise from the mind, the mind is itself the mirror and the mirror is itself the mind; they are non-dual and without distinction, and one cannot discuss any characteristics of difference between them."
If the mind is defiled, it is the mundane; if the mind is free from defilement, it is the supramundane mind.
The above constitutes the Chapter on the Hundred-Syllable Stage.
As the explanation is not yet clear, you should inquire further.
However, the general purport is that [this state] is accomplished through prior cultivation of yoga, even to the point of being extremely vast and universal.
Yet, if one does not use this wisdom and skillful means to contemplate emptiness and the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) in order to cleanse the mind, it remains merely a worldly phenomenon.

Therefore, one must perform this contemplative practice to enter the true reality (*tattva*) of the maṇḍala, forming a mandala of great emptiness wherein nothing is not present, which is eternal and ultimately pure.
This is a general outline. 22. Chapter Twenty-Two:

The Recitation for the Accomplishment of the Hundred Syllables (19). Next, the Sūtra on the Chapter Twenty-Two: The Recitation for the Accomplishment of the Hundred Syllables states: "Listen attentively, O Lord of Secrets!"
"The Mantra-Savior’s body is not different from [one's own] body" means that one's body is not distinct from that [Mantra] body.
This refers to abiding within the mind while employing the body of that mantra.
"Mind arises from mind": the former refers to the mind that is subject to birth, while the latter refers to the pure mind; it is capable of purifying and removing [impurities] from the mind.
"Light universally flows forth from those places": it flows forth from the pure mind.
The phrase "that" refers to the aforementioned mind.
The light arises in conjunction with yoga; because it is in conjunction with yoga, this light is produced from that mind.
That which fools are perpetually unable to know is called "that which cannot be known by fools"; they fail to penetrate and realize this path.
Even as for the parts produced from the body, those parts are not different from the body itself.
That which arises from the body is itself the body, and it exists in immeasurable varieties.
Since the bodies are immeasurable, the verbal expressions of these mantras are likewise immeasurable.
It is like the *cintāmaṇi*—the wish-fulfilling jewel—which accomplishes whatever benefit is desired.
In this way, for the body of the Illuminator of the World, all benefits are accomplished.
Lord of Secrets, how is it that, being non-conceptual, the Dharma-realm accords with and turns according to all that is done?
"O Lord of Secrets!
Furthermore, it is like the realm of space," and so forth.
The Buddha told the Lord of Secrets, "Listen attentively: the mantra-saviors are non-different from body to body."
One should properly and thoroughly purify the arising of mental formations.
From that place, light flows forth everywhere, reaching all corresponding limbs and members.
This path is unknown to the foolish, extending even to the various immeasurable kinds of bodily constituents that arise.
This is also a scriptural passage.
Because it involves the retention of mantras, this statement differs [from others].

"Arising from the mind" means that one is able to thoroughly purify what has flowed forth from that [mind]; thus, by means of this very body—not distinct from that body—one is born from one's own self, which is precisely what is meant by "arising from the mind."
Because all defilements have been purified, all tasks are accomplished.
Possessing this virtue, light radiates from each of its parts to perform the work of a Buddha.
Matters such as these cannot be known by the ordinary and foolish.
Because they do not know this path, they receive the name "fools.
This path is the practice of mantra (vidyā), for through the perfection of mantra one attains *siddhi*.

From this body, further bodies arise—namely, those of the desire realm, the form realm, and so forth, of which there are many varieties—all of which emerge from a single mantra as infinite bodies, speech, and minds, just as it was explained above that from the Buddha’s superior, middling, and inferior divisions, infinite bodies are produced.

This practitioner is also like this: according to the superior, middling, or inferior capacity of their faculties, they can manifest four Buddhas, four Bodhisattvas, or even the various classes of the Eight Divinities, as described in the *Mahākaruṇāgarbha-sūtra*, in numbers that are immeasurable.
Furthermore, a doubt is raised:
It was stated above that mantras are signless and objectless, identical to great emptiness and thus incapable of differentiation.
How is it that these various matters exist? Answer:
It is like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) that fulfills all wishes; even the three matters can be purified by it.
If a person desires purity of body, by the power of the jewel, their body becomes like lapis lazuli.
If they desire purity of speech and mind, these too are purified according to their respective parts.
If even worldly phenomena are thus, how much more so the Tathāgata’s wondrous jewel of the wish-fulfilling gem—could it not perform such deeds?
Like a worldly jewel, although it performs various functions and fulfills various aspirations, it remains tranquil and unmoving, without thought or volition, neither coming nor going.
If this is so for the accomplishment of all things, how much more so for the Great Jewel of the Tathāgata?

Therefore, within the non-conceptual dharmadhātu, like a great dragon dwelling in its palace, it does not stir the mind or give rise to thoughts, yet it brings down various distinct flavors according to the power of karma.

For this reason, within the signless emptiness, one manifests immeasurable activities of body, speech, and mind through the universal gate; thus, the [Buddha] body can indeed be attained—there is no need for doubt.
Furthermore, it is like space, which is not included among the categories of sentient beings, yet is that upon which sentient beings depend.

It is not a self, nor a life-principle, nor a person, nor an agent, nor an experiencer; all conceptual constructions are eliminated, it is entirely free from discrimination, and it neither comes nor goes.

Yet it is not different from the realm of sentient beings; all the activities upon which sentient beings rely are accomplished through this, and it nourishes and benefits sentient beings by producing various things.
One cannot, however, because space can accomplish all things, conclude that space is conditioned or possesses characteristics.
Now, this great empty maṇḍala is also like this: ultimately pure and capable of accomplishing all things, it abides eternally in stillness yet is not empty of its accomplishments.
Therefore, the Sūtra encourages faith, saying: "One should know it thus; do not give rise to doubt.

At that time, the World-Honored One further proclaimed the phrase on the purification of the inexhaustible realm of sentient beings, the phrase on the outflow of samādhi, the phrase on the inconceivable, and the phrase on the gateway of transformation for others.
If primordial birth is non-existent and one accords with worldly phenomena, how can one know emptiness? How can one give rise to a practitioner?
If self-nature is thus, awakening cannot be apprehended; one should maintain a mind equal to space, give rise to the birth of Bodhi, and give rise to compassion, thereby acceding to all the world.
The above is the scriptural passage.
"Abiding in the purification of the inexhaustible realm of sentient beings" means that one originally established a vow, desiring to purify all sentient beings within the inexhaustible worlds.

Because sentient beings possess defilements, they are unable to save themselves; now, I wish to universally open for them the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision so that they may attain purity, causing their spheres of body, speech, and mind to all become pure and free from defilement.

One should know that this phrase "the inexhaustible purification of sentient beings" is a phrase flowing forth from samādhi; the phrase flowing forth from samādhi is an inconceivable phrase; and the inconceivable phrase is a phrase that turns toward the gateway of others.

It is called the "phrase of the gate of transforming others" because it transforms the defilements of others into the purity of one's own nature, and transforms the ignorance of others into the illumination of the Tathāgata.
"Others" refers to sentient beings.
It is by transforming the defiled into the pure that this Dharma-gate is taught.
Regarding the statement "originally non-existent": if there were originally nothing at all, yet one arises in accordance with the world, how then should one know emptiness?
That is to say, how should one proceed? It means knowing that all phenomena are empty.
As for the arising of this yoga, the verse itself contains the question; this question arises through the empowerment of the Buddha's spiritual power.

If it is said that the original birth is non-existent, yet there is that which accords with the world, how then can that practitioner cause this emptiness to arise within the practitioner—that is, what is called pure emptiness?
If one says that it does not exist, how could this pure emptiness arise?
If it were fundamentally non-existent, then this arising would also follow that fundamental non-existence, which is precisely "fundamental non-arising."
What is a yogin? How does one realize emptiness?
This very emptiness is the nature of mantra.
What is meant by one who gives rise to yoga?

If the intrinsic nature is thus, then the name "awakening" (bodhi) cannot be apprehended; that is to say, one contemplates that names cannot be apprehended. This is precisely what constitutes contemplation (vipaśyanā), for contemplation and awakening are identical.
"When the mind that is equal to emptiness arises" means that the bodhicitta arises; this introduces the ten similes explained above.
Because awakening is fundamentally unarisen, signless, and ungraspable, one attains this mind that is equal to emptiness.
Purity, non-discrimination, and so forth—as mentioned above—are not merely emptiness, but rather the arising of wisdom, which is called *bodhi*.
"One should give rise to compassion and accord with all worlds; abiding in the practice of mere ideation (*saṃjñā-mātra*), one is then named a Buddha."

This means that the Tathāgata has thoroughly realized that all dharmas are fundamentally unarisen and fundamentally non-existent; yet, they exist for the purpose of delivering sentient beings by conforming to worldly conventions. This "existence" refers to the manifestation of various skillful means through the universal gate to benefit sentient beings, which exists due to the causes and conditions of their responsive resonance, while being fundamentally non-existent.

The nature of sentient beings is fundamentally non-existent; through cultivation, one realizes that this nature of sentient beings is empty and quiescent. Because one awakens to the fact that this nature is empty, it exists only as a name and cannot be apprehended.
This means that the nature of the emptiness of emptiness exists only as a name; ultimately, it cannot be found when sought. This is precisely the "emptiness of the unfindable.
It is not like those of inferior wisdom who cling to this emptiness-nature as being substantially existent.

One observes that sentient beings are identical to space; the intrinsic nature of space is free from contemplation and observation, and is devoid of all deluded thoughts and conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
When one thus understands space, one knows the principle of reality; one should not, however, grasp at this dharma of emptiness.

Because this space cannot be apprehended, it is not a state of total non-existence; rather, it truly possesses its own intrinsic nature (svabhāva). That which is called the intrinsic nature of emptiness is itself non-empty.
One should know that this "not empty" is precisely the mind equal to space.
The mind equal to space is pure bodhi; from this pure bodhicitta, the mind of great compassion arises.
Why is this so? Because once a practitioner has fully realized this bodhicitta, they form this thought:
"All sentient beings are exactly like this; they all possess the treasure-store of the Tathāgata, yet they do not themselves perceive or know it."
"For these reasons, one undergoes weariness and suffering in vain, without any benefit.
It is for these four reasons that the Bodhisattva gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
Because they do not understand this mind, they wander aimlessly through the cycle of birth and death without end;
yet, upon understanding it, they are Bodhisattvas.

Seeing that all sentient beings possess the nature capable of awakening yet are unable to realize it themselves, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion for their sake, intending to explain skillful means to provide them with protection and rescue.
Precisely by means of this great compassion, in order to eliminate the defilements of inexhaustible sentient beings, one employs skillful means in accordance with the world.

Because the types within the inexhaustible realm of sentient beings differ according to their various dispositions, inclinations, faculties, and conditions, the Bodhisattva guides and transforms them by conforming to those differences; therefore, it is said that he "accords with the world."
Abiding in the perception that "mind-only" exists is itself called being a Buddha.
One should know that this arises from the construction of perceptions.
That which is called "emptiness" is established from within these very perceptions.
Having abided in mind-only, one returns to this very mind-only to establish all phenomena.
Regarding the phrase "contemplating this as empty-of-emptiness," it means that the designation "empty-of-emptiness" arises from contemplation; it is merely a name, for emptiness arises from the mind.
