The method of calculating the lower numbers proceeds by turning; from the divisions of one, two, and three, they are spoken of as distinct, meaning these ones, twos, and so forth are different.
This "fen" (分) is pronounced with a departing tone (*qùshēng*). O Diligent One!
That emptiness is thus; even unto its increase, it follows the sequence, namely these syllables beginning with *a*.
The term "perception" (*saṃjñā*) refers solely to the meaning of perception.
As stated above, this syllable *a* is itself perception.
Furthermore, self-arisen wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*) is the Buddha, which refers to that which is empowered by the Buddha.

If one constructs the conceptualization of emptiness or non-emptiness, observing the shifting of the lower numerical methods, they begin with the differentiation of one, two, and three; thus, those empty heroes increase according to their respective sequence.
The letter *A* is this initial syllable; it is the natural wisdom (*svayambhūjñāna*) through which empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is applied.
This is the scriptural passage.
What was previously described as attaining the mind of emptiness is precisely the arising of the bodhicitta.
Bodhi means awakening; how could this mind be empty?
It is, in fact, fully endowed with merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Although it possesses the immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata, it is without marks and without name, and thus cannot be displayed.

As the proponents of the *lakṣaṇa* (characteristics) school speak of sixteen kinds of emptiness, and as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* speaks of eighteen kinds of emptiness and so forth, all are intended to clarify this meaning.
If emptiness were merely a total absence of any nature whatsoever, how could such inconceivable miraculous transformations and virtues be accomplished to deliver sentient beings?
One should know that this emptiness is the principle of self-realization.
Since conceptualization is empty and non-existent, names are likewise so; this state cannot be demonstrated, for words and their characteristics are quiescent.
If one were to explain such a self-realized Dharma to ordinary, ignorant people, it could never be grasped.
One should know that this possesses only a name; among the eighteen kinds of emptiness, it stands supreme, being the Great Emptiness of all Buddhas, which is in truth not empty.

Regarding the analogy of calculation herein: it is like the method of accounting used by people in the world. At the very beginning, one places down a single character as the foundation; in the Western system of calculation, all figures are inscribed upon the ground, and even when the process is not yet finished, one simply continues to inscribe more. Thus, numbers up to billions and asaṃkhyeya are all produced from this. Nevertheless, before the first figure was inscribed, that number did not exist at all.
From this empty space, which originally contains no calculation, one places down a marker—whether two, three, or even immeasurable.
Once the calculation is finished, all the positions are removed, returning to emptiness as it was before.
However, as for the numbers thus calculated, those who perform the reckoning will personally verify them in their own minds, perceiving them exactly as they are without any loss.
Although numbers are established from within primordial non-existence, they now appear as they were originally, yet in reality, they do not exist at all.
However, when the dharmas of enumeration are maintained within the mind without loss, this is precisely "non-existence yet existence" and "existence yet non-existence.
Now, this gateway of the letter A is likewise: from within primordial non-arising, for the sake of conforming to the world, it sequentially brings forth immeasurable dharma-gates.

Although these immeasurable skillful means are manifested, they do not differ from the meaning of the letter A’s fundamental nature of non-arising; it is just as those numbers do not depart from the number one.
Since the initial method of calculation begins with one, all numerical phenomena do not depart from one; even ten thousand is simply ten times one, and they cannot be separated.
All other enumerations can be understood accordingly.
It is for this reason that all dharmas cannot be separated from the letter "A. Furthermore, there is a master of treatises who offers another analogy:

it is like the movement of insects; as immeasurable insects follow one another without interruption, they form a path, which may take various forms such as square, circular, or winding. If these were separated and treated as distinct entities, each would simply be an individual insect, devoid of any characteristics such as curvature, straightness, length, or shortness.
This Dharma is likewise: within the ultimately self-realized, inconceivable, and empty Dharma, all merits are fully present.
Yet, arising from conditions, it has no original birth; it does not depart from the One, for its fundamental nature is the principle of non-substantiality.

Regarding the statement that "this letter A is the foremost, and through the empowerment corresponding to natural wisdom (svayambhū-jñāna), it is spontaneously known": because this gateway of letters is empowered by natural wisdom, immeasurable speech arises; within speech there are immeasurable sounds, and within sounds there are immeasurable principles. Thus, each and every one of them pervades all, equal in number to those [immeasurable phenomena].
The Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*) is likewise: it possesses all phenomena and pervades all phenomena.
This syllable *A* is also thus; all gateways of mantra arise from the syllable *A*, just as the myriad forms arise from space. It does not merely give rise to all letters.
Within each of these gates through which the syllables thus produced arise, the principle of non-arising is revealed.
It continues: "O Lord of Mysteries!
Contemplate how, within this emptiness, that which is conventionally established as flowing and dispersing is sustained by the empowerment of the letter A, thereby accomplishing the path of samādhi."
Lord of Mysteries!

Thus, this letter A is arrayed in various positions within the mandala; even that which has form and that which is formless, that which has characteristics and that which is characteristicless—all arise from the letter A.
"Placing the positions" refers to various adornments.
"The observer" refers to causing the Lord of Secrets to observe this;
that is, abiding in various forms and adornments while discerning their respective positions.
Because these dharmas are fundamentally unarisen, they manifest their own form; this own form is precisely the letter A.
Within this own form, fundamental non-arising is manifested.
"O Lord of Mysteries! The letter A is thus:
when various positions are arranged and distributed, I perceive that they abide in non-arising, and the self-forms of all phenomena are revealed.
This is the scriptural passage."
Contemplate this syllable *A* as it flows forth from space to produce the myriad phenomena of the world; all worlds arise from this, yet they are fundamentally unarisen.

Through the empowerment of the provisional establishment of the syllable *A*, one achieves samādhi; by realizing this samādhi and possessing *prajñā*, the myriad practices are accomplished—all through this syllable *A*. The perfection of merit and wisdom is attained entirely through this gateway of the syllable *A*.

This syllable can produce various colors—namely blue, yellow, red, white, black, and even infinite varieties of mixed hues—as well as various shapes, such as triangles, squares, circles, and crescents, and countless different forms of deities and so forth.
If one realizes the true meaning herein, there is nothing that does not enter the gateway of the letter *A* in its entirety, becoming identical to Vairocana.
The gateway of the letter *A* explained above is precisely the manifestation of one’s own self; it is that my very self is fundamentally unborn and likewise unceasing.
That which is neither born nor extinguished is the body of the Tathāgata; one should observe it in this manner.
Therefore, it is said that the letter *A* manifests its virtue through its own form.
Next, it may signify the meaning of non-apprehension.
The syllable *vaṃ* reveals the meaning of unattainability; this *vaṃ* serves to realize primordial non-arising (*mūlānutpāda*).
The manifestation of the form of *vaṃ* is precisely the meaning of the severance of the path of speech mentioned in the subsequent text.
What does this clarify?
The Buddha said:
"The letter A possesses all merits; alternatively, it is explained by means of the gateway of the letter A as 'primordial non-arising'."
Alternatively, it may be revealed through other gateways, namely the various syllable-gates such as *va* and so forth.

Although their meanings differ and the gateways themselves are distinct, there is no difference in the meaning of the self-nature of the "I" (*ātman*) that they demonstrate—the fact that it is fundamentally unarisen.
If a phenomenon possesses oneness, it is a state of arising and is thus a characteristic that can be described; it is not a phenomenon for which the path of language has been severed.
Because the syllable *va* represents the severance of language and the cessation of mental activity, one enters the gateway of the syllable *a*.
Because of the syllable *A*, one knows that this *Va* is ineffable and cannot be demonstrated.
All that follows consists of various synonymous designations (*paryāya*).
Alternatively, because all phenomena are free from conditioned activity (*abhisamskāra*), the form of the syllable *Ka* appears.
This clarifies the single gateway of the letter A; however, because one wishes to clarify that all phenomena are originally unconditioned (*akṛta*), this letter Ka is manifested.
Yet, this letter Ka itself elucidates the meaning of the letter A.
It is like the letter *ka*: if the horizontal stroke is not placed above it, the sound of the letter *ka* is not formed.
The reason it is not formed is that the sound of *a* is missing from within the *ka*.
At the top of this letter *ka*, there is the form of *a*; one should know that all these hundred letters are likewise so, as can be understood by the following examples.
If the sound *a* were not present within them, they would not open their mouths, and they would likewise have no sound of their own.
Alternatively, because all phenomena are like space, the letter *kha* appears.
Alternatively, because activity is unattainable, the letter *ga* appears.

Alternatively, because a unified characteristic is unattainable, the letter *gha* appears; the *ālayavijñāna* contains all seeds of defilement and purity, which is the meaning of "containing" (*ālaya*).
Alternatively, because all phenomena are free from arising and ceasing, the character *cha* (􄑼) appears as a negation; its direct opposite carries the meaning of death and cessation.
Alternatively, because all phenomena lack images, the character *cha* (􄒪) appears; it is like worldly phenomena, wherein an image arises through the conjunction of causes such as the sun and trees.
Alternatively, because all phenomena are devoid of arising and cannot be apprehended, the syllable *ja* appears.
Alternatively, because all phenomena are devoid of adversaries, the syllable *dha* appears; this means "this exists" and "that exists," and where there is "this" and "that," there is an adversary.
Alternatively, all phenomena are free from inferiority. The character *ṭha* manifests the meaning of "ṭha" as self-exaltation through pride; in contrast to this, there is inferiority.
If there is pride and inferiority, there is the sense of arising and ceasing, which does not correspond with the letter A.
Because the sound *a* is situated in the middle, it clarifies the meaning of being neither base nor arrogant.

Alternatively, because all phenomena are free from nourishment, the form of the syllable *ṭha* manifests the meaning of growth and establishment; for example, by harmonizing soil and water, one nurtures the roots of trees, whereby they attain growth and sustenance.
However, all phenomena enter into the letter A.

Because of the separation from enmity, the form of the letter NA appears; "enmity" refers to being exclusively intent on committing evil toward oneself in all places, and this evil constitutes the duality in relation to that which is non-evil.
Alternatively, because it signifies separation through calamity and transformation, the form of the letter *ḍa* manifests as the meaning of calamity and transformation;
that is to say, it refers to worldly anomalies such as locusts, water, and fire, as well as the arrival of robbers and military invasions.

Alternatively, because all phenomena are detached from suchness (*tathatā*), the letter *ta* manifests; yet if one contemplates suchness as being existent, there is an object of observation. Because there is an object of observation, there is arising and ceasing, which is not in accord with the letter *a*.
Therefore, even *tathatā* (suchness) must be transcended.

Alternatively, because all phenomena are devoid of a place of abiding, when the form of the letter *tha* appears—whether there be a state of possibility (*sthāna*) or impossibility (*asthāna*)—the mind of "is" or "is not" arises, which does not correspond with the letter *a*.
Alternatively, all phenomena are devoid of giving; if the letter Na appears, it signifies that if there are objects to be given, such as this or that, they do not correspond with the Path.
As stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, "all dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*) are unobtainable. The character *Dha* manifests as the realm, signifying that each maintains its own position.
While the various dharma-realms have myriad forms, the term "realm" (*dhātu*) carries the sense of a multitude of images contained therein.
This realm is unattainable;
or rather, since the truth of all phenomena is unattainable, even the manifestation of the letter *ba* as the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is likewise unattainable.
Alternatively, all phenomena are identical to foam and lack solidity; the manifestation of the letter *pha* signifies that foam is insubstantial.
To be free from this insubstantiality is precisely the virtue of the letter *a*.
Alternatively, because all phenomena are free from bondage, the form of the letter *ma* appears; yet if one perceives the existence of bondage or liberation, this is due to a mind of grasping.
Entering the letter *a*, there is neither bondage nor liberation, for they do not arise.
Alternatively, one contemplates all phenomena as unattainable; the manifestation of the syllable *VA* is itself the contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*).
Through the perfection of this observation, there arises a place of rebirth.
If one realizes that [all things] are fundamentally non-existent, then there is neither arising nor contemplation.
Regarding the explanation of the character here, it is not appropriate to explain this character "ma" (麼).
This is a separate explanation of the meaning of emptiness; the text contains an error.

Alternatively, "vehicle" (*yāna*) refers to the fact that all phenomena are unattainable; it manifests through the form of the letter *ya*. Here, "vehicle" refers to the three vehicles (*triyāna*). Generally, the meaning of a vehicle—such as a boat or a chariot—is that which brings one to a destination. All such things share this common sense.
If there is something mounted upon, then there is something attained.
Alternatively, when all dharmas and sense-objects (*viṣaya*) are detached, the syllable *ra* appears;
*ra* signifies "staining" (*rañjana*). Staining refers to the staining of pure form; this is precisely the staining by sense-objects.
All phenomena are free from all defilements.

Alternatively, all phenomena are signless (*animitta*); if the syllable *la* were to manifest as having a sign, it would then be in opposition to the signless and would not correspond with the syllable *a*.
Alternatively, because all phenomena are beyond verbal expression, the syllable VAḤ appears;
or, because all phenomena are free from quiescence, the syllable ŚAḤ appears—where "śa" signifies the meaning of being tranquil.
If there is stillness, there is distraction; where there is neither stillness nor distraction, such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Alternatively, all phenomena are by nature dull and insentient; the syllable *sa* appears as a form, and "sa" signifies that which is ignorant and lacks discernment.
Folly and wisdom constitute a loss when they do not correspond with the fundamental essence.
Alternatively, the truth (satya) is unattainable; the syllable *sa* manifests this truth, which signifies reality.
Truth and untruth constitute duality; this is a worldly phenomenon, and it is here that the letter *kṣa* (kṣara) is manifested.

Regarding the manifestation of the letter *kṣa*, all the merits of every gateway to the Dharma are contained within it. Alternatively, all phenomena are free from causes; the letter *kṣa* manifests the meaning of "reproach" (*kṣepa*), for *kṣepa* signifies the sense of causality.
If there is a cause, there is an effect; this is the nature of arising and ceasing.
Entering the gate of non-arising means there is neither cause nor effect; others should follow this example.
O Lord of Mysteries!
Entering each of these samādhi-gates in turn, O Lord of Mysteries, observe this: even the thirty-two marks of a great man all arise from within them.
Āṅgā, Raṅgā, Naṅgā, Maṅgā, and so forth, exercise sovereign mastery over all phenomena.
These manifest as the secondary marks (anuvyañjana) that perfect the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
And as for these secondary marks of a Samyaksaṃbuddha, O Guhyapati!
Master, enter each and every gate of samādhi and see them thus. O Guhyapati!
The scriptural passage continues: "Even the thirty-two marks of a great man all arise from within this.
Within each and every one of these characters, there are thirty-two gates of samādhi.
Because these thirty-two gates enter into one another, they are able to accomplish the thirty-two marks.
That is to say, the twenty syllables beginning with *ka*, the eight syllables beginning with *ya-ra*, and these four syllables together constitute the thirty-two.
Within each individual syllable lies a samādhi, all of which are endowed with the thirty-two marks.
Next, the five syllables *oṃ, ra, ja, na, ta* revolve with sovereign mastery over all phenomena.
These constitute the accomplishment of the secondary marks (anuvyañjana) of a Perfectly Enlightened One, as they appear in the scriptural texts.

These five syllables pervade both meditative concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā); they can accomplish samādhi, they can accomplish wisdom, and they can universally accomplish the eighty secondary marks of a Tathāgata.
Therefore, those who cultivate the practice of mantra (vidyā) should recognize the meanings of these characters.
If such characters appear within a mantra, one will understand its intent by correlating them with their respective meanings.
This clarifies such matters.
Because it clarifies this meaning, one thereby knows that this mantra possesses such powers, functions, and so forth.

Within this [text], there is a verse beginning from "The Bodhisattva of the Mantra Gate, Lord of Secrets" and ending with "the hundred-syllable samaya-born"; this is a passage from a different location and should not have been included here—the original text was erroneous.

One also understands that these Buddhas have extensively performed this for me, and thus one attains the status of a World-Honored One among all Buddhas. As with the aforementioned thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, all causes for attaining Buddhahood and all merits are accomplished through these extensive practices; it is by means of these practices that all Buddhas become Honored Ones among devas and humans.
If a practitioner practices in this manner, they shall likewise become a venerable one among men.
Thus ends the Chapter on the Accomplishment of the Hundred-Syllable Recitation.
23. Chapter on the Ritual of the Hundred-Syllable Mantra (19). Next, O Lord of Secrets! Regarding the twenty-third chapter, the Ritual of the Hundred-Syllable Mantra: Furthermore, O Lord of Secrets!
Within this gateway of samādhi, through the empowerment of emptiness, one attains perfect awakening with mastery over all phenomena.
Therefore, this syllable is the first phrase of the mantra of the Honored One, ĀḤ.
Furthermore, Guhyapati!
The syllables of the gateways of samādhi are empty within this.
Because the Buddha has attained mastery over all phenomena through empowerment, these are the seed-syllables of the deities.
"The letter A is the foremost phrase; it clarifies that the Dharma is universally pervasive, encircled by letters.
That Honored One is without marks, being far removed from the perception of marks."
"The signless Honored Ones of the Noble Ones appear from within the midst of signs.
The first phrase, the letter *A*, clarifies that the Dharma universally surrounds all.

As for those signless Honored Ones appearing from within the midst of the signs of the signless Honored Ones who have transcended signs: it is because the Buddha wishes to fulfill and bring to completion those practitioners of the true mantra-conduct (*mantracaryā*) that he further expounds these words of samādhi.
In this context, "emptiness" refers to the syllable *a*.
The syllable *a* is the emptiness of primordial non-arising and unobtainability.
Just as this ultimate emptiness of unobtainability is unobtainable, it is fully endowed with all virtues and universally encompasses all Buddha-dharmas.
This "gathering" (*saṃgraha*) refers to the gathering of the Brahma-sound, in the sense of drawing all things into oneself, as if collecting various objects and placing them within one's own body.
By means of the empowering power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of this emptiness, one is able to gather all phenomena and attain Buddhahood.
In this context, "sovereignty" (*vaśitā*) differs from the sovereignty of Avalokiteśvara; here it carries the sense of "gathering," meaning the ability to gather all phenomena.
Just as a king within his realm may seize whatever he desires with complete sovereignty,
so too is the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, sovereign over all phenomena.
Therefore, this syllable is the most venerable; it is said that this syllable is itself the Honored One, being both heaven and the divine.
Heaven is the foremost among all beings, and this syllable is likewise so.

Among all phenomena, it is the most honored; just as Śakra is foremost among the world’s rulers of the earth, the Brahmā King is foremost among the sages and saints of the world, and the Buddha is foremost among all noble wisdoms, so too this syllable *A* is the foremost among all gateways of mantras.
Because this single syllable accomplishes immeasurable merit, it is unsurpassed.
"Vidyā" is an alternative name for mantra.

Regarding the statement that the vidyā-dharma is universally surrounded by syllables: this means that from a single syllable, immeasurable syllables arise, and immeasurable vidyās surround it on all sides, just as the previously described wheel of syllables (*akṣaracakra*).
Although there is such surrounding, its essence is empty, quiescent, and signless.
Within the signless, one perceives signs; yet within these very signs, one is detached from signs.
Furthermore, within the state of signlessness (animitta), there yet manifest phenomena such as coming and going that universally respond to the world;
one should know that these are all the power of the inconceivable empowerment (adhiṣṭhāna) of mantra.
By consecrating oneself with the syllable A, one becomes identical with emptiness; within this emptiness, all Buddha-dharmas are accomplished.

Just as the myriad things of the world are brought into existence by means of space, yet the essence of space is signless (animitta), so too do various forms and sounds manifest within that signlessness.
The "Venerable One" (Bhagavān) refers to the meaning, while "syllables" (akṣara) refer to the signs; this is identical in meaning to the preceding chapter.
From syllables arise words, and from words arise mantras.
Through mantras, the fruits of mantra-attainment are produced; these are the voices of all World-Saviors.
Sound issues forth from syllables, and syllables give rise to mantras; mantras establish the fruit—this is what the Protectors of the World have taught.
One should know that the nature of sound is empty, and that it is a construction produced by emptiness.

All classes of sentient beings grasp at things according to words as being false attachments; yet it is neither emptiness nor sound that is so grasped. It is for the sake of practitioners that emptiness is taught.

Knowing that all things in the world produced by emptiness are likewise grasped falsely according to their respective types—neither as that emptiness nor as sound—it is for the sake of practice that this is taught: through sound one attains penetration, which is the realization of samādhi.
Place the corresponding syllables according to the ritual method, illuminating the various characteristics of the mantra phrases of the letter *A*.
This is the scriptural text.

Relying upon the letter *A* as being identical to space, one should know that it is originally free from all characteristics; yet, while free from characteristics, there are the characteristics of coming and going, and from the letter *A*, sound is produced.
The letter A is fundamentally empty. Why is this so?
This sound exists through a multitude of conditions;

that is to say, it arises when various conditions such as the throat, tongue, and palate come into contact. It belongs solely to these conditions and possesses no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of its own.
Furthermore, these very conditions that can produce [a result] also arise from conditions; one should know that this is precisely primordial non-arising (*an-utpāda*).
Yet, through the mantra arising from causes and conditions, the mantra itself brings about the accomplishment of the fruit.
This is precisely what the Savior has taught.
If one recognizes that this sound is empty and so forth, it arises from emptiness; the sound expresses the syllable, and the sound and emptiness are mutually dependent.
If one knows this, then the myriad aspects of all worldly activities performed will not transcend the gateway of the letter A.
Because they accord with the world, they arise through conceptual differentiation.
Those who do not understand give rise, based on this, to various conceptualizations and grasping minds regarding states of being.
However, since both space and sound are in fact devoid of duality, this is precisely what is taught by the practitioners of the True Word (mantra).
If one understands this, then these very verses explain one another; this is the liberation through sound.
This is called attaining mastery over sound: by understanding that its intrinsic nature is empty, one realizes samādhi.
Sound manifests emptiness, and emptiness reveals conditions; these explain one another. This causes one to enter the emptiness of both together.

Sound and the ear are themselves empty; this very principle is itself endowed with all virtues. Because one realizes that consciousness, sound, and so forth are empty, one enters the principle of true nature. Entering true nature is precisely abiding in samādhi. To be in accord with this samādhi is the Dharma—ask further regarding this.

Although fundamentally unborn, it gives rise to all phenomena; that is, it illuminates based upon this [nature] the various colors such as blue and yellow, the various shapes such as square, round, and triangular, and even the immeasurable and ineffable distinctions of characteristics.
Both self and other are empty; establishing principles from within emptiness is entirely the function of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
To "enter" means to penetrate thoroughly.
To abide in this principle is itself to abide in samādhi.
Having realized this, one establishes the correspondence according to the Dharma; this correspondence also achieves union.
"Establishing" (zhì) is synonymous with "arranging" (bù).
This character serves as illumination; illumination means the perfection of its virtues.
Furthermore, the "A" syllable and its like are intended to serve as an analogy for all syllables.
The "contemplation" (saṃjñā) of various mantra forms refers to the sense of making distinctions.
By analogy with this single syllable, it encompasses the meaning of all mantras.

One should change the visualization to the differentiation of various mantra names; that is to say, within a single syllable, immeasurable meanings are manifested and immeasurable explanations are revealed. For each class of sentient beings, immeasurable languages are manifested, all of which arise from this single syllable. It is upon this basis that the numerous names of mantras are established.

For one who realizes this principle, one should place the corresponding syllables according to the method; that is, within the single syllable mentioned above, one places immeasurable syllables, each with a distinct form and color, as manifested in such things as the hundred-syllable wheel (*śatākṣara-cakra*). All of these appear based upon this.
One should thus illuminate and understand it through observation.
It should be known that the letter A possesses immeasurable meanings, and the same applies to the various and immeasurable distinctions of mantras.

The meaning of these words extends even to the fact that from the very beginning, the Way of the Buddhas has been the same; this meaning of the words of ultimate truth, as well as these practices such as the mantras which are the wondrous gateway for accomplishing spontaneous wisdom, were not established by worldly people.

This is the gateway to the Tathāgata’s spontaneous wisdom; it does not arise from another, nor was it established by the Tathāgata for the sake of a particular class of sentient beings. Rather, the Way is identical for all Buddhas, and the dharma-position is eternally abiding.
Although it is spontaneously accomplished from the very beginning, it must nevertheless rely upon conditions and skillful means to become clearly manifest.
Herein, though only a single character is explained, the dharma-gate of all one hundred characters can be understood; therefore, it is called the "Gate of One Hundred Characters."
This means that by citing a single character, one hundred characters can be understood.
This concludes the "Chapter on the Dharma of the Hundred Characters. Here, "dharma" refers to a multitude of meanings; it is not the dharma of the *Dharmapada*.
This refers to the ritual procedure of the hundred syllables (*śatākṣara*).
From within these hundred syllables, various virtues arise; this is called the Dharma.
The final fascicle, together with the second *Hongji* (Extensive Record), enters into a small portion of the first chapter of the sutra.

24. Chapter on the Nature of Bodhi (19). Following the Chapter on the Nature of Bodhi, the twenty-fourth, this chapter explains the meaning of the "Chapter on the Hundred-Syllable Dharma" by means of parables.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Just as the directions of space, like space itself, are eternally pervasive throughout all directions;
so too, the Mantra of the Savior of the World is eternally pervasive throughout all phenomena, yet remains without any dependence."
The Mantra Savior has no basis in any phenomena, just as space is not based on things such as smoke or clouds.

Although one perceives it, space and the like have no basis; although one perceives all things such as the sun, moon, smoke, and clouds, they are empty and have no basis in space, nor do those things depend upon that space.
The Mantra Savior is likewise not that upon which others rely;
this is as taught and is universally established in the world.
Space is detached from the three times, and the Mantra Savior is also detached from the three times.
The Mantra-Savior is identical to space; he is equally detached from the three periods of time.
This is the scriptural text.
Just as space pervades all places and all phenomena depend upon it for their establishment, yet space itself has no basis of dependence.
All such mantras depend upon this mantra, the Savior of the World.
This vision is a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*); it is just like seeing smoke and so forth without staining the sky.
Abiding in the practice of "mere name," one remains far removed from such things as an agent.
Regarding "space, conventional designations, and so forth"—the phrase "and so forth" refers to various other conventional designations.
This means that when worldly people speak of "space," it is merely a conventional designation.
That which is proclaimed by the Teacher—the essence of this mantra, which is fundamentally unborn—is a teaching without basis, like space, pervading all places.
Furthermore, it is like when people in the world observe space and claim there is something seen; yet in reality, this observation of space is such that no observation at all confronts the eye.

While space possesses all characteristics, it is not itself those characteristics; and while space possesses all characteristics, space likewise does not enter into those characteristics, being free from both self and other.
One should know that this Mantra-Savior is likewise; he is no different from space.
Although there is nothing he does not possess, his ultimate purity is identical in essence to space.
Although it is identical to empty space—ultimately pure and devoid of any obtainable phenomena—it is that which is not non-existent and that which is not unaccomplished.
Furthermore, it is like empty space, which transcends the three periods of time: namely, the past, the future, and the present.

Mantras are likewise; because they conform to worldly conventions, it is said that they exist in the three times—namely, those to be cultivated, those already cultivated, and those currently being cultivated; and similarly, those to be realized, those already realized, and those currently being realized.
The essence of the mantra transcends the three periods of time and is equal to empty space; how much more so when it accords with worldly convention by speaking of the three periods.

As for the "Savior of the World," this refers to the various dharmas distinguished within the view of emptiness; since these dharmas arise from that which is fundamentally unarisen, one should know that their essence is likewise identical to the fundamental source.

Furthermore, all those who perform actions are merely designated by names; they are equally free from the conventional designations of space and so forth. It is taught that the Teacher does not depend upon any name or substance.
As with space, so it is with the mantra; the mantra is self-existent, and this syllable is its manifestation.
This is also the meaning of the sutra text.
Just as empty space dwells solely within the formations of names, these formations can also be "approached"; this is called the "approach of names.
That is to say, the approach of mere names is simply that names themselves are the approach.
The term "destination" (*gati*) established here is also intended to mean "speech.
Terms such as "space" and "provisional designation" are established in accordance with worldly convention; they are merely conceptual constructs.
The preceding verse states that emptiness exists as a mere name; the intent of the subsequent verse is that this name, too, is identical to emptiness and cannot be apprehended.
There is only the name, which is unapprehendable and devoid of an agent.

Just as people in the world, due to the characteristics of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), grasp at this characteristic of emptiness as being truly existent and give rise to various false imaginings:
some say that space is eternal;
others say that it is the void within that which is surrounded by various forms, and so forth.
Some say that this emptiness arises based on the locus of an agent.
Such views are immeasurable and boundless, as explained at length in the sūtras and śāstras.
To state the essential point: they do not deviate from the two views of annihilationism and eternalism.
Even the teachers of the worldly Hīnayāna establish empty phenomena as being substantially existent; for this reason, there are immeasurable faults.

Even names do not exist and are likewise identical to empty space; the Lord of Mantras is also thus, seen as abiding in provisional designations, which refers to the immeasurable conventional establishments.
The various "non-" [prefixes] and so forth do not refer to birth through either purity or impurity.
Alternatively, it may mean that even the fruit cannot arise; this likely carries the sense of being manifold, implying that various fruits likewise do not arise.
If one is free from such various worldly discriminations and constantly and diligently practices therein, seeking the phrases of omniscience—this refers to being intent on seeking this very state.
What is here called "space" is precisely the emptiness of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*), which is the great emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*).
Furthermore, emptiness exists only as a name, yet its substantial reality is not empty; it is free from the characteristics of both emptiness and non-emptiness.
Out of skillful means, the Teacher employs provisional verbal expressions to awaken sentient beings.

However, even this name "emptiness" is unattainable; if there were a name that could exist, it would constitute a mark (*nimitta*), and where there is a mark, the mind undergoes birth and cessation and fails to enter true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). How, then, could it be called the natural wisdom of the letter A, the wisdom of the true mark?
Just as space has nothing upon which it relies, one should know that mantras are likewise; ultimately, they have nothing upon which they rely.

Through skillful means, the Buddha desires to lead all sentient beings universally into the Buddha-wisdom; thus, he establishes the provisional based on emptiness, causing them to rely on this provisional to reach the ultimate principle.
Since emptiness is fundamentally unborn, from what could the provisional [phenomena] that depend upon emptiness arise?
One should know that they arise from substantialist views.
Such knowledge and vision is itself the nature of bodhi; and the nature of bodhi is nothing other than the mantra.
The meaning of this mantra is itself enlightenment (*bodhi*); it is impossible for there to be enlightenment existing apart from this.

It is not fire, water, wind, or earth; it is not the grasping of the sun or moon; it is not day or night; it is not birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); it is not injury; it is not moments (*kṣaṇa*) or *muhūrta*s; it is not years and so forth; it is not the number of eons of formation and destruction; it is neither pure nor impure; and as for the fruit of rebirth, it is either born or unborn.
If one does not engage in such various worldly conceptualizations, but instead applies oneself diligently to them, one should cultivate the aspiration for the state of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
This is the scriptural passage.

Regarding the nature of mantra: it is not earth, water, fire, or wind; rather, it is like space, which pervades earth, water, fire, and wind. While these four elements rely upon space to accomplish all things, space itself has no basis.
Within this mantra, the inconceivable functions of earth, water, fire, wind, and so forth rely upon the gateway of the letter A; yet this letter A is not a term for earth, water, fire, or wind.
Neither the sun nor the moon—namely, the nine planets and other celestial bodies—are established by worldly convention alone and are not ultimately real.
Now, this nature of bodhi is devoid of distinctions such as ignorance or the absence of ignorance; how, then, could there be any difference between day and night?
Being eternally abiding in the true reality (dharmatā) apart from causes and conditions is precisely the essence of Mahāvairocana Tathāgata; how then could it not be free from birth and death?
"Harm" (hai) carries the meaning of injury or damage, as well as the meaning of decay and exhaustion.

Furthermore, the nature of this mantra is eternal and unchanging; it is free from all decline, affliction, and the process of transformation and decay, and possesses no characteristics of temporal duration or the kalpas of formation and destruction.
One should thus correctly contemplate the nature of the mantra, not relying on false attachments.

It is neither formed at the beginning of an eon nor destroyed at the end of an eon; its origin is without beginning and its end is without cessation. Therefore, it is free from the divisions and calculations of eons.
Because there is nothing that is not present, it is not pure; because it is ultimately empty, it is not impure.

All sentient beings possess all defiled dharmas by means of this letter A, while the Tathāgata accomplishes all meritorious virtues by means of this very same letter; therefore, it is neither pure nor impure.
If one says that [the body] arises from contemplation, it is because there is something contemplated and something accomplished, and thus one undergoes birth according to one's practice;
however, mantras are entirely free from this.

Even the attainment of a mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) arising from the merit of pure contemplation or from immeasurable merit is likewise non-existent; therefore, there is no fruit of undergoing birth.
Since all such things are dharmas that involve apprehension, whereas the nature of the mantra is natural, true wisdom, which finds nothing at all among all dharmas;
one should know that the various kinds of conceptual distinctions mentioned above are not the vision of reality, and their number is immeasurable.
To state it briefly: the nature of mantras is that they are all free from such worldly views of conceptual discrimination.
If one understands this and practices the conduct of mantras accordingly, that is the very word of omniscience.
As for "desire," it is accomplished according to one's will.
A "phrase" (pada) has the meaning of a dwelling place; the dwelling place of all-knowledge is precisely the dwelling of the Buddha.
One should know that the nature of bodhi is equal to space, and space is equal to the nature of bodhi.
The nature of bodhi is the syllable *A*, the gateway to the phrase of omniscience. Chapter 25:

The Practice of the Three Samayas (19). Next, in the twenty-fifth chapter, "The Practice of the Three Samayas," at that time, Vajrapāṇi asked about these words regarding the dharma of the three samayas. Then, the Secret Lord Vajradhara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, you have spoken of the three samayas."
"Why is this Dharma taught as the three samayas? Having spoken thus,
the Buddha next addressed the Lord of Secrets, Vajrapāṇi, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Guhyakādhipati!
You have asked me about such a meaning. Guhyakādhipati!”
"You should listen attentively and apply your mind with great care;
I shall now expound it. Vajrapāṇi replied, "So be it."
“World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it.
This is said because, although it was previously explained, it was not yet complete; thus he rose up and asked.
The meaning of the question is as follows:
regarding these three samayas, what dharma constitutes the three samayas?

Because the Buddha considers this question to involve a matter of great significance, he offers words of praise and then exhorts [the assembly] to receive the teaching with careful attention; the passage continues until "Thus it is; we shall receive the instruction," which may be understood according to the text.

These three samayas are explained extensively in the *Mahāmūla* with approximately one thousand two hundred verses; here, only their essential principles are presented, for no further meaning exists outside this framework.
The Buddha said: "There are three kinds of dharmas that continue in succession; this succession is birth. The removal of obstacles corresponds to being free from obstacles.

To speak of the removal of obstacles is precisely the arising of the correspondence with being free from obstacles; it is called the three samayas. Because they correspond with yoga, being free from obstacles is itself the three samayas."
What is the continuity of those phenomena?
In the Buddha’s subsequent answer, the first three phenomena refer to continuity without interruption; this is the meaning of *samaya*.
However, in the Sanskrit sound, "continuity" (*saṃtati*) shares the same phonetic root as "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*); thus, it may also encompass both meanings.
If there is an interruption in this continuity, it is no longer the *samaya*; this constitutes an obstacle to its arising, and thus it possesses both meanings [of "continuity" and "vow"].

That which is called "uninterrupted continuity" refers to the continuity of speech and action, and the correspondence between mind and mouth; once the resolve has been made, the conduct of body and mouth does not deviate from it. Whatever is vowed by the mouth, the mind and practice likewise cultivate accordingly—this is termed *samaya*.
The Sūtra says:
"If the initial mind does not contemplate one's own nature, wisdom will arise from this.
Next, the knowledge of reality (yathābhūta-jñāna) arises, and the inexhaustible net of conceptual discrimination is abandoned; this is the second characteristic of the bodhicitta."
It is not a conceptualized Buddha-phrase.
It is the vision of the inexhaustible realm of sentient beings as it truly is. O Lord of Secrets!

When the bodhicitta arises through the sovereign turning of compassion and the objectless contemplation (*anālambana-bhāvanā*), it is called the bodhicitta free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), the signless (*animitta*) bodhicitta, and the settling of sentient beings in their abode—these are the three *samayas*.
This is also the meaning of the sutra text.
"The initial stage" refers to not yet contemplating one's own nature or original essence; from this point, wisdom is generated and the wisdom of suchness arises.
This means that one has realized the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), and this realization is itself wisdom.
To be free from the inexhaustible net of conceptual discrimination is called the second mind.

O Lord of Mysteries! Regarding the state of non-conceptual triply-enlightened awakening (*tri-bodhi*) which is the characteristic of bodhi, once one has seen it as it truly is, one contemplates the inexhaustible realm of sentient beings; through the sovereign turning of compassion, the non-referential contemplation (*anālambana-dhyāna*) arises, and the bodhicitta is born.
This refers to being free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and establishing all sentient beings so that they dwell in the mind of non-conceptual bodhicitta.
This "establishing all sentient beings in non-conceptual bodhicitta while being free from all conceptual proliferation" is what is called the vow of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
These are called the three samaya phrases.

Among these three, the first merely involves generating the aspiration and vowing to attain Buddhahood; however, one has not yet been able to correctly contemplate the merits of the Tathāgata, nor can one fully understand by what dharma one attains Buddhahood, as one has not yet possessed the wisdom of contemplative insight.
Merely possessing the aspiration for Buddhahood, yet not yet having fully realized what inherent merits exist within the fundamental nature of one's own body—
merely possessing this wisdom-nature and being able, amidst birth and death, to first give rise to the mind seeking the fruit of Buddhahood— this is the first samaya.

Following this mind, there arises the wisdom that accords with reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), by which one is able to discern through insight (*prajñā*) and clearly understand what constitutes merit and what does not, as well as the characteristics of the possible and the impossible, and the erroneous and the correct.

By attaining suchness-wisdom (*yathābhūtajñāna*), one is able to leave behind the net of inexhaustible false views and conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*), skillfully extinguishing all discursive elaborations and abiding securely within the true nature of reality (*tattvalakṣaṇa*).
However, this true wisdom is itself the bodhicitta.
"Samaya" has the meaning of "equality," and because this mind arises as equal, it is called samaya.

Although the initial resolve does not yet possess actualized true wisdom, it nonetheless vows to attain buddhahood and deliver sentient beings; as this is a mind of equality, it also receives the name "samaya."

From this mind, the second mind continues in succession without interval or obstruction; immediately thereafter, having discerned the true and the false within these very words of reality, one gives rise to great compassion toward all inexhaustible sentient beings—this is the third samaya.
Since all sentient beings possess this same nature yet are unable to realize it themselves, they undergo the cycle of birth and death without end.
Having now personally awakened to this myself, I shall universally open the light of the Buddha’s wisdom so that all may become like me; this is Great Compassion.

Because one sees reality, that which is unreal is eliminated of its own accord; no external dharma comes from outside to enter the body. When delusion is removed, the true nature (dharmatā) manifests spontaneously.
It was stated above that this sutra contains three points of meaning:
the bodhicitta as the seed is the first point, and great compassion as the root is the second.
Previously, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) was taken as the root; why is it now placed third?

In this context, clear discernment (*pratisaṃvid*) is the root, for it is through the ability to clearly discern right from wrong that one is able to give rise to compassion; thus, their meanings are mutually established.
The third skillful means is the ultimate; here it is called great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), which also functions in mutual completion with the former.
Because one gives rise to great compassion, one employs skillful means to gather in all beings.
These three matters, proceeding in continuous succession from beginning to end without interruption, are called the Three Samayas.

By abiding in truth and realizing that delusion is false, one gives rise to great compassion for the sake of those sentient beings, thereby eliminating the conceptual proliferation of all sentient beings.
From this point onward, he performs the Buddha-work through skillful means.

As for "idle proliferation" (*prapañca*): it is like a worldly entertainer who, with a distracted mind, performs various actions of body and speech merely to please others, yet without any real purpose.
Now, that which is produced by those with false views is likewise like that; therefore, it is called frivolous conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

As for "bodhi and sentient beings abiding," it means causing sentient beings to abide in this Dharma so that they are no different from myself; this is precisely the meaning of dwelling securely within the secret treasury of all sons.
Next are the three samayas.
Having first attained buddhahood through the skillful means of great compassion, furthermore, O Lord of Secrets!
What are these three samayas?
The first is called the Buddha.
The initial mind of perfect enlightenment is the second, named the Dharma. The subsequent minds that arise in succession are what is known as the Saṃgha.
The Guide has thus spoken of these three samayas.
Abiding in these three equalities, one practices the conduct of enlightenment.

Next, regarding the various leaders—meaning the extensive dissemination of the various gates of guidance—for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, one shall attain the realization of enlightenment and manifest the mastery of the three bodies.
Furthermore, from the Buddha comes the Dharma, and from the Dharma comes the Sangha; these three are of one essence, for in reality they possess no dual nature.
Because of this equality, it is called *samaya*. A previous interpretation at another time stated:
*sa* means Buddha, *ma* means Dharma, and *ya* means Sangha.
Furthermore, regarding the three samayas: it means that by abiding in these samayas, one immediately attains bodhi.

Abiding in bodhi for the sake of sentient beings, one manifests various forms and teaches various paths; one should know that this very mind is able to encompass the three bodies—this is the meaning of samaya.
As stated above, the Three Jewels are the three *samaya*s.
*Samaya* has the meaning of "equality"; because these Three Jewels are equal, they are called the three *samaya*s.
Following these three samayas, one next possesses the three bodies; these are also called the three samayas.
Because one abides in the three bodies, there is the activity of benefiting others.
What is the benefit? It is precisely the benefiting of sentient beings.
Abiding within the three bodies (*trikāya*), one manifests various paths and likewise gathers in sentient beings; "gathering" here has the meaning of sovereign inclusion.
Lord of Secrets!

The Buddha’s true teaching is expressed as the empowerment of the single body; that which is called the "first emanation body" refers to the twelvefold division of the teachings, which contain various skillful means therein.
"Lord of Secrets!
Because the Samyaksaṃbuddhas establish the teaching, they empower a single body, namely, the first, the nirmāṇakāya.
Furthermore, Lord of Secrets!"
Next, within a single body, he manifests three aspects, namely: the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Furthermore, O Lord of Mysteries, from this point on, he establishes the teaching of the three vehicles, extensively performs buddha-activities, and manifests parinirvāṇa.
The maturation of sentient beings and the benefiting of sentient beings are both sustained by a single body, namely the nirmāṇakāya (transformation body).
Because it abides in the samaya, such benefit is realized.

Next, within a single body, the three bodies are manifested—namely, the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha—which constitute the Three Jewels as a single essence; one should know that all of these arise from within this one body.
Among these, the three samayas follow one another in succession, each arising from the preceding one.

Following this succession, there further arises that which is produced: namely, manifesting and teaching the Three Vehicles, extensively performing Buddha-works to guide sentient beings, and upon having accomplished what was to be done, entering into nirvana.
Furthermore, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he continues to bring immeasurable sentient beings to accomplishment.

This refers to those classes of sentient beings who were unable to resolve their minds toward enlightenment while the Buddha was still present, but who achieve it either because of the Buddha’s passing or during the period of the Semblance Dharma (śāsanapratirūpaka).
O Lord of Secrets!
By contemplating those three samayas, one comes to know all the gateways of mantra.
O Lord of Secrets!

Observe those bodhisattvas who have realized the three samayas and practice the path to enlightenment through the gateway of mantras; they achieve accomplishment according to the rules of the mantra-dharma.
He is not attached to any false conceptualizations, and nothing can act as an obstacle for him.

Regarding this, there are alternative names [for these obstacles]: to eliminate lack of desire, laziness, and unprofitable talk; to prevent the failure to generate faith and the accumulation of merit; and furthermore, one should not perform two things, namely: drinking various intoxicants and sleeping on a bed.

The practitioner of the bodhisattva path who maintains and recites the rules of the mantra-dharma does not cling to any false attachments and dwells as one free from the obstructions of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This is the scriptural text.
The Buddha told Vajrapāṇi: "Observe what has been explained above; all of it arises from abiding in the three samayas.
By abiding in these samayas and reciting according to the Dharma without interruption in thought after thought—namely, by not clinging to any false attachments—one attains this."
Because of false attachments, various obstacles arise; however, if one abides in the equality of these three, one will not cling to any single false attachment.
This very equality of the three is itself bodhi—how then could any obstacles arise? This is the great principle for being free from all obstacles.

Furthermore, there is another cause for the arising of obstacles, namely "lack of desire. This means that because obstacles exist within this very practice of *mantra*, one suddenly finds no basis for the inclination toward it.
Alternatively, it may arise from a mind of lack of desire, which thus obstructs entry;
"lack of desire" refers to the absence of aspiration and so forth.
"Laziness" is due to a lack of diligent progress.

Just as when drilling for fire, if one stops breathing before it has grown hot, it obstructs the entry [of the spark]; likewise, idle talk is of no benefit, and failing to maintain recitation or diligently practice the mantra path causes time to be wasted in vain, thereby providing an opportunity for obstacles to take advantage of the situation.
Lack of faith: because of this lack of faith, one is obstructed from attaining ease.
Furthermore, one amasses vast wealth and resources, yet in seeking them, one is moved by anger; in guarding them, one undergoes arduous toil; and when they are lost, one suffers.
Through various causes and conditions such as these, they enable the practitioner to fall into the grasp of obstacles.
All of the above are conditions for the arising of obstacles.
Furthermore, there are two [other] types, namely: not drinking alcohol.
Alcohol is the primary cause for the arising of obstacles; this is the first.
Because of drinking alcohol, various unwholesome states arise.
Furthermore, one must not lie upon a bed; this is the second.
If one sleeps peacefully upon a bed, various desires and thoughts of negligence will arise; therefore, one shall not attain [the goal].
One should instead spread a mat of grass; those who practice recitation in the West mostly use auspicious *kuśa* grass as their mat.
This has many benefits:

first, because it is the place where the Tathāgata sat when he attained enlightenment, and because all the world regards it as auspicious, those who maintain and recite [the mantra] upon it will find that obstacles do not arise.
Furthermore, if various venomous insects or similar creatures encounter this [grass], none shall be able to reach its location.
Moreover, its nature is exceedingly fragrant and pure.
Furthermore, this grass is extremely sharp; upon touching the body, it pierces it like the shape of a double-edged blade.

When the practitioner has finished reciting and rests during their leisure time, they lie upon this grass mat; however, if they become heedless and indulge themselves, it will cause injury. Therefore, one must not act with negligence or arrogance.
Furthermore, the reason the Buddha personally used this grass was to eliminate the prideful mind of the world.
When he was a prince, he indulged in various forms of luxury, sitting upon jeweled couches and having his feet rested upon jeweled stands.
If one who has left the household life still practices such things, they are no different from when they were originally a layperson.

Because they are able to renounce such matters and sit upon a grass mat, all humans and devas will give rise to a heart of reverence; they will likewise emulate this by eliminating arrogance and entering the True Dharma.
"If even the Buddha is thus, how much more so should we be?

Chapter 26: Clarifying the Tathāgata (19). Second Part: Clarifying the Tathāgata, Chapter Twenty-Six. At that time, the Vajradhara Lord of Mysteries addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

At that time, the World-Honored One Vairocana surveyed the entire great assembly and addressed the Vajradhara Lord of Secrets, saying:

It is well that you are able to ask me about such a meaning.
Listen attentively and apply your mind with great care; I shall now expound the path of the Mahāyāna.
Awakening has the characteristic of space and is free from all conceptual discrimination.
One who joyfully seeks that enlightenment is called a Bodhisattva.

Having accomplished the ten stages and so forth, they attain mastery and skillful penetration; they know that all phenomena are empty like illusions, and they realize that all these things are identical. This is what is meant by "knowing that all these things are identical."
Because he knows the destinies of all worlds, he is called a Buddha. The Dharma has the characteristic of space;
it is non-dual and possesses but a single characteristic. Perfectly awakened and endowed with the ten powers—this is named *samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Only that which harms by means of wisdom" refers to both the act and its attainment; that is, harming the afflictions through wisdom.
Because its intrinsic nature is ineffable and it is the wisdom of self-realization, it is called the Tathāgata.
What is awakening?
This is my doubt; O Guide, remove it! The Great Muni has cast aside all uncertainty.
The Bodhisattva of great renown shall practice the unsurpassed conduct of the King of the Mahāyāna.
The above questions have this underlying meaning:
since the Buddha has previously taught the Dharma, he has at various points referred to himself as either a "Buddha" or a "Bodhisattva."
Although I have heard this, I have not yet received a definitive determination regarding the characteristics of these names and meanings.
For what reason does one receive the name "Bodhisattva," the name "Buddha," the name "Tathāgata," and the name "Honored One among Men"?
Does he possess this title from the very moment he was born of his parents,
or does he only attain this title once his virtues are perfected and his conduct fulfilled?
This question is posed while praising the Buddha’s virtues, for there is no king of Mahāyāna practice who is superior to him.
The Buddha again praised him, saying "Excellent," and so forth, until he commanded him to listen attentively before finally answering:
"The Mahāyāna path is the emptiness of Bodhi; it is free from all conceptual discrimination. If one joyfully seeks that Bodhi, one is called a Bodhisattva."
This is the answer regarding the name "Bodhisattva.
Space has no marks, and awakening (*bodhi*) is likewise; it is just as space is markless and non-conceptual.
Furthermore, although space is markless, it is the basis upon which all virtues depend, and the myriad phenomena rely upon it to exist.
Bodhi is likewise: ultimately signless and non-conceptual, yet it possesses all meritorious qualities.
To seek realization of this suchness is what is called bodhi.
Next, the meaning of "Buddha" is explained:

Having attained perfection in the ten stages, possessing mastery and excellent penetration, knowing that all phenomena are empty like illusions—this is the practice of those who follow the same path; by knowing all worlds, one receives the name "Buddha."
This is the answer to the Buddha’s meaning.

It refers to the fulfillment of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) through sovereign penetration; that is, within each and every stage, one thoroughly penetrates and attains mastery, realizing that all phenomena are identical to emptiness and illusion, while also knowing the various inclinations and the deep mental activities of sentient beings.
Because he possesses these virtues, all the worlds designate him as "Buddha," and it is from this that the name "Buddha" arises.
The nature of space and the nature of phenomena are non-dual, being of a single characteristic.
The "Ten Powers" (*daśabala*) is the name of the Buddha and a title for the Perfectly Awakened One; it also explains the meaning of "Buddha.

Previously, it was merely stated that he knows phenomena are empty and like illusions; now it is said that the phenomena of space are of one mark, which is marklessness. Because he has realized this through penetration, he possesses the Ten Powers to universally know all phenomena, such that there is nothing he does not know.
As stated in the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*, the ten powers (*daśabala*) are extremely vast.
This bodhi is like space, devoid of dual characteristics; with a mind that abides nowhere within even a single characteristic, one thereby attains the ten powers of a Buddha.
By virtue of abiding correctly in these ten powers, one is called the Perfectly Enlightened One (*samyaksaṃbuddha*).
"Buddha" and "Perfectly Enlightened One" differ in name but are identical in essence.
Because he has skillfully disciplined body, speech, and mind, and possesses mastery over subduing them, he is able to conquer all Māras.

Not only does he subdue external māras, but he also completely subdues internal obstacles; because he is honored among both the mundane and the supramundane, he is further titled the Honored One Among Men.
This meaning is omitted from the sūtra and not explained there;
other passages explain it in this way:
the wisdom that destroys [ignorance] is solely ineffable; it is called self-nature and self-attesting gnosis, and this is said to be the Tathāgata.
This answers the name of the Tathāgata.
This wisdom is able to destroy ignorance; therefore, it is called "wisdom-destroying.
Although the word "ignorance" is not explicitly mentioned, that which is destroyed is precisely ignorance, and its meaning is thus naturally revealed.

This realm of self-realization transcends the path of language; knowing that self-realization cannot be expressed and transmitted to others, one abides in such wisdom and thus attains the name "Tathāgata."
Furthermore, because one realizes and knows the principle of the Buddhas spontaneously, one is called a Tathāgata.
Moreover, because I likewise proceed along the path traversed by all Buddhas and to the place of spontaneous realization, I am called a Tathāgata.
The *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (The Awakening of Faith) contains detailed answers to these questions, each consisting of more than a hundred verses.
The transmitters of the Dharma have merely summarized their essential points by providing a single verse for each answer; nevertheless, the general meaning remains fully preserved.

27. Chapter on Homa (19–20). Part Two: The Twenty-seventh Chapter on Homa. In the non-Buddhist scriptures of the Vedic treatises on pure conduct, there are rites for fire worship; likewise, within the Mahāyāna Mantra Vehicle, there are also fire rites.
The reason for this is that, in order to subdue a certain class of people, he employed the matters of the Vedas to win them over.
Nevertheless, their underlying significance remains as incomparable as heaven and earth.

Now, wishing to distinguish between the characteristics of the heterodox and the orthodox so that practitioners may no longer harbor further doubts, the transmitters of the Dharma have extensively set forth the causal origins within this chapter.

Desiring to eliminate the prideful minds of those practitioners of purity in future ages, the Buddha himself recounted his past lives, including when he acted as a Brahmā King and expounded the external Vedas, thereby causing the hearts of those of heterodox schools to submit; only thereafter did he teach this correct practice of the gateway of mantras.
Furthermore, Guhyakādhipati!
Once in the past, when I was a bodhisattva, I dwelt in the Brahma-heaven practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva.
That very Brahma-abode is this Brahma-heaven.
At that time, Brahmā asked Mahābrahmā, wishing to know how many kinds of fire there are.
Then I spoke thus; that is to say, I addressed him with these words.
That fire is named the Spontaneous Fire of Self-Grasping (*asmimāna*).
Next is the fire produced by the Son of Brahmā, named *Pavaṅgu*, which is the very first fire in the world.
This refers to when, in a previous life while practicing the bodhisattva path, I manifested as the King of Brahmā; at that time, various practitioners of the Brahma-faring came to question me:
"How many kinds of fires are there in the ritual of fire-sacrifice?
I explained them all to him. Now that I have attained perfect enlightenment, I realize that what was previously stated was incorrect, and what is now being stated is correct.

Therefore, practitioners should from this time forth correctly practice the fire ritual (agnihotra) according to the True Dharma; it is not appropriate to employ the previously held false and incorrect methods.

The Buddha’s intended meaning is as follows:

However, at that time, I did not yet understand the intrinsic nature of fire nor its functional activity; because of this ignorance, you should know that whatever was performed then cannot be called "well-done," nor can it be termed *homa*.
