31. Chapter Thirty-one: Entrustment (20). Next, regarding the "Chapter on Entrustment," the Buddha addresses the great assembly; this refers to the passage at the beginning of the sutra concerning the Vajra Bodhisattvas, numbering as many as the atoms in ten worlds.
Now that the preaching of this sutra is about to conclude, I therefore add this entrustment.
"You all should abide in non-negligence" is a continuation of the preceding text.
This esoteric teaching of the Mahāyāna should be transmitted according to such a dharma-method.

If the manner of giving and receiving is improper, it constitutes a case where the donor acts according to their own whims and transgresses the rules; therefore, it is said that one must abide in non-negligence.

Furthermore, regarding the meaning of the aforementioned three phrases—the practice of benefiting oneself and others—you all should perform Buddha-works while abiding within the secret teaching of the meaning of the letter *A*.
If one does not follow this, it constitutes dwelling in negligence.

Because the teaching is bestowed according to individual capacities, there is the risk of damaging their roots of goodness; thus the Sūtra says: "Those with wisdom who hear this can immediately believe and understand, whereas those without wisdom who harbor doubt and regret will suffer eternal loss."

If a bodhisattva, without deeply contemplating the fundamental causes, conditions, characteristics, and essential nature of sentient beings, were to transmit the Dharma impulsively, they would become an enemy to humans and devas; this constitutes a great act of heedlessness.
Therefore, it is stated next that if one does not know those faculties (*indriya*), one must not bestow [the precepts].
"Faculties" refers to the characteristics of sharpness or dullness regarding the five faculties, such as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth.
"With the exception of my disciples" means that only those who already abide by my teaching and whose mental disposition is characterized by genuine trust are fit to receive them.

If there are others among the world’s non-Buddhist practitioners who have not yet entered the True Dharma and whose faith is not yet firm, one should for the time being instruct, benefit, and encourage them through other profound teachings; one must not hastily preach [this teaching] to them.
If a bodhisattva illuminates the capacities [of sentient beings], this is certainly due to their own power of wisdom.
Now, for the sake of those who transmit the Dharma in the final age, I shall further clarify the external traces that may be transmitted.

The preceding sutra first clarified the characteristics for selecting disciples; now it speaks of them again, though both instances merely provide a summary of the essential points, while the full details are clearly explained in the *Mahāvaipulya* (the Great Root Text).

Regarding those born at an auspicious time, the *Mahāvaipulya* explains in detail how they were born under such a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), such a governing planet (*graha*), and at such a season, whereby they possess such faculties (*indriya*) and such physical marks (*lakṣaṇa*), and thus should be given such a teaching; its words are extremely extensive.
Furthermore, each of these has both a superficial and a profound secret explanation; here, I have merely set forth their general outlines.
To seek the supreme matter is precisely to resolve upon bodhicitta, seeking solely the practice of the Tathāgata’s complete path.
Whatever they undertake is not for the sake of seeking other matters; their conduct is vast, universal, and sublime.

As for being "subtle," it means that upon hearing a single word or phrase, they are able to use their own power of wisdom to extensively understand immeasurable meanings and principles, and to expound them broadly without any partiality.

One who contemplates the debt of gratitude does not forget to repay it, even for the meaning of a single phrase heard from a teacher; until they attain Buddhahood, they always remain mindful of and repay that kindness.
"Those who thirst and yearn" refers to those whose minds are earnestly seeking the sublime Dharma, such as Sadāprarudita and his like; for them alone may one preach.
"Those who dwell in joy" refers to those whose hearts leap with delight upon hearing the wondrous Dharma, such that this joy pervades both body and mind.
"One who does not seek those dharmas" refers, for instance, to one who does not accept even a single word from other sutras.
Next, its external characteristics are explained.
To speak briefly of its color, it is blue and white; that is, it is neither white nor very black, and is thus an auspicious color.
The Great Text explains this extensively; here, I have merely cited one corner of the matter.
Regarding the width of the head: as with Rāhula, for example, the crown of the head should be like the handle of a parasol.
It must not be too wide, nor should it be too small; it is essential that the proportions be balanced and the features complete.
"High neck" means that the neck is neither too long nor too short.
To state it briefly, it must be straight and of medium length, without being excessive.
"Broad and majestic forehead" also means that while it is extremely broad according to principle, it must likewise be fully endowed with the marks of dignity and solemnity.
Regarding the "long nose": it means it is neither too prominent nor too flat; it should be like a gold ingot, for example.
This is a brief description of the physical and mental characteristics that make one a fit vessel for the Way; such a person is capable of receiving and practicing the teachings.

"One who possesses the marks" refers to a son of the Buddha; such a person should be given [this teaching], and one should diligently embrace and instruct them. This is as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* regarding the Ten Stages (*Daśabhūmi*).

Furthermore, one should exhort and entrust [the teachings] specifically to those who are capable of continuing the transmission; they should be diligently instructed so that the [teachings] do not fall into disuse at the proper time.

At that time, Vajrapāṇi and others endowed with great virtue—namely, the assembly mentioned above—hearing this being spoken, received and upheld with the highest reverence all the instructions taught by the various deities.
This means that having already received the King’s instructions, they shall practice and propagate them, and perform offerings.
At that time, the assembly rose again to pay homage to the Buddha, requesting his empowerment so that the Dharma might endure for a long time.
Having received and upheld what the Buddha has taught with the utmost reverence, they prostrated before the Omniscient One and requested the Tathāgata’s protection. Why was this?
For the Buddha had already entrusted them with such a secret treasury; to shoulder this heavy responsibility and carry out the work of the Tathāgata is no light task.
Nevertheless, even while the Tathāgata was in the world, this sublime Dharma encountered much resentment and hostility; how much more so in the evil age of the final dharma-period!
Yet we have already made a sincere vow that such a sutra as this shall be widely circulated and propagated.
Therefore, we entreat the Buddha to empower us with his sovereign spiritual power so that our aspirations may be fulfilled.
That the Eye of the Dharma and the Way may long abide in the world and pervade all places is precisely the vow to propagate this sutra.
By the empowerment of the Buddha, may this Dharma-eye long endure in the world.
This is the path of great wisdom that opens up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; it is the path traversed by all Buddhas, and is therefore called the "path of the Dharma-eye."
I shall cause this path to abide long in the world until the end of the realm of sentient beings, and furthermore, to spread throughout the entire universe so that it is not without circulation.
This is what is meant by the statement of Shangxing and others: "Wherever the traces of the Buddha remain, I vow to transmit this Dharma."
This was originally intended as an inquiry into the purpose of propagating the sūtra.

At that time, because the Buddha accepted his request, he immediately empowered this dharma with mantras, as explained in the sūtra. As for the meaning of the phrases not yet spoken, [the interlocutor] asked further.
At that time, the leading bodhisattvas and others, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, received and upheld it with their heads bowed.
This concludes the extensive exposition of the Mahāvairocana-bodhy-abhiṣeka-vikurvāṇa-sūtra.
Question regarding the first three phrases:
first, the bodhicitta as the seed; second, great compassion as the root; and third, skillful means as the culmination.

Now, explaining this in terms of the Great Compassion Treasury Maṇḍala: the central terrace represents the bodhicitta, the subsequent eight petals represent great compassion, and the outer three enclosures represent skillful means.
The answer is:
There are two kinds. One is spoken from the perspective of the causal stage for those who practice; the other is spoken from the perspective of the resultant stage of a Tathāgata.

For instance, the worldly deities such as the eight classes of spirits in the outermost enclosure correspond to the period from the initial understanding and observance of the precepts within the first eight mental states, up until the enjoyment of the fruits and so forth.
However, when roots of goodness are developed and correspond with the Right Path, this is the cause for the Flower Pedestal of the Matrix of Great Compassion (*Mahākaruṇā-garbha*).
The Tathāgata guides them through the power of skillful means, leading them until they achieve the eight worldly minds; this constitutes the rank of the Outer Court.
Next, gradually moving inward, even the followers of the Two Vehicles are within this interior.
Furthermore, knowing there is the supreme mind of the superior Dharma, one is further led into the second and third stages; all of these are phrases of great compassion.
Next, attaining the fruit of Buddhahood and entering the central womb is precisely the phrase regarding skillful means (*upāya*).
Now, are these eight petals and the five Buddhas and four Bodhisattvas within the central womb not one and the same body?
This is none other than Vairocana himself.
However, in order to differentiate the virtues of the Tathāgata’s internal realization and manifest them externally, he manifests an eight-petaled division within the single Dharma-realm.
Furthermore, regarding the four bodhisattvas, who is the one in the southeast, Samantabhadra?
Samantabhadra is the bodhicitta.
Without this wondrous cause, one can never reach the unsurpassed great fruit; therefore, he is given this name at the very beginning.
Next, Mañjuśrī represents great wisdom.

First, one gives rise to the pure bodhicitta according to the sequence of the *Samantabhadra-bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna-sūtra*, up until the point where Vairocana pervades all places and is perfected through the inclusion of the perfections such as permanence, bliss, self, and purity; all of these constitute the pure bodhicitta.
Next, the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) is explained:
"My own mind is inherently empty; good and evil have no master. To contemplate that the mind is no-mind and that dharmas do not abide in dharmas is precisely wondrous wisdom (*prajñā*).

By means of this sublime wisdom of the emptiness of the ultimate truth, one purifies that bodhicitta which is pervasive throughout all places; with the sharp blade of equanimous wisdom, one severs the root of beginningless ignorance and immediately enters the stage of the Bodhisattva’s correct position.
Therefore, although one possesses the bodhicitta, if there is no practice of wisdom, the fruit cannot be attained; hence, Mañjuśrī is explained next.
Next is Maitreya in the northwest, who represents both great kindness and great compassion; these are both the meanings contained within the second phrase.
Because this treasury of great compassion causes the branches, flowers, and leaves of the wondrous Bodhi tree to grow and flourish, Maitreya is mentioned next.
If there were wisdom without compassion, then skillful means would be incomplete; one would thus fail to achieve Bodhi and be unable to fully embody the six perfections to gather in sentient beings.
Next, Avalokiteśvara in the northeast represents "realization" (zhèng).
Realization refers to the fulfillment of practice and vows, whereby one attains entry into this Flower Terrace Samādhi (*puṣkara-ṭala-samādhi*).
If viewed from the perspective of the period prior to the attainment of fruition, these then represent a sequence of varying degrees of depth.

Now, when observed through the Tathāgata’s impartial wisdom, from cause to fruit, these are merely the single body and single wisdom of the Tathāgata; therefore, all eight petals are of one essence with Mahāvairocana Tathāgata.
If the Tathāgata were to abide solely in the dharma of his own realization, he would be unable to deliver sentient beings.
Why is this? This state is subtle, tranquil, and absolute, transcending the measure of the mind; what could be taught or shown to others therein?
Therefore, it flows out gradually, entering the first courtyard, then proceeding to the second courtyard, and then to the third courtyard.

Although it flows out in this manner, it does not depart from the body of the Universal Gate; for the assemblies of the eight classes of beings are all the realm of the Body that Universally Manifests Form.

If one speaks according to the capacities and dispositions of sentient beings, then the three tiers of mandalas proceed from the profound toward the shallow; even the meaning of the worldly *mantras* is shallow, being merely the path of the *nirmāṇakāya*, wherein the skillful means are not yet ultimate.
If one reveals the true nature, how would the worldly mantras differ from the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana?
From the perspective of the Tathāgata, they proceed from the profound to the shallow and from the inner to the outer, forming the threefold maṇḍala.
Following the principle of sentient beings, the three-layered altar is formed by proceeding from the shallow to the deep and gradually from the exterior to the interior.
Furthermore, this sequence corresponds precisely to the meaning of the characters themselves.

The initial syllable *A* is in the eastern direction; like the Sanskrit sound *A*, it carries the meaning of "moving the head. Because, according to worldly convention, the east is considered the foremost among all directions, it serves as a metaphor for the bodhicitta being the very beginning of the myriad practices. Its name is Ratnaketu Buddha (Jewel Banner Buddha).
Next, the character "A-ping" (阿平) signifies practice (*caryā*).

If one possesses only the bodhicitta but does not fully cultivate the myriad practices, one will ultimately fail to achieve fruition; this is no different in meaning from the previous four types of bodhisattvas.
That Buddha is precisely the blossoming of the flower.
Next is the syllable "Aṃ," which signifies *samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Because of the myriad practices, he attained perfect enlightenment; that Buddha is named Amitābha, which refers to the Western Quarter.
Next, the sound of the drum is the Great Parinirvāṇa; the syllable *e* (惡) is the fruit of Perfect Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), and it is mentioned next because it is the fruit.
Next is the entry into the long-syllabled *e* within the center, which is the skillful means (*upāya*).

This is the body of the original ground of Vairocana Buddha, the substance of the flower pedestal; it transcends the eight petals and is beyond spatial location. It is not a realm accessible to the conscious mind, known only by Buddha after Buddha.

In order to reveal the treasury of great compassion by recollecting their original vows and to universally lead sentient beings into the wisdom of the Buddha, they further employ the power of their sustaining grace (*adhiṣṭhāna*) to universally manifest body, speech, and mind throughout the realm of birth and death; you should know that this is precisely their skillful means (*upāya*).
If one is devoid of skillful means, even the Tathāgata’s fundamental ground cannot be described, let alone shown to others.
It cannot be explained to bodhisattvas who are leaders among the ranks, much less to those who have entered into the cycle of birth and death.

By this expedient means, they manifest various forms within the Great Emptiness; one should know that all the great assembly maṇḍalas are but a single body without distinct bodies—this is the Universal Gate Body, the Dharma-realm Body, and the Vajradhātu Body.
Furthermore, the yellow color of Bodhi represents the nature of the Vajra.
Next, the red color of practice signifies fire, which is identical to the meaning of Mañjuśrī.
The myriad practices are guided by wondrous wisdom; one cannot have activity apart from wisdom.
Next, the white color of the attainment of Bodhi signifies the ultimate meaning of perfect luminosity, and it also carries the meaning of water.

"As I have previously vowed, it is now fulfilled; I shall transform all sentient beings and cause them all to enter the Buddha-way"—it is for this purpose, and because of the arousal of great compassion, that this occurs.

Next is Great Nirvana: when the traces have reached their limit and one returns to the source, the fire of the Tathāgata’s skillful means is extinguished once the fuel of sentient beings' karmic conditions is exhausted; therefore, it is called Nirvana.
The Buddha-sun has already set behind the mountain of nirvāṇa; therefore, its color is black.
Its center is empty, yet it contains all colors; this is the universal assembly of the maṇḍala of the empowered world, which is ultimately pure and lacks nothing.
The reason why this hundred-syllable wheel proceeds from the outside toward the inside is also for this same purpose.
Just as with the central terrace, it is said that all deities are likewise so.
Just as with the seed-syllable *vaṃ* of Vajrapāṇi, the syllable *va* constitutes five things:
*va* is the bodhicitta; *ṃ* is conduct; *ṃ* is the three types of enlightenment (*trividhabodhi*); *ṃ* is nirvāṇa; and *ṃ* is skillful means (*upāya*).
This is why it is said that "expedient means is the last"; this is the meaning.
For example, the Lotus Honored One also has five aspects: *sa* is the bodhicitta, *va* is practice, *dha* is the attainment of enlightenment, *na* is nirvāṇa, and *ma* is expedient means.

Just as Mañjuśrī takes the syllable *vaṃ* as his seed-syllable, it likewise possesses five meanings: *vaṃ* is the bodhicitta; *vaṃ* is practice; *vaṃ* is the attainment of enlightenment; *vaṃ* is nirvāṇa; and *vaṃ* is skillful means.
All other seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the various honored ones are likewise explained in detail in this manner.

For this reason, Vajrapāṇi is none other than Mahāvairocana Tathāgata; Avalokiteśvara is also Mahāvairocana Tathāgata; Mañjuśrī is also Mahāvairocana Tathāgata; and even down to each of the eight classes of spirits (*aṣṭavidha-gaṇa*), they all possess this same significance, being likewise the realization of Mahāvairocana Tathāgata.
Although their essence is one, their meanings differ.
Thus, it is said in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*: "Vairocana says:
'I am Mañjuśrī, Avalokiteśvara, and so forth.'"
"I am indeed the devas, I am indeed humans;
I am indeed ghosts and spirits, I am indeed dragons and birds"—
it is for this reason that it is said, "there is nothing that is not indeed [I]."

Furthermore, it is said: "The positions, forms, colors, and other attributes of these deities of the Great Compassion Treasury (Mahākaruṇāgarbha) vary individually; however, because beginners who have not yet deeply entered yoga do not correctly visualize the deity, the Buddha employed this skillful means to provide an object for their minds."

When the contemplation is perfected, through the empowerment of the Dharma, one naturally and constantly accords with the assemblies of the Buddhas; even without forming a deliberate thought, one remains clearly aware, let alone when applying the contemplation itself.
At such a time, one spontaneously perceives the true maṇḍala.
This ground is none other than the pure bodhicitta.
All that has been represented above are the marks of the sublime adornment of the Dharmakāya of Mahāvairocana Tathāgata.
Furthermore, Avalokiteśvara, Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and Maitreya are already present within the eight petals; they are, in fact, the Great Dharma-body of Mahāvairocana Tathāgata.

For the sake of delivering sentient beings, they gradually emerge outward; therefore, Mañjuśrī, Avalokiteśvara, and others appear again in the subsequent diagram, which can be understood through this analogy.

Furthermore, it says: "As within the eight petals, Samantabhadra is the bodhicitta, Mañjuśrī is wisdom, and Maitreya is compassion; this bodhicitta is none other than Mahāvairocana Tathāgata, yet he possesses bodhicitta."
Great Wisdom (Mahāmaitrī) is none other than the Tathāgata Vairocana; there is no wisdom apart from this Tathāgata Vairocana.
Compassion (Karuṇā) is none other than the Tathāgata Vairocana; there is no compassion apart from the Tathāgata Vairocana.
One should know that, based on this explanation, it is the same for all ten thousand virtues.
This accords with the meaning of the Dharma-body, Prajñā, and Liberation as taught at Tiantai: if one refers to them by the name of the "Dharma-body" alone, it is of this same category.
Question:
Regarding the outer and inner hundred-syllable wheels, does each one follow such a sequence as the meaning of being introduced into the maṇḍala and gradually gathered into the center?
Answer: This refers to the sequence of cause and effect.

If a practitioner first gives rise to the bodhicitta, next proceeds in practice, next attains perfect enlightenment, next abides in nirvāṇa, and next manifests skillful means, it is precisely according to this order.

If explained from the perspective of the ground of one’s own fruition (*svaphala-bhūmi*), then the syllable *ka* (𑀓) is innermost; next is *kha* (𑀔); next is *bodhi* (𑀪𑀺𑀧𑀺); and finally, *upāya* (𑀉𑀧𑀸𑀬) is outermost.
The letter *ka* is identical in essence to the letter *a*; it constitutes the fruit of the dharma-body and is not taught as the causal ground of the bodhicitta.

Arising from the dharma-body, it subsequently flows outward to deliver sentient beings, just as [light] issues from the central terrace of a maṇḍala and reaches the stations of the eight classes of worldly deities.

Furthermore, one introduces the fruit of Buddhahood from the outside, just as in a maṇḍala, from the beginning stages up to the eight minds, and continuing until the completion of the skillful means for attaining bodhi.

As for the syllables such as *yaṃ*, *raṃ*, *ñaṃ*, and *naṃ*, they also follow the sense of entering and exiting; they may be within the hundred syllables or outside the hundred syllables—this is further questioned.

He asked again: "Regarding the contemplative practice within the mind of the practitioner, does the meaning of the Maṇḍala as the Treasury of Great Compassion take the central platform as the bodhicitta, and then proceed gradually outward, even to the positions of the worldly deities, as the skillful means?"
Answer: For all practitioners, there is a sequential order.

First, one should recite according to the dharma, performing mantra-recitation, mudrās, and so forth, while contemplating the perfect luminosity; or one may contemplate only the syllables, or only the mudrās. When any one of these matters is accomplished, all three are accomplished.
At first, one cannot perceive the perfect luminosity even while observing it; however, through the mudrās, mantras, and the recollection of the deity, the three karmas gradually become purified.
Because the mental obstructions are purified, one then gradually perceives the perfect luminosity.
When you perceive this perfect luminosity, there may appear within it the original seed-syllables, clearly manifest according to their respective forms and colors.
When such a vision is attained, the discursive thoughts of one's own mind are stilled; the mind becomes profoundly tranquil and constant in its unity, no longer moved by external conditions.
Having seen it thus, this is still an external condition; next, one should draw the mind inward and observe in this way:
"This perfect luminosity emerges from my own mind; know that the internal is likewise so."
Now, "perfectly bright and pure" is the very essence and nature of the mind; there is no separate dharma.

Because one diligently employs skillful means to observe the internal mind, one sees that these characters "perfectly bright" are nothing other than one's own mind, and no longer relies on external conditions.
Even up to the point where one clearly perceives the external circle and the central deity through the aforementioned skillful means,
when now performing internal visualization, it is one's own body that becomes the central deity, such as Vairocana.
Since this is thus in accord with the principles of yoga, it constitutes an achievement according to one's capacity.
Through such correspondence with yoga, that which is contemplated will be accomplished according to one's wish.

One should then contemplate this mind as an eight-petaled lotus according to the aforementioned expedient means; the heart-cakra of this lotus serves as the central womb (*garbha*) of the maṇḍala, and the eight petals outside it are likewise arranged according to the positions of the Buddhas. It is further stated:
"These eight petals constitute the first enclosure of the Great Compassion Treasury (*mahākaruṇā-garbha*)."

At that time, the practitioner visualizes the eight-petaled heart as the central womb; he visualizes his own body as the maṇḍala: from the heart upward is the first court, from the heart downward to the navel is the second court, and from the navel downward is the third.

The celestial courts of the world and the forms, colors, and marks of the various honored ones appear with their respective distinctions vividly clear; these manifest within one's own body as if facing them directly, just as if one had personally entered the Buddha’s assembly.
However, those who have not yet seen the Truths are still unable to perform various supernatural transformations like Vairocana; they merely achieve realization through the contemplation of the mind.
Yet there is one thing that is true and not false: it is precisely this "I" itself.
As for the statement "I am that," one must resolutely and truly believe that I am the Dharma-realm, I am Vairocana, and I am the universal gate of all bodies; this matter is not erroneous.
As stated above in the section on the meaning of empowerment through mantras, "I am indeed the Dharma-realm.
It further states:
"The Dharmakāya possesses sovereign, miraculous transformations and empowerments."
This need not be doubted.

As cited in the *Yogatantra-vajraśekhara*, hundreds of analogies are presented; the extensive version explains their meaning in detail, stating: "It is like Śakra dwelling within his celestial palace, where the entire ground consists of lapis lazuli, pure both inside and out."
Each member of the celestial host, while remaining within their own palace chamber, perceives Śakra as always being present in his palace, as if they were facing one another directly.

Why is this? Because this ground and all else are composed of exquisite jewels that reflect one another and mutually stimulate one another; thus, he does not come here and they do not go there, nor do they actually conjoin, yet because the conditions are complete, it appears so. In reality, however, there is no arising and nothing exists.
One must not fail to believe this.

Furthermore, when the various devas in the Garden of Joy (Nandana) become excessively heedless, at that time, by the power of their past karma, there arises from within the leaves of the trees the sound of the Dharma teaching, rebuking them and urging them to abide in right conduct.
At that time, the devas immediately ceased their heedlessness for a moment and turned their minds toward virtuous conduct.

Yet, in reality, this matter cannot be found by seeking it within each individual leaf, nor does it arise from the bodies of the devas, nor from themselves, nor from others; and yet, this matter is accomplished.

Furthermore, when waging war against the asuras, the celestial drum emits a sound that consoles the heavenly hosts, inciting thoughts of courage and vigor, and causing the asuras to be struck with fear and retreat.

In reality, this drum has no form and no dwelling place; it is produced solely by the various conditions of the merits of the devas, all of which are inconceivable—how much more so, then, is the Dharma-body?

Furthermore, it is like the Great Brahmā King who, while remaining within his own palace, appears before all the hosts of devas whenever they desire to see him; there are none to whom he does not manifest.

Because all these devas know his pure conduct and because his physical marks and signs of excellence are foremost, their afflictions, cravings, and other defiled thoughts subside. Consequently, they give rise to immeasurable virtuous aspirations and cultivate pure conduct according to their respective capacities.

Yet, while the Brahma King remains within his own palace, neither moving nor wavering, and without forming the thought, "I shall manifest myself before them all," he appears before each and every one of them.
Each of them thought to themselves:
"He has manifested for me alone; he is preaching the Dharma for me.

If such inconceivable efficacy exists even for those in the world who possess but meager merit and vows, how much more so for the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata—could it not accomplish such sovereign spiritual powers, empowerments, and miraculous transformations?

However, in conventional explanations of the Dharma, one speaks either of "dharma-nature" (dharmatā) or "dharma-body" (dharmakāya), which are quiescent like space and devoid of activity; such accounts never mention that they are fully endowed with such powers and functions.
To think that all manifestations of spiritual transformations are merely the power of the samādhi of a conditioned mind, without speaking of the essence of the Dharma—
such is a failure to understand this.
Question:

In the eastern sector of the first enclosure of the maṇḍala, there are only three things—the triangular space-eye (ākāśacakṣus) and the wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi)—while the remainder is empty; why is this so?
Answer:

As in the case of mantras and mudrās, such as the *ūrṇā-kośa* (hair-treasure) of the Tathāgata, the tongue of the Tathāgata, the tusks of the Tathāgata, the teeth of the Tathāgata, the navel of the Tathāgata, and the fingernails of the Tathāgata—all these are included here; they shall now be listed in sequence.
The Buddha’s crown protrusion (uṣṇīṣa) is located in the third enclosure; it is not present here.
Question:
What is the meaning of "Jeweled Banner" (Ratnaketu) Buddha?
Answer: This is the bodhicitta.
It is like a banner in a worldly army; it is the emblem of the commander-in-chief among the ranks, gazed upon by all, and there is no movement or stationing that does not follow its lead.
Just as all myriad practices are for the sake of this bodhicitta, it is named after that which serves as its banner and its master.
Next, why is the Jewel Banner (Ratnaketu) called the Flower-Blossoming Buddha?
From this point onward is the practice of the meaning [of the perfections].
The ten perfections and myriad practices support the bodhicitta; as they unfold in succession, their sprouts, stems, flowers, and leaves flourish and become lovely, and thus they receive their names.
Next, regarding the statement that "when the flowers bloom, it is called Amitābha," what does this mean?

This refers to the Sambhogakāya Buddha (the Enjoyment Body), which is the attainment of the great fruit; it is the enjoyment of that fruit—the immeasurable and inconceivable bliss of the present reality—and all such states may be given this name.
Next, as for the Buddha Drum-Sound (Dundubhisvara), this refers to skillful means (*upāya*).

Having already attained the great fruit, it would be merely for one's own enjoyment; however, he universally expounds it for the sake of all sentient beings through various skillful means and the wisdom of accomplished action (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). It is named such because it accomplishes its activities without thought, just like the sound of a celestial drum.

Furthermore, as for the previous statement that Akṣobhya is in the north, that is an error in the scripture; this is according to the *Yogācāra* system, which does not correspond with this [text], as it establishes Drumakinnararāja (Drumaghoṣa) as the fixed [Buddha of the north].

The Commentary on the Meaning of the Mahāvairocana Sūtra, Fascicle Twenty. On the twentieth day of the second month in the second year of the Kōhō era, the Great Sōjō of the Kan’on-in received this at the eastern meditation chamber in the inner precinct of Kongōbu-ji.
The Great Sōjō Kōi of Onkōin was the successor to the Dharma of Shinshin of Daigoshitsu.

The Minister of Ceremonial, Prince Atsunen, resided at Tōji; during the lifetime of the Second Chōja, he retired to Kōyasan for seclusion, and so forth. From the second year of Kashō to the sixth year of Kōei, it is five hundred and thirty-five years.
Guangze received this Dharma, and his final provisions for manifesting realization were recorded herein.
